en: The Jewel Garland of the Meaning of the Sūtras
Now begins the first chapter.
Now begins the first quarter.
In this chapter, the reconciliation of words consisting of names that are generally well-known in other [contexts] with the Supreme Self is demonstrated.
Herein, it is established that "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken.
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman.

Is it not the case that this treatise is not to be commenced? For inquiry, which consists of the investigation of logic, is itself not to be undertaken. And it is not to be undertaken because of reasons such as its lack of a subject matter (*aviṣayatva*). To explain: the Brahman intended as the subject matter is not distinct from the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), because there is no means of valid knowledge (*māna*) [for such a distinction]. Is this means of knowledge perception, inference, or scripture? Not the first, because no difference between the individual soul and the Lord is perceived, unlike [the difference] between a jar and a cloth. Not the second, because [inference] depends on one's whim. Not the third, because of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*).

Since the scripture concerning difference (*bheda*), whose intended meaning has been determined through the methods such as the opening context (*upakrama*) and so forth, would otherwise result in the invalidation of its literal sense—as seen in passages such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*)—it is impossible for it to possess authority regarding difference. Therefore, one must assert that the scripture, whose intended meaning has been determined through the opening context and other means, possesses authority regarding difference. Consequently, once the investigation consisting of the examination of the opening context and so forth has proceeded according to the treatise, the establishment of difference is achieved by means of the Veda, whose intended meaning has thus been determined.

If that [Brahman] were established, Brahman—which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva)—would fall into a state of doubt, and thus there would be no engagement with the scripture. Furthermore, if [Brahman] were of the nature of the individual soul, it could not be the subject matter [of the inquiry], because it would be eternally established as self-luminous. Nor could it be for the sake of another. For the purpose of another must be either worldly prosperity, such as heaven and the like, or liberation (mokṣa). It cannot be the former, because that is accomplished by easier means. Nor can it be liberation, because liberation is not perceived immediately following the desire to know (jijñāsā). Or, let it be granted that Brahman is distinct from the individual soul.

Even so, inquiry does not cause that [realization] by way of direct perception (*aparokṣa*), because it is not observed even in those such as Vasiṣṭha who have directly realized Brahman; for there would be no object or purpose [for further inquiry]. Now, since no qualified person (*adhikārī*) is possible for what is taught by the words [of the scripture], there is no one entitled to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). For this very reason, there is also no connection [between the inquiry and its result]. To this objection, the Sūtra speaks in order to refute it: [The Sūtra: *athāto brahmajijñāsā* (Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman). **Explanation:** The opponent argues that the inquiry into Brahman is useless because it cannot produce direct realization through mere reasoning, as evidenced by the case of Vasiṣṭha and others who possessed direct knowledge yet did not engage in such inquiry. Furthermore, since the scripture itself does not specify a particular qualified seeker, there is no candidate for this inquiry, and consequently, no relationship between the inquiry and its result can be established. The Sūtra is introduced to resolve these objections.

"Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā). Its meaning is as follows: "Now" (atha) means after the attainment of the qualifications consisting of Vedic study, tranquility, self-control, and so forth. "Therefore" (ataḥ) means because [Brahman] possesses the fruit called liberation, which is produced by the knowledge generated by oneself. The meaning is that the desire to know (jijñāsā)—that is, the inquiry in the form of hearing and so forth—concerning Viṣṇu, who is Brahman complete in all attributes, must be undertaken.

Thus, the inquiry into Brahman must indeed be undertaken, because it possesses a purpose. Nor can it be countered by the objection that it lacks a subject matter; for since Brahman, which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), can serve as its subject matter, the charge of being devoid of a subject matter is unproven. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for this distinction, as the very fullness established by the scriptural injunction "seek to know That" serves as such evidence. Nor is the reason [fullness] non-exclusive with respect to insentient objects, because what is intended as the logical mark is precisely that fullness of attributes which is impossible for the individual soul. Finally, an inference does not follow one’s mere whim.

It should not be argued that there is a circularity (anyonyāśraya) in the following manner: first, because the scripture states "He is distinct and inconceivable," [the distinction is established]; second, upon engaging in inquiry in the form of an investigation into the opening statements (upakrama) and so forth, the determination of the purport (tātparya) of those scriptures—such as "He is distinct and inconceivable"—is made regarding their difference; third, when that [determination] exists, the subject matter of the inference under discussion is established as being distinct from the individual soul (jīva) by virtue of its being a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); and fourth, once that is established, the engagement in inquiry occurs. This is because inquiry is required only when there is a doubt regarding the purport. [In our view,] it is precisely when such a doubt exists that inquiry is necessary.

Otherwise, for the sake of determining the purport regarding the meaning of the *upakrama* (introductory statement) and so forth, one would have to search for yet another *upakrama* and so on, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, since Brahman as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) is not subject to doubt, there is no counter-argument based on the lack of a subject matter (*aviṣayatva*). Furthermore, because the pervaded (*vyāpya*) purpose exists, the pervader—the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*)—is also established; therefore, there is no counter-argument based on its absence either.

[Objection: But surely, since liberation is not observed even in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others who have directly realized Brahman, it is unproven that [liberation] has a real purpose. [Reply: This is not so. Is this non-observation by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or by means of perception in general? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and such things also do not exist. As for the second, is it the non-observation of their existence at the present time, or at any time whatsoever? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that the performance of sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma would never occur. Nor can it be the second.

Because it is heard in scripture that Vasiṣṭha and others attained liberation after the dissolution of Brahmā, the objection regarding the absence of a relationship [between the means and the goal] is thereby refuted; and even in the absence of that [relationship], there is no counter-argument (satpratipakṣa). Therefore, since inquiry must indeed be undertaken, it is established that the treatise (śāstra) should be commenced.
Thus concludes the section on the desire to know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa).
Here, the definition of Brahman is stated.
[The Brahman is that] from which there is the origin, etc., of this [world].

Is it not the case that this Brahman is the individual soul (jīva) and not Viṣṇu? For there exists the presence of conventional usage (rūḍhi) that establishes the soul. Nor can it be Viṣṇu alone on the grounds of the existence of etymological derivation (yoga) that establishes Viṣṇu; for conventional usage is more primary than etymological derivation, and one cannot abandon the primary meaning in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka). Nor is the very fact of being the object of inquiry (jijñāsyatva) a subverting factor; for the word *jijñāsā* denotes the desire for knowledge (*jñānecchā*) and does not have "inquiry" (vicāra) as its meaning.

Furthermore, since the term "Brahman" primarily denotes the Jīva, once it is established that this Brahman is the Jīva, and since that [Jīva], being self-luminous, is not a subject for doubt and thus not something to be investigated, the word "jijñāsā" (desire to know) must be taken in its figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) as something consistent with the context; thus, because the desire to know is not something prescribed by rule, the "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not possible—this being the prima facie view, the author recites the aphorism.

"From which there is the birth, etc., of this. This is its meaning: "Of this"—of this world-complex consisting of the known living and insentient beings—"from which," from that [source], "birth, etc."—meaning the eightfold group consisting of creation, sustenance, dissolution, governance, knowledge, ignorance, bondage, and liberation—"comes," as is heard in scripture; that alone is Brahman, and nothing else—this is the sense.

And thus, because the word *brahman* possesses both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings when applied to Viṣṇu, this *brahman* is indeed Viṣṇu. Even though the word *brahman* has a conventional meaning in reference to the individual soul (*jīva*), it is logical to determine its referent based on the fact that "learned convention" (*vidvad-rūḍhi*) is stronger than mere convention. Alternatively, even if the convention were restricted to the soul alone, the primary meaning must still be abandoned due to the impossibility [of the soul] possessing the qualities of being the cause, the sustainer, the destroyer, and the goal attained by the liberated, as stated in the preceding sentence, "From which...". Furthermore, those qualities cannot possibly belong to the individual soul.

Since their exclusive devotion to Viṣṇu alone is established by the passage beginning with "ya utridhā tvā," the word *jijñāsā* is either conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) in the sense of inquiry or used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). In either case, because of the designation of the Śruti text "ātmā vā are," it refers specifically to inquiry; thus, contrary to that, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not intended here. Consequently, the status of Brahman as the object of inquiry, as previously stated, is established as being distinct from the individual soul.
Thus ends the section on birth.

Here, in order to avoid the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the previously stated definition of Brahman—consisting in being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world—to Rudra and others, the proof for the world-cause is stated:
"Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

Is it not the case that there is no over-extension [of the definition] to Rudra and others, because their status as the cause of the world is untenable due to the consequence of self-dependence? For the definition intended by the proponent (siddhāntin) does not apply there; thus, it is improper to charge over-extension by establishing that Rudra—who is not accepted by the proponent—is the cause of the world. Furthermore, is the state of being bound by Viṣṇu and so forth, which is intended by the author of the Sūtras, admitted in the case of Rudra and others or not? In the first case, his status as a cause is impossible, because one who is bound is equivalent to Devadatta and others.

If it is argued that in the second case, one must simply state that [the definition] is impossible, because the agency over the bondage and liberation of the world residing in Rudra—which is accepted by the Siddhāntin—is absent in Viṣṇu; we reply: this would indeed be a fault if an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) were being alleged against the definition intended by the author of the Sūtras. But it is not so. Rather, it concerns precisely the definition stated in the Śruti, "Mayo bhuva" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6.1). Furthermore, the causality of bondage and so forth residing in Rudra and others is not what is intended by the Śruti, because Rudra, being equal to Viṣṇu, is devoid of bondage, ignorance, and the like.

If the scriptural meaning were that agency regarding bondage and so forth resides in a non-existent Rudra and others, then the agency of a jar regarding bondage and so forth would also have to be the scriptural meaning. Consequently, the scriptural meaning would be the non-agency of Mahat and others alone, not that which was stated by the author of the Sūtras; for [agency] is established in Rudra and others through inference. Thus, there is indeed the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For this very reason, there is no possibility of a quibble (*chala*) either. As for the proof, it is as follows: Śiva is the creator of the world, because, while possessing the desire for it, he is equal to Viṣṇu, who is the creator of it. This is the evidence.

And because this [meaning] is established for all the world, there is no minor obstacle such as non-establishment [of the term]. Consequently, since there is no sublation in the sentence "Seek to know Him" when Rudra and others are understood, and because of the existence of conventional usage (rūḍhi), it follows that Rudra alone is intended, not Viṣṇu. To this, the Sūtra says:

"Because it has the Veda as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*). This is the meaning: the causality of the world cannot be attributed to Rudra and others through such inferences as "Śiva is the creator of the world, because, while possessing that desire, he is equal to Viṣṇu, who is the creator thereof. Why? Because it has the Veda as its source. "Veda" refers to the form of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas; "source" means the cause of knowledge; that which has this is "having the Veda as its source. Therefore, Brahman is the cause of the world, because it is to be known solely through the Veda—this is the meaning.

And thus, the causality of the world belongs to Viṣṇu alone, and not to Rudra and others, because qualities such as being the cause of bondage for Rudra and others are impossible in the case of Rudra and the rest. Nor should it be argued that the scriptural passage "from which [all this arises]" (yato vā) does not have the sense of being the cause of Rudra and others; for by the word "these" (imāni), all objects established by valid means of knowledge as possessing origination and so forth are included, and Rudra himself is established by valid means of knowledge as possessing origination and so forth. Or, let it be that the meaning of the scriptural passage "from which" is simply the agency of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.

Nevertheless, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to Rudra and others, because causality is to be known solely through scripture (*śāstra*) and thus lacks the possibility of being established by inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, the inference put forward by the opponent is incapable of proving [the point], as it is beset by defects such as the non-establishment of the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*). Nor can it be argued that there is no non-establishment [of the reason] because it is well-known to all the world; for since we and others do not accept it, there is an absence of universal worldly consensus. Moreover, the cognition of common folk (*pāmara*) is incapable of serving as proof due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And likewise, because there exists a subverting factor—namely, the impossibility of the definition stated in the Śruti applying to Śiva and others—it is established that Viṣṇu alone is intended by the phrase "seek to know That," and thus He alone is the object of inquiry.
Thus concludes the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] entitled "Having Scripture as its Source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa).
In this [sūtra], it is established that Viṣṇu alone is known through the scriptures as the cause of the world, and not others.
"But that [is so] because of the harmony [of the texts]. (1.1.4)

But surely, just as Viṣṇu, so too others must be accepted as having the status of being the source of the scripture (*śāstrayonitva*) by virtue of being the cause of the world; for just as the purport regarding Viṣṇu is determined through Āgamas such as the Pañcarātra, which are commentaries on the Veda, so too it is determined regarding Śiva and others through Āgamas such as the Pāśupata, composed by those who profess omniscience, which are commentaries on the Veda and establish their status as the cause through portions of the Veda that express this causality.

Since the validity of all Vedic exegeses is possible, there is no reason to reject the validity of the Pañcarātra and other such texts while accepting the validity of the Śaiva and other Āgamas; for, just as the quality of propounding Viṣṇu is clearly perceived in certain specific portions [of the latter], the quality of being devoted to Śiva and others is likewise clearly perceived in other specific portions, and thus the correspondence with actual experience is equal in both cases. Nor is it impossible for many things to function as causes.

For it is established by the experience of all people that many individuals who are individually incapable of lifting a very heavy burden can do so when acting together. Nor is there any contradiction with such scriptural passages as "All the Vedas," for that statement means "all the Vedas" insofar as they are endowed with words and marks well-known to refer to Viṣṇu. Nor is there any contradiction with passages such as "Nārāyaṇa alone [is the cause]," which negate Rudra and others as being the cause.

Since those [passages] are intended to praise Viṣṇu as the cause—just like the statements that censure the offerings made before or after sunrise—they have no underlying intent (*tātparya*) to negate Śiva and others as causes. Nor is there a contradiction with the opening context (*upakrama*) and so forth; for an interpretation based on the opening context and other criteria is more powerful because it was composed by an omniscient being. Therefore, since Śiva and others are also the cause according to the scriptures, the definition of "being the source of the scripture" (*śāstrayonitva*) overextends (*ativyāpta*) to the status of being the cause of the world. This being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra:

"Because of the harmony [of the texts]. This is its meaning: the word "tu" (but) has the sense of "only. That alone—namely, Brahman called Viṣṇu—is the primary source of the scripture, not Rudra and the others. Why? Because of "samanvaya," which means because of the signs of purport such as the concordant opening statements and so forth.

And thus, since Śiva and others lack the status of being the cause of the world due to the absence of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition]. Nor is the Veda, whose purport has been determined by the Śaiva and other Āgamas, a means of knowledge (*māna*) in that regard; for the Śaiva and other Āgamas, which would establish a purport in the Veda regarding Śiva and so forth, are not authoritative when they contradict the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and other criteria. Nor is the reverse the case, because those [Vedic criteria] are stronger due to their being more internal (*antaraṅga*). Furthermore, since the introductory passages and so forth must be followed in order to ascertain the purport of the Śaiva and other Āgamas, the latter do not possess the status of being self-sufficient foundations (*upajīvyatva*).

Nor is the authority of scripture dependent on its conformity with empirical cognition, because it lacks conformity with the cognition that arises from a preliminary investigation of the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth. Furthermore, mere conformity with superficial cognition is not a determining factor. Moreover, although the censure of the *uditahoma* (sacrifice at sunrise) and the like does not intend to negate them—since they have been prescribed—the statements negating Śiva and others as the cause do indeed intend their own literal meaning, as the causality of Śiva and others is unestablished by valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*). Therefore, it is established that the definition of Brahman is "being the cause of birth and so forth," which is not over-pervasive (*ativyāpta*).
Thus concludes the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).
Here, the expressibility and totality implied by the word "sam" (together/completely) are raised as objections and then resolved:
"On account of seeing, [the pradhāna] is not that which is not based on scripture."

Now, an objection may be raised: Is not Brahman, which was denoted by the word "That" (*tat*) in the preceding Sūtra, within the range of words and the cause of the world as taught by the Śāstra? No, it is not the primary meaning of the Śāstra. Why? Because it is inexpressible (*avācya*). Furthermore, its being the primary meaning is established by such scriptural texts as, "From which speech turns back," and so forth. Indeed, that which is inexpressible cannot possibly have the status of a primary meaning. Thus, it might be concluded that the status of being the cause of the world as taught by the Śāstra does not belong to Him. To this, the author states the following Sūtra:

"Because of seeing, it is not that which is not denoted by words. This is its meaning: That Brahman is not "aśabda," meaning it is not inexpressible; rather, it is indeed expressible. Why? Because of "īkṣati"; *īkṣati* means knowledge. The meaning is: because [Brahman] is the object of that [knowledge].

Thus, since expressibility (*vācyatva*) itself is established through the very necessity that otherwise [the Lord] could not be perceived, inexpressibility (*avācyatva*) remains unestablished. Nor should it be said that "perceptibility" (*īkṣaṇīyatva*) is unestablished, for it is established by the scripture: "He [beheld] from this" (*sa etasmāt*). Nor does the inference of expressibility suffer sublation by such scriptures as "from which speech turns back," because the scriptural passage "from which speech turns back" expresses well-known [reality] and does not express inexpressibility; for the Smṛti states: "[That which is] unknown is inexpressible.
Therefore, in the absence of any subverting evidence in the form of inexpressibility, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the cause.
If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self."

[Objection: But surely, because the reason "being worthy of being seen" (*īkṣaṇīyatva*) is unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhatva*), the "Self" mentioned in such scriptural passages as "one should see the non-Self within the Self itself" refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*), who is called the "secondary Self" (*gauṇa-ātman*) because he is bound by qualities such as *sattva*. Therefore, since it would otherwise be impossible [to maintain the opposite], even the "denoted" (*vācya*) [meaning] must be that very same [individual soul] and not the attributeless Supreme Self (*paramātman*). To this, the Sūtra says: *janmādyasya yataḥ* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2). [Response: Since the origin, etc., of this [world] proceed from Him... [The Sūtra continues]. (Note: The provided text contains an objection regarding the *īkṣati-adhikaraṇa* of the *Brahma-sūtra*, specifically concerning whether the "Seer" (*īkṣitṛ*) is the individual soul or the Supreme Self.)

"If it be argued that [the term 'Self'] is secondary, we say no, because of the word 'Self'. This is its meaning: if it is argued that the one spoken of in the scriptural passage concerning "seeing" (*īkṣati*) is merely the individual soul (*jīva*), who is bound by qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and is thus secondary—[we reply] no. Why? Because of the word "Self"; that is to say, because in the object to be seen, there is the hearing of the word "Self" in the injunction, "one should see the Self."

And thus, because the word "Self" (ātman) is heard in such passages as "He who [is endowed] with all qualities on every side" and "There are indeed two Brahmans," and because that [Self] is described as being devoid of qualities such as sattva, and because the purport of the text of "He from this" must be stated as referring precisely to that [Brahman], since the meaning of a Vedic text (śruti) is precisely what is obtained through its designation (samākhyā); and since it is possible for the primary sense of "Self"—which refers to the qualityless Brahman taught by the scripture of "seeing" (īkṣati) as the object of vision—to be intended, there is no justification for adopting a secondary sense of the primary term "Truth" (satya). Therefore, it is established that the qualityless Brahman alone is what is denoted, and not the individual soul (jīva).
Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that.

Surely, the word *ātman* would refer to the secondary self (*gauṇātman*) in its primary sense [only if it were otherwise established]; for, since it has not been stated that in the cited Śrutis and Smṛtis the word *ātman* is primary with respect to Viṣṇu (who is devoid of qualities) and secondary with respect to individual souls (*jīva*), it is possible for the words *ātman* and *anātman* to have as their objects the sentient and the insentient respectively. If those two words refer to the well-known sentient and insentient, there would be straightforwardness (*ārjava*) in the Śruti; this is because it does not abandon the conventional meaning and avoids the conceptualization of multiple meanings for the word *rūpa*.

To dispel the doubt that—since defects such as suffering are merely adventitious (aupādhika), and since scripture teaches that the individual soul (jīva) is naturally (svabhāvataḥ) free from defects, it is therefore logical for [the scriptural statements] to have natural state as their subject matter—the author recites the Sūtra.

"Because liberation is taught for one who is established in that. This is the meaning: "established in that" refers to the knower of the Supreme Self. "Because liberation is taught" means that liberation is heard of in such passages as "He by whom this is known," and so forth; therefore, the primary denotation of the word *ātman* is not the individual soul (*jīva*).

And thus, for a knower of the Self whose soul is bound by qualities, liberation in the form of the cessation of the bondage of qualities is not possible; for it is heard in the scripture, "By whom this is known," that liberation is taught for the knower of Brahman. Furthermore, since the word "Self" (ātman) refers primarily to Viṣṇu alone according to the scripture, "This Self is Brahman," it is established that the Self is not secondary, but is indeed the qualityless Brahman. "And because there is no mention of its being something to be abandoned."
The author of the Sūtras states that, because of another logical reason, the word "Self" (ātman) does not denote [the individual soul] in a figurative sense.

"And because there is no statement of its being something to be abandoned. This is the meaning: because there is no statement of its being something to be abandoned—since, for the sake of liberation, Brahman is not presented primarily as something to be abandoned in the form of ignorance; on the contrary, because there is no statement that it is not to be known, as in "Know [Him]"—the term "Self" does not denote a secondary (gauṇa) entity, but rather refers exclusively to Viṣṇu who is devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa). This is the sense.

And thus, it is not only because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to Him, but also because the Śruti—specifically the passage "Him alone as the one"—does not state that the Self (ātman) is to be abandoned; and furthermore, because the passage "Cast off other words" declares that which is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation. The intention is that the term "Self" does not refer to something secondary, but rather to Viṣṇu Himself, who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Thus, it is established that even the Self mentioned in the Śruti regarding "seeing" (īkṣati) is indeed devoid of qualities. And it is established that He is the primary denotation (vācyatva) [of the word Brahman] precisely because "seeing" would otherwise be inexplicable.
On account of deep sleep.
He introduces the aphorism which establishes, by yet another argument, that Viṣṇu, though devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), is expressible by words.

"Because of merging into itself" (svāpyayāt). This is its meaning: because of the merging (apyaya) of the self into itself—since the word *apyaya* denotes dissolution (*laya*)—the one described in the Śruti as "he causes himself to dissolve" is indeed the Nirguṇa [Brahman] and not the secondary (gauṇa) one. For this very reason, he is denotable by words; such is the meaning.

And thus, because the Śruti text "Full is that" (*pūrṇam adaḥ*) speaks of fullness characterized by the term "dissolution" (*svāpyaya*), and because it speaks of one's own dissolution into oneself; because the clear Smṛti text "That God" (*sa devaḥ*) states "he dissolves in the Self alone" (*ātmany eva vilāpayati*), thereby speaking of one's own dissolution into oneself; because the Smṛti declares that He is established in the qualities of Hari; and because there can be no dissolution of the faultless [Self] into a secondary (inferior) Self—it is established that this [Self] is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and not secondary.
Because of the commonality of their destiny.

[Objection: Granted that it may be possible for the qualityless Viṣṇu to be the denotable object [of scripture], and thus his being known through scripture as the cause [of the world] is established; and so, by the force of the opening statements (*upakrama*) and other criteria, it is concluded that he is taught as the cause only in those well-known recensions (*śākhā*). However, let some other [deity] also be spoken of as the cause in the less well-known recensions. For they do not fail to exist, since their number cannot be determined due to their infinity. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies:

Regarding the phrase "due to the commonality of the goal" (gatisāmānyāt), its meaning is as follows: because of the commonality of the goal—that is, because the knowledge produced by the various recensions (śākhās) is heard to be of a single nature—no one other than Viṣṇu is taught in another recension as the cause. This is the sense.

And thus, by the Paiṅgi-śruti stating "all the Vedas," all the Vedas and Itihāsas—whether by way of their subject matter or their modes—reveal the single nature of Brahman, which is of the essence of knowledge, due to the absence of contradiction. Since it is stated that the knowledge produced by all the Śākhās is of one kind, and since there is no contradictory teaching in any of the Śākhās, it follows as a conclusion that Viṣṇu alone is propounded as the cause in all the Śākhās.
And because it is so stated in scripture.
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras states, by way of the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokana) maxim, that Brahman is to be denoted as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
"And because it is heard [in scripture]. The meaning of this is: since it is stated in scripture that "the God is one," Brahman is not something that cannot be denoted by words. This is the sense.

And thus, from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad statement, "In this way, the one God [resides] in all beings," it is declared that the subject to be denoted is the attributeless (nirguṇa) [Brahman], which is free from the bondage of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest. For an entity that is inexpressible cannot be expressed by the words of the Śruti; moreover, it is improper to conceive of Brahman—which is inexpressible—as being merely indicated (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, the opponent himself has admitted that Brahman is indeed expressible by all words. Consequently, since there is no subverting factor consisting of its inexpressibility, when an inquiry is conducted based on the marks of the opening passage and so forth, it is understood that He alone is the cause. And because of the uniformity of the scriptural approach (*gatisāmānya*), it is established that His alone is the causality.
Thus concludes the section concerning "Iksati" (the act of seeing).

Here, the reconciliation in Brahman of words denoting the possessor of qualities—which are indicated by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and which are not well-known in other [contexts] than the Vedic—is established.
[The Sūtra: "That which consists of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition. (1.1.12)

Is it not the case that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is non-different from the four-faced Brahmā? No, because of the confusion of names. Indeed, the word "Brahman" residing in the four-faced one is found in the one consisting of bliss, since the word "Brahman" is heard in the passage concerning the one consisting of bliss: "He is Brahman. Furthermore, the name "Śatānanda," which has the same meaning as "one consisting of bliss," applies to Hiraṇyagarbha. Or rather, Rudra is the one consisting of bliss; for the one consisting of bliss is declared to be the Sun in the passage, "And he who is that Sun," and being within the Sun is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Rudra.

It may be Indra, because he is the presiding deity of the sun and possesses the characteristic marks of Indra; or it may be Bṛhaspati, because he possesses the characteristic marks of Bṛhaspati. Or it may be the conscious primordial nature (*cit-prakṛti*), because of the desire for multiplicity expressed in the passage "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*) regarding that which identifies itself as "I"; or it may be the unconscious primordial nature (*acit-prakṛti*), due to its state of multiplicity. Or it may be all individual souls (*jīva*) residing within those respective bodies, because of the context of the "consisting of the essence of food" (*annarasamaya*) being primarily concerned with the soul, and because the status of being a soul must be attributed to those "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others by virtue of their identification with the transformations of food and so forth. Nor is the word "Brahman" a sublater [of these interpretations].

"Since all living beings are Brahmanīs, the word 'Brahman' is heard even with respect to the individual soul (jīva). This being the prima facie view, the author states the aphorism as a resolution: "The one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) [is Viṣṇu], because of repetition. The meaning of this is as follows: that which is denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" and so forth is Viṣṇu alone, not Prakṛti or others. Why? Because of repetition; that is to say, because the word "Brahman" is heard in every section concerning the one consisting of bliss and so forth.

And thus, He is not non-existent; for it has been stated in such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as "If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he becomes non-existent himself; if one knows Brahman as existent," that the word "Brahman" possesses its supreme primary denotation only with respect to Viṣṇu. It is therefore established that even the one denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is Viṣṇu alone.
"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the meaning of 'Self'] because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance."

Now, an objection may be raised: since the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), and because the material cause (*prakṛti*) consists of its modifications, and because the conscious material cause and others possess the conceit of being such modifications, it would follow that the terms "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and so forth refer only to the material cause and the like, and not to the Supreme Self. This is because the Supreme Self is changeless and free from such conceit. To refute this, the Sūtra speaks, raising the objection and then providing the resolution: [The Sūtra: "But [the Self] consisting of bliss is the one within, on account of the repetition. (BrSū 1.1.13) This is the meaning: the term "consisting of bliss" refers to the Supreme Self, which is the innermost Self. Why? Because of the repetition. For the word "Self" (*ātman*) is repeated in the text: "From him, verily, is born the Self consisting of food... the Self consisting of breath... the Self consisting of mind... the Self consisting of understanding... the Self consisting of bliss. Since the word "Self" is applied to each preceding stage, it is understood that the same "Self" is intended for the final stage as well. Furthermore, the attributes of fearlessness, immortality, and non-duality are declared for this very "Self consisting of bliss," which is possible only if it is the Supreme Self. Therefore, the "Self consisting of bliss" is the Supreme Self. It is not a modification; rather, the suffix *mayaṭ* here denotes abundance (*prācurya*). Thus, the objection is refuted.

"Because of the word denoting a modification; if it be said [that Viṣṇu is not meant], we say no, because of abundance. This is its meaning: "Because of the word denoting a modification"—that is, because of the suffix *mayaṭ* which signifies a modification—if it be argued that Viṣṇu is not the referent of the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and so forth, we say no. Why? Because of abundance; the meaning is that the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes fullness as expressed by the word "abundance" (*prācurya*).

And thus, because the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies abundance of bliss, even in the case of "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others, there is no absence of the sense of modification for the *mayaṭ* attached to them, since they are Brahman. Nor does the word *annamaya* and the others imply a limited meaning when they signify the abundance of food and so forth; for by the etymologies "it is eaten" (*adyate*) and "it eats" (*atti*), the very meanings of the word *annamaya* are being the sustenance of all beings and being the eater of all, respectively. This is because the intention is that being the sustenance of others is itself what constitutes "being eaten."

Since it is inappropriate to assume two distinct meanings for the suffix *mayaṭ* when it occurs in a list of primary terms (*prāyapaṭhita*), and since such usage is justified as a specific designation—just as one speaks of the sun as "abundant light" (*pracuraprakāśa*) with respect to Hari, whose essential nature is bliss and so forth—it is established that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and the others are indeed Viṣṇu alone.
And because its cause is designated.

He introduces the sūtra which establishes the reason—namely, abundance (*prācurya*)—as the meaning of the suffix *-maya*, serving as another ground for the fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Viṣṇu.

"And because of the designation of its cause. The meaning of this is as follows: the word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. "Of that" refers to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Regarding his being Viṣṇu, it is because of the "designation of the cause," namely the reason called "the impeller of the world's activity," since this is stated in the Śruti passage, "Who indeed could breathe? Therefore, the meaning is that the one consisting of bliss is indeed Viṣṇu alone.

And thus, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), not only because of the repetition of the word "Brahman," but also because in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss, Viṣṇu’s state of being "consisting of bliss" is due to his fullness of bliss; furthermore, since the suffix -maya is shown to mean "abundance," and because the reason known as "being the cause of the world's activity" is stated, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" precisely by virtue of his fullness of bliss.
And it is sung as having the color of emerald.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the word *brahman* can be applied to the individual soul (*jīva*) as the lower *brahman*, and even though it has its primary sense in the supreme *brahman*, its acceptance of a non-primary meaning is justified by the subverting evidence (bādhaka) found in statements such as Viṣṇu being described as a limb of the *ānandamaya*. To this, the author states the Sūtra:

"And it is sung as being based on the words of the mantra. This is its meaning: since Brahman—described in the words of the mantra as "Brahman is that infinite knowledge, the essence of food"—is "sung," that is, established by means of terms such as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that Brahman alone is denoted by the terms beginning with "consisting of bliss."

And this being so, since the words "truth," "knowledge," and so forth, as well as the words "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth, are perceived to have a single meaning when considered together, there is no contradiction in the statement that Brahman is the "tail" (support) of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), even though that [bliss] itself is Brahman; for the Śruti passage, "He is the head, He is the right [side]," speaks of the limbs belonging to the whole itself. Thus it is established that Brahman alone is what is denoted by the words "consisting of bliss" and the rest.
Not the other, because it is not possible.

[Objection: Surely, because the word "Brahman" is common [to many], and because the designation of that cause does not clearly appear as residing in Viṣṇu, and because the appellation based on the wording of a mantra is weaker than other indicative marks (liṅga) and so forth and thus has room for another interpretation, and because there is no other cause established otherwise, it follows that the Ānandamaya and others must be Viriñca and the rest. To this, he introduces the Sūtra: *nanu brahmaśabdasya sādhāraṇatvāt | taddhetuvyapadeśasya viṣṇuniṣṭhatayā spaṣṭamapratibhānāt | mantravarṇasamākhyāyāścānyaliṅgādibhyo durbalatvena sāvakāśatvāt | ananyathāsiddhahetvantarasya cābhāvāt | ānandamayādayo viriñcādaya eva syuriti prāpte sūtramavatārayati ||*

"Nor any other, because of impossibility. This is its meaning: "any other," such as Caturmukha (Brahmā) and so forth, is not [the one referred to]. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because it is impossible for him to be the object of the knowledge that produces liberation, as stated in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

Thus, by means of the terms *annamaya* and so forth—which convey the aforementioned attributes such as being the bliss of hundreds of Brahmas, having eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*), and manifold existence—it is established that Viriñca (Brahmā) and others are not what is denoted. This is because liberation is impossible through knowledge of anyone other than Viṣṇu, such as Viriñca; for the Śruti, "He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme," declares that the objects of the knowledge which is the cause of liberation are the *ānandamaya* and the rest, and thus it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the terms *ānandamaya* and so forth.
And because there is a designation of difference.
He introduces the sūtra which refutes the view that Brahmā and others consist of bliss by means of a different reason.

"And because there is a designation of difference. The meaning of this is: because qualities that distinguish the four-faced [Brahmā] and others from the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) are stated, the one consisting of bliss is not anyone other [than Brahman]. This is the sense.

And thus, because in the passage "those who are a hundred [of them]" it is stated that Viriñca possesses a bliss a hundred times greater than Rudra's; because in the passage beginning with "from which words turn back," the Ānandamaya is stated to possess immeasurable bliss; because it is stated that Rudra's bliss is only a hundredth part of Viriñca's; because it is stated that the bliss of Bṛhaspati and the others is each a hundredth part less than the one preceding them; and because in the context of invisibility and other qualities, there is heard mention of distinctive attributes such as independence (svātantrya) which are incompatible with Prakṛti and the rest.

Because, in the passage "He who is this [and that]," there is stated a distinguishing attribute—the state of all living beings, from the unexalted to the exalted—pertaining to the entire collection of souls beginning with Brahmā; and because the meaning of such scriptural texts as "That thou art" must be interpreted otherwise; and because the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been established, it is proven that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) and so forth is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
And because it is directly perceived, there is no dependence upon inference.

Now, one might object: even if there is no contradiction with scripture regarding the statement of difference, there would still be a contradiction with the following inferences: "The individual soul (jīva) is non-different from Brahman because it is conscious, like Brahman"; "Difference is false because it is a difference, like the [apparent] difference in the moon"; and "The bodies under dispute are the abodes of my enjoyment because they are bodies, like my own body. Having raised this objection, the author introduces the Sūtra.

"And because [the inquiry proceeds] from desire, there is no dependence on inference. This is its meaning: since there is no inference that is favorable to the Śruti of non-duality, and since mere inference proceeds according to one's own desire—that is, by following one's own whim—there is no dependence on inference. The meaning is that one should not rely on "dry" (unfounded) inference regarding objects that transcend the senses.

And thus, since inference that contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, and which lacks the support of scripture, possesses no causal efficacy toward the knowledge of reality; furthermore, because it is possible to infer [the contrary] that "God is not independent because he is conscious, like Devadatta and others"; and because if even that which contradicts perception and so forth were to be a valid means of knowledge, then consciousness and the like would also possess validity due to there being no distinction between them—therefore, a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) against the opposing position is possible. This is because, in the Skanda Purāṇa passage beginning with "as one desires," mere inference is stated to be subject to one's own whims.
Since the difference between the individual soul and the Lord is established, it is proven that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and so forth is indeed Brahman.
And [the scripture] teaches his union with that in this [state].

"Granted that there may be a difference between the Brahman consisting of bliss and the individual souls such as Hiraṇyagarbha; nevertheless, that difference is merely empirical (vyāvahārika) and not ultimate (pāramārthika), because even in liberation it persists, since the cited scriptural passages can be reasonably interpreted as referring to worldly difference. To this position, the Sūtra states:

"And it teaches its connection with that in this [context]. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) signifies a conjunction of reasons. Because in this section concerning the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), the Scripture teaches—that is, establishes—the connection of this individual soul (jīva) even with liberation to those [states] beginning with the one consisting of bliss; therefore, the meaning is that the one consisting of bliss and so forth is indeed Brahman, and not the body or other such things.

Thus, from such statements as "In the abode-less [Brahman] there is fearlessness" and "This is the one consisting of bliss," it is established that upon liberation, the knower of Brahman attains his own appropriate desires along with the omniscient Jñānin and Caturmukha; and because it is stated that [the path] leads the soul that has departed from the body into the proximity of the Supreme Self who is full bliss. Therefore, since the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is proven to be ultimate, it is established that the one consisting of bliss and so forth is not Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning that which consists of bliss (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa).

Here, for the purpose of establishing the coordination of names such as Indra—which are well-known in the context of the deities—with the [Supreme Self], the coordination of the mark consisting in "dwelling within the body" is now undertaken.
