[Objection: Surely the one spoken of as being "within" must be Indra, because of the mention of "Indra"; or it must be Sūrya, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the "Lord of Heaven"; or Varuṇa, because of the indicative mark of Varuṇa; or Tvaṣṭṛ, because of the mention of Tvaṣṭṛ; or Agni and Bṛhaspati, because of the mentions of Agni and Bṛhaspati. Indeed, the words "Indra" and so forth cannot be applied elsewhere, because they are conventionally established (rūḍha) only among the gods, and because their grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta), such as sovereignty and the like, belong only to them. Nor can the one within be Viṣṇu on account of indicative marks such as invisibility (adṛśyatva) and so forth, because a mere indicative mark is weaker than direct scriptural statement (śruti) and the rest. To this, the author of the Sūtra replies: *na vakturātmopadeśāditi cedadhyātmasambandhabhūmā hyasmin* || 1.2.29 || [Response: It is not so, because there is instruction regarding the Self of the Speaker; for in this [passage], there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections. (Sūtra 1.2.29) The word "not" (na) negates the previous position. The phrase "because there is instruction regarding the Self of the Speaker" means that the instruction concerns the very Self of the Speaker, who is the Lord (Iśvara). How so? Because there is an abundance of internal connections in this passage. The term "abundance" (bhūmā) refers to the multitude of statements concerning the internal Self. These are: "He who dwells in the breath and is within the breath," "He who dwells in the eye and is within the eye," "He who dwells in the mind and is within the mind," "He who dwells in the understanding (vijñāna) and is within the understanding," and "He who dwells in the bliss and is within the bliss. Since these many internal connections are found here, the one within must be the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) is used primarily for the Supreme Self, as seen in passages such as, "The Self alone is to be meditated upon. Moreover, the word "Person" (puruṣa) is used in the sense of the Supreme Self in the passage, "The Person who is seen within the eye. Also, the word "Brahman" is used in the sense of the Supreme Self in the passage, "That which is the Brahman within the city of the body (pura). Therefore, since the word "Self" and others are used in this context, the one within is the Supreme Self. As for the objection that the word "Indra" and so forth cannot be applied elsewhere, we reply: those words are indeed applied to the Supreme Self in the sense of its attributes, such as sovereignty and the like. This is seen in the passage, "He is Indra by name, Śakra by name, and the Powerful One (Purandara) by name. Thus, the conclusion is that the one within is the Supreme Self. This is stated in the commentary: "The word 'Indra' is applied to the Supreme Self in the sense of its sovereignty. The word "Śakra" is applied in the sense of its power to accomplish all tasks. The word "Purandara" is applied in the sense of its destruction of the cities of the demons. Similarly, the word "Varuṇa" is applied in the sense of its quality of encompassing all things. The word "Tvaṣṭṛ" is applied in the sense of its fashioning all forms. The word "Agni" is applied in the sense of its quality of leading all beings to their respective ends. The word "Bṛhaspati" is applied in the sense of its being the lord of the great Veda. Therefore, the one within is the Supreme Self. This is the meaning. End of section. End of second quarter of the first chapter. End of first chapter. (Note: The provided text contains a portion of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* by Śaṅkarācārya on Sūtra 1.2.29.)

"Because of the teaching of His attributes within. This is its meaning: "Within"—that is, that which is heard to have entered within the heart—is Brahman alone, not Indra or others. Why? Because of the teaching of His attributes. That is to say, because the attributes of Viṣṇu—such as residing in the midst of the milk-ocean, abiding in the ocean of dissolution, and being the seed of the cosmic egg—are heard in the scripture in passages such as "within the ocean" and so forth.

And thus, since it is logical that the signs which have scope are sublated by the signs which leave no room for alternative interpretation, it is established that this one situated within is indeed Viṣṇu.
And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the aggregate].

Now, one might raise this objection: since Viṣṇu is "situated within" (antaḥstha) based on such marks as residing in the ocean and so forth, let there then be non-difference between that Viṣṇu situated within and Indra and the other gods, because there also exists scriptural testimony and other evidence establishing Indra and the rest. Furthermore, since scriptural testimony and the like, by their very nature, possess greater force than a mark (liṅga) which lacks a specific scope (niravakāśatva), it is impossible to determine one side over the other through the sublation of either. Thus, when both the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions are devoid of a mutual relationship of sublated and sublator, the conclusion that Indra and the others are non-different from the Viṣṇu situated within follows by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (anyathānupapatti). Anticipating this doubt, he presents the following Sūtra to resolve it:

"And because of the designation of difference, [He] is other. This is its meaning: Viṣṇu is not only the one dwelling within; rather, He is also other than Indra and the rest. Why? Because of the designation of difference. The meaning is that this is because we hear of distinguishing attributes such as His being the inner controller (antaryāmin) of those [deities] and His being their impeller.

And thus, because of the hearing of attributes that distinguish [the inner being] from others in such scriptural passages as "the Self of Indra," "the Self of Vāyu," and "within the sun," one might argue that this [inner being] must be postulated through the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (anyathānupapatti) since both [sets of evidence] apply. However, this is not so; for it is logical that the scriptural texts and indicative marks (liṅga) which apply to others and possess other scopes are sublated by the indicative marks of Viṣṇu, which are without scope elsewhere. Therefore, it is established that this one situated within is indeed Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the section concerning the state of being intermediate.

In this case, the Lord—who is indicated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), which is not well-known in common worldly usage [as referring to the physical element]—is shown to be the substratum of all sounds whatsoever, including those pertaining to the physical realm.
"The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark."

Now, it might be argued that the "ether" mentioned in the Śruti passage, "Of this world," is indeed the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), because the word "ether" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense. Nor should it be said that this ether is Viṣṇu, on the grounds that the word "ether" is applied there etymologically (*yogika*) and thus constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*). For an etymological meaning is of inferior strength and therefore cannot serve as a counter-argument.

Nor should it be argued that because the ground for the application of the word "ether" (ākāśa)—namely, "providing space" (avakāśatva)—exists in Hari as well through the relationship characterized by independence (svātaṃtrya), just as it exists in the elemental ether through inherence (samavāya), and thus the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is identical in both cases, making it impossible to determine from convention alone that it refers to the elemental ether; for ether is insentient and lacks dependence upon the Lord, and therefore the quality of being ether does not reside in Him through the relationship of master and servant (svasvāmibhāva).

Thus, since the "ether" mentioned in the *Chāndogya* Śruti is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), the ether mentioned in the *Taittirīya* Śruti must also, by the force of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), be the elemental ether; for it is stated that "all these [beings] come from this ether," thereby describing that ether as the cause of the elements. Furthermore, since the observation that activity within an effect depends upon its cause provides scope for the mark (*liṅga*) of being the "mover of the world" mentioned in the Śruti—"Who indeed other than He could breathe?"—it does not constitute a sublation [of the conventional meaning]. Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that "the ether is not Viṣṇu," the following is set forth in the Sūtra:

"Ākāśa [is Viṣṇu], because of His characteristic marks. This is its meaning: "Ākāśa"—that which is denoted by the word *ākāśa*—is indeed Viṣṇu, not the well-known elemental ether. Why? "Because of His characteristic marks" (*talliṅgāt*); that is to say, because the characteristic marks such as being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) are heard in relation to the *ākāśa* mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

And thus, because of the unimpeded Viṣṇu-indications such as "being higher than the high" (parovarīyastva), and because the word *ākāśa* has its primary meaning in that very [Viṣṇu] due to the existence of both great etymological derivation (*mahāyoga*) and the conventional usage of the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*), it follows that if the *ākāśa* mentioned in the Chāndogya Śruti is Viṣṇu, then the one mentioned in the Taittirīya [Śruti] is also Viṣṇu by the force of the indication of being the "mover of the world" (*jagacceṣṭakatva*). This is because "being a mover" is primarily applicable to an agent, and when the primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one.

Since the state of being the mover of all is pervaded by the state of being the supreme among all, and since the state of being the supreme among all is absent in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), it follows that the state of being the mover of all is also absent there. Nor can bliss arise for even an insentient entity through the favor of a sentient being, because such a claim lacks scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*). Therefore, it is established that Ākāśa is indeed Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the section concerning space.
Here, the reconciliation of the word *prāṇa*—which, by its very nature, indicates all words that are not well-known in common usage elsewhere—with Brahman is established.
Therefore, [the subject] is *prāṇa*.

Now, is this *prāṇa* not simply air (*vāyu*)? For the word *prāṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense, whereas it lacks such conventional usage in reference to Viṣṇu; thus, the scriptural mention of *prāṇa* finds no scope there. Furthermore, since the etymological meaning—being the cause of life—is observed in air alone through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that *prāṇa* is indeed air. To this, the Sūtra states:

"Therefore, [He is] Prāṇa. This is its meaning: "That very You became Prāṇa"—the Prāṇa mentioned here is Viṣṇu alone, and none other. Why? "For this very reason," that is, for the reason of the mark (liṅga) of being the Lord of Śrī, as stated in the words "and Śrī [is yours]."

And thus, because of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of being the Lord of Śrī-Lakṣmī, which leaves no room for another interpretation; because the term "Īśāna," "Prāṇada," and "Prāṇa" exist in Viṣṇu through the established usage of the learned (*viddhr-ruḍhi*), as well as through great yoga (*mahā-yoga*); and because even the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of life residing in the vital breath is dependent upon the Blessed Lord according to the scripture "not by breath" (*na prāṇena*); therefore, it is established that the one denoted by the word "Prāṇa" is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).

Here, the reconciliation of the term "Light" (jyotis)—which is well-known elsewhere in common usage as indicative of all the various words occurring in those respective Sūtras—is established with respect to Brahman. [Sūtra: "Because of the mention of the feet. (1.1.24)

Is it not the case that this light is indeed Agni? For this hymn is an *agni-sūkta* (a hymn dedicated to Agni). Nor can it be argued that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the mark (*liṅga*) because the mark is weaker than the context, on the grounds that the mark of being "hidden in the cave" overrides the context; for the direct scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotiḥ-śruti*) is firmly established in reference to Agni, whereas it does not apply to Viṣṇu. Furthermore, one should not say that the mark overrides both the scripture and the context simply because the mark has no other possible application (*niravakāśatva*); for even the mark finds its application in the digestive fire (*jāṭhara-jātavedas*). Even if the mark were indeed without other application, its strength would be of precisely this kind [i.e., limited].

However, because direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) possess greater force due to being employed in multiple ways—and because direct statement also possesses greater force by virtue of its inherent nature—it is proper that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) be set aside by both direct statement and context. Thus, when it is argued that "the light is fire," the Sūtra states:

"Because of the mention of feet in the case of light. This is its meaning: "Light" refers to Brahman alone, which is denoted by the word *jyotis*, and not anything else. Why? Because of the mention of feet—that is, because of the mention of the ears and other limbs as the feet [of the one described]. The meaning is that it is heard that light is entirely beyond the reach of the ears and other senses.

And thus, because the strength of being "without scope" (*niravakāśatva*)—which arises from the Viṣṇu-liṅga known as "being far from Karṇa and others"—is more powerful than both types of strength (namely, the strength of plurality and the strength of natural power), it is logical that this liṅga sublates the Śruti and the Context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, since the Śruti has its primary meaning in Viṣṇu alone due to the existence of both Great Etymology (*mahāyoga*) and conventional usage among the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*), it is established that this light is indeed Viṣṇu, and that He alone is situated within the cave of the heart.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
Here, the application of all the terms beginning with "Gāyatrī" as they occur in the context of the secondary wife (adhivedana) is established. [Sūtra:
"If it be argued that this is not so because of the mention of meters, we say no; for there is a declaration of the fixing of the mind in that way, and such is seen [in scripture]."

Objection: Gāyatrī is indeed the metre, because the word "gāyatrī" is conventionally established in that sense alone, and because of the scriptural injunction: "Speech, verily, is Gāyatrī. Nor can it be argued that the word "gāyatrī" applies primarily to the Lord Himself because Gāyatrī is dependent on Him; for since Gāyatrī is a specific Vedic metre, being eternal, it cannot be dependent on another. Therefore, since it follows that Gāyatrī is merely a specific metre, the author reads the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But on account of the statement of its feet and so forth [the Lord is Gāyatrī]. (1.1.25) This means: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view. It is the Lord who is Gāyatrī. Why? Because of the statement of His feet and so forth. For it is said: "The earth is one foot of Her," and so on, up to "The immortal glory in heaven is Her fourth foot. Since these feet and other attributes belong to the Lord, He alone is Gāyatrī. Furthermore, the word "Gāyatrī" is derived from the root *gai* (to sing), meaning "She who sings," and thus refers to the Lord as the singer of all things. Moreover, the word "Gāyatrī" is used in the sense of the Lord in the passage: "He who knows this Gāyatrī as having eight syllables and four feet, and who knows its Brahman as life-force (*prāṇa*), does not fall before the day of death. Therefore, the Lord alone is Gāyatrī. As for the argument that the word is conventional in the sense of a metre, that is not so; for even though it is conventional, it is not impossible for it to denote the Lord through etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*). Just as the word "lion" (*siṃha*) is applied to a man, so too the word "Gāyatrī" may be applied to the Lord. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural statement "Speech is Gāyatrī," for that is intended to show that speech is a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Lord. Thus, the conclusion is that the Lord alone is Gāyatrī. This is stated in the *Vedāntasūtramuktāvalī*: "But on account of the statement of its feet and so forth, the Lord alone is Gāyatrī. For it is said: 'The earth is one foot of Her,' and so on. And because the word 'Gāyatrī' is derived from the root *gai*, it denotes the Lord as the singer of all things. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding speech, for that is intended to show that speech is a manifestation of the Lord. Thus it is established.

"Because of the mention of a *chandas* [Vedic meter], it is not [Viṣṇu]; if this is argued, it is not so, because of the declaration of the fixing of the mind [upon Him] in that way; for there is a scriptural vision [to that effect]. This is its meaning: "Because of the mention of a *chandas*. Now, since the word *gāyatrī* found in the *Chāndogya* Śruti denotes a *chandas* consisting of twenty-four syllables, one might argue that Viṣṇu is not the referent of the word *gāyatrī*. If this is said, it is not so. Why? Because "there is a scriptural vision [to that effect]. For (*hi*)—that is, because—in that way, by reason of His being the agent of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*).

There is a scriptural text (*śruti*) that establishes Viṣṇu as the referent of the word *gāyatrī*. Therefore, it was stated [in the commentary], beginning with "tathā" (likewise), that there is no futility in designating Viṣṇu by the term *gāyatrī*. The meaning of "tathā cetorpaṇanigadāt" is as follows: because of the mention in scripture (*nigadāt*) regarding the fixing of the mind (*cetorpaṇa*) upon Viṣṇu—meaning for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*) through the fixing of the mind on Him as possessing the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as *gāyatrī* and so forth; thus, there is no futility. This is the intended sense.

And thus, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the agent of singing and protection, there is no sublation of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) on the grounds that the *liṅga* lacks scope; for the direct scriptural statement regarding the Gāyatrī is primary in that context due to its conventional usage in the Purāṇas and because of the etymological derivation mentioned in scripture. Furthermore, from the statement "by her own nature," it follows that the Gāyatrī is dependent upon the Lord. Thus, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the referent denoted by the word "Gāyatrī."
And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "bhūta" is thus appropriate.
He introduces the aphorism which establishes the identity of Gāyatrī with Viṣṇu by means of another reason as well.

"And because the designation of the quarters beginning with 'beings' is appropriate [only] thus. This is its meaning: the word "thus" (evam) is repeated. It is appropriate that Brahman alone is denoted by the word Gāyatrī. Why? Because the designation of the quarters beginning with "beings" is appropriate only thus. For it is stated that it possesses parts consisting of beings and nectar, in the passage: "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. And the meaning is that this is possible only in the case of Viṣṇu, while it is impossible in any other case.

And thus, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, by the passage "This [Gāyatrī] is four-footed," the sixfold nature of the Lord named Gāyatrī—consisting of the previously mentioned speech, earth, body, and heart—is restated; having then enjoined His four-footedness as consisting of the possession of four parts (aṃśas), the mantra of the Puruṣasūkta is cited as an authoritative designation (samākhyā) for the very point just stated. The four-footedness of the Lord is clearly and favorably expressed by a Ṛgvedic mantra.

Nor is it untenable to describe Viṣṇu as having the elements as His feet on the basis of His being distinct from the elements, as is the case with the Gāyatrī; for there is the scriptural text: "The golden casket. Nor should it be said that the Puruṣasūkta is not a context concerning Viṣṇu; for by the Smṛti statement, "At that time, He was the Great King," the fact that the context concerns Viṣṇu is certain. Therefore, it is established that the one denoted by the word Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
If it be argued that [the meditations] are not identical because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case.

Now, having raised an objection based on the statement beginning with "because the two sections concerning the Gāyatrī and the Jyotis have different meanings due to a difference in instruction," he states the sūtra as a resolution:

"If it be argued that [the two are] not [one] because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. This is the meaning: If it be argued that they are not one because of the difference in instruction—that is, because of the difference between scriptural passages teaching contradictory attributes such as being situated in the heavens (*dyusthatva*) and being beyond the heavens (*divaḥ paratva*) regarding Gāyatrī and Jyotis, and therefore they are not a single entity called Viṣṇu but rather distinct things—[we reply] "no. Why? Because there is no contradiction in either scriptural statement, even though they establish a single object; the meaning is that there is no contradiction when the seven-times-three worlds are intended [to be encompassed].

And thus, since for one and the same entity both "dwelling in heaven" and "being beyond heaven" are possible through a difference in intended meaning, there is no difference in their referents. Therefore, it is established that Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation of meters.

In this [section], the concordance of the name "Prāṇa"—which is not established as referring to anything other than Viṣṇu in common worldly usage—is demonstrated. "Prāṇa [is Viṣṇu] because of the [contextual] correspondence."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the vital breath (prāṇa), and not Viṣṇu, is the subject here? For it has been stated, "These indeed were so many," and because [the prāṇa] is enumerated among the group of sense organs. Or rather, it is the individual soul (jīva), because of the characteristic mark of the soul found in the passage, "He [it] illumined this world. Or perhaps it is the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), because of its characteristic mark in the passage, "They did not injure him. This being the position reached, the author presents the aphorism:

"Likewise, Prāṇa [is Viṣṇu], because of the following [of characteristics]. This is its meaning: "Likewise" means that just like the Prāṇa mentioned in the Taittirīya, "tadvaitvam," the Prāṇa mentioned in the Aitareya, "tā vā," is also Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the following; that is to say, because of the repeated hearing of words such as "Brahman," which are marks of Viṣṇu regarding the deity to be meditated upon and so forth.

And thus, in the passage "He is this *asu*," he is described as *asu* because he dispels the wicked; as the nature of supreme bliss because he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and as both prosperity and its opposite because he bestows the sovereignty of knowledge and so forth upon the gods while being the cause of the sovereignty of ignorance and so forth upon the *asuras*. Furthermore, in the passage "These indeed are those," he is described as being declared by all the Vedas; in "This is that *prāṇa*," as being the charioteer of the body; and in "The gods struck him down," as being the object of worship for all the deities.

Nor is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) strengthened by the fact that its indicative mark (liṅga) is without scope; for in the passage "they breathe through him" (*prāṇayanta*), he is described as being worshipped by all the deities. Nor is the prima facie argument strengthened even by the absence of scope for its indicative mark, because being enumerated along with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) can possibly belong to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Even if [the prima facie mark] were stronger, a definitive conclusion is still possible because the Siddhāntin’s indicative mark is superior, being stronger in two ways compared to the prima facie mark which is strong in only one way.

In this context, because of the repeated use of the term "Brahman" in its exclusive sense—as in "this is Brahman," "the world of Brahman," "Brahman [leads] this person," "they call the belly Brahman," and "A is Brahman"—it is established that this Prāṇa is indeed Viṣṇu alone.

"If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the Supreme Self because of the instruction concerning the speaker's own self, we reply: no, for there is an abundance of references to the connection with the inner self (adhyātma) in this [section]."

"Is it not the case that this Prāṇa is not Viṣṇu, but rather Indra himself? For, by the statement 'I am indeed Prāṇa,' Indra taught his own self as Prāṇa to Viśvāmitra, who was the reciter of a thousand Bṛhatī verses?"—having raised this objection, the author states the Sūtra to provide the resolution.

"If it be argued that [the Prāṇa] is not Viṣṇu because of the instruction regarding the Self by the speaker—[we reply: no, for there is an abundance of internal connection in this [passage]. This is its meaning: the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. "By the speaker" means toward Viśvāmitra, the reciter of a thousand Bṛhatī verses. "Because of the instruction regarding the Self" means because of the instruction of the Self—that is, of Himself—as the Prāṇa. If it be argued that "this Prāṇa is Indra alone and not Viṣṇu," the word "no" (na) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Its repetition connects back to the phrase "because of the following" (anugamāt). Thus, for the reason of the aforementioned following, the Prāṇa is not Indra.

Even so, there is no contradiction with the scriptural teaching (upadeśa). Why? Because in this context, the Lord’s abundant connection with the inner self (adhyātma-sambandha-bhūmā)—that is, His connection with many bodies such as those of Indra, Viśvāmitra, and others—is stated. This is the meaning. Alternatively: for (hi) because, in this Indra, there exists an abundance (bhūmā)—meaning a great quantity—of the connection with the Supreme Self (adhi-ātman), that is, of the connection consisting of His descent (āveśa); therefore [there is no contradiction]. This is the meaning.
And thus it is established that the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
But the instruction is given from the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva.

Now, if by the word "prāṇa" Viṣṇu alone is indeed denoted by Indra as being all-pervasive within his own self and so forth, then the designation would have been "prāṇa is in me," and not "I am [the prāṇa]. Since it is argued that the teaching in the form of "I am [the prāṇa]" and so forth would be inappropriate for Viṣṇu, the author reads the sūtra which provides the resolution.

"But the instruction is from the perspective of the Śāstra, as in the case of Vāmadeva. This is the meaning: the word "but" (tu) has the sense of "only" (eva). "As in the case of Vāmadeva" means just as the sage Vāmadeva, with the intention of referring to the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin), declared his own identity with Manu, Sūrya, and so forth, saying, "I was Manu," and so on; similarly, from the perspective of the Śāstra—where "Śāstra" is that which rules all, namely the Inner Ruler—the instruction, the designation "I am Prāṇa," is made solely with the intention of referring to that [Inner Ruler], and not by way of actual identity.

Thus, because this instruction regarding the Self as the vital breath (prāṇa) of Indra proceeds with the intention of referring to the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), otherwise the designation "Thou art the prāṇa" would be untenable. However, in the case of the Lord (Īśvara), since words such as "I" and so forth are employed from the perspective of the scriptural vision (śāstradṛṣṭyā), there is no contradiction; for it is stated in scripture that "Viṣṇu is designated by those various names. Therefore, it is established that this prāṇa is indeed Viṣṇu.

If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital air (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefoldness of meditation, and because here [in this context], their connection is based on that [Brahman].
Having raised the objection regarding redundancy, he presents the sūtra as a resolution.

"If it be argued that [the one referred to] is not [Viṣṇu] because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, because [these marks] are resorted to [by Viṣṇu], and because of their connection with Him here. This is its meaning: "Because of the marks of the individual soul"—such as having a lifespan of a hundred years and so forth—and "because of the marks of the chief vital breath"—in the form of the dialogue with the senses and the gods and so forth—[it may be argued] that the Prāṇa is someone else and not Viṣṇu. If this is said, we reply: "No. Why? "Because of the underlying connection" (anugama). Nor is there a contradiction with the marks; for it should be supplied that these marks are explained by their referring to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), and so forth.

To the question, "For what purpose is the discussion of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin)? it is said: "Because of the threefold nature of meditation" (*upāsātraividhyāt*). This means that because the meditation on Brahman is threefold—distinguished as internal, external, and all-pervading—and because this threefold nature is relied upon and stated in this context, it is due to the fitness of those qualified aspirants for these three types of meditation. Thus is the meaning.

Thus, the intention is that it is appropriate to describe the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) through various terms for the sake of meditation according to the differences among the respective qualified aspirants. Therefore, since this Prāṇa is indeed Viṣṇu—as previously stated—and since that very Prāṇa is the Ānandamaya, it is established that the desire to know Him (taj-jijñāsā) is justified.
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath at the end of the feet.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter.
Hari.
Now begins the second quarter of the first chapter.
In this section (pāda), the application of words whose primary meaning consists of gender (liṅga) to Viṣṇu is demonstrated primarily.
Here, the gender-characteristic (liṅga) consisting of the state of being omnipresent, which is well-known elsewhere [as belonging to other deities], is shown to be in harmony with Brahman.
"Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere. || ||

Surely, this [Self] must be the all-pervading Sun itself, because of numerous scriptural passages such as "He is that Sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6) and others; and because of the citation of the solar mantra, "The Sun is the Self" (Sūrya Ātmā); and because there is the indicative mark of its not being mentioned among the Sun, whereas it has been mentioned in relation to earth and the other elements in the passage "This one in this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.14). Or else, this all-pervasiveness belongs to all individual souls (jīvas), because of the indicative marks such as "consisting of the eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.18). Nor can the marks such as "consisting of the eye" refer to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), since, being unlimited, it would be impossible for Him to have a "small abode" as stated in the phrase "dwelling in all beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.15).

Therefore, since it might be argued that the previously mentioned state of being the vital breath (*prāṇatva*) and the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) belong not to Viṣṇu, but to someone else who is all-pervading, the Sūtra states:

"Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere. This is the meaning: the word "that" (tat) carries over from the previous context. That entity being spoken of in relation to everything—earth and so forth—is indeed Brahman called Nārāyaṇa, and nothing else. Why? Because of the teaching of what is well-known (prasiddhopadeśāt). The meaning is that in the case of this all-pervading reality, we hear the word "Brahman"—which is well-known in the Śrutis and other sources as denoting Nārāyaṇa—used in the statement, "This very one is Brahman."

And thus, in this very manner, it is established that Nārāyaṇa alone is the reality residing within all beings; for, by virtue of being taught through the word "Brahman"—as made famous by the scripture stating "He who is this [Self]"—Nārāyaṇa alone is declared to be present as the inner self within all beings, since He is the sole ultimate ground of everything.
And because the qualities intended [to be described] are applicable [to Brahman].
He introduces the sūtra which, by means of another scriptural passage, establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the all-pervasiveness mentioned here.

"Because the qualities intended [to be expressed] are applicable [only to Him]. This is the meaning: the word "ca" (and) denotes either conjunction or emphasis. The phrase "by scripture regarding the omnipresent one" is the ellipsis. Therefore, since the qualities such as "not being heard" and so forth—which are intended to be expressed hereafter, which are fit to be stated by scripture as residing in the omnipresent one, and which will be mentioned later—apply only to Viṣṇu due to His fitness, and because they are not applicable elsewhere, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the omnipresent one.

And thus, by such scriptural passages as "He who is unheard from this," "Not those, O Viṣṇu," and "He is Savitṛ," it is established that Nārāyaṇa alone is the one spoken of everywhere, since the qualities to be described—such as being unheard and so forth—which are suitable to be predicated of him who is omnipresent and the ultimate reality, are fitting for Viṣṇu alone.
But because of the impossibility [of it being so], it is not the embodied soul.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as Viṣṇu is declared to be omnipresent based on the word "Brahman" along with such marks as "unheard-of-ness" (aśrutatva) and so forth, so too, based on the word "Āditya" in the passage "The Āditya is the essence," and because the mark of being "consisting of sight" (cakṣurmaya)—which is well-known to apply to the individual soul (jīva) due to its identification with a body whose nature is the instrument of knowledge—is found in the scripture, it follows that either the Āditya or all individual souls might be [the referent]. To this, the Sūtra provides the following response:

"But because of impossibility, it is not the embodied one. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: the word "but" (tu) has the sense of "only"; "the embodied one" (śārīraḥ) refers to the individual soul (jīva) or the sun. It is not omnipresent. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because it is impossible for a single individual soul to reside within all bodies.

And thus, because it would be contradictory for all living beings to have an identical form of experience, and because it is impossible for each individual soul to reside within every body; furthermore, if a single soul—or even the sun—were to reside in all bodies, it would follow that it would experience all the pleasures, pains, and so forth [of all beings], which would render its omnipresence untenable and result in the scripture having a sublated subject matter. Therefore, it is established that Nārāyaṇa alone is what is spoken of as being present within all beings.
And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the object and the agent of action.
He introduces the sūtra which refutes the all-pervasiveness of the embodied soul by means of another argument.

"And because of the designation of [the Self] as both object and agent. This is its meaning: since there is a designation of "Self" (*ātmānam*) as the object (*karman*) with respect to an all-pervading entity, and a designation of agency (*kartṛtva*)—which is contradictory to that—in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), and because this has been stated, the meaning is that the individual soul is not all-pervading.

And thus, since it is stated everywhere that this very Self—which is omnipresent and under discussion—is the object (*karman*) in the act of praising in the Aitareya Śruti through the expression "this Self" (*etam ātmānam*), while the embodied soul (*śārīra*) is designated as its agent (*kartṛ*) in that same passage through the expression "he [is] this Self" (*sa etam ātmānam*); and because, in a single action, those two are generally subject to the rule of being distinct in the absence of any cause for exception, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one spoken of everywhere.
Because of the distinction in the word.

Now, it is not tenable to claim that Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent based on the word "Brahman," because that word also applies to the individual soul (jīva). Nor can it be argued that the soul is not grasped [as the referent] because its usage there is secondary; for it is possible to accept even a secondary meaning by the force of subverting factors such as its being "consisting of sight" and so forth. Nor is the soul excluded by the subverting factor of its form being devoid of qualities such as "not being heard" and so on, since the Bhagavad Gītā states, "Even having heard this," thereby describing the soul as marvelous and so forth. Furthermore, the impossibility of residing in a single body is not a subverting factor, as that [impossibility] applies equally to Viṣṇu as well.

Nor can it be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is not [all-pervading] because of the sublation [of such a view] by its being composed of the eye and so forth; for it is logically possible for a single entity to be both the agent and the object of action. Thus, when it is concluded that the jīva is indeed all-pervading, the following aphorism is stated:

"Because of a specific word": this is its meaning. In the sentence "This very [is] Brahman," the word *brahman* does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), because it possesses the qualification known as the word *eva*, which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). This is the meaning.

And thus, because the word *brahman* used in the present context within the stated sentence possesses the specific quality of being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇatva*) by virtue of its function as a reason, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the referent of the word *brahman* accompanied by the particle *eva*, it would follow that the soul is the primary *brahman*. But that is untenable, since it is well-known that the soul is not *brahman*. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the omnipresent one.
And because of Smṛti.
He presents the sūtra which establishes the all-pervasiveness of Viṣṇu even by means of the designation of scripture (śruti-samākhyā).

"And because of Smṛti. This is its meaning: [the word "and" indicates] a conjunction. It means that the word *brahman* does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) not only because it is stated in Śruti, but also because of the existence of Smṛti such as "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa," and so forth; thus, the word *brahman* does not refer to the individual soul.

And thus, from the aforementioned scriptural statement, it is established that the author of the Sūtras did not intend to propound the falsity of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara); furthermore, because such a conception would contradict authoritative sources such as the verse beginning with "dvā suparṇā," it should not be so conceived, and it is therefore proven that Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because of its having a small abode and because of being designated as such, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the individual soul (jīva) alone is omnipresent and not Viṣṇu? For, in the passage beginning with "in all beings," His presence is stated as being universal; and because attributes of the individual soul are predicated of Him. Since such dual designations would be impossible for one who is unlimited and devoid of the attributes of the individual soul, [the opponent] arrives at this conclusion. To this, the author presents the aphorism as a resolution: sūtra 2.3.29: jīvamukhyaprāṇaliṅgānneti cennopāsātraividhyādāśritatvādiha tadyogāt|| If it be argued that [Viṣṇu is not the subject] because of the indicative marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), we say no; because there is a threefold nature of meditation, and because those [marks] are applicable here due to their being based on [the individual soul]. The meaning is as follows: The term "individual soul" (jīva) refers to the individual soul, while "chief vital breath" (mukhyaprāṇa) refers to the vital air. Because there are indicative marks of both, it cannot be Viṣṇu. However, this is not so. Why? Because of the threefold nature of meditation. The threefold nature of meditation consists of: meditation on the individual soul, meditation on the chief vital breath, and meditation on the Supreme Self. Among these, the meditation on the individual soul is intended for those who have attained the state of *prāptabhūmikā* (one who has reached the stage of realization); the meditation on the chief vital breath is for those who have attained the state of *anugrāhyabhūmikā* (one who is to be favored); and the meditation on the Supreme Self is for those who have attained the state of *anugrāhakabhūmikā* (one who is the favorer). Since the individual soul and the chief vital breath are dependent upon the Supreme Self, the indicative marks pertaining to them are also applicable to the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the subject. Furthermore, the word "all" (sarva) in the phrase "in all beings" does not mean every single thing, but rather refers to all living beings. This is because the context concerns the individual soul, and because the word "all" is used in a relative sense, just as when one says, "All the Brahmins have arrived. Moreover, the word "all" is used in a limited sense in other scriptural passages, such as "All this is indeed Brahman. Thus, the doubt is resolved. Furthermore, the statement "He who dwells in the eye" and so forth indicates that the individual soul is the subject, because it is described as having a specific location and size, and because attributes of the individual soul are predicated of it. Also, the statement "He who dwells in the earth" and so forth indicates that the chief vital breath is the subject, because it is described as having a specific location and size, and because attributes of the chief vital breath are predicated of it. “If it be said that [Brahman] is not [the subject of the passage] because of its having a small abode and because of the designation of that [individual soul], we say no, because it is to be perceived in this way, and like space. This is the meaning: “Because of its having a small abode,” since it is stated that the omnipresent reality has a small location in the form of the space within the hearts of all living beings; and “because of the designation of that,” because that [individual soul] is designated by means of scriptural texts, indicative marks, and so forth, and because it has been so described. If it be argued that Brahman alone is omnipresent and thus [the passage does not refer to Him], we say no. Why? Because it is to be perceived in this very manner, and because it is like space.

The phrase "because [the qualities] such as being the object of vision apply to Viṣṇu" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Nor is there any pointlessness [to these attributes], because He is to be meditated upon in this way—that is, because Viṣṇu alone is the object of meditation in the form of having a small abode and so forth. Thus, the sense is that there is no pointlessness. The intention is that there is no contradiction with those [scriptural passages], since the direct statements (śruti), indicative marks (liṅga), and so forth, have Brahman as their ultimate purport. To the question, "How can the all-pervading Viṣṇu reside in a small place?", it is said: "And like space. The meaning is that just as space, though all-pervading, resides in specific locations such as houses, so too does Viṣṇu.

And thus, the statement that the Lord—who is of an unlimited nature and so forth—dwells within a small space (the heart) would be either purposeless or illogical. It is not the first case, because there is a purpose for designating Him as the object of meditation in that form. Nor is it the second case, because even though the ether is all-pervading, a portion of it is seen to occupy a small space; and since He is non-different from that, it is logical that the Lord occupies a small space in His entirety, just as the ether does. Furthermore, since the Lord is the master of all the senses, it is also logical that He consists of the eye and so forth.

Nor is there a contradiction with the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of "not being mentioned" regarding the Sun; for since the state of residing in the Sun was already stated in the preceding passage, "And he who is that [Self] in the Sun," the claim of "not being mentioned" is unestablished. Therefore, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent.
If it be argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment [in the world of Brahman], we say no, because of the difference in nature.
Having raised the objection regarding the redundancy, he states the sūtra as a resolution:

"If it be argued that [Brahman] would experience [suffering], we say no, because of its distinction. This is the meaning: if it is argued that since Brahman, like space, resides within the bodies of all living beings, it would follow that it experiences enjoyment—that is, it would undergo identical experiences [of suffering]—and therefore, due to this objection, Brahman is not omnipresent; [we reply] "no. Why? Because of its distinction (*vaiśeṣyāt*), meaning because Viṣṇu possesses a specific, extraordinary capacity. Thus, the sense is that He does not undergo experiences identical to those of the individual soul (*jīva*).

And thus, because of the distinction between omniscience and limited knowledge, and due to the excellence of His power—just as there is an absence of burning for one who possesses the power to arrest fire—it is established that Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent, since equal enjoyment is not attained [by others].
Thus concludes the section on omnipresence.

In this [sūtra], the concordance of the mark of being the "eater" (attṛtva)—which is mentioned together with the word "iti" that is well-known elsewhere than in the worldly sense—is established with reference to Hari:
"The Eater, because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving."

[Objection: Let the quality of being the devourer—which is synonymous with being the destroyer, as mentioned in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 1.1.2)—belong to Aditi alone on the basis of the statement "whatever he [Aditi] eats" (*sa yadyadeva...*) and because of the irrefutable indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the direct scriptural mention (*śruti*) of Aditi. Nor can the scriptural mention of Aditi be interpreted as referring to Viṣṇu through the power of etymological derivation (*yoga*), since the indicative mark of being Aditi is otherwise without scope. Furthermore, there is no inconsistency regarding the masculine gender of the pronoun "he" (*sa*), for the masculine gender is appropriate here just as in such expressions as "the immutable (*akṣara*) is called the eternal one (*kūṭastha*)" because it is endowed with the power of the male (*puṃśakti*). This being the position reached, the author reads the Sūtra: sū || ādityānāmādityo 'ntaryāmīti vācyam | kutaḥ | taddharmavyapadeśāt | tasya paramātmano dharmāṇāṃ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāmabhyantaratvasarvādhipatitvādīnāṃ vyapadeśāt śravaṇāt || 20 || Sūtra: It must be stated that the Āditya among the Ādityas is the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*). Why? Because of the declaration of His attributes; that is, because of the scriptural declaration of the attributes of that Supreme Self, such as being within all beings and being the sovereign lord of all. || 20 || [Commentary: It must be stated that the Āditya among the Ādityas is the Inner Ruler. Why? Because of the declaration of His attributes. For the scriptural text declares the attributes of that Supreme Self—such as being within all beings and being the sovereign lord of all. Moreover, the scriptural mention of Aditi is not without scope, as it refers to the Supreme Self by way of metaphorical identification (*upacāra*), based on the fact that He is the cause of her existence. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the masculine gender, for the Supreme Self is designated as "He" (*sa*) because He possesses the power of the male, just as the term "He" is applied to the Immutable (*akṣara*) in the sense that it is the source of the power of the male. "The Eater [is Viṣṇu], because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: The Eater—who is called the "Eater of All" because he eats everything—is indeed Viṣṇu, and not Aditi. Why? Because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving; that is to say, because the scripture states that "all," consisting of the world of sentient and insentient beings (the moving and the unmoving), is the object to be eaten.

And thus, because the moving and the non-moving are grasped as being "eaten" (adana), there is no contradiction with the scriptural text regarding Aditi. This is because it can be established, on the strength of the scriptural text "He who is the name of the gods," that the mention of Aditi has Viṣṇu as its ultimate referent. Nor is there a contradiction with the indivisible attribute (akhaṇḍadharma) of being Aditi; for since Viṣṇu is also the object of the conventional usage among the learned (vidvad-ruḍhi), the indivisible attribute of being Aditi is necessarily present in him as well. Therefore, since Viṣṇu alone is the subject of this passage as the "Eater" (attṛ), it is established that the previously stated definition does not suffer from the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti).
And because of the context.

When it is established that the Eater is indeed Viṣṇu by the sublation of the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the "Eater of all" (sarvātṛtva), which has no other scope, by the indicative mark of being the "Eater of food" (annātṛtva) from the Śruti and so forth, which does have other scope—then what more need be said regarding the case where the indicative mark is conjoined with a context (prakaraṇa) that has no other scope? With this meaning, he recites the Sūtra which establishes the point.
"And because of the context. The meaning of this is: by the force of the context concerning Viṣṇu in the passage "There is nothing here whatsoever," the sense is that Viṣṇu alone must be the subject.

And thus, by the passage beginning with "In the beginning, there was nothing here at all" and "the creation of the year," and by the force of the context of Viṣṇu which leaves no room for another, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is [the subject].
Thus ends the section concerning the non-eater.
Here, the concordance of the mark consisting in being the enjoyer of the fruits of actions—well-known in the world as belonging to others—is established with respect to Viṣṇu.
"For the two selves have entered the cave, because that is seen [in scripture]."

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the statement of the sentence, "The two who drink the *ṛta*," two individual souls (*jīva*) are meant, and not the Supreme Lord alone? For the dual number is heard [in the text], and the dual number cannot apply to a single entity. And thus, like Indra (*hari*), the soul would also be an independent drinker; consequently, like him, it would also be the eater of all. Since there is no reason to deny this for an independent entity, there would therefore be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Alternatively: In the statement of that same sentence, the two refer to the soul and the Supreme Lord, because of the hearing of the dual number. Even so, the soul alone would be the drinker, and not the All-pervading Lord.

For one who is free from the bondage of karma, it is impossible to be a consumer of the fruits of karma. Nor does this contradict the statement that [the Supreme] is the "consumer of all" (*sarvāttṛ*), because such a contraction of meaning is possible when there is a conflict with the Śruti text, "Eating [yet] not eating, the other" (*anaśnannanyo*). Nor does it contradict the statement that "the two are drinking," for we accept that the status of being a drinker is applied figuratively according to the logic of the *chatri-nyāya* (the rule of the umbrella-bearers). If it is asked, "Even so, what is the reason for [one] being the individual soul (*jīva*) and [the other] the Lord (*īśvara*)?"—once the status of being the individual soul is established for one on the grounds that the status of being a drinker cannot otherwise be explained, the second must necessarily be understood as belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*).

Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be two living beings (jīvas), because it is impossible for two living beings who are enjoyers to exist within a single body. Therefore, only the living being and the Lord (jīveśau) can be accepted [as the subject and object of the "eater" metaphor]. Even so, since the living being alone is the eater, its "all-consuming nature"—which is intended as the defining characteristic—is impossible. Alternatively, let us assume again that there are indeed two living beings. Nor is there an impossibility of two living beings who are enjoyers in a single body, on the grounds that the existence of a living being about to be born in a body such as rice is established by other means of knowledge, yet that being lacks the status of an enjoyer. If this is argued, we say no.

Because, although there is an absence of being an enjoyer with respect to the limitation of that [individual] body, in reality the state of being an enjoyer exists; and thus, since God lacks the status of being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma, [the Lord] would be impossible—this being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"Indeed, the two selves have entered the cave, because of the vision thereof. This is its meaning: the word "tat" (that) follows by way of grammatical modification. The two "selves" (ātmānau)—derived from the etymology *ā-deya* (to be taken) and *mā-trī* (measurer), thus referring to those who drink the *ṛta*—are the enjoyers of the fruits of auspicious karma denoted by the word "drinkers" (*pibantau*) found in the scripture; they are the two forms of Viṣṇu known as the Inner Self (*antarātman*) and the Self (*ātman*). They are not, however, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Why? Because of the word "hi" (indeed); since those two have entered the cave, therefore [they are the two selves]. This is the sense.

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates the scriptural renown of the mark consisting in abiding in the cave, as expressed in the passage "he who knows. He states the proof for His abiding in the cave of the body in two forms with the words "because that is seen. The meaning is: because it is stated in scripture—specifically in the passage "His qualities are on all sides"—that Hari exists in the cave of the heart within the body in a twofold manner.

Furthermore, the two who are said to be "drinking" in this spoken passage are indeed forms of Viṣṇu, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having entered the cave. It should not be argued that this indicative mark does not establish their identity as Viṣṇu because it also applies to the individual soul (*jīva*); for the state of being hidden in the secret place is well-known to belong to the Lord (*Īśvara*), and what is well-known must be accepted [as the primary meaning]. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural mention of the dual number; for that is accommodated by intending two forms. And it is not the case that the presence of two forms is negated simply because they enter by means of each form individually.

The phrase "the dharmas are encompassed on all sides by the threefold" establishes that even within a single body, two distinct forms are indeed proven to exist. Nor does the acceptance of Viṣṇu as the drinker contradict such scriptural passages as "none other eats," for since Viṣṇu’s status as a drinker is established by the authority of the text "He drinks what is auspicious," that scripture refers specifically to the absence of the experience of the inauspicious. Furthermore, there is no impossibility of experiencing the fruits of karma for the Perfect One, as He is free from the bondage of karma.

Since enjoyment is possible by one's own will even when it does not occur as a matter of necessity, it is established that the definition of "eater" (attṛtva) characterized by the state of being a consumer is properly applicable to Viṣṇu alone as the eater.
And because of the qualification.

Since the mark (*liṅga*) of being situated in a cave that admits of no other possibility is stronger than even the dual-numbered *śruti* which does admit of other possibilities, and since it is possible for Viṣṇu to be the enjoyer who is the primary sense of the word "nature" (*prakṛti*), it is established that He alone is the protector (*pāti*). The author now cites the sūtra which establishes this meaning by showing that it is so even by means of an *śruti* that admits of no other possibility.

"And because of the qualification. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the arguments. Because of the qualification by the singular number in the phrase "He who is the bridge" (yaḥ setuḥ), there is only one protector. And since he is qualified by attributes such as being the bridge and being Brahman, the meaning is that he is Viṣṇu alone, not the individual soul (jīva).

And thus, it is established that those two who drink are indeed Viṣṇu not only by the force of the mark of "having entered the cave," but also because of the qualification in the Śruti text, "He who is the bridge for the sacrificers," by means of the singular words denoting Brahman. Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is the protector.
Thus concludes the section concerning the cave.
In this context, the mark of being "within" is harmonized with Brahman:
"On account of the appropriateness of what is within."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the fire mentioned in the passage 'This which is within the eye' must be the very same fire [referred to] by the statement 'This which is the sun,' since that [latter] declares the fire's residence in the sun? And even if the fire resides in the sun, why should it reside in the eye? For it is stated in scripture, 'The sun, having become the eye...'; moreover, because the eye and the sun are identical, the fire's residence in the eye is established through its residence in the sun. Furthermore, why should the fire be the one taught in the words 'I am He'? Because in this teaching, there are many scriptural references to fire. [Response: This is not so. The fire mentioned in the sentence "This which is within the eye" is indeed the one residing in the eye. Since the text "This which is the sun" identifies the very same fire as residing in the sun, and because the sun and the eye are non-different according to the Śruti, "The sun, having become the eye...", the fire's residence in the eye is proven by its residence in the sun. Nor can it be asked why the fire is the one taught in "I am He," for in this instruction, there exist numerous scriptural mentions of fire.

Nor can it be argued that Viṣṇu alone, residing in the sun, is meant by the force of the designation "He who is that," because the practice of identifying "I am He" is more powerful than mere designation; nor does the acceptance of Viṣṇu sublate the novelty of the teaching or the practice itself, since the statement "He who knows thus" is an explanatory praise (arthavāda), and an explanatory praise possesses greater authority regarding what is previously unknown. Thus, when it is concluded that Agni resides in the sun and from there resides in the eye, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But on account of the connection with what follows. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7) This means: But [the person in the eye is] the Self, because of the connection with what follows. For in the subsequent passage—"Now, he who knows this, when departing from this world, enters into this very self"—it is the supreme Self that is referred to as the object of entry. And the supreme Self is none other than the one whose nature is being taught here. Furthermore, the word "Self" is used in its primary sense for the supreme Self, whereas it is used in a secondary sense for the individual soul (jīva). Moreover, the phrase "I am He" is a statement of identity, and identity is possible only between two things of the same kind. Therefore, the person within the eye is the supreme Self. This is the meaning.

"Because of the appropriateness [of the attributes] in the intermediate space. This is the meaning of that [sūtra]: That which is called "the one within the eye" in the Śruti is indeed Viṣṇu residing within the eye, and not Agni. Why? Because of the appropriateness; for such qualities as immortality and the term "Brahman" are heard in reference to the one within the eye, and these are appropriate only for Viṣṇu—this is the sense.

And thus, because of the hearing of attributes such as immortality and fearlessness in the passage "and this is immortal and fearless," and because of the hearing of words such as "Brahman" and so forth, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the "inner eye."
And because of the designation of place and so forth.
He introduces a sūtra that establishes Viṣṇu’s presence within the eye by means of another argument.

"And because of the designation of its location and so forth. This is the meaning: because there is a designation of the power of the eye, which is the locus of Brahman, and of the power of Brahman that presides over it—as it is stated, "He pours either clarified butter or water"—the sense is that Viṣṇu alone is the one residing within the eye.

And thus, since it is stated in the Śruti that "He is either clarified butter or water" regarding the power of His abode (*sthāna-śakti*), and in the Caturvedaśikhā that "Vāmanī and Bhāmanī" regarding the power of His essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), and because these two powers cannot exist elsewhere, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one residing within the eye.
And also because of the very designation of [the state] as distinguished by happiness.
By the force of the context, he introduces the aphorism which establishes that the eye is situated within Viṣṇu.

"And also because of the mention of that which is distinguished by bliss. This is its meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. Because of the mention of that which is distinguished by bliss—that is, because of the mention of the supreme bliss (as opposed to the previously mentioned bliss) in passages such as "Kaṃ is Brahman"—Viṣṇu alone is the one within the eye. The sense is: how much more so [is it Viṣṇu] on account of the mention of perfect knowledge in the passage "What is Kha is Brahman"?

Thus, since this section is devoted to Viṣṇu—given that at the beginning it is heard that "Prāṇa is Brahman" and "Ka is Brahman," and because therein "Kha is Brahman" is designated as full bliss and full knowledge—the term [full] bliss intends infinite, absolute fullness of bliss. Since the primary meaning is possible, a secondary one is not appropriate; therefore, it is established that the one within the eye is indeed Viṣṇu.
And because there is a mention of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads.

But surely, even though pleasure and knowledge were mentioned at the beginning, it is not proper to conclude that the section concerning what is situated in the eye has Viṣṇu as its subject. For in the Chāndogya, after teaching the knowledge that "Prāṇa is Brahman" and the knowledge that "He who is in the sun," it is stated by the fires to Upakośala that "our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self have been taught"; thus, it is appropriate that the first [knowledge] concerns Viṣṇu and the second concerns Agni. Furthermore, the knowledge concerning what is within the eye—"He who is within the eye"—must have the same meaning as the knowledge concerning the sun.

Nor is there a contradiction with the opening statement; for that opening statement is consistent, just as in the case of "Invoke Agni, O Agni. Since the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā) has been mentioned separately, it is impossible for our present knowledge to have the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) as its object. Therefore, the conclusion reached was that the knowledge concerning what is within the eye has Agni as its subject matter. To this, the Sūtra states:

"And because of the mention of the path for those who have heard the Upaniṣads. This is its meaning: for men who have heard the Upaniṣads—that is, those by whom this knowledge has been heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon—by which [agent]? By Vāyu. Of which two? Of the effected Brahman and the Supreme Brahman. Because of the mention in the Śruti, "He leads them to Brahman," it follows that the one within the eye is indeed Viṣṇu alone. This is the sense.

And thus, by the statement "and so he [leads] them" in the concluding summary, since the knowledge (vidyā) residing in the eye has Viṣṇu as its object, and because it is impossible for one vidyā to result in the attainment of another, the Vaiṣṇava nature of this section is established.
"And because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other."

One might object: "By assuming that the instruction 'That thou art' and so forth refers to the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), Viṣṇu's presence in the eye would not be apprehended; why then could Agni's presence in the eye not likewise follow from the force of the instruction itself? To this, the author recites the sūtra, providing the resolution that it is because of the existence of a subverting argument (bādhaka).

"Because of non-abiding and because of impossibility, it is not the other. This is the meaning of the sūtra: "The other" refers to Agni. The internal eye is not Agni, but Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of non-abiding: if the individual soul (jīva) Agni were the controller of another individual soul, then since that [second] soul would likewise be no different from a soul, one would have to admit yet another controller for him, and for him yet another; thus there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). Furthermore, it is impossible for a soul such as Agni to be the controller of another soul. This is the meaning.

And thus, since it is impossible for fire to be the controller by virtue of being a living soul (jīva), there is no possibility of its being located within the eye. Or, even if such a possibility were somehow admitted, fire should not be accepted as residing within the eye; for if fire were a living soul, another living soul would have to exist to impel it, and for that one as well, and for that one as well—thus there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, Viṣṇu alone, abiding in the eye and the sun, is the object of perception; hence, He alone is the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), and it is established that liberation arises from the knowledge of Him alone.
Thus ends the section concerning the intermediate state.
In this context, the *liṅga* (inferential mark) consisting of the activity of internal control, accompanied by the state of being situated within, is shown to be consistently applicable to Brahman:
"The Inner Ruler with respect to the gods and so forth, because of the designation of His attributes."

Is it not the case that *prakṛti* itself is the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*), because of the designation of having the earth and so forth as its body in the passage beginning with "of whom the earth"? For the word "body" is seen to be used even for one's own essential nature, and thus its application there is justified. Nor is there a contradiction with the statement "he who is in the earth," etc., which speaks of abiding within the earth and so forth; for it is said that "the cause pervades the effects," and thus its presence there is logical. Furthermore, it is not impossible for *prakṛti* to be the regulator of the earth and so forth, despite its insentience.

Since an effect is dependent upon its cause, it is logical to figuratively attribute the status of a controller even to the conscious primordial nature (prakṛti). Nor is there any contradiction with its immortality; for that [immortality] can be established here through metaphorical application (yoga), just as it is in the case of Viṣṇu. Alternatively, this state of being the inner controller (antaryāmitva) may belong to those respective individual souls (jīvas), since it is very easy to establish for them the possession of bodies such as the earth and so forth. Consequently, since the immortality heard in that context belongs to the inner controller of activity and the like, it does not prove that the one residing in the eye is Viṣṇu. To this, the Sūtra states: [The answer: This is not so, because of the mention of "immortality" and other attributes. For immortality and the rest are not possible in the case of the individual soul or the primordial nature. Even if the immortality were attributed to the inner controller who is a soul, it would still not be possible for the soul to be the inner controller of the earth and so forth, because it is impossible for a soul to have the earth and the rest as its body. Furthermore, the immortality mentioned in the text is not merely figurative, because it is connected with the term "Self" (ātman); for the word "Self" is never used in a figurative sense. Moreover, the immortality is not merely relative, because it is stated in connection with the phrase "not trembling at anything. Therefore, it is established that the one residing in the eye is indeed Viṣṇu. || 1.2.8 || [Sūtra 1.2.8] || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 || || 1.2.8 ||
