"Antaryāmin (the Inner Ruler) [is Viṣṇu] because His attributes are designated in the sections concerning the deities and so forth. This is the meaning: The Antaryāmin spoken of in the scripture as "This is your Self, the Antaryāmin," is indeed Viṣṇu and not the Pradhāna or others. Why? Because in the sections concerning the deities, the self, and the elements—namely, the *adhidaiva*, *adhyātma*, and *adhibhūta* contexts—His attributes are designated; that is to say, because the attributes of Brahman, such as being unknown, which are stated in the scripture regarding that Antaryāmin in the passage "Whom the earth does not know," are designated there. This is the sense.
And thus, because the qualities designated as "inner" (antara) are unknown to the deities of the earth and so forth, it is established that the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
And it is not based on Smṛti, because there is no mention of its specific characteristics.

Having thus established Viṣṇu’s status as the inner controller (antaryāmin) by means of an argument that leaves no room for alternative interpretations, the Sūtra now states a verse which, through reasoning, refutes the possibility of Prakṛti and others being the inner controller—a position shared by both the proponents of Prakṛti and those of the individual soul (jīva).

"And it is not the Smārta [Pradhāna], because its characteristics are not mentioned. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of conjunction. "Smārta" refers to that which is stated in the Smṛti of Kapila; it is neither the Pradhāna nor the individual soul (jīva) who is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī). Why? Because its characteristics are not mentioned—that is, because the characteristics of the Pradhāna and the individual soul, such as consisting of the three guṇas, being subject to saṃsāra, and so forth, are not stated. This is the meaning.

Thus, since there is no mention of attributes such as being the material cause, the state of being the Pradhāna, the nature of having the three guṇas, or being subject to transmigratory existence—attributes which are unique to Kapila’s Smṛti and not shared by Viṣṇu, just as there is no mention of attributes like being the earth or being unknown which are unique to Viṣṇu—it is established that the Inner Controller is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
For both the bodily [self] and the other are indeed distinguished from this [Self].

Although the soul's status as an inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) has already been refuted by the absence of evidence to establish it, the author introduces the following sūtra to refute it once more by means of a specific argument termed a "refutation" (*bādhaka*).

"And the embodied one, for both [recensions] read of him as distinct. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to draw forward the negative particle (nañ). "For" (hi) means because. "Both" refers to the Mādhyandinas and the Kāṇvas. They read of this [one], namely the individual soul (jīva), as distinct—that is, as different—from the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin), using the words "the inner one from the Self," "the inner one from consciousness," and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that the embodied one, the individual soul, is not the Inner Ruler.

Thus, since both schools teach the individual soul (*jīva*) as distinct from Brahman—by stating "the Self is within" and "it is within"—it is established that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is indeed Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī).
Here, the mark known as the absence of visibility and so forth is shown to be consistently applicable to Brahman:
"That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the mention of its attributes."

Now, one might object: that which is described as having the qualities of being "unseen" and so forth is not Viṣṇu, but rather the insentient *prakṛti*. For the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is heard in the passage, "From the Akṣara it is born. Nor is the term "akṣara" applicable to Viṣṇu, because what is higher than it is subsequently mentioned; and there is nothing higher than Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the status of being the cause of the world through its nature as material cause (*upādāna*) is declared by means of the analogies of the earth and other elements. Thus, these qualities such as being "unseen" belong only to the conscious *prakṛti*, for the application of the word "akṣara" to her is established by the Smṛti in the sense of the "immutable" (*kūṭastha*).

The statement that the cause of the world is subject to modification is appropriate because [Hiraṇyagarbha] identifies with those modifications. Furthermore, the phrase "beyond the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ*) is also justified through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "beyond the Imperishable. Alternatively, this invisibility and so forth belong to Hiraṇyagarbha, because of the word "Brahman" in the passage beginning with "that knowledge of Brahman" (*sā brahmavidyā*). Or else, this invisibility and so forth belong to Rudra, because of the hearing of the word "Lord" (*īśa*) in the passage "the maker, the Lord" (*kartāram īśam*). This being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"Because of the mention of attributes such as invisibility, [it is] He who possesses those qualities. This is the meaning: He who possesses attributes such as invisibility—that is, Viṣṇu alone, denoted by the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) as qualified by the attributes of invisibility and so forth mentioned in the scripture, "That which is invisible"—and not *prakṛti* (primordial matter) or anything else. Why? Because of the mention of attributes; that is to say, because the attribute of being the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures, which is a characteristic of Viṣṇu, is stated in the scripture, "By whom... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6).

And thus, since it is stated in the subsequent section that the one possessing qualities such as invisibility is the subject of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one possessing qualities such as invisibility.
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two.

Now, one might object: "Since there exist [scriptural passages] that lead to the inert Prakṛti, as well as those leading to Viriñca (Brahmā) and Rudra—just as there are those leading to Viṣṇu as the subject of the higher knowledge (paravidyā)—why could these [latter] not also possess qualities such as being 'unseen' (adṛśyatva) and so forth? To this, the author recites the Sūtra, refuting the objection with a specific argument: sūtraṃ paṭhati || [The author recites the Sūtra.]

"And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, the two others are not [the cause]. This is the meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction. "The two others" refers to the two sources of origin, namely Viriñca (Brahmā) and Rudra. They do not possess qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*) and so forth. Why? Because of the distinction and the designation of difference. In the two propositions, each reason is applied respectively. "He who is omniscient" is because of the distinction [of attributes] such as omniscience; and "from that, this [was produced]" is because of the statement of the difference between the Imperishable (*akṣara*) characterized by invisibility and the other two, Viriñca and Rudra. Thus is the meaning.

And thus, because there is an absence of the attributes such as omniscience—which are incompatible with being insentient primordial matter (*jaḍaprakṛti*)—there is no possibility [of this being Prakṛti]; because there is an absence of the designation of difference—which is incompatible with being Brahmā (Viriñci) expressed by "this from that" (*tasmādetat*); and because there is an absence of the designation of Rudra-ness—which is incompatible with "when he sees another who is adored" (*juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyatyanyam*). Nor should it be said that Viṣṇu is not [the one referred to] because of the mention of "that which is beyond the beyond" (*parataḥ para*), for since the name consists of three syllables—"the other" (*aparam*), "indeed" (*tu*), and "the imperishable" (*akṣaram*)"—it is possible for it to mean "beyond" in the sense of being beyond the middle syllable; thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one possessing qualities such as invisibility.
And because of the presentation of form.
He introduces the sūtra which, by means of another scriptural passage, establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the qualities of being invisible and so forth.

"And because of the presentation of form. The meaning of this is as follows: since the text "when the seer sees" presents a golden form that is unique to Viṣṇu, the sense is that He alone, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, is the one intended.

And thus, because the unique golden form of Viṣṇu is established here, and because it has been stated in the passage "Nārāyaṇa is one" that forms such as white and so forth are mixed [with others] in humans and the like, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is the one characterized by qualities such as invisibility.
Thus ends the section concerning invisibility (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa).

In this context, the application of the name Vaiśvānara to Brahman is established for the purpose of proving the consistent application of numerous marks, such as being the "Cook" (pācaka) and so forth.
Vaiśvānara [is Brahman], because of the distinction of a common term.

Now, it may be argued that this Vaiśvānara is not Viṣṇu, because he lacks the supporting evidence (sādhaka) [for being Viṣṇu]. This is because the mark (liṅga) of omnipresence is sublated by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) regarding Vaiśvānara, which is well-known to refer to something else. Nor can it be said that the scripture is sublated by the mark on the grounds that the mark has no other scope (niravakāśatva); for the scripture, too, has no other scope. Since the Vaiśvānara-śruti lacks any sublatant proof and is common to both Agni and Viṣṇu, it does not determine anything else. Thus, the prima facie conclusion (pūrva-pakṣa) being that Vaiśvānara is not Viṣṇu, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] so [stated] because of the teaching of the measure. (1.2.7)

"Vaiśvānara [is Viṣṇu] because of the distinction of a common term. This is the meaning of the sūtra. Vaiśvānara—that which is denoted by the word "Vaiśvānara" and so forth occurring in the passage beginning with "He who [knows] this"—is Viṣṇu alone, and not Agni. Why? Because of the distinction of a common term. The meaning is that the word "Vaiśvānara," which is common to both Agni and Viṣṇu, is specified by the word "Self" (ātman) in the Śruti text, "The Self, Vaiśvānara."

And thus, although the word *vaiśvānara* is common [to many], it can be established as referring to Viṣṇu alone because it is qualified by the word *ātman* in the passage "the Self, Vaiśvānara," which is proven by Śruti and other authorities; since well-known usage and the like can be explained otherwise, there is no cause for a definitive conclusion [other than this]. Therefore, due to the specific word—the word *ātman*—it is established that Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu.
"That which is being remembered would be an inference."

Now, it might be argued that it is not tenable to say that this Vaiśvānara is Viṣṇu alone, because of the contradiction with grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), since there exists evidence establishing his nature as Agni just as there is evidence establishing his nature as Viṣṇu. To this objection, the author states the Sūtra:

"Smṛyamāṇamanumānaṃ syāditi"—the meaning of this is as follows: "Thus being remembered" refers to Viṣṇu’s status as Vaiśvānara, which was stated in the passage, "I indeed became Vaiśvānara. "Anumānam" means it serves as an inference; that is, it would be the inferential proof for the fact that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā has the Blessed Lord as its object, as stated in the Gītā. This is the sense.

And thus, since the Gītā Smṛti takes the form of a statement equating itself with the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it serves as a decisive authority due to this common designation; therefore, it is established that Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the one taught here] because of its being established within sound and so forth, we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [the other sense-objects] are impossible [therein], and they also study this [Self] as being of the form of a person.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "O Immortal, [I praise] Agni Vaiśvānara, the unborn"—thus, the word *agni* is applied to Vaiśvānara. Furthermore, because there is the scriptural mention of the marks of fire, such as "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire," and because of the mention of his being the internal abode through his nature as the cooker (as in "by whom this food is cooked"), these [marks] find no place in Viṣṇu. Having thus raised an objection against Vaiśvānara being Viṣṇu, the author states the sūtra to provide a resolution.

"Because of the word [Vaiśvānara] and so forth, and because of his abiding within, it is not [Viṣṇu]; if this is argued, we say no, because of the teaching of viewing Him as such, because of impossibility, and because they study Him also as being of human form. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of combining arguments. "Because of the word and so forth" means because of the word [Vaiśvānara], and because of the indicative marks such as being the locus of the oblation (the fire). "Because of his abiding within" means because he dwells inside the body as the digestive fire. If it is argued that Vaiśvānara is not Viṣṇu but rather Agni alone, we say no. Why? Because of the teaching of viewing Him as such.

The meaning is that because Agni and the others are taught as objects of meditation (upāsana) by virtue of possessing characteristics and functions [associated with them], such as being fire; thus, since the scriptural mentions and indicative marks (liṅga) of Agni and the others find their scope in Viṣṇu, there is no contradiction with Him—this is the sense. Furthermore, Vaiśvānara must be Viṣṇu alone, because the attributes of being the Self (ātmatva) and being Brahman mentioned here are impossible in Agni and the others. Moreover, the Chāndogas study this Vaiśvānara as "having the form of a person" (puruṣavidha), meaning they declare Him to possess the very same qualities as Nārāyaṇa, who is expounded in the Puruṣasūkta.
The meaning is that for this reason as well, it is Viṣṇu alone; by the word "ca" (and), he indicates that the Puruṣasūkta's focus on Viṣṇu is established by many authorities.

And thus, because in the *Mahopaniṣad*—through such passages as "He who has all names" and "He who performs all actions"—the instruction is given for the practice of viewing [the Self] through those respective names and marks; because the inquiry begins with Viṣṇu alone in the words "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"; and because in the passage beginning with "The moon was born from the mind," Vaiśvānara is declared to possess that same nature; therefore, it is established that Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu.
Therefore, it is neither a deity nor a living being.

Now, since the word *vaiśvānara* is well-known to denote both the element fire (*tejas*) and the deity Agni, it might be argued that here too it must refer to those; in order to refute this, he presents the following sūtra.

"Therefore, it is neither the deity nor the elemental being. This is its meaning: the deity is that which has the form of Agni and so forth; and the elemental being is the element of fire (tejas) presided over by that deity. Neither of these is denoted by the word Vaiśvānara. Why? "For this very reason," meaning for the same reasons already stated, such as the presence of the term *ātman* (Self), which would have no other scope [if applied to either of those].
And thus, since the word "Self" (ātman) is heard here without any other possible application, it is established that the one denoted by the word Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu alone.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception.

Now, since it is observed in both worldly usage and the Veda that words such as "Agni" and others are commonly employed to denote things other than the Lord (Īśa), and since there is no other cause for this usage, one must admit that these words have other denotations because their application [to the Lord] would otherwise be inexplicable; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. This being the prima facie view, the author explains the Sūtra in order to refute it.

"Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even in the direct [sense]. This is its meaning: "Directly" means in the primary sense (*mukhyavṛttyā*). "Even" (*api*) means even though Brahman is denoted by words such as "fire" (*agni*) and so forth. "No contradiction" (*avirodham*) means the absence of any contradiction regarding those respective words in relation to fire and so forth, due to other causes such as ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like. The meaning is that the teacher Jaimini declares this.

Thus, although words such as "fire" (agni) do not denote Brahman in the same way that [the word "Brahman"] does, they are nonetheless used by those who are proficient for the sake of conveying knowledge of fire and so forth elsewhere. However, because those who are unproficient employ these words in their primary sense—namely, fire and the like—due solely to their ignorance of the Lord, who is the supreme primary referent, the establishment of their conventional usage is justified; therefore, words such as "fire" are denoters of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, there is no mutual contradiction between the views of Jaimini and others and the view of Vyāsa.

In relation to the great space known as *jñāna*—which resides within the mind of Vyāsa and is synonymous with *matā* (the doctrine)—certain thinkers such as Jaimini and others employ their respective systems by accepting limited objects such as space delimited by houses and the like. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that [these views arise] "from the space residing in the mind of Vyāsa. Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction among those doctrines.
"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya.

[Objection: Granted that worldly convention may be explained otherwise because it is rooted in ignorance and so forth; nevertheless, since the Vedic conventions regarding hymns (*sūkta*), mantras, and the like concerning Agni and others cannot be explained otherwise, Agni and the rest must indeed be the referents of the words "Agni" and so on occurring in those hymns and mantras. For in that case, it is impossible to assume a root in ignorance, as there is no other way to explain it. Nor can it be explained otherwise on the grounds that it serves merely for practical usage (*vyavahāra*), because such usage is beginningless (*anāditva*). This being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"Because of manifestation, so says Āśmarathya. This is its meaning: because of manifestation—that is, when the meditation on Brahman has been performed upon fire and the other [deities], Brahman becomes manifest within them; therefore, the restriction to the hymns (sūktas) of fire and the others is caused by that manifestation—this is what the teacher Āśmarathya maintains.

And thus, since the recitation of specific hymns (*sūkta*) is possible for worshippers through the manifestation of the Lord within Agni and other deities by means of the *Agnisūkta* and so forth, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the words "Agni" and the rest. Consequently, it is established that there is no contradiction according to the view of the teacher Āśmarathya.
Bādari [maintains that the soul's ascent] is due to remembrance.
He introduces the aphorism which explains the alternative justification for the rule regarding the *sūkta* and so forth, by stating it in another way:

"Because of remembrance, Bādari [says so]. This is its meaning: because of remembrance—that is, because of the continuous contemplation by those who worship the respective hymns (*sūkta*) and so forth upon Agni and the other deities alone—the cause being this remembrance—Bādari declares that there is a fixed distribution (*vyavasthā*) according to the hymns dedicated to Agni and the others. This is the sense.

Thus, since Viṣṇu is to be remembered within Agni and the other deities by those who worship them through the hymns (sūktas) dedicated to Agni and the rest, the application of these specific hymns is possible; therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words "Agni" and so forth. Consequently, it remains settled that this does not contradict the view of Śukācārya, the son of Badara.
"Jaimini [holds that the fruit arises] from attainment, for thus the scripture shows."
He explains the sūtra, which demonstrates that the restriction regarding the hymns can be accounted for otherwise through a different method.

"Because of attainment, Jaimini [says so], for thus the scripture shows. This is its meaning: "hi" means because; for there is a well-known scriptural passage, "As that [is]," which shows in such a way—that is, it establishes the view of Jaimini. Therefore, Jaimini, in accordance with the scripture favorable to his own statement, says that due to "attainment"—meaning the cause for the attaining of Agni and others by those who meditate on the hymns (sūkta) dedicated to Agni and others—there is a restriction regarding the hymns and so forth, intended to express that very attainment. This is the meaning.

Thus, even though in the Agni-sūkta and other such hymns the Supreme Brahman alone is primarily the subject to be propounded, the restriction of these specific hymns is nevertheless appropriate; for those who worship the Lord attain [the status of] Agni and the other deities. Therefore, Jaimini considers that there is no contradiction with worldly usage. Consequently, it is established that the restriction of the hymns must be accepted.
And they record this [Self] in this [body].

Now, an objection may be raised: it is not proper to say that a worshiper of Brahman attains Agni and the other deities through the hymns (sūktas) dedicated to Agni and others; for, as stated in passages such as "My devotees go [to Me]," it is illogical for a worshiper of one thing to attain something else, and because this [attainment of others] was not accepted in the Sūtra [3.3.34], "On account of scriptural statement" (*śruteḥ*). To this, the author states the following Sūtra:

"And they enjoin Him in this [fire], etc."—the meaning of this is as follows: the word "ca" (and) serves to remove doubt. Because they enjoin this Viṣṇu in the fire and other elements—scriptural texts such as "He who dwells in the fire" (*yo 'gnau tiṣṭhan*) and others establish Him as residing therein—therefore, the doubt as to how the attainment of the fire and so forth can result from the worship of Viṣṇu in the fire and other elements is removed. Why? Because by the words "fire" and so forth, what is intended is precisely the attainment of the Blessed Lord residing therein; such is the meaning.

And thus, since it is intended that those who worship various specific hymns (*sūkta*) attain Viṣṇu—who is contained within those [deities] such as Agni—by means of the words "Agni" and so forth, it is illogical to state that a worshipper of Viṣṇu attains Agni and the others. Nor is it unestablished that Viṣṇu is contained within Agni and the rest, for there is the scriptural text beginning with, "He who dwells in fire... Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the words "Agni" and so forth.
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.
Śrī.
Hari.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
In this [section], the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of words well-known in both [Brahman and other things] with Viṣṇu is generally performed.
Here, the mark (*liṅga*) of being the substratum of all, which is well-known in both [contexts], is reconciled with Brahman:
"The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, because of its own word."

[Objection: Might not Rudra alone be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth? For the quality of being the support of the vital breaths (prāṇas), mentioned here, is perceived in him through such texts as "Thou art the knot of the prāṇas"; and because the quality of being the abode of the mind is stated in him alone by "The mind is woven [in him]"; and because he is perceived as the Lord of the prāṇas through the mark of being their support, as in "He is the Lord of the prāṇas. Or, it might be the individual soul (jīva), since marks of the jīva are perceived in him by such texts as "This one moves within. This being the position reached, the author presents the Sūtra.

"The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Viṣṇu], because of the word 'Self'. This is its meaning: The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—in which all things such as heaven and earth mentioned in the scriptural passage have their support—is Viṣṇu alone, and not anyone else. Why? Because of the word "Self" (*sva-śabdāt*). "Sva-śabda" means the word "Self" (*ātman*); that is to say, because of the word "Self," which denotes Brahman as grasped by the term "Self."
And thus, because of the use of the word "Self" in the phrase "that very one Self," it is established that Viṣṇu is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated.

Now, an objection may be raised: even though the word "Self" (ātman) primarily denotes Viṣṇu, in the passage "like the spokes in the nave of a wheel," it possesses the characteristic mark of a living being (jīva)—namely, the state of being born in many ways. Since its status as a living being is established by that very fact, it follows that the living being alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. To this, the author reads the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the Self] is Brahman, on account of the designation of the quarters and so forth. (1.3.1) This means: although the word "Self" primarily denotes Viṣṇu, in the passage "like the spokes in the nave of a wheel," it is not the living being that is intended, because of the designation of the quarters and so forth. For the quarters and so forth are designated as being within Him, and they cannot exist within a living being. Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman alone. Thus, the prima facie view having been stated, the Sūtra is recited.

"Because of the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated. This is its meaning: The state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth belongs not to anyone other than Viṣṇu, but to Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated (*muktopasṛpya*). This [term] emphasizes the state [of being]. The meaning is that because it is stated—by the words "this is the bridge to the immortal"—that the reality which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is to be reached by the liberated, and because such a thing is impossible in any other [deity].

Thus, it is established that Viṣṇu is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, because of statements such as "He is the bridge to immortality" and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," which declare that He is the goal to be reached by the liberated.
There is no inference from this, because of the word "not-that."

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since there exist means of attaining Rudra and Prakṛti just as there are means of attaining Viṣṇu, it follows that these two also should be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. To this, the author reads the Sūtra:

"Nor is it inference, because of the absence of words denoting that. This is the meaning: "Inference" (anumāna) means either the act of inferring or that which is established through inference. It refers to the Pāśupata and other scriptures whose authority is established by inference, wherein Rudra, Pradhāna, and so forth are postulated as the support of all things, such as the abode of heaven, earth, and so on. Why? Because of the absence of words denoting that; that is to say, because there is an absence of scriptural words and indicative marks (liṅga) such as the wearing of ashes, ferocity, and the like.

And thus, since words such as "Rudra" and others have other possible referents (sāvakāśatva), they cannot establish that the statement beginning with "of the vital breaths" (prāṇānām) refers to Rudra; furthermore, there is an absence of words like "ash-bearer" (bhasmadhara) or "fierce one" (ugra) which would have no other possible referent (niravakāśa). Consequently, it is established that Viṣṇu is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
And [the word] "living being" (prāṇabhṛt) [is also used].

Now, an objection may be raised: since in the passage "He who is this" (*sa eṣa*) there is heard the mark of the individual soul (*jīva*) consisting in its being born, and because the state of being a living being is established; and since it is heard that the support of the world which is the object—expressed in the words "By air, O Gautama, as by a thread, is this world [held together]" (*vāyunā vai gautama sūtreṇāyaṃ lokaḥ*)—resides in air, it follows that air might be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. To this, the author presents the Sūtra.
"And because [the Self] is a living being": the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) also, for this very reason, is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

And thus, even though there exist proofs with scope that were mentioned previously, it is established that neither the individual soul nor the vital air (vāyu) can be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; for while the scriptural passage beginning with "not being born" (*ajāyamāna*)—which is intended to establish that [abode]—is possible only in reference to Viṣṇu, the word "Self" (*ātman*), which has no other scope, is absent [in those passages]. Therefore, the status of being the abode of heaven, earth, etc., does not belong to the individual soul or the vital air.
Because there is a designation of difference.

Now, one might object: "What is the use of the effort to establish that the individual soul (jīva) is Viṣṇu? For even if the individual soul alone were the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, Viṣṇu would still be attained through that [attainment]. Nor is there a contradiction with the reasons already stated; since the word 'Self' (ātman) and other terms can be appropriately applied to the individual soul as well, with the intention of asserting the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord, it follows that the individual soul itself must be the one propounded as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. To this, the Sūtra states:

"Because of the designation of difference. This is its meaning: the sense is that because of the statement of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśa) in the words "another Lord," there is no identity between them.

And thus, since in the passage "When he sees the one being served... the individual soul under discussion is designated as distinct from the Lord denoted by the word Īśa by virtue of being the agent of seeing, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one propounded as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Because of the context.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Is it not the case that the individual soul (jīva) is said to be different from some Lord, but not from the Supreme Self (paramātman)? Therefore, there is no difference between the two. Anticipating this, the author states the aphorism as a refutation:

"Because of the context" (prakaraṇāt). This is its meaning: because the passage beginning with "another" (anyam) and so forth occurs within the context of Viṣṇu; here, only the difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Viṣṇu is stated, and not the difference [of the soul] from something else—this is the sense.

And thus, since the subject matter of "two kinds of knowledge" (*dve vidye*) is studied here as the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), and because this constitutes a context concerning Viṣṇu, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, as the designation of difference is understood to refer to the Supreme Self alone.
And on account of abiding and eating.

Thus, it is understood that not only from the scriptural text "the one who is enjoyed" (*juṣṭam*)—which expresses a distinction—is the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) intended in this context, but also from an indicative mark (*liṅga*); so says the author of the Sūtras.

"And by [the reasons of] abiding and eating" (sthityadanābhyām). The meaning of this is as follows: it must not be asserted that there is identity between the Lord (Īśa) and the individual soul (jīva), based on two reasons stated in such passages as "Two birds... (dvā suparṇā), namely, the Lord's non-participation in the fruits of action while abiding [in the same tree], and the soul's participation in those fruits while eating [them]. This is the sense.

And thus, since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) is established by the scripture cited above, it is proven that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not the individual soul, but Viṣṇu alone.
Thus concludes the section concerning heaven, earth, and so forth.
Here, the concordance of the name "Bhūman" with Viṣṇu is established:
"Bhūman [is Viṣṇu], because of the instruction following from the state of supreme serenity."

[Objection: It might be the vital breath (prāṇa) called Bhūman; for after stating that the prāṇa is the highest, the text does not mention anything higher than it, as the Bhūman is what is taught [therein]. Furthermore, because of the hearing of the mark of departure in the passage, "The prāṇas having departed, [he pierced him] with a spear," this mark cannot apply to Viṣṇu, since He is all-pervading. Moreover, the word "prāṇa" denotes air (vāyu). Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is also that very same [air]. To this, he presents the aphorism: *na vaktur ātmopadeśād iti cedadhyātmasambandhabhūmā hy asmin.* (1.1.29) [Response: It is not so, because of the teaching of the Self by the Speaker; for in this [text], there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections. (1.1.29) This means: It is not the case that the one consisting of bliss is the vital breath. Why? Because of the teaching of the Self by the Speaker. For the Speaker here is Nārada, who is the speaker of the knowledge of Brahman. And the teaching of the Self by him occurs thus: "He who knows the Self as 'I am He'... and so forth. Nor can the vital breath be the Self, because it is subject to transmigration. Furthermore, there is an abundance of internal connections in this [text], such as "He who knows the Self as 'I am He' attains all worlds and all desires. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the Supreme Self. Thus, the doubt regarding the one consisting of bliss being the vital breath is refuted. Furthermore, the vital breath is not the highest, because it is mentioned immediately after the statement of the prāṇa's supremacy, and because the mark of departure is heard in the passage, "The prāṇas having departed, [he pierced him] with a spear. Nor is this mark applicable to Viṣṇu, due to His omnipresence. And the word "prāṇa" primarily denotes air. Consequently, the conclusion was reached that the one consisting of bliss is also that very same [air]. To this, he presents the aphorism. (Note: The provided text contains a portion of the commentary on *Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.29.)

"Because of the teaching that [He] is superior to the state of perfect serenity. This is the meaning: In the scriptural passage, "The Bhūman, verily, is bliss," the one denoted by the word *bhūman*—the Full—is Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the teaching of His being the state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*), for it is stated in the text, "That is His bliss," that He is of the nature of full bliss denoted by the term *saṃprasāda*. Furthermore, because of the teaching of superiority; that is to say, because the *bhūman* is designated as being higher than even Name and the rest, as the most excellent among the deities presiding over Name and so forth.

And thus, this Bhūman is indeed Viṣṇu, because he possesses full bliss and because [the quality of fullness] has no other scope. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that this Bhūman is taught as being above all; nor does it have scope elsewhere. Nor should it be asked how this can be Viṣṇu given the hearing of the word "prāṇa" at the beginning, for Viṣṇu is also denoted by the word "prāṇa. Nor is there any contradiction with the marks such as "departing" (utkramaṇa) and so forth, since its primary application to Viṣṇu alone is established by the scriptural text, "Him who has departed" (tam utkrāntam).

Alternatively, this "prāṇa" may indeed be the wind; nevertheless, it does not attain the status of being the "Full" (bhūman). For, by supplying the missing questions and so forth indicated by the words "But he [said]... and so on, the text declares that Viṣṇu is greater than prāṇa, since the "Full" is subsequently taught. Furthermore, because Viṣṇu is designated as the supreme among all things beginning with Name, it is established that the "Full" is Viṣṇu alone.
And because of the logical consistency of Dharma.
He recites the sūtra which establishes the all-pervasiveness (bhūmatva) of Viṣṇu by means of another argument.

"And because of the occurrence of attributes" (dharmopapatti). This is its meaning: because attributes such as omnipresence are heard in the passage beginning with "That indeed is below," and because those [attributes] can belong to Viṣṇu alone; the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the Infinite (bhūman).

And thus, since Viṣṇu, who is within the wind, is denoted by the word "prāṇa," it is like the case where, in the passage "From the Self, space [was produced]," although the word "saṃbhūta" (produced) denotes the production of the nature of the elemental body presiding over that [space], it also denotes the manifestation of the connection with a body for Hari, the one who presides over it; likewise, even though the passage "The Infinite (bhūman) is indeed superior to prāṇa" denotes the superiority of the Infinite's own nature, [it also denotes its superiority over others].

Because it is possible for the term "Bhūman" (the Infinite) to be applied to the subtlest form within the air—characterized by its state of being oriented toward clarity—and because it is thus possible for it to withstand the questions and answers [of the text]; furthermore, attributes such as omnipresence and so forth are heard in the scripture regarding Bhūman in the passage beginning with "He alone is below. These [attributes] find no place elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no other possibility for these qualities such as omnipresence, it is established that Bhūman is indeed Viṣṇu, and that he alone is the one whose nature consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
Thus concludes the section concerning the Infinite.
Here, the coordination of the name "Akṣara" is established:
"The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports that which ends with the ether."

But surely this middle *akṣara* is none other than the *Śrītattva*, because of the scriptural statement, "It is unseen" (*adṛṣṭam*), and because its status as the substratum of the moon, sun, and so forth—understood through the passage beginning with "I am Soma"—is known to be an attribute of that [Śrītattva], and because the *akṣara* is perceived through the passage beginning with "The sun and the moon. And it should not be argued: "If the *akṣara* is called the *Śrītattva* on the strength of being the substratum of the moon, sun, and so forth—which are well-known as marks (*liṅga*) of the *Śrītattva*—then why should it not be Viṣṇu himself on the strength of invisibility (*adṛśyatva*) and other qualities which are well-known as marks of Viṣṇu? [This objection is invalid.]

As for the attributes such as "unseen-ness" (adṛśyatva), they have scope elsewhere because of the statement, "the imperishable (akṣara) is indefinable," and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "Since there is equality between the middle and the highest imperishables regarding the scriptural mention of 'imperishable' (akṣara) and the marks such as 'unseen-ness,' what is the reason for determining that only the middle one is spoken of here? For it is stated of this imperishable, "it eats nothing at all" (na tadaśnāti kiṃcana); and that is contradictory to Viṣṇu, since it has been stated [in the scripture] that "He is the eater, because of His grasping of the moving and the unmoving. However, there is no contradiction in accepting the non-eating of the middle imperishable. Thus, when it is reached that this imperishable is indeed the middle Śrī-tattva, the Sūtra states: [The answer: It is not so, because of the mention of the eating [of food]. (1.2.9) It is not the case that the imperishable mentioned here is the middle one; rather, it is the highest. Why? Because of the mention of eating. For it is said: "That which is the eater of all beings, whose own body all beings are, who controls all this from within—that is the imperishable, that is the Brahman, that is the True, that is called the Self" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.4). And eating is impossible for the middle imperishable. Therefore, this is the highest imperishable. Furthermore, the word "imperishable" (akṣara) is primarily applied to the highest, as in the passage: "Higher than the imperishable is the Supreme Being" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2). Moreover, the attributes such as "unseen-ness" are more appropriate for the highest, as they are described as being beyond the reach of speech and mind, etc. Nor is there any reason to restrict the meaning to the middle one, for the mention of eating establishes the identity with the highest. As for the objection that the term "imperishable" applies to both, we reply that while it may apply to both, the specific mention of eating serves as the deciding factor. And eating is not contradictory to the middle imperishable. Therefore, the conclusion is that this is the highest imperishable. This is established by the Sūtra: But on account of the mention of the eater, it is the highest. (1.2.10) It is the highest imperishable. Why? On account of the mention of the eater. For it is said: "The eater of all beings... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1). Eating is impossible for the middle imperishable. Therefore, it is the highest. "Because of the support of everything up to the ether. This is its meaning: that which is denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) in the phrase "That indeed is the akṣara" is Brahman alone, not the material nature (cit-prakṛti). Why? Because of the support of everything up to the ether; for it is heard in scripture that within this very akṣara, "in this akṣara," there is the sustaining of all things ending with space (ākāśa). This is the sense.

Thus, having stated that space alone is that in which [all things] are woven crosswise and lengthwise—thereby declaring that the primordial nature (prakṛti) called "space" is the support of all—and having heard from the passage beginning with "In this Imperishable indeed" that the Imperishable is the support of that [space], it is established that the one denoted by the word "Imperishable" is Viṣṇu alone.
And that [power] is due to his command.
He explains the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara) through another argument.

"And that [support] is from command" (sā ca praśāsanāt). The meaning of this is as follows: "ca" means "because"; "sā" refers to the support of the ends of space; it exists "from command," that is, by the mere command of Viṣṇu alone—this is stated in the Śruti passage beginning with "of Him. Therefore, for this reason as well, Brahman alone is denoted by the word "Akṣara" (the Imperishable), and not the non-intelligent primordial nature (prakṛti); such is the meaning.

And thus, because it is heard that the Imperishable (akṣara) alone is the support of all by its mere command, and because of the scriptural statement, "The seven half-embryos," it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word "Imperishable."
And because of the exclusion of other states.
He states the sūtra which establishes Viṣṇu’s nature as the Protector through another argument:

"And because of the exclusion of other states" (anyabhāvavyāvṛtteśca). This is its meaning: because the Śruti text, "Not gross, not subtle," describes the non-existence of the exclusion of other states—that is, the intrinsic natures of things other than Viṣṇu, such as grossness and so forth—within the Imperishable (akṣara), the meaning is that Brahman alone is the Imperishable.

Thus, by the statement beginning with "not gross" (*asthūlam*), since the exclusion of the natures of other entities—such as grossness and so forth—is expressed, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the referent denoted by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*).
Thus concludes the section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa).
The passage beginning with "Existence alone" (*sadeva*) and so forth, which consists of various sections, is connected [to this topic].
He [is Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*).

[Objection: Surely "Being" (sat) must be the Pradhāna alone, not Viṣṇu; for it is heard that Being undergoes modification called becoming manifold, as in the text, "May I be many. And such mutability is impossible in the Supreme Self, because He is immutable, as stated in passages such as "He is changeless and eternally pure. Therefore, since "Being" is the Pradhāna, the agency of the world belongs to that alone. To this, the Sūtra replies: *na vilakṣaṇatvād asya tathātvaṃ ca śabdāt* || (BS 2.1.4) [The world] cannot [be the effect of the Pradhāna] because it is of a different nature from it; and its being so [different] is known from Scripture. (BS 2.1.4) [Commentary: It is not possible that the world has the Pradhāna as its material cause. Why? Because the world is of a different nature from the Pradhāna. The Pradhāna is non-intelligent, insentient, and composed of the three guṇas; the world, however, is intelligent, sentient, and devoid of the three guṇas. Furthermore, the Pradhāna is homogeneous, while the world is heterogeneous. Moreover, the Pradhāna is unevolved, whereas the world is evolved. Thus, the world is of a different nature from the Pradhāna. Since the material cause and its effect must be of the same nature, the world cannot have the Pradhāna as its cause. Furthermore, the fact that the world is of a different nature from the Pradhāna is known from Scripture, as in, "From that, which is the existent and the non-existent, was born the manifest and the unmanifest" (MuU 1.5.18), and "Two birds, inseparable friends... (ŚU 1.1). Therefore, the world has Brahman as its material cause. || 4 ||

"Because of the designation of the object of seeing, it is He. This is the meaning: that which is denoted by the words "Being" (sat) and so forth occurring in the context of the passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was Being alone," is Viṣṇu alone, not the Pradhāna. Why? Because of the designation of the object of seeing; that is to say, because there is the mention of the action called "seeing," characterized by the word "It saw" (tadaikṣata), which resides in a conscious being.

And thus, because of the hearing of the activity called "seeing" in the passage "It thought (aikṣata)," there is obtained the quality of acting with foresight; for seeing is in no way possible in the non-intelligent *pradhāna*. If it is argued: "Let the *prakṛti* then not be non-intelligent; why should it not be intelligent?"—[the answer is] that an intelligent *prakṛti*, being female [in gender], cannot be an independent creator. Nor should it be said that He is not Viṣṇu because of the hearing of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *pradhāna* known as "becoming manifold."

Because the statement "though unborn, he is born in many ways" is applicable [to Viṣṇu] as well, since it is heard that even the unchanging undergoes manifoldness; and because it is established that by the word "Being" (sat) Viṣṇu alone is denoted, and he alone possesses the nature of the creator.
Thus ends the section on the six bases.

In this context, the concordance of the mark of being located in the heart-lotus—whether directly or indirectly—with Brahman is established on the grounds that it is the support of all and that which is to be sought after. "The small [ether] [is Brahman], because of the subsequent [reasons]. || 1.3.14 ||

But surely, the ether itself must reside within the lotus of the heart; for we hear of the "small [ether] within this," which refers to the existence of the small ether residing in the lotus, and because of the explanation that "at its end there is a cavity. If by the word "ether" (ākāśa) only the cavity is intended, and if—by the phrase "that which is within it"—the ether situated in the lotus of the heart were meant as the support of all, then the syntactical connection of the passage would be untenable. To explain: ... [The remainder of the argument follows] ... Thus, indeed:

In this context, if the intention were that Viṣṇu is meant by the word "in that" (tasmin), there would be an inconsistency regarding the intent of the phrase "as far as" (yāvān vai) and so forth; for, without a response such as "Brahman exists there" to the question "What is found there?", the purpose of that respectful expression would not be coherent. However, in the case of the ether (ākāśa) being the subject, this connection is appropriate. When it has been stated that the object of meditation is situated in the ether of the heart, the question "What is stationed there? is answered by the phrase "as far as," which specifically summarizes the previously mentioned ether through the concluding response beginning with "both of these in this."

Furthermore, the logical connection [of the passage] is not established by the argument that Viṣṇu, named Ākāśa, is understood as the support of all through the phrase "as vast as" (na ca yāvān) and so forth; for this would contradict the direct statement that the cavity itself is the support of all in the words "everything is established in it" (tasmin sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitam). Therefore, it follows that it is the element Ākāśa itself, as the support of all, that resides in the heart-lotus. Consequently, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) being reached—that the Imperishable (akṣara) which is the support of the moon, sun, and so forth, is indeed something other than the Blessed Lord—the following was stated in the Sūtra:

"Because of the subsequent [passages], [it is] the small one. This is its meaning: Viṣṇu alone—not the individual soul (jīva) or others—is the agent residing in the small space within the heart-lotus, as stated in the passage, "In the small [space] is a small lotus-palace. This is because of the subsequent [passages], that is, because of the attributes such as being free from sin mentioned in the following passages beginning with, "That Self which is free from sin... and so forth.

Thus, He who resides in the small lotus must be Viṣṇu alone. This is because in the subsequent passage beginning with "free from evil" (apahatapāpman), qualities such as being free from evil are heard of in relation to Him who resides in the heart-lotus. While the absence of evil and so forth might somehow be possible in another [deity], the possession of qualities such as having true desires (satyakāmatva) and the rest is impossible elsewhere in any way whatsoever. This is according to the Śruti text, "He who [is not affected] by hunger," and because absolute (nirapekṣa) qualities do not exist elsewhere. Furthermore, there is the statement, "He who has eternally crossed over. Between that which is dependent and that which is independent, the independent must be accepted. Therefore, it is established that He who resides in the heart-lotus is indeed Viṣṇu.
On account of the movement and the word; for thus is the mark seen.
He introduces the aphorism that establishes Viṣṇu’s abiding within the heart-lotus by means of another argument.

"By the movement and the word; for thus the mark is seen. This is the meaning: by the two reasons—the movement and the word heard in the passage "Every day they go to this world of Brahman"—namely, the state of being reached by one who has fallen asleep and the word "Brahman," [the one situated in] the lotus within the heart of the *dahara* is indeed Brahman. Furthermore, because in the scripture beginning with "the spokes," it is likewise established that [it] is reached by one who has fallen asleep, just as [the word] is well-known to reside in Viṣṇu.

The *liṅga* (indicative mark) consisting of the world's abiding within the ocean of nectar called the *araṇī* is stated to be seen as residing in the heart-lotus; for this reason also, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone resides in the heart-lotus of the *dahara*.

And thus, because it is stated that they go there daily, and because the state attainable in deep sleep is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu—according to the Śruti, "He goes to Being"—and because the heart-lotus is seen to possess the characteristic mark of being the locus for the two oceans of nectar named Ara and Ṇya, as per the Śruti, "Ara and..."—it is therefore established that Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus.
This is also because His greatness, consisting in His sustaining [the world], is perceived in Him.
He recites the sūtra which establishes, by means of another reason, that Viṣṇu resides within the heart-lotus.

"And because of the support, and because His greatness is perceived in this [context]. This is the meaning: Because of the support—since it is heard in the scripture that He who resides in the heart-lotus is the support of all, in the passage "He is the bridge, the divider"—it is Viṣṇu alone who resides in the heart-lotus. Furthermore, because of the perception—that is, the hearing—in the Vājasaneyaka text "He is the Lord of All," of the greatness such as being the Lord of All attributed to Him who is stated to reside in the heart-lotus in the Chāndogya; and also because of the common designation [of both texts], it is Viṣṇu alone who resides in the heart-lotus.

Now, one might ask: "Why is it Viṣṇu alone [who is meant] even by virtue of the name? To this it is said: "Of this," and so forth. The meaning is: because of the hearing of this greatness of Viṣṇu in this Vājasaneyaka passage.

And thus, in the Vājasaneyaka passage, after stating "He who is here within the heart," and so forth, it is declared by the words "He is the Lord of all," and so on, that Viṣṇu resides in the heart; for this is the designation [of Viṣṇu]. Furthermore, because the indicative marks (liṅgas) stated in such Śruti and Smṛti passages as "In this very Imperishable," "For He is the Overlord of all," and "Viṣṇu alone is the sole Lord of all" have no application elsewhere, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the lotus of the heart.
And because it is well-known.
He recites the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu resides in the space within the heart-lotus, by means of reasoning other than the argument based on etymological designation.

"And because of its renown. The meaning of this is: because of the renown in scripture that Viṣṇu resides within the heart-lotus—as in the passage "the small, free from evil"—He alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus; such is the meaning.

And thus, because of the scriptural mention of the name "the small, sinless one" (*daharaṃ vipāpmam*) and the well-known fact from other texts that Viṣṇu resides within the heart-lotus, there is no inconsistency between the question and the answer. Since the status of the one residing in the heart-lotus as Brahman is already established by the very term "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*), a question regarding its mere essential nature would be inappropriate. Rather, with the intention of asking "What is it like?", the question "What is that? is posed; and the answer beginning with "As large as... (*yāvān*) is appropriately connected for the purpose of defining the essential nature of Brahman.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that Viṣṇu is directly present within the lotus—whether by taking the word "cavity" (*suṣira*) to mean "space" and thus accepting that the space within the lotus is Viṣṇu himself, or by accepting that the small lotus is space while Viṣṇu resides within that space, thereby maintaining his status as the support of all—there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding the cavity, because it is the cavity itself that is declared to be the support of everything.

Just as an object situated inside a chest is designated as being "in the chest," so too here, because of the scriptural mention of a "cavity" (suṣira)—which directly teaches that space alone is the support of all—the scripture containing the word "cavity" is applied with reference to the Supreme Self residing within the cavity of the lotus. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone resides in the heart-lotus.
If it be argued that "He" refers to the other [the individual soul] because of the subsequent reference to it, we say no, because of impossibility.

"Surely, since space (*ākāśa*) is the support of all things, it would be the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that resides within the heart-lotus; for later on, there is a reference to that which dwells in the heart-lotus as 'the supreme light' (*paraṃjyoti*), and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being situated in the small [space] (*dahara*). Nor is there an impossibility of syntactical connection (*anvaya*); for just as the sentence can be construed with Viṣṇu, it can likewise be construed with the individual soul. Having thus raised an objection regarding the Lord’s residence in the heart-lotus, the Sūtra provides the following resolution:

"If it be argued that it is the individual soul because of the reference to 'the other,' we say no, on account of impossibility. This is the meaning: "Because of the reference to the other"—that is, because of the reference (grahaṇa) by means of the word "this Self" (*eṣa ātmā*) to the individual soul previously mentioned as "attaining perfection in its own form," which resides as the Self within the heart-lotus. If it be argued that it is the individual soul alone who resides in the heart-lotus, we say no. Why? Because of impossibility; the meaning is that the qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth, which are heard in scripture as residing in the heart-lotus, are impossible for the individual soul to possess independently.
Thus, since qualities such as being free from sin are impossible for the individual soul (jīva), it is established that Viṣṇu alone resides within the heart-lotus. [Objection:
If it be argued that this is so because of what follows in the subsequent section, then let it be the case that the one whose nature has become manifest [is meant].

Now, since the soul (jīva) described as "this serene being" (saṃprasāda) is perceived to possess true desires through the passage beginning with "he moves about there," and since freedom from sorrow and other qualities are established by that very fact, the aforementioned qualities are possible; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the one residing in the heart-lotus is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*). To this, the author recites the aphorism (*sūtra*) which provides the resolution: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] Brahman, on account of the subsequent [statement]. (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.20) This means: But it is the Supreme Brahman who resides in the heart-lotus, because of what follows in the text. For the subsequent passage—"He thinks, 'Why did I not eat of the white? Why did I not eat of the black?'... He becomes like this world"—indicates that he possesses the power to create the entire universe. Such power does not belong to the individual soul, but belongs to the Supreme Lord alone. Therefore, the one in the heart-lotus is Brahman. Furthermore, the term "serene being" (*saṃprasāda*), which denotes the state of deep sleep, refers to the Supreme Self, as seen in the passage: "This is his true form, in which he is serene, passed beyond evil, free from old age, free from death, free from grief, free from hunger and thirst, whose desire is the True, whose resolve is the True. Since the individual soul is subject to transmigration, it cannot be designated as "passed beyond evil" or "free from grief. Thus, the one in the heart-lotus is none other than the Supreme Brahman.

Regarding the statement, "If it be argued that [it is the individual soul] because of what follows, [we reply] 'No, for its true nature has become manifest'": the meaning of this is as follows. The word *tu* (but/for) has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). The word *na* (not) is to be supplied as a remainder. Thus, from the subsequent sentence, "He moves about there" (*sa tatra paryetā*), the individual soul is perceived to possess the quality of having true desires and so forth; and from that very fact, the state of being free from sorrow and other such qualities is possible. If it be argued that "that [soul] alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus," we say no. Why? Because, by the force of the subsequent phrase "by his own [nature]" (*svena*) in that passage, it is the liberated soul alone whose manifested true nature (*āvirbhūtasvarūpaḥ*) is being taught, not the mere individual soul.

Furthermore, the liberated soul does not possess qualities such as being "free from evil" (apahatapāpmā) by its own nature; therefore, the meaning is that even for it, there is no abiding within the heart-lotus.

Furthermore, since the liberated soul (*muktajīva*) is spoken of in the subsequent passage, it is impossible for that which resides in the heart-lotus to be liberated while remaining within the body. Nor should it be argued that even if this passage concerns the liberated state, since a liberated soul remains a *jīva*, the absence of the possibility of being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth implies that it is the *jīva* itself—possessing those qualities—that is described as residing in the heart-lotus by way of its future attainment. For even in the case of the liberated soul, the manifestation of those qualities occurs solely through the grace of the Lord; they cannot exist inherently (*svataḥ*).
Thus, it is established that the one residing in the heart-lotus is Viṣṇu alone.

The meaning is that this is because of the Vedic revelation stating that "by its light all this shines," which establishes that the world has the radiance of the Supreme Self as its illumination.

And thus, because it is heard in scripture that the splendors of the sun and other luminaries are dependent on Viṣṇu—as in "shining after Him alone"—and because His light is declared to be the illuminator of the entire universe; and because both of these marks (the mark of being the source of light and the mark of universal illumination) are understood to be marks of Viṣṇu through the Śruti text "I am that light" and the Smṛti text "That which is in the sun," there is no contradiction with the scriptural mention of bliss. "But with reference to the heart, [it is said so] because the qualification belongs to humans. This is its meaning: the word *tu* (but) has the sense of *eva* (only/precisely) and the sense of *api* (even/although). Thus, although Viṣṇu is omnipresent, the statement that He is "the size of a thumb" is made with reference to the heart—that is, with reference only to the space of the heart measured by a thumb. The meaning is that one should not understand from this that Viṣṇu is limited in extent. Now, since animals and the like lack thumbs, how can a statement regarding that measure be applicable to all qualified beings? To this it is said: "because the qualification belongs to humans."

And likewise, because this meditation on the knowledge has human beings as its qualified practitioners, and because the engagement in this knowledge is possible for them; the sense is that there is no fault even in the absence of a thumb in the case of Īśvara and others.

And thus, since the thumb-sized dimension is mentioned in the Śruti solely for the purpose of meditating upon the Supreme Self manifested within the space of the heart—given that it is impossible to assume an intention to exclude other dimensions—it follows that even though other living beings lack thumbs, the mention of being "thumb-sized" is appropriate because only humans have the qualification for Vedic knowledge. Therefore, it is established that the Lord (Īśāna) is indeed Viṣṇu, and that the qualities of lordship and the state of being the object of inquiry belong to Him alone.

In this regard, the qualification of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman is established:
"And also above that [the world of the ancestors], Bādarāyaṇa [maintains it] because of the possibility."

But surely, the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of the Vedas is not possible; for whether their status is eternal and beginningless, or whether it is a status attained through knowledge and other means, eligibility is impossible. Since the gods have attained their status, they have already achieved all human goals other than liberation; thus, being omniscient and knowing that liberation has been attained, no desire whatsoever can arise in them.

If gods were subject to birth and destruction, then prior to their existence as gods, there would be an absence of deities; consequently, the rites such as the "Hundredfold" sacrifice performed by gods for the sake of attaining godhood would be *vyaṅgya* (unmanifested), and thus could not lead to the attainment of the status of a god and so forth. For a *vyaṅgya* rite does not produce a fruit, as that would entail the absurd consequence that even sacrifices and the like performed by outsiders would produce fruits. Thus, since one observes no eligibility for a non-existent entity such as the son of a barren woman, it follows that gods have no eligibility [for Vedic rites]. To this objection, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: *Devānāṃ ca*... [and of the gods... (Sūtra 1.3.27) This is the established conclusion.

"Even beyond that, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains there is eligibility], because of the possibility. This is its meaning: even beyond that—that is, not only during the state of being human, but also after attaining the status of gods and so forth—there exists eligibility for Vedic knowledge for those humans who are capable of becoming deities. Why? Because of the possibility; for even they possess the specialized intellect that serves as the cause for eligibility. This is the meaning of what the venerable Bādarāyaṇa declares.

And thus, it is not impossible for the gods to possess the qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas, as is the case with animals and the like; for the necessary conditions, such as superior intelligence and so forth, exist. And when such possibility exists, this formal argument arises: "The gods possess the qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas, because even above that [human state], there exists—on account of their attainment of divinity—the possibility of both capacity and learning which are conducive to divine qualification, precisely because they possess desire and the fitness for the excellence of liberation."

Nor is it a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) to claim that gods do not possess the qualification for knowledge because they are non-human, like animals and so forth; for the probans (*upādhi*) "being devoid of specific intellect and the like" is fallacious. Nor can it be argued that this is not a valid probans because, although Jaritāri and others lacked such qualification, they nonetheless possessed specific intellect and the like—thus the probans would fail to pervade the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) due to the absence of "being devoid of specific intellect and the like" in them. This is because, if they did possess qualification, the probandum in the form of "lack of qualification" would be absent in those cases, as evidenced by the Vedic text: "O Agni, [this is] for you, O Jaritāri. [Objection: But if they too possess qualification, does this not contradict the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*)?

If it be argued that [the gods lack qualification] because of their non-human nature, and because of the prohibition [of such status], we say no; for this is due to a misunderstanding of the matter. In the previous case, the lack of qualification for the "thumb-sized" (aṅguṣṭhamātra) meditation was stated on account of the absence of a physical thumb in the qualified person. Here, however, having accepted what was stated there, the qualification for other meditations is being declared. Therefore, it is established that the gods possess the qualification for Vedic knowledge.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no; for we observe the attainment of various [bodies].

Now, one might object: "If the second alternative—that the gods are perishable along with their bodies—is accepted, then the statement regarding the eligibility of the gods for Vedic knowledge is untenable. For if the gods are perishable along with their bodies, there would be an absence of presiding deities prior to that [present creation]; consequently, since there would be no recipient for the rituals performed in a previous cycle, a contradiction known as 'futility' (vaiyarthyam) would arise. Having raised this objection, the author recites the Sūtra which provides the resolution.

"If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding ritual action, we say no, because we observe the attainment [of divinity] by many. This is the meaning: if the gods and others were subject to beginningless ritual action—that is, with respect to rituals such as sacrifices performed in previous kalpas—there would be a contradiction, namely the contradiction known as "futility" caused by the absence of a [new] objective. If this is argued, we say no. Why? Because of the attainment by many; for it is observed that many qualified humans attain the status of deities, as stated in the scripture: "In whomsoever [it was] before," and so forth.

And thus, because these [groups] are beginninglessly eternal by way of their continuous flow (*pravāha*), even in the absence of one set of gods, other deities exist. This is because the scripture, in the passage "They indeed [attain] the heavenly world" (*te ha nākam*), shows that through knowledge and action, infinite humans who are fit for divinity and so forth attain the status of the respective preceding deities, group by group. Consequently, it is established that there is no contradiction known as "futility" (*vaiyarthyākhya*).
If it be argued that [the world] is [produced from] sound, we say no; because [the world] originates from this [Brahman], as is known through perception and inference.

Now, since the authority of the Vedas would be untenable if they were non-eternal, their eternity must necessarily be accepted, as per the Vedic revelation: "By speech, which is multiform... If the deities expressed by those [Vedas] were non-eternal, then it would have to be admitted that the Vedas abandon their previous deities and come to express different deities. But this is not possible, because of the natural relationship between a sentence and its meaning. Indeed, no sentence, having conveyed a certain meaning at one time, abandons it to convey a different meaning at another time; this is due to the natural relationship [between word and meaning].

Indeed, it has never been observed that a sentence, having conveyed a certain meaning at one time, abandons it to convey a different meaning at another time—such that this might also be the case with the Veda. One who accepts such a thing regarding the Veda must necessarily accept that its connection with its meaning is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). Furthermore, since a conceptual connection entails a lack of authority, the Veda would consequently be invalid.

Even if a conceptual relationship were the basis for the authority [of the Veda], the authority of the Veda would still not be established. For even if there were a rule regarding the succession of deities based on authoritative tradition, since there is no such authority, there would be no rule regarding the succession of deities in subsequent kalpas either; thus, the conceptual relationship itself would be absent. Having raised this objection, the author states the sūtra as a response: [The sūtra: "But because of the non-difference of the word and its meaning, there is no contradiction. (JS 1.3.30) This means that because the word and its meaning are non-different across time, there is no contradiction. Since the relationship between words and their meanings is eternal, the conceptual relationship is not lacking. Therefore, the authority of the Veda is established.
