“If it be argued that there is contradiction because of the Word, we say no; because [the gods] originate from this [Word], as is known through perception and inference. This is the meaning: the word “contradiction” (virodha) carries over. If the gods were to have a beginning and an end, there would be a contradiction with the Word—the Veda—since the words of the Veda, established by scripture as eternal, would at some point be devoid of referents. If this is argued, we say no, because of the Vedic statement, “As the Creator [ordained]...,” and likewise because of perception and inference: from the direct perception of great beings, and from the evidence proving the continuous production of the gods.

The meaning is that it is logical because of "origination" (prabhavāt); for in every kalpa, origination—denoted by the word *prabhava*—is understood to occur as a rule. Thus, what was stated is appropriate.

And thus, because of the Vedic revelation, "The sun and the moon," because it is perceived by great beings, and because there exists the inference that "the subsequent Kalpa possesses deities, since it is not a time of dissolution," one should not say that the relationship [between the deity and the mantra] lacks the capacity to produce validity due to its being conceptual. This is because the relationship with various other deities is established as valid by virtue of being beginningless and endless, and therefore is not merely conceptual. Thus, it is proven that there is no contradiction characterized by futility.
And for this very reason, there is eternality.
He introduces a sūtra that establishes the eternality of the stream of deities through another argument:

"And for this very reason, [the Veda] is eternal. Its meaning is as follows: "For this very reason"—that is, precisely because of the eternality of the Veda asserted by the opponent—it is established that the stream of deities who are its referents is also eternal, since otherwise [the Veda's eternality] would be untenable. This is the sense.

And thus, since the eternity of the stream of deities is established precisely by the impossibility of the eternity of the Veda as spoken by another being otherwise, the eternity of speech in this form is not tenable if the object denoted lacks eternity; for, because they are subject to production and destruction, their eternity in terms of intrinsic nature is impossible, and thus their eternity is established only in the form of a continuous stream.
And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of repeated cycles, as is seen from scripture and from tradition.

Now, even if there is a continuity of deities, the authority of the Veda would still be untenable. For if those liberated in a previous *kalpa* were to return again in a subsequent *kalpa*, it would contradict the definition of liberation as being "non-return. Furthermore, if others were to return, then even if no contradiction arose regarding the impermanence of the deities who constitute the substrata (*dharmin*), a contradiction would nonetheless arise due to the diversity of attributes such as names and forms. This is because the expressive Veda remains uniform across all *kalpas* without any difference in its recension, whereas the expressed deities possess various names and forms. To this objection, the author states the following Sūtra:

"And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, on account of both scripture and tradition. This is its meaning: "Even in the case of recurrence (*āvṛtti*), that is, even though those gods who were liberated in a previous cycle do not exist again in their own positions, there is no contradiction—meaning there is no contradiction known as the invalidity of the uniform Veda which establishes that [recurrence]. Why? Because names and forms are the same (*samānanāmarūpatvāt*); for even the gods produced in this present cycle possess names and forms identical to those of the past."

And thus, since that which is to be established is also of a single nature, the meaning is that there is no lack of authority in the Veda which makes that known. As for the question "Why is it of a single nature?", it is said: "Because of [Vedic] revelation and tradition. This means: because of the Śruti text, "As in the beginning," and because of the Smṛti text, "Without beginning or end."

Thus, since the names and forms of the deities such as Indra and others that are propounded in the Veda are admitted to belong to those very same deities who are born in another kalpa, and because their authoritative status is established by both the Vedic revelation stating "as before" (yathā pūrvam) and the Smṛti stating "without beginning or end" (anādinidhana), it is proven that there is no contradiction known as the invalidity of the Veda.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations because they are impossible [for them].

Now, it may be argued that it is not appropriate for the gods to have the qualification for Vedic knowledge (*vedavidyā*). Vedic knowledge is of two kinds: that which aims at its primary fruit, and that which aims at other fruits. Even those aiming at fruits other than liberation are of two kinds, distinguished by whether they concern Brahman or ritual action—namely, the Madhu-vidyā and the Agniṣṭoma-vidyā. Among these, first of all, it is not fitting for the gods to have the qualification for the two kinds of knowledge that aim at fruits other than liberation.

Among those things to be accomplished by that [knowledge], since there is no desire for some fruits other than liberation—because they have already been attained by those who are fit, and because they cannot be attained by those who are unfit—the Sūtra speaks, having established a general prohibition regarding eligibility for Vedic knowledge according to the view of Jaimini.

"Jaimini [holds that] there is no entitlement [to these meditations] because of the impossibility [of it for gods] in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and others. Regarding the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations taught in passages such as "That yonder sun is indeed honey," the teacher Jaimini maintains that there is no entitlement—that is, an absence of eligibility—for the gods. Why? Because of impossibility; the meaning is that desire, the capacity for those states, and so forth, are not possible for them.

And thus, because it is impossible for [the qualification] to exist in the first of the two sections, as well as in the first of the second; and because, in the second of the second, there is an absence of interest [in the ritual], which results in a prohibition of the qualification—not a prohibition of the qualification alone—there is no contradiction with the view of the teacher Jaimini. This is established.
And because [the qualities] exist in light.

[Objection: "Granted that the gods lack the qualification for those vidyās whose fruits are other than liberation; nevertheless, they will possess the qualification for those vidyās aimed at liberation, such as 'Truth, Knowledge, Infinite,' because the possibility of their desiring [liberation] exists there. Anticipating this doubt, he recites the sūtra which refutes it:

"Because [the knowledge] of the luminaries exists [in them]. This is its meaning: since the knowledge of the luminaries (*jyotiṣ*) consists in the knowledge of the gods, and because all things are included within their scope, it is not logical for the gods—who possess perfected knowledge—to have a need for knowledge; thus, they have no qualification for the sciences of liberation (*mokṣavidyā*). This is the sense.

And thus, since the gods possess omniscience—meaning they have necessarily attained all knowledge achievable through Vedic rituals and sciences—and for that very reason are seers of the Vedas (*vedadraṣṭṛ*), it follows that there is no possibility of them having a desire for knowledge achievable through both types of science (Vedic and worldly). Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction with the opinion of Jaimini.
But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that there is indeed [the existence of the soul after death], for it exists.

Thus, since the gods have already attained fruits other than liberation that are appropriate for them, and because it is impossible for them to attain what is inappropriate; and since liberation is effectively obtained by virtue of their being knowers of Brahman; and because, due to the absence of desire, they lack qualification for any of the meditations (vidyās)—the author now presents the sūtra which establishes their qualification once again, countering the argument supported by the school of Jaimini.

"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that there is [eligibility], for it exists. This is its meaning: Bādarāyaṇa, however—because (hi) even for the gods there exists a particular manifestation of the prior [karma] to be accomplished through knowledge, and because there is an excellence regarding the fruit of liberation—therefore, he considers that there is "bhāva," meaning the existence of eligibility for the gods. It should be understood, however, that Jaimini’s opinion intends that there is no eligibility for the gods for the sake of obtaining the fruit of knowledge already attained.

And thus, although the gods have attained their station, have realized Brahman, and have already secured the fruits of liberation and other goals—thereby making further attainment impossible and rendering higher fruits unsuitable for them—nevertheless, even for these gods who have attained their station, there exists the possibility of desiring [liberation]. This is because, through the sequential practice of meditation on the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations as taught in the Upaniṣads, they may attain specific distinctions of fruit; and because, by means of the mere knowledge appropriate to their respective capacities—which cannot be accomplished otherwise—they can achieve excellence in the fruit of liberation. Thus, the desire for that goal is possible.

Because there exists the possibility of qualification even for the sake of knowledge, due to the presence of the fruit of liberation—which is the fruit of *vidyā* consisting of the excellence of bliss—as evidenced by the Skanda Purāṇa statement, "as long as one is intent on service"; because, since those other than the Blessed Lord lack unqualified omniscience, the attainment of knowledge through the inquiry into *vidyā* is possible; and because the position of Jaimini is not contradictory when intended to mean that the gods have no qualification for [further study] since they have already attained the fruit.

Thus, since it has been stated by the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa that the gods lack any further qualification for the remaining [levels of] ignorance beginning with the Madhu-vidyā, it is established that Viṣṇu’s being worshipped by all the gods is logical.
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities.
Here, the eligibility of the Śūdra—who is other than the three [higher] castes—for the knowledge of Brahman taught in the Vedas is refuted.
For it is indicated by the hearing of that contempt for Śuka and by his running toward him.

[Objection: Surely Śūdras must have the qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas (vedavidyā), because of the Vedic revelation (śruti) stating, "Ahaha! Bring it hither," and because they are human beings. The Blessed Author of the Sūtras has indicated this by stating that the qualification [for study] is based on being human (*manuṣyādhikāratvāt*). Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, even one belonging to the three higher castes would not possess such qualification. Furthermore, a Śūdra possesses specific intelligence and other such qualities, as is seen from the fact that Pautrāyaṇa, who was a Śūdra, studied the Saṃvarga-vidyā of the Vedas. This being the position reached, [the author] provides the following sūtra: *na śūdrasyādhikāraḥ, śravaṇādhyayanārthapratiṣedhāt smṛteḥ* || (Sūtra 1.3.38) [Reply: There is no qualification for a Śūdra, because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda], according to the Smṛti. (Sūtra 1.3.38) [Commentary: It is not so. A Śūdra does not have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. Why? Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding the Veda, as stated in the Smṛti: "The Veda must not be recited to a Śūdra, nor should he be made to hear it. And: "If the Veda is recited in his presence, the wind carries away the syllables. Also: "A Śūdra is outside the pale of the sacred law (*dharma*). Furthermore, the word "Śūdra" is derived from the root *śuc* (to grieve), meaning "one who grieves," and thus denotes a person of low birth. Moreover, the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman requires the performance of rituals such as the Agnihotra, which are preceded by initiation (*upanayana*) and the like; and these are not permitted for a Śūdra. Therefore, the Śūdra lacks the qualification. As for the mention of the Śūdra in the Veda, that refers to a different caste entirely, or is used figuratively. Thus, the conclusion is established. As for the argument that the Śūdra possesses specific intelligence and so forth, and that Pautrāyaṇa studied the Saṃvarga-vidyā—this is refuted by the fact that the qualification depends upon the injunctions regarding the means of knowledge, such as hearing and reflection, which are restricted by the aforementioned prohibitions. The mention of Pautrāyaṇa is merely an incidental reference (*arthavāda*) to praise the excellence of the knowledge, not an injunction establishing a Śūdra's right to study. Therefore, the Śūdra is excluded from the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. Thus ends the section.

"Because of hearing that disregard for him, and because of his running toward that [disregard], he is indicated by the word 'hi' (for/indeed). This is its meaning: "Of this king named Pautrāyaṇa; because of hearing that disregard—namely, the cause of hearing the swan’s disregard expressed as *gaccha enam* ('go to him')"; *śukaḥ* means sorrow (*śokaḥ*). To the question "Even so, why is there sorrow?", it is said: "For he is indicated. For (*hi*) because he is indicated by the subsequent sentence, "As he was indeed rising up," and is thus known; therefore there is sorrow. It is on account of this very cause.

The king was addressed as "Śūdra" by the seer Raikva; however, the meaning is that this was not intended to imply his inferiority in terms of caste (varṇa). Thus, the point is that one should not conclude, on the strength of this indicative evidence, that a Śūdra possesses the qualification for Vedic knowledge.

And thus, because [the qualification] is devoid of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and because study and so forth depend upon purificatory rites; and because the statement "not fire" is intended to prohibit purificatory rites for the Śūdra—it is established that there is a prohibition of the Śūdra, who is other than the three castes, from the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
And because of the understanding of his being a Kṣatriya later on, on account of the indicative mark [found] in the case of Caitraratha.

[Objection: Should not the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) alone be accepted for the word *śūdra*, since conventional meaning is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*)? For the eligibility of a Śūdra for Vedic study is established by the very example of Pautrāyaṇa; since we see that even the Śūdra Pautrāyaṇa studied the Vedic Saṃvarga-vidyā. Nor should it be said that Pautrāyaṇa was not a Śūdra at all, because he was addressed as "O Śūdra, bring the firewood! Thus, when this [objection] has been raised, the author states the Sūtra in order to refute it.

"And because his status as a Kṣatriya is understood later, on account of the indicative mark [consisting] of Caitraratha. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to collect another indicative mark. "Later" refers to the subsequent sentence, "This is the chariot drawn by mules" (*ayamaśvatarīrathaḥ*). The word "heard" (*śrutena*) is to be supplied. "By Caitraratha" means by the indicative mark consisting of the connection with a chariot yoked to mules, derived from the word *citra*. And "because his status as a Kṣatriya is understood"—that is, because of the knowledge that he is a Kṣatriya—means that Pautrāyaṇa is not a Śūdra.

And thus, since there is no evidence for Pautrāyaṇa’s being a Śūdra, the address by the word "Śūdra" lacks authority. Nor is that very address by the word "Śūdra" proof in this matter; for the term "Śūdra" was applied there due to his running away out of grief, and therefore it cannot establish that he belongs to a lower caste as understood by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Furthermore, this Pautrāyaṇa was not a Śūdra, because great men are known to have been Kṣatriyas.

Furthermore, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of Caitraratha—the statement "This is the Aśvatarī-chariot of others"—it is understood that he was a Kṣatriya. Consequently, it is established that a Śūdra lacks the qualification for the Vedas.
Because of the grasping at mental formations and because of the expression of their non-existence.

Now, one might object: "Could it not be that a Śūdra also has the qualification for the Vedas? For even he can be a charioteer (*rathin*). Since the chariot is pervaded by the Veda—meaning wherever there is a chariot, there is the Veda—and since that [Veda] is absent in a Śūdra, the chariot must also be absent," such a doubt does not arise; for it is accepted that even a Śūdra possesses the qualification for the Vedas. This being the position, the author recites the Sūtra to refute it:

"Because of the reference to sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and because of the statement regarding the absence thereof. This is its meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the probandum. Because of the reference to sacraments, [in the text] "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age; one should teach him"—by the use of the pronoun "him" (*tam*), there is a mention of one who is endowed with the sacrament called initiation (*upanayana*). Because of the statement regarding the absence thereof, [in the text] "For a Śūdra there is no fire, no sacrifice," there is a declaration of the absence of sacraments. The meaning is that he has no entitlement to the Vedas and so forth.

And thus, since it is understood that the purpose of study involves dependence upon *saṃsāra*, and since it has been stated that there is an absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for the *śūdra*, whereas for women of the higher castes there is no such [absence] as there is for the *śūdra*—as seen in their eligibility for [rites] such as those involving a co-wife—and because of the *Vyāsa-smṛti* which states, "For women, the act of giving in marriage is indeed [the primary rite]," it is established that the *śūdra* lacks eligibility for the Vedas.
And because [the person] engages in activity for the sake of determining the non-existence of that [object].

Now, one might argue that even so, the Śūdra’s eligibility for the Vedas is logical; for since there is no prohibition stating "one should not initiate a Śūdra," the possibility of his receiving the sacraments (saṃskāra) exists. Furthermore, in the Śruti passage beginning with "Not fire," only the absence of the sacraments is mentioned, and since there is no absolute prohibition stating "it must never be done," there is no contradiction [with the claim of eligibility]. To this, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"And because of the engagement [of Gautama] when there was a determination of his absence from that [status]. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis. "When there was a determination of his absence from that" means precisely when there was the ascertainment of the person named Satyakāma’s lack of Śūdra status. "Because of the engagement" means because Gautama engaged in initiating him. The meaning is that, based on this indicative mark (jñāpaka), the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) is not appropriate for a Śūdra.

And thus, because Gautama’s action is justified either by his statement of a subverting argument against the contrary position or by his statement of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), which establishes that Satyakāma lacks the status of a *śūdra*; and because of the scriptural text, "This is not a non-Brāhmaṇa," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) signifying the prohibition of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the lack of qualification for the Vedas on the part of a *śūdra* is established.
Because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda], and because of Smṛti.

[Objection: But surely, according to the reasoning stated by the word "on account of distinction" (*viśeṣāt*), the eligibility of even a Śūdra would be established because he possesses specific intelligence and so forth; otherwise, his eligibility even for [the worship of] deities and the like would not be established. To this, the author states the Sūtra:

"Because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning [of the Veda], and because of Smṛti. This is its meaning: "Because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning"—because for a Śūdra, the hearing of the Veda, its study, and the ascertainment of its meaning are prohibited by the Śruti, which states that "upon hearing [the Veda], one's ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac"; and "because of Smṛti"—because of the prohibitive Smṛti stating, "There is neither fire nor sacrifice for the Śūdra"—the meaning is that he has no entitlement to the knowledge of the Veda.

And thus, since for a Śūdra the hearing of the Veda, its study, and the comprehension of its meaning are prohibited; and since, such prohibition existing, the possession of specific intelligence and so forth is accepted as the sole determinant of eligibility for the Veda, and that [qualification] is absent in the Śūdra; and since Smṛti makes known the prohibition of study for him alone; and since Vidura and others, by virtue of possessing the special knowledge that has arisen within them, are not subjects of the prohibition but rather subjects of exceptions;
therefore, it is established that because Śūdras and others lack eligibility, the Blessed Lord Hari cannot be known through the wisdom of the Veda by Śūdras and the like.
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras.
Here, the name "Vajra" is applied to Brahman because of its trembling.

Now, one might object: "What is this that has been stated here? This must be the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the weapon of Indra, because of the direct scriptural mention (*śruti*) of 'thunderbolt' and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being raised. Thus, it is appropriate that it refers to a weapon. It should not be argued that it is Viṣṇu because liberation is said to result from the knowledge of the thunderbolt; for direct scriptural mention is more powerful than a mere indicative mark. Nor can it be claimed that the indicative mark is more powerful due to its being "without scope" (*niravakāśa*); for both the direct scriptural mention and the indicative mark are equally without scope.

It should not be argued that this being so, the fact that the mark (*liṅga*)—consisting in being the object of the knowledge that produces liberation—is restricted solely to Viṣṇu is not undermined, and thus it is not undesirable for the thunderbolt (*vajra*) to be Indra’s weapon (*indrāyudha*). For even if the mark consisting in being the object of the knowledge that produces liberation as qualified by its result (*phalopahita*) remains unimpaired, the mark in the form of *yogyatva* (fitness) is indeed undermined in its restriction to Viṣṇu alone. Consequently, since the thunderbolt is merely Indra’s weapon, liberation does not arise from the knowledge of Viṣṇu alone. To this, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the word 'thunderbolt'] refers to the body, on account of the context" (Brahmasūtra 1.3.42). This means: the word "thunderbolt" denotes the body of Viṣṇu, because it occurs in a context concerning Him. Just as the word "Indra" denotes the body of Viṣṇu in the passage, "He who is Indra among the gods," so too here the word "thunderbolt" denotes His body. Therefore, the meaning is that liberation arises from the knowledge of Viṣṇu alone. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement, "From fear of Him the wind blows. This is established. Furthermore, the word "thunderbolt" is well-known to denote Viṣṇu in the passage, "The thunderbolt is Viṣṇu; He is the great Indra. Hence, the conclusion is that the word "thunderbolt" refers to the body of Viṣṇu. This is the meaning. || 42 ||

Regarding the phrase "Because of trembling" (*kaṃpanāt*): its meaning is as follows. In the expression "the great fear, the thunderbolt" (*mahadbhayaṃ vajram*), that which is denoted by the word "thunderbolt" (*vajra*) is Viṣṇu alone, and not the rainbow of Indra. Why? Because of trembling; that is to say, because there is heard a scriptural mark (*liṅga*) consisting in being the mover of all activity, expressed by the word "trembling" in the passage "all breaths tremble" (*sarvaṃ prāṇa ejati*).

And because it is said that "it moves thus," which refers to its trembling; and because it is stated that "they are immortal," which denotes being the object of the knowledge that produces liberation endowed with its fruit. Nor is there a contradiction with the mark of being "upraised" (*udyatatva*); for the mark of being upraised has scope as it means "being about to strike. Nor is there a contradiction with the Vedic text concerning the *vajra*; for even the text regarding the *vajra* has scope, since it is stated that "it is called *vajra* because of its warding off (*varjana*) [of evil]. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the *vajra*, and that he alone possesses the fitness for the knowledge that produces liberation.
Thus concludes the section concerning trembling.
In both these passages, the name "Light" (jyotis), which is not well-known in either context, is construed as referring to Brahman,
because of the mention of seeing the Light.

Is it not the case that this light is indeed the individual soul (jīva)? For there are marks of the soul, such as "he is common" (*sa samānaḥ*), and the scriptural statement, "this world. Furthermore, after stating that the self is light through the passage beginning with "the sun is his light," the text asks, "Which is the self? and then records the description of light. That [description] cannot belong to Viṣṇu, because of passages such as "the sun does not shine there. Nor can it be argued that the one for whom the sun and other lights are stated to be his light must simply be the individual soul.

Having stated that the Supreme Self possesses the nature of light in the passage "of that very [Self]," and having addressed the question "Which is the Self? by declaring that the Self is Viṣṇu because He is the Light mentioned in the Veda, it follows that—since the Supreme Self is eternally existent as being devoid of rising, setting, and so forth—the restrictive statement "by the sun alone this [person shines]" and so on would be inappropriate. Furthermore, this is because there is a recognition of the very same meaning in the text: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. Therefore, the opponent's position—that this light is the individual soul (jīva) alone, and thus the citation of the ancient Brahman-text is incorrect—is reached. To this, the author states the Sūtra: *na ca smārtamataddharmābhilāpāt* || 1.3.18 || [The light is] not the one taught in the Smṛti, because there is a mention of attributes other than those [belonging to it]. (Sūtra 1.3.18) This means: the light under discussion is not the one described in the Smṛti (the *Yoga-sūtra*), because attributes contrary to its own are mentioned here. For instance, the Smṛti describes the light as being subject to rising and setting, whereas the present text speaks of a light that is eternal and free from such changes. Moreover, the Smṛti identifies that light with the individual soul (*jīva*), while the present text identifies it with the Supreme Self. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the word "light" (*jyotis*) is used in the Smṛti in a figurative sense to denote the mind (*manas*), whereas here it is used in its primary sense to denote the Supreme Lord. "Because of the vision of light" (jyotirdarśanāt). This is its meaning: That which is designated by the word "light" as "this light within" is Viṣṇu alone, not the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the vision [of scripture]; that is to say, because of the scriptural statement that Viṣṇu alone is the light.

And thus, Viṣṇu alone is this light, because the scriptural term "light" (jyotis) refers exclusively to Viṣṇu; for it is only when the primary meaning is impossible that a secondary meaning can be accepted. Nor can the individual soul (jīva) be accepted as the meaning—even in a secondary sense—under the view of Viṣṇu, on the grounds that moving between both worlds would be untenable for him; for even in that case, his existence [in those worlds] is established by the authority of the text "with the intelligent Self" (prājñena ātmanā), and thus there is no obstacle to accepting the primary meaning. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the indicative marks (liṅga) stated in the passage beginning with "this world" (imaṃ lokam).

Since those [passages] are also capable of being accommodated by having their meaning internalized (*antarṇīta*), there is no contradiction with the luminosity of the sun and other celestial bodies; for that [luminosity] is admitted to belong to the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor is there a failure to designate luminosity on the grounds that the soul is already well-known through its own self-luminosity (*svayaṃ-jyotiṣṭva*) and is thus unfit to be the subject of a question. Furthermore, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is not untenable, as it serves to indicate the primacy of that [soul] among the various forms of Brahmanic light. Alternatively, it excludes others, since such exclusion is impossible given the existence of speech and the other organs.

Furthermore, the statement that the Lord is "light" (jyotis) in a specific sense should be understood as intending that there is no other light during His sleep. Therefore, it is established that this light is Viṣṇu, and thus the status of Viṣṇu previously demonstrated in the aphorism *jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt* is not contradicted.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
In both these cases, the term "ether" (ākāśa), which is not well-established as referring to the Brahman, is harmonized with the Brahman:
"The ether [is Brahman], because of its designation as being different from other things, and so forth."

Now, in the passage "This indeed is that which is called space," the term *ākāśa* must refer to the well-known physical ether (*prasiddhākāśa*). This is because the word is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of ether, whereas it is only etymological (*yogika*) when applied to Viṣṇu. Furthermore, conventional meaning takes precedence over etymological meaning. If one were to abandon the well-known ether and accept Viṣṇu based on the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being the support of all, there would be a contradiction with the two particles "vai" and "nāma" used in the text. On the other hand, since the mere quality of being the sustainer of names and forms is well-established for the ether, there is no contradiction regarding those particles in that view.

In the case of Viṣṇu, both [the attributes]—being Viṣṇu and being the sustainer thereof—are unestablished. In the case of Ākāśa, however, only the quality of being the sustainer thereof is unestablished; thus there is a disparity. Since the mark of being the sustainer of name and form is possible for Ākāśa because it is the material cause (upādāna), but not for Viṣṇu, the Sūtra says [in response]:

"Ākāśa [is Viṣṇu], because of the designation of being something other [than the unmanifest], etc. The Ākāśa mentioned in the Śruti passage, "Indeed, He is named Ākāśa," is Viṣṇu alone; it is not the unmanifest (avyākṛta) ether. Why? Because of the designation of being something other, etc.; for in the sentence "That which is within them," there is stated Viṣṇu’s state of being distinct from name and form (the meaning of "otherness"), as well as His being Brahman and His immortality, which are included by the word "etc."—this is the meaning.

Thus, because of the existence of the two aforementioned reasons; because being devoid of name and form is established by scripture as its defining characteristic through the statement "He is colorless" (*avarṇa*); because there is no contradiction between the two particles [in the phrase] "One alone supports," since this is not an unfamiliar claim; and because scriptural renown is more authoritative than worldly renown, it is that [scriptural entity] alone which must be accepted—on the contrary, if it were space (*ākāśa*), there would be a contradiction precisely in its inclusion as having name and form. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the space, and He alone is the support of all.
Thus ends the section concerning space (ākāśādhikaraṇa).
Here, the mark of being the seer of dreams and so forth is shown to be consistent with Brahman, [as stated in the sūtra]:
"Because of the difference between deep sleep and departure."

But surely this must be the individual soul (jīva), the seer of dreams and so forth, because [the attributes] are well-known of it; because, due to the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord, the mark of being "unattached" cannot possibly apply even to the individual soul in its primary sense; because Viṣṇu, being bodiless, cannot be the seer of dreams and so forth; because even if that which resides in the cause can exist in the effect, that which resides in the effect cannot reside in the cause; and because the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord is established precisely by the otherwise inexplicable grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the two qualifying epithets.

Just as the treasury, though a quality not common to the king, resides in the minister, so too, by the force of scripture, it is possible that non-attachment—an attribute not common to the Lord—resides in the individual soul (jīva). This being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

Regarding the sūtra *suṣuptyutkrāntyorbhedeneti* ("On account of the difference in deep sleep and departure"): its meaning is as follows. The one who sees whatever he may see there [in the state of dream], as stated in the Śruti, is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), not the individual soul (*jīva*). Why? Because the reason—"on account of the mark of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) declared in the text 'for this person is unattached' (*asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ')"—must be supplied from outside [the sūtra]. Now, one might object that even for the individual soul, the declaration of non-attachment is possible due to its non-difference from the Lord; therefore, it is said: "on account of [the difference in] deep sleep," and so forth.

And likewise, in the contexts of deep sleep and departure, it is stated that [the soul] is "completely embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā saṃpariṣvaktaḥ*) and "mounted upon the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanānvārūḍhaḥ*). Because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) are thus described as distinct—that is, as different—it follows that there is no identity between the two. This is the meaning.

Thus, by the mark of "unattached-ness" (*asaṅgatva*), this [state] is possible for Viṣṇu alone, but not for the individual soul (*jīva*), because the latter is bound. Furthermore, since the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord is absent—given that their distinction is declared in the contexts of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and departure (*utkrānti*)—it follows from the mark of unattached-ness as it relates to the relationship of quality and qualified that Viṣṇu alone is the seer of dreams and so forth. Moreover, unattached-ness resides in the Lord alone; therefore, the statement "for this person is indeed unattached" refers exclusively to the Lord, as there is no evidence to the contrary. Thus it is established that unattached-ness does not reside in another, just like the wealth of a king.
Thus concludes the section on deep sleep.
In this [section], the term "Brāhmaṇa" is connected with the word "brahmāṇi," because of words such as "pati" (husband) and others.

Surely this Brāhmaṇa must be Viriñca (Brahmā), because the word "unborn" (*aja*) is heard many times in reference to him. It should not be argued that the word "unborn" finds its scope in Viṣṇu through the application of the quality of being unborn; for the word "unborn," when recited in conjunction with the word "Brāhmaṇa," has no scope in Viṣṇu. Nor should it be argued that the word "unborn" finds scope in Viṣṇu due to its being recited alongside the word "self-born" (*ātmaja*); for the word "self" (*ātman*) is also applied to Viriñca, as seen in such passages as "the self is Viriñca."

Nor should it be said that Viriñca is not [the Supreme Being] because the mark of being "unattached" finds no scope [in him]; for since Viṣṇu and Viriñca are non-different, the mark of being unattached is possible in him as well. Thus, when it is argued that the previously stated eternal majesty of Viṣṇu is untenable because Viriñca is a Brāhmaṇa, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But on account of the word 'Brāhmaṇa' [being applied to Him], [He is the Supreme Being]. (Brahmasūtra 1.3.20) This means that the designation "Brāhmaṇa" applies to the Supreme Lord, and therefore His eternal majesty is indeed established. Furthermore, the term "Brāhmaṇa" here refers to one who is characterized by the quality of Brahman (purity/omniscience), and not merely to a member of the social class. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "from words such as 'Lord' (pati) and so forth": the Brāhmaṇa mentioned in the Śruti text, "This is the eternal glory of the Brāhmaṇa," is indeed Viṣṇu alone, not Viriñca (Brahmā). Why? Because of words such as "Lord" and so forth; that is to say, because of Śruti passages expressing universal sovereignty and other such attributes, such as "the Lord of all."

And thus, because words such as "Lord" (*pati*) and so forth exist in the revealed scriptures (*śruti*) as they have been pointed out, there is no contradiction with the word "unborn" (*aja*) even if Viṣṇu is a Brāhmaṇa. This is because the word *aja* is justified through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "he who is not born" (*na jāyate*). Furthermore, since the word "Brāhmaṇa" is justified by the derivation "he who is addressed by the Veda" (*brāhmaṇā vedena bhaṇyate*), it does not exclude the application of the word *aja*. Nor is it possible for lordship and the like to belong to Viriñca simply because of non-difference [from Viṣṇu], for there is no evidence for such non-difference; moreover, the two words "Brāhmaṇa" and "aja" are explained in the manner already stated.

Since there is an abundance of scriptural texts regarding their differentiation—such as "From that, these were born"—there is no evidence for their non-difference. Consequently, it is established that this Brāhmaṇa is indeed Viṣṇu himself, possessing eternal majesty and other attributes.
Thus ends the section concerning the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.
Śrīḥ.
Om. May there be auspiciousness. May Hari protect you.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the first chapter.
In this pāda, it is demonstrated that even those words well-known in other [contexts] apply exclusively to Viṣṇu when taken as a whole, by means of specific reasons.
Here, words whose meanings are otherwise established—such as "inferiority" (avara) and "suffering" (duḥkha)—are shown to be in harmony with Brahman.

"If it be argued that for some there is also what is inferential, we say no; because [the text] shows that [the word 'small'] is understood as referring to what was presented in the metaphor of the body, and Scripture also demonstrates this. (Sūtra 1.2.24)

Objection: Is it not the case that Pradhāna and so forth alone are denoted by terms such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) and the like? For those terms are well-known to refer to Pradhāna and its derivatives. Nor can they have application to Viṣṇu; for in that context, the Unmanifest is heard to be subordinate to the Puruṣa, whereas it is impossible for Viṣṇu to be so, as it would contradict the authoritative testimony: "Neither one equal to nor superior to Him is seen. Furthermore, this is established by the Sāṃkhya-inferred arguments such as: "The Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are produced from causes similar to themselves, because they are effects, like a jar."

Furthermore, since the Unmanifest (avyakta) is heard to possess supreme greatness, the Pradhāna alone must be denoted by the word "Unmanifest. Moreover, because [the Unmanifest] is perceived as being subject to suffering and bondage, the individual souls (kṣetrajña) alone are denoted by the word "jīva," and not Viṣṇu. Since, for these reasons, certain Vedic branches state that the Pradhāna and so forth are denoted by words such as "Unmanifest," the previously asserted claim that all words denote the Supreme Lord is incorrect. To this, the following aphorism is stated:

"Even that which is inferential [is taught] by some; if this is argued, it is not so, because [the scripture] shows that what is grasped is that which was placed in the form of the body's metaphor, and because it declares [this]. This is the meaning: the word "api" (even) has the sense of "only," and "ca" (and) is for the purpose of collecting the Smṛti. Since "that which is inferential"—meaning precisely the Pradhāna and so forth imagined through the inference of the Sāṃkhyas—is expressed by terms such as "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) found in the passages of certain reciters of the Vedas (e.g., "From the Unmanifest, the Puruṣa"), therefore it is not logical that Viṣṇu is denotable by all words. If this is argued, it is not so; for Viṣṇu alone is denotable by terms such as "unmanifest."

It is not Pradhāna and so forth. Why? Because of the Śruti stating "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and the Smṛti stating "the Unmanifest is the Imperishable" (*akṣara*). [The word] "shows" means that it establishes that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as "Unmanifest. If one asks, "How then is the term 'Unmanifest' and so forth used elsewhere? it is said: "Because of the grasping of what is set forth through the metaphor of the body," and so on. The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of contempt. Thus, [it refers to] the grasping [of the Supreme Self] through what is presented by way of the metaphor of the body; just as the body is dependent upon the Person (the Self).

Likewise, because the body is contemptible by virtue of its dependence on the Supreme Self; and because, in reality, it is the Supreme Self alone—who is bodiless and resides within the primary matter (pradhāna) and so forth—who is grasped by terms such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta); thus, the meaning is that the conventional usage of terms like "Unmanifest" for other things such as primordial nature (prakṛti) occurs solely due to their connection with the Supreme Self.

Thus, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is denoted by words such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta), because He is the master of the grounds for applying those terms, and because He is the ultimate locus of those grounds of application in their highest sense; for since the grounds for applying those terms depend upon the Lord, He too is accepted as their primary referent. Therefore, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is the one denoted by words such as "the Unmanifest."
But that [knowledge] is subtle because of its fitness for such a state.

Now, it may be granted that, by the force of their usage in the Śruti and Smṛti, words such as "unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth denote the Blessed Lord; nevertheless, even so, they would not possess the highest primary sense (*parama-mukhyatva*) therein, because their usage in the Śruti and Smṛti is possible even for a non-primary referent. To this objection, the Sūtra states:

"But that [Pradhāna] is subtle because it is worthy of that [designation]. This is the meaning: since that which is "subtle" (sūkṣma) is indeed subtle, denotable by such terms as "unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth; why? Because it is worthy of that—because that subtle entity possesses the fitness to be the ground for the application of the term "unmanifest. And in this context, subtlety belongs to Viṣṇu alone; therefore, the meaning is that He alone is denotable by the term "unmanifest."

Thus, since the excellence of subtlety—which serves as the basis for the application of the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) and is conducive to its unmanifest nature—belongs to Viṣṇu alone; and since it is improper to apply a secondary sense where the primary sense exists; and because of the scriptural text, "That which is subtle"; therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as "unmanifest."
Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful.

Granted that the primary denotation of the nominal stems *avyakta* and so forth may indeed belong to Viṣṇu alone; nevertheless, in passages such as "the Puruṣa is higher than the unmanifest" (*avyaktāt puruṣaḥ paraḥ*), it is not proper to understand the words *avyakta* and the rest as referring to Viṣṇu. For if that were the case, those texts would become purposeless, as their meanings would be impossible with respect to the Lord due to contradiction with authoritative evidence such as: the scriptural statement "higher than the Great One" (*mahataḥ param*); the use of the ablative case in "than the unmanifest" (*avyaktāt*), which expresses a limit in relation to something inferior; the direct scriptural statement "he is inferior" (*so 'varaḥ*); and the scriptural statements regarding living beings, such as "they are miserable and bound," which would contradict evidence like "He is free from all defects" (*niraniṣṭaḥ*). Thus, those [passages] would result in meaninglessness.

Thus, since it has been argued that—due to this sublation—the terms "Unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth must necessarily be understood as denoting the Pradhāna and its like, even if only in a secondary sense, the following was set forth as a Sūtra:

"Because it is dependent on that, it is meaningful. This is the meaning [of the sūtra]. The word "and" (*ca*) from the preceding sūtra, "And [the scripture] shows," is carried over here. The entire collection of words denoting the high, the low, suffering, bondage, and so forth, applies to the Supreme Self alone; they are "meaningful," that is, they possess a meaning consisting of a ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and are not meaningless. Why? Because they are dependent on that—that is, because those attributes such as being high or low, which reside in primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the like, are dependent upon the Lord. Thus, the sense is that even by virtue of the ground for application consisting in being the owner of what resides in another, the employment of words such as "high" and "low" with respect to the Lord is entirely appropriate.

And thus, since it is accepted that whatever depends upon a quality for its designation is called the "possessor of that quality" (guṇin)—and because the Lord is the substratum (adhikaraṇa) for the ground of application (pravṛttinimitta) which depends upon Him—it follows that He too is the denoter of that [ground]. Consequently, there is no pointlessness in the entire collection of words denoting both qualities and defects, such as "unmanifest" (avyakta), being endowed with the object known as the ground of application when referring to Him alone. Therefore, it is established that the collection of words such as "the highest" (para) and "the lower" (avara) is appropriately applied to Viṣṇu.
And because [the Lord] is not mentioned as being an object of knowledge.

Thus, because the terms "unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth primarily denote the Blessed Lord alone—due to the two excellences of application mentioned in the first and second [sūtras] regarding Vedic and Smṛti usage—and because the primary meaning must be accepted in the absence of any sublation; and because the sublation by the scriptural passage concerning inferiority and so forth has already been removed in the third [sūtra], the sūtra now states the following to establish, by another line of reasoning, that the Blessed Lord alone is the denotable object of the terms "unmanifest" and so forth, as previously asserted.

"And because of the non-statement that [others] are to be known. This is its meaning: because it is Viṣṇu alone who is stated to be the object of knowledge for the sake of liberation in the passage, "Know Him alone as the One"; because others are not so stated; and because, on the contrary, they are stated to be things to be abandoned in the passage, "Cast off [them]. The meaning is that by the words "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth occurring here, Viṣṇu alone is to be denoted.

And thus, since the aforementioned scriptural statements declare that Viṣṇu alone is the object of knowledge for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), whereas Pradhāna and the rest lack that status; and since the Vedas, which have liberation as their fruit, are engaged solely in making known Brahman—the object of the knowledge that causes liberation; and since the fact that every sentence has Him as its ultimate purport is established by such statements as "in the beginning and at the end" and so forth; it must be accepted that He alone, whose knowledge leads to liberation, is the subject to be propounded. Since there is no reason to abandon the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) which is self-evident, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as *avyakta* (the unmanifest) and the like, and not Pradhāna or anything else.
If it is argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one does not [speak].

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that there is no scriptural statement regarding the Pradhāna being known for the sake of liberation? For there exists the statement, 'without beginning and without end'. Having raised this objection, the author states the sūtra as a response:

"If it be argued that [the scripture] says so, we reply: 'No, for it is the Wise One. This is its meaning: Now, one might object that the Kāṭhaka passage beginning with "without beginning or end" speaks of the Pradhāna—that is, the Pradhāna is what is being propounded—and by the word "it," its status as an object of knowledge is established. If this is said, we say: no. Why? Because (hi), since (yataḥ), it is the Wise One—the Supreme Self alone denoted by the word "Wise"—who is propounded there, not the Pradhāna. Therefore, the meaning is that its status as an object of knowledge should not be considered.

And thus, even though Viṣṇu is stated to be superior to everything, the superiority of the "Great One" (mahat) over everything gross is established by implication through the Śruti text, "greater than the great. Therefore, it is established that by the force of this statement, it is the Blessed Lord alone—and not anything else—who is to be known for the sake of liberation.
Because of the context.

Now, an objection may be raised: since we have already admitted that the specific mark of the Pradhāna—namely, its being "greater than the great" (mahat)—is not used in its primary sense, there would be no reason to accept that the passage concerning "without beginning, without end," and so forth, refers to Viṣṇu; rather, it follows that the Pradhāna alone is spoken of here. To this, the Sūtra replies:

"Because of the context (prakaraṇāt). The meaning of this is as follows: by the force of the context of the three Vaiśvānara passages, the Supreme Intellect (Prājña) alone is to be understood here; this is the sense.

And thus, because this section is Vaiṣṇava—since it states that the worshiper of the meaning of this section attains the station of Viṣṇu—and because of the scriptural text, "He [travels] the path," it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the subject to be expounded in this section.
And thus there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone.
He introduces the sūtra which, by means of another reason, refutes the claim that anything else could be the subject matter of statements such as "beginningless and endless."

"Furthermore, there is the presentation and the question of only three. This is its meaning: the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because" for the purpose of combining arguments; the word "eva" (only/just) refers to the threefold nature of the categories. Thus, because only these three—namely, the gratification of the ancestors (*pitṛsaumanasya*), the heavenly realm (*svargya*), and the supreme Self (*paramātman*)—are involved, the question was asked by the seer Naciketas to Yama regarding only these three. Furthermore, only their presentation and the corresponding answers are seen in this section.
Therefore, the meaning is that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is not what is being propounded here.

Furthermore, because such questions and answers regarding these three alone are seen in that context; and because there is no contradiction with the statement "a request for what is not understood"; therefore, by the reason already stated, it is established that the passage beginning with "without beginning or end" has the Blessed One as its subject matter.
And like the Great [Self].

Now, it is argued that it is incorrect to say that Viṣṇu alone is the primary denotation of words such as "unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth, because those terms are well-known to denote the Pradhāna and other such entities. Nor can it be said that the primary status of those words resides in Him alone on the grounds that the ground for their application (pravṛttinimitta) exists in the Lord in its primary sense; for it has never been observed that a word's primary denotation must reside in that where it is already established, nor that a thing's primary status consists in having a primary ground for its application.
Since, in the absence of an illustrative example, it is impossible to establish that [the Lord] possesses a superior causal agency, the Sūtra states:

"And like the word 'Great' (mahat)": this is its meaning. The particle "ca" (and) serves to collect the illustrative example. Just as the word "Great" occurring in such passages as "the Great, all-pervading Self" refers exclusively to Viṣṇu and not to the principle of Mahat-tattva, so too it is with words such as "Unmanifest" (avyakta). This is the sense.

And thus, since the word *mahat* itself serves as the illustrative example, there is no contradiction with common usage. Although the word *mahat* is well-known in the Śruti in the sense of the *mahat-tattva*, it is accepted that its primary denotation applies to the Blessed Lord because it possesses the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) known as "supreme greatness. Similarly, although words such as *avyakta* are well-known elsewhere, they are accepted as having their supreme primary application in Him alone because He possesses the grounds for application such as "supreme unmanifestness.
Thus, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the denotable object of words such as *avyakta*.
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction.

[Objection: "Granted that even if there is an excellence (*atiśaya*) as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of these terms] to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), words such as 'the Unmanifest' (*avyakta*) do not have their primary sense (*paramamukhya*) there. This is because, due to the absence of established usage (*prasiddhi*) therein, they lack even the status of being denotable (*vācyatā*). Rather, like the word 'lion' applied to a man of great endurance, they possess only a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*). Thus, it is incorrect to say 'and like the word *mahat*' (BrSū 1.4.6). For while the word *mahat*—being by its very nature a designation for the Lord (*bhagavat*)—can attain primary status through the abundance of its ground for application, this is not the case for words such as 'the Unmanifest,' since they lack the status of being designations for the Lord at all; thus there is a disparity. To this, the author of the Sūtras provides the following reply: *na vā prakaraṇabhedāt parovarīyastvādivat* || BrSū 1.4.7 || [Response: "Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of 'higher than the high' (*parovarīyastva*) and so on. Just as in the passage beginning with "The ether is indeed the high" (*ākāśo vai nāma nityaḥ paraḥ*), the word 'high' (*para*) is shown to denote the Lord through the context of the Upanishadic discourse (*brahmakāṇḍa*), despite the absence of established worldly usage; so too, in the context of the Upanishads, words such as 'the Unmanifest' denote the Lord.
