"Like the *camasa*, because there is no distinction. This is its meaning: Just as in the case of the *camasa*—where the word *camasa*, though well-known [in common usage] as a sacrificial vessel, denotes the head by the force of the scriptural text "This is that head"—so too, although words such as *avyakta* (the unmanifest) are well-known to denote the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth, they denote Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the scriptural text, "All names... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5]. Now, even if that is so, why do they denote Viṣṇu? To this it is said: "Because there is no distinction. The meaning is that, according to the scriptural text "All names... [ibid.], there is no distinction between this [Viṣṇu] and [other things] due to the scriptural statement [that He is everything].

And thus, although the word *camasa* is well-known as a specific sacrificial vessel and is not well-known as a denoter of the head, its status as a denoter of the head is established by the force of the scriptural statement, "This is His head. Similarly, although words such as *avyakta* are not well-known as denoters of the Blessed Lord, it is possible to ascertain their denotative power for the Blessed Lord through the force of the scriptural injunction in the form of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), "They are names [of the Supreme]. This is because there is no difference between those two scriptural statements—namely, "This is His head" and "They are names"—in their status as injunctions.
Consequently, since Hari indeed becomes denotable by words such as "the unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth, it is established that his being denotable by all words is logically consistent.
Thus ends the section concerning those who rely on inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa).

In this [section], it is established that words such as *jyotiṣṭoma* and others, which are well-known to denote specific ritual acts and their constituent parts, actually refer to the Blessed Lord. "But because it begins with light, for thus some read."

Now, an objection may be raised: words such as *jyotis* (light) and so forth do not denote Viṣṇu, but rather denote rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and their constituent parts, because they are well-known in that very sense. If these were to denote Viṣṇu, there would arise the contradiction known as "non-existence" (*tadabhāva*), due to the absence of anything that could express time, ritual action, sequence, and so on. Consequently, since there would be no other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to express those [ritual elements], it would follow that the performance of enjoined rites would be abandoned. To this, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the word] 'Light' [denotes Him], because of the teaching of what is not seen. (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.24) This means: the word *jyotis* does indeed denote Viṣṇu. Why? Because of the teaching of what is not seen—that is, because of the scriptural declaration of the unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa-phala*). For example, the scripture says: "He who knows this becomes light itself" (*sa ya etad evaṃ vidvān amum lokam abhisambhavati sa jyotir eva*). Since the attainment of the world of light is an unseen result, the word *jyotis* must refer to the Supreme Being, who is the cause of that attainment. Furthermore, the word *jyotis* denotes Viṣṇu because of the connection with the term "Self" (*ātman*), as in: "The Self is hidden in all beings, and He is the Light beyond darkness" (*tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvam tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti*). Also, because of the mention of "bliss" (*ānanda*), as in: "He is bliss, He is Brahman" (*ānando brahma iti*). Moreover, because of the mention of "immortality," as in: "He is the immortal, the fearless" (*eṣa hy evānandayāti*). And because of the mention of "freedom from fear," as in: "When one sees Him, the formless, the bodiless, the colorless, the pure, then he transcends all sorrows" (*yadā paśyaḥ paśyate rukmavarṇam kartāram īśam puruṣam brahmayonim | tadā vidvān puṇyapāpe vidhūya nirañjanaḥ paramaṃ sāmyam upaiti*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme goal," as in: "He is the supreme goal, the highest support" (*sa eṣa sarvasyeśānaḥ sarvasyādhipatiḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme ruler," as in: "He is the Lord of all, the King of all" (*sa eṣa sarveśvaraḥ sa eṣa bhūtādhipatiḥ*). Furthermore, because of the mention of "the supreme lordship," as in: "He is the supreme lord, the supreme refuge" (*sa eṣa sarveśvaraḥ sa eṣa parameśvaraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme abode," as in: "He is the supreme abode, the supreme light" (*sa eṣa parāyaṇaḥ sa eṣa jyotiḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme light," as in: "He is the supreme light, the supreme truth" (*sa eṣa satyaḥ sa eṣa jyotiḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme truth," as in: "He is the supreme truth, the supreme reality" (*sa eṣa satyam sa eṣa paramārthaḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme reality," as in: "He is the supreme reality, the supreme essence" (*sa eṣa paramārthaḥ sa eṣa sāraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme essence," as in: "He is the supreme essence, the supreme bliss" (*sa eṣa sāraḥ sa eṣa ānandaḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme bliss," as in: "He is the supreme bliss, the supreme peace" (*sa eṣa ānandaḥ sa eṣa śāntiḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme peace," as in: "He is the supreme peace, the supreme liberation" (*sa eṣa śāntiḥ sa eṣa mokṣaḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme liberation," as in: "He is the supreme liberation, the supreme freedom" (*sa eṣa mokṣaḥ sa eṣa nirvāṇaḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme freedom," as in: "He is the supreme freedom, the supreme state" (*sa eṣa nirvāṇaḥ sa eṣa padaṃ paramam*). And because of the mention of "the supreme state," as in: "He is the supreme state, the supreme goal" (*sa eṣa padaṃ paramaṃ sa eṣa gatiḥ parā*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme goal," as in: "He is the supreme goal, the supreme refuge" (*sa eṣa gatiḥ parā sa eṣa śaraṇam paramam*). And because of the mention of "the supreme refuge," as in: "He is the supreme refuge, the supreme protector" (*sa eṣa śaraṇam paramaṃ sa eṣa trātā parameśvaraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme protector," as in: "He is the supreme protector, the supreme master" (*sa eṣa trātā parameśvaraḥ sa eṣa svāmī paraḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme master," as in: "He is the supreme master, the supreme lord" (*sa eṣa svāmī paraḥ sa eṣa patiḥ paraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme lord," as in: "He is the supreme lord, the supreme deity" (*sa eṣa patiḥ paraḥ sa eṣa devaḥ paraḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme deity," as in: "He is the supreme deity, the supreme god" (*sa eṣa devaḥ paraḥ sa eṣa suraḥ paraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme god," as in: "He is the supreme god, the supreme divinity" (*sa eṣa suraḥ paraḥ sa eṣa daivataṃ paramam*). And because of the mention of "the supreme divinity," as in: "He is the supreme divinity, the supreme being" (*sa eṣa daivataṃ paramaṃ sa eṣa bhūtaṃ paramam*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme being," as in: "He is the supreme being, the supreme soul" (*sa eṣa bhūtaṃ paramaṃ sa eṣa ātmā paraḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme soul," as in: "He is the supreme soul, the supreme self" (*sa eṣa ātmā paraḥ sa eṣa puruṣaḥ paraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the supreme person," as in: "He is the supreme person, the supreme Puruṣa" (*sa eṣa puruṣaḥ paraḥ sa eṣa pūrṇaḥ paraḥ*). And because of the mention of "the supreme fullness," as in: "He is the supreme fullness, the supreme infinite" (*sa eṣa pūrṇaḥ paraḥ sa eṣa anantaḥ paraḥ*). Also, because of the mention of "the

"But because [the passage] begins with light, for thus some read. This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) has the sense of "only. That which is denoted by the words "light" and so forth mentioned in such sentences as "One should sacrifice with light" (jyotiṣā yajeta) is Brahman alone, and not the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice or the like. Why? Because (hi), since (yasmāt), some followers of a Vedic branch (eke śākhinaḥ), having begun [the section] with "This one... (eṣa imam...), read and recite that very Hari as the referent of all words in the passage "So many indeed are these... (tāvā etā...). Therefore is the meaning.

And thus, Hari alone is denoted by words such as "light" (*jyotis*) and so forth; for, beginning with the passage "He [entered] this world," it is stated that "these are those," thereby declaring His denotability by all words. Nor is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) intended in the Śruti, since the application of terms such as "the hundred-versed ones" (*śatarcī*) is explained as being through figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nor should it be argued that because these words are conventionally established (*ruḍha*) elsewhere, they cannot be the subject of the primary purport (*mahātātparya*), whereas Viṣṇu—the conventional meaning—is merely the subject of a secondary purport (*avāntaratātparya*) due to being a non-primary object.

Therefore, because the primary meaning [of the word "Śatarcin"] is set aside by this etymological application (yoga), one asks: "Why is that? It is because it is understood that they designate this Supreme Self—which is primarily of etymological meaning—by names such as "Śatarcin" and so forth, but they do not designate the sages [as Śatarcin] even though [the term] has a conventional meaning (rūḍhi), since the sages are not the primary object of the Great Intention (mahātātparya). Thus, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as "Jyotis" (Light) and the like.
And because there is instruction regarding [the Lord] as a mental construct, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth.

Are words such as *jyotis* (light) and others denoters of the Supreme Self by convention (*rūḍhi*), or by etymological derivation (*yoga*)? Not the first, because that convention does not exist and because the perfection of all attributes (*guṇapūrti*) remains unestablished. Nor the second, because it is impossible for an etymological meaning to override a conventional one. Furthermore, even etymological derivation is not possible; for in the case of words like *jyotiṣṭoma*, the derivation must be stated in the form "the soma-sacrifice of lights" (*jyotiṣāṃ stomaḥ*). Indeed, derivation is not possible unless it is admitted that words such as *stoma* refer to something other than their primary sense, which would result in the fallacy of repeating the Lord’s own names.

If it is admitted that those words [jyotis, etc. have another referent, then what specific offense has been committed by the words "Jyotiṣṭoma" and so forth? Consequently, since words such as "jyotis" do not denote the Lord, the application of the *samanvaya-sūtra* would be untenable; this being the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the following was formulated as a sūtra:

"And because of the teaching of [divine] imagination, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. This is its meaning: the word "ca" (and) signifies either "only" or "conjunction. Thus, just as in the case of honey and so forth—meaning that even though words such as "honey" occurring in the Madhu-vidyā and other contexts denote Viṣṇu, there is no contradiction—likewise, even when it is accepted that the Supreme Self is denotable by all words, there is no contradiction with the absence of [ordinary] action and so forth. Why? Because, having accepted that words possess the functions of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) elsewhere, one accepts the function of great etymological derivation (*mahā-yoga-vṛtti*) in the case of the Lord; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

And why is that? Because of the teaching of figurative designation (*kalpanopadeśāt*). For it has been stated that Viṣṇu’s being denotable by all words is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), which is designated by the term "figurative designation" (as in *prāṇa ṛcaḥ*). And the meaning is that this [designation] is impossible without the "great etymological function" (*mahāyogavṛtti*), which consists in his possessing both the primary and secondary meanings of all words.

And thus, just as in the Madhu-vidyā, although the instruction is given for the worship of the Supreme Self through the objects such as honey by means of the passage beginning with "That indeed is honey, that is the sun," there is no contradiction due to the absence of those [objects] because of the lack of words denoting worldly honey and so forth; for it is accepted that the words "honey" and so on function with respect to the Lord and other [meanings] through the mode of great metaphorical application (mahā-yoga-vṛtti), without setting aside their conventional usage elsewhere. Likewise, even when it is accepted that the Supreme Self is denotable by all words, it is still admitted that something else may also be the object propounded by a particular sentence.

This is because another case-ending is accepted for that purpose. Nor does it follow that there is an absence of the object (karman) and other factors; nor is there an impossibility of origination, nor the undesirable consequence that all [words] would be denotative of the agent (vidhātṛ). Therefore, it is established that Hari is denoted by words expressive of the object and its accessories.
Thus concludes the section concerning the commencement with light.

Here, the syntactic coordination is established between words denoting things qualified by the number "plurality"—whether through the nominal stem or through the suffix—and words denoting the locus and the thing located.
[This is so] even because of the inclusion of numbers, due to their manifold nature and because of their surplus.

Objection: Viṣṇu cannot be the referent of words such as *pañcajana* (the five people), for what else could it be? This is because such words denote objects qualified by the number "many," and plurality is incompatible with God, who possesses unique attributes. Nor can it be argued that even though He Himself lacks plurality, the word denoting plurality applies to Him because He is the controller of the plurality residing in others, thereby allowing God to acquire the unique attribute of being the controller of plurality. For we do not observe the use of a word denoting plurality in reference to a king, even when he has brought many people under his control.

Nor is there a possibility of [the word "Brahman"] functioning [metaphorically] even when its primary sense is not perceived, as is the case with words such as "inferior" (*avara*). For, once it is established by the force of scriptural texts such as "He is inferior" (*so 'varaḥ*) that the word "inferior" denotes [Brahman], one must admit that being the regulator of inferiority is merely the occasion for its application (*nimitta*). However, in the present context, no such regulator exists; because the statement "That state which all the Vedas seek" can be subject to restriction, it lacks the power to serve as a regulator.

Since the two forms—the individual self (ātmā) and the inner self (antarātman)—are established by authoritative means for every body, duality is possible in such passages as "The two who drink the Truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*). However, because there is no evidence for a multiplicity of forms within each body, plurality is untenable. Consequently, it is argued that the term "five people" (*pañcajana*) and similar words cannot denote [the five elements]. This being the position reached, the Sūtra states: [1.4.12]... [Sūtra follows].

"Nor [is there a contradiction] because of the inclusion of a number, due to their manifold nature and because of the excess. This is its meaning: "Because of the inclusion of a number" means because of the expression of a plural number in the phrase "in whom the five groups of five" (*yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ*). Furthermore, "because of the designation of the relationship between locus and located" in the phrase "in whom" (*yasmin*), there is no contradiction in Viṣṇu being denoted by words such as "five groups of five. Why? Because of their manifold nature (*nānābhāvāt*); that is, because the Blessed Lord possesses many forms. And "because of the excess" (*atirekāt*); the meaning is that the form of the locus mentioned in "in whom" and the form of the located mentioned in "the five groups" are non-different despite having specific distinctions.

Thus, the Blessed Lord alone is that which is denoted by the word *pañcajana* and the like, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). Nor is there any impossibility regarding plurality; for, since there is no subverting evidence, plurality is established through His manifold forms for the purpose of governing the five classes of beings, beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Nor is there any impossibility regarding the relationship between the container and the contained, because His status as the substratum is proven by scripture in such passages as "The Blessed One in His own greatness" (*sve mahimni*). Thus it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one denoted by the word *pañcajana* and the like.
The vital breaths and so forth [are the objects of meditation], because of the remainder of the passage.

Granted that plurality and so forth may be logically established; nevertheless, since there is no specific reason for *pañcajana* to be Viṣṇu, and because the phrase "all the Vedas" is common [to many] and thus capable of being restricted [to a specific sense], it lacks the power of a definitive determinant. Therefore, even though plurality is possible, the conclusion reached is that Hari is not denoted by the word *pañcajana* and the like. To this, the author states the Sūtra:

"Prāṇa and the others [are meant] because of the remainder of the passage. This is its meaning: The five *pañcajana*s, who have been described as having the form of the Blessed Lord, are indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest. "Prāṇa and the others" refers to those designated in the accusative case—the vital breath, eye, ear, food, and mind—and these are to be understood as such. Why? Because of the remainder of the passage. And they are specifically particular forms of the Blessed Lord. Why? Because of the remainder of the passage beginning with "the breath of the breath," which establishes that the status of being the source of the vital breath (*prāṇa-prāṇatva*) and so forth is impossible for anyone other than Viṣṇu. This is the meaning.

And thus, because in the supplementary portion of that very sentence, "of that breath," it is stated that the breath and the others possess the status of being the "breath" (prāṇa), and because that [status] is a characteristic mark of Viṣṇu; therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words "five people" (pañcajana) and so forth.
According to some, [the ritual] is performed with light when food is not available.

Objection: Viṣṇu is not the one denoted by the term "pañcajana. For although the Prāṇas and others—mentioned in the Mādhyandina recension as being the "breath of breaths" (prāṇaprāṇa) and so forth—are indeed Viṣṇu, in the Kāṇva recension only four are mentioned in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). Consequently, the meaning of the phrase "in whom" (*yasmin*) from the preceding sentence must differ [from the meaning of the *pañcajanas*]. Furthermore, in this case as well, the supplementary passage must necessarily have a meaning distinct from "in whom," because a single entity cannot simultaneously possess the relationship of both container and contained. Therefore, since the *pañcajanas* are not Viṣṇu, [the Sūtra] reads: [The author] states the Sūtra: [1.4.12] *jyotiḥ* (Light).

"According to some, by means of light, even though food is not [explicitly] mentioned. This is its meaning: according to some, such as the followers of the Kāṇva school, in their recension, even though "food"—that is, the form of the Lord known as food—is not mentioned, the completion of the number five is to be understood by means of "light," that is, by the form of the Lord known as light.

And thus, even though in this supplementary statement "the food of food" has been mentioned, there is no lack of identity of subject matter with the phrase "that [is] the light of lights," which was stated somewhat further on, because both can be understood as referring to the number five. Therefore, it is established that Hari alone is the one denoted by words expressing the number of plurality.
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number.
Here, the concordance of the terms "ether" and so forth—which denote an intermediate cause—is established in Brahman:
"And [Brahman is the cause] because of the mention of ether and the rest as being designated as the cause."

Is it not the case that Viṣṇu is not denoted by words such as "ether" (ākāśa), because those [elements] are heard in scripture to be effects of the Self (ātman) and so forth? And such a relationship is not possible for the Supreme Self, according to the scriptural text, "He is not born. Furthermore, in the world, the relation of cause and effect is observed only between two distinct things, not between non-distinct ones; therefore, such a state of affairs is contradictory given the non-difference of the Self and ether. Nor should it be argued that the term "become" (saṃbhūta) is appropriate because the origination of ether and the rest is dependent upon Him, for we do not observe the use of the word "born" (jāta) with respect to the progenitor when a son is born.

If the ether (*ākāśa*) were the regulator of the production of forms residing elsewhere, the word "Self" (*ātman*) would be useless; consequently, the phrase "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*) would be syntactically disconnected. Therefore, since Viṣṇu alone—the primary cause denoted by the word "Self"—is the subject, and not the intermediate causes such as ether and the rest, this being the position reached, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"And because of the mention [of Him] as the cause in the case of ether and so forth, according to how He was described. This is its meaning: In passages such as "From the Self, ether was produced; from ether, air," although [ether and the rest] are effects, it is Viṣṇu alone who resides within ether and the other elements, being denoted by the words "ether" and so forth which signify intermediate causes in the form of causality. He is spoken of both as the cause and as the effect, but not as a mere elemental substance. Why? Because of the mention [of Him] exactly as He was described.

The meaning is that Viṣṇu is the one referred to in passages such as "He who is unheard from here," for He is designated by such characteristics as being unknown, since it is stated in the passage beginning with "Whom the ether does not know" that He possesses those very same attributes within the ether and other elements.

Thus, since He is an effect, Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the words "ether" and so forth found in scriptural passages such as "the ether was produced," which designate Him as the cause. This is because of the Śruti text, "All names [belong to Him]. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between His being the effect and His being the cause; for upon the production of the ether and other elements, the Lord becomes manifest within that ether, and His causality is established by His being the cause of the manifestation of the forms of air and the subsequent elements. Therefore, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words "ether" and so forth, which refer to Him as the intermediate cause.
Thus ends the section concerning space (ākāśādhikaraṇa).
In this regard, having raised the objection that the previously stated concordance of all words is impossible with respect to Viṣṇu by way of another interpretation, it is now refuted:
"Because of the drawing together."

Now, even so, it may be argued that it is not possible for the Blessed Lord to be denotable by all words. For if all words were to denote Him primarily, there would follow the absence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—whether in the form of verbal usage or in the form of acceptance and rejection—with respect to anything other than Him; and this would lead to the undesirable consequence of such transaction being lost. Furthermore, the restrictive determination that "the Supreme Self alone is primarily denotable by all words" would be untenable. This being the position reached, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: *na caikasya... (not so, because of the non-contradiction of the nature of things)*. (Brahmasūtra 2.3.1) This means: It is not the case that the Blessed Lord cannot be denoted by all words. Why? Because of the non-contradiction of the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). Just as the single moon is perceived by many people simultaneously, yet each perceives it according to their own capacity, so too, although the one Supreme Lord is the primary object denoted by all words, He is understood through those words in accordance with the respective capacities of the speakers and the listeners. There is no contradiction here, just as there is no contradiction when many people see the same moon. Nor does this imply the loss of worldly transaction, for the Lord, being the inner self (*antarātman*) of all, is the substratum of all linguistic usage; thus, all transactions involving acceptance and rejection proceed with respect to His limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which are the objects of ordinary experience. Therefore, the restriction that the Supreme Self alone is the primary denotation of all words is indeed established. Thus, the Blessed Lord is denotable by all words. ||| End of section ||| 2.3.1 ||| End of chapter ||| End of book ||| End of part ||| End of volume ||| End of work ||| End of series ||| End of Regarding the phrase "because of attraction" (*samākarṣāt*): its meaning is as follows. Since words that primarily denote the Supreme Self by their own inherent power are drawn from there and accepted as having the capacity to denote other things, there is no consequence of the cessation of conventional usage elsewhere. This is the sense.

And thus, since words primarily denoting the Supreme Self are drawn elsewhere for the sake of conventional usage by the Supreme Lord through His own convention (*saṃketa*), all worldly transactions are thereby rendered possible. This is supported by the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "they are the denoters of the Supreme. Consequently, it is established that Hari is the ultimate primary referent (*paramamukhyārtha*) of all words.
Because of the mention of the world.

Now, if words are primary (mukhya) with respect to the Supreme Self and secondary (amukhya) elsewhere, then they ought to be established as such only in that [Supreme Self]. How then can there be a primary establishment elsewhere? Thus, since the primary meaning cannot otherwise be accounted for, it must be postulated that something else alone is the primary denotation. To this objection, the author reads the Sūtra: [The opponent argues: "If words are primary with regard to the Supreme Self and secondary elsewhere, then they must be established as such only in that [Supreme Self]. How can there be a primary establishment elsewhere? And thus, because the primary meaning would otherwise be impossible, one must assume that something else is the primary denotation. Having reached this point, he recites the Sūtra.

"Because it denotes the world" (jagadvācitvāt). The meaning of this is as follows: since words are known to denote the world through worldly usage, it is logical that their well-known application (*prasiddhi*) is directed toward that [world].

And thus, because worldly activity occurs within the world alone due to the outward orientation of the world, words are established through their derivation (*vyutpatti*) therein; however, since there is no such derivation with respect to the Supreme Self, it is logical that there is no established usage for It. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu is the primary denotation of all words.
If it be argued that this is because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), [we reply] that this has already been explained.

Granted that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is primarily denoted by the word [Brahman] because He is the sovereign lord (*svāmin*) who is the cause of its application; nevertheless, an objection is raised: why should it not apply to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) as well? For their sovereignty over all things is established by such scriptural passages as "When one branch [of the body]... and "By means of Vāyu, indeed, all the worlds...". Having thus raised the objection, the author presents the Sūtra to provide the resolution.

“If it be argued that [the passage refers to] the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) because of their characteristic marks (liṅga), this has already been explained. This is its meaning: In the sentences, “When the individual soul leaves one branch,” and “For by Vāyu the worlds are led,” there is the hearing of the characteristic marks of both the individual soul and the chief vital breath; therefore, it might be thought that both of them possess the primary denotation of those respective terms. If this is argued, the answer is no. Why? Because that entire collection of passages has been explained as being directed toward their respective inner rulers (antaryāmin). Such is the meaning.

And thus, because the explanation given for the Vedas—that they concern the Lord contained within them and that there is a threefold nature of meditation—establishes that Viṣṇu alone is primarily the referent of the word [Brahman].
Jaimini, however, [holds that the mantras] have another purpose, on account of both questions and explanations; and some [teachers] likewise [hold this].

Now, as for what was previously stated—that because of the process of attraction (*samākarṣa*), one [name] has primary denotability while another has supreme primary denotability due to being denotable by its own nature—that has been answered. Since the Veda does not function for the sake of desired fruits, there is no purpose in such an attraction. Thus, it follows that one [name] lacks even basic denotability, whereas the other, Viṣṇu, possesses denotability only in the primary sense, but not in the supreme primary sense. To this, the author recites the Sūtra:

"But Jaimini [holds that the words refer] to another meaning, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus it is likewise. This is its meaning: the word *tu* (but) has the sense of *eva* (indeed). By this, it is also logical to draw the words away from Viṣṇu to establish [the nature of] ritual action (*karman*) and so forth. Why? Because they are for another purpose—that is, solely for the sake of knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). If it is asked how that is known, the teacher Jaimini maintains it is because of both the question and the explanation: from the question of Śvetaketu and from the statement of Uddālaka, "Come, my dear" (*yathā saumya*).

Furthermore, certain followers of other Vedic branches clearly state that the knowledge of other things is for the sake of knowing the Supreme Self, in the passage beginning "He who does not know Him. The meaning of the word "tasmāt" (therefore) is "for this reason as well."

Thus, it is indeed logical that the Veda teaches ritual action and so forth through the process of "summoning together" (samākarṣa). If one asks, "Why is the knowledge of ritual action and the like for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman?"—the answer is found in Śaunaka’s question, "When all this is known, what is it that, being known, brings about the fruit? Since the mere knowledge of this [world] is fruitless, Aṅgiras explains in his commentary that "all this becomes known through the lower knowledge (aparavidyā)," and "that which is known becomes fruitful through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is the object of the higher knowledge (paravidyā)."

Moreover, those who follow a single Vedic branch (eka-śākhinaḥ) recite: "He who does not know that... and so forth. Therefore, the teacher Jaimini maintains that the knowledge of ritual action and the like is for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the Blessed Lord. Consequently, it is established that Viṣṇu is the primary and most direct denotation [of the word "Brahman"].
Because of the syntactical connection of the sentence.

One might object: "It need not be that ritual action and the like must be taught by the Veda for the sake of knowledge of the Supreme Self; for even if the Veda speaks only of the Supreme Self without mentioning anything else, such knowledge is possible. Nor can it be argued that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) would be impossible, because words such as 'Jyotiṣṭoma' lack conventional denotation (*rūḍhi*) for Viṣṇu, and because etymological derivation (*yoga*) is untenable—since if one does not admit that the constituent parts of the word 'Jyotiṣṭomena' refer to something else, no derivation is possible. This objection is invalid, because we do admit that even a single broken-off part of a word may denote something else.
Thus, since there is no purpose in mentioning [the other] elsewhere, it follows that a coordination (samākarṣa) therein is not appropriate; to this, the author recites the Sūtra.

"Because of the syntactical connection" (vākyānvayāt). Its meaning is as follows: having observed the syntactical harmony of sentences with respect to Brahman, it follows that even ritual action and so forth must be taught by the Veda.

And thus, it is established that not only is the syntactic coordination of words (*padasamanvaya*) intended with respect to the Supreme Self as heard in scripture, but rather the coordination of sentences (*vākyasamanvaya*) as well; and since this [sentence-level coordination] cannot be established elsewhere in the absence of a drawing together [of the meanings], it must be stated that there is such a drawing together. This is proven.
Āśmarathya [holds that] there is a sign for the establishment of the proposition.
Now, it was stated that ritual action and so forth are taught for the sake of the knowledge of the Supreme Self; in response to the inquiry as to by what means this is so, he introduces the aphorism.

"Because the fulfillment of the proposition is the sign, [the Veda teaches ritual action and so forth]; thus says Āśmarathya. The meaning is as follows: the teaching of ritual action and the like by the Veda serves as a "sign" (liṅga) for the fulfillment of the proposition—that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation and nothing else—since this establishes the sense of the proposition "There is no other path. Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya considers that the teaching of those [rituals] is appropriate because of its utility toward that [knowledge].

And thus, by the statement "there is no other path," it is asserted that liberation is attained through the knowledge of Brahman. To establish this, ritual action (*karman*) and its auxiliaries are described, and it is stated that their fruit is characterized by impermanence and suffering. Ācārya Āśmarathya maintains that the purpose of the discourse on ritual action is precisely this: to establish, by way of showing that action and the like have impermanent fruits, that there is indeed "no other" [path]. Consequently, it is established that ritual action and the like are taught for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the Blessed Lord.
"Auḍulomi maintains that [the soul] departs from its state of being in this very manner."
He introduces the sūtra which demonstrates, by another method, the utility of the Lord’s knowledge for the teaching of karma and so forth.

"Because [the seeker] is about to depart from this state of being, so says Auḍulomi. This is its meaning: for the qualified seeker who desires liberation through knowledge and is "about to depart" from this state of being, since ritual action and the like are also to be performed as means to that knowledge, the Teacher Auḍulomi considers it entirely appropriate that the Veda teaches ritual action and so forth as means to the knowledge aimed at liberation.

Thus, for one who desires liberation and seeks to transcend saṃsāra, just as knowledge is required, so too is respect for ritual action (karman) necessary; because it is to be accomplished as a means to the knowledge of the Lord—which is itself a means to liberation—by way of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the teacher Auḍulomi maintains that the Vedas must necessarily denote ritual action and the like. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural declarations of the fruits of ritual action, since those declarations are intended to generate an inclination toward such action. As it has been said: "It is logical. Thus, the point is established.
"Because of the abiding [of the Self in all beings], so says Kāśakṛtsna."
He recites the sūtra which demonstrates, by another method, the utility of the mention of karma and so forth for the knowledge of Brahman.

"Because of the abiding [of all things]—thus says Kāśakṛtsna. This is its meaning: because action and the rest abide—that is, because they reside—in the Blessed Lord, who is the support of all; the Teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that the Veda teaches the nature of action and the rest, which constitute the supported, in order to make known the Blessed Lord's status as the substratum of action and so forth. It should be understood that there is no contradiction among these views, as each pertains to different levels of qualification.

Furthermore, because in such passages as "Thus indeed is the bridge, the support" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5), the abiding in the Supreme Self is declared, and because that [abiding] must be known as being the support of all, and because this [supporting] is impossible without knowledge of that which is supported, the Veda prescribes ritual action and so forth for that purpose. Thus, since the Veda provides the specific mode—namely, that the Supreme Self is the support of everything other than itself—which is required by the seeker of knowledge as to how Brahman is to be directly known, the Veda’s mention of the world of ritual action and so forth is for another purpose, namely, for the sake of the knowledge of the Supreme Self.

The teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains this view; and thus, since the usage of Vedic words for the sake of the Lord’s knowledge is established by drawing them together elsewhere, it is proven that Hari is the supreme primary referent of all words.
Thus concludes the section concerning the extraction [of mantras].
Here, the concordance of words denoting women with Brahman is established:
"And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples."

[Objection: Is it not the case that Hari is not denotable by words such as *prakṛti* (nature), because the absence of femininity—which is the pervader of being denotable by feminine gendered words—is present [in Him]? This is because His femininity is denied in the passage, "Not her" (*nainam*). Nor should it be argued: "Why could the occurrence of the word 'woman' not apply to Him, just as the occurrence of neuter words does? For such a supposition is untenable. Furthermore, one might argue: "Even though He has become a woman, He is denotable by that word because He is the controller of women. But this is not correct, for it would lead to the absurd consequence that a husband who has brought his wife under his control would also be denotable by that word. Therefore, since words such as *prakṛti* do not denote the Supreme Self, the *Samanvaya-sūtra* is untenable. To this, the author states the Sūtra: *janmādyasya yataḥ* || 1.1.2 || [The origin, etc., of this [world] from whom. [This is the response: It is not so. Although the Supreme Self is devoid of all gender, He is nevertheless denoted by feminine words such as *prakṛti*. Just as the word *prajāpati* is applied to the Supreme Self despite its masculine gender, so too is the word *prakṛti* applied to Him despite its feminine gender. Nor is there any contradiction with the denial of femininity in the passage, "Not her," because that denial refers to the feminine gender associated with the individual soul (*jīva*), not to the feminine gender associated with the Supreme Self. Nor is it possible to conceive of the word *prakṛti* as having a neuter application; for the word *prakṛti* is well-known in the world as being feminine. Furthermore, even if He were to assume a female form, He would not be denotable by that word merely on the basis of being a controller of women, for that would lead to the aforementioned absurdity regarding a husband who controls his wife. Therefore, since words such as *prakṛti* do indeed denote the Supreme Self, the *Samanvaya-sūtra* is perfectly consistent. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established. || 2 ||* *Note: The provided text contains a portion of the commentary on the first Sūtra of the Brahma-sūtras.*

"And [the Lord] is also the material cause (prakṛti), because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative example. This is its meaning: The Lord is not denoted solely by masculine terms; rather, He is also the material cause. Furthermore, He is denoted by feminine terms such as "this very material cause" (saiṣā prakṛtiḥ) and others mentioned previously. Why? Because only in this way is there no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative example—namely, the non-contradiction, or lack of conflict, with the proposition "He entered into it" and the example of the river and the ocean introduced by the word "as. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between them. This is the sense.

And thus, Hari alone is denoted by such terms as "Prakṛti" (Nature) and the like. For in the Śruti, having first asserted that Viṣṇu is denotable by all words in the passage, "He [the Creator] created this very Puruṣa," the text then provides the analogy of the river and the ocean with respect to that very same [Viṣṇu]. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the initial proposition and the illustrative example. Therefore, it is established that Hari alone is denoted by such terms as "Prakṛti."
And because of the teaching of covetousness.

Having thus established by means of general evidence that Hari is denoted by words such as *prakṛti*, the author now recites the aphorism which specifically establishes the evidence for His being denoted by the word *prakṛti* as the indicator of all feminine terms whatsoever.

"And because of the teaching of *abhidhyā*. The meaning of this is as follows: *Abhidhyā* refers to the will (*icchā*) of Īśvara. Because of the teaching in the scripture, "But [it was] Māyā," that she is denoted by the word *prakṛti*, and because the Will, which is non-different from Īśvara, is also denoted by that same word—this is the meaning.

And thus, since it is stated in the Śruti, "But Māyā is Prakṛti," and in the Smṛti, "Prakṛti is indeed vāsanā," that the term *prakṛti* denotes the will which is non-different from the Lord; and because of the Smṛti passage, "That [will] is abhidhyāsa" (creative contemplation), it is established that Prakṛti is indeed Brahman—not only for the general reason previously mentioned, but also because it is declared to consist of the will denoted by the word *prakṛti*.
And because both are explicitly recorded in the sacred tradition.

Now, even if it be granted that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word *prakṛti* through the mediation of His will, He is not directly denoted by that word, because there is a lack of evidence; for the possibility of restricting the Vedic text "His names" (*nāmāni*) exists. This being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra:

"And because both are directly declared. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of emphasis. "Directly" means without any intermediary. "Because both are declared" means that by the statement, "This is woman, this is man," it is stated that the Lord is denotable by the words signifying both Prakṛti and Puruṣa; thus, the meaning is that it is necessary for the Lord to be denotable by such terms as Prakṛti and so forth.

And thus, since the Lord is designated as "Prakṛti" (Nature) in this very scripture, it is established by this same scriptural statement that He is denoted by the word "Prakṛti," even without the mediation of His will; otherwise, He would not be denoted by the word "Puruṣa" (Spirit) either, as there is no distinction between the two cases. Therefore, it is proven that Viṣṇu alone is the one denoted by words such as "Prakṛti."
Because of self-creation and transformation.

Now, an objection is raised: although it is stated in scripture that the Blessed Lord is denoted by the word *prakṛti*, this is not tenable when [the meaning of the word] is established, because there is no ground for its application to Him; for the proponents of the Siddhānta do not accept that [the relationship between word and meaning] is based on mere convention. To this objection, the author states the aphorism as a rebuttal: [The Sūtra: "But [it is so] because of the existence of the word. (sū. 1.4.3) This means: the word *prakṛti* applies to the Blessed Lord because of the existence of that very word [in scripture]; for the application of a word to an object is established by the fact of its being used to denote that object, and not merely by the presence of a formal cause (*nimitta*) for such application. Furthermore, the view that the relationship between word and meaning is based on mere convention is not accepted by the Siddhāntins. Therefore, the Blessed Lord is indeed denoted by the word *prakṛti*. Thus, the objection is refuted.

Regarding the phrase "because of the self-creation through transformation" (ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt), its meaning is as follows: having brought about the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) and for the sake of impelling it, because of his own creative act consisting of making himself manifold, the one denoted by the word "prakṛti" is indeed Viṣṇu; this is the sense.

And thus, because the reason "possessing an excellent form" is unestablished due to the impossibility of its connection with *yoga*—since *prakṛti* lacks the inherent capacity for transformation, [the Lord] abides within it, transforms it, and by acting as the director of the *mahat* and other principles, makes Himself manifold; for there is the Śruti, "He indeed is the Self," and the Smṛti, "The Supreme is changeless. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words *prakṛti* and so forth.
For it is indeed sung as the womb.

[Objection: Even if the Supreme Self were female, and even if there existed authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) declaring that She is denoted by the word "Prakṛti," it is not proper for Her to be denoted by the feminine word [“strī”]. This is because that word is necessarily restricted to denoting an agent of birth without any mediation; and such [birth] does not exist in the case of the Supreme Self. Furthermore, in the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka), the pervaded (vyāpya) cannot logically exist. Since the statement declaring that She is denoted by the word “Prakṛti” is somehow non-literal—just like the statement "the clay said" (mṛd abravīt)—this being the position reached, the author recites the aphorism as a rebuttal: naivaṃ vācyam | yathā hi loke mṛdabravīdityādivākyaṃ gauṇārthakaṃ tathā prakṛtiśabdavācyatvābhidhāyakavākyasyāpi gauṇatvopapatteḥ | na ca strīśabdasya sūtikartṛtvamātraniyatatvam | strīliṅgasya śabdasya dravyaguṇakriyādyarthavācakatvasyāpi darśanāt | tasmāt paramātmano 'pi strīliṅgaśabdavācyatvaṃ nānupapannam || 1.4.25 || It should not be argued thus: just as in the world the sentence "the clay spoke" has a figurative meaning, so too the sentence declaring that She is denoted by the word "Prakṛti" can have a figurative sense. Nor is it the case that the feminine word is restricted solely to denoting an agent of birth, since feminine words are seen to denote substances, qualities, actions, and so forth. Therefore, it is not illogical for the Supreme Self to be denoted by a word in the feminine gender. 1.4.25.

"And because He is indeed sung of as the *yoni*. The meaning of this is as follows: "For" (*hi*) means "because. Since the Lord is sung of—that is, established—as the *yoni* by the Śruti text, "He who is the source (*yoni*) of all beings," and since He is the producer of offspring from His own body, therefore He is denotable by feminine gendered words such as *prakṛti* (Nature) and so forth; this is the meaning.

And thus, because of the Smṛti statement "and so by way of intervention," and because the status of being a source (yonitva) is also established by Śruti, the absence of a pervading [reason] is not proven. Consequently, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by all words signifying "woman"; thus, the Sūtra on Concordance (Samanvaya-sūtra) is validated.
Thus concludes the section concerning primordial matter (prakṛti).
In this regard, words whose meanings consist in the negation of that which is to be negated are seen to be in harmony with Brahman.
By this, all [such passages] have been explained—yes, they have been explained.

Now, it may be argued that Viṣṇu alone is not the referent of words such as "non-existent" (asat) and the like; for some of these words denote non-existence, while others denote the absence of essential nature (niḥsvarūpa). Since the Supreme Self is of the nature of existence, it is not logical for Him to possess non-existence and so forth. Nor can it be said that even if He Himself lacks the absence of essential nature, the application of those words to Him occurs because non-existence is dependent upon Him; for that which is devoid of its own essential nature cannot logically be subject to governance. To this objection, the author reads the following Sūtra:

"By this, all [terms] are explained, they are explained. This is the meaning: by this very reason stated previously, all words such as "void" (śūnya) and so forth primarily denote the Blessed Lord alone; this is the sense. The repetition at the end of the chapter is for the purpose of emphasizing that the meaning stated from the beginning of this chapter until its conclusion is exactly thus.

And thus, [the Supreme Self exists] due to this collection of arguments, such as its being dependent on the Supreme Self. Nor can it be argued that it does not exist because it lacks the quality of being known through negation (*niṣedha-mukha-vedyatva*) and so forth; for even in the absence of being known through negation, it is logically established that it is denotable by words such as "void" (*śūnya*) and the like, based on its being unmanifest to the wicked and through such yogic applications as "he makes [the world] devoid [of dharma]," etc., as per the Śruti: "For He alone is the Void. Nor should it be said that its dependence on another is untenable because it lacks a nature to be governed; [this is not so].

Even though there is a lack of positive form (*svarūpa-vaidhurya*), attributes such as being knowable through negation (*niṣedha-mukha-vedyatva*) and so forth are dependent upon Him; therefore, since it is established that Hari is the denotable object of words such as "non-existent" (*asad-ādi*), it is logical that Viṣṇu’s status as the source of the entire scripture—consisting of all sounds, phonemes, words, and sentences—is proven, as well as His authorship of the birth of the universe and His possession of primary, infinite qualities.
Thus, by this, all the topical sections (adhikaraṇas) have been explained.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter.
Thus the first chapter is completed.
Prosperity!
Hari.
Now begins the second chapter.

In this chapter, [the author] demonstrates the absence of contradiction regarding the meaning established in the preceding chapter—that Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the universe through the synthesis of all the Vedas.
Now begins the first quarter.
In this quarter [of the verse], he demonstrates the absence of contradiction with reasoning.

In this context, with the intention that the contradiction with Smṛti—which consists of four types of contradictions—is more powerful than each individual contradiction and must therefore be refuted first, the non-contradiction with Smṛti is now examined.
"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis [that are not in conflict]."

Now, it may be argued that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is not tenable due to a lack of evidence. Nor should it be said that such scriptural passages as "from which [all this arises]" constitute proof; for if this scripture were intended to establish Viṣṇu’s causality, it would be rendered invalid by its contradiction with the Śaiva and other Āgamas composed by omniscient authors. Thus, due to the contradiction of such reasoning, the scripture cannot have the intention of establishing Viṣṇu’s causality. Furthermore, even if there were validity regarding a particular state of being, there could be no non-contradiction across different places and times.

Since it is observed that Viṣṇu and others are declared superior to Rudra and others in their respective scriptures, and since they testify to this, it follows that Viṣṇu is not the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). To this objection, the Sūtra states: [I.1.1] *athāto brahmajijñāsā*.

"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. This is the meaning: Since there would be the consequence of the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis—namely, that because the Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata and others would have no scope (being set aside) by the Śrutis which, having no scope [elsewhere], are intent upon Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world, there would arise the fault of contradiction, resulting in the defect known as lack of authority—it is therefore not logical that the Śrutis are intent upon Viṣṇu’s status as the cause.

But [it may be argued that] it is more appropriate [to interpret the text] as being intent upon Śiva and others as the creator. If this is said, we reply: no. Why? Because of the consequence of the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. For there would be the consequence of the fault of finding no scope for other Smṛtis—such as the Pañcarātra and others—which are stronger than the Pāśupata and other texts because they are in harmony with the Śruti and were composed by Viṣṇu and others who are omniscient even in comparison to Rudra and the rest; and because, since these [stronger] Smṛtis find no scope in attributing the agency of the world to Rudra and others, there would be the consequence of the defect [of falsity] in those Smṛtis like the Śaiva which contradict them.
The meaning is that, by accepting a connection with the defect known as invalidity (aprāmāṇya) in its highest degree, the contradiction [of that validity] becomes irrelevant.

And thus, because there exists the authority of scriptural passages such as "From whom [it proceeds]," even if one were to abandon the primary purport (*tātparya*) regarding Viṣṇu and instead accept a purport regarding Śiva and others, it would result in the invalidation of the Śruti due to its contradiction with the Smṛtis composed by the most authoritative beings, Viṣṇu and the rest. Nor can it be argued that there is no final determination because both Smṛtis lack authority; for the Pāśupata and other such Smṛtis are non-authoritative insofar as they contradict the Śruti. Furthermore, it should not be said that the Śruti is weak because its expression is indistinct, since its strength is established by its being consistent with the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis.
And thus it is established that there is no contradiction between Viṣṇu and His being the cause of the world as declared by the Śruti.
And because others are not perceived.

Now, an objection is raised: "It was stated that because the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis were composed by the Supreme Self (Paramātman), Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is established by the powerful Śrutis associated with them; however, this is not correct, for if that were so, it would follow that the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis are invalid, since it is impossible for those [Smṛtis] spoken by authoritative persons (āpta) to lack validity. To this, the Sūtra says:

"And because of the non-perception of others. This is its meaning: the term "non-perception" (anupalabdhi) is repeated. The word "and" (ca) indicates the admission of some perception of results. Thus, because of the non-perception—that is, the lack of direct observation—of those other than the supersensuous [results], namely the distinct results mentioned in the Pāśupata and other systems which are perceptible, as well as the undesirable [consequences] resulting from the performance or abandonment of the practices prescribed therein, it is logical that they possess no authority at all. This is the meaning.

And thus, even if the result described in the Śaiva Āgamas—which is capable of being perceived—is occasionally observed when one performs the practices prescribed therein, its lack of certainty as an authoritative source (āptatva) remains due to its non-occurrence as a rule; and so it is established that the Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata and others possess no authority whatsoever.
By this, Yoga is refuted.

Now, even so, it may be argued that not all non-Viṣṇuite Smṛtis lack authority on account of the aforementioned grounds; for since the results described in the Yoga-smṛtis—such as sweating and the breaking of limbs—are invariably observed, it is possible to determine that they were composed by authoritative persons (āpta). To this, the author reads the Sūtra: *na śiṣṭāparigrahāḥ...* [Sūtra 2.1.12] (Those [Smṛtis] which are not accepted by the learned [are not authoritative]).

"By this, Yoga is refuted. This is its meaning: by this very reason previously stated—namely, the non-observation of results—the "Yoga," that is, the Yoga-śāstra, is "refuted," meaning it is rejected.

And thus, since the first stage is fomentation (*svedana*) and the second is the breaking of the limbs (*gātrabhañjana*), and so forth—as stated in the authoritative texts—there is no certainty regarding the authoritativeness of such descriptions of the stages of practice (*abhyāsāvasthā*) and their progressive perfection, because these are not perceived [by ordinary means]. Consequently, since the cause for obtaining the result is not established by necessity, it is impossible to ascertain the authoritativeness of what was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). Therefore, the Yoga-smṛti lacks authority. Since all non-Vaiṣṇava smṛtis likewise lack authority, it is established that there is no contradiction with Viṣṇu being the cause of the universe.
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti.
In this context, the contradiction with reasoning regarding the authority of the Vedas and other sources cited as proof for Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is resolved:
"Not so, because of its dissimilarity; and its being such [is known] from scripture. (Sūtra 2.1.4)

[Objection: Surely the Vedas and the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis are not authoritative, because even when their injunctions are performed, the result is not perceived. If they were authoritative despite the non-perception of results, then—since the non-perception of results is equally present for the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis as well—there would be no basis for distinguishing why authority belongs only to the Vedas and so forth and not to the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis. Consequently, if a portion of the Vedas and so forth is unauthoritative due to the non-perception of results, there would be a lack of confidence in the authority of its other portions; thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world cannot be established. To this, the Sūtra states: *Śāstrayonitvāt* (Because He has the scripture as His source). [2.1.3] This means: It is not the case that the Vedas and the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis are not authoritative. Why? Because they are the source (*yoni*) of the *śāstra*. That is to say, the omniscient Lord, who is the author of the Vedas and the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis, is Himself the source of the scripture. Therefore, the Vedas and the Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis are indeed authoritative. Furthermore, it is not the case that the non-perception of results invalidates them. For even though results may not be perceived immediately, they are understood through inference based on the observation of the world’s variety, and the fact that the Vedas and Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis are the source of the scripture is established by the very fact that the scripture itself is the source of all knowledge. Moreover, the non-perception of results does not prove the non-authoritativeness of the Vedas and Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis, because the results of Vedic actions are often experienced after a long time, and because the fruits of knowledge depend upon the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nor is there a lack of a basis for distinction; for the difference between the Vedas and the Pāśupata Smṛtis is established by the fact that the former are the source of the scripture, while the latter are not. Thus, since the Vedas and Vaiṣṇava Smṛtis are authoritative, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is established. This is the meaning. || 3 ||* (Note: The provided text ends with the objection; the response begins with the Sūtra and its commentary.)

"Because it is different in character from that [Smṛti], and its suchness is established by the Word. This is the meaning: "Of this"—that is, of the Śruti and the Smṛtis conforming to it—"there is no lack of authority, unlike the Smṛtis of the Śaivas and others. Why? Because it is different in character (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*). It is different in character from others insofar as it possesses what is called intrinsic authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, because it possesses the difference characterized by the eternity of the Śruti, and because the Smṛti possesses the difference characterized by its conformity to the Śruti, there is no lack of authority.
And "its suchness"—that is, its possession of the aforementioned differences—is ascertained "by the Word," meaning from the scripture: *vācā virūpanityayā* (with the multiform, eternal speech)."

And thus, the Veda and so forth are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) and because they conform to that [reality]. Nor should it be asked, "From where does this lack of human origin derive? For the lack of human origin has already been established through the previously mentioned methods of general proof and elimination (*sāmānyasiddhi-pariśeṣa*), as well as by the scriptural statement: "One should fashion speech as being without a personal author" (*vācā virūpanityayā*). And so, since there is no contradiction with their status as valid means of knowledge, it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe.
But it is indeed seen.

Now, even for one who maintains that the authority of scripture and other sources is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it must necessarily be admitted that non-authority arises upon perceiving a defect. Thus, since non-authority must be asserted even in the case of the Veda due to the defect of not observing the results mentioned therein, the author reads the Sūtra [in response].

"But it is seen" (dṛśyate tu). This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) is for the sake of distinction. Since the fruit declared by the Śruti and other authorities is seen—that is, perceived—by those specific qualified persons who are fit for that fruit, therefore there is no lack of authority; this is the meaning.

Thus, since the non-perception of results by those entitled [to perform rites] is accounted for by defects in the performer and so forth—given that the perception of results by others is established—the discrepancy regarding results is otherwise explained. Furthermore, because it has been stated that the Pāśupata and other non-Vedic traditions do not result in the attainment of perceived fruits, their lack of authority is certain. Therefore, it is established that Hari’s status as the cause of the universe is logical, as there is no contradiction with reason regarding the authority of the Vedas.
Thus ends the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] on "On account of having different characteristics."
Here, the absence of contradiction with firm reasoning regarding the aforementioned matter—the validity of the Veda which establishes Viṣṇu as the creator of the world—is stated:
"But the designation [of the elements] refers to their presiding deities, because of the distinction and the conformity."

But is it not the case that the Veda is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For [the Veda] speaks of things such as clay being the agent of creation—as in "Clay said," and so forth—and this is contradicted by reasoning such as the fact that [clay] is insentient. Furthermore, if a portion of the Veda were invalid, then the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*), which is the very proof for the Veda's validity, would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that very instance; thus, due to its lack of certainty, it would fail to establish [validity]. Moreover, one cannot assume a different meaning for the scripture in order to avoid contradiction with reason. Finally, if there were a presiding deity (*abhimānidevatā*) possessing a body even in a single part [of the Veda], it would follow that [that deity] would be perceived; yet if there is no body, speech and the like would be impossible.

Because there is no connection with a deity; because, if it were to arise in another location devoid of that [deity], it would follow that [the deity] is useless; and because there is no proof for the existence of a deity; and because the Śruti is not intended to be authoritative in this regard—this being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"But the designation [of the elements] is based on those who possess self-conceit (abhimānin), because of distinction and conformity. This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. "The designation of those who possess self-conceit" means that in passages such as "the clay spoke," there is indeed a designation—that is, a statement—referring only to sentient beings who possess self-conceit, and not to insentient things. Why? Because it would contradict reason, as clay is not a speaker due to its insentience. And thus, there is no loss of authority for the Veda.

Now, one might ask: since the possessor of egoity (abhimānin) cannot be disembodied and must therefore possess a body, how is it possible for him to be invisible, to speak by presiding over other objects, and to be the presiding agent over many things he identifies with? To this, it is said: "By specific power," and so forth. "Specific power" (viśeṣa) means capacity; "concomitance" (anugati) means pervasion of all that is identified with.
The meaning is that everything is possible through these two.

And thus, the statement "the clay spoke" is consistent with reason when understood as referring to the presiding deity (abhimānidevatā) of the Veda; for there is no contradiction with logic. Since it is possible to find the primary meaning by interpreting the Śruti in another sense rather than its literal appearance, the text remains authoritative. There is no sublation of the Śruti by reason, because there exist deities who possess bodies and whose activities extend over that which they preside over. In the case of great beings, the fact of their being perceived is accepted as a matter of course, since this is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); whereas for those who are ignorant, such beings are simply beyond the range of their perception.

Since direct perception alone is the means of valid knowledge for great beings regarding the existence of deities, it follows that the proof of the Blessed One’s status as the cause of the universe is logical, provided there is no contradiction with reason in the authority of the Veda; thus, it is established.
And it is also observed.

Now, one might argue that rather than postulating deities and their powers—which lack any basis in valid cognition—it is better to postulate the non-authoritativeness of the Veda; for this is simpler (lāghava), and because it is illogical to assume those [deities] residing as presiding entities over things such as forests, given the absence of any evidence for such specific powers, and because the authority of the Veda is contested. To this, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [it is not so], because there is no contradiction with the Vedic statement. (JS 2.1.5) This means: It is not the case that the Veda is non-authoritative. Why? Because there is no contradiction with the Vedic statement. That is to say, the Veda itself declares: "The gods, having attained immortality through the sacrifice, protect the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.8.3). Furthermore, the fact that the Veda is the source of knowledge regarding Dharma is established by the very same means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the existence of the self and other such entities. Therefore, the Veda is authoritative. As for the claim that the Veda is non-authoritative because its author is unknown, we reply: even if the author were unknown, the Veda would still be authoritative, just like the perception of a person born blind. Alternatively, the Veda is authoritative because it was spoken by a trustworthy person (āpta), just like the words of Manu and others. How so? Because the Veda is accepted as authoritative by those who are themselves trustworthy. And how is it that they accept it? Because they see that it is consistent with the means of valid cognition. And how do they see this consistency? By observing that the injunctions of the Veda produce results that are seen, such as rain, and results that are unseen, such as heaven. Thus, since the Veda is authoritative, the existence of deities and their powers is established by that very authority. Consequently, the objection that there is no evidence for their specific powers is refuted. As for the claim that it is simpler to assume the Veda is non-authoritative, we reply: simplicity is not a valid reason here, because the assumption of non-authoritativeness would entail a greater complexity (gaurava) by requiring one to reject the Veda's status as a means of valid cognition and instead posit a new, unestablished entity. Therefore, the Veda is indeed authoritative. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

"And it is seen" (dṛśyate ca). The meaning of this is as follows: the capacity [of the subtle body] is perceived by yogins within the presiding deity; therefore, for this reason as well, there is no contradiction with non-perception. This is the sense.

And thus, since the utterances are justified by the existence of specific capacities [within them], because the perception of excellence is a valid means of knowledge regarding that distinction, and because of the Smṛti statement that [the deities] preside over earth and the other elements; therefore, it is established that the proof of the Lord’s authorship of the world through the Veda is logical, as it is not contradicted by reason.
Thus ends the section concerning the one who possesses the conceit.

Here, the contradiction with the reasoning that establishes that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—which is subordinate to scripture—is the agent of the world’s creation, in the context of Brahman being the creator of the world, is refuted:
"If it be argued that [the world] was non-existent, no; because [the term 'non-existent'] is a mere negation."

Objection: It is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, because there is a lack of evidence. Nor should it be said that such scriptural passages as "That from which [it arises]" constitute evidence; for Brahman cannot be the cause of the world, since it did not exist prior to that. Since it is logically contradictory to say that what does not exist prior to something cannot be its cause, the scripture lacks authority regarding its literal meaning. Furthermore, the reason is not unestablished, as it is established by the scripture stating, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent."

Nor should it be argued that if Brahman were not the cause, the world would result in being causeless; for, by the force of the scriptural statement "from non-being, being was born," non-existence itself must be accepted as the cause. Furthermore, there is no logical contradiction in accepting non-existence as the cause, just as there is none in accepting Brahman as the cause; on the contrary, there is even an inference supporting the view that non-existence is the cause of the world: "The cause at the time of dissolution must be non-existent (asat), because it is a real entity (vastu), like the effect."

Therefore, since it would follow that the world has non-existence (*abhāva*) as its cause rather than Brahman, the definition-sūtra (*lakṣaṇasūtra*) would be untenable; having reached this conclusion, the author states the sūtra which refutes it.

“If it be said that [the cause] is non-existent, no, because it is a mere negation. This is the meaning: “The non-existent” refers to the prior absence of the universe. If it be argued that the Lord is not the creator of the world, we say no. Why? Because it is a mere negation; the meaning is that it is an object of the cognition of negation by its very nature, without possessing the character of an absence (abhāva-dharma).

And thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world, and not the non-existent (asat), because the latter is the object of the cognition that negates causality, namely, "it has no cause. Therefore, since reasoning and the like serve as illuminators rather than contradictors, it is established that the Sūtra defining [Brahman] is logically sound.
"Because of the consequence that [the world] would likewise [merge] into dissolution, it is inconsistent."

Now, as for what was said—that because it is a mere negation, non-existence cannot be a cause due to its contradiction with reason—that is not correct. For there is no sublation [of our position] if one accepts that some kind of non-existence, even if contradicted by reason, possesses agency on the strength of scripture. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the prior non-existence of a jar and so forth would also possess agency.

Just as there is a distinction among positive entities (bhāvas) such that some possess agency while others lack it, so too can a distinction be established among negative entities (abhāvas): for instance, the prior non-existence of a jar lacks agency, whereas the prior non-existence of the entire universe lacks agency by virtue of scriptural authority (śruti), such as "only the non-existent existed. Having reached this position, the author states the aphorism (sūtra) as a response: [The sūtra: "But [the non-existence] of the effect is not [non-existent], because of the impossibility of its being the agent of its own production. (NS 4.1.14) This means that the prior non-existence of an effect is not itself non-existent, because it is impossible for it to be the agent of its own production. Since the prior non-existence of an effect cannot act upon itself, it must be admitted to exist as a distinct category from absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva). Thus, the distinction between these two types of non-existence is established.

"In dissolution, there would be the same consequence; therefore, it is inconsistent. This is the meaning: "In dissolution," that is, at the time of pralaya; "there would be the same consequence," meaning there would be the consequence of [the world] being merely non-existent; "the agency of the non-existent" is "inconsistent," meaning it is illogical.

And thus, if at the time of dissolution (pralaya) all that exists were non-existent, there would remain only non-existence; for it is a rule that upon the destruction of an effect, only the cause remains. Furthermore, one could argue that this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), such that even time itself would not exist. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
But it is not so, because of the existence of examples.

Now, anticipating the objection that "this does not result in an undesirable consequence for us either, since we also desire that at the time of dissolution only non-existence remains," he introduces the aphorism as a refutation.

"But not because of the existence of an example" (na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt). The meaning of this is as follows: the word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. It is not tenable that everything becomes non-existent at the time of dissolution. Why? Because at that time, an example exists precisely because all things are present; the meaning is "because of their existence."

And thus, the origination of that which exists must be possible because it possesses the property of having an origination, just like the origination of a jar. Furthermore, the destruction under dispute is accompanied by a remainder because it is a destruction, just like the destruction of a jar. Since the existence of the entity at the time of dissolution is established by these two inferences, the denial of it constitutes a loss of authoritative truth and thus results in an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*). Therefore, in the absence of contradiction, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logical.
And because of the defects in one's own position.

He introduces the sūtra which demonstrates that the undesirable consequence of universal non-existence at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) follows not only from the abandonment of what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but also because [the world] would otherwise lack such validity.

"And because of the defect in one's own position" (svapakṣadoṣāt). The meaning of this is as follows: "In one's own position"—that is, in the position that everything is non-existent at the time of dissolution (pralaya)—"because of the defect," namely the defect known as the absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntābhāva), that position is not tenable; such is the meaning.

And thus, the non-existence of everything during the dissolution (*pralaya*) is unproven. To explain: regarding the non-existence of time and other entities existing during the dissolution—is this cognizable through perception, or cognizable through scripture, or cognizable through inference? It cannot be the first, because [these entities] are not in contact with the senses. Nor can it be the second, because such a scripture does not exist. Nor can it be the third, because of the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and so forth.
