Thus, since the position that everything is non-existent during the dissolution lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), its acceptance is undesirable; therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
"Because reasoning is not firmly established, if it is argued that the object can be inferred otherwise, even so there follows the consequence of no liberation."

"Now, is it not the case that this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta) are untenable? For, since there is no establishing proof [to fix] that 'inference is limited to just this much,' it is possible to infer otherwise than what has been stated. Having thus raised an objection regarding the proof or refutation of the causality of the existent and the non-existent, the author states the aphorism as a resolution: [The Sūtra: "Because of the impossibility of the production of the existent and the non-existent, and because of the absence of a cause for the destruction of the existent, [the non-existent cannot be the cause]. (NS 4.1.14) This is the intended meaning: Since the production of an existent thing from a non-existent cause is impossible, and since there is no cause for the destruction of an existent thing [if it were already existent], the non-existent cannot be the cause. Furthermore, if the existent were the cause, its prior non-existence would be required; however, since an existent thing cannot be produced from a non-existent cause, and since an existent thing cannot be destroyed without a cause, neither the existent nor the non-existent can be the cause. Thus, by refuting the arguments for and against the causality of the existent and the non-existent, he provides the resolution.

"Because reasoning is not firmly established, if it is argued that the object of inference can be established otherwise, even so there would be the consequence of no liberation. This is the meaning: "Because reasoning is not firmly established" means because reasoning—consisting of such things as the absence of a corroborative instance—is not firmly established, i.e., is unsettled. "Otherwise" means in a manner different from the way the proponent has stated their position. "The object of inference could be established" means it could be proven by a counter-reasoning. [The answer is] "No"—this is the ellipsis. Why? Because "even so," that is, this being the case, when mere reasoning lacks authority.

There would be the consequence of no liberation at all; that is, there would be the consequence of the loss of even liberation, which is accepted by all proponents of established systems as the purpose of their respective treatises. Why? Because, since it must be proven by inference alone for one who is in disagreement, it is possible to assert its lack of authority in that same manner—this is the meaning.

And thus it must be stated here: can that which is authoritative and established by reasoning be refuted by counter-reasoning, or is it non-authoritative? The second [alternative] is what you intend; however, regarding the first, does liberation exist according to the view of such a disputant, or not? If the position is "no," then because he is not a proponent [of liberation], he is to be disregarded. Since he does not obstruct the objects of knowledge accepted by the final Siddhāntin, his [arguments for] being the cause of the world and so forth remain exactly as they are. As for the first [alternative], if reasoning were non-authoritative, then liberation itself would not be established, due to the absence of any means to achieve it.

Nor can its establishment be achieved through scripture, because one who does not accept liberation cannot acknowledge the authority of such scripture. Furthermore, since the two types of reasoning—establishing that existence is causeless and establishing that non-existence has a cause—are themselves unauthoritative, it is impossible to negate [the self] by means of them. Therefore, in the absence of contradiction, it is established that the Sūtra defining [the self] is logically sound.
By this, those other refined persons who do not accept [the authority of the Vedas] are also explained.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the principle of non-existence (abhāva-tattva), denoted by the word 'non-being' (asat), is not the cause of the world; nevertheless, it is still impossible for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world. For the world, which is a matter of dispute, must be either causeless, or have a non-conscious entity as its cause, or have the individual soul (jīva) as its cause, because it is an effect—just like the falling of a riverbank or the curdling of milk. Thus, there is a contradiction with the reasoning that establishes causelessness and so forth. Nor should it be said that reasoning devoid of scriptural basis is ineffective, since [the claim of causelessness] is rooted in the Śruti statement, 'It arose spontaneously' (akasmāt). Anticipating this doubt, he presents the Sūtra to dispel it: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] not so, on account of the observation of effects [having causes]. (na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt) [Commentary: It is not the case that Viṣṇu cannot be the cause of the world. Why? Because we observe that effects possess causes. Just as a potter is the cause of a jar, goldsmiths of golden ornaments, and weavers of cloth, so too the world, being an effect, must have a cause. The argument that the world is causeless is refuted by the very fact of its being an effect. Furthermore, the claim that it has a non-conscious entity as its cause is untenable, because consciousness is observed in the world. The claim that the individual soul is the cause is also incorrect, because the soul is itself subject to bondage and liberation and lacks the power to create the entire universe. Therefore, the reasoning that supports causelessness and other such views is contradicted by the observation of effects having causes. Nor is it the case that reasoning devoid of a root is ineffective, for this reasoning is supported by the Śruti: "From Him, indeed, was born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses... from Him were born fire, water, and earth, the supporter of all" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3). Thus, the objection is refuted.

"By this, those who are not accepted [as authorities] are also explained. This is the meaning: by this—namely, the reason consisting in the presence or absence of supporting examples for one's own and opposing positions—those "not accepted" (aparigrahāḥ), meaning those devoid of acceptance by the Veda and those contrary to it; the "remaining" (śiṣṭāḥ) or residual positions, such as those asserting the soul (jīva), time (kāla), inherent nature (svabhāva), or a creator (kartṛtva)—are "explained," which means they are rejected and refuted.

And thus, since the doctrines that the world has non-intelligent causes—such as being caused by Māyā, by Brahman alone, by Time, or by inherent nature—have been refuted both on the grounds of their lack of supporting examples and because they contradict the Vedas; and since such scriptural passages as "This [world] arose from nothing," "This was produced from Pradhāna," and "Beings arise from the Jīva" actually have Viṣṇu as their intended meaning; therefore, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct, as there is no contradiction due to the fallacious nature of the arguments and other such means.
Thus ends the section on the non-existent.
In this regard, the contradiction is resolved by means of a powerful and firm argument established through abundant scriptural authority.
If it be argued that there is no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] because of the departure [of the soul from the body], we say: it would be as in the case of the world.

[Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world and so forth is untenable? Because he is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), agency and the like cannot logically belong to one who is non-different from the individual soul. If it is asked, "From what [source] is his non-difference from the individual soul [known]?"—it is because of the scriptural text: "In the supreme, imperishable, all become one. Therefore, since the Lord is non-different from the individual soul, his status as the cause of the world and so forth is untenable; thus, the Sūtra containing the definition is not tenable. To this, the author presents the Sūtra.

"Because of the attainment of the state of the enjoyer, there is non-distinction, as in the case of the world. This is the meaning: "Because of the attainment of the state of the enjoyer," since it is heard in the scriptural statement that "they become one with the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]" that the individual soul (jīva), the enjoyer, attains the state of Brahman; therefore, there is "non-distinction" between the two, meaning the absence of difference. If it be argued that, for this reason, it is not logical for Brahman—which is non-different from the limited individual soul—to be the cause of the world, [the answer is] "No"—this is the remainder [of the sūtra]. Why? Because it is "as in the case of the world. Just as in the world, although the individual souls are non-different from the universal soul, they do not lose their distinctness while remaining in the body, so too here. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Because, as in the world—just as in common worldly usage there is a statement of the unification of one water with another water, so here too, based on the identity of location and other factors, the statement of the unification of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) as "they become one" would be figurative; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply. This is the meaning.

And thus, because there is no identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), the Lord’s status as the cause of the world and so forth is not contradictory. Nor can it be argued that there is an absence of oneness based on the scriptural text, "In the supreme, immutable [Brahman], all [become one]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7); for that scriptural statement lacks such an intended meaning due to its contradiction with the connected passage, "The stainless one attains the highest equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). If it is asked, "What then is the recourse for the scriptures concerning non-difference?"—the answer is that it is established as figurative, based on the identity of location and other factors, just like the expression "the waters have become one."

Nor can it be argued that the demonstration of the difference between the liberated soul (mukta) and the Lord (īśvara) does not constitute the meaning of this sūtra because it pertains to the *Phalādhyāya* (the fourth chapter on the fruits of knowledge). Although this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed connected to the *Phalādhyāya*, it is specifically distinguished here as being included within the *pāda* whose subject matter consists of the removal of contradictions—such as the one expressed by the words "na hy anyasya" (for [the world] belongs to no other). Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra (*lakṣaṇa-sūtra*) is valid, as there is no logical contradiction regarding Viṣṇu being the cause of the universe.
Thus ends the section on the existence of the Buddha.
Here, the contradiction with many arguments regarding Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world is resolved:
"Its non-difference [from Brahman] follows from such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa) and others."

Now, an objection is raised: "The creation under dispute must depend upon independent external instruments, because it is a creation, like the creation of a jar and other objects. Consequently, God is merely the agent of creation and so forth by depending on independent instruments; thus, His status as the cause of the birth of the universe does not establish His perfection in all attributes. To this, the Sūtra states:

"Non-difference from that [is established] on account of the words concerning 'origin' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. This is the meaning: "non-difference from that" means that the effect is non-distinct from its independent cause, Brahman. Why? "On account of the words concerning origin and so forth. That is to say, on account of the scriptural passage beginning with "What is the origin? which, through the inquiry into the substratum and other such questions, indicates the result; and on account of logical arguments such as the impossibility of independence [of the effect].

And thus, it is not possible to assert by the power of inference that the creation of the Lord is accomplished through many independent means. For the Śruti, "What indeed was there? [Rig Veda 10.129.5], indicates that the Lord is devoid of independent means, since He is capable of creating while setting aside any other means—by way of contrast, like a potter. Likewise, the Lord is devoid of independent means, because He employs means according to His own will. One who is devoid of independent means does not employ means according to his own will.

However, [the Lord] possesses the means [of action] because of the fear that the effect would not arise in the absence of those means (the counter-example). For instance: "The Lord is independent, because he is the provider of the existence of the means; by contrast, [he is not like] a potter," and so forth—such arguments establish his independence. Thus, since there is not even a scent of contradiction in the Lord’s being the creator of all things through his own independence, it is established that he is complete in all qualities.
And because [the object] is perceived when there is existence.
He introduces the sūtra which refutes the independent proof by means of another argument.

"And because of perception when there is existence. This is its meaning: since there would be the consequence of perception—that is, observation—when there is the existence (bhāve), that is, the presence, of an independent means other than God; therefore, for this reason also, there is no such independent means. This is the sense.

And thus, if there were any independent means of proof other than God, it would be perceived through the authoritative means such as the Vedas; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, it does not exist, because of the existence of this subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*). If it is asked, "Could a thing not exist even if it is not perceived by the means of knowledge? [the answer is: A thing that is not mentioned in the five Vedas does not exist. Why? Because of the statement: "That which is not mentioned by the five [Vedas] exists only if it is established by some means of knowledge. Thus, since there is no contradiction, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct.
And because of the existence of what follows.

[Objection: Since it is understood from the Śruti text, "He was born from water," and from the Smṛti text, "Having taken hold of my own nature (prakṛti), I manifest [myself] age after age," that there exists a material cause other than the Blessed Lord—an independent means such as primordial matter (prakṛti)—the objection is raised that this merely establishes what is already accepted by us. To this, he introduces the Sūtra.

"And because of the existence of the subsequent [world]. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of restriction. Because of the very existence of the subsequent world—that which has no independent means of proof—the statement that [the world] was produced from the unmanifested (adṛbhyas) becomes focused on that [subsequent world], and thus there is no contradiction with that [scriptural authority]. This is the meaning.

And thus, because the existence of the very means [of creation] is heard [in scripture], it has that as its object. Consequently, that whose perception is being attributed [to the Lord] does not itself have perception; and that which is perceived is not an independent means. Therefore, since there is no instance of proving what is already accepted [as true], one should not say: "In this scriptural passage, only the means is understood, but not its dependence on the Blessed One; so why might it not be independent, following worldly usage? For there is the scriptural text: "Time existed."

Since origination is established through antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), and since there is no other cause for that origination, the fact that Hari alone is the creator of the universe is established. Therefore, it is proven that the definition [of Brahman] as the cause of the universe is logical.
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [non-existent] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for there is another attribute [intended], as is clear from the remainder of the passage.

Now, one might object that since the Śruti text "Non-being existed not" declares the non-existence of everything, it is improper to describe the dependence of that [non-being] upon the Lord by first admitting another means of proof; having raised this objection, he presents the Sūtra as a resolution.

"Because of the designation of non-existence; if it be said [that this is] not so, we say no, because [it refers to non-existence] by means of another attribute, according to the remainder of the passage. This is its meaning: If it be argued that because of the designation of non-existence—in the statement "Non-being was not," which speaks of the non-existence of something else—it is not logical for there to be the existence of anything else, we say no. Why? Because that negation is consistent with another attribute, namely, a specific attribute such as lack of independence (asvātantrya) and so forth. How is this known? From the remainder of the passage. That negation is consistent with another attribute, namely, a specific attribute such as lack of independence and so forth. How is this known? From the remainder of the passage; the meaning is: from the remaining portion of the sentence, "Darkness existed" (tama āsīt).

Thus, in the Śruti text "Non-being existed," non-existence is predicated with respect to attributes such as unmanifestness, dependence on another, inferiority, having a modified form, and perishability; it is not intended to mean absolute non-existence. Why? Because the supplementary statement "Darkness existed" declares the existence of another means [of manifestation]. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the non-difference of the conscious and unconscious phenomenal world from Brahman.

By this, the interpretation of others—that the world is non-different from Brahman because of the scriptural statement "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*)—is refuted. This is because the doctrine of the falsity of the universe contradicts the scripture "for [Brahman] is unborn and one," and because it contradicts the Smṛti text "unreal and without foundation. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence elsewhere, given the existence of such logical arguments as: "The individual soul is not different from Brahman, because it is conscious, like Brahman," or "The phenomenal world is sublatable, because it is an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell."

Since even pure reasoning that is not in conformity with Śruti and Smṛti lacks authority, it is established that the definition of the world's causality is valid, as there is no contradiction [with scripture].
On account of reasoning and another scriptural passage.

One might object: "Rather than admitting other means [of creation] and then stating that they are dependent on God, it would be better simply to state the absence of such means; for by admitting that one devoid of means is the creator of the world and so forth, one gains a superior degree of greatness. Anticipating this objection, he presents the Sūtra as follows:

"From reasoning (yukti) and from another scriptural statement (śabdāntara). This is its meaning: regarding dissolution (pralaya), it is logical because, just as one who walks while leaning on a staff does not suffer lameness, it is likewise logical for the Blessed Lord—who relies on His own independent means—to act out of divine play (līlā). "From another scriptural statement" means that it is stated to be logical based on specific traditional authority (āgama), such as the passage beginning with "Even though He is capable... (tasmācchakto 'pi). Thus, what has been said is justified.

And thus, since the fact that activity even by means of other independent instruments indicates supreme sovereignty is established by the Smṛti in the passage beginning "of the instruments" (Sūtra 1.4.2), there is no contradiction; furthermore, because other instruments are mentioned in the Śruti passage, "Hiraṇyagarbha was born from the waters... eight [instruments]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.18.1). Moreover, for the sake of establishing the preeminence of Viṣṇu’s greatness, it must be admitted that even at the time of dissolution (pralaya), lower instruments exist. Therefore, in the absence of any contradiction, it is established that the Sūtra defining [the Lord] is appropriate.
And like a cloth.

The author of the Sūtras states that the lack of attachment to those [objects] is due not only to their being established by scripture, but also because the existence of the means [of liberation] is established by reasoning.
"And like a cloth" (paṭavat): the meaning of this is that, just like the creation of a cloth, the creation of the universe as well must be accomplished by means other than the agent.

And thus, it is not only on the basis of scripture; rather, because it is established by reasoning such as: "The creation under dispute is dependent upon means other than its agent, because it is a creation, like the creation of a jar," there is no contradiction. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is appropriate.
Just as, for example, the vital breath and so forth.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If this were so, then creation, being subject to dispute, would require independent means other than a creator, because it is a creation, like the creation of a jar," and so forth; thus, there would also be independence on the part of the instruments. Anticipating this doubt, the author reads the following Sūtra:

"Just as [the body does not exist] without breath"—this is its meaning: just as the vital breath, the body, the senses, and so forth are not independent, so too are other means such as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest.

And thus, since the entry of the Supreme Self into primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth—just as into the body, senses, and so on—is established by scripture in such passages as "primordial matter and the person" (*prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ ca*), the opponent's argument is subject to sublation because its scope is invalidated; for the act of entering implies impelling, and therefore the instruments lack independence. Since the collection of instruments is not independent, as it has entered into them for the purpose of impelling by the Lord, just like the body, senses, vital breath, and so forth—this powerful inference serves as a counter-argument to the inference put forward by the proponent.
Therefore, since there is no contradiction in the Lord’s independent status as the creator of all, it is established that He is complete in all auspicious qualities.
Thus concludes the section on "Designation" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa).
December 4, continuation:
Here, the position that the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses agency as established by scripture is refuted in detail.
"Because of the designation of another [as the agent], there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial, and so forth."

But surely the individual soul (*jīva*) is itself independent as the agent of effects such as jars and the like; for we have the experience that the soul gathers the necessary materials and performs whatever action it intends, thinking "I am doing this. Furthermore, there is the inference: "The potter is the agent of the jar and so forth, because he possesses an effort directed toward them, just as I do. Nor should it be argued that even if the soul is an agent by virtue of the force of experience, its agency might still be dependent upon an inner ruler (*antaryāmin*); for there is no evidence of a soul-governing deity within the body of the individual soul, and if such a being were present, it would be perceived.

For it cannot be said that the Lord exists within the body of the individual soul (*jīva*), and yet the soul is subject to His control, while He does not perceive Him; this is because those who are subject to control must necessarily perceive their controller. Even if one were to conceive of such a Lord, there would be the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*), due to postulating the Lord’s residence within the body of the individual soul and His status as its controller—both of which lack scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*). Thus, once it is established that the visible objects such as jars are produced by the individual soul as their agent, it follows that even effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest have as their agent Brahman, who is not a Lord (i.e., not a transcendent creator).

Potters and the like are not under the control of Brahman; for the claim that Brahman is the controller of all is contradicted by the Śruti text: "From the Jīva, beings arise. However, there is no loss for us if this Śruti is understood as referring to Brahman by way of its identity with the Jīva. For we—who maintain that all Jīvas acting together are the cause of the entire universe—also accept that this text declares that Mahat and the other principles are produced from Brahman, which is equivalent to the Jīva, just as pots and the like are produced from a potter.

Furthermore, if it were intended to refer to Brahman as characterized by supreme sovereignty and so forth, that very [Brahman] would be non-existent [in that context]. Therefore, since the individual soul (jīva) possesses agency by its own nature on the strength of scripture and other authorities, the definition provided in the Sūtra is impossible; such being the position reached, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Because of the designation of another, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial, and so forth. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: the words "if that were so" (*yadi tarhi*) are to be supplied as the remainder. Because of the designation of another—since the scripture states that [the individual soul] comes into being from the individual soul (*jīva*)—it follows that the soul alone is the agent, and not the Lord. If that were so, then there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth; that is, the consequence of the faults of non-performance of the beneficial and performance of the harmful residing in the individual soul. The sense is that these two would not occur [if the soul were independent], because the individual soul is independent. Yet these two are indeed found in the individual soul. Therefore, the meaning is that the individual soul is not an independent agent.

And thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not an agent by its own independence, but rather the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). This is because [the contrary view] is contradicted by reasoning (*tarka*). If it were an agent by its own independence, then there would be no occurrence of non-performance of what is beneficial and the performance of what is harmful; yet both of these are observed. Therefore, it is not an independent agent, because defects such as the failure to perform what is beneficial would necessarily attach to the individual soul, which makes them incompatible with the Supreme Lord as an independent agent. Thus, since the independent agency of the individual soul is untenable, it is established that the definition of Hari as the cause of the universe is correct.
But it is more, because of the specific mention of distinction.

Now, if the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is refuted on account of even some slight defect, then it would follow that Brahman also cannot be the agent, since He too is subject to defects such as fatigue and so forth. Thus, when the two positions appear equal, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that one must simply accept the agency of the individual soul as established by experience and other means; in response to this, the author states the aphorism (*sūtra*) which sets aside that objection: [The sūtra: "But [the agency] belongs to Him alone, because of the teaching [of scripture]. (Brahmasūtra 2.3.40) This means: But the agency belongs to Him alone—that is, to the Supreme Lord—because of the scriptural teaching. For the scriptures declare that the Lord, who is free from all defects, is the agent of all actions. As it is said: "He who dwells in the self, within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who controls the self from within—he is your inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22). Furthermore, the agency of the individual soul is merely figurative, based on its being an instrument for the Lord's activity, just as a woodcutter is said to be the agent of cutting through his relationship with the axe. Therefore, the agency of the individual soul is not real. Thus, the conclusion is that the agency of the individual soul is refuted by the very same arguments that establish the agency of the Lord. Hence, the agency of the individual soul is not tenable. This is the meaning.

"But [Brahman is] superior because of the specification of difference. This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) excludes the equality with the individual soul (jīva). Brahman, however, is superior to the individual soul. Why? Because in passages such as "the hearer, the thinker," etc., specific attributes such as being a hearer are stated; this is the meaning.

Thus, since the absence of fatigue and other such defects in the Lord (Īśvara) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objection that these would apply to Him results in proving what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). Furthermore, since defects such as failing to act for the benefit of living beings (*jīva*) are indeed attested in the case of the individual soul, the objection that they would not apply to it is undesirable; therefore, there is an inequality [between the two cases]. Moreover, because the Lord possesses superior power, defects such as fatigue and anxiety do not affect Him, as is known from the scriptural texts: "He hears without ears" and "He who is beyond hunger and thirst. Consequently, it is established that the Sūtra defining [the Self] is logically sound.
And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is untenable.

Now, even so, since the individual soul (jīva) is an independent agent because it is conscious, like the Lord (Īśvara), it follows that the soul must also be an independent, sole agent; anticipating this objection, the author recites the Sūtra to refute it.

"And as in the case of stones and so forth, that is untenable. This is its meaning: the word "ca" (and) also conveys the sense of "api" (even). "As in the case of stones and so forth" means like a stone or similar object. "Even though the individual soul is sentient," "that is untenable" means that due to a lack of independence, independent agency is impossible.

And thus, since it is possible to establish even the absence of independence by means of the reason of "independence" itself, and because the reason of "consciousness" (*cetanatva*) is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), so too, although both consciousness and lack of independence exist in the individual soul (*jīva*), it is not tenable to prove the soul's inherent agency (*kartṛtā*) on the basis of its consciousness alone—just as in the case of stone pillars and the like. This is because the reason of consciousness is non-conclusive and is countered by the reason of lack of independence, as evidenced by the scriptural statement, "made of clay" (*dārumayīm*).
Therefore, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* is appropriate, as there is no contradiction.
If it is argued that [the world] is not [produced by Brahman] because we observe [processes such as] contraction and so forth, [we reply: no, for it is like milk.

Now, one might object: "Is it not logical that the individual soul (jīva) lacks independent agency? For we observe completion [of actions], since whatever effect the soul begins, it brings to completion. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism as a refutation.

"If it be argued that [Brahman is not the agent] because we see the completion [of an action by another], [we reply] 'no, for it is like milk. This is the meaning: "Because we see the completion"—that is, because we observe the finishing of an effect begun by the individual soul (jīva)—it was said that Brahman is not the agent; if this is argued, we say no. Why? Because, as in the case of milk—which is seen among cows—the completion performed by the individual soul is likewise performed by the Supreme Self alone. By the word "for" (hi), the scriptural authority for this point, namely the passage beginning with "food" (anna), is indicated.

And thus, even though milk is seen in cows, just as [the world] is dependent on the primary vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) by virtue of its being authoritative, so too is this [world] logically established as dependent on the Supreme Self (paramātman). Because of the statement that "food" exists in the form of essence (rasa) and so forth, the fact that the withdrawal of effects is experienced by oneself and observed by others is not proof for the individual soul (jīva) being the agent; for, due to the absence of independence, the Supreme Lord alone is the cause thereof. Thus, since there is no contradiction with reason, it is established that the Sūtra defining [the Lord] is logical.
And also because [the soul] is like the gods and others in the world.

Now, it may be argued that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) cannot be said to be dependent on the Lord (Īśvara). This is because the Lord, as the controller of the soul, is not perceived within the body of the soul. Nor can the existence of the Lord be established by such scriptural texts as "He is indeed the ruler of all," for that [scripture] is sublated by the mark of non-perception. Furthermore, even if one were to postulate His existence, it would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava); for it is not possible that the soul, being controlled by Him, acts according to His command while remaining ignorant of Him. Therefore, since there is no Lord residing within the belly of the soul's body who controls it, [this objection] having been raised, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [the Lord exists] because of the designation of the relationship between the two. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.20) This means: But [the Lord exists], because of the designation of the relationship between the two—the Lord and the soul—as master and servant, which is found in the scripture: "He who dwells in the soul, yet is within the soul, whom the soul does not know, whose body the soul is, and who controls the soul from within, He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22). Since this relationship is designated, the Lord must exist. As for the argument regarding non-perception, it is refuted by the fact that the Lord is supersensible (atīndriya), like the ether (ākāśa) or the self-nature of the soul. Nor is there any logical necessity (niyama) that whatever is supersensible must be non-existent; for if that were so, the self itself would also have to be denied. Furthermore, the scripture stating "He is indeed the ruler of all" establishes the Lord's existence, and it is not sublated by non-perception, because non-perception is merely the absence of perception, and the absence of perception does not prove the absence of the object. Moreover, the assumption of the Lord is not complex, for the scripture itself declares His existence. It is not possible for the soul to act under His command without knowing Him; rather, just as a person may perform actions under the influence of another without knowing their specific intent, so too the soul acts under the Lord's direction while remaining unaware of it. Thus, the Lord certainly exists as the controller of the soul within its body. Therefore, the conclusion is established.

"Also because [it is seen] in the world, like gods and others. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: Just as it is fitting that the Lord of beings is not perceived, even though he exists, so too is it fitting for him to be unseen, like gods and others. To the question "How is this so?", it is said: "In the world. The meaning is that in the world, in the universe, even beings such as *piśācas* are observed to possess powers such as invisibility; what then need be said of the Lord of all?

And thus, although [the Lord] is not perceived through direct perception—just like gods and others—due to His power of invisibility, He is nonetheless perceived through scripture. If it is argued that it is not logical for the Lord to possess the power of invisibility like gods and others, because that power is to be accomplished through meditative worship (*upāsanā*) and is therefore absent in the Lord; then, by that logic, even *piśācas* and the like would not possess it, since they lack such worship. If, on the other hand, the power of invisibility established by valid means of knowledge cannot be denied of *piśācas* and others, then some other cause must be postulated [for its absence in the Lord]. [But this is not the case, as the cause is simply] the absence of worship.

Now, if it is argued that the power of invisibility established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the case of Piśācas and others cannot be abandoned and must therefore be assumed to have a cause, then since that which is "invisible" is established by valid means of knowledge, it cannot be abandoned; thus, let it be assumed to be eternal. This is because of the statement "not through the application of reasoning" (*na yuktiyogāt*), which implies that statements in the form of Śruti and Smṛti cannot be refuted—either as non-authoritative or as non-probative—in any matter by means of the method characterized as reasoning.

In the absence of such contradiction, it is established that the definition-sūtra is valid, for it is only those arguments which follow a single consistent discourse that can establish the meaning, and not dry, isolated arguments. Thus, due to the lack of contradiction, the definition-sūtra is proven correct.
Either there would be the consequence of [the whole] being entirely affected, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness.
He presents the sūtra, refuting the soul's inherent agency by means of another argument.

"Either there would be the consequence of [the soul's] acting as a whole, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts declaring its partlessness. This is the meaning: the word "or" (*vā*) indicates the presentation of a fault based on a distinction between alternative positions. If it is admitted that the individual soul (*jīva*) is inherently an agent and acts in its entirety, then there follows the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of "acting as a whole" (*kṛtsnaprasakti*), which is the implication that all its capacities would be employed even in every action such as the grasping of grass and so forth.

And if, in order to avoid that, one accepts that it acts only through a single part, then there would be a "contradiction with the scriptural texts declaring its partlessness" (*niravayavatva-śabdakopa*), meaning there would be a conflict with such Vedic revelation as "He is eternal and partless."

And thus, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were an independent agent by its own nature, it would have to be an agent of all its own actions either in their entirety or in part. In the first case, if the soul were an agent of all its own actions in their entirety, it would follow that it is an agent even in the taking up of grass and such [insignificant acts] in their entirety; this constitutes a contradiction with reasoning (*tarkavirodha*). In the second case, if the soul were an agent of its own actions only in part, then there would be a lack of authority for the scriptural texts (*śruti*) which establish that the soul is partless; this also constitutes a contradiction with reasoning.

Furthermore, agency consists of activity both in its entirety and in part; thus, if one accepts the independence of the individual soul (jīva), agency itself would be impossible because activity—which is the pervader—would be incompatible with it. Therefore, independence must be abandoned. If it is argued: "There is no room for this objection even if the soul possesses agency by its own nature, because since it possesses parts produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the contingency of total involvement does not apply. And since there is no inherent [independent] part, there is no contradiction with scripture," then we must ask: Is every soul equally possessed of adjuncts, or is it only a part thereof?

The first [position] is not tenable; for if every living being were conditioned (*upahitatva*), everything would be swallowed up by the condition, and thus it would be impossible for a part to be conditioned. In the second [position], there is no state of being conditioned; for the "part" must be asserted to exist even prior to its connection with a condition. If that [part] were also produced by another condition, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued: "Let the agency of the living being (*jīva*) be caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), as it is charming only when left unexamined because it contradicts reason," we say no. This is because being caused by ignorance lacks scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*). For that which is said to contradict reason also contradicts authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, since independent agency is untenable for the individual soul (jīva), it is established that the defining characteristic of Hari as the cause of the universe is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the other.
Here, the contradiction with powerful arguments regarding Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is resolved:
"But [it is so] because of scripture, for [the Lord] has sound as His basis."

Objection: Is it not the case that it is not logical for the Lord to be the creator of the world by virtue of His own independence? For if the Lord were the creator, He would have to possess activity either in its entirety or in part; yet such [activity] is not possible in the case of the Lord. Thus, because this is contradicted by reasoning (*tarka*), [the position is untenable]. Response: This is not a fault. One should not say that the very acceptance of the individual soul (*jīva*) as the agent implies the non-acceptance of the Lord as the agent. This is because there is no activity in the Lord other than that which is employed to eliminate defects [in the soul]. Otherwise, that same defect would not apply to the individual soul either.
Therefore, since it has been established that Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is not tenable due to its contradiction with reason, the Sūtra speaks as follows, refuting that position:

"Because of the fact that [the Lord] has scripture as His source. This is its meaning: in the view that God is the agent, the defect of contradiction with the arguments stated regarding the view that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent—such as "the consequence of the entire [world] being produced at once," and so forth—does not exist. Why? Because of scripture; for that which is [otherwise] contradictory is [established] by scripture alone. Now, one might ask: how does this much resolve the contradiction with reasoning? To this it is said: "Because He has scripture as His source. Since God and His attributes have scripture as their sole means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and are not objects of reasoning, no contradiction with reasoning applies there.
But it is not so with the living self (jīva); the meaning is that it is cognizable even by other means of knowledge.

And thus, there is no contradiction with reason regarding the independent agency of God. This is because the reasoning that establishes a contradiction depends upon the scripture that apprehends the subject (the locus), and therefore the very reasoning [of the opponent] lacks authority in proving that [contradiction]. Furthermore, since God possesses inconceivable power, it is logically possible for Him to perform the functions of a part even while being a whole, by virtue of that power; for the Scripture states that those qualities which are contradictory in the world exist in God without contradiction.

Since the quality of being knowable solely through verbal testimony—which serves as the means for avoiding contradiction with reason—exists in God (Īśvara), the lack of distinction [between Him and other objects] is not established. Furthermore, it is impossible to negate an object of knowledge taught in scripture by means of "dry" (abstract) inference alone. Therefore, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is logically consistent, as there is no contradiction.
And likewise in the self, for [the world] is indeed manifold.

He introduces the sūtra which, by means of another argument, establishes this point: that the contradiction with reason applies only to the position that [the world] has a living being (jīva) as its cause, and not to the position that it has the Lord (īśvara) as its cause.

"Thus, indeed, [these] diverse [powers] are in the Self alone. This is its meaning: the first word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis; the second is for conjunction; and the word "hi" (indeed) indicates well-known fact. Thus, by virtue of the word "hi," [it is established that] these very powers—diverse, inconceivable, and known through scripture as "diverse power"—reside in the Self, which is the Lord alone, and not in the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, the contradiction with reasoning applies only to the position of the individual soul, and not to the position of the Lord; this is the meaning.

And thus, since only Īśvara possesses these diverse powers while others lack them—according to the Śruti, "He is the one controller"—the diversity of power is established through the discernment that it consists in the performance of various effects, such as activity and so forth, by means of a single part of both the Jīvas (who are devoid of distinct limbs) and Īśvara. Therefore, in the absence of any contradiction with reason, it is established that the Sūtra defining [Īśvara] is logical.
And because of the defects in one’s own position.

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is no fault in the contradiction with reasoning regarding Viṣṇu because He is rooted in scripture and possesses diverse powers, so it might be for the individual soul (jīva) as well; for it is possible to establish that the contradiction with reasoning—based on marks such as its being conscious—is not a real contradiction. To this, the author states the sūtra as a reply:

"And because of the defect in its own position" (svapakṣadoṣāt). This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of restriction. Thus, since the defect of contradiction with reasoning has been stated in the scripture specifically regarding the position of the individual soul (jīva), that [contradiction] must not be led to the status of being non-defective; rather, the meaning is that only the position of the Lord (īśvara) is to be led to the status of being free from defects.

And thus, it is impossible to assert that the individual soul (jīva) possesses agency independently; for since the soul is subject to defects and lacks the capacity for such creative imagination, its defects cannot be interpreted as non-defects. This is because of the scriptural statement, "Now, that which is the defect [is the Lord]," and because the logical contradictions—such as the consequence of the entire [Brahman] being affected—have already been stated as defects specifically regarding the position of the individual soul. Furthermore, there exists the defect known as the contradiction between the statements concerning the soul's possession of defects and the Lord's freedom from defects. Therefore, in the absence of such contradictions, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is logically sound.
"He is endowed with all [powers], because of the perception of that."

One might object: "Is it not reasonable that there is no contradiction in God because of His power of diverse capacities? For when a capacity does not have a certain thing as its object, or when it ceases to exist, then at that time, since the occurrence of a defect in that regard is inevitable, it is not tenable to avoid that [defect] by means of such a capacity. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the sūtra:

"And she is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen. This is the meaning: since the deity called the Supreme Self is not merely possessed of various powers in a general sense, but is "endowed with all," meaning possessed of powers regarding all objects at all times; for what reason? Because of that vision, and because of the scriptural statement that she is "joined with all. Therefore, the meaning is that one should not suspect any contradiction with reasoning regarding the Lord.

Thus, because the Lord is always possessed of manifold powers regarding all objects, it is stated in the Śruti that the power of the Supreme Self is "always endowed with all powers," meaning it pertains to all objects and exists at all times; for it is declared that He possesses all powers, and it is therefore appropriate to resolve any contradiction with reasoning by means of such power. Consequently, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is free from contradiction with reasoning.
If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered.

Now, one might object: even so, because the Lord is devoid of organs (vikaraṇatva), His status as the creator of the world is not logical. Furthermore, since all contradictions have already been resolved by the power of His diverse and infinite capacities in the very sūtra "sarvopeta" (II.1.30), there is no room for doubt; thus, the present sūtra would be redundant. Having raised this objection, the author presents the sūtra while providing a resolution.

"If it be said that [the Lord cannot be the agent] because of His being devoid of instruments, that has already been answered. This is the meaning of the passage. The word "no" (na) is repeated. "Because of being devoid of instruments": since scripture states, "He has neither hand nor foot," it is understood that the Lord is devoid of organs such as hands. If it be argued that "no"—that is, the agency of the Lord is not tenable—[we reply: why? Because "that has already been answered. By such scriptural passages as "In Him there is no such thing... and so forth, it was previously stated that the absence of instruments refers only to the domain of material (prākṛta) senses. Therefore is the meaning.

Furthermore, in the Śruti passage stating "thus [He is] handless and footless," although the Lord's grasping and so forth are described despite His being devoid of hands and feet, this very lack of hands and feet is established as pertaining to the material realm, while His supreme excellence and supreme power are demonstrated by such statements as "there is no action for Him. Consequently, the reason put forward by the opponent is both inconclusive (*aprayojaka*) and unestablished (*asiddha*).

Moreover, even though the resolution of all contradictions has been made in a general sense, there is no pointlessness to the Sūtra, because the doubt is presented once again with the desire to demonstrate the reasoning conducive to resolving this specific objection. Therefore, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* is appropriate, as there is no contradiction with reasoning regarding Viṣṇu’s being the creator of the world.
Thus concludes the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "But because scripture is its source" (Śrutestu śabdamūlatvāt).
Here, the contradiction with arguments such as the lack of purpose regarding the Lord’s status as the creator of the world is resolved:
"Not so, because there is no need for a motive."

Now, an objection is raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu possesses the quality of being the creator of all, and so forth. In this regard, is it said that Viṣṇu performs creation and other acts with a specific purpose in mind, or without such a purpose? In the first case, he would be incomplete. In the second case, since activity itself would be impossible, his status as the creator of all would be even more untenable. Since there is no other alternative, his being the creator of all is indeed unestablished—this being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from compassion. (1.1.3) [Commentary: It is not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is illogical. For it is established that the Lord, out of compassion for the world, undertakes creation and other acts solely for the sake of the welfare of others, without any personal motive. Just as a father acts for the sake of his son, so too does the Lord act for the sake of the world. Therefore, because He is perfectly complete, His undertaking of creation and so forth is entirely consistent with His nature as the creator of all. Thus, the objection is refuted.

"Not because of having a purpose. This is its meaning: the Lord's engagement in creation and so forth is not for the sake of attaining some purpose of his own. Why? Because he possesses no further purpose; that is to say, because, being full bliss, he has already attained all that is to be attained.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is indeed logical. This is because, being full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), he has already attained everything that is to be attained; therefore, he does not engage in activity for the sake of a result, as is known from the scripture: "He is this very one who goes beyond. Likewise, since his desires are fulfilled, there is no fruit to be accomplished through compassion; thus, it is impossible for him to engage in creation and so forth even for the sake of another's purpose. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, the aphorism defining [the Lord] is established. "But like the world, His activity is mere sport (*līlā-kaivalyam*)."

He introduces the sūtra while refuting the objection: "How can there be activity on the part of the Lord without aiming at a fruit?"—an objection based on the contradiction with the following reasoning: "The Lord must have activity without aiming at a fruit because he is conscious, like Yajñadatta. The sūtra states: na prayojanavattvāt || 2.1.32 || [This is not so], because [the Lord's activity] is not for the sake of a purpose. (2.1.32) The commentary explains: "Because the activity of the Lord is not for the sake of a purpose, the aforementioned reasoning is not valid. For it is observed that even in the case of one who acts out of compassion, such as a physician, activity occurs without aiming at a fruit for himself; therefore, the probans 'because he is conscious' is inconclusive. Furthermore, the sūtra continues: lokavat tu līlākaivalyam || 2.1.33 || "But, as in the world, it is mere sport (līlā). (2.1.33) The commentary explains: "Just as in the world, kings and others engage in activities such as hunting or sports without any external purpose, so too the activity of the Lord is mere sport. Therefore, the objection is set aside. And further: vaiṣamyanairghṛṇye na sāpekṣatvāt tathā hi darśayati || 2.1.34 || "Inequality and cruelty do not [apply to the Lord], because He is dependent [on other factors]; for thus Scripture shows. (2.1.34) The commentary explains: "The Lord does not create inequality or act with cruelty toward His creatures, because He is dependent on the merit and demerit (dharma and adharma) of those very creatures. For Scripture shows this: 'For I am the cause of the origination, sustenance, and dissolution of all beings; and action is what causes their differentiation' (Gītā 18.46), and 'I distribute Myself by My own power through the division of the three guṇas' (Gītā 7.12). And finally: sarvadharmopapatteśca || 2.1.35 || "And because all attributes are possible [in Him]. (2.1.35) The commentary explains: "Moreover, all the attributes mentioned in the scriptures regarding the Supreme Brahman are possible in the Lord alone. Therefore, He alone is the cause of the origin, etc., of the world. Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter. This concludes the section concerning the non-origination of the world. The doubt as to whether the world is real or unreal has been resolved by establishing its non-origination. Now, the doubt arises as to whether the individual soul (jīva) is different from Brahman or not. To resolve this, the second quarter begins. First, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is presented: "The individual soul is different from Brahman, because of the difference in nature. To refute this, the following sūtra is introduced: janmādyasya yataḥ || 2.1.1 || "That from which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]. (2.1.1) The commentary explains: "By the word 'this,' the world consisting of names and forms, which is well-known through perception and other means of knowledge, is referred to. The phrase 'birth, etc. denotes origination, subsistence, and dissolution. The compound 'janmādi' is a karmadhāraya, meaning 'that whose beginning is birth. The word 'yataḥ' (from which) signifies the cause. The meaning of the sūtra is: That from which the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of this world proceed is Brahman. The commentary continues: "Now, it may be asked: how is it known that the birth, etc., of this world proceed from Brahman? To this we reply: It is known from Scripture. For Scripture declares: 'From whence indeed these beings are born, by what they, once born, live, and into what they enter at death—seek to know that; that is Brahman' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1). And again: 'He who, dwelling within the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your inner self, the ruler and immortal' (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3). And so forth. The commentary concludes: "Since the birth, etc., of this world proceed from Him, He is the cause of the world. Moreover, the birth, etc., of this world are possible only if the cause possesses omniscience and omnipotence, and not otherwise. Therefore, Brahman alone is the cause of the world. Thus ends the first sūtra of the second chapter. This concludes the section concerning the definition of Brahman. Now, the doubt arises as to whether the attributes of omniscience and omnipotence belong to Brahman or not. To resolve this, the following sūtra is introduced: śāstrayonitvāt || 1.1.3 || "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source. (1.1.3) The commentary explains: "It is established that Brahman is the cause of the world. But how is it known that He possesses omniscience and omnipotence? To this we reply: Because He has the scripture as His source. The word 'source' (yoni) here means 'cause' (kāraṇa). The meaning is: because the scripture is the cause of the knowledge of Him. The scripture declares: 'Whose greatness is revealed by the hymns' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.11.6), and 'From whom the Vedas arise' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.2). Since the scripture, which is the work of one who knows all things, sets forth the attributes of omniscience and omnipotence in relation to Brahman, it is established that Brahman possesses those attributes. The commentary continues: "Furthermore, the scripture is the source of the knowledge of Dharma, and since Dharma is something beyond the senses, it cannot be known through perception or inference. Therefore, the scripture is the sole authority for Dharma. Likewise, since Brahman is also beyond the senses, the scripture is the sole authority for knowing Him as well. Thus, because the scripture is the source of the knowledge of both Dharma and Brahman, it is established that Brahman possesses the attributes of omniscience and omnipotence. The commentary concludes: "Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the cause of the world, possesses the attributes of omniscience and omnipotence, and is the object of the inquiry into Brahman. Thus ends the third sūtra of the first chapter. This concludes the section concerning the source of the knowledge of Brahman. Now, the doubt arises as to whether the scripture is the source of the knowledge of Brahman or not. To resolve this, the following sūtra is introduced: tattu samanvayāt || 1.1.4 || "But that [Brahman is known] through the harmony [of the texts]. (1.1.4) The commentary explains: "The word 'but' (tu) removes the doubt. The word 'that' (tat) refers to Brahman, the subject under discussion. The meaning is: Brahman is known through the harmony of the texts. The word 'samanvaya' means 'harmony' (anvaya) characterized by 'sam' (complete). The meaning is: because the texts, when taken together, lead to the conclusion that Brahman is the sole cause of the world. The commentary continues: "For instance, the text 'In the beginning, this was indeed Being alone, one only, without a second' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) establishes that Being is the cause of the world. The text 'From whence these beings are born' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) establishes that Being is the source of the world. The text 'All this, verily, is Brahman' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1) establishes that Brahman is the material cause of the world. The text 'He thought: May I be many, may I grow forth' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3) establishes that Brahman is the efficient cause of the world. Thus, through the harmony of these and other texts, it is established that Brahman is the cause of the world. The commentary concludes: "Therefore, it is established that the scripture is the source of the knowledge of Brahman, and that Brahman is the object of the inquiry into Brahman. Thus ends the

"But like the world, [His activity is] mere sport. This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) has the sense of "only" (eva). "Like the world" means that the Lord's activity is like the behavior of a drunkard or the like in the world. "Mere sport" means that it consists solely of play (*līlā*), and not the pursuit of some purpose for Himself.

If it is argued that, in this case, activity without a specific aim toward a fruit is untenable, we say no; for such activity is possible through mere play (*līlā*), as is seen in the world. Indeed, play does not require another purpose, since we observe that even for one who is intoxicated, there is no further purpose for activities such as dancing and singing. Furthermore, the inference put forward by the opponent is fallacious (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the intoxicated person and others, because such actions lack a purpose, just like the movement of hands during the time of explaining a text. Moreover, the activity of the Lord is accepted as being for the sake of favoring the world (*lokānugraha*).
Therefore, since there is no contradiction, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is valid.
Thus ends the section concerning the purpose.
Here, the contradiction with the reasoning concerning the previously mentioned result in the form of another's purpose is resolved.
[The Lord is] not [subject to] partiality or cruelty, because He has regard [for other factors]; for thus [the scripture] shows.

Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is untenable, because he would be subject to defects such as partiality? To this, one must ask: when the Lord, having produced living beings in various wombs such as gods, humans, and animals, bestows upon them happiness and suffering according to their distribution, is that in accordance with their karma, or independently of it? In the first case, there follows a lack of independence, since it is a rule that one who is necessarily dependent on karma lacks independence. In the second case, however, partiality and cruelty result.

Because [the Lord] bestows pleasure and pain through the differentiation of signs (nirnimitta-vibhāga). Furthermore, there is no proof for the Lord’s status as a creator. For the Veda, which is accepted as a means of valid knowledge, lacks authority—just like the Vedic texts that enjoin the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. The lack of authority of those Vedic texts regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth is established because the Lord does not independently bestow pleasure and the like based on the dharma and other factors described therein as the means to pleasure and pain. Thus, since it is impossible for Hari to be the creator of all, the Sūtra cannot be a definition; such being the prima facie view, the following is stated in the Sūtra: [The Lord is the cause,] because of the distribution of pleasure and pain through the differentiation of signs.]

"Partiality and cruelty do not [apply to the Lord], because He has regard [for other factors]; for thus the Scripture shows. This is the meaning: if, for the sake of establishing His sovereignty, one admits that the Lord’s bestowal of fruits upon living beings depends upon their karma, then the partiality and cruelty—that is, the state of being uneven and merciless—of Him who bestows fruits would follow as being without cause; yet these do not exist. Why? Because He has regard [for other factors], since it is accepted that the Lord takes the karma into account. Why is that? Because the Śruti, in the passage "By merit, merit," shows—that is, establishes—it as such. Therefore is the meaning.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world and so forth is indeed logical; for, by accepting that He bestows fruits in accordance with various karmas, there is an absence of partiality and cruelty. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is valid.
"If it be argued that [the distinction between soul and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no, because [the cycle] is beginningless."

[Objection: Surely, since there is an absence of action (karman) by way of dependence [on God], it is not possible to avoid defects such as partiality (vaiṣamya) by depending on that [action]. Nor can it be said that prior action exists, for in the scripture stating "He alone indeed... (Eṣa hy eva...), even that is heard to be dependent upon the Lord. Since partiality and other defects cannot be overcome even when the granting of fruit is considered in relation to what is performed by oneself, [the opponent] having reached this conclusion, the Sūtra says: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] because of His dependence on that [action]... (Sūtra 2.1.34).

"If it be argued that [the Lord is not the cause] because of the non-distinction of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness. This is its meaning: To avoid the defects of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*), one might argue that there is no karma to be depended upon by the Lord; thus, there is a qualified negation [of His dependence on karma]. Why? Because of "non-distinction" (*avibhāga*); that is, because that karma is not distinct from things that are not independent (meaning, they are dependent). Thus, if it is argued that partiality and so forth cannot be avoided due to dependence on karma that is under His own control, we say no. Why?

The meaning of "because of beginninglessness" is "because of the beginninglessness of the succession of karma. Thus, the point is that there is no such fault [in our position], because by accepting that the Lord causes the successive karma to be performed by the individual soul (jīva) in dependence upon each preceding [action], it follows that karma is indeed dependent [on prior causes].

And this fault would indeed arise if the prior karma were caused by God independently [of anything else]. But it is not so; rather, it was caused in accordance with prior karma. Since the fault begins from that very point where the process culminates, there is no contradiction because the succession of karma is beginningless, as indicated by the statement "merit, demerit, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is stated without any inconsistency.
And it is both logically established and empirically observed.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even so, it is not logical for God to be the giver of fruits in dependence upon karma, because that would entail a lack of His independence. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism:

"And it is both logical and observed. This is its meaning: even if God depends upon karma, His sovereignty is indeed logical and consistent, because karma itself is under His control. Now, one might object that dependence on karma—which is under His own control—would result in the emergence of partiality; to this it is said: "And it is observed. The meaning is that such partiality is known from scripture, through the text "He causes [them] to act," to be no fault.

Thus, even though Īśvara is dependent upon karma, His sovereignty remains intact; for dependence on that which is under one's own control does not contradict sovereignty. Nor should it be argued that, such being the case, defects like partiality (vaiṣamya) would again arise, because this is actually accepted—as indicated by the very mention of "partiality" [in the Sūtra]. Therefore, since there is no contradiction in Hari’s being the creator of all, the definition-sūtra is established as valid.
Thus concludes the section concerning partiality and cruelty.
In this regard, the absence of contradiction with reason is stated concerning Viṣṇu’s possession of all auspicious qualities and His freedom from all defects:
"And because all attributes are possible [in Him]."

"Now, is it not the case that Viṣṇu is not full of all attributes? Because he is sentient; otherwise, even Devadatta and others would possess such a nature. Furthermore, since all contradictions with reason have been refuted, the subsequent sūtra would be redundant. To this objection, the author states the following sūtra as a rebuttal:

"And because all attributes are possible. This is its meaning: since all attributes—consisting in the presence of qualities and the absence of defects—are possible in Brahman, being appropriate to It by virtue of Its independence and other such characteristics, one should not suspect any logical contradiction regarding Its being full of all auspicious qualities. This is the sense.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s possession of all perfect qualities is indeed logical, because of His independence and because of the scriptural statement, "The qualities have been heard [in the Vedas]. In the preceding sections, the absence of defects regarding each individual quality was established by resolving contradictions. Furthermore, since this section concludes the discussion on His being full of all qualities by removing the contradictions of the arguments that might arise, there is no pointlessness to the sūtra. Moreover, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is ineffective, as it is contradicted by scripture.
And thus, since there is no contradiction regarding Viṣṇu’s being complete in all attributes, it is established that everything stated is logically consistent.
Thus concludes the section on the arising of all phenomena.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter.
Śrīḥ!
Hari.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.
And according to the principle that "others are not perceived," this chapter (pāda) provides a specific refutation of those whose doctrines have already been refuted in general.
Here, the doctrine of the activity of the insentient is refuted:
"And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of a non-intelligent cause]."

Now, an objection is raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world. For, according to the Sāṃkhya system, [it is established] by the inference—"The Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are produced from a cause similar to themselves, because they are effects, like a jar"—that Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is the cause. Since it is stated that this [matter], being independent of anything else, is directed toward the production of effects, it follows that Primordial Matter alone, by virtue of its independence and its orientation toward all effects, possesses agency; thus, it is not logical for [Viṣṇu] to be the cause of the world. To refute this, the author states the following sūtra:

"And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [to prove the Pradhāna]. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: that which is inferred is "inference" (anumāna). The Pradhāna postulated by the Sāṃkhya through inference is not the creator of the world. Why? Because the formation [of the world] is impossible. Since the Pradhāna is insentient, its spontaneous activity is impossible; furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for the spontaneous activity of an insentient entity—this is the meaning.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world is indeed logical. For, since the Pradhāna—which is postulated as the cause by the inference that "an effect must possess a cause similar to itself"—is insentient, it lacks the capacity for spontaneous orientation toward an effect. Furthermore, the objection that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the Pradhāna lacks inherent activity has been refuted by pointing out the reason known as its insentience; for it is precisely the presence of a property contradictory to that [activity] which proves its absence.

Since the previously mentioned inference establishes merely the state of being a cause and does not establish that [the cause] is inherently directed toward an effect, and since there is no other means of valid cognition [to prove otherwise], the definition of the cause of birth and so forth is established as correct; for, as the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya lacks scriptural authority, there is no contradiction with it.
And because of the activity [of the world].

Having thus refuted the Pradhāna’s status as an agent acting spontaneously by means of its insentience, its lack of spontaneous activity, and the absence of any proof [for such agency], the author introduces the Sūtra which refutes it through yet another argument.

"And because of activity" (pravṛtteśca). The meaning of this is: since activity is observed to belong only to a conscious being, in the form "I am acting," the Pradhāna is not the creator of the world. This is the sense.

Furthermore, because the activity of a potter and others in the creation of a jar and so forth is established by experience through the thought "I am doing it"; and moreover, since the creation of cloth and other things is observed to follow the will of a conscious agent, the creation of the *mahat* and other principles must likewise be accepted as such. For the creation of the *mahat* and so forth follows the will of a conscious being, because it is a creation, like the creation of a jar—this being so, [the Sāṅkhya position] contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The activity of a conscious being is action; and that is not possible without volition (*kṛti*), nor is that possible without desire (*icchā*).

And since that [activity] does not exist without knowledge, it is possible to establish that activity is preceded by desire, because effects such as activity are invariably concomitant with their respective causes; therefore, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logical.
If it is argued that [the soul] is like milk and water, even in that case [the same objection applies].

"Now, it may be argued that even in the case of milk and water, which are insentient, spontaneous activity is observed; therefore, because the reason 'being insentient' is seen to deviate [from the conclusion] in those very instances, and since that same example will serve for the spontaneous activity of the insentient,"—having reached this position, the Sūtra speaks in order to refute it:

"If it be argued that it is like milk and water, [we reply] 'even there'. This is the meaning: the word "api" (also/even) is intended to draw in the activity of a conscious being. If it is argued that just as the activity of insentient milk and water is observed, so too may it be for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), we say no. Why? Because even in those cases, such as milk and water, the activity ultimately proceeds from the Lord alone; the meaning is that there is no activity originating from themselves (*svataḥ*).

And thus, since the scripture stating "by the command of this very Imperishable" establishes that even in those cases there exists activity caused by the Lord, it follows that the corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) cited by the opponent—such as milk, water, and so forth—actually possesses the probandum (sādhya) accepted by the proponent. Consequently, the opponent's inference is neither countered by an equally valid counter-inference (satpratipakṣa) nor is it subject to the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra). Therefore, it is established that the definition consisting of being the cause of birth and so forth is logical.
And because there is no establishment of a distinction [between cause and effect], owing to their independence.

One might object: "Granted that there is no deviation [from the rule] regarding the activity of milk and water, since their functioning is dependent on the will of the Lord as established by the authority of scripture; nevertheless, once the activity of insentient things such as magnets and the like is established, there will be a deviation in those cases. Furthermore, when the spontaneous activity of Pradhāna is to be proven, examples such as magnets and so forth will serve as the proof, because one need not adhere to a restriction regarding the choice of examples. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "Not so, because of the difference in nature. (Sūtra 2.1.24) This refutes the objection by showing that the case of insentient objects like magnets is fundamentally different from the case of Pradhāna. While a magnet acts toward iron through a specific, inherent power (śakti), Pradhāna lacks such a directing intelligence. Therefore, the example of the magnet does not invalidate the argument against the independent activity of Pradhāna. The Sūtra thus establishes that the analogy fails due to the essential disparity between the two cases.

"Because of the non-existence of anything apart [from Him], and because of independence. This is the meaning: "Because of the non-existence of anything apart [from Him]" means that, according to the scripture *ṛte* (without), it is understood through the Veda that no action whatsoever exists apart from the Lord.
