Precisely for that reason, since the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya—that insentient matter acts spontaneously—is unauthoritative, and therefore, because of such independence and because it is to be disregarded by the wise, there is no contradiction with the agency of Viṣṇu. This is the sense.

And thus, because the scripture "Nothing is done without you" reveals that everything is dependent upon the Lord, and because there is no deviation from the reason of insentience—given the scriptural teaching that no action whatsoever can exist apart from or without the Lord—and because the opponent's proposed inference lacks a supporting example, and because the inference devised by the Sāṃkhya school is unauthoritative, contradicted by valid means of knowledge, and not accepted by great men, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined through inference is not the creator of the world.

Therefore, since the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya lacks authoritative validity, there is no contradiction with it; thus, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world].
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the self] is not like grass and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for the Lord to be the agent through His own independence, because the production of the world is possible from Pradhāna alone when favored by the Supreme Lord—just as the production of a sprout occurs from the earth when favored by rain. Therefore, since it is not logical for the Lord to be the cause of the world through His own independence, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from Him [the Lord], because of the declaration of His being the source. (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.3) This means: But the agency of the Lord is indeed logical through His own independence, because of the scriptural declaration that He is the source of all things. Just as a chariot moves when its parts are joined together, so too the world comes into being when Pradhāna and other factors are presided over by the Lord. Furthermore, the Lord's agency is established by the fact that He possesses the power to produce effects; for even though the Lord is eternal, He acts by employing various instruments such as time, karma, and the like, just as a potter produces a jar by using clay, a wheel, and other tools. Thus, the objection that the Lord cannot be the independent cause of the world is refuted.

"And because [the effect] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. This is its meaning: Just as in the case of effects such as grass produced from the earth, rain is merely a cooperative cause (*sahakāri*), so too in the case of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) produced from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*) is a supportive factor; He is not independent. Thus, the position of the Theistic Sāṃkhya (*seśvara-sāṃkhya*) is also not tenable. Why? "Because it does not exist elsewhere. The meaning is that the world does not exist elsewhere than through God—that is, without His impulsion—and because God bestows existence and other qualities upon primordial nature.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe; for there exists no entity whatsoever that can function independently or without His impulsion, and even Prakṛti, which serves as the root cause, possesses its existence only by depending upon Him. Therefore, since the doctrine of Sāṃkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṃkhya) lacks scriptural authority and is not contradictory [to our position], it is established that the definition of the cause of the universe is valid.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence elsewhere.
Here, the position of the Lokāyatikas is refuted:
"Even if [the existence of the self] were admitted, it would be devoid of purpose."

[Objection: Surely it is not logical for God to be the agent by virtue of His own independence, because the production of each subsequent effect from each preceding one is possible even without a God; and because the arising of consciousness is also established through its own inherent nature (svabhāva), just like the arising of intoxication from wine. Nor is there any sublation by scripture (śruti) and so forth, since that [scripture] lacks authority. Nor does the lack of authority of that [scripture] entail the non-establishment of dharma and other matters, because we accept the non-existence of supersensuous entities. Therefore, since God does not exist, it is not logical for Him to have the characteristic of being the cause of the world. To this, the author of the Sūtras recites the following:

"Even if [it were] accepted, because of the absence of a purpose. This is the meaning: the word "no" (na) carries over from the previous context. Even if it is not accepted—that is, even if the Cārvākas do not accept that their own treatise possesses the status of a *siddhānta*—our desired conclusion is established. However, even if it were accepted, there would be a self-contradiction because of the absence of a purpose; for they would be admitting the non-existence of both the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), which are pervaded by the status of being a *siddhānta*. Therefore, that position also is not tenable. This is the meaning.

And thus, it is entirely logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world; for there is no contradiction [with our position] because the Cārvāka system is devoid of subject matter and purpose, and is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). To explain: first of all, the subject matter of that system is not supersensible (*atīndriya*), because such things do not exist [for them]. Nor is it sensible (*aindriyaka*), because that which is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) has no need for scripture (*śāstra*). Nor is heaven, liberation, and so forth the fruit for the listener, because those are not attained [by following their system]. Nor is it wealth and the like seen in this world, because that can be achieved through easy means such as agriculture.

Nor can it be said that the purpose [of the treatise] belongs to the author, nor that its purpose is the benefit of the world by means of establishing the non-existence of dharma and so forth; for upon the knowledge of the non-existence of dharma and so forth, only harm—such as mutual injury—is likely to result. Furthermore, benefit itself is not an intrinsic purpose, because it lacks the nature of being the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain. Nor is there any further purpose to be accomplished by such a benefit. Thus, a qualified person (adhikārī) is utterly excluded. Due to the absence of that very qualification, the relationship [between the subject matter and the purpose] is also absent. Therefore, since the system of the Cārvākas is devoid of authoritative validity, it is established that the Sūtra on Definition is correct.
Thus concludes the section on the admission [of the opponent's position].
Section on Legal Jurisdiction.
Here, the doctrine that the agent is the material cause (prakṛti) subordinate to the Person (puruṣa) is refuted.
[Objection: "If it be argued that it is like the case of the person and the stone, even in that case..."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Hari to be the cause of the world; for we observe that a body, which is subordinate to a conscious being, acts as an agent in tasks such as carrying stones, and thus the production of the world is possible through Pradhāna alone, which is subordinate to Puruṣa. Furthermore, because Pradhāna possesses spontaneous activity due to the proximity of a conscious being—despite its own insentience, like a body—it follows from the existence of such reasoning that God himself does not exist. Consequently, the definition of Him as the cause of the world is utterly discarded. To this objection, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from Him [the Lord], because of the impossibility [otherwise] and because of the teaching. (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.37) This means: But [the world arises] from Him, the Lord, because [production from Pradhāna] is impossible otherwise, and because of the scriptural teaching. It is not logical that the world could arise from an insentient Pradhāna, even when conjoined with Puruṣa. For an insentient thing cannot act toward a purpose unless impelled by a conscious being. Just as a chariot, though yoked to horses, does not move toward a destination on its own without a driver, so too Pradhāna, being insentient, cannot act toward the production of the world without being directed by a conscious being. Nor is it logical that the world could arise from Puruṣa alone, who is immutable and devoid of desire. Therefore, the world must arise from a conscious Being who is both the efficient and material cause, namely, the Supreme Lord. This is established by the scriptural teaching: "He thought, 'May I be many, may I grow forth,'" and so on. Thus, the definition of the Lord as the cause of the world is not discarded.

"If it be argued that it is like a man and a stone, [we reply] 'even there'. This is the meaning: if it is argued that just as an insentient body acts toward carrying stones and so forth due to its connection with a man, so too does the insentient *prakṛti* act due to its connection with a sentient being—this is not so. Why? Because even in that case of the body's activity, since the sentient Lord alone is the agent, there is no supporting instance (*dṛṣṭānta*); such is the meaning.

And thus, it is indeed logical that Hari alone is the cause of the world. For, in establishing primordial nature (prakṛti)—subordinated by the Puruṣa—as the cause of the world, there is an absence of any corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta). Nor should it be argued that the body itself serves as the instance; for according to the Śruti, "Nothing is created without You," even the activity of the body is dependent upon the Supreme Self, and thus the instance would be devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala). Consequently, since there is no contradiction with other systems of thought, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logically sound.
Because the status of being a whole (aṅgin) is untenable.

Having thus stated the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example by means of the reason characterized as scriptural testimony (*śruti*), he introduces the aphorism (*sūtra*) in order to establish that same deficiency in the example by means of another reason.

Regarding the phrase "because being an 'aṅgin' is untenable": its meaning is as follows. If it were admitted that the Puruṣa is an *aṅga* (subordinate member), then in the statement "the *aṅga* is the *aṅgin*," it would be untenable to speak of *aṅgitva*—that is, primacy. The meaning is that there is no illustrative example for the position that the Prakṛti is subordinate to the Puruṣa and that agency belongs to the former.

And thus, if the body alone, being subordinate to the person, were the agent, then the authoritative and worldly usage that "the person is the principal and the body is the accessory" would not exist; yet such usage does exist. Therefore, this is not a valid illustration.

Therefore, if it were asserted that the body conjoined with the person acts spontaneously by itself, then because the person would necessarily be subordinate and not primary, the conventional designation of the person as the "principal" (aṅgin) in the Smṛti—where it is stated that "the body is the limb"—would be untenable as an instruction regarding the person's primacy relative to the body. Likewise, in the case of the subject of the illustration, the person would fall into being a subordinate limb of the Pradhāna, and thus the conventional designation of the person as the "principal" would be untenable. Consequently, both the absence of a valid illustrative example and a contradiction [with established doctrine] have been shown. Thus, it is established that the definition of the Lord as the cause of the world is correct, as it is free from contradiction with other philosophical systems.
Thus concludes the section concerning the stone for the man.
Here, the doctrine that the person (puruṣa) is the agent with nature (prakṛti) as a subordinate factor shall be refuted;
otherwise, because there would be a dissociation from the power of consciousness in the case of inference.

Now, it may be objected that it is not logical for Hari to be the cause of the world; for since the production of the world is possible from Pradhāna (primordial matter) and Puruṣa (the individual soul) alone—with Pradhāna acting as the subordinate and Puruṣa as the principal—God would be redundant. Accordingly, the formal argument is as follows: "The activity under dispute is dependent upon a non-conscious entity acting as a subordinate to Puruṣa, because it is an activity, like the activity of carrying stones and so forth. Since this is the case, the definition [of Brahman] as the cause of the world is untenable. To this, the author states the Sūtra: [Note: The Sūtra itself is not provided in the source text.]

"And because of the absence of the power of consciousness in the inference of [the self] in another way. This is the meaning: there is an attraction (samākarṣa) of the phrase "because of the impossibility of being the principal [agent] by means of the word [‘puruṣa’]. Even if one attempts to infer—by a method other than the previous position—that the person (puruṣa) is the agent with the prakṛti as a subordinate factor, [it fails] because of the absence of the power of consciousness. That is to say, because the conscious individual soul (jīva) lacks the power of activity for the sake of connection with a body, it is precisely due to the impossibility of being the principal [agent].

And thus, it is indeed logical that God alone is the cause of the world; for there is no evidence for the agency of a Puruṣa who has Primordial Matter (prakṛti) as a subordinate factor. Now, if it is thought that [the world] is inferred otherwise than according to the ancient doctrine, that being the case, the probandum would be absent in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). If one were to admit the power of activity in the [Purusha] alone, the body would be useless. If not, then by the consequence of the absence of connection with a body, there would be no activity such as bringing stones and so forth; yet such activity does exist.

Therefore, since an Īśvara must be admitted as the one who effects the connection between the person and the body and bestows powers such as the ability to move stones and so forth, how can the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) be said to be devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala)? Thus, it is established that the definition [of Īśvara] as the cause of the world is logical.
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent.
Having thus refuted the non-theistic doctrines individually, the Sūtra now recites [the following] while also refuting them through a general refutation.

"And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. This is the meaning: because of contradiction—that is, because it is opposed by all scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and reasoning (*yukti*)—the doctrine that there is no Lord (*anīśvara-mata*) is inconsistent; the meaning is that it is illogical.

Furthermore, because there is no statement that contradicts the following: the scriptural texts such as "Thus generating heaven and earth" (RV 10.121.1) and "From whom [the world arises]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1); the traditional authorities (smṛti) such as "The creator, the protector, and likewise the consumer"; and the logical arguments such as "The subject of dispute has an agent because it is an effect," and "Consciousness and its mental states are governed by something else because they lack independence. This is because [the opponent] asserts a doctrine of the independence of primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth, which contradicts these sources.

Consequently, because it contradicts all of Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, every non-theistic doctrine is invalid. Therefore, it is established that there is no impossibility of the definition [of God] due to conflict with the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and others.
Thus ends the section on inference based on other [premises].
Here, the doctrine of the commencement [of the world] by atoms is refuted:
"Or [the world] is like the large and the long, from the short and the spherical."

Now, are there not exactly seven categories, beginning with substance? Among them, substances are exactly nine, starting with earth; qualities are twenty-four, beginning with color; action is fivefold, such as upward throwing; generality is of many kinds, being both of the nature of a genus (*jāti*) and of the nature of an adjunct (*upādhi*); inherence, however, is only one; and particulars are infinite. This triad [of inherence, generality, and particularity] is exclusively eternal. Among these, the non-eternal is produced by a triad of causes. That in which an effect inheres when it is produced is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), which is precisely a substance such as an atom.

In that process, atoms initiate a composite whole (*avayavin*) through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. An inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is that which is proximate to the effect and whose causal capacity has been ascertained. Among these, the conjunction of the parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*) alone serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the effect-substance by virtue of its proximity to the effect within a single object (*kāryaikārthapratyāsatti*). Furthermore, the qualities and actions of the causes serve as the non-inherent causes of the qualities of the effect by virtue of their proximity to the effect within a single object.

Regarding action, that which resides in the cause is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the quality or action in the effect, by virtue of the proximity consisting in having a single object as the effect. In this regard, dimension residing in the cause becomes the non-inherent cause of the dimension residing in the effect. However, the dimensions residing in atoms, dyads, and cotton-wool are not the non-inherent causes of the dimensions residing in dyads, triads, and cotton-balls; rather, it is only the number residing in the dyad and triad that is [the cause]. As for the dimension of the cotton-ball, however, it arises from aggregation (*pracaya*).

This other cause, the instrumental factor, consists of God (Īśvara), unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), time, and so forth. Among these, God is a specific kind of self (ātman). While the [ordinary] self is endowed with fourteen qualities beginning with number (saṃkhyā), the Supreme Lord possesses only five qualities beginning with number. Furthermore, since He is possessed of knowledge, will, and effort—which are necessary for agency—and is thus fit only for the remaining six qualities, how can it be logical that He possesses infinite qualities? Therefore, the previous chapter is entirely useless. To this objection, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Or, like the large and the long from the short and the spherical. This is its meaning: according to the Vaiśeṣika system, just as dimension arises in the *caturaṇuka* (four-atom aggregate) and so forth from the largeness and length residing in the *tryaṇuka* (three-atom aggregate) and so forth; likewise, dimension would also arise in the *tryaṇuka* and *dvyaṇuka* from the shortness and sphericity residing in both the *dvyaṇuka* and the atom (*paramāṇu*). This is the sense.

Alternatively, the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) is that the production of an effect would not occur even from largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*). Therefore, the intention is that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is untenable.

And thus, it is indeed logical that Hari possesses the characteristic of being complete with infinite qualities; for the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are unauthoritative, as their assertions are untenable. As for what was said—that minute (*aṇu*) and atomic (*parimaṇḍala*) dimensions do not possess the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—that is not so. For if that were the case, it would follow that large (*mahat*) and long (*dīrgha*) dimensions also lack that status. Since [large and long dimensions] act as causes for [larger and longer effects], these two [minute and atomic dimensions] would likewise be equal in that regard, as there is no distinction [in the nature of the cause]. Therefore, because they are contrary to production [of further dimension], those two do not possess the status of non-inherent causes.

However, the claim of the Vaiśeṣikas and others that these two [attributes] belong exclusively to these [two] is indeed inconsistent; therefore, there is no contradiction with the infinite qualities of the Lord, and it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] does not exist.

Thus, intending that by the method of refuting the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) such as largeness and length according to the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, the category of non-inherent cause itself is rejected, he introduces the Sūtra which likewise refutes the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

"Even in both ways, there is no action; therefore, there is an absence of that [effect]. This is the meaning: even in both ways—that is, in either of the two positions regarding the nature of God's will, whether eternal or non-eternal—there is no possibility of the production of motion in the atoms. Therefore, "there is an absence of that" means that, consequently, there would be an absence of the effects such as the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth.

If it is argued that the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), is that will eternal or non-eternal? In either case, the motion of atoms (*paramāṇu-karman*) is not possible. If the will of God were eternal, then since it exists even during the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*), there would be no motion of atoms at other times as well due to its constant presence. If, on the other hand, it were non-eternal, then because of the absence of a cause for its production, the will of God would never arise, and thus there would be no motion of atoms. Nor can it be said that the will belonging to a previous cycle (*kalpa*), though non-eternal, serves as the efficient cause like a sacrifice (*yāga*); for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*) for this.

Now, if the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is not the cause, then let that [will] itself be the cause; however, in that case, there would be no cause for anything else either. According to the opponent's view, due to the absence of action in atoms, there is an absence of conjunction, and consequently, an absence of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). But in the Vedic position regarding God, even though the will of God exists, the fact that all effects are not produced is explained solely by the inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*) of God. And this is not the same in the opponent's position, because for them God is known through inference (*anumāna-gamya*), whereas for us God is known through the Vedas alone (*vedaika-gamya*).
Therefore, since the assertions of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are inconsistent, it is established that the defining characteristic of Hari is His possession of infinite qualities.
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being on the same footing.

Having thus demonstrated the impossibility of an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) according to the positions of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the author states the aphorism while also refuting the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

"And because of the acceptance of inherence, due to parity, there is an infinite regress. This is the meaning: because the Vaiśeṣikas accept inherence—that is, they admit the relation of inherence—on the grounds that the parts and the whole, and so forth, are distinct; and because of parity, since the inherent cause and the non-inherent cause are likewise equally distinct; and because if inherence must also be accepted in those cases, it leads to an infinite regress; and because of this infinite regress, their doctrine is untenable. This is the sense.

And thus, as for the claim that a substance such as an atom (*paramāṇu*) is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), that is not correct. For the inherence (*samavāya*) is postulated only after one has accepted the difference between the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) in order to establish the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Since inherence itself possesses the same quality of being distinct [from its relata], there would have to be a further inherence required to establish the relationship of qualifier and qualified—such as "the inherence of the clay in the jar. If that were so, the same logic would apply there as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, because the very relationship between the fundamental parts and the whole remains unestablished, that [inherence] is also unestablished.

For other relations would have to be admitted to establish the first relation among them, yet those further relations remain utterly unestablished. Furthermore, if inherence (samavāya) is held to be self-establishing—meaning it is accepted that it itself generates the cognition of the qualifier-qualified relationship within itself—then inherence remains unestablished.

Since it is simpler to accept the non-difference of quality, the qualified, and so forth, and to establish that a single substance alone is self-sustaining—rather than accepting their difference and then postulating an inherence (*samavāya*) as its own sustainer, which would render inherence redundant—it is established that the definition-sūtra is logically sound.
And because it exists eternally.
Thus, having refuted creation by means of the rejection of the three causes according to the opponent's view, he introduces the aphorism intended for the purpose of refuting dissolution.

"And because [the cause] exists eternally. This is its meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the defects. Since causes such as the will of God (*īśecchā*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist at all times, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, there would be the production of effects eternally—that is, always—and not only occasionally. This is the sense.

And thus, in the view of the opponent, dissolution (laya) is impossible. This is because, given the presence of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), there can be no non-production of an effect due to a lack of causes. If the inherent causes—the atoms—are eternal, and one accepts that inherence itself is produced, then every effect would be eternal and subject to production. Furthermore, when the production of an effect ceases while the inherent causes and other factors remain present, an effect could never arise from them again. For if an effect is not produced despite the presence of a complete set of causes, it is illogical for those factors to be considered its causes. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because it possesses form and so forth, the opposite [of the atom's indivisibility] follows, as is seen [in experience].
Thus, having accepted the permanence of atoms, the doctrine that they are the originators [of composite objects] has been refuted. Now, he introduces a sūtra that negates their permanence.

"And because they possess form and other qualities, there would be the opposite [of eternity], due to observation. This is its meaning: Furthermore, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, since the atoms of earth, water, and fire possess form and other qualities, there would be the opposite—namely, non-eternality, which is the reverse of eternality. Why? Because of observation; that is to say, because of the observed pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever possesses form and other qualities is non-eternal," as seen in the case of jars and the like.

And thus, in reality, the eternality of atoms is not tenable, because they necessarily possess a primordial nature (prākṛtarūpa). Indeed, it is observed in the world that whatever possesses a primordial form and so forth is impermanent. Since the atoms of earth, water, fire, and air possess material color, taste, smell, and touch, they are impermanent. Therefore, it is established that the previously stated definition-sūtra [of atoms] is invalid due to the absence of eternality in atoms.
And because there is a fault in both cases.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "whatever possesses color and so forth is impermanent" is a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), whereas "whatever substance is partless is eternal" is a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) that is more powerful? Therefore, because it is sublated by that [specific pervasion], the possession of color and so forth cannot prove the impermanence of atoms. Or, let it be granted that atoms have a beginning; even so, there would still be no absence of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). For if atoms were produced by some other cause, the production of dyads and so forth from them would be possible. To refute this, the author states the aphorism: *na kāraṇāvayavabhāvāt* (Sūtra 4.2.23). [Translation of the Sūtra: Not [so], because [atoms] do not exist as parts of a cause. [Commentary: This means that since atoms do not exist as constituent parts (*avayava*) of any other substance that could serve as their cause, they are themselves the ultimate causes. Consequently, there is no possibility of atoms being produced by another cause, and thus the aforementioned objections do not apply. Furthermore, if atoms were produced, they would necessarily possess parts, and being composite, they would be non-eternal. Thus, the existence of atoms as eternal, partless substances remains unrefuted. Therefore, the production of dyads and subsequent effects from atoms is established. Thus ends the section.

"And because there is a fault in both ways. This is the meaning: for the Vaiśeṣika, in both ways—that is, in either of the two positions consisting of the permanence or impermanence of the soul—there is a fault. The meaning is that, just as in those cases, since there is the fault of the non-existence of a cause for the production of everything being permanent, that position is not tenable.

And thus, as for what was stated—that "whatever possesses color and so forth is impermanent" constitutes a general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti)—that is not correct. This is because there is no specific means of valid cognition (viśeṣapramāṇa) that would exclude impermanence from that which possesses color and so forth. Nor is partlessness (niravayavatva) such a specific means of valid cognition, since it is possible to prove the absence of that [partlessness] in an atom (paramāṇu) by virtue of its possessing color and so forth. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no fault regarding impermanence, that too is not correct.

In your view, since atoms lack a cause, they cannot arise; consequently, there exists a subverting argument (bādhaka) characterized by the undesirable consequence that effects such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth would not be produced. Thus, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct, as both positions are vitiated by defects.
And because there is no sense of possession, there is absolute lack of expectation.

Having thus refuted the doctrine of the commencement [of the world] by atoms through its conceptual proliferation, the Sūtra speaks in order to refute it also on the grounds of its lack of authoritative basis:

"And because it is not accepted [by the Vedas], there should be absolute disregard for it. This is its meaning: "Because it is not accepted" means that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is devoid of acceptance by the Śrutis and other authoritative sources, and because it is contrary to them. In this regard, "absolute disregard" means that one should show no respect for it.

And thus, because the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is not accepted by any of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and so forth, and because it is contrary to them; because it is to be disregarded even more than the theory that Pradhāna is the cause [of the world]; and because it is censured in the Mokṣadharma section of the Mahābhārata as "Anvīkṣakī" (speculative reasoning); therefore, since the theory of the world's origination from atoms is untenable, it is established that the Lord’s possession of infinite, perfect qualities—as stated in the preceding chapter—is free from contradiction.
Thus ends the section concerning the Vaiśeṣika.
Here, the view of those who maintain that [the world] is a collection of atoms is refuted:
"Even if the aggregate were caused by both [atoms and a creator], that [result] would not be attained."

Now, it may be objected that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world, because this contradicts the doctrines of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas. Indeed, the entire world, existing in the form of matter (rūpa), consciousness (vijñāna), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra), is ultimately real only as an aggregate of atoms; there is no such thing as a "whole" (avayavin). For when the cognition of a jar or similar objects is accounted for by the mere collection of atoms, the postulation of a "whole"—whether as the dimension of the atom itself or as something produced from them—is useless.

Moreover, everything that exists is strictly momentary; for there is no pervasion of non-existence by momentariness, since in the absence of a pervader, the pervaded cannot logically exist. Furthermore, this entire collection of effects arises solely through the causes of time, karma, and form; it does not depend upon a material cause (*upādāna*). Consequently, because preceding atoms perish, even in the absence of a material cause, the creation of subsequent atoms occurs through time, karma, and so forth alone—so what need is there for a Lord (*īśvara*)? Nor is there any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a Lord, since the Vedas and other such sources lack authority.
Therefore, since the Lord himself does not exist, it follows that his being the cause of birth and so forth is untenable; this being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"Even if the aggregate were caused by both [the atoms and their conjunction], that [aggregate] would not be attained. This is its meaning: since even if an aggregate—meaning a collection of atoms consisting of a plurality—is accepted as being caused by many atoms joined together, or if it is accepted as being caused by many [atoms] that are separate, "that non-attainment" (tadaprāptiḥ) means the non-attainment, i.e., the impossibility, of such an aggregate caused by many separate [atoms]. Why? Because of defects such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), etc.—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. This has been established in the *Ṭīkā*.
Therefore, the Buddhist position—that the pot is merely a heap of atoms (*paramāṇupuñja*) and not a composite whole (*avayavī*)—is also untenable; this is the sense.

Thus, the designation of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is indeed logical. This is because the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas lack authority, as their doctrines are untenable. As for what was stated—that a composite aggregate arises through causes such as time and karma, based on momentary atoms, and that no "whole" (avayavin) exists at all—that is not correct. In this regard, is this aggregate caused by a single atom or by multiple atoms? It cannot be the first, because the notion that an aggregate arises from a single [atom] is a contradiction.

Regarding the second [position] as well, does it have multiple causes that are conjoined or multiple causes that are dispersed? Not the first, because conjunction itself constitutes a composite whole, which leads to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, if one accepts a causal relationship between two composites, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); and if one accepts a plurality of individual instances, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is the latter [the case], because since a stream of dispersed atoms would exist at all times, it would follow that there could never be a dissolution (*pralaya*) characterized by the absence of the composite effect.

Therefore, since there is no attainment of a composite whole, and because the position that there exists some "whole" (avayavin) perceivable by the cognitions of cows, jars, and so forth is untenable, it is established that the definition of the cause of the world is correct.
If it is argued that [the world] exists because of mutual dependence, we say no, because that is merely the cause for their arising.

"Granted that there may indeed always be the arising of aggregates; nevertheless, there is no absence of dissolution. Since dissolution is established precisely because of the absence of cognition and worldly activity,"—this being the position reached, the Sūtra says:

"If it be argued that [the world] exists because of mutual dependence, we say no, because that is merely a cause for the conventional usage of 'origination. This is the meaning: Now, even if the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-puñja*) exists at all times, there is no inconsistency regarding dissolution (*pralaya*) in our position. Why? Because the conventional usage of those [atoms], and so forth, is due to mutual dependence. That is to say, [the usage] "this and this" is caused by the relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*) of the atoms toward one another. Thus, since the conventional usage of the aggregate and so forth does not exist at a time when such a cognition is absent, dissolution is possible. If this is argued, we say no. Why?

Because atoms are causes merely for the production of their own aggregates—that is, they are causes merely for the production of their own collections—the word "merely" (mātra) implies that it is not possible for even the notion of relative expectation (*apekṣābuddhi*) and so forth to arise from them. Thus, the meaning is that in the doctrine of momentariness, conventional usage and the like caused by those [notions] can never possibly occur.

Furthermore, since there would never be a connection between perception and linguistic usage, it would follow that creation itself does not exist. To explain: the sequence is that first there is the perception of atoms, then the mental requirement (apekṣā), and then linguistic usage; yet this sequence is untenable. Because atoms are momentary, they perish immediately after producing their effect. For it is impossible for perception to occur in one place, the requirement in another, and the linguistic usage in yet another; such a conclusion would lead to an over-extension of the principle (atiprasaṅga).

In the same way, regarding the person (puruṣa) as well, if one were to admit the stability of aggregated atoms produced by sparse atoms, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the production of effects at every moment. And thus, even in a very short time, there would be the consequence of filling the potter’s workshop with numerous effects produced from each individual aggregate of atoms in the form of a jar. Therefore, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logical.
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises.

Thus, having accepted the production of conjoined atoms from sparse atoms, the impossibility of worldly transaction and so forth has been demonstrated. Now, he introduces a sūtra which also refutes the production of dissimilar effects.

"And because of the cessation of the preceding upon the arising of the succeeding. This is its meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) serves both to restrict and to aggregate. The word "not" (*na*) is understood from the context; the phrase "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) is the ellipsis. Thus, not only is the conventional usage of a "collection" untenable in the doctrine of momentariness, but moreover, the production of specific effects is also illogical. Why?

Furthermore, since a cause possesses the capacity to produce an effect similar to itself upon the arising of a subsequent [moment], one might ask: "What is the fault if that cause first produces something similar to itself and subsequently produces a dissimilar effect? For this reason, he says: "Upon the arising of the subsequent. Thus, the meaning is that when the subsequent [moment] arises—that is, when there is the production of an effect similar to itself—the preceding cause must cease; therefore, it is impossible for it to subsequently produce a dissimilar effect.

And thus, according to the opponent's view, the production of a specific effect is impossible, because an effect has the inherent nature of producing an effect similar to itself; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of a cloth being produced from a jar. Nor can it be argued that after producing an effect similar to itself, it subsequently produces dissimilarity, because by the time the effect is produced, the cause has perished, making the production of dissimilarity impossible. Therefore, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logical.
If it were non-existent [at the time of production], there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity.
Thus, having refuted conventional discourse and the like by negating the production of dissimilar effects, he now introduces the sūtra which negates the very production of an effect at every moment.

"Otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the thesis or simultaneity. This is its meaning: In the doctrine of momentariness, the production of an effect at every moment is not tenable. Why? Because if one accepts that an effect arises when the cause is absent, there would be a "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñoparodha*); having previously asserted that "this is the effect of that," there would be a contradiction—that is, a loss—of the established system of conventional discourse. Alternatively, if one accepts that an effect arises when the cause is present, there would be "simultaneity" (*yaugapadyam*), meaning the consequence that causes would exist together with their effects all at once.

And thus, if one accepts the production of an effect at every moment, does the effect arise when the cause is absent, or when it is present? In the first case, there is a contradiction of your own thesis. In the second case, if the sparse atoms produced in the first moment were to persist even at the time of the production of the effect, then—due to the absence of the rule of momentariness—they would remain until the occurrence of their destruction.

Furthermore, according to that view, since there is the rule that "when the cause exists, the effect necessarily arises," the effect would arise again and again; thus, all effects would occur simultaneously. Consequently, it would follow that a potter’s workshop would be filled with pots within a single *ghaṭikā*. Alternatively, because atoms are momentary, the effect would exist in the very same moment as the atoms; thus, there would be no temporal sequence between cause and effect. And a moment possesses no prior, posterior, or middle part.

Since it would follow that in the first moment there is the arising of atoms, while in the second moment there is the production of the effect, the definition-sūtra is therefore established as correct.
Cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, and non-attainment do not exist [as separate entities], because they are not subject to interruption.
Having thus refuted the arising of effects within the doctrine of momentariness, he introduces a sutra that refutes [their] destruction as well.

"Non-attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation [is asserted] because there is no interruption. This is its meaning: thus, in the view that things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), there is non-attainment—that is, the impossibility—of analytical and non-analytical cessation, which consist respectively in the destruction of the continuum at every moment and the non-destruction of the continuum. Why? Because there is no interruption; the meaning is that according to that system, since effects arise, non-effects would not be interrupted.

And thus, in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), destruction is not logically tenable. In that system, destruction is of two kinds: first, having produced an effect, it abandons it and perishes at that very moment; and of that [momentary entity] as well, the same occurs—thus there is destruction at every moment. This very destruction of the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the cause has perished even without a [further] continuum. The other kind, however, is when, after producing an effect, [the cause] perishes in a mere instant along with that effect due to a blow from a hammer or the like.

That very destruction of the continuum is also designated as "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Of these, the first [position] is untenable. Since there is the rule that after producing an effect, at the time of abandoning it, [the cause] must exist and thereby possess the capacity to produce an effect, it would simply produce another effect rather than perish. This would likewise apply at the time of its separation [from the effect]; thus, destruction could never be a state devoid of a continuum. Nor is the destruction of a continuum tenable. For the absolute destruction of an existing jar would mean that, because it exists, it would produce an effect rather than perish.

Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, because [the cause] exists, it must produce an effect and cannot perish; therefore, since there is no occasion for the interruption of the continuum, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logical.
And because there is a fault in both cases.

Now, even so, it cannot be denied that existing entities (*bhāva-padārtha*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Existence (*sattva*) is defined as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). And this is not possible without momentariness. If a jar, having produced another jar in its first moment, were not itself to perish, then it would produce yet another jar in the second moment and so forth; and since those other jars would likewise do the same, there would follow the absurdity of an infinite series of effects. Therefore, in order to establish existence—which consists in the capacity for causal efficiency—the momentariness of entities must be accepted. To this objection, the author states the aphorism: [The opponent argues: "Even so, it is impossible to deny the momentariness of existing entities. Existence is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency. And that [capacity] is not tenable without momentariness. If a jar, having produced another jar in its first moment, did not itself perish, then it would produce yet another jar in the second moment and so on; and those other jars would do the same, leading to the consequence of an infinite number of effects. Therefore, for the sake of establishing existence in the form of causal efficiency, the momentariness of entities must be admitted. To this, he states the Sūtra:

"And because there is a fault in both cases. This is its meaning: in both cases—namely, the position that an effect necessarily arises when a cause exists, and the position that it does not—the fault exists; that is, the fault known as the non-arising of specific effects from specific causes. Therefore, the meaning is that the momentary theory is not tenable by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on adopting either of these two positions.

And thus, if one accepts the momentariness of entities, [one must hold that] existence (*sattva*) consists in their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and that momentariness follows from the impossibility of this [existence] otherwise. For one who asserts this, the rule relied upon—that "when a cause exists, the effect necessarily arises"—is it real or not? In the first case, since cause and effect would be simultaneous like the left and right horns of a cow, there could be no relation of cause and effect. In the second case, if the effect is not produced in the first moment, it would lack existence due to the absence of causal efficiency.

Consequently, at some point, the production of effects would cease to occur; and thus, momentariness—which is postulated because existence is otherwise inexplicable—would not exist. By this, it should be understood that the opponent's own position suffers from defects in both ways, whereas our own position is free from defects. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logically sound.
[Sūtra: "And because there is no distinction in the case of space."

Now, let it be granted that momentariness is not established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). It will be established by inference as follows: "Whatever is existent is momentary, like a lamp and so forth; and these entities, these objects, are existent. Nor should it be argued that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). For instance: "Whatever is the locus of contradictory properties is manifold, like a jar and a cloth; and this lamp is the locus of contradictory properties in its prior and subsequent moments, because such a distinction is observed"—this being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra: *Pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhāprāptirvicchedāt* (2.2.21). [This refers to the refutation of the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness.]

"And because there is no distinction in the case of space. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "also. When momentariness is established for the world by means of the example of a lamp and the reason of existence, there arises the contingency of also establishing non-momentariness by means of the example of space. Now, [one might object] that the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya); to this it is said: "because there is no distinction in the case of space. The meaning is: because no specific dimension (parimāṇa), which would serve as a prover of momentariness, is observed [in the case of space].
And thus, since this reason is counterbalanced (satpratipakṣa), momentariness is not established by it; such is the sense.

And thus, since it is possible to prove even non-momentariness by means of the argument: "Whatever exists is momentary, like space," there is no absence of the probandum (sādhya) in space. This is because, due to the absence of specific perception (*viśeṣadarśana*), there is no proof for momentariness [in that case]. Nor is it established by another reason, because that [momentariness] is not admitted therein as being distinct from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). If you say that existence (*sattva*) does not exist in space, then what is this "existence" which is absent in space? If you say it is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), [then...]

O Venerable One, according to the manner previously stated, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because no entity whatsoever possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Furthermore, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) lacks the probandum (*sādhanavikalatā*). Alternatively, if "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*) means "existence" or "the state of being non-existence," that too exists in space (*ākāśa*), so the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is difficult to avoid. Therefore, since the reason of "existence" (*sattva*) is countered by itself, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is not established even by this [reason]. Thus, it is proven that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because of mindfulness.
Having thus refuted the inference of a sentient being by means of a counter-argument, he introduces the sūtra to refute it further by means of sublation by valid cognition (pramāṇa).

"And because of recollection" (anusmṛteśca). The meaning of this is as follows: because there is recognition (pratyabhijñāna) in the form "this is that very same thing," and because [the theory of momentariness] contradicts that, it is not logical to establish momentariness by means of the reason "existence" (sattva). This is the sense.

And thus, there is a contradiction with the proposition that "this is that very jar," as well as the establishment of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Nor can this be a mere error in the proposition, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) to the contrary. Furthermore, the argument—"this jar is the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in each subsequent moment, because it possesses the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), like a jar struck by a mallet in a single moment"—is refuted by the method already stated. Moreover, by using the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) to indicate atoms (*paramāṇu*), and the word "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) to intend atom-ness (*paramāṇutva*) itself as the reason, [the argument is shown to be flawed].

Alternatively, it might be intended that the aggregate itself is made the subject (*pakṣa*) and "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) alone is intended as the reason (*hetu*). Not the first [alternative], because a pot struck by a mallet lacks the status of an atom (*paramāṇu*) insofar as it is an aggregate; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible due to the absence of the reason in that instance. Nor the second, because since you yourself must prove momentariness only for what exists, proving it for a non-entity (*avastu*) is useless.

Therefore, since the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas are untenable and thus do not constitute a contradiction, it is established that the definition of God as the cause of the entire universe is correct.
Thus concludes the section concerning the aggregate.
Here, the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) is refuted:
"Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed."

[Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is untenable? Because it contradicts the doctrine of Śūnya (the Void). The doctrine of Śūnya holds that there is only one [reality], the Void; therein, the welfare of others is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). From that alone the entire world arises. Nor is its impossibility due to [Viṣṇu] being unattached (*asaṅga*), for its possibility is established through the connection with conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Vedas (*śruti*), because their authority is not accepted. Therefore, since it contradicts the doctrine of Śūnya, the definition of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is untenable. To this, the Sūtra states: [Answer: This is not so. Why? Because it is not contradictory to the Śruti. For the Śruti is authoritative for us. And the Śruti declares that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world. Moreover, the Śruti does not teach the doctrine of Śūnya. How so? Because it teaches the existence of the Self (*ātman*). For the Śruti says: "The Self, dear one, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while simultaneously teaching that the Self is to be seen and so forth. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by means of negating the attributes of the non-Self. For the Śruti says: "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Therefore, because it is not contradictory to the Śruti, Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is indeed tenable. Thus, the Sūtra concludes: "But [it is] from Him [alone]. (Brahmasūtra 2.1.14) "But" indicates the refutation of the objection. "From Him" means from Viṣṇu alone. "Arises" means originates. "The entire world"—this is the subject. "Without a second"—this is an adjective qualifying the world. "As taught in the Śruti"—this is the reason. The sense is: because the Śruti teaches that the world arises from Viṣṇu alone, who is without a second. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as agency and enjoyership. For the Śruti says: "It thinks, as it were; it moves, as it were" (*tad dhy eva manyate tad dhy eva vicetati*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that it thinks and moves. Moreover, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as the body and the senses. For the Śruti says: "This person consists of the essence of food, the essence of water, and the essence of heat" (*annamaya... āpomaya... tejomaya... puruṣaḥ*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self consists of food, water, and heat. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as pleasure and pain. For the Śruti says: "It is neither pleasure nor pain" (*na vai saśarīrasya sataḥ priyāpriyayor apahatir asti... aśarīraṃ vāva santaṃ na priyāpriye spṛśataḥ*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is untouched by pleasure and pain when embodied. Therefore, because it is not contradictory to the Śruti, Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is indeed tenable. Thus, the Sūtra concludes: "But [it is] from Him [alone]. "But" indicates the refutation of the objection. "From Him" means from Viṣṇu alone. "Arises" means originates. "The entire world"—this is the subject. "Without a second"—this is an adjective qualifying the world. "As taught in the Śruti"—this is the reason. The sense is: because the Śruti teaches that the world arises from Viṣṇu alone, who is without a second. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as birth and death. For the Śruti says: "He is neither born nor dies" (*na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścit*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is neither born nor dies. Moreover, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as increase and decrease. For the Śruti says: "It is never diminished by action" (*na karmaṇā vardhate no kanīyān*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is never diminished by action. Therefore, because it is not contradictory to the Śruti, Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is indeed tenable. Thus, the Sūtra concludes: "But [it is] from Him [alone]. "But" indicates the refutation of the objection. "From Him" means from Viṣṇu alone. "Arises" means originates. "The entire world"—this is the subject. "Without a second"—this is an adjective qualifying the world. "As taught in the Śruti"—this is the reason. The sense is: because the Śruti teaches that the world arises from Viṣṇu alone, who is without a second. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as the intellect and the mind. For the Śruti says: "It is neither intellect nor mind" (*naiva vācā na manasā prāptuṃ śakyaḥ*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self cannot be reached by speech or mind. Moreover, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as the elements. For the Śruti says: "It is beyond earth, water, fire, air, and ether" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is beyond the elements. Therefore, because it is not contradictory to the Śruti, Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is indeed tenable. Thus, the Sūtra concludes: "But [it is] from Him [alone]. "But" indicates the refutation of the objection. "From Him" means from Viṣṇu alone. "Arises" means originates. "The entire world"—this is the subject. "Without a second"—this is an adjective qualifying the world. "As taught in the Śruti"—this is the reason. The sense is: because the Śruti teaches that the world arises from Viṣṇu alone, who is without a second. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established. Furthermore, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as the organs of action. For the Śruti says: "It is neither the organ of speech nor the hand" (*naiva vācā na hastena*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is neither speech nor hand. Moreover, the Śruti teaches the existence of the Self by negating the attributes of the non-Self, such as the organs of perception. For the Śruti says: "It is neither the eye nor the ear" (*na cakṣuṣā gṛhyate nāpi vācā*). It is not possible for the Śruti to teach the non-existence of the Self while teaching that the Self is not grasped by the eye or the ear. Therefore, because it is not contradictory to the Śruti, Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is indeed tenable. Thus, the Sūtra concludes: "But [it is] from Him [alone]. "But" indicates the refutation of

"Because the non-existent has not been observed. This is its meaning: it is not logical for the non-existent—that is, the void—to be the creator of the world. Why? Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); this is the implied remainder [of the argument]. Why is that? "Because it has not been observed," that is, because the causality of the non-existent has never been seen anywhere. Therefore, the meaning is that even inference and other means of knowledge are absent [in this case].

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, because the doctrine of Śūnya lacks authoritative foundation. There is no evidence for the claim that Śūnya alone is the cause of the world; such evidence would have to be either perception, inference, or scripture. It cannot be perception, because the state of having Śūnya as the cause is not perceptible. Nor can it be inference, because there is a lack of a corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta). Even though causality is observed in things like jars, these do not serve as a valid instance [for a cause that is non-existent].

In your own view, however, because [the opponent] does not accept its existence, and since the opponent has not perceived causality, it is possible for him to infer the absence of causality; thus, your argument suffers from the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Furthermore, as for scripture (*āgama*), would it be a Buddhist scripture or one such as the Veda? It cannot be the first, because the opponent does not accept its authority. Nor can it be the second, because the proponent does not accept its authority, and moreover, no such Veda is ever observed.
Therefore, since the doctrine of the Void (*śūnyavāda*) is untenable, it is established that the definition of God as the cause of the world is logical.
And thus, even for those who are indifferent, success is achieved.

[Objection: "But what is the fault in accepting that even the unperceived state of being the cause of the world belongs to the Void (śūnya)? Nor has it been said that because it is unperceived, it is unauthoritative and thus unfit for acceptance. For even if an inference based on what is perceived (dṛṣṭānumāna) is impossible due to its not being perceived, an inference based on general observation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa) is possible. For, once the existence of the cause as a real entity—just like the effect—is negated, the birth of that which is non-existent will be established by the reason of its being an effect. [Reply: Anticipating this doubt, he presents the Sūtra: *naikasminnasaṃbhavāt* (Because of the impossibility in one). [Explanation: This refutes the aforementioned doubt. For, while the existence of the cause as a real entity is denied, the very fact that it is an effect serves as the reason to establish that it is indeed non-existent; thus, the Sūtra is introduced to dispel that expectation.

"And thus there would be the production [of effects] even from indifferent things. This is the meaning: if it were admitted that an effect can be produced from what is non-existent (*asat*), then the accomplishment of effects such as *sāra* and *arbha* would result even from "indifferent" things—namely, sky-flowers and the like—which are not objects of the cognition of what is to be avoided or accepted. The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that otherwise, no effect could arise even from the void (*śūnya*).

And thus, if that which is non-existent could be a cause, it would follow that even things like sky-flowers—which are devoid of being objects for the cognition of what is to be rejected or accepted—could produce effects such as fragrance; for it is possible to formulate a negative inference (*vyatirekī-anumāna*) in that case as well. Furthermore, the inferences favored by our opponents are sublated by logical reasoning (*tarka*). Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
Not non-existence, because it is perceived.

Now, one might object: "This criticism would indeed apply if the world were produced from the reality of emptiness (*śūnya-tattva*) as an ultimate truth, like a jar from a lump of clay. But it is not so. Rather, since we accept that even the void appears in the form of the world through a transformation (*vivarta*)—known as an appearance arising from a specific kind of ignorance termed 'conventional' (*saṃvṛti*), just as the form of silver [appears] from what is non-existent—the objection falls away. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the aphorism:

"Nor is there non-existence, because of perception. This is its meaning: the world is not non-existent (asat). Why? Because of perception; that is to say, because it is perceived as being existent (sat).

And thus, if one accepts that the void (*śūnya*) manifests in the form of the world, it follows that the world must be false (*mithyātva*). Nor is this a desired conclusion, because the world is perceived as being real (*sat*). Furthermore, if the void were to appear in the form of silver, experience establishes that it is the mother-of-pearl itself that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition of silver; the void cannot be its substrate. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logical.
And because of the difference in nature, [the dream analogy does not apply], as in the case of dreams and the like.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since even that which is perceived as 'existent'—such as the states of dreaming and waking, or a snake in a rope—is actually non-existent, why should the world not likewise be non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, the author presents the aphorism to dispel it.

"And because of dissimilarity, [the world] is not like a dream and so forth. This is its meaning: the world is not non-existent in the same way that a dream and so forth are—like the state of being "waking" superimposed upon dream-objects. Why? Because of dissimilarity; that is to say, because the waking-state within a dream possesses a distinct property known as sublation (*bādhyatva*), whereas such a property is absent in the [actual] world.

And thus, this [dream] is merely a dream, whereas this [waking world] is not like a rope-snake; for there is a disparity because, while the former is the object of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), the latter lacks such a subverting cognition in the present case. By this, it has been stated that the counter-inference (*pratipakṣānumāna*) propounded by the opponent possesses the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) of being the object of a subverting means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that its counter-position lacks this. Therefore, since even the doctrine of the Void (*śūnyavāda*) is untenable, it is established that the definition of the Lord as the cause of the world is correct.
Thus concludes the section on the non-existent.
Here, the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda) is refuted:
"There is no [external] entity, because it is not perceived."

Now, an objection may be raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, because this contradicts the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins (Idealists). Indeed, only the reality of consciousness—eternal and stainless—is existent; this entire world is nothing but that, and there exists nothing whatsoever beyond it. Therefore, since there is no purpose for a Lord in the production of the world, the definition-sūtra is untenable. To this, the author states the following sūtra:

"Existence does not [occur], because of non-apprehension. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: the world is not existence, even though it consists of cognition; for there is no apprehension of non-difference between cognition and the object of cognition—this is the sense.

And thus, Hari’s status as the cause of the world is indeed logical, because the system of the Vijñānavādins (Idealists) is untenable and therefore non-contradictory [to our position]. If it is argued that the world does not exist apart from consciousness and is merely superimposed upon the reality of consciousness—on the grounds that it cannot be a false imposition since it is perceived as "existent"—or if it is argued that there is no difference between the reality of consciousness and the world because the world consists of the nature of cognition, we reply: there is no evidence for the world having the nature of cognition. Nor should it be said that there is no difference between blue and its cognition because they are necessarily perceived together; for this contradicts the perception of their difference.

Nor is that [perception] an error, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*). Since blue and other objects possess non-difference from their own cognition—just as difference also possesses non-difference from its own cognition—they are real; therefore, it is impossible for the cognition of them to be erroneous. Furthermore, since concomitance (*sāhitya*) is pervaded by difference, the proposition that "there is non-difference because of simultaneous perception" involves a contradiction between the thesis and the reason. If it is argued: "Whatever is manifest is consciousness, just like consciousness itself; and blue and other objects are manifest. Thus, by this inference, the nature of consciousness is established for blue and the rest."

If, by the phrase "it shines forth" (prakāśate), one accepts that [consciousness] is an object of knowledge, then the Māyāvādin’s objection regarding the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*)—based on the contradiction of consciousness acting upon itself—is rendered untenable. Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to ignorance (*ajñāna*). If, on the other hand, one accepts that it possesses the quality of luminosity (*prakāśatva*), then the probans is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Therefore, since the Buddhist doctrine lacks scriptural authority, there is no contradiction; thus, it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe.
And because of momentariness.
He introduces another aphorism which refutes the view that the world consists of consciousness by means of yet another argument.

"And because of momentariness. This is its meaning: since cognition exists for only a single moment while the world is enduring, there is a contradiction between them; therefore, they cannot be identical—this is the sense.

And thus, since knowledge is momentary while the world is enduring, their identity is impossible; for momentariness entails the nature of perishability. Therefore, it is established that the definition [of Brahman] as the cause of the world is logical.
And because it is impossible in every way.
Having thus refuted each of the Buddhist systems, such as those of the Vaibhāṣikas and others, he introduces a scriptural passage that further undermines them with a general refutation.

"And because it is untenable in every way. The meaning of this is as follows: because the Buddhist tenet system is untenable in every respect—being devoid of reason and contradictory [to valid cognition]—it is not to be accepted. This is the sense.

Thus, in the postulation of the momentariness of perception, the postulation of arising and destruction at every moment, the postulation of the non-duality of the Void (*śūnyādvaita*), or the postulation of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*)—whether in their manifestation or concealment—it is not possible [to maintain these] without contradicting such Śruti texts as "Whatever was here, that was Brahman alone," and such Smṛti texts as "That very same [Brahman] again," as well as the reasonings stated in the Sūtras. Since all these positions held by those who hate the Vedas are untenable, it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world.
Thus ends the section on non-perception as a cause.
Here, the doctrine of the Syādvādins is refuted:
"Because [the contradictory properties] cannot exist in one [entity]."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world, because this contradicts the Jaina doctrine. The Jainas, however, describe the world through the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). To explain: "existent" is one mode; "non-existent" is another; "both existent and non-existent" is the third; "neither existent nor non-existent" is the fourth; "existent while being distinct from the existent" is the fifth; "non-existent while being distinct from the non-existent" is the sixth; and "both existent and non-existent while being distinct from both existent and non-existent" is the seventh.

Furthermore, since the production of the world is possible from the individual soul (jīvātman)—which is of the same size as the body—through seen and unseen means, what need is there for a Lord (īśvara)? Thus, the objection being raised that the definition-sūtra is incorrect, the author states the following sūtra to refute it:

"Because [the sevenfold predication] is impossible in one [entity]. This is its meaning: the seven modes asserted by the Jainas are not tenable in a single entity. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because they are unestablished by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they cannot possibly exist in one place. The seven modes should be understood as follows: existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, being different from existence, being different from existence while possessing existence, being different from non-existence while possessing non-existence, and being different from both existence and non-existence while possessing both existence and non-existence.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world, because the Jaina doctrine lacks authoritative validity. As for what was said—that the world consists of sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī)—that is not so; for a mode of existence other than being and non-being is unauthoritative, and because [contradictory attributes] cannot coexist in a single entity. Nor is it reasonable to claim that a position is accepted simply because a fault exists when each individual aspect is affirmed; if that were the case, one would have to abandon everything out of fear of faults.

Since the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) regarding a single entity is even more untenable—given that the alternatives of "existence" and "non-existence" are themselves unproven by valid means of knowledge—it follows that the Jaina doctrine is logically inconsistent. Thus, it is established that the definition-sūtra is indeed free from contradiction.
And thus, the self would not be a whole.

As for what was stated by the Jina—that because it is impossible for a soul that is atomic (aṇu) to experience sensations throughout all its limbs, and because if it were all-pervading (vyāpta) there would be the undesirable consequence of experiencing sensations even when one has gone to another body, the soul must be of the same size as the body—[we ask]: is that [size] accepted for the sake of accounting for the occurrence of movement perceived in all of one's own bodies, or rather because the self lacks an intrinsic dimension apart from being delimited by the body? To refute the first position, he states the following Sūtra:

"And thus, there would be non-omnipresence of the self. This is its meaning: if it is accepted that the self has the same dimensions as the body, then when the self—which previously occupied the body of an ant and was limited to that body—attains the body of an elephant, a donkey, or the like, there would be "non-omnipresence," meaning a lack of fullness. Likewise, it should be understood that when the self that occupies an elephant's body attains the body of an ant, there would be both non-omnipresence and excess.

Thus, even if one accepts that the self has the same dimensions as the body, since it would fail to produce all the movements in all bodies that it might occupy, the following would occur: when a self of the size of an elephant or a donkey, by the force of karma, enters the body of an ant or similar creature, there would be a redundancy [of space] within that very small body. Consequently, the doctrine of the self having the dimensions of the body would be destroyed. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And even by way of figurative interpretation, there is no absence of contradiction, because of [the necessity of] transformation and so forth.

"Now, it may be argued that the self is not restricted to the size of a single body, but rather assumes whatever size corresponds to whichever body it attains at any given time; and since this is so, the defects previously mentioned do not follow. To this objection, the author presents the sūtra as a refutation:

"And there is no non-contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and so forth. This is its meaning: "Through succession" means through sequence; that is, even by accepting that [the self] possesses the dimensions of various bodies in sequence, "there is no non-contradiction"—meaning the aforementioned fault does not apply—this is not tenable. Why? Because succession is not tenable. And why is that? "Because of transformation and so forth": for if that were the case, there would be a difference in the substance due to the difference in dimensions at those respective times, which would result in the self undergoing transformation. Consequently, the faults of impermanence, lack of liberation, and so forth would follow. This is the meaning.

Thus, because the Self would be subject to modification, the consequence of its impermanence follows; and consequently, there would follow the impossibility of liberation and the futility of the scriptures.
