Furthermore, if one were to accept that the Self residing in bodies such as those of an elephant or an ant possesses a size corresponding sequentially to each respective body, the aforementioned defects would not be avoided, as it would result in the Self being subject to modification and thus falling into impermanence. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both [the soul and the body] would be eternal, there would be no distinction.

Now, [the author] presents the sūtra while refuting the second position, which asserts that because the self lacks its own inherent dimension in the absence of limitation by the body, it must therefore be admitted to have the same dimension as the body.

"And because of the final state, and because of the permanence of both, there would be no distinction. This is its meaning: from the previous sūtra, the word "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*) is supplied by ellipsis. The phrase "because of the final state" (*antyāvasthiteḥ*) is repeated. The word "and" (*ca*) serves both to emphasize and to connect. Thus, it follows that if the soul's size were admitted to be equal to the body, then—supplying the remainder—"there would be the consequence of a final state. The meaning is that even in liberation (*mokṣa*), the existence of a body would have to be admitted for the soul that exists [then]. Why? Because of the final state. And because of the permanence of both.

The meaning is that the persistence of the final dimension of the pearl must necessarily be admitted. Why? "And because of the persistence of the final [dimension]. This is because the persistence of the final dimension of the pearl must necessarily be accepted; for it is impossible for the dimension being delimited (the delimited) to exist without a body that serves as the delimiter (the delimiting). This is the underlying sense. He says "final" also to explain why there must be a dimension at all.

The sense is that for the final state, which consists of the nature of a liberated pearl, its existence as a real entity is impossible without a dimension (parimāṇa). To the question, "Let there be a body even in liberation; what of it?", it is said: "Because both would be eternal. This means that if that were so, it would follow that both—the body and the self existing at the time of liberation—are eternal. To the question, "Let the eternity of the liberated body be granted; what of it?", he says: "And from that, everything would be eternal. Here, the sentence stating the undesirable consequence (*āpādyavākya*) must be supplied.

For this very reason, the word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction; its meaning is that all present bodies would likewise be eternal. Why? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction" (aviśeṣāt). This means that there is no difference between the bodies existing at the time of liberation and those existing now, insofar as they are both "bodies. Therefore, the view that the self is co-extensive with the body is not tenable; this is the intended sense.

And thus, if there were an absence of dimension in the soul upon liberation, it would follow that the very nature of the self ceases to exist; for there is no substance devoid of dimension. If it does exist [without a body], it is because dimension is impossible apart from a body. Even in that case, if that body were non-eternal, it would result in the soul possessing the same attributes as those in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). If it were eternal, then since there is no distinction in its being a "body," the present body as well would have to be eternal. Therefore, the position that the self has the dimension of the body is not tenable. Consequently, since the Jaina doctrine is untenable and thus non-contradictory [to our own system], it is established that the definition of the cause of the world is valid.
Thus ends the section on non-multiplicity in a single substratum.
Here, the Pāśupata position is refuted.
On account of the lack of consistency regarding the Lord.

Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is untenable? For it contradicts the Pāśupata tradition. Indeed, Paśupati alone possesses qualities such as omniscience; taking Māyā as his material cause, he performs all acts, including the production of the world consisting of Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others. There are also Śruti and Smṛti texts to this effect. Therefore, the Sūtra defining [Brahman] is incorrect. To this, the following Sūtra is recited: [The Sūtra: janmādyasya yataḥ || 1.1.2 || (From which the birth etc. of this [world proceed).)

"Because of the lack of consistency regarding the Lord (pati). This is its meaning: the status of being the cause of the world is not logical for the Lord Paśupati. Why? Because of "lack of consistency," which means because he possesses defects such as dependence, birth, and so forth.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is logical. Since the Pāśupata system lacks authoritative validity, Paśupati is not the creator of the world, because he is tainted by the defects of dependence, birth, and death. Nor is this reason unestablished, for it is established by the Śruti text: "Whomever I desire, him I make fierce. Furthermore, since the Śruti text "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" indicates the non-existence of Paśupati at the time of dissolution (pralaya), the Pāśupata system is untenable and therefore cannot constitute a contradiction. Thus, it is established that the *Lakṣaṇa-sūtra* is logically sound.
And because a relationship is untenable.
He introduces another aphorism which refutes the status of Paśupati as the cause of the world by means of a further argument.
"And because a relationship is untenable. This is its meaning: since Śiva is bodiless, a relationship with the world is untenable; therefore, he cannot be the creator—this is the sense.

And thus, not only because of dependence and the like, but also because of being bodiless (*aśarīratva*), it is impossible for Paśupati to be the creator of the world. For the agency of one who is bodiless is never observed, such that it could belong to him in this way. Nor should it be argued that even for one who is bodiless, a mere relationship with the world as an effect is possible—just as the ether (*ākāśa*) has conjunction with jars and the like; for, unlike a person who has abandoned the body, there is an absence of the specific relationship consisting of agency. Therefore, since it is impossible for Paśupati to be the creator of the world, the definition-sūtra is established as correct.
And because a substratum is untenable.
He introduces a sūtra that refutes Paśupati’s status as the cause of the world by means of another reason.

"And because a substratum is impossible. This is its meaning: since everything has perished at the time of dissolution (pralaya), it is impossible for Paśupati to have a substratum such as the earth at the time of renewed creation; therefore, he cannot be the creator of the world—this is the sense.

And thus, since the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) cannot be the agent due to the non-perception of a substratum, and because we observe effects such as jars produced by potters and others who reside in a substratum like the earth—whereas for this [alleged creator] such a substratum is absent; and because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) has been demonstrated through the general example of the substrata of the earth and so forth by means of the reason stated in the Sūtra; therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logically sound.
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [the existence of] experience and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that at the time of dissolution, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest do not exist as permanent entities in such a way that they could be directly presided over by an effort like the body and so forth. Nor is there a requirement for a body for the sake of impelling what is directly presided over by effort; for if that were so, it would lead to the absurd consequence of requiring another body even for the impelling of the [first] body. Thus, since there exists a substitute for the body and other such requirements, agency is established. To this, the author presents the Sūtra: [The opponent's position: It might be argued that at the time of dissolution, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest do not exist as permanent entities in such a way that they could be directly presided over by an effort like the body and so forth. Nor is there a requirement for a body for the sake of impelling what is directly presided over by effort; for if that were so, it would lead to the absurd consequence of requiring another body even for the impelling of the [first] body. Therefore, since there exists a substitute for the body and other such requirements, agency is established. To this, the author presents the Sūtra:

"If it be argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, we say no, because of enjoyment and so forth. This is its meaning: Now, if it is argued that since the collection of means belonging to Paśupati is "like an instrument"—that is, like a body and equivalent to a body, and equivalent to a locus—therefore the aforementioned defect does not apply, we say no. Why? Because of enjoyment and so forth; that is to say, because of the defects such as the arising of the experience of pleasure and pain produced by a body, birth, death, and the rest.

And thus, since the aggregate of causal factors (*kārakasamūha*) is equivalent to the body, it would follow that birth and death would occur through the acquisition and abandonment of those [factors] just as they do through the acquisition and abandonment of the body; and from that, the experience of pleasure and pain would result. For we observe that in the case of Yajñadatta and others, when there is the acquisition and loss of a body—which is essentially a modification directly presided over by effort—there is the perception of arising and destruction caused by those two [acquisitions and losses]. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience.

He recites and explains the Sūtra which, by means of the two [reasons] "because a relationship is impossible" and "and like an instrument," refutes the aforementioned positions regarding the existence and non-existence of a body through further logical fallacies.

"Either finitude or non-omniscience [would follow]. This is its meaning: since, in the two positions regarding Śiva’s having a body or not having one, there would respectively be finitude—which is the state of being subject to destruction—and non-omniscience—which is the absence of omniscience—it follows that [the position] is not tenable. This is the sense.

And thus, if one accepts Paśupati as the creator of the world, there arises the contingency of his being subject to destruction if he possesses a body; if, however, he lacks a body, there follows the absence of knowledge. These defects do not apply to the case of Viṣṇu, because the absence of knowledge has been refuted by such scriptural texts as "He is possessed of intelligence and mind," and because defects such as finitude have been dispelled by such passages as "Of what nature is the Blessed Lord. In that context, it is stated that the body of the Blessed Lord is of the same nature as His own essence, consisting of knowledge and so forth.

In this very manner, the conventions (*samaya*) of the Śākta, Saura, Skānda, and Gāṇapatya [sects] are to be understood as refuted. Therefore, since the convention of the Pāśupatas is untenable and thus non-contradictory [to our position], it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct.
Thus ends the section concerning the husband.
Here, the position of those who maintain that [the world] arises from primordial matter (śakti) is refuted:
"Because of the impossibility of origination."

Now, an objection may be raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe, because this contradicts the Śākta doctrine. Indeed, it is Śakti alone—endowed with qualities such as omniscience—who is proclaimed in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas as the mother of the entire world. Therefore, the aphorism defining Hari is not appropriate. To this, the author presents the following aphorism: [The author] states the aphorism in response to the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) that has been reached.

"Because of the impossibility of origination. This is its meaning: Śakti is not the cause of the world. Why? Because of the impossibility of origination; that is to say, because it is impossible for offspring to be produced from mere females designated by the word "Śakti."

Thus, according to the view of the Mahāvāmas, the claim that Śakti alone—unaided by Puruṣa—is the cause of the world is not tenable. This is because the proposition that Śakti alone, unaided by Puruṣa, is the cause of the world is not observed in any authoritative scripture (pramāṇa), and because it is impossible for her in isolation to be the creator of the world. Furthermore, the scriptural passages cited by others, such as "the one unborn female" (ajāmekām), do not have that as their intended meaning, since they declare that she is the cause of the world only through dependence upon Īśvara. Therefore, it is established that the doctrine of the Mahāvāmas is invalid and that the definition of the cause of the world [as being dependent on Īśvara] is correct.
And there can be no instrument for an agent.

Now, it might be argued that Sadāśiva, though devoid of qualities such as omniscience, exists as the bestower of grace upon Śakti; and that when Śakti, thus graced by him, is the cause of the universe, the scriptural text "the one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*) and so forth serves as its authority. In order to refute the view of the Madhyamas and Vāmas—who maintain that the cause of the universe is Śakti graced by Sadāśiva—the author of the Sūtras presents the following aphorism:

"And there is no instrument for the agent. This is its meaning: because there is no cause—meaning no means such as knowledge—for the agent, who is Śiva, the one who bestows grace upon [the individual's] power; therefore, it does not possess the quality of being a bestower of grace upon that power. This is the sense.

And thus, since Sadāśiva lacks omniscience and other such qualities, he cannot function as a bestower of grace; furthermore, because he lacks the knowledge and so forth necessary for creation, as well as the sense organs required for its accomplishment, and the causal body that serves as their basis, it follows that even the power (śakti) presided over by him cannot produce the universe. Therefore, since the doctrines of the Madhyama and Vāma schools are unauthoritative, it is established that the definition of the cause of the universe [as held by our school] is the correct one.
Or, if consciousness and the other [aggregates] exist, there is no negation of that [self].

Now, it is not merely said that the production of the world from *śakti* (the primordial power) is logical because of the absence of a person (*puruṣa*) who could favor that power; rather, this is stated in order to refute the view of those who follow the doctrine of atoms (*aṇuvādins*), who maintain that the production of the world from *śakti* is even more logical precisely because of the existence of that Person’s omniscience and other such qualities. To this end, he presents the aphorism (*sūtra*).

"Or, if there is the existence of consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that. This is the meaning: "Or, if there is the existence of consciousness and so forth"—that is, if it is admitted that Śiva possesses knowledge, will, and the rest—"there is no negation of that": there would be no negation or refutation of that Śaiva position; rather, an inference [in its favor] would have been established. And that [position] has indeed already been refuted; such is the meaning.

And thus, if it is accepted that there exists a sentient being possessing a body and sense organs whose consciousness is the agent of the empowerment of powers and who is instrumental in the production of the world, then—since the production of the world and so forth would be possible for the agent Śiva and others through the empowerment of powers alone, without depending on any other agent—the doctrine of Power (Śaktimata) would become identical with the Pāśupata doctrine; and since that [Pāśupata doctrine] has already been refuted, there would be no further reason to refute it. Therefore, the view of the Atomists (Aṇuvādins) is unauthoritative, and it is established that the definition of the cause of the world [as a conscious agent] is logical.
And because of contradiction.
Having thus refuted the three Śākta doctrines individually, he now introduces the sūtra, which refutes them by means of a collective critique as well.
"And because of contradiction. This is its meaning: because it contradicts all the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the Śākta doctrine is inconsistent; that is to say, it is irrational.

Thus, because it contradicts such Śruti passages as "There is no one else but Nārāyaṇa," such Smṛti passages as "He alone [is the cause]," and the previously stated reasons, and because it is censured by cultured people (śiṣṭas), the entire Śākta doctrine is indeed untenable; therefore, it is established that the definition of Viṣṇu as the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe is correct.
Thus ends the section concerning origination.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
Śrīḥ!
Hari.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.
According to the principle that "others are not perceived," this chapter (pāda) provides a specific refutation of those whose doctrines have already been refuted in general.
Here, the doctrine of the activity of insentient matter is refuted:
"And because the formation [of the world] is inexplicable, there is no inference [of a creator]."

[Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is not tenable? For in the Sāṃkhya system, it is established through the inference: "The Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are produced from a cause similar to themselves, because they are effects, like a jar," that Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is the cause. Since it is stated that this [matter], being independent of anything else, is oriented toward the production of effects, and since Primordial Matter alone—being independent and oriented toward all effects—is the agent, there is no agency belonging to God; thus, His status as the cause of the world is not tenable. To this, the author states the aphorism which refutes [the objection]: *na vilakṣaṇatvād asyato nānumānam* || 2.1.4 || [Translation of the aphorism: "Because this [world] is of a different nature [from Primordial Matter], [the Sāṃkhya position] is not [tenable]; therefore, [their] inference is not [valid]. [Commentary: This means: Because this world is of a different nature from Primordial Matter, it cannot be an effect produced by Primordial Matter. Therefore, the inference [of the Sāṃkhyas] is not valid. Furthermore, the world is not of the same nature as Primordial Matter, because it possesses qualities such as consciousness (*caitanya*), while Primordial Matter lacks them. Moreover, the world is not of the same nature as Primordial Matter because it is composed of parts (*sāvayava*), whereas Primordial Matter is partless (*niravayava*). Thus, the world is of a different nature from Primordial Matter. Consequently, the inference [of the Sāṃkhyas] is not valid. Therefore, Primordial Matter is not the cause of the world. Hence, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world. || 4 || [Objection: Even if Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, He cannot be its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), because He is eternal and immutable. Therefore, He cannot be the efficient cause of the world. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world. || 5 || [Objection: Even if Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, He cannot be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), because He is formless (*amūrta*), whereas the world has form (*mūrta*). Therefore, He cannot be the material cause of the world. [Commentary: The word "from" (*pratyakṣānumānābhyām*) here indicates the means of knowledge. Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world. || 7 || [Objection: Even if Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, He cannot be the cause of the world's destruction, because He is compassionate. "And because the formation [of the world] is not possible, there is no inference [to prove the Pradhāna]. This is the meaning of that [sūtra]: "Inference" (anumāna) refers to that which is inferred; [it refers to] the Pradhāna postulated by the Sāṃkhyas. That Pradhāna is not the creator of the world. Why? Because the formation [of the world] is not possible. Since the Pradhāna is insentient, its spontaneous activity is not possible; and because there is no evidence for the spontaneous activity of an insentient entity—this is the meaning.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world is indeed logical. For, since the Pradhāna—postulated as the cause by the inference that "an effect must possess a cause similar to itself"—is insentient, it cannot spontaneously be directed toward the production of an effect. Since the absence of such spontaneous activity in the Pradhāna is established by pointing out the reason known as its insentience, any objection based on the impossibility of that [activity] is refuted; for it is precisely the occurrence of what is contrary to that [insentience] which proves the absence of such [spontaneous activity].

Since the previously mentioned inference establishes only the status of being a cause in general, and not the fact of being spontaneously directed toward an effect, and since there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition [to prove it], the definition consisting of being the cause of birth and so forth is established as valid; for there is no contradiction with the atheistic Sāṃkhya doctrine, which lacks scriptural authority.
And because of the activity [of the world].

Having thus refuted the Pradhāna’s status as an agent of spontaneous activity by means of its insentience, the absence of spontaneous activity, and the lack of any proof [for such a claim], the author presents a further aphorism that refutes it through another argument.

"And because of activity" (pravṛtteśca): the meaning of this is that since activity is observed only in a conscious being, such as in the thought "I am acting," the Pradhāna is not the creator of the world. This is the sense.

And thus, because the activity of a potter and others in the creation of a jar and so forth is established by experience through the thought "I am doing it"; furthermore, since the creation of cloth and other things is observed to follow the will of a conscious being, the creation of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest must likewise be admitted to be so. [Otherwise], there would be a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), namely: "The creation of the Great Principle and the rest follows the will of a conscious being, because it is a creation, like the creation of a jar. The activity of a conscious being is action (*kriyā*); and that is not possible without volitional effort (*kṛti*); and that, in turn, is not possible without desire (*icchā*).

And since that [desire] cannot exist without knowledge, it is possible to establish that activity is preceded by desire, given that effects such as activity are invariably concomitant with their respective causes. Therefore, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the universe is logical.
If it is argued that [the soul] is like milk and water, even in that case [the same objection applies].

"Now, it might be argued that even milk and water, though insentient, are seen to act spontaneously; therefore, since the reason 'being insentient' is shown to be fallacious in those very cases, and since they will serve as the illustrative examples for the spontaneous activity of the insentient,"—having reached this position, the Sūtra speaks in order to refute it.

"If it be argued that it is like milk and water, we say: 'Even there [it is so]'" (payo'mbuvad cet tatrāpi iti). The meaning of this is as follows: the word "api" (even/also) is intended to draw in the activity of a conscious being. If it is argued, "Just as the activity of insentient milk and water is observed, let the activity of the Pradhāna be likewise," we say no. Why? Because even in those cases, such as milk and water, the activity ultimately proceeds from the Lord alone; the meaning is that there is no activity by itself.

And thus, since the scripture states, "by the command of this very Imperishable," it is understood that even in those cases there exists activity caused by the Lord; consequently, because the probandum accepted by the proponent (the Siddhāntin) is indeed present in the examples cited by the opponent for his counter-inference—such as milk, water, and so forth—neither is that inference subject to being countered by an equal argument (satpratipakṣatā), nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra). Therefore, it is established that the definition consisting of being the cause of birth and so forth is logical.
And because there is no establishment of a distinction [between cause and effect], since [the effect] is independent.

"Because of the non-existence of anything apart [from Him], and because of independence. This is the meaning: "Because of the non-existence of anything apart [from Him]" means that according to the scriptural text "Not so, not so" (*neti neti*), it is understood that no action whatsoever exists apart from the Lord. For that very reason, since the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya—which holds that insentient matter acts spontaneously—is unauthoritative, and precisely because of this independence (of the Lord), such views are to be disregarded by the wise; therefore, there is no contradiction with the fact that Viṣṇu is the creator. This is the sense.

And thus, since the scripture stating "nothing is done without you" reveals that everything is dependent upon the Lord, and because there is no deviation from the reason of insentience—given the scriptural teaching that no action whatsoever can exist apart from or without the Lord—and because the example for the inference put forward by the opponent cannot be found, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined by the Sāṃkhya is not the creator of the world; for their inference lacks authoritative basis, contradicts valid means of knowledge, and is not accepted by the great community of people.

Therefore, since the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya lacks authoritative basis, there is no contradiction with it; thus, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is valid.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world].
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the soul] is not like grass and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for the Lord to possess agency through His own independence, since the production of the world is possible from the Pradhāna alone when favored by the Supreme Lord—just as the production of a sprout occurs from the earth when favored by rain. Therefore, it being established that it is not logical for the Lord to have the status of the cause of the world through His own independence, the Sūtra states:

"And because [the effect] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. This is the meaning: just as in the case of effects such as grass produced from the earth, rain is merely a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), so too in the case of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) produced from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*) is a supportive factor (*anugrāhaka*); He is not independent. Thus, the position of the Theistic Sāṃkhya is also not tenable. Why? "Because it does not exist elsewhere. The meaning is that the world does not exist apart from the Lord—without His impulsion—and because the Lord bestows existence and other qualities upon primordial nature.

And thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe; for there exists no entity whatsoever that functions independently or without being impelled by Him. Furthermore, even *prakṛti*, which serves as the root cause, possesses its existence solely through dependence upon Him. Therefore, since the doctrine of Sāṃkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṃkhya) lacks authoritative validity and is not contradictory [to our position], it is established that the definition of the cause of the universe is logically sound.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence elsewhere.
Here, the position of the Lokāyatikas is refuted:
even if [the existence of the self] were admitted, it would be devoid of purpose.

[Objection: Is it not the case that it is not logical for God to be the agent by virtue of His own independence? For even without a God, the successive production of later effects from earlier causes is possible; and the arising of consciousness is also established through its own nature alone, just like the arising of intoxication from fermented liquor. Nor is there any sublation by scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, because such scripture lacks authority. Nor does the lack of authority of scripture entail the impossibility of establishing *dharma* and other categories, since we accept the non-existence of supersensible objects. Therefore, since God does not exist, it is not logical for Him to possess the characteristic of being the cause of the world. To this, the author of the Sūtras recites the following: [Response: [Sūtra 2.2.37] "But [the world] is seen to arise from that which possesses intelligence, as in the case of a bed, a chair, and so forth. (NS 4.1.21) [Note: The provided text contains a portion of the objection leading into the response. [The author] reads the Sūtra: "But [the world] is seen to arise from that which possesses intelligence, as in the case of a bed, a chair, and so forth" (NS 4.1.21). [This is the response to the objection.]

"Even if [it were] accepted, because of the absence of a subject matter (*arthābhāvāt*). This is the meaning: the word "not" (*na*) carries over from the previous context. Even if it is not accepted—that is, even if the Cārvākas do not accept that their own treatise possesses the status of a *siddhānta* (established doctrine)—our desired conclusion is proven. However, even if it were accepted, because of the absence of a subject matter: since they would have to admit the non-existence of both the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), which are pervaded by the status of being a *siddhānta*, there would be a self-contradiction; thus, that position is also not tenable. This is the meaning.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is indeed logical; for there is no contradiction with the Cārvāka system, as that system is devoid of subject matter, purpose, and so forth, and is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). To explain: first of all, the subject matter of that system is not supersensible (*atīndriya*), because such a thing does not exist [for them]. Nor is it sensible (*aiṃdriyaka*), because what is established by perception requires no dependence upon scripture. Nor is heaven, liberation, and the like the fruit for the listener, because those are not obtained [by following their system]. Nor is wealth and the like the visible fruit, because that can be achieved through easy means such as agriculture.

Nor can it be said that the purpose [of the treatise] belongs to the author, nor that its purpose is the benefit of the world by means of establishing the non-existence of *dharma* and so forth; for upon the knowledge of the non-existence of *dharma* and the like, only harm—such as mutual injury—is likely to result. Nor is benefit itself the purpose, since it lacks the nature of being either the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain. Furthermore, there is no further purpose to be accomplished through that [benefit]. Thus, a qualified person (*adhikārī*) is utterly excluded. Due to the absence of such a person, the relationship [between the subject matter and the purpose] also does not exist. Therefore, since the system of the Cārvākas is devoid of authoritative validity, it is established that the Sūtra providing the definition [of the treatise] is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section on the admission [of the opponent's position].
The Section on Legal Proceedings.
Here, the doctrine that the agent is the primordial matter (prakṛti) subordinate to the Person (puruṣa) is refuted. [Objection:
"If it be argued that it is like the case of the person and the stone, even there... [The sūtra continues: "Even in that case, [it is not so]."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Hari to be the cause of the world; for we observe that a body, which is subordinate to a conscious being, acts as the agent in tasks such as carrying stones, and thus the production of the world is possible through Pradhāna alone, with Puruṣa as its subordinate. Furthermore, Pradhāna possesses spontaneous activity due to the proximity of consciousness, yet because it is insentient, it is like a body; this is established by inference. Therefore, since the Lord himself does not exist, the claim that He alone possesses the characteristic of being the cause of the world is utterly discarded—this being the position reached, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from Him, because of the observation of design. (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.1) This means: But [the world arises] from Him (the Lord), because of the observation of design (in the world). Just as a chariot and other objects, which possess a specific arrangement of parts, are seen to have an intelligent maker, so too this earth and other things, which possess a specific arrangement of parts, must have an intelligent maker. Thus, the Lord exists as the cause of the world. This refutes the objection that the existence of the Lord is unproven. Therefore, the definition of His being the cause of the world stands firm.

"If it be argued that it is like a man and a stone, we say: 'In that case also [it is not so]'"—this is the meaning [of the sūtra]. The sense is as follows: if it is argued that just as an insentient body acts toward carrying stones and the like through its connection with a person, so too does the insentient *prakṛti* act through its connection with a sentient being, we say no. Why? Because even in that instance of the body's activity, the sentient Lord alone is the agent; therefore, there is an absence of a valid illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntābhāva). This is the meaning.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Hari alone is the cause of the world. For, in establishing that primordial nature (prakṛti), which is subordinate to the Puruṣa, is the cause of the world, there is an absence of any corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta). Nor should it be argued that the body itself serves as the instance; for according to the Śruti, "Nothing is created without You," even the activity of the body is dependent upon the Supreme Self, and thus the instance would be devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala). Consequently, since there is no contradiction with other philosophical systems, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logically sound.
Because the status of being a constituent part (aṅgin) is untenable.

Having thus stated the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example by means of the reason characterized as scriptural testimony (*śruti*), he introduces the aphorism (*sūtra*) in order to establish that same deficiency in the example by means of another reason.

Regarding the phrase "because being a principal [agent] is untenable" (aṅgitvānupapatteḥ): its meaning is as follows. If it were admitted that the Puruṣa is a subordinate member (aṅga), then in the statement "the member is the principal" (aṅgam aṅgī), the mention of "being a principal" (aṅgitva)—that is, primacy—would be untenable. The sense is that there is no illustrative example for the position that the Puruṣa is a subordinate factor serving as the agent of the primordial matter (prakṛti).

And thus, if the body alone, being subordinate to the person, were the agent, then the authoritative and worldly convention that "the person is the principal and the body is the subordinate" would not exist; yet this convention does exist. Therefore, this is not a valid illustration.

Therefore, if it were asserted that the body conjoined with the person acts spontaneously by itself, then because the person would necessarily be subordinate and not primary, the conventional designation of the person as the "principal" (aṅgin) in the Smṛti—where it is called an "organ" (aṅga)—would be untenable as a teaching regarding the person's primacy relative to the body. Likewise, in the case of the subject of the illustration, the conventional designation of the person as the "principal" would be untenable due to the consequence of the person being a subordinate part of the Pradhāna. Thus, both the absence of a valid illustration and a contradiction have been shown.
Consequently, since there is no conflict with other doctrines, it is established that the definition of the Lord as the cause of the world is logical.
Thus concludes the section concerning the stone for the man.
Here, the doctrine that the person (puruṣa) is the agent—subordinate to primordial nature (prakṛti)—is refuted;
for otherwise, in the case of inference, there would be an absence of the capacity for knowledge.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Hari to be the cause of the world; for since the production of the world is possible from Pradhāna (primordial matter) assisted by Puruṣa (the individual soul), God would be superfluous. Thus, the formal argument is as follows: "The activity under discussion is dependent upon a non-conscious entity assisted by Puruṣa, because it is an activity, like the activity of carrying stones [by a servant]. Therefore, having reached the conclusion that the definition of being the cause of the world is untenable, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [that] is not so, on account of there being no such power in non-intelligent things. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.4) This means: It is not the case that Hari cannot be the cause of the world. Why? Because non-intelligent things lack such power. That is to say, non-intelligent things do not possess the capacity to produce the world. How so? Because they are non-intelligent. Just as a stone does not have the power to produce a pot. And this is established by the fact that non-intelligent things are devoid of purposeful action. Furthermore, the scripture declares that the Lord is the cause of the world: "He who, dwelling within the earth, yet is distinct from the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3). Likewise: "He who dwells in all beings, yet is distinct from all beings, whom all beings do not know, whose body all beings are, and who controls all beings from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.15). And: "He who dwells in the self, yet is distinct from the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.22). And: "He who dwells in the intellect, yet is distinct from the intellect, whom the intellect does not know, whose body the intellect is, and who controls the intellect from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.23). And: "He who dwells in the unmanifest, yet is distinct from the unmanifest, whom the unmanifest does not know, whose body the unmanifest is, and who controls the unmanifest from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.24). And: "He who dwells in the darkness, yet is distinct from the darkness, whom the darkness does not know, whose body the darkness is, and who controls the darkness from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.25). And: "He who dwells in the light, yet is distinct from the light, whom the light does not know, whose body the light is, and who controls the light from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.26). And: "He who dwells in the deathless, yet is distinct from the deathless, whom the deathless does not know, whose body the deathless is, and who controls the deathless from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.27). And: "He who dwells in the death, yet is distinct from the death, whom the death does not know, whose body the death is, and who controls the death from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.28). And: "He who dwells in the desire, yet is distinct from the desire, whom the desire does not know, whose body the desire is, and who controls the desire from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.29). And: "He who dwells in the anger, yet is distinct from the anger, whom the anger does not know, whose body the anger is, and who controls the anger from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.30). And: "He who dwells in the procreation, yet is distinct from the procreation, whom the procreation does not know, whose body the procreation is, and who controls the procreation from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.31). And: "He who dwells in the semen, yet is distinct from the semen, whom the semen does not know, whose body the semen is, and who controls the semen from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.32). And: "He who dwells in the elements, yet is distinct from the elements, whom the elements do not know, whose body the elements are, and who controls the elements from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.33). And: "He who dwells in the senses, yet is distinct from the senses, whom the senses do not know, whose body the senses are, and who controls the senses from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.34). And: "He who dwells in the mind, yet is distinct from the mind, whom the mind does not know, whose body the mind is, and who controls the mind from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.35). And: "He who dwells in the understanding, yet is distinct from the understanding, whom the understanding does not know, whose body the understanding is, and who controls the understanding from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.36). And: "He who dwells in the bliss, yet is distinct from the bliss, whom the bliss does not know, whose body the bliss is, and who controls the bliss from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.37). And: "He who dwells in the darkness, yet is distinct from the darkness, whom the darkness does not know, whose body the darkness is, and who controls the darkness from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.38). And: "He who dwells in the light, yet is distinct from the light, whom the light does not know, whose body the light is, and who controls the light from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.39). And: "He who dwells in the highest, yet is distinct from the highest, whom the highest does not know, whose body the highest is, and who controls the highest from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.40). And: "He who dwells in the unseen, yet is distinct from the unseen, whom the unseen does not know, whose body the unseen is, and who controls the unseen from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.41). And: "He who dwells in the ungraspable, yet is distinct from the ungraspable, whom the ungraspable does not know, whose body the ungraspable is, and who controls the ungraspable from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.42). And: "He who dwells in the unattached, yet is distinct from the unattached, whom the unattached does not know, whose body the unattached is, and who controls the unattached from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.43). And: "He who dwells in the unmanifested, yet is distinct from the unmanifested, whom the unmanifested does not know, whose body the unmanifested is, and who controls the unmanifested from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.44). And: "He who dwells in the fear, yet is distinct from the fear, whom the fear does not know, whose body the fear is, and who controls the fear from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.45). And: "He who dwells in the fearless, yet is distinct from the fearless, whom the fearless does not know, whose body the fearless is, and who controls the fearless from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (ibid., 3.7.46). And: "He who dwells in the desire, yet is distinct from the desire, whom the desire does not know, whose body the desire is

"And because of the absence of the power of cognition in the case of an inference in another way. This is the meaning: there is an attraction (*samākarṣa*) of the phrase "because of the impossibility of being the principal [agent] by means of the word [‘puruṣa’]. Just as in the case of inferring—i.e., establishing—the agency of the person (*puruṣa*) as subordinate to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) in a manner other than the previously mentioned position, [the same applies here]: "because of the absence of the power of cognition" means because of the absence of the power of activity for the sake of the individual soul (*jīva*)’s connection with a body; that is to say, precisely because of the impossibility of being the principal [agent].

And thus, it is indeed logical that Īśvara alone is the cause of the world; for there is no evidence for the agency of the *puruṣa* when nature (*prakṛti*) is merely subordinate. Now, if it is thought that this is inferred differently from the previous view, that being the case, the probandum (the property to be proven) would be absent in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If one were to admit the power of activity in the [puruṣa] alone, the body would be useless. If not, then due to the consequence of an absence of connection with a body, there would be no activity such as the carrying of stones and so forth; yet such activity does exist.

Therefore, since a Lord who establishes the connection between the person and the body and bestows powers such as the ability to move stones must be admitted, how can the illustrative example be devoid of the probandum? Consequently, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logical.
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent.
Having thus refuted each of the non-theistic views individually, he recites a sutra that also negates them by means of a general refutation.

"And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent"—this is its meaning. "Because of contradiction" means because it is opposed to all Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning; thus, the doctrine of non-theism is "inconsistent," that is, irrational.

And thus, because there is a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "producing heaven and earth," "from whom [all this]," and "He who is all-knowing"; with such Smṛti passages as "the creator, the protector, and likewise the consumer"; and with such logical arguments as "the subject of dispute has an agent because it is an effect" and "consciousness and its mental states are governed by something else because they lack independence"—there is no statement from anyone else that contradicts the assertion that the meaning [of the texts] consists in the independence of *prakṛti* and so forth.

Consequently, because it contradicts all scripture, tradition, and reasoning, every non-theistic doctrine is invalid. Therefore, it is established that there is no impossibility of the definition [of Brahman] due to conflict with the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and others.
Thus ends the section on inference based on other [premises].
Here, the doctrine of the commencement [of creation] by atoms is refuted:
"Or, like the large and the long, [the world arises] from the short and the spherical."

Now, are there not exactly seven categories, beginning with substance? Among these, substances are exactly nine, starting with earth; qualities are exactly twenty-four, beginning with color; action is fivefold, such as upward throwing and so forth; generality is of many kinds, being both of the nature of a genus (*jāti*) and of the nature of an adjunct (*upādhi*); inherence, however, is only one; and particulars are infinite. This triad [of generality, particularity, and inherence] is exclusively eternal. Among them, that which is non-eternal is produced by a triad of causes. That in which an effect inheres as it arises is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and this is precisely substance, such as atoms and the like.

In that process, atoms initiate a composite whole through the sequence of dyads and so forth. An inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is that which is proximate to the effect and whose causal capacity has been determined. Among these, the conjunction of the parts of a produced substance becomes the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by virtue of its proximity to the effect within a single objective context. Furthermore, the qualities and actions of the causes become the non-inherent causes of the qualities of the effect by virtue of their proximity to the effect within a single objective context.

Regarding action, that which resides in the cause—namely quality and action—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the effect through the mediation of a single objective (*ekārtha*) relation. Among these, size (*parimāṇa*) residing in the cause becomes the non-inherent cause for the size residing in the effect. However, the size residing in atoms, dyads, or cotton-balls is not the non-inherent cause for the sizes residing in dyads, triads, or cotton-clumps; rather, it is only the number (*saṃkhyā*) residing in the dyads and triads [that serves as the cause]. As for the size of a cotton-clump, however, it arises from aggregation (*pracaya*).

This other cause or instrumental factor consists of God (Īśvara), unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), time (kāla), and so forth. Among these, God is a specific kind of self (ātman). A [generic] self is endowed with fourteen qualities beginning with number (saṃkhyā), whereas the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) possesses only five qualities beginning with number. Furthermore, He is possessed of knowledge, will, and effort suitable for agency, and is unfit for the remaining six qualities; thus, how can His possession of infinite qualities be logical? Therefore, since the previous chapter is rendered useless, this objection having been raised, the following is stated in the aphorism:

"Or, like the large and the long from the short and the spherical. This is its meaning: according to the Vaiśeṣika system, just as dimension arises in the *caturaṇuka* and so forth from the largeness and length residing in the *tryaṇuka* and so forth, so too would there be the production of dimensions in the *tryaṇuka* and *dvyaṇuka* from the shortness and sphericity residing in both the *dvyaṇuka* and the atom (*paramāṇu*). This is the sense.

Alternatively, the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) is that the production of an effect would not occur even from largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*). Therefore, the intention is that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is untenable.

And thus, it is indeed logical that Hari is characterized by the perfection of infinite qualities, because the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are unauthoritative due to their propounding what is untenable. As for what was stated—that minute dimension and atomic dimension do not possess the status of non-inherent cause—that is not so; for if that were the case, it would follow that large dimension and long dimension also lack that status. Since these two [large and long dimensions] are causes, the same logic applies to these two as well, as there is no distinction between them. Therefore, because they are incompatible with production, those two do not possess the status of non-inherent cause.

However, the claim of the Vaiśeṣikas and others that these two [attributes] belong to these [two beings] alone is indeed inconsistent; therefore, there is no contradiction with the infinite qualities of the Lord, and thus it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] is non-existent.

Thus, intending that by the method of refuting the non-inherent causality (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) of largeness, length, and so forth in the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, all non-inherent causes are thereby rejected, he introduces the aphorism which likewise refutes the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

"Even in both ways, there is no action; therefore, there is an absence of that [effect]. This is the meaning: "In both ways"—that is, in either of the two positions regarding the nature of God's will, whether it be eternal or non-eternal—there is no possibility of the production of motion within the atoms. Therefore, there is an absence of that; the meaning is that there would be an absence of the effects beginning with the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth.

If it is argued that the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), is that will eternal or non-eternal? In either case, the motion of atoms is not possible. If the will of God were eternal, then even during the period of dissolution (*pralaya*), when that will exists, there would be an absence of atomic activity; consequently, there would be an absence of such activity at other times as well. If, on the other hand, it were non-eternal, then due to the absence of its cause, the will of God would not arise, resulting in the absence of atomic motion. Nor should it be said that the will belonging to a previous cycle (*kalpa*), though non-eternal, serves as the efficient cause like a sacrifice (*yāga*); for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this.

Now, if the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is not the cause [of motion], then let that alone be the cause. In that case, there would be no cause for anything else either. According to the opponent's view, due to the absence of atomic action, there is an absence of conjunction, and consequently, an absence of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). However, in the Vedic position regarding God, even though the will of God exists, the fact that all effects are not produced is accounted for solely by the inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*) of God. This is not the same in the opponent's position, because their God is known through inference (*anumāna*), whereas our God is known exclusively through the Vedas.
Therefore, since the arguments of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are inconsistent, it is established that the definition of Hari as possessing infinite qualities is correct.
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being subject to the same [objections].

Having thus demonstrated the impossibility of an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) according to the positions of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the author states the sūtra which refutes the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as well.

"And because of the acceptance of inherence (samavāya), and because of its equality [to other relations], there is an infinite regress. This is the meaning: since the Vaiśeṣikas accept inherence—that is, they admit the relation of inherence—as the cause for the distinctness of parts, wholes, and so forth; and because of its equality, meaning that inherence and non-inherence are likewise equal in being distinct; and because if one accepts inherence even in those cases, it leads to an infinite regress; and because of this infinite regress, their doctrine is untenable. This is the sense.

And thus, as for the claim that a substance such as an atom (*paramāṇu*) is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), that is not so. For one accepts the existence of inherence (*samavāya*) only after admitting the difference between the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*), in order to account for the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Since inherence itself is equally distinct [from the related entities], there would be a need for another inherence to account for the relationship of qualifier and qualified in such cases as "the inherence of the pot in the clay. If that were the case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, since the very relationship between the fundamental parts and the whole remains unestablished, inherence itself is unestablished.

For the sake of establishing their first relation, other relations would have to be admitted, yet these are even more utterly unestablished. Furthermore, if inherence (*samavāya*) were held to be self-establishing—meaning it is accepted that it itself generates the cognition of the qualifier-qualified relationship within itself—then inherence itself would remain unestablished.

Having accepted the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality (guṇa-guṇin) and so forth, as well as their inherence (samavāya), one must postulate that these [categories] are self-sustaining; however, by contrast, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to accept the non-difference of quality and its possessor, whereby the single substance itself can be established as self-sustaining. Thus, since inherence would be redundant, it is proven that the definition-sūtra is logically sound.
And because it exists eternally.
Thus, having refuted creation by means of the rejection of the three causes according to the opponent's view, he introduces the sūtra intended for the purpose of refuting dissolution.

"And because [the cause] exists eternally" (nityameva ca bhāvāt). This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the defects. Since causes such as the will of God and atoms exist at all times, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, the production of effects would occur eternally—that is, always—and not only occasionally. This is the sense.

And thus, in the view of the opponent, the dissolution [of the world] is impossible. This is because, given the presence of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa), there can be no non-production of the effect due to a lack of causes. If the atomic inherent causes were eternal and one were to admit that inherence itself is produced, then every effect would be eternal and subject to production. Furthermore, when the production of an effect ceases while the inherent causes and other factors remain present, the effect could never arise from them again;

for if an effect is not produced despite the presence of its full set of causes, it is impossible for those factors to be considered its causes. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because they possess form and other qualities, there is a reversal [of their nature], as seen from observation.
Thus, having accepted the eternity of atoms, the doctrine that they are the constituent causes [of composite objects] has been refuted. Now, he introduces a sūtra which rejects their eternity.

"And because they possess color and other qualities, there would be the opposite [of permanence], since it is observed. This is the meaning: furthermore, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, because the atoms of earth, water, and fire possess color and other qualities, there would be the "opposite"—that is, impermanence, which is the reverse of permanence. Why? Because of observation; the meaning is that this is due to the observed pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever possesses color and other qualities is impermanent," as seen in the case of a jar and similar objects.

And thus, in reality, the eternity of atoms is not tenable, because they necessarily possess a natural form. Indeed, it is observed in the world that whatever possesses a natural form and so forth is impermanent. Since the atoms of earth, water, fire, and air possess material color, taste, smell, and touch, they are impermanent. Consequently, it is established that the previously stated definition-sūtra [of atoms] is invalid due to the absence of their eternity.
And because there is a fault in both cases.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "whatever possesses color and so forth is impermanent" is a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), whereas "whatever substance is partless is eternal" is a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) that is stronger? Therefore, because it is sublated by that [specific pervasion], the possession of color and so forth cannot prove the impermanence of atoms. Or, let it be granted that atoms have a beginning; even so, there would still be no absence of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). For if atoms were produced by some other cause, the production of dyads and so forth from them would be possible. To this, the author states the aphorism (*sūtra*) while refuting [the objection]: *na karmānityatvāt* (VS 4.2.23). [Commentary: This is not so. Because action is impermanent, the production of atoms from action is impossible. If atoms were produced from action, they would be impermanent, just like action itself. Since atoms are eternal, they cannot be produced from action. Furthermore, since the production of dyads and so forth from atoms has already been established, the claim that atoms are produced from something else is refuted. Thus, the existence of atoms is proven. Moreover, if atoms were non-eternal, the world would be subject to total destruction (*pralaya*) at every moment, and thus the world-process (*saṃsāra*) would be impossible. Therefore, atoms are eternal. Furthermore, if atoms were non-eternal, there would be no basis for the production of gross objects, as the causal series would lack a stable foundation. Consequently, the existence of atoms is established. Thus, the view that atoms are produced from action is rejected. This concludes the section on the eternity of atoms. Now begins the examination of the nature of the whole (*avayavin*). Some say: "The whole does not exist as a distinct entity separate from its parts. Others say: "It exists, but it is merely a collection of parts. Still others say: "It exists as a distinct entity, but it is nothing more than a configuration (*saṃsthāna*). To refute these views, the author states the following: *avayavāvayavinoḥ nātyantabhedaḥ* (VS 7.1.1). [Commentary: There is no absolute difference between the part and the whole. If there were an absolute difference, the whole could never be perceived when its parts are not perceived, and the whole would be unrelated to its parts. Therefore, the whole exists as a distinct entity from its parts, yet it is not entirely different from them. This establishes the reality of the whole. Now begins the examination of the nature of space (*ākāśa*). Some say: "Space is merely the absence of obstruction. Others say: "It is a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To refute these, the author states: *ākāśasyāvagāhanam liṅgam* (VS 2.1.20). [Commentary: The fact that things occupy space (*avagāhana*) is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of space. Since all corporeal things require a medium for their occupation, and since no other substance can serve as that medium, space exists as a distinct, eternal substance. Thus, the existence of space is proven. Now begins the examination of time (*kāla*). Some say: "Time is merely a mental construct based on change. Others say: "It is a property of the soul. To refute these, the author states: *kālaḥ parāparavyatikarayaugapadyāyaugapadyacirakṣiprapratyayaliṅgaḥ* (VS 2.2.6). [Commentary: Time is that which is inferred from the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness. Since these notions cannot be attributed to substances like earth or qualities like color, there must be a distinct substance called time. Thus, the existence of time is proven. Now begins the examination of the self (*ātman*). Some say: "The self is merely the body. Others say: "It is the sense-faculties. Still others say: "It is consciousness itself. To refute these, the author states: *ātmasamanvaye sukhaduḥkhajñānaniṣpattiviśeṣāt* (VS 3.2.1). [Commentary: Because of the specific production of pleasure, pain, and cognition upon the conjunction with the self, the self exists as a distinct substance. Since these experiences are not found in external objects or the sense-faculties, there must be an internal agent, the self. Thus, the existence of the self is proven. Now begins the examination of the mind (*manas*). Some say: "The mind is merely the body. Others say: "It is the sense-faculties. To refute these, the author states: *prayatnāyaugapadyāj jñānāyaugapadyācca pratiśarīramekatvam* (VS 3.2.1). [Commentary: Because efforts are not simultaneous and cognitions are not simultaneous, the mind is one in each body. If there were multiple minds, all efforts and cognitions would occur simultaneously. Since this is not the case, the mind is a single, atomic substance in each body. Thus, the existence of the mind is proven. Now begins the examination of the nature of the self. Some say: "The self is eternal and partless. Others say: "It is perishable. To refute these, the author states: *saṃdigdhatvādahetuḥ* (VS 3.2.3). [Commentary: Because [the reason] is doubtful, it is not a valid proof. If the self were perishable, there would be no memory of past experiences, as the subject who experienced them would no longer exist. Since memory occurs, the self must be eternal. Furthermore, if the self were partless, it could not undergo transformation. Since it does undergo transformation through the acquisition of merit and demerit, it must possess parts. Thus, the self is both eternal and possessed of parts. Now begins the examination of the nature of the self's attributes. Some say: "Pleasure and pain are properties of the body. Others say: "They are properties of the sense-faculties. To refute these, the author states: *sukhaduḥkhe ātmāntaraguṇānām akāraṇatvād ātmāntarair asamānadharmā* (VS 3.2.15). [Commentary: Pleasure and pain are not the qualities of other selves, because they do not serve as causes for the qualities of those other selves. Therefore, the self possessing pleasure and pain is not identical to any other self. Thus, the plurality of selves is established. Now begins the examination of the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*). Some say: "Liberation is the total annihilation of the self. Others say: "It is the attainment of a state of pure bliss. To refute these, the author states: *duḥkhābhāve saṃyogābhāvo 'prādurbhāvaśca mokṣaḥ* (VS 5.2.18). [Commentary: Liberation is the non-appearance of the self due to the cessation of the conjunction [of the self with the body], resulting in the absence of suffering. It is not the annihilation of the self, nor is it the attainment of a new state of bliss. Rather, it is the permanent cessation of the cycle of birth and death. Thus, the nature of liberation is established. This concludes the examination of the categories. Now begins the examination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Some say: "There is only one means of knowledge, perception. Others say: "There are two: perception and inference. Still others say: "There are three: perception, inference, and verbal testimony. To refute these, the author states: *pratyakṣānumānopamānaśabdāḥ pramāṇāni* (VS 2.1.1). [Commentary: Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of knowledge. Perception is the direct apprehension of an object through the contact of the senses with it. Inference is the knowledge of an object derived from a sign (*liṅga*) that is known to be invariably concomitant with it. Comparison is the knowledge of an object through its similarity to a known object. Verbal testimony is the knowledge of an object derived from the words of a reliable person. These four are the means of knowledge. Now begins the examination of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Some say: "Only the self is the object of knowledge. Others say: "All things are objects of knowledge. To refute these, the author states: *ātmendriyārthasannikarṣād yan ni

"Because there is a fault in both ways. This is its meaning: for the Vaiśeṣika, in both ways—that is, in either of the two positions consisting of the eternity or non-eternity of the soul—there is a fault; because, as in that case, there is the fault of the existence of that production being caused by the absence of a cause for the eternity of all things, that position is not tenable. This is the meaning.

And thus, as for what was stated—that "whatever possesses color and so forth is impermanent" constitutes a general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti)—that is not correct. This is because there is no specific means of valid cognition (viśeṣapramāṇa) that would serve as an exception to the impermanence of that which possesses color and so forth. Nor can partlessness (niravayavatva) serve as such a specific means of valid cognition, since it is possible to prove the absence of that [partlessness] even in an atom (paramāṇu) by virtue of its possessing color and so forth. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no fault regarding impermanence, that too is not correct.

In your view, since atoms lack a cause, they cannot arise; consequently, there exists a subverting argument (bādhaka) characterized by the undesirable consequence that composite effects such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth would not be produced. Thus, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct, as both positions are flawed by defects.
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of dependence.
Having thus refuted the theory of the composition of atoms through its conceptual proliferation, the Sūtra now states [the following] to refute it on the grounds of its lack of authoritative basis:

"And because it is not accepted, there is absolute disregard. This is its meaning: "Because it is not accepted" means that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is devoid of acceptance by the Vedas and other authoritative sources, and because it is contrary to them. In this regard, "absolute disregard" means that one should show no respect for it.

Thus, because the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is not accepted by any of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other authoritative texts, and because it is contrary to them; because it is to be disregarded even more than the theory that Pradhāna is the cause; and because it is censured in the Mokṣadharma section of the Mahābhārata as "Anvīkṣakī" (speculative reasoning); therefore, since the theory of the commencement [of the world] from atoms is untenable, there is no contradiction, and it is established that the Lord's possession of infinite, perfect qualities, as stated in the previous chapter, is correct.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Vaiśeṣikas.
Here, the view of those who maintain that [the world] is an aggregate of atoms is refuted:
"Even if the collection were caused by both [atoms and space], that [collection] would not be attained."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world, because this contradicts the doctrines of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas. Indeed, the entire world, existing in the form of matter (rūpa), consciousness (vijñāna), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra), is ultimately real as a collection of atoms; there is no such thing as a "whole" (avayavin). Since the cognition of jars and other objects is accounted for by the mere collection of atoms, the postulation of a whole—whether as the dimension of the atom itself or as something produced from them—is redundant.

Furthermore, everything that exists is indeed momentary, because there is no pervasion of momentariness by existence; for in the absence of a pervader, the pervaded cannot exist. Moreover, this entire collection of effects arises solely through the causes of time, karma, and form; it does not depend upon a material cause (*upādāna*). Consequently, since the preceding atoms perish, even in the absence of a material cause, the creation of subsequent atoms occurs through time, karma, and so forth alone—so what need is there for a Lord (*īśvara*)? Furthermore, there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the Lord, because the Vedas and other such sources are not authoritative.
Therefore, since the Lord himself does not exist, it follows that his being the cause of birth and so forth is untenable; this being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"Even if the aggregate is admitted to have both [types of] causes, that [aggregate] is not attained. This is its meaning: since, even when an aggregate (*samudāya*)—which consists of the number of plurality (*anekatva-saṃkhyā*) in a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-samudāya*) and is caused by many atoms joined together—is accepted, or even when it is accepted as being caused by many [atoms] situated at a distance (*viralāneka-hetuka*), "that is not attained" means that such an aggregate, which would be caused by many [atoms] at a distance, is not attained; that is, it is untenable. Why? Because of defects such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), etc.—this is the remainder of the sense. This has been established in the *Ṭīkā*.
Therefore, the Buddhist position that the pot is merely a heap of atoms (*paramāṇu-puñja*) as a composite whole (*avayavin*) is also not tenable. This is the meaning.

Thus, the designation of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is indeed logical. This is because the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas lack authority, as their doctrines are untenable. As for what was stated—that a composite aggregate arises through causes such as time and karma, based on momentary atoms, and that no "whole" (avayavin) exists at all—that is not correct. In this regard, is this aggregate caused by a single atom or by multiple atoms? It cannot be the first, because it is contradictory to say that an aggregate arises from a single [atom].

Regarding the second [position] as well, is it caused by multiple [atoms] that have conjoined, or by multiple [atoms] that are dispersed? It cannot be the first, because conjunction itself constitutes a composite whole, which leads to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, if one were to accept a causal relationship between two such composites, it would lead to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); and if one were to accept a plurality of individual instances, it would result in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor can it be the latter, because since a stream of dispersed atoms would exist at all times, it would follow that there could never be a dissolution (*pralaya*) characterized by the absence of the composite effect.

Therefore, since there is no attainment of a composite whole, it is established that the definition of the world’s cause is correct, because the position that there exists some "whole" (avayavin) perceivable by the cognitions of cows, jars, and so forth, is untenable.
If it is argued that [the world] exists because of mutual dependence, we say no, because that is merely the cause for their arising.

"Let it be granted that there is always the arising of a collection; nevertheless, there is no absence of dissolution. Since dissolution is established precisely because of the absence of mental activity and worldly transaction, [the opponent] having thus argued, the Sūtra says:"

"If it is argued that [the world] exists because of mutual dependence (*itaretara-pratyayatva*), we say no, because that is merely a cause for the appearance [of conventional usage]. This is the meaning: Now, one might object: "Even if the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-puñja*) exists eternally, there is no inconsistency regarding dissolution (*pralaya*) in our position. Why? Because the conventional usage of those [atoms] and so forth arises from mutual dependence (*itaretara-pratyayatva*). That is to say, the conventional designation 'this and this' is caused by a relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*) among the atoms themselves. Thus, at a time when such a cognition is absent, since the conventional usage of the aggregate and so forth does not exist, dissolution is logically possible. If this is argued, we say: No. Why?

Because atoms are merely the cause of their own aggregation—that is, they are merely the cause for the arising of their own collection—the word "merely" (mātra) signifies that it is not possible for even the cognition of expectation (*apekṣābuddhi*) and so forth to arise from them. Thus, the meaning is that in the doctrine of momentariness, conventional usage and the like, which are caused by those [cognitions], can never possibly occur.

Moreover, since there would never be a connection between perception and linguistic usage, it would follow that creation itself does not exist. To explain: the sequence is that first there is the perception of atoms, then the desire [to act], and then the linguistic usage; yet this sequence is not tenable. Because atoms are momentary, they perish immediately after producing their effect. For it is impossible for perception to occur in one place, the desire in another, and the linguistic usage in yet another; otherwise, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

Likewise, in the case of the person (puruṣa) as well, if one were to admit the stability of aggregated atoms produced by sparse atoms, there would follow the consequence that an effect would be produced at every moment. And thus, even in a very short time, there would be the consequence that the potter’s workshop would be filled with numerous effects arising from each individual atom-cluster constituting the jar. Therefore, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the world is logical.
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises.

Thus, having accepted the production of conjoined atoms from rarefied atoms, the impossibility of conventional discourse and so forth has been demonstrated. Now, he introduces a sūtra which also refutes the production of dissimilar effects.

"And because of the cessation of the preceding upon the arising of the succeeding. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves both to restrict and to aggregate. The word "not" (na) is understood from the previous context; "by implication" (sāmarthyāt) is the ellipsis.
