Thus, not only is the conventional usage of a "collection" untenable in the doctrine of momentariness, but furthermore, the production of specific effects is also illogical. Why?

Furthermore, since a cause possesses the capacity to produce an effect similar to itself upon the arising of a subsequent [moment], what fault could there be in that cause first producing an effect similar to itself and subsequently producing a dissimilar effect? For this reason as well, he says: "Upon the arising of the subsequent. Thus, the meaning is that when the subsequent [moment] arises—that is, when its production of an effect similar to itself occurs—there is the cessation of the preceding [cause]; because of the destruction of the preceding cause, it is impossible for it to again produce a dissimilar effect.

And thus, according to the opponent's view, the production of a specific effect is impossible, because an effect has the inherent nature of producing an effect similar to itself; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of a cloth being produced from a jar. Nor can it be argued that after producing an effect similar to itself, the cause subsequently produces dissimilarity, for since the cause perishes at the moment the effect is produced, it is incapable of generating dissimilarity. Therefore, it is established that the definition of the cause of the world [as Brahman] is logical.
If it were non-existent [at the time of production], there would be a contradiction with one's own thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity.

Having thus refuted conventional discourse and other such phenomena by rejecting the arising of dissimilar effects, he now introduces the sūtra which rejects the very notion of the arising of an effect at every moment.

"Otherwise, there would be either a contradiction of one's own thesis or simultaneity. This is its meaning: In the doctrine of momentariness, the production of an effect at every moment is not tenable. Why? Because if one accepts that an effect arises even when the cause is absent, there would be a "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñoparodha*); having previously asserted that "this is the effect of that," one would incur a loss or abandonment of the established system of discourse. Alternatively, if one accepts that an effect arises only when the cause is present, there would be "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*), meaning that the causes would necessarily exist at the same time as the effect.

And thus, if one accepts the production of an effect at every moment, does the effect arise when the cause is absent, or when it is present? In the first case, there is a contradiction of your own thesis. In the second case, if the sparse atoms produced in the first moment were to persist even at the time of the production of the effect, then—due to the absence of the rule of momentariness—they would remain until the arrival of their destroyer.

Furthermore, according to that view, because of the rule that "when the cause exists, the effect necessarily arises," the production of the effect would occur again and again; thus, all effects would occur simultaneously. Consequently, it would follow that a potter’s workshop would be filled in a single *ghaṭikā*. Alternatively, since atoms are momentary, the effect would exist in the very same moment as the atoms; thus, there would be no temporal sequence between cause and effect. Moreover, a moment possesses no prior, posterior, or middle part.
Since the production of atoms would occur in the first part, while the capacity to produce an effect would occur in the second part, it is established that the definition-sūtra is indeed appropriate.
Cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, and non-attainment [are not interrupted] because there is no interruption.
Having thus refuted the arising of an effect within the doctrine of momentariness, he introduces the sūtra which also refutes its destruction.

"Non-attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation [is asserted] because there is no interruption. This is its meaning: thus, in the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*), there is a non-attainment—that is, an impossibility—of analytical and non-analytical cessation; this refers to the non-attainment of the destruction at every moment and the non-destruction of the continuum [respectively]. Why? Because there is no interruption; the meaning is that, according to that system, since effects arise [continuously], there is no interruption even among those things that are not effects.

Thus, in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), destruction is not logically tenable. In that system, destruction is of two kinds: first, having produced an effect, the cause abandons it and perishes at that very moment; since this process repeats itself, there is destruction at every instant. This is precisely what is called "destruction of the continuum" (*saṃtānavināśa*) or "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), because the cause has perished even without [the intervention of] a further continuum. The other kind, however, is when, after producing an effect, the cause perishes in a mere instant along with that effect due to such factors as the blow of a hammer.

That very destruction of the continuum is also designated as "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Of these, the first [position] is untenable. For, according to the rule that after producing an effect, at the time of its relinquishment, [the cause] must exist as a reality and thereby possess the capacity to produce an effect, it would simply produce another effect rather than perish. Since this would also apply at the moment of separation from that [effect], there would never be a destruction devoid of a continuum. Nor is the destruction of the continuum itself tenable; for the absolute destruction of an existing jar would mean that, because it exists, it must produce an effect and not perish.

Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, because [the cause] exists, it produces only an effect and does not perish; therefore, since there is no occasion for the interruption of the continuum, the definition-sūtra is established as logical.
And because there is a fault in both cases.

Now, even so, it might be argued that it is impossible to negate the momentariness of existent entities (*bhāva-padārtha*). Existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); and this is not possible without momentariness. If a jar, having produced another jar in its first moment, did not itself perish, then it would produce yet another jar in the second moment and so on; and since those other jars would likewise do the same, there would be the consequence of an infinite series of effects. Therefore, since existence—defined as the capacity for causal efficiency—is established only through the momentariness of entities, momentariness must be accepted. To this, the author states the aphorism: [The opponent's position: Even so, it is impossible to negate the momentariness of existent entities. Existence is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency. And that [capacity] is not tenable without momentariness. If a jar, having produced another jar in its first moment, were not itself to perish, then it would produce yet another jar in the second moment and so forth; and since those other jars would likewise do the same, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of effects. Therefore, for the sake of establishing existence in the form of causal efficiency, the momentariness of entities must be admitted. To this, the Sūtra says:

"And because there is a fault in both cases. This is the meaning: whether one adopts the position that an effect necessarily arises when its cause exists, or the position that it does not, a fault exists—namely, the fault known as the non-production of specific effects from specific causes. Therefore, the position of momentariness is not tenable through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) by relying on either of these two positions. This is the sense.

And thus, if one accepts the momentariness of entities, [one must hold that] existence (*sattva*) consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and momentariness follows from the impossibility of that [efficiency] otherwise. For one who asserts this, is the rule relied upon—that "when a cause exists, the effect necessarily arises"—real or not? In the first case, since cause and effect would be simultaneous like the left and right horns of a cow, there could be no relationship of cause and effect. In the second case, if the effect is not produced in the first moment, it would lack existence due to the absence of causal efficiency.

Consequently, at some point, no effect whatsoever would arise. And thus, momentariness—which is postulated because existence cannot otherwise be accounted for—would not exist either. By this, it should be understood that the opponent's own position is flawed in both ways, whereas our own position is free from defect; therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct. [Sūtra: "And in the case of space, because there is no distinction."

Now, let it be granted that momentariness is not established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). It will be established by inference as follows: "Whatever exists is momentary, like a lamp and so forth; and these entities, these objects, exist. Nor should it be argued that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for instance: "Whatever is the locus of contradictory properties is manifold, like a jar and a cloth; and this lamp is the locus of contradictory properties in its preceding and succeeding moments, because such a distinction is observed. To this, the author states the aphorism: [The opponent argues: "If it is said that 'whatever is the locus of contradictory properties is manifold, like a jar and a cloth,' and since this lamp is the locus of contradictory properties in its preceding and succeeding moments—because a specific difference is perceived—then [momentariness is established]. To this, the Sūtra says:

"And because there is no distinction in the case of space. This is its meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also. When momentariness is established for the world using the example of a lamp as a reason for existence, there arises the contingency of establishing non-momentariness as well by means of the example of space. Now, one might object that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*); to this it is said: "because there is no distinction in the case of space. The meaning is that no specific dimension (*parimāṇa*) is observed in space that could serve as a proof for momentariness, as [you] have stated.
And thus, since this reason is counterbalanced (satpratipakṣa), the momentariness [of things] is not established by it; such is the sense.

Furthermore, since it is possible to prove even non-momentariness by means of the following [inference]: "Whatever exists is momentary, just like space," there is no absence of the probandum (sādhya) in space. This is because, due to the absence of any specific observation, there is no proof for momentariness [in that case]. Nor can that [non-momentariness] be established by another reason, because that [space] is not admitted to be distinct from the five aggregates (skandhas). If it is argued that "existence does not exist in space," then what is this "existence" that is absent in space? If it is defined as "the capacity for causal efficiency" (arthakriyākāritva), [then...]

O Venerable One, according to the previously stated method, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because nothing whatsoever possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); furthermore, the example (*nidarśana*) lacks the probandum (*sādhanavikalatā*). Alternatively, if you mean "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*), this refers either to existence or to the nature of non-existence; since that too exists in space (*ākāśa*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is difficult to avoid. Therefore, because the reason of "existence" (*sattva*) is countered by itself, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is not established by this [reason] either. Thus, it is proven that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because of recollection.
Having thus refuted the inference of a sentient being by means of a counter-argument, he introduces a sutra that refutes it even by means of sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*).

"And because of recognition" (anusmṛti). The meaning of this is as follows: because there is recognition in the form "this is that very same thing," and because [momentariness] contradicts that, it is not logical to prove momentariness by means of the reason of existence; such is the meaning.

And thus, there is a contradiction with the proposition [of yours] that "this is that very jar," as well as because its momentariness would be established. Nor is the proposition erroneous, for there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, the argument—"This jar is the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in each subsequent moment, because it possesses the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*), like a jar struck by a mallet in a single moment"—is refuted by the aforementioned method. Moreover, having indicated the atoms (*paramāṇu*) by the word "jar," the word "nature of a jar" intends to express "atom-ness" (*paramāṇutva*) itself as the logical reason (*hetu*).

Or, is it intended that the aggregate itself is made the subject (*pakṣa*) and "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) alone is stated as the reason (*hetu*)? Not the first [alternative], because a pot struck by a mallet lacks the nature of an atom (*paramāṇu*) insofar as it is an aggregate; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible due to the absence of the reason in that instance. Nor the second, because since you must prove momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) only for that which exists, proving it for a non-entity (*avastu*) is useless.

Therefore, since the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas are untenable and thus do not constitute opposition, it is established that the definition of God as the cause of the entire universe is correct.
Thus concludes the section concerning the aggregate.
Here, the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) is refuted:
"Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed."

[Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is untenable? Because it contradicts the doctrine of Śūnya (the Void). The doctrine of Śūnya alone is the truth; therein, the supreme benefit is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). From that alone the entire world arises. Nor is its impossibility for one who is unattached (*asaṅga*) a problem, because its possibility is established through conventional connection (*saṃvṛtti-sambandha*). Nor is there a contradiction with the Vedas (*śruti*), because their authority is not accepted. Therefore, since it contradicts the doctrine of Śūnya, the definition of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is untenable. To this, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Because it is not seen [to exist] in the case of the non-existent. This is its meaning: it is not logical for that which is non-existent—that is, a void—to be the creator of the world. Why? Because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Why is that? Because it is not observed; for nowhere is the causality of the non-existent ever seen. Therefore, the meaning is that even inference and verbal testimony are absent [in this regard].

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world, because the doctrine of Śūnya lacks authoritative foundation. There is no proof for the claim that Śūnya itself is the cause of the world; such proof would have to be either perception, inference, or scripture. First of all, it cannot be perception, because the state of having Śūnya as the cause is not perceptible. Nor can it be inference, because there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Even though causality is observed in things like jars, these do not serve as valid instances [for a cause that is non-existent].

In your view, however, because [the opponent] does not accept its existence, the opponent has not perceived its causality; thus, since the absence of causality can be inferred by him, your argument suffers from the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). As for scripture (*āgama*), it would have to be either Buddhist scripture or the Veda and so forth. It cannot be the first, because the opponent does not accept its authority. Nor can it be the second, because the proponent does not accept its authority, and furthermore, such a Veda is not observed to exist.
Therefore, since the doctrine of emptiness is untenable, it is established that the definition of God as the cause of the world is correct.
And thus there is accomplishment even for those who are indifferent.

Surely, what fault is there in accepting that even though it is unobserved, emptiness (*śūnya*) is the cause of the world? Nor has it been said that because it is unobserved, it is unauthoritative and thus unfit for acceptance; for although a specific inference (*dṛṣṭānumāna*) may not arise due to its being unobserved, an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is possible. Indeed, if the existence of the cause as a real entity—just like the effect—is denied, one might suspect that birth from a non-existent thing alone will be established by the reason of "being an effect. Anticipating this objection, the author introduces the aphorism (*sūtra*) which refutes it.

"And thus there would be the production [of effects] even from indifferent things. This is the meaning: if it were accepted that an effect can arise from what is non-existent (*asat*), then the production of effects such as curd and the like would occur even from "indifferent" things—such as sky-flowers and the like—which are not objects of the cognition of what is to be rejected or accepted. The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that otherwise, no effect could arise even from the void (*śūnya*).

And thus, if that which is non-existent were a cause, there would follow the absurd consequence that even things like sky-flowers—which are devoid of being objects of the cognition of what is to be avoided or accepted—could produce effects such as fragrance; for it is possible to formulate a negative inference (*vyatirekī-anumāna*) in that case as well. Furthermore, the inferences favored by opponents are sublated by logical reasoning (*tarka*). Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
Not non-existence, because of perception.

Now, this objection might indeed hold if the world were produced from the reality of emptiness (*śūnya-tattva*) in an ultimate sense, like a jar from a lump of clay; but it is not so. Rather, since it is accepted that even the void appears in the form of the world as a "transformation" (*vivarta*)—an appearance arising from a specific ignorance designated as "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*), just as [the appearance] of silver arises from what is non-existent—the author states the aphorism to dispel such a doubt: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from the power of illusion (*māyā-vaśāt*). (Brahmasūtra 2.1.14) This means: the world is not produced from the reality of emptiness in an ultimate sense, like a jar from a lump of clay. On the contrary, it is accepted that even the void appears in the form of the world as a transformation—an appearance arising from a specific ignorance designated as "conventional reality," just as the appearance of silver arises from what is non-existent. Thus, the author states the aphorism to refute this doubt.
"Nor is there non-existence, because of perception. This is its meaning: the world is not non-existent (asat); why? Because of perception—that is, because it is perceived as being existent (sat).

And thus, if one accepts that the void (*śūnya*) functions in the form of the world, it follows that the world must be false (*mithyātva*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the world is perceived as being real (*sat*). Furthermore, if the void were to appear in the form of silver, experience establishes that it is the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) alone that serves as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition of silver; the void lacks such a status as a locus. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logically sound.
And because of the difference in nature, [the dream analogy] does not apply, as in the case of dreams and the like.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since even that which is perceived as 'existent'—such as the states of dreaming and waking, or a snake in a rope—is actually non-existent, why should the world not likewise be non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, the author presents the following sūtra to resolve it:

"And because of dissimilarity, [the world] is not like a dream and so forth. This is its meaning: the world is not non-existent in the same way that a dream and so forth are—like the state of being "waking" superimposed upon dream-objects. Why? Because of dissimilarity; that is to say, because the waking-state within a dream possesses a distinct property called "sublatability," whereas that [property] is absent in the [actual] world.

And thus, this [world] is merely a dream; it is not like the waking state, for there is a disparity due to the absence of a subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) in the present case—unlike the instance where one recognizes, "This is a rope, not a snake," which serves as the object of a subverting cognition. By this, it has been stated that the counter-inference (pratipakṣānumāna) propounded by the opponent possesses the fallacy of a limiting condition (upādhi), namely, being the object of a subverting means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), whereas its counter-part lacks such a condition. Therefore, since the doctrine of Śūnyavāda is likewise untenable, it is established that the definition of the Lord as the cause of the world is correct.
Thus concludes the section on the non-existent.
Here, the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda) is refuted:
"There is no [external] entity, because it is not perceived."

Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is untenable? For this contradicts the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins (Idealists). Indeed, only the reality of consciousness—which is eternal and stainless—exists; this entire world is merely that, and there is nothing whatsoever beyond it. Therefore, since there is no purpose for a Lord in the production of the world, the definition-sūtra is incorrect. To this, the author states the sūtra: *janmādyasya yataḥ* (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.2). [Translation of the sūtra: "That from which [proceed] the birth and so forth of this [world]. [Commentary: This is stated to refute the objection that the definition-sūtra is improper because the Lord has no function in the creation of the world, given the Idealist position that the world is nothing but consciousness. By asserting that the world originates from Him, the sūtra establishes that the Lord is indeed the cause of the universe, thereby refuting the Idealist view. Thus, the status of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is established.

"Existence does not [arise], because of non-apprehension. This is its meaning: the world is not an existence, even though it consists of cognition; for there is no apprehension of non-difference between the cognition and the cognized object—this is the sense.

And thus, Hari’s status as the cause of the world is indeed logical, because the system of the Vijñānavādins (Idealists) is untenable and therefore does not constitute a contradiction. If it is argued that the world is superimposed upon the reality of consciousness—on the grounds that no world exists apart from consciousness—that is incorrect, because it is impossible for something to be superimposed while being perceived as "existent. If it is argued that there is non-difference between the reality of consciousness and the world, that is also untenable, because there is no evidence for the world having the nature of cognition. Nor should it be said that non-difference between blue and its cognition follows from the rule of their simultaneous apprehension; for this contradicts the perception of their difference.

Nor is that [perception] an error, because there is no sublation (bādhaka). Since blue and other objects, like their own cognition, do not differ from it, their difference is also consistent with their own cognition; thus, it is impossible for that cognition to be erroneous. Furthermore, since coexistence is pervaded by difference, the claim that "there is non-difference because they are perceived together" involves a contradiction between the proposition and the reason. If it is argued that the nature of blue and other objects as cognition is established by the inference: "Whatever is manifest is cognition, just like cognition itself; and blue and others are manifest," [we reply: [The opponent continues: But surely, that which is manifest is cognition, just as cognition is; and blue and other objects are manifest. Thus, by this inference, the status of blue and other objects as cognition is proven.

If one accepts that [the world] "shines forth" (prakāśate) by taking this to mean being an object of cognition, then the Māyāvādin’s objection—that there is a lack of proof regarding consciousness due to the contradiction of a thing acting upon itself—would result in him being left without an answer. Furthermore, there would be a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of ignorance (ajñāna). If, on the other hand, one accepts "shining forth" as the nature of luminosity (prakāśatva), then the reason is unestablished (asiddhi). Therefore, since the Buddhist doctrine lacks scriptural authority, there is no contradiction; thus, it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe.
And because of momentariness.
He introduces another aphorism which refutes the view that the world consists of consciousness by means of yet another argument.

"And because of momentariness" (kṣaṇikatvāt). The meaning of this is as follows: since cognition exists for only a single moment while the world is enduring, there is a contradiction between the two; therefore, they cannot be identical. This is the sense.

And thus, since cognition is momentary while the world is enduring, their identity is impossible; for momentariness entails the nature of perishability. Therefore, it is established that the definition [of Brahman] as the cause of the world is logical.
And because it is untenable in every way.
Having thus refuted each of the Buddhist systems, such as the Vaibhāṣika and others, he introduces a scriptural passage that further undermines them with a general critique.

"And because it is untenable in every way. This is its meaning: because the Buddhist tenet system is untenable in every respect—being devoid of logical justification and being contradictory [to reason]—it is not to be accepted. This is the sense.

Thus, in the case of the hypothesis of the momentariness of perception—the hypothesis that things arise and perish at every moment—the hypothesis of the non-duality of the Void (Śūnyādvaita), or the hypothesis of the non-duality of Consciousness (Vijñānādvaita)—whether in their manifestation or concealment—these are untenable. This is because they contradict such Śruti passages as "Whatever existed here was Brahman alone," and such Smṛti passages as "He Himself [became] manifold again," as well as the reasonings set forth in the Sūtras. Since all these positions held by those who hate the Vedas are logically inconsistent, it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world.
Thus ends the section on non-apprehension as a non-probans.
Here, the doctrine of the Syādvādins is refuted:
"Because [the contradictory properties] cannot coexist in one [entity]."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world, because this contradicts the Jaina doctrine. The Jainas, however, describe the world through the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). To explain: "existent" is one mode; "non-existent" is another; "both existent and non-existent" is the third; "distinct from both existent and non-existent" is the fourth; "existent while being distinct from the existent" is the fifth; "non-existent while being distinct from the non-existent" is the sixth; and "both existent and non-existent while being distinct from both existent and non-existent" is the seventh.

Furthermore, since the birth of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the body of the world is possible through seen and unseen means, what need is there for a Lord? Thus, the objection that the defining sutra is improper having been raised, the author states the following sutra to refute it.

"Because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] in one [entity]. This is its meaning: the sevenfold categories asserted by the Jains are not tenable in a single entity. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because they are impossible in one place due to their lack of authoritative foundation (*aprāmāṇikatva*). The sevenfold categories should be understood as follows: existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, distinctness from existence, distinctness from non-existence while being existent, distinctness from existence while being non-existent, and distinctness from both existence and non-existence while being both existent and non-existent.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is indeed logical, because the Jaina doctrine lacks authoritative validity. As for what was said—that the world consists of sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī)—that is not correct, because a mode distinct from both existence and non-existence lacks authoritative validity, and because [contradictory attributes] cannot coexist in a single entity. Nor is it reasonable to claim that a position is accepted simply because a fault exists when one individual aspect is affirmed; if that were the case, one would have to abandon everything out of fear of faults.

Since a "sevenfold predication" (saptabhaṅgī) regarding a single entity is even more untenable—given that a "sevenfold predication" distinct from both existence and non-existence is itself unauthoritative—it follows that the Jaina doctrine is logically inconsistent. Thus, it is established that the definition-sūtra [of our system] is free from contradiction.
And thus, the self would not be omnipresent.

As for that which was stated by the Jina—that because it is impossible for a soul to experience sensations throughout all its limbs if it were atomic, and because if it were omnipresent there would be the undesirable consequence of experiencing [sensations] even when one has gone to another body, the soul must be of the same size as the body—[we ask]: is that [size] accepted for the sake of accounting for the occurrence of movements perceived in all of one's own bodies? Or is it because the self lacks an inherent dimension of its own, except for being delimited by the body? To refute the first position, he states the following Sūtra:

"And thus, there would be non-omnipresence of the self. This is its meaning: if it is accepted that the self has the same dimensions as the body, then when the self—having previously occupied the body of an ant and being limited to that body—attains the body of an elephant, a donkey, or the like, there would be "non-omnipresence," meaning a lack of fullness. Likewise, it should be understood that when the self occupying an elephant's body attains the body of an ant, there would be non-omnipresence and [subsequent] deficiency.

Thus, even if one accepts that the self has the same dimensions as the body, since it would be incapable of producing all the activities within all bodies that it might occupy, the following would occur: when a self of the dimensions of an elephant or a donkey, by the force of karma, enters the body of an ant, there would be an excess [of space] within that very [ant] body. Consequently, the doctrine that the self has the dimensions of the body would be destroyed. Therefore, it is established that the *lakṣaṇasūtra* is correct.
And even by way of figurative interpretation there is no absence of contradiction, because of transformation and other such reasons.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the self is not restricted to the size of a single body, but rather assumes whatever size corresponds to whichever body it attains? And if this were so, the previously mentioned defects would not follow. To this, the author presents the aphorism as a refutation.

"And there is no absence of contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and so forth. This is its meaning: "Through succession" means through sequence; even by accepting that [the self] possesses the dimensions of those respective bodies in sequence, it is not tenable to say "there is no contradiction," i.e., that the aforementioned fault does not exist. Why? Because succession is not tenable. And why is that? Because of "transformation and so forth": if that were the case, since there would be a difference in the substance due to the difference in dimensions at those respective times, it would follow that the self undergoes transformation. Consequently, because of impermanence, there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation and other such faults. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, because the self would thus be subject to modification, it would follow that it is impermanent. Consequently, there would be the consequence of no liberation and the futility of the scriptures. Moreover, if one were to accept that the self residing in bodies such as those of an elephant or an ant possesses a size corresponding sequentially to each respective body, the aforementioned defects would not be avoided; since it would incur modification, it would fall into the error of impermanence. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
And because of the final state, and because both [the soul and the body] are eternal, there is no distinction [between them].

Now, he presents the sūtra while refuting the second position, which asserts that because the self lacks its own intrinsic dimension in the absence of limitation by the body, the self must therefore be admitted to have the same dimensions as the body.

"And because of the final state, and because of the permanence of both, there would be no distinction. This is its meaning: from the previous sūtra, the word "and thus" (evam ca) is supplied by ellipsis; the phrase "because of the final state" (antyāvasthiteḥ) is repeated; and the word "and" (ca) serves both to emphasize and to aggregate. Thus, it follows that if the soul's size is admitted to be equal to that of the body, then the consequence of "the final state" arises—this is the remainder of the sense. The meaning is that even in liberation (mokṣa), the existence of a body would have to be admitted for the soul that persists. Why? Because of the final state.

The meaning is that the persistence of the final dimension of the pearl must necessarily be admitted. Why? "And because of the persistence of the final [dimension]. This is because the persistence of the final dimension of the pearl must necessarily be accepted; for it is impossible for a delimited dimension to exist without a body that serves as its delimiter—this is the sense. He states further why there must be a dimension at all: "And because of the final... [and so forth].

The meaning is that for the final state, which consists of the nature of a liberated pearl (mauktika), it is impossible for its essential existence (*svarūpasattva*) to persist without a measurement (*parimāṇa*). To the question, "Let there be a body even in liberation; what of it?", it is said: "Because both would be eternal. This means that if that were the case, it would follow that both—the body and the self existing at the time of liberation—are eternal. To the question, "Let the eternity of the liberated body be granted; what of it?", he says: "And from that, there would be the eternity of everything"—this sentence of the consequence (*āpādya*) is to be supplied.

For this very reason, the word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction, meaning that all present bodies would have to be eternal. Why? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction" (aviśeṣāt). This means that there is no difference between the bodies existing at the time of liberation and those existing now, insofar as they are both "bodies. Therefore, the view that the self is of the same size as the body is not tenable; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, if the soul lacks dimension upon liberation, it would follow that its very nature as a self is non-existent; for there is no substance devoid of dimension. If it were to exist [without a body], it would be impossible for it to possess dimension in the absence of a body. Even if such a body were to exist, if it were impermanent, it would result in the soul possessing the same attributes as those in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). If it were permanent, then because the quality of being a "body" is indistinguishable, the present body would also have to be permanent. Therefore, the position that the self has the dimension of the body is not tenable. Consequently, since the Jaina doctrine is untenable and thus not a source of contradiction, it is established that the definition of the cause of the world is valid.
Thus ends the section concerning "not in one [locus]."
Here, the Pāśupata position is refuted.
On account of the inconsistency of [the Lord] being the master.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is untenable? Because it contradicts the Pāśupata tradition. Indeed, Paśupati alone possesses qualities such as omniscience; having taken *māyā* as his material cause, he performs all acts, including the creation of the world consisting of Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others. There are also Śruti and Smṛti texts to this effect. Therefore, the aphorism defining [Brahman] is incorrect. To this, the author reads the following aphorism: [The author] states the aphorism in response to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

"Because of the inconsistency of the Lord [as cause]" (Sūtra 2.2.37). The meaning of this is as follows: it is not logical for Paśupati, the Lord, to be the cause of the world. Why? Because of inconsistency; that is to say, because he would possess defects such as dependence and birth.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is logical. Since the Pāśupata doctrine lacks authoritative validity, Paśupati is not the creator of the world, because he is tainted by the defects of dependence, birth, and death. Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), for it is established by the Śruti text: "Whomever I desire, him I make fierce. Furthermore, from the Śruti text, "Nārāyaṇa alone existed," it is understood that Paśupati does not exist at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). Therefore, since the Pāśupata doctrine is untenable and thus non-contradictory [to our position], the definition-sūtra is established as logical.
And because a relationship [between them] is untenable.
He introduces another aphorism which refutes the status of Paśupati as the cause of the world by means of a further argument.
"And because a relationship is untenable. This is its meaning: since Śiva is bodiless, a relationship with the world is untenable; therefore, he cannot be the creator—this is the sense.

And thus, not only because of dependence and so forth, but also because of being bodiless (*aśarīratva*), it is impossible for Paśupati to be the creator of the world. For the agency of one who is bodiless is never observed, such that it could belong to him in that manner. Nor should it be argued that even for one who is bodiless, a mere connection with the effect—the world—is possible, as in the case of the conjunction of the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth with a jar and the like; for, unlike a person who has abandoned the body, there is an absence of the specific type of connection characterized by agency. Therefore, since it is impossible for Paśupati to be the creator of the world, it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct.
And because a substratum is untenable.
He introduces a sūtra that refutes Paśupati’s status as the cause of the world by means of another reason:

"And because a substratum is untenable. This is its meaning: since everything has perished at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), at the time of renewed creation, a substratum such as the earth is untenable for Paśupati; therefore, he cannot be the creator of the world—this is the sense.

And thus, because the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) cannot be the agent due to the non-perception of a substratum, and because we observe effects such as jars produced by potters and others who reside in a substratum like the earth, whereas such [a substratum] is absent for him; and since the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyāpti) has been demonstrated through the general example of the substratum of the earth and so forth by means of the reason stated in the Sūtra—therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is logical.
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of enjoyment and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that at the time of dissolution, primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest do not exist as permanent entities that could be directly presided over by effort like the body and so forth; nor is there a requirement for a body to instigate what is already directly presided over by effort, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of requiring yet another body to instigate the first body. Therefore, since there exists a substitute for the body and such, agency is established. To this position, the author presents the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] not so, on account of the impossibility of the absence of a body. (2.1.31) This means: It is not the case that agency is possible even in the absence of a body. Why? Because of the impossibility. For the Lord, who is the agent, must possess a body, just as we see in the case of ordinary agents. If one were to argue that He does not require a body because He is eternally free from all defects, we reply: no, because the very nature of being an agent implies the necessity of a body. Even if one were to claim that He acts through His mere will, that too is untenable, as it would entail the aforementioned infinite regress. Thus, the conclusion remains that agency is impossible without a body.

"If it be argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [the consequences of] experience and so forth. This is its meaning: Now, if it be argued that since the collection of instruments belonging to Paśupati is like a cause—that is, like a body, equal to a body, and equal to a locus—therefore the aforementioned defect does not apply, we say "no. Why? Because of "experience and so forth"; that is to say, because of the defects such as the arising of the experience of pleasure and pain produced by a body, death, and so on.

And thus, since the aggregate of causal factors (*kārakasamūha*) is equivalent to a body, there would follow birth and death through the acquisition and abandonment of that [aggregate], just as there is birth and death through the acquisition and abandonment of a body. Consequently, there would be the experience of pleasure and pain. For it is observed that when Yajñadatta and others acquire or abandon a body—which is essentially a modification directly governed by effort—there occur production and destruction caused by those two [acquisitions and abandonments]. Therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct.
Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience.

He recites and explains the Sūtra—“Because a relationship is impossible” and “And because [the soul] is like an instrument”—which refutes, by means of another logical flaw, the very two positions regarding the existence or non-existence of a body that were previously stated, by way of an analysis of alternatives.

"Either [the Lord] would be finite or he would be non-omniscient. This is its meaning: since, under the two alternatives of Śiva having a body or not having one, there would respectively be finitude—which is to say perishability—and non-omniscience—which is to say a lack of omniscience—it follows that [the position of those who assert his corporeality] is untenable. This is the sense.

And thus, if one accepts Paśupati as the creator of the world, there arises the contingency of his being subject to destruction if he possesses a body; if he lacks a body, however, there would be an absence of knowledge. These defects do not apply to the case of Viṣṇu, because the absence of knowledge is precluded by such scriptural texts as "He is possessed of intelligence" and "He is possessed of mind," and because defects such as finitude are refuted by passages like "Of what nature the Blessed Lord is. In that context, it is stated that the body of the Blessed Lord is of the same nature as His own essence, consisting of knowledge and the rest.

In this very manner, the conventions (*samaya*) of the Śākta, Saura, Skānda, and Gāṇapatya [sects] are to be understood as refuted. Therefore, since the convention of the Pāśupatas is untenable and thus non-contradictory [to our position], it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct.
Thus ends the section concerning the husband.
Here, the position of those who maintain that [the world] arises from primordial matter (śakti) is refuted: "Because of the impossibility of its arising."

Now, an objection is raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, because this contradicts the Śākta doctrine. Indeed, it is taught in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that Śakti alone—endowed with attributes such as omniscience—is the mother of the entire universe. Therefore, the aphorism defining Hari is not appropriate. To this, the author presents the following aphorism:

"Because of the impossibility of origination. This is its meaning: Śakti is not the cause of the world. Why? Because of the impossibility of origination; that is to say, because the birth of offspring from mere females denoted by the word "Śakti" is impossible.

Thus, in the view of the Mahāvāmas, that which is asserted—namely, that Śakti alone, unaided by Puruṣa, is the cause of the world—is not tenable. This is because the proposition that Śakti alone, unaided by Puruṣa, is the cause of the world is not seen to be supported by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); for it is impossible for her in isolation to be the creator of the world. Furthermore, the scriptural authorities cited by others, such as "the one unborn female" (ajāmekām) and so forth, do not have that as their intended meaning, since they declare that she is the cause of the world only through dependence upon Īśvara. Therefore, it is established that the doctrine of the Mahāvāmas is invalid, and that the definition of the cause of the world [as being dependent on Īśvara] is correct.
And there is no instrument for the agent.

But surely Sadāśiva, though devoid of qualities such as omniscience, exists as the bestower of grace upon Śakti; and since Śakti, when graced by him, is the cause of the world, the scripture stating "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*) and so forth serves as its authority. In response to those of the Madhyama and Vāma schools who maintain that the cause of the world is Śakti as graced by Sadāśiva, the author of the Sūtras sets forth the following aphorism to refute their view:

"And there is no instrument for the agent. This is its meaning: since the instrument—the means such as knowledge and so forth—is not the cause of the agent, Śiva, who is the benefactor of [the soul's] power; therefore, it does not possess the status of being a benefactor of that power. This is the sense.

And thus, because Sadāśiva lacks omniscience and other such qualities, he cannot be the one who bestows grace; furthermore, due to the absence of the knowledge and so forth necessary for creation, as well as the sense organs required for its accomplishment, and the causal body [that serves as their basis], it is impossible for the world to arise even from a power (śakti) conjoined with a person (puruṣa). Therefore, since the systems of the Madhyama and Vāma schools lack scriptural authority, it is established that the definition of the cause of the world [as belonging to Śiva] is correct.
Or, if consciousness and the other [aggregates] exist, there is no negation of that [self].

Now, it is not merely said that the production of the world from *śakti* is logical because of the absence of a person who would favor that *śakti*; rather, for those who maintain that the production of the world from *śakti* is even more logical because of the existence of that Person’s omniscience and other qualities, [the author] presents the aphorism in order to refute their view.

"Or, if [Śiva] possesses consciousness and so forth, there is no refutation of that. This is its meaning: "Or, if consciousness and so forth exist"—that is, if it is admitted that Śiva possesses knowledge, will, and the rest—"there is no refutation of that": there would be no refutation, i.e., no rejection, of that Śaiva position; rather, an inference [in its favor] would have been made. And the sense is that this [position] has indeed already been refuted.

And thus, if it is accepted that there exists a sentient being possessing a body and sense organs whose consciousness is the agent of the world's production through the favoring of [primordial] powers (śakti), then—since the production of the world and so forth is possible for the agent Śiva and others by means of that very favoring of powers, without depending on any other agent—the doctrine of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimata) becomes identical with the Pāśupata doctrine; and since the latter has already been refuted, there is no further reason to refute it. Therefore, the doctrine of the Atomists (Aṇuvādins) is unauthoritative, and it is established that the definition of the cause of the world [as a conscious agent] is logical.
And because of contradiction.
Having thus individually refuted these three Śākta doctrines, he introduces the aphorism while further undermining them by means of a collective refutation.
"And because of contradiction. This is its meaning: because it contradicts all the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the Śākta doctrine is inconsistent; that is to say, it is illogical.

Thus, because it contradicts such Śruti passages as "There is no one else but Nārāyaṇa," such Smṛti passages as "He alone [is the cause]," and the previously stated reasons—and because it is censured by cultured people (śiṣṭas)—the entire Śākta doctrine is indeed untenable; therefore, it is established that the definition of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world's birth and so forth is correct.
Thus concludes the section on origination.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
Śrīḥ!
Hari.
Now begins the third quarter of the second chapter.

In this section (pāda), [the author] resolves the mutual contradictions among the scriptural texts concerning the individual self (jīva), the supreme self (paramātman), the presiding deity over the elements (adhibhūta), and the presiding deity over the divine powers (adhidaiva).
Here, the contradiction with scriptural passages concerning the origin of ether is resolved:
"Ether does not [originate], because it is not mentioned [in that context]."

Objection: It is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, because of the scriptural text, "This ether is indeed without beginning. Since ether is without beginning, it cannot have a cause. Nor can it be maintained that the Self is the cause of ether on the basis of the scriptural text, "From the Self, ether was produced," for that scripture lacks authority as it contradicts direct experience, reasoning, and many other statements. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that this scripture is not unauthoritative because the word "produced" (*saṃbhūta*) refers to something else; for if that were so, the same would apply to the passages concerning air and the rest.

For it is not possible that where a word is heard in its primary sense elsewhere, it should be drawn as secondary in this instance while being primary there. Therefore, since the scriptural mention of ether lacks authority [in this context], it is improper to establish Brahman as the cause of the universe through the concordance of the scriptures regarding ether. To this prima facie view, the Sūtra states:

"Because there is no scriptural statement [of its origin], the ether [is unproduced]. This is the meaning: "viyat" means the ether (ākāśa). It is not without origin; rather, it indeed has an origin from the Lord (Īśvara). Why? Because of the absence of scriptural statement (aśruteḥ); that is to say, because there is no scriptural passage regarding the non-origination of the ether.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe. Since there is no contradiction regarding the causality of space—even though space is not explicitly mentioned as being produced, its status as having an origin is established by its non-eternality—and since there is no sublation to its being the cause of space; nevertheless, if it is argued that Viṣṇu is not the cause of all because the causality of the individual soul (*jīva*), time (*kāla*), and so forth has not been stated, [we reply] that this is not so, because by the term "space" (*viyat*), the individual soul, time, the great principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the rest are indicated as representative examples (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, since the production of everything other than the Blessed Lord is established without contradicting the scriptures, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures (*śrutisamanvaya*) is properly established in the Supreme Brahman, the cause of all.
But it does exist.

Now, it might be argued that no proof need necessarily be stated for the absence of the production of ether (*viyat*), since its existence [as unproduced] is established simply by the absence of proof for its production; for once there is an absence of proof regarding a jar, there would be no further need for proof. To this objection, the Sūtra replies:

"But there is [a scriptural statement]"—the meaning of this is as follows: regarding the origin of space, there indeed exists a scriptural statement, namely, "From the Self, space was produced. This is the sense.

And thus, because of the existence of the scriptural text stating that "space was produced from the Self," non-origination is not established by this [other] scriptural passage. Therefore, since the origination of space and the rest is established in a manner consistent with scripture, it is proven that the concordance [of the Vedānta texts] is logical.
Because figurative application is impossible.

Now, one might object: "Is it not impossible to establish the origination of the ether (viyat) from the Self on the basis of the Śruti stating 'from [the Self] as space' (ātmana ākāśaḥ), because this contradicts other Śruti passages declaring its beginninglessness, such as 'it is without origin'? Anticipating this doubt, the author states the Sūtra.

"Because a figurative sense is impossible": this is its meaning. The scriptural text, "Or rather, this ether is beginningless," is figurative; it refers to a non-primary (secondary) kind of beginninglessness. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because if it were taken in its primary sense, it would be inconsistent with the numerous scriptural texts concerning its origination.

Furthermore, because the scriptural texts concerning beginninglessness must be understood as figurative; for it is established that those texts are figurative since the numerous scriptural passages on origination can otherwise be explained [as referring to the manifestation of the unmanifest]. Moreover, since the scriptural passages on origination possess their primary sense, they apply to all things. If one were to accept the aforementioned arrangement in accordance with the texts on beginninglessness and thus maintain that space is in no way originated, it would follow that those [scriptures on origination] would lose their authority.

Since abundance is a cause of preponderance, even the scriptural statement regarding origination possesses strength; thus, it is impossible to declare that [the scripture] lacks authority. Therefore, in order to maintain the authority of both scriptural passages, one must necessarily resort to the aforementioned distinction. Consequently, since the origination of ether is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the harmony [of the Upanishads with Brahman] is logical.
And from scripture.

He introduces the aphorism which establishes that the aforementioned arrangement is not only proven by the reasoning of impossibility, but is also established by scripture: [The aphorism: "But [the soul] is of the same size as the body, because that is seen [in scripture]. (2.3.29) This aphorism presents the meaning that this arrangement is established by both logic and scriptural authority.

"And because of the scriptural statement. The meaning of this is as follows: on the strength of the scriptural statement, "Now, indeed, they are eternal," the scriptural passage concerning their beginninglessness must be understood in a figurative sense.

Thus, the established position as stated is indeed logical, for the Bhāllaveya Śruti declares, "Now, these [elements] are indeed eternal. By this, the contradiction regarding [the claim that they arise] from experience is resolved. Therefore, it is established that the systematic reconciliation of the Śrutis with the Lord is consistent and free from conflict with the scriptures.
And it may belong to one [entity], as in the case of the word "Brahman."

Now, one might object: "How can the scriptural statement regarding beginninglessness be considered figurative, given that there is no sublation of its primary meaning? Otherwise, even such passages as 'It is not born, it does not die' would have to be taken in a figurative sense. To dispel this doubt—namely, that since the word expressing non-origination ("it is not born") is seen to have its primary meaning in the Supreme Self, it is appropriate that the scriptural statement on beginninglessness, which has the same referent, should likewise be so understood—the author presents the following sūtra.

"And it may belong to one [entity], like the word 'Brahman'. This is its meaning: the particle "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. Just as in the case of the single word "Brahman," which has a primary sense when applied to Viṣṇu and a secondary sense when applied to the individual soul (*jīva*), so too a single word denoting impermanence may have its primary meaning apply to Brahman. That is to say, it could be so.

And thus, while the word "unborn" (anutpatti) would be primary elsewhere, it would be secondary when applied to space (ākāśa), because its primary meaning is contradicted in the case of space by numerous scriptural texts concerning origination. Furthermore, we observe that even the word "Brahman," though primary when applied to Brahman, is used in a secondary sense for Viriñci and others due to the force of contradicting evidence. Therefore, it is established that the systematic reconciliation of the scriptures (śrutisamanvaya) is valid only when it does not conflict with the scriptures themselves.
There is an abandonment of the thesis because there is no distinction from the words.

Now, an objection may be raised: "It is indeed appropriate that the word *brahman* has its primary sense (*mukhya*) in the Supreme Brahman and a secondary sense (*amukhya*) elsewhere, because of the presence or absence of the cause for the application of the word—namely, the existence or non-existence of the nature of being full of all attributes (*guṇapūrṇatva*). However, it cannot be said that the same applies to the word *anutpattimat* (that which is unoriginated), since we do not perceive any such cause in the present case, namely, the presence or absence of the fullness of the grounds for the word's application. To dispel this doubt, the following sūtra is presented:

"Relinquishment of the proposition [would result] because space is not distinct from sounds. This is its meaning: if one were to state that space has no primary origination, there would be a relinquishment of the proposition; namely, a relinquishment of the proposition that Viṣṇu is the creator, expressed in the text, "He created all this. Why? Because of non-distinction—that is, because space is not distinct from the referents of all words. Furthermore, it is determined from such clear scriptural texts as "The Self, verily, was this in the beginning," and so forth, that the primary non-origination belongs to Brahman alone and not to anything else.
Therefore, what was stated is logical; this is the meaning.

And thus, since space (*ākāśa*) also possesses primary eternity like Brahman, if one were to accept that it is primarily denoted by words signifying "that which is unproduced," there would result a contradiction with the proposition [of the scripture] that "He created this. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction with the proposition simply because it is not explicitly stated here that "He created space"; for space is included by the very word "all" (*sarva*), as there is no reason to restrict the scope [of "all"], and because of the scriptural text: "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone, one only. Therefore, it is established that the systematic reconciliation (*samanvaya*) is consistent with the scriptures.
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world.

The Sūtra introduces [the following argument], establishing by means of inference that Brahman alone is beginningless while all others are beginningless, for the purpose of determining the primary and secondary senses of the scriptural texts concerning non-origination.

"But as far as there is modification, there is division, according to worldly usage. This is its meaning: the word *yāvat* is used in the sense of restriction; *yāvadvikāram* is an indeclinable compound; and the particle *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). Thus, it is established as a rule that "as far as there is modification" (*yāvadvikāram*)—that is, only that which is undergoing change—is "division," meaning it possesses limited power and nothing else. Therefore, "according to worldly usage" (*lokavat*); that is, "like in the world" (*loka iti*). Just as in the world, in the case of a jar and so forth, because they are divided, their state of being modified is accepted.

In the same way, even for space and so forth, their state of being subject to modification is established by the reason of their being divisible; from that very fact, it follows that they are also beginningless—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, space possesses origination because it has limited power, like a jar and other such objects; thus, since the origination of space is established through inference, the scriptural texts concerning its beginninglessness must be understood figuratively. Moreover, there exists the following reasoning: Brahman does not possess origination because it is undifferentiated, whereas the opposite is the case for a jar. Nor does the statement "Prakṛti and Puruṣa" contradict ancient scripture which speaks of "eternal and non-eternal Puruṣas," for that text merely declares the absence of origination—in the sense of coming into being after not having existed—with respect to the essential nature of Prakṛti and the rest.

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction here due to the difference in scope between the statement regarding origination—which consists in the attainment of a specific state dependent on another—and [the statement regarding non-origination], it is established that the harmony of the scriptures with Brahman as the cause of all is valid, because the origination of everything other than the Blessed Lord is proven in accordance with the scriptures. Thus, it is settled.
Thus ends the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa).

Here, for the sake of establishing the concordance of the scriptures with respect to the Lord, the contradiction among scriptural passages concerning the origin of the primary vital air (mukhyavāyu) is resolved.
By this, Mātariśvan is explained.

But is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is untenable? For according to the Śruti, "Vāyu alone [is the cause]," Vāyu lacks causality due to his lack of origination. Nor can this Śruti be considered figurative (gauṇī) like the one regarding the non-origination of ether (ākāśa); for after stating the eternity of ether with the Śruti, "Now, these [elements] are eternal," the Śruti declares the eternity of Vāyu as well. Otherwise, the specific mention of his eternity would be improper. Furthermore, if Vāyu were subject to origination, he would not possess the supreme degree of consciousness relative to all else, nor would he be the object of worship for all the gods.

Since the Śruti states that air has neither beginning nor middle, thereby declaring its beginninglessness, and further mentions its rising and setting, it is logical to conceive of its production as being devoid of those two [beginning and end]. If one were to accept that air—which possesses the means of proof (sādhaka)—is subject to production simply because one observes the production of the object to be proven (sādhya), there would be a contradiction with experience. Therefore, since air lacks production, the scriptural statement regarding its production lacks authority; thus, it is argued that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world based on the harmony of the Śrutis. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra: "But [air] is like the ether. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.1) This means: Just as the ether, though beginningless, is produced by the will of the Lord, so too is air. Or, just as the ether, though unproduced, is designated as "produced" in relation to its effects such as sound, so too is air. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that air is eternal in the sense of being non-produced (*ajanya*): "From which all beings arise, by which, when born, they live, and into which they enter upon death—desire that Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). This indicates that air is eternal insofar as it is not produced from anything else. Moreover, the Śruti speaks of its production in reference to its manifestation as a specific effect, such as sound, just as one says "the jar is produced" even though the clay is eternal. Therefore, air is both eternal and produced. Consequently, the non-authoritativeness of the Śruti regarding air’s production is untenable, and it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world through the harmony of the Śrutis. Thus ends the section concerning air. Now begins the consideration of fire. Regarding this, the following doubt arises: Is fire produced from air, or is it not? On this point, the following prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is presented: "Fire is not produced from air, because of the Śruti stating 'fire arose from air' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1). Since the Śruti uses the word "arose" (*ajāyata*), which denotes birth, and since air is established to be beginningless, it is logical to assume that fire, being devoid of those two [beginning and end], is likewise unproduced. If one were to accept that fire—which possesses the means of proof—is produced simply because one observes the production of the object to be proven, there would be a contradiction with experience. Therefore, since fire lacks production, the Śruti regarding its production lacks authority; thus, it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world based on the harmony of the Śrutis. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra: "But [fire] is like the ether. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.2) This means: Just as the ether, though beginningless, is produced by the will of the Lord, so too is fire. Or, just as the ether, though unproduced, is designated as "produced" in relation to its effects such as sound, so too is fire. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that fire is eternal in the sense of being non-produced: "From which all beings arise, by which, when born, they live, and into which they enter upon death—desire that Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). This indicates that fire is eternal insofar as it is not produced from anything else. Moreover, the Śruti speaks of its production in reference to its manifestation as a specific effect, such as light, just as one says "the jar is produced" even though the clay is eternal. Therefore, fire is both eternal and produced. Consequently, the non-authoritativeness of the Śruti regarding fire’s production is untenable, and it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world through the harmony of the Śrutis. Thus ends the section concerning fire. Now begins the consideration of water. Regarding this, the following doubt arises: Is water produced from fire, or is it not? On this point, the following prima facie view is presented: "Water is not produced from fire, because of the Śruti stating 'water arose from fire' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1). Since the Śruti uses the word "arose," and since fire is established to be beginningless, it is logical to assume that water, being devoid of those two, is likewise unproduced. If one were to accept that water—which possesses the means of proof—is produced simply because one observes the production of the object to be proven, there would be a contradiction with experience. Therefore, since water lacks production, the Śruti regarding its production lacks authority; thus, it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world based on the harmony of the Śrutis. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra: "But [water] is like the ether. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.3) This means: Just as the ether, though beginningless, is produced by the will of the Lord, so too is water. Or, just as the ether, though unproduced, is designated as "produced" in relation to its effects such as sound, so too is water. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that water is eternal in the sense of being non-produced: "From which all beings arise, by which, when born, they live, and into which they enter upon death—desire that Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). This indicates that water is eternal insofar as it is not produced from anything else. Moreover, the Śruti speaks of its production in reference to its manifestation as a specific effect, such as fluidity, just as one says "the jar is produced" even though the clay is eternal. Therefore, water is both eternal and produced. Consequently, the non-authoritativeness of the Śruti regarding water’s production is untenable, and it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world through the harmony of the Śrutis. Thus ends the section concerning water. Now begins the consideration of earth. Regarding this, the following doubt arises: Is earth produced from water, or is it not? On this point, the following prima facie view is presented: "Earth is not produced from water, because of the Śruti stating 'earth arose from water' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1). Since the Śruti uses the word "arose," and since water is established to be beginningless, it is logical to assume that earth, being devoid of those two, is likewise unproduced. If one were to accept that earth—which possesses the means of proof—is produced simply because one observes the production of the object to be proven, there would be a contradiction with experience. Therefore, since earth lacks production, the Śruti regarding its production lacks authority; thus, it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world based on the harmony of the Śrutis. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra: "But [earth] is like the ether. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.4) This means: Just as the ether, though beginningless, is produced by the will of the Lord, so too is earth. Or, just as the ether, though unproduced, is designated as "produced" in relation to its effects such as sound, so too is earth. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that earth is eternal in the sense of being non-produced: "From which all beings arise, by which, when born, they live, and into which they enter upon death—desire that Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). This indicates that earth is eternal insofar as it is not produced from anything else. Moreover, the Śruti speaks of its production in reference to its manifestation as a specific effect, such as solidity, just as one says "the jar is produced" even though the clay is eternal. Therefore, earth is both eternal and produced. Consequently, the non-authoritativeness of the Śruti regarding earth’s production is untenable, and it is established that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world through the harmony of the Śrutis. Thus ends the section concerning earth. Now begins the consideration of the self (ātman). Regarding this, the following doubt arises: Is the self produced from earth, or is it not? On this point, the following prima facie view is presented: "The self is not produced from

"By this, Mātariśvan is explained. This is the meaning: by this aforementioned reason of being differentiated and so forth, Mātariśvan—the primary wind—is explained; that is to say, he is stated to possess an origin.

Thus, it is logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe. This is because air possesses an origin, as evidenced by the scriptural authority of the Śruti text: "From Prāṇa came Vāyu. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning non-origination; for those texts are secondary (gauṇa) in nature, intending to convey that its essential nature (svarūpa) is not produced. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the specific declarations regarding air’s superior eternality and consciousness if it lacks primary non-originatedness. This is because the possibility of such attributes—superiority and so forth—is established by intending the eternality of knowledge distinct from its essential nature.
Therefore, since the origin of air is proven without contradicting the Śruti, it is established that the definition of being the cause of the universe is appropriate [for Viṣṇu].
Thus ends the section concerning Mātariśvan.
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the origin of the Blessed One is resolved.
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is logically untenable.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the cause of the world based on the concordance of the Vedas (*śrutisamanvaya*), because as something subject to origination, he cannot be the cause of the world. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, since the scripture states: "From the non-existent, the existent was born. Nor can the origination [of Brahman] be denied on the grounds of being contradicted by scriptural texts concerning his beginninglessness; for the scripture regarding origination is stronger, as it is supported by reasoning, namely: "Brahman has origination, because it is not distinct from that which possesses origination. Since the non-existent alone is its cause, there is an absence of origination due to the absence of a cause.
Therefore, since even Brahman possesses an origin, it is argued that its status as the cause of all things is untenable; this being the position reached, the following is stated in a Sūtra:

"But the non-origination of that which exists, because it is illogical. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]. The word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. "Of that which exists" (sataḥ) refers to Viṣṇu. "Non-origination" (asaṃbhavaḥ) means precisely no birth; it does not mean that origination from non-existence is to be asserted on the basis of the scriptural text, "From non-existence, existence was born. Why? Because it is illogical (anupapatteḥ). Therefore, the meaning is that since origination from non-existence is impossible for Viṣṇu.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world; for since the arising of existence from non-existence is never observed anywhere, origination from what is non-existent is untenable. According to the scriptural text, "Whether Brahmā be non-existent or existent, he is the vital breath," the meaning of the Śruti is that the wind originates from Brahman. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement in the Bhāgavata: "O Lord, [I take refuge] in Your divine power. Nor is there any contradiction in Hari being born in the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, because those forms are manifestations (*prādurbhāva*), and thus birth is not logically inconsistent with them.

Because of the statement that Hari is directly perceptible, and because the beginninglessness of Brahman is thus established without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that its status as the cause of the world is logical through the harmonization of the Śruti with respect to Him.
Thus ends the section on impossibility.
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the origin of fire is resolved:
"Fire [originates] from this, for so the scripture says."

An objection may be raised: it is not appropriate to declare that Viṣṇu’s status as the unique cause of the world is established by the concordance of the Śruti texts. This is because there exists scriptural evidence that fire is born from air; thus, since air is also a cause of fire—just like Viṣṇu—there is no distinction for Viṣṇu. Nor can it be said that the Śruti intends to declare that [fire] is born from the Supreme Self through the medium of air. For if Brahman were intended to create fire without the medium of air, then the mention of that medium would be useless; if, however, it is used, then the equality between the two (Viṣṇu and air) becomes unavoidable. Therefore, it is not logical that the concordance of all Śruti texts regarding the cause of the world refers to Viṣṇu. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra: "But on account of the word ‘Self’ (Ātman), [the cause is Viṣṇu]. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.18) [Commentary: The word "but" (tu) is used to remove the doubt. It is indeed Viṣṇu who is the cause of the world, as established by the concordance of the Śruti texts. Why? Because of the word "Self" (Ātman). In the passage, "From this Self, verily, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), the word "Self" is applied to Him alone, as He is the Self of all. Furthermore, the word "Self" is used in relation to the creation of fire, as in: "From this Self, fire was produced" (ibid.). Since the word "Self" is applied to Him alone, it is understood that He is the cause of the world.
