Moreover, the word "Self" is used in relation to the creation of air, as in: "From this Self, air was produced" (ibid.). Therefore, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world. As for the argument that air is also a cause of fire, that is not a fault; for air is merely an instrument (nimitta) for the manifestation of fire, whereas Viṣṇu is the material cause (upādāna). Thus, there is no equality between them. Consequently, the concordance of all Śruti texts regarding the cause of the world is properly established in Viṣṇu. ||| End of section ||| 18 ||| End of chapter ||| 3 ||| End of book ||| 2 ||| End of "Fire [is produced] from that, for thus [the scripture] says. This is its meaning: "Fire" means the element of fire. It is produced from *that*—namely, from Brahman alone—and not from air. Why? Because of the word "hi," which signifies "for"; that is, because the Śruti says, "That [Brahman] created fire. "Thus" means in the manner stated; it "says" or declares. Therefore is the sense.

Thus, it is entirely logical that the causality of the universe resides in Him alone through the harmonization of all scriptural texts (*sarva-śruti-samanvaya*). This is because, according to the scripture "He created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*), fire is born from Viṣṇu. Nor is there any contradiction with such scriptures as "From air [comes] fire" (*vāyoragniḥ*); for in those passages, it is stated that fire is born from Brahman by way of air as an intermediate medium. Furthermore, one should not argue that both air and Brahman must be causes based on the principle of "the inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) regarding the necessity of a medium; for it is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) that even though Brahman is inherently capable, He acts as the cause by resorting to a medium solely through His own will.
Therefore, since it is established that fire is born from Brahman without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that Hari is the cause of the universe through the harmonization of all the Śrutis.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
Here, the contradiction with the Vedic texts concerning the origin from water is resolved:
"The waters."

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Hari to be the cause of the world based on the concordance of the Vedas (*śrutisamanvaya*), because [water] is produced from fire according to the scriptural authority of the text, "From water, fire" (*apām agneḥ*). Nor can the scriptural statement "He emitted water" (*tad apo 'sṛjata*) be rendered invalid regarding its apparent meaning by the contradiction of the text stating it is born from fire; for the latter is stronger due to being supported by reasoning, such as: "Water is born from fire, because it possesses the nature of water (*aptva*), like sweat. This is also confirmed by the scriptural text, "That fire thought" (*tat teja aikṣata*). Therefore, since Brahman cannot be the cause of the world through the concordance of the Vedas, the following Sūtra is stated: [The opponent's position having been established, the author states the Sūtra:]

"Water (āpaḥ)"—this is its meaning. Here too, the phrases "therefore" (ataḥ) and "for thus it says" (tathā hyāha) carry over from the previous context. Thus, water has its origin from Viṣṇu alone and not from anything else. Why? Because the scripture declares, "This is indeed Brahman. Therefore is the sense.

Thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world. The scriptural statement, "From fire, water," intends to show that water arises from the Supreme Self through fire as an intermediary; this is consistent with the scripture, "Brahman alone existed in the beginning. Nor can it be argued that, due to the apparent contradiction between these two scriptural passages, Brahman and fire must both be causes in equal measure, for that would contradict the declaration: "Viṣṇu is indeed the creator of all. Therefore, since it is established that water is born of Brahman without contradicting the scriptures, it is proven that Hari’s status as the cause of the world is consistent with the harmony of the Vedas.
Thus concludes the section on the non-obstructed.

Here, in order to establish the concordance [of the Vedānta texts] regarding the cause of the world through another means, the contradiction with scripture concerning water being the door to Brahman is resolved:
"On account of earth, the subject matter, form, and other words."

Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s being the cause of the world is not tenable? For the Śrutis concerning the causes of the door [the elements] are devoid of authority due to their mutual contradictions. To explain: in the passage "They created food," the immediate succession of the creation of food to the creation of water is stated; and in "From water, earth," the immediate succession of the creation of earth to the creation of water is stated. Due to this contradiction, neither [sequence] is possible. Nor can it be argued that in that context the word "food" (anna) intends to refer to earth alone; for since the term "food" is well-known to denote actual food, it is more meritorious to follow the majority of the scriptural statements.

Therefore, since it is well known from the scriptural mark (*liṅga*) that "wherever it rains, [from that comes food]," and since the term "earth" does not include food, and because if one accepts that food is created from water alone, it would contradict the Śruti text "From water, earth [arose]"; nor can there be a simultaneous production of both earth and food from water, as that would contradict the aforementioned Śruti; nor can there be a separate creation of food from water, for that would lead to the unwarranted assumption of multiple origins even for plants from water. Thus, since the two Śruti texts are mutually contradictory, they lack authority altogether, and a systematic reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of the Śrutis is not tenable—this being the position reached, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: *tadabhidhyānādeva tu talliṅgāt saḥ* (But he [the Lord] [creates] from that very intention, on account of the mark thereof). This means: But He (the Supreme Lord) creates all this—from water, earth, and so forth—precisely through His volition (*abhidhyāna*), because the Śruti bears the mark of His agency. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. The phrase "on account of the mark thereof" refers to the Śruti passage: "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" which indicates His creative intent. Furthermore, the statement "From water, earth [arose]" is not intended to establish a direct causal origin of earth from water alone; rather, it is a figurative expression (*upacāra*) based on the fact that water is the primary material cause for the manifestation of earth. This is because the Śruti also says, "From earth, herbs [arose]," and "From herbs, food [arose]. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two Śruti texts, and the systematic reconciliation of the Śrutis is indeed appropriate.

"Because of the context, the form, and other words, such as 'the earth'. This is the meaning: "The earth" means the earth itself. That which is spoken of by the word "food" (*anna*) in the scriptural passage, "They created food," is not ordinary, well-known food. Why? Because of the context, the form, other words, and so forth. "Context" refers to the section concerning the primary elements (*bhūta*). "Form" refers to the mention of the black form (*kṛṣṇarūpa*). "Other words" means a specific term; that is, because of the specific scriptural statement, "The earth, indeed, is food.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the reasoning that a sentence which is free from defects due to its non-human origin cannot lack authority.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the universe is indeed logical, because there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages. To explain: in the passage "That [became] food," the word "food" (anna) is intended to signify the earth, because the context concerns the elements (beginning with "That created fire"), and because the blackness of food is heard in the phrase "that which was red. Nor is this merely figurative, for in another scriptural text, "Water and earth are food," the earth is explicitly stated to be denoted by the word "food. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the indicative mark (liṅga) of being born from rain.

Since earthly objects are logically accounted for as being produced by rain, there is no lack of authority due to a contradiction between two scriptural texts resulting from the impossibility of interpreting one scripture in another sense. To say that the Veda is not authoritative because it lacks the causes of unauthoritativeness—namely, defects—is contrary to the statement that it is like perception [in its authority]. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, the consistent interpretation of the scriptures is established.
Thus concludes the section concerning the earth.

In this regard, the contradiction with scripture concerning Brahman’s being the agent of the withdrawal of the previously mentioned objects—the adhibhūta and adhidaiva—is resolved [by the following sūtra]:
"But he [is the agent] because of his meditating upon that, on account of the scriptural indication thereof."

Now, it may be argued that Viṣṇu is not the destroyer of all, but rather Rudra alone, based on the Śruti text: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths. Nor can this scriptural statement be taken as referring to Viṣṇu simply because he is denoted by the word "all," for even if it refers to Rudra, it merely describes him as the instrument (the door). This contradicts worldly experience; for in the world, a father does not kill his son, and even one who kills is merely a fool, not a wise man. Consequently, if one accepts that the Lord, who is the father, is the destroyer of the universe, it would imply nothing but folly, and since that is not tenable, the contradiction with worldly experience is unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that even though Viṣṇu is the destroyer of all, the existence of the scriptural text "yat prayanti" (that toward which they go) remains valid; for that [text] lacks authority due to its contradiction with this more powerful scriptural text. Thus, when it is concluded that Viṣṇu is not the destroyer of all, the Sūtra states:

"But from His meditation alone, on account of His characteristic mark, He [is the agent]. This is its meaning: the word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. By the word "meditation" (abhidhyāna), desire is expressed. By the pronoun "He" (sa), Viṣṇu is understood. Thus, Viṣṇu alone is the agent of dissolution, not Rudra. Why? Because of "His meditation"; that is, because it is stated in the Śruti: "from His meditation."

The meaning is: from that very mark (liṅga) of Viṣṇu—characterized by the specific desire to withdraw (saṃjihīrṣā), which is made known by the word "contemplation" (abhidhyāna)—and which serves as the proof for His being the destroyer of the world beginning with [the egg], etc.; the particle "eva" (only/just), according to the method of the Bhāṣya, indicates the argumentum ad absurdum (kaimutya), implying "how much more so on the basis of the Śrutis."

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the destroyer of all is indeed logical. This is because the scripture, in the passage beginning with "From meditation upon Him," declares that the cessation of bondage is dependent on the will in the form of grace produced by such meditation. Furthermore, His agency is inferred from the fact that [the cessation of bondage] is dependent on His will. Thus, it is established that He is the agent of the dissolution of even beginningless bondage, let alone the agent of the destruction of the world, which has a beginning; for the scripture states, "He who dissolves all this."

There is no contradiction, because the scriptural passage that enjoins [the Lord] as the agent of the dissolution of Rudra and others does not enjoin Him as the instrumental cause [of that dissolution]. Nor does it follow that the Lord would be subject to delusion by being a destroyer due to His fatherhood; for while worldly fathers are possessed of possessiveness and thus lack the capacity to kill, their delusion is accepted as being caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In the case of the Lord, however, since that [possessiveness] is absent, His status as the destroyer is established even without [the charge of] delusion.
Therefore, in the absence of any contradiction with scripture, it is proven that Viṣṇu is the agent of the dissolution of all things.
Thus ends the section concerning meditation upon that.
Here, the contradiction with scriptural texts concerning the sequence of the dissolution of the elements and so forth, which was previously set forth as an objection, is resolved:
"But the reverse order is logical, and it is also supported by reasoning."

Objection: It is not logical that the Lord’s role as the destroyer occurs out of sequence by virtue of the harmony of the Śruti texts, because a Śruti text that teaches an out-of-sequence order lacks authority. For instance, there is the Śruti text beginning with "Therefore, indeed, this [world]... which teaches dissolution according to a specific sequence, and that is in accordance with direct perception. There are Śruti passages such as "It is dissolved in sequence" which support this point. Consequently, since this [sequence-based] Śruti is more powerful, the Śruti teaching an out-of-sequence order is simply non-authoritative; thus, [the opponent's position] being established, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But on account of the harmony of the Śruti. (Sūtra 2.3.14) This means: But on account of the harmony of the Śruti, the Lord’s role as the destroyer is indeed through an out-of-sequence order. Why? Because the Śruti text "He [the Lord] absorbs them all together at the end" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2) teaches a simultaneous destruction. Furthermore, the Śruti text "He absorbs all these beings together at the end" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17) also indicates a simultaneous destruction. Therefore, the Śruti text "It is dissolved in sequence" is not intended to teach a sequential order, but rather to indicate the manner of the Lord’s activity, namely, that He first withdraws the subtle elements from their effects and then those elements themselves from one another. Thus, the Śruti text "Therefore, indeed, this [world]... is not contradictory to the Śruti text "He absorbs all these beings together at the end," for both are in agreement regarding the simultaneous destruction of all things. Hence, the claim that the Śruti teaching an out-of-sequence order is non-authoritative due to contradiction with the stronger Śruti is incorrect. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the Śruti text "He absorbs all these beings together at the end" is not contradicted by the Śruti text "Therefore, indeed, this [world]..."; rather, it is consistent with it. Therefore, the conclusion is that the Lord’s role as the destroyer is indeed through an out-of-sequence order. This is the meaning. "But the sequence [of dissolution] occurs by way of reversal from this; such is the meaning. Here, the word *tu* (but) serves as an exclusion. The word *ataḥ* (from this) recurs. "From this" means from the sequence of origination (*utpatti-krama*). "By way of reversal" means by way of inversion. "Sequence" refers to the sequence of dissolution (*laya-krama*), and not the sequence of origination. For this very reason, it is "out of order," according to the scripture itself. Furthermore, this out-of-order sequence is logical (*upapadyate*) and appropriate (*yujyate*). Why?

Because those things that have originated earlier possess greater capacity than those originating later, and thus it is logical that they should persist for a longer duration of time; such is the meaning.

And thus, dissolution by way of reverse order alone is logical. This is because the scriptural mention of sequential order is not a subverting factor, as it possesses its own scope. Furthermore, even in the word "reverse order" (*vyutkrama*), there is an inclusion of "order" (*krama*); for in the Bhāllaveya-śruti, which teaches dissolution by way of sequence, dissolution is taught by way of reverse order. This is also supported by the statement, "The order is according to fitness. Nor is there any contradiction with worldly experience; rather, since each preceding [cause] possesses greater capacity than the succeeding one, this very [process] is consistent with worldly experience.
Therefore, since dissolution by reverse order is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Hari is logical.
Thus concludes the section on error.
Here, by means of the previously mentioned reverse order of dissolution, any suspicion of an exception regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the others is refuted.

If it be argued that the intermediate [elements], consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the mind (*manas*) dissolve in sequence because of their respective signs, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the scriptural statement].

But is it not the case that it is not logical for Viṣṇu to be the agent of dissolution through a transposition of all [elements]? Rather, he is the agent of dissolution through a transposition between the intellect (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*). For it is said, "of the mind, the intellect," and because we hear of the dissolution of the principle of the mind into the principle of the intellect in the passage, "he should dissolve that [mind] into the self which is the intellect. This is also consistent with common worldly experience, as dissolution is seen in the world both in regular order and by way of transposition. Nor does this contradict the gradation of capacities.

Since there is no contradiction in accepting that while the mind possesses a preponderance of capacity regarding the object of origination, consciousness possesses a preponderance of capacity regarding the object of dissolution, it follows that the scriptural text concerning the sequence [of creation] lacks authority as it contradicts the observation of logical signs supported by reasoning. Therefore, when it is argued that a systematic coordination of the scriptures is not tenable, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the order of dissolution is] the reverse of that [of creation], because it is so observed. (Vyāsasūtra 2.3.14) This means: the order of dissolution is the reverse of the order of creation, because it is so observed in the world; for instance, a clay pot is dissolved into its cause, the clay, and cloth is dissolved into its cause, the threads. Furthermore, since the scripture teaches that the order of creation is from the unmanifest (avyakta) to the intellect (buddhi), and since the scripture also teaches that the order of dissolution is from the gross elements to the unmanifest, the claim that the scriptural text on sequence is invalid is refuted. Thus, the systematic coordination of the scriptures is indeed appropriate.

“If it be argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*) [dissolve] sequentially because of their respective indicators, we say no, because there is no distinction. This is its meaning: “Consciousness and mind” refers to the principle of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) and the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). “Without interval” means not elsewhere; there is no dissolution for these two either, whether sequentially or out of sequence. Why? Because of their respective indicators. In the passage, “The mind dissolves into consciousness,” even though the mind has already arisen prior to consciousness, one observes a supporting proof in the statement, “He restrains both speech and mind,” which declares its dissolution first. If this is argued, we say no. Why? [Because...]

"Because there is no distinction" means that, regarding the manner in which the principles of consciousness (vijñāna) and mind (manas) arise and dissolve, there is an absence of any specific authoritative evidence (pramāṇa).

And thus, it is indeed logical that Viṣṇu’s role as the destroyer of all occurs in reverse order; for even in the case of the intellect (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*), their dissolution in reverse order is accepted due to the absence of any subverting evidence. Since there is no specific authoritative proof to the effect that "all this arises in a sequential order and dissolves in a sequential order," the consistency [of the Upaniṣadic texts] is established, because the dissolution of all things in reverse order is proven without contradicting the Śruti. Thus it is settled.
But the designation [of the Self] as "moving" and "non-moving" is figurative, based on its dependence on those [bodies], because it exists when they exist.

Now, an objection is raised: since the scripture states "and from mind, consciousness," the principle of consciousness arises from the principle of mind; therefore, if one accepts the dissolution of the principle of mind into the principle of consciousness, a contradiction indeed results. Having reached this point, the author presents the aphorism that refutes it.

"But that designation [of the mind] based on the moving and the non-moving would be figurative (bhākta), because it is sublated by the actual state of those [objects]. This is its meaning: "Based on the moving and the non-moving" means common to the senses, their functions, cognitions, and objects, which are designated by the terms "moving" and "non-moving. "That designation," namely the Vedic usage "the cognition of the mind" (*manasaś ca vijñānam*), is "figurative," that is, partial (*ekadeśa*). It refers only to the objects of the cognitions of the functions of the senses, which constitute a part of the referent of the term "cognition of the mind," and not to the [mind's] true nature (*tattva*). For what reason?

Because it is produced by that state, there is no occurrence of that [inference] with respect to that object denoted as "moving and non-moving," namely, the sentient and insentient; for it is produced—that is, brought into being—by that state, which is the state of the mind, namely, by the act of perception. Therefore, the meaning is that the observation of the aforementioned mark (liṅga) is not a sublater [of this inference].

Thus, there is no contradiction in what has been stated, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the scripture. For that scripture, being devoted to that [subject], does not declare the origination of the principle of consciousness from the principle of mind. What then? It declares the origination of knowledge from the sense-organ of the mind, based on the statement, "From the Supreme, the Unmanifest. And thus it is established that the concordance of the scriptures with Hari is logical, provided there is no contradiction with the scripture.
Thus concludes the section concerning the intermediate state.
Here, the resolution of the contradiction with scriptural passages concerning dissolution into the Supreme Self is undertaken.
The self is not [denied], because it is not heard [in the Upanishads] as such, and because of its eternity, on account of those [scriptural passages].

But is it not the case that the scriptural concordance regarding Viṣṇu is not tenable? For he too is perishable, according to the scripture: "He is dissolved in the inner darkness. Nor can one argue that this contradicts the scripture stating, "He is eternal among the eternal"; for the scripture concerning his perishability is stronger when supported by reasoning, namely, that "The Lord is perishable because he is a conscious being. Nor is it impossible for him to perish on the grounds that his non-origination has been established through the reason of his independence; for even in the case of one who is independent, the occurrence of unavoidable calamities is possible when he assumes a physical form for the sake of divine play (līlā).

Just as for one leaping from wall to wall, the falling [is as effortless] as the rising; yet it is not that the rising is "effortless" while the falling is also "effortless"—rather, the falling is unavoidable due to other causes. Therefore, since there is a contradiction with scripture supported by reasoning, the authority of one of the scriptural passages is lost, and thus the aforementioned reconciliation (samanvaya) is not tenable. To this, the author reads the Sūtra: [The opponent argues: Since there is a contradiction between [the Upaniṣads] supported by reasoning and [other] Śruti, the lack of authority of one of the Śrutis renders the stated reconciliation untenable. To this, he recites the Sūtra.

"Nor the Self, because of its not being heard [of as merging] and because of its eternity, on account of those [scriptural texts]. This is the meaning: the Self, that is, the Supreme Self, does not dissolve. Why? Because of its not being heard; for its dissolution is nowhere mentioned in scripture. Furthermore, because of those [texts] such as "He is eternal, devoid of qualities," and so forth—meaning, because of His eternity and because Viṣṇu is understood to be eternal—there is no destruction of Him.

Thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the universe is indeed logical, because the dissolution [of the world] lacks scriptural authority. Nor is the Śruti passage stating that "He is merged in the inner darkness" a proof for this [dissolution], because after saying "merged in the inner darkness," the text continues with "the Puruṣa, etc.," which shows that the word "merged" (nilīna) here carries the sense of being "concealed" (apahita). Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with many Śruti passages such as "The eternal among eternals. Therefore, since the dissolution of the Supreme Self has been refuted in accordance with the Śruti, it is established that the stated systematic concordance (samanvaya) is logical.
Thus ends the section on the Self.
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is resolved.
For this very reason, [the self] is a knower.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for the Blessed One to be the cause of the world, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is unproduced, according to the scriptural text: "The eternal among the eternals. Nor is there a scripture stating that even in the case of production, "all these [are produced]. This is because the scriptural text concerning beginninglessness is more powerful, being supported by such reasoning as: "The soul is not subject to production, because it is beginningless, like the Lord. Furthermore, the reason [of being produced] is not qualified by "having a beginning," since by the word "beginningless" what is intended is the fact that its existence is from time immemorial. Moreover, there is no dispute regarding the existence of the souls and other entities during the dissolution (*pralaya*).

This being the case, due to the absence of the individual soul (jīva), its attribute—namely, adṛṣṭa (unseen merit/demerit)—would also necessarily be absent; consequently, in the absence of a cause, the very production of the world would be impossible. Alternatively, if "beginninglessness" is intended to mean being devoid of a cause, there is no dispute even on that point, since no cause is perceived. Thus, it having been argued that it is not logical for [Brahman] to be the cause of the world, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from Him, because of the declaration of His being the source. (brahma-tu-arthāntaratvādivyapadeśāt) *Note: The provided text contains the argument leading up to the Sūtra, but does not include the full Sūtra itself or its commentary. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument presented.*

"Jño'ta eva" (The knower [is born] from Him alone). This is its meaning: the "knower" (jña) is the individual soul (jīva), who also indeed arises from Viṣṇu. Why? "From Him alone"—that is, precisely because of the scriptural statement that they arise without having perished.

And thus, the systematic concordance (samanvaya) is indeed appropriate; for it is by the scriptural statement "these [breaths] were born from them" that the birth of the very souls, who are beginningless and eternal, is enjoined. Nor is there an absence of a cause, since the Supreme Lord alone is the cause. Therefore, since the fact that the soul is born from Brahman is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the systematic concordance regarding Him is logical.
And because of logical reasoning.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even though the birth of the soul—which is eternal and beginningless—is heard in scripture, to accept its birth would be as contradictory as a statement that a woman is a mother after first admitting she is barren; for it is a contradiction to accept its eternity and yet speak of its birth again. Anticipating this doubt, the author presents the Sūtra.

"And because of reasoning" (yukteśca). The meaning of this is as follows: since even for the soul (*jīva*), which is beginningless and eternal, its "origination"—in the form of being dependent on a body—is logical, the meaning is that the soul indeed possesses origination.

And thus, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is eternal, its "origination" is logically established in view of the arising of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Even so, since what is intended here is not origination in the sense of acquiring its own essential nature—which it never lacks—but rather origination in the sense of attaining specific qualities dependent on another, the absence of such [essential] origination is accepted. Therefore, since the fact that the individual soul is born from Brahman is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the texts with respect to Brahman is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning knowledge.
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding atomicity is resolved in respect to the dimension that is an attribute of the individual soul (jīva).
[The Sūtra teaches] the departing, the going, and the returning.

Therefore, by process of elimination, the all-pervasiveness of the Self must indeed be accepted. Consequently, since the scriptural text regarding atomicity lacks authority—and given that there is no certainty that scripture as a whole possesses authority—the reconciliation of the scriptures (śrutisamanvaya) is not tenable; such being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

Nor is there a proof of its being something else (anyatā) by virtue of having a middle-sized dimension (madhyama-parimāṇa), because that has been refuted due to the consequence of its being non-eternal (anityatva).
Therefore, since the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the reconciliation of the scriptures is logical.

"If it be argued that there is a difference in the mode of abiding, we say no, because it is admitted [by scripture] that [the soul] abides in the heart. Or [the Lord is designated as such] because of His qualities, like light.

"Or [it is] due to its quality, like light. This is the meaning: the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative mode. Since this is possible, there is no contradiction known as the impossibility of full cognition. Here, the contradiction between scriptural passages concerning the soul's being of a single nature and its being of multiple natures is resolved.

Now, it may be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not delimited by multiple bodies at once, but rather by only one at a time, according to the scriptural statement, "It is one. Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of both [the body and the senses], the yogins possess a non-corporeal nature due to being endowed with the power to accomplish the impossible, and that their drinking of the ocean and such feats have been observed. Therefore, since this contradicts scripture supported by reasoning, the multiplicity of forms mentioned in other scriptural passages lacks authority; thus, the harmonization of the scriptures (śrutisamanvaya) is not tenable. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra states: "But [it is] on account of the word [of scripture]. (sū. 3.2.14) [Note: The provided text contains the objection leading into the Sūtra. For if that were so, it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that the soul becomes equal to the Lord in attributes. Furthermore, the drinking of the ocean and similar acts performed by them are merely illusory appearances (māyāmayam), like the drinking of the ocean by the sage Agastya. Thus, since the soul is indeed non-corporeal, the harmonization of the scriptures is indeed tenable. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the statement regarding the soul's non-corporeality is based on its essential nature (svarūpataḥ); however, when it assumes a body through its own power, it is designated as "corporeal" in a figurative sense (upacārataḥ). Just as light, though possessing the power to illuminate, is not considered corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to illuminate objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is all-pervading (vibhutvāt). Just as space (ākāśa), though possessing the power to manifest sound, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to manifest knowledge, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is eternal (nityatvāt). Just as time (kāla), though possessing the power to cause the manifestation of things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to bring about the manifestation of objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is partless (niravayavatvāt). Just as the atom (paramāṇu), though possessing the power to produce effects, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to produce knowledge, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of form (amūrtatvāt). Just as the wind (vāyu), though possessing the power to move objects, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to move objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of color (arūpitvāt). Just as the ether (ākāśa), though possessing the power to provide space for things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to provide space for objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of touch (asparśatvāt). Just as the mind (manas), though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of taste (arasatvāt). Just as water, though possessing the power to nourish things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to nourish objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of smell (agandhatvāt). Just as earth, though possessing the power to support things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to support objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of sound (aśabdatvāt). Just as the ear, though possessing the power to hear sounds, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to hear sounds, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of number (asaṃkhyatvāt). Just as the quality of number, though possessing the power to qualify things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to qualify objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of dimension (aparimāṇatvāt). Just as the quality of dimension, though possessing the power to qualify things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to qualify objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of conjunction (asaṃyogatvāt). Just as the quality of conjunction, though possessing the power to connect things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to connect objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of disjunction (avibhāgatvāt). Just as the quality of disjunction, though possessing the power to separate things, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to separate objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of priority and posteriority (aparatvāparatvābhāvāt). Just as the qualities of priority and posteriority, though possessing the power to qualify things, are not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to qualify objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of weight (agurutvāt). Just as the quality of weight, though possessing the power to cause things to fall, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to cause objects to fall, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of fluidity (adravatvāt). Just as the quality of fluidity, though possessing the power to cause things to flow, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to cause objects to flow, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of viscidity (asnehatvāt). Just as the quality of viscidity, though possessing the power to cause cohesion, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to cause cohesion among objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of sound (aśabdatvāt). Just as the quality of sound, though possessing the power to be perceived, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of touch (asparśatvāt). Just as the quality of touch, though possessing the power to be perceived, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of color (arūpitvāt). Just as the quality of color, though possessing the power to be perceived, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of taste (arasatvāt). Just as the quality of taste, though possessing the power to be perceived, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of smell (agandhatvāt). Just as the quality of smell, though possessing the power to be perceived, is not corporeal, so too the soul, though possessing the power to perceive objects, is not corporeal. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the soul is non-corporeal because it is devoid of number (asa

"Separation [is possible] like that of fragrance; and thus the scripture shows. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is a conjunction of the Smṛti statement "in an inconceivable manner. "Like fragrance" means just as in the case of fragrance—for example, the separation of the fragrance of a flower from its own parts—so too is separation by means of its own parts possible for the atomic individual soul (jīva) through the power of the Lord. Why does it establish this? Because the Śruti, with the words "from whence," shows it to be so; that is the meaning of "for this very reason."

Thus, there is no rule that the individual soul (jīva) possesses only a single form; rather, through the grace of the Lord attained by yoga and other means, some souls may simultaneously possess a single form. Nor is it impossible for a part to go elsewhere leaving the whole behind; for indeed, it is observed that even a quality such as fragrance moves elsewhere, leaving its substratum. This being so, what inconsistency is there? Furthermore, regarding the movement of a substance’s part to another place while leaving the whole behind, there is no contradiction with the Śruti text stating "at once" (ekadā), because that text refers to the oneness of essential nature (svarūpa-ekya).

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement that "He is indeed one," and because the multiplicity of forms of the individual soul (jīva) is thus logically established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the harmonious reconciliation (samanvaya) is valid.
Thus concludes the section on negative concomitance (vyatirekādhikaraṇa).
Here, the contradiction with the scriptures concerning the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from the Supreme Self (paramātman) is resolved:
"Because of the teaching of their distinction."

Indeed, the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), based on such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Although this scripture directly teaches the identity of Śvetaketu alone, it nevertheless serves as a means of valid knowledge for the non-difference of all individual souls, because its purport lies in the non-difference of all souls. Furthermore, that individual soul is not a partial manifestation (*aṃśa*) of the Lord like Rāma and others, since this is understood by considering the preceding statement, "Not so, O Soma."

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in their status as living beings (*jīva*), it is impossible for some to be non-different from Brahman while others are not. Therefore, intending to express the non-difference of all living beings from Brahman, that [text] declares its non-difference from Him. Nor is there any scripture such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) that supports the contrary view; for the non-dualistic (*advaita*) scriptures are more powerful, being endowed with the sixfold marks of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*) along with supporting arguments. Thus, since the non-dualistic scripture intends non-duality alone, the scriptural texts regarding difference—which contradict it—are merely informative of what is not reality (*atattvāvedaka*). Consequently, the conclusion that the Lord's [teaching] is not in harmony with the scriptures (*śrutisamanvaya*) having been reached, the following was stated in the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: *na ca smārtam adhyātmopadeśād viśeṣācca* (And it is not the Smṛti [view], because of the teaching concerning the Self and because of the specific distinction). [Commentary: It is not the case that the dualism taught in the Smṛti is the intended meaning here. Why? Because of the teaching concerning the Self (*adhyātmopadeśa*) and because of the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). The teaching concerning the Self is seen in passages such as, "Having known Him, one transcends death; there is no other path" (*tameva viditvāti mṛtyumeti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate'yanāya*). Furthermore, the specific distinction is observed in the passage, "The two unborn ones, the Lord and the individual soul, are seated in the heart" (*dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samāne vṛkṣe...*), where the Supreme Lord is distinguished from the individual soul. Therefore, the dualistic Smṛti is not authoritative regarding the ultimate truth. As for the objection that the non-dualistic scripture is contradicted by the dualistic scripture, that is not so; for the non-dualistic scripture is stronger due to its possession of the aforementioned marks of intention. Thus, the harmony of the scriptures with the Lord's teaching is established.

"Because of the separate instruction. This is its meaning: the individual soul (jīva) is distinct and different from the Supreme Self (paramātman). Why? Because of the instruction; that is to say, because of the scriptural statement: "He is different and inconceivable."

Thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed distinct from the Lord, according to the scriptural statement: "He is distinct and inconceivable. Nor should it be argued that there is no scripture supporting non-difference; for the scripture concerning difference is more powerful, as it is supported by reason, given that two substrates possessing contradictory attributes cannot be identical. Therefore, since the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the reconciliation of the scriptures with Brahman is logical.
But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that [name], just as in the case of the conscious one (the individual soul).

Now, one might raise the objection that if this were so, then non-dualistic scriptures such as "Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*) would lack a subject matter and consequently result in invalidity; in order to dispel this doubt, he presents the following sūtra:

"But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that [name], just like the Intelligent One. This is the meaning: "Just like the Intelligent One" means just as in the case of the Intelligent One, which is Brahman—as in the statement "All this is indeed Brahman," there is a declaration of non-difference between the world and Brahman—so too in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*). "Designated by that" means that the declaration of identity with Brahman, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), is appropriate. Why? "Because its essence consists of those qualities"; that is to say, because the individual soul has as its essential nature qualities such as consciousness and bliss that resemble the qualities of Brahman. This is the reason.

Thus, the authority of the scriptural texts on non-difference is also established; for even so, because the individual soul (jīva) possesses qualities such as bliss that are similar to the qualities of the Supreme Self (paramātman), words like "Brahman" occurring in such scriptures as "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi) apply to the individual soul through a secondary sense (gauṇī vṛtti). This is because non-difference based on similarity is the intended meaning of the scripture. Furthermore, just as one accepts a secondary application of a word denoting Brahman—such as in "That thou art" (tattvamasi)—to the individual soul, even if one accepts a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) for the word "art" (asi) when referring to the soul, there is still the cognition of non-difference based on similarity.

Even in the absence of actual non-difference, the designation of non-difference is seen in passages such as "All this, indeed," because [the world] has that [Brahman] as its essential quality (*tadguṇasāratvena*). This is because the identity of the two qualified entities (*viśiṣṭa*) denoted by the words *tat* and *tvam* is sublated; and because, since two things devoid of attributes cannot stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), it is impossible for them to convey non-difference. For non-difference [is understood] through that [relation], as in the case of "The lotus is blue. Furthermore, since two things devoid of attributes cannot stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, it is impossible for them to convey non-difference.

Because non-difference, as in the case of "the blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and so forth, must be understood precisely through the medium of that [identity]. Just as in common worldly sentences such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the sentence-meaning is mediated solely by the secondary (gauna) sense of words like "Gaṅgā" and not by their primary (mukhya) sense; it is not so in the Veda. For the Veda, having first established the meaning of its own words through modes such as *mahāyoga*, subsequently establishes another meaning through secondary modes (*gauṇī*) and so forth—so he says. This is because, according to the opponent's own system, since the attainment [of the goal] already exists, there can be no possibility of negating what has not been attained (*aprāpti*).
Therefore, since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that the harmony [of the texts] is logical.
Thus ends the section on separate [entities].
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the eternity of the individual soul (jīva) is resolved:
"And because it exists as long as the self exists, there is no fault; for that is seen [in scripture]."

Indeed, the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-eternal, because of the scriptural statement regarding its non-eternality: "O Brahman, it goes to dissolution. Nor can it be argued that there exists no scriptural statement for its eternality such as "it is beginningless," because the scriptural statement of non-eternality is stronger due to its being supported by reasoning. For the origin of the soul has indeed been stated [in the Sūtra]: "Therefore, it is a knower" (*jño 'ta eva*). Consequently, the soul is perishable, because of the existence of the following inference: "It is perishable, because while being an entity, it possesses an origin. Nor can it be said that in that context the origin of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) alone was stated, and not that of the soul.

Since the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is subject to origination, its destruction inevitably entails the destruction of the reflection; therefore, because it contradicts scripture supported by reasoning, and since the claim of its beginningless connection with karma lacks validity, the scriptural harmony regarding that [reflection] is untenable—this being the prima facie position, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"And because it exists as long as the self does, there is no fault on account of seeing that [fault]. This is the meaning: "Because it exists as long as the self" means as long as the Supreme Self exists; that is to say, because of its eternity. "There is no fault" means there is no fault regarding the lack of authority in the Śruti which teaches the connection between merit and demerit for that [jīva] which is beginningless. Why is this so? "On account of seeing that," meaning because its eternity has been stated in the text "The jīva is eternal," and also because of the two Smṛti passages stating "The Self is eternal" and "The jīva is eternal."

And thus, the *jīva* is indeed eternal. For in the Śruti, by stating "The Supreme is eternal," the eternity of the *jīva* is declared just like that of the Self (*ātman*). Likewise, in the Smṛti, having stated the eternity of the *jīva* in the phrase "The Self is eternal," the non-eternity of its body and so forth is specified. Nor is it difficult to avoid the conclusion that the reflection—the *jīva*—is destroyed upon the destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because the *jīva* is not actually a reflection. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the Śruti passage "form after form" establishes the *jīva* as a reflection.

Since that [reflection] is dependent upon it, it refers to a secondary reflection characterized by similarity to it, and thus does not indicate a primary reflection. Furthermore, it is not possible for there to be a reflection of this [one] alone and not of another within a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), as that would lead to the same contingency in the case of a mirror and so forth. Moreover, because of the rule that a reflection must reside in one part of the limiting adjunct, it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*) resides in only one part of the body of Consciousness.

Furthermore, if the soul exists as a reflection within the external body, then upon the destruction of that external body, the destruction of the soul would be unavoidable. Moreover, in such passages as "In its absence, however, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the soul is said to be twofold," the statement that it is an adjunct would become entirely untenable. If the statement regarding its being an adjunct is figurative, then let the statement regarding the body of consciousness (ciccharīra) also be figurative; for it is illogical to apply the principle of "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya). Or, let the soul indeed be a reflection.

Nevertheless, because the reflection, the limiting adjunct (upādhi), and their proximity are eternal, there is no destruction of the individual soul (jīva), as there is an absence of any cause for such destruction. Scriptural statements regarding the non-eternality of the adjunct refer only to external adjuncts. Therefore, since the eternality of the soul is established in accordance with scripture, it is proven that the systematic concordance (samanvaya) is logical.
Thus ends the section on legal cases.
Here, the contradiction between the scriptural statements regarding the soul's nature as bliss and so forth, and the statements regarding its absence thereof, is resolved:
"But [the manifestation of the soul's qualities] occurs like manhood and so forth, because there is a connection with their manifestation while [the soul] exists."

Objection: Is it not the case that the individual soul (jīva) does not have knowledge, bliss, and so forth as its nature? For the Śruti states, "It is free from pleasure and pain. Nor can it be argued that even if it has the nature of bliss and so forth, there is no Śruti stating "Bliss alone is its essence," and thus a determination that it lacks the nature of bliss and so forth is impossible. Response: The individual soul does not have bliss and so forth as its nature. This is because, while being capable of being perceived as such, it is not perceived as such—this is established by the existence of the mind (mānasadbhāvena). Thus, the scriptural statement that it is not bliss is supported by reasoning.

Nor can it be argued that non-perception is due to the force of an obstruction, and that effort is possible for the sake of removing it; for since the individual soul (jīva) is eternally manifested as "I," it is logically impossible for there to be any obscuration of its own essential nature. Furthermore, if it is claimed that "obscuration" means ignorance, and that non-experience occurs by the power of that [ignorance], this is untenable as a rebuttal when it is objected that if the soul's nature consists of bliss and so forth, then ignorance of bliss and so forth is itself illogical—how then could one say that ignorance is established by the power of ignorance? If it is argued that the obscuration is the body and so forth, [the response follows...]

Since it is also possible to state the opposite, and thus, due to contradiction with reasoned scripture (*yuktika-śruti*), other scripture is indeed not authoritative, the conclusion reached is that the concordance of scripture (*śruti-samanvaya*) with respect to God (*īśvara*) is not tenable; to this, the author states the Sūtra: [The opponent argues: Since the opposite can also be asserted, and because of the contradiction with reasoned scripture, other scripture is indeed non-authoritative; therefore, the concordance of scripture with regard to the Lord is not tenable—this being the position reached, the Sūtra says:

"Because there is a possibility of manifestation for that which exists, just like virility and so forth. This is the meaning: the word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "eva" (indeed). Just as in the case of virility and so forth—meaning, although the capacity to produce offspring exists in men, women, and others by their very nature, its manifestation occurs at a specific time; likewise, because there is a possibility of manifestation for this [bliss, knowledge, etc. which exists even prior to liberation by virtue of being the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), and because of the connection with liberation as the cause of that manifestation, the scriptural statement "he becomes blissful" is justified.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction with scripture regarding the soul's nature as bliss and so forth; thus, the soul is indeed of the nature of bliss and the like.

And thus, the individual soul (jīva) indeed exists in the form of bliss and so forth, because it is so heard in scripture. Nor does this contradict the scriptural statement, "He becomes blissful" (ānandī bhavati). Just as, although men, women, and others possess the inherent power to produce offspring, the expressions "this person was not a man before, but is a man now," and so on, are appropriate due to the manifestation of that power at a particular time; likewise, since the knowledge, bliss, and other qualities exist in the very nature of the soul even prior to liberation, the designations such as "he becomes blissful" are justified by the manifestation of these qualities through the grace of the Lord (Īśvara).

Nor is there an impossibility of effort, for such effort is indeed possible for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) precisely for the sake of manifesting that [bliss]. Nor is there an impossibility of concealment, because it is admitted that concealment is indeed ignorance (avidyā), which is distinct from the mere absence of knowledge. Thus, since the nature of the individual soul (jīva) as consisting of bliss and so forth is established without contradicting scripture, the conclusion of the concordance (samanvaya) is proven.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other.

Now, an objection may be raised: it is improper to say that bliss and other qualities, which constitute the very nature of the individual soul (jīva) yet were previously unmanifest, become manifest at liberation; for the nature of the soul is eternally manifest. To this, the author states the Sūtra:

"Otherwise, there would be the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other. This is the meaning: the word "or" (*vā*) signifies a fixed alternative. "Perception" (*upalabdhi*) means experience. Otherwise—that is, if one accepts that the individual soul (*jīva*) has the nature of bliss and so forth, but does not accept its concealment—there follows the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception. The connection [of the terms] is according to their respective fitness: for those fit for liberation, there would be the constant experience of bliss and so forth; for those fit for darkness (*tamas*), there would never be the experience of bliss.

However, there would be only the experience of suffering inherent in its own nature. Thus, for intermediate beings, there would be a fixed rule regarding one or the other—namely, a state of equality in the experience of either pleasure or pain. This refers to the meaning of the sun being within the obscuring veil that acts as a hindrance. Therefore, the implication is that an obscuration must be admitted for the individual soul (jīva).

And thus, if one accepts that the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of bliss and so forth, yet fails to accept the cessation of its obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), and claims that the absence of obscuration is the root [of experience], then it would follow that gods, demons, and humans would eternally perceive their own true nature; for in the absence of obscuration, the lack of experience is impossible. Conversely, if one fails to accept the cessation of obscuration, it would follow that gods, demons, and humans would never perceive their own true nature, because the obstructing factor would be present at all times. Furthermore, such a view contradicts the scripture stating "eternal bliss" (*nityānanda*).
Therefore, since it is established that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the nature of bliss and so forth without contradicting the Śruti, the concordance [of all Vedānta texts] is proven.
Thus concludes the section on the qualification of males.
Here, the contradiction with the Śruti regarding the soul's status as the agent is resolved:
"He is the agent, because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the agent? For scripture states, "There is no other agent. Nor is the scriptural passage, "Whatever action one performs," a proof for the soul's agency; this is because the scriptural teaching of its non-agency is stronger due to its being supported by reasoning. Indeed, the agency belonging exclusively to the Lord has already been established in such passages as "Because of the designation of another [as the agent]" (BS 2.3.40). Consequently, since the soul possesses no agency at all, the systematic interpretation (*samanvaya*) of passages such as "He alone causes him to perform good actions" is untenable. To this, the author reads the following sūtra:

"Because the scripture would otherwise be purposeless. This is its meaning: the individual soul (jīva) is also an agent. Why? Because only if that were so would the scripture have a purpose; that is, the scripture consisting of injunctions and prohibitions would possess utility. Otherwise, it would follow that it is useless.

Thus, the reconciliation of the scriptural texts as stated is indeed logical. For since the individual soul (jīva) is also an agent, it is possible for it to be the impeller [of the Lord]. Otherwise, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered purposeless; for the scriptures, which would otherwise be like lamentations in a wilderness, could not have any meaningful purpose in the absence of an agent. Therefore, since the agency of the individual soul is established without contradicting the Śruti, the reconciliation of the scriptural texts is proven.
Because of the teaching on the dwelling.

Now, even so, one might still object: "The agency of the individual soul (jīva) cannot be accepted as real. Even though the soul lacks inherent agency, there is indeed a grasping at that agency as one's own with respect to the agency residing in another [the Lord]. Therefore, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions may apply to the soul which possesses only imagined agency. Anticipating this doubt, the author presents the following sūtra to dispel it:

"Because of the teaching concerning his abiding (vihāra). The meaning of this is as follows: since it is stated that even in liberation he "eats, plays, and so forth," which describes him as the agent of abiding, the soul is indeed an agent in the ultimate sense, not merely a figurative agent.

And thus, because it is taught that even in liberation one performs acts of wandering by means of women or vehicles and so forth, and because it is impossible for that which exists in liberation to possess a merely empirical (vyāvahārika) nature, it is established that the harmony [of the scriptures] is logical, since the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is proven without contradicting the Śruti. This is settled.
Because of appropriation.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Let it be then that the soul's agency in liberation is ultimate (pāramārthika), since that is supported by authoritative means of knowledge; however, in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), it is merely conventional (vyāvahārika). By this much, the purposefulness of the scriptures would be established. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism [to refute it]:

"Because of appropriation" (upādānāt). The meaning of this is: because we observe the performance of means for the sake of the soul's liberation, and because we observe the resulting fruit from that [performance], it follows that even in saṃsāra, the soul is not a merely imaginary agent. This is the sense.

And thus, since one is observed to undertake means for the sake of liberation, it cannot be said that even those [means] are merely superimposed upon the individual soul (jīva) as belonging to another [the Lord], for that would result in the absence of any fruit. Therefore, since the agency of the individual soul is established in accordance with scripture, the concordance [of all texts with the doctrine of Brahman] is proven.
And because of the designation [of the agent] even in the absence of action; if it is argued that this is not so, then there would be a reversal of the grammatical instruction.

Thus, having established the agency of the individual soul (jīva) through the reasoning that the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless within the context of saṃsāra, and through the perception of undertaking means such as spiritual practice, the Sūtra speaks in order to support that [agency] by means of scripture as well.

"And because of the designation [of the agent] in the case of action; if not, there would be a reversal of the instruction. This is its meaning: "In the case of action"—that is, in the act of meditation mentioned in the passage, "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world"—"because of the designation," that is, because the individual soul (jīva) is designated as the agent. Therefore, the soul is the agent. "If not"—meaning if it were not the agent—"there would be a reversal of the instruction. This means that there would be a contradiction in the instruction, which speaks of the soul as the agent and the Lord as the object, resulting in a reversal of the form of the statement, such as "one should meditate on the Self [as the object]."

Furthermore, because the individual soul (jīva) is designated as the agent in the scriptural passage, "In this way, one should worship the Self alone as the world," if the soul were not intended by the scripture as the agent in the act of worship, then—since an action cannot be without an agent and an insentient being cannot be an agent—the scripture would be rendered purposeless. To avoid this consequence, if the Supreme Self alone were intended as the agent of the action, the designation would have been "the Self alone is the world. Since, however, the individual soul is designated as the agent, it follows that the individual soul is indeed the agent.

And thus, because he is the agent, there is no such contrary instruction; therefore, since the conclusion of the reversal—that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a non-agent but indeed an agent—is established through the proof of the soul's agency, it is proven that systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) with the scriptures is logical.
There is no fixed rule, just as in the case of perception.

[Objection: "But if the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the agent, how is it that in such passages as 'Because of the designation of another' (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.22), it is established that the Lord alone is the agent? And how can the scriptural statement that 'there is no other agent' be justified? Therefore, there is certainly a contradiction. Anticipating this doubt, the author reads the following sūtra:

"Like perception, there is no fixed rule. This is its meaning: "Like perception" means just as in the case of perception—that is, in the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva)—there is no fixed rule, such that knowledge is not obtained according to one's own will; so too, it is logical that there is no fixed rule regarding action.

And thus, even when there is the desire "may I know this," the individual soul (jīva) does not obtain knowledge according to his own will; likewise, even in the resolve "I shall do this," the accomplishment of the task does not occur according to his own will. However, for the Lord (īśvara), the accomplishment of the task occurs according to His own will. Therefore, with the intention of expressing His sovereignty, it is said that the Lord alone is the agent and not the individual soul. Consequently, since the individual soul lacks such necessity regarding action while the Lord possesses it, [the Lord alone is the agent].

Since it was previously stated that agency belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) not in the same sense as it belongs to God (*īśvara*), which is intended here to mean agency independent of anything else, but rather with the intention that there is no total absence of agency, there is no contradiction with what was said before. Therefore, since the agency of the individual soul is established without contradicting scripture, the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) is justified; this is proven.
Because of the reversal of capacity.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no distinction [between them] insofar as both the Lord and the individual soul (jīva) possess agency that depends upon means (sādhana), from what source does this [distinction] arise—that independence belongs to the Lord alone and not to the individual soul? Anticipating this inquiry, he sets forth the aphorism (sūtra) as a response.

"Due to the reversal of power" (śaktiviparyayāt). The meaning of this is as follows: because of the reversal of power between the Lord (Īśa) and the individual soul (jīva)—that is, with reference to the distinction between their powers as being complete or incomplete—their agency (kartṛtva) is also distinguished by the difference between independence and dependence. Alternatively, it means that because the individual soul lacks complete power like that of the Lord, he does not possess independent agency.

Thus, because Īśvara possesses independence regarding the means of accomplishment by virtue of being the controller of all such means, and because the attainment of the effect depends upon that independence; whereas for the *jīva*, due to the absence of independence regarding the means, there is an absence of independence regarding the fruit—therefore, it is established that the concordance (*samanvaya*) is logical on account of the *jīva*’s limited power and lack of independence.
And because of the absence of meditative concentration.
He introduces the aphorism which establishes the independence of the Lord and the dependence of the individual soul by means of another argument.

"And because of the absence of *samādhi*. The meaning of this is as follows: *Samādhi* is the sense of sufficiency (the feeling of having enough). Due to its absence, the individual soul (*jīva*) does not possess independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*), but rather possesses only dependent agency (*paratantra-kartṛtva*). This is the meaning.

Thus, because the Lord possesses the fulfillment of all desires, He has independence regarding the fruit [of action], whereas the individual soul (jīva), lacking that, lacks such independence. Consequently, since independence and dependence are perceived in the case of the individual soul and the Lord, one must understand the necessity and lack of necessity regarding action based on those two causes. Therefore, it is established that systematic harmony with the scriptures is logical, provided there is no contradiction with the sacred texts.
And just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways.

Now, if the individual soul (jīva) does not possess agency independently, then how is it described as "the agent" in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts? For, since the term "agent" is never applied to one who acts without independence, that term is understood to indicate only independent agency. Having raised this objection, the Sūtra provides the following refutation:

"And just as the carpenter [is said to act] in both ways"—this is the meaning of that [sūtra]. The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the illustrative example with the subject at hand. Just as a carpenter or woodworker is designated as the agent in both ways—namely, by virtue of being impelled by one who commissions the construction of a palace or similar structure, and by virtue of being the actual doer thereof—so too it can be said that the individual soul (jīva), though directed by God, is the agent. This is the sense.

Thus, even though the agent is not independent, we observe the usage "this carpenter is the builder of the palace"; since there is no rule that the word *kartṛ* (agent) must denote only an independent agent, and because the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed subject to the Lord's control while still possessing agency with respect to jars and other objects, it is established that the soul’s agency is proven, and therefore the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the Upanishadic texts] is logical. This is settled.
But [the soul is] from the Highest, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.

Now, is the power of agency belonging to the individual soul (jīva) dependent solely on the soul itself—just as the agency of a carpenter is? Or is it dependent on the Lord (īśvara), as in the case of receiving wages and so forth; that is, is the power of agency also dependent on the Lord? In the first case, the position that agency belongs to the Lord alone has already been refuted. In the second case, it would follow that the soul possesses no power of agency at all. To this, the author states the aphorism (sūtra) as a resolution:

"But from Him [proceeds] that, because of scriptural statement. This is its meaning: the power of agency belonging to the individual soul (jīva) exists only by following after the Supreme Self (paramātman) and is dependent upon Him alone. Why? "Because of scriptural statement" (tacchruteḥ); that is to say, because scripture declares that both agency and causality depend upon the Lord (Īśa). Thus is the sense.

And thus, since agency and instrumentality belong to the individual soul (jīva) by virtue of the authority of scripture, it is accepted that the soul’s power of agency is dependent upon the Lord; for, given the existence of the Lord’s capacity to act, not to act, or to act otherwise, it is observed that the attainment of agency and so forth by the souls and others occurs solely through His will. Therefore, it is established that systematic reconciliation (samanvaya) with scripture is indeed appropriate.
But [the Lord] depends on the effort performed [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons.

"Now, it may be argued that even in this view a fault has been stated: if the power of agency belongs to the Lord, then agency itself belongs to Him alone and not to the individual soul (jīva). In that case, as with a wooden statue moved by another, the scripture would again fall into the error of being purposeless. Having raised this objection, the author states the aphorism (sūtra) which refutes it.

"But [the Lord] has regard for the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth. This is the meaning: the word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. Since the Supreme Self has regard for the effort made [by the soul]—on account of the fact that otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be meaningless, and for the sake of avoiding [the charge of] partiality and cruelty toward Himself—the Lord impels the soul only while having regard for the fitness of the soul's own karma and effort; He does not do so without such regard.
Therefore, the meaning is that even though the power of the soul is dependent upon the Lord, it nonetheless possesses the quality of being characterized by the effort required [for action].

Thus, in order to avoid the futility of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, and to avoid [the Lord's] own partiality and cruelty, it is accepted that the Lord impels the individual soul (jīva) only in consideration of the soul’s past karma, effort, and capacity; for it is stated: "and [in consideration of] previous karma and effort.

Even though the soul is impelled by the Lord regarding its knowledge of the injunctive texts and their meanings, its desire for the means and fruits produced thereby, and its volitional effort toward those means, there is no inconsistency in its being the object of injunctions or its being the recipient of karmic fruits; therefore, there is no futility in the operation of the scriptures.

For even in the case of a member of the three higher castes or others who possess desires produced by royal officers and the like, as well as in the case of one conscripted for forced labor, we observe injunctions regarding the performance of twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the carrying of burdens; thus, these two cases are explained simply by the fact of being an agent who lacks independence, just like that [dependent agent]. Therefore, since the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established without contradicting the scriptures, it is proven that the reconciliation of the scriptures (*śrutisamanvaya*) is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning agency.
Here, the contradiction regarding the individual soul (jīva) found in the Śruti is resolved:

"He is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of multiplicity, and also because otherwise; moreover, some record that He possesses the nature of the fisherman, the kitava-player, and so forth."

Is it not the case that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a part (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Lord? For there is a lack of evidence for that. Nor can the authority of the scripture stating "these individual souls are indeed parts" be accepted; because that scripture lacks the capacity to determine its own meaning—being sublated by the scriptural statement "it is certainly not a part"—it is invalid. Furthermore, since the difference between the individual soul and the Lord has been established, it is impossible for that which is distinct to be a part. Moreover, the earlier scripture whose meaning is impossible is set aside by the stronger, subverting scripture whose meaning is possible, namely, "it is certainly not a part."

Thus, because the scripture regarding [Brahman] being a part lacks authority, its reconciliation [with other scriptures] is not tenable. Alternatively, according to the method stated in the *Ṭīkā*, the two scriptural passages are simply non-conclusive due to their mutual contradiction. Nor is an option (*vikalpa*) like that between the *vrīhi* and *yava* injunctions appropriate, because an option regarding a real entity (*vastu*) is impossible. Nor is an option established by difference of place or time appropriate, because there is no specific evidence for such a distinction. Therefore, since both scriptural passages lack authority, the aforementioned arguments are not tenable. This being the position reached, the Sūtra says:

"Aṃśa (a part) [is the soul], because of various designations, and also because otherwise it is taught that the one [Lord] is the fisherman, the kitava, and so forth. This is its meaning: The individual soul (jīva) is indeed a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman). It is a part by virtue of being entirely dependent upon Him through relationships such as father and son, and so on; however, it is never the object of dependence like the Lord Himself. Why? Because of "various designations" (nānāvyapadeśāt); for in passages such as "May He protect me," the soul's relationship with the Lord is stated in various ways, such as fatherhood, brotherhood, and so forth.
