Furthermore, because certain followers of particular recensions (eke śākhinaḥ) [teach this].

By such passages as "The other is the Supreme, the other is the individual soul (jīva)," they study—that is, they recite—this *jīva* as distinct from the Supreme. Furthermore, other followers of different Vedic branches (*śākhins*) study that the Supreme Brahman possesses the state of being the *dāśas*, *kitavas*, and so forth; this means that Brahman exists in the form of the *jīvas* associated with specific castes denoted by the terms *dāśa* and *kitava*, which amounts to saying there is non-difference [between them]. Moreover, they study that the *dāśas*, *kitavas*, and others are not Brahman. Therefore, the meaning is that [the *jīva*] possesses the nature of being a part (*aṃśatva*).

Thus, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed a part (aṃśa) of the Blessed Lord, because the soul's relationship with the Lord is designated in various ways, such as "May He protect me," and so forth; for that very relationship consists in being His part. Therefore, since it is established that the soul is a part of the Lord without contradicting the Śruti, the systematic harmony (samanvaya) is proven.
From the wording of the mantra.
Having thus established through reasoning that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Lord (īśvara), the Sūtra proceeds to prove that same point by means of scripture as well.
"From the words of the mantra": the meaning of this is that, according to the Śruti text "A foot of Him," the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Supreme Self (paramātman).

And thus, because of the Vedic mantra stating, "His foot is all beings," it is declared that all individual souls (jīvas) are portions (aṃśas) of this Supreme Self (paramātman). Consequently, since it is established that the individual soul is a portion of the Lord, the concordance of the Śruti with Hari is proven.
It is also recorded in the Smṛti.
He introduces the aphorism which establishes, even by means of Smṛti, that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Supreme Self (paramātman).

"Also, it is recorded in Smṛti. The meaning of this is: the fact that the individual soul (jīva) is a part [of the Lord] is stated by Kṛṣṇa and others in the Smṛti text, "A portion of My very self," and so forth.

And thus, because it is stated in the Smṛti that "He is indeed a portion of Myself," the Lord, at the time of the soul's acquisition of a body, draws forth the sense organs from their primary cause, and [withdraws them] from the body in the reverse order of their emergence; yet, while remaining [in the body], He does so from the physical sockets and so forth—since the soul is thus declared to be a portion of the Supreme Self, the harmony [of the scriptures] with respect to the soul being a portion of the Lord is established. This is proven.
The Supreme is not like this, as in the case of light and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper for the individual soul (jīva) to be a part of the Lord? For if that were so, since there would be no distinction in their being parts, it would follow that souls are identical to milk and other such things; furthermore, this would contradict scriptural texts stating that the soul has no parts. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism as follows:

"Like light and so forth, the Supreme is not thus. This is its meaning: The individual soul (*jīva*) is a distinct part (*bhinna-aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self, like light and so forth—specifically, like a portion of light that identifies with a firefly and the like. But the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, appearing in forms such as the Fish and others, is "not thus"; He is not a distinct part like the individual soul. Rather, like light and so forth—specifically, like a portion of light that identifies with the fire at the end of time (*kālāgni*) and the like—He is indeed a non-distinct part (*abhinnāṃśa*) of the Lord. This is the sense.

Thus, because the scriptural texts concerning "non-limbarhood" (anaṃśatva) intend to convey the absence of being a limb of the essential nature—just as in the case of the fish and other [manifestations]—therefore, there is no equality with the fish and others in terms of happiness and so forth. Furthermore, it would be incorrect to claim a disparity such that, due to the commonality of the mention of "limbarhood," the individual souls (jīvas) are limbs of a different kind while the fish and others are limbs of the essential nature; for even though fire, the fire at the end of time, fireflies, and so on, share the commonality of being mentioned as "limbs of light," a disparity is observed between them in the form of being limbs of the essential nature versus being limbs of a different kind. Therefore, since the soul's status as a limb of the Lord is established, the concordance of the scriptures with respect to Hari is proven.
And they remember it.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since a mere illustrative example is not decisive, even if things like the fire at the end of time and fireflies lack a common aspect of form, why could there not be both a sharing of essential nature and non-difference between the fish and other such beings and the individual souls? Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism as follows:

"And they remember" (smaraṃti ca). The meaning of this is as follows: the rememberers (smartāraḥ) state—by means of such Smṛti texts as "these are portions and parts of My own self"—that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) are either distinct parts or non-distinct parts. This is the sense.

And thus, for the devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavata*), because [the Lord] has stated in the passage beginning with "these are portions and parts of His own self" (*svāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ*) that the Boar-incarnation and others are non-differentiated parts (*abhinnāṃśa*); and because, subsequently, in the passage beginning with "that which is unmanifest" (*yadavyaktam*), He declares that individual souls (*jīva*) are differentiated parts (*bhinnāṃśa*).

Moreover, by the statement "both as its own part (*svāṃśa*) and as a distinct part (*vibhinnāṃśa*)," it is not merely a matter of the non-saṃsāric and saṃsāric states, or of being protected and unprotected, that the identity and difference between the whole (*aṃśin*) and the individual souls such as the fish are established; rather, because the fish and others possess the characteristics of being parts of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), while the individual souls possess the characteristics of being distinct parts (*bhinnāṃśa*), there is a similarity in their identity and difference with the whole based on this distinction between parts of the essential nature and parts that are not. Since the definition of these two has been stated following this division between parts of the essential nature and parts that are not, it is established that the harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the Upanishadic texts] with respect to the soul is logical, as the soul's status as a part is proven.
The permissions and prohibitions [of ritual acts] apply because of the connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.

Thus, because the distinction and non-distinction between souls—such as fish and so forth—and the possessor of those parts (the Lord) exist sequentially, it has been stated that [the relationship] is not of a single uniform kind. And now, refuting that uniformity by means of another argument, he introduces the aphorism:

"Permission and avoidance [of action] result from connection with a body, as in the case of light and so forth. This is the meaning: just as in the case of light and so forth—where, due to the connection with various bodies, such as the eyeball and so on, there occurs the activity and so forth of deities residing therein by the permission of the Sun, Varuṇa, and others—the individual soul (*jīva*) likewise, because of its connection with various bodies, experiences permission and avoidance; that is, the engagement in activity and the avoidance of bondage dependent upon the Supreme Self’s permission. This is not the case for the Fish-incarnation and others.

However, just as in the case of the deities presiding over light and so forth—such as the sun’s radiance—who possess activity and other functions independent of that [source], so too does the individual soul (jīva) possess activity independent of the Lord (Īśvara). For this reason also, the jīva is a distinct part (bhinnāṃśa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman); whereas the Fish-incarnation and others are non-distinct parts (abhinnāṃśa). This is the meaning of the established distinction.

And thus, from the liberation and activity that are entirely dependent on another, it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) is a distinct part [of the Supreme], based on the Śruti: "The Self which is within," and the Smṛti: "Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa," and so forth. The Fish-incarnation and others do not have activity dependent on their own parts, because of their connection with bodies produced by the karma of their own parts; for the formal argument (prayoga) is possible: "[The incarnations] are like the conceit of light and so forth residing in space."

Due to the soul's connection with a body, there is an absence of power—just as in the case of fish and other creatures—and consequently, there is dependence upon the grace of the Lord; from that very [grace], liberation from bondage occurs, according to the Śruti: "The white and the black. Therefore, since the soul's status as a part (aṃśa) of the Lord is established without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that the concordance of the Śrutis regarding Hari is logical.
And because there is no continuity [of the soul], there is no confusion [of karmic results].
He introduces another aphorism which refutes the identity of living beings such as fish and others by means of a further argument.

"And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion. This is the meaning: "Because there is no continuity" means that the individual soul (jīva) lacks the complete capacity [for omniscience], whereas fish and other such beings possess it. "No confusion" means the absence of any reversal of the stated principle—that the individual soul and the Lord are neither entirely different nor identical parts.

Thus, even though the Fish and other incarnations are declared by Śruti to be partial [manifestations], there is no contradiction with what was stated previously, because they possess full power (*pūrṇa-śakti*), whereas individual souls (*jīva*) lack that. For in the Śruti passage beginning "Of this very one... (*tasya ha vā etasya...*), after stating the twofold nature of sentient beings through the distinction between the higher and the lower, it describes Nārāyaṇa’s forms as possessing qualities such as fullness and so forth, while describing the other individual souls as being incomplete, bound, not eternally liberated, and so on. Therefore, since the status of the individual soul as a part of the Lord is established without contradicting Śruti, the conclusion of the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) is proven.
And it is merely an appearance.
He introduces the aphorism which establishes the point already stated by means of another argument.

"And [it is] merely a reflection" (ābhāsa eva ca). This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of conjunction. Since the individual soul (jīva) is merely a reflection—that is, a mere image—of the Supreme, whereas the fish and so forth are not so, for this reason also there is no contradiction with what was previously stated.

And thus, because it is stated that "He became a counterpart to every form" (*evaṃ ca rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva*), which indicates that individual souls (*jīvas*) are reflections; and because fish and other beings are described as being portions of His own nature (*svarūpāṃśas*); and because the scriptural texts stating that the soul is "without parts" (*anaṃśa*) refer specifically to the absence of being a portion of the essential nature—since the entire class of living beings, like the fish and others, exists as reflections of the Supreme Self and their functions are dependent upon Him; therefore, it is established that the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the scriptures is logical and free from contradiction.
Thus concludes the section on the portions (Aṃśādhikaraṇa).
Here, the contradiction regarding the scriptural statements concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) as a reflection of the Lord (*īśvara*) is resolved. [Sūtra 3.2.20:
"It is not seen [as such], because of the lack of restriction."

[Objection: It may be argued that the individual souls (jīvas) are not reflections of the Lord. For scripture states, "Neither a part, nor a reflection, nor a connection. Nor should it be said that even if they were reflections, there is a scriptural text stating "form after form," because the scriptural statement "nor a connection" is supported by reasoning. Indeed, the individual souls are diverse, distinguished as gods, humans, animals, and so forth; and such diversity is not possible if they are reflections of a single source. Therefore, since the souls are not reflections, and since the scriptural statement regarding reflection is contradicted by the scriptural statement regarding [non-reflection] supported by reasoning, the reflection-scripture must be unauthoritative. Thus, the previously stated harmonious consistency (samanvaya) is not established. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies with the following aphorism: *na ca smārtamataddharmābhilāpāt* || 2.3.17 || [Response: It is not so, for the Smṛti [which speaks of the soul as a reflection] does not contradict our position, because it describes attributes other than those of the reflected object. The Smṛti passage, "As the one fire, entered into the world, becomes many forms according to its entry into various fuels, so the one Self, entered into the world, becomes many forms according to its entry into various bodies" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan), clearly indicates that the soul is a reflection. Furthermore, the Smṛti passage, "As the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the external defects of the eyes, so the one Inner Self of all beings is not stained by the suffering of the world, being beyond it" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan), shows that the soul, as a reflection, is distinct from the limiting adjuncts. Moreover, the Smṛti passage, "Just as the one ether, when enclosed by jars and the like, appears as many, so the one Self, though one, appears as many through its connection with bodies" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa), confirms that the soul is a reflection. Nor is the scriptural statement "nor a connection" contradicted, for it refers to a relationship other than that of reflection—namely, the relationship of identity (tādātmya). The statement "neither a part" excludes the relationship of being a constituent part (avayava). Thus, the Smṛti is consistent with scripture. Furthermore, the diversity of the souls is due to their association with various limiting adjuncts (upādhis), just as the same space appears diverse when limited by jars and other objects. Therefore, the souls are indeed reflections of the Lord, and the previously stated harmonious consistency is established. || 2.3.17 ||

"Because of the lack of restriction [imposed] by the unseen [force]" (adṛṣṭa-aniyamāt). This is the meaning: the term "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) indicates ignorance (avidyā), karma, and mental impressions (saṃskāra). "Restriction" (niyama) means being of one uniform nature; "lack of restriction" (aniyama) means having manifold natures. Thus, there is diversity; and because of this diversity, it is logical that even for the individual souls (jīvas) who are reflections, there exists diversity such as being gods, demons, humans, and so forth. This is the sense.

Thus, the aforementioned defect would occur only if the soul were a reflection in the literal sense, like a face in a mirror; but it is not so. Rather, its being a "reflection" is technical, consisting in its similarity [to Brahman] while being dependent upon Him. Nor is there a lack of diversity in this view, for we observe diversity among sons who, though similar, are dependent on their father. Or, let it be that the soul is a reflection exactly like a face in a mirror; even so, there is no inconsistency regarding diversity, because of the existence of causes such as the diversity of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) and so forth.

If it is asked how there is such variety in the unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, [the answer is] that even that is dependent upon the variety of prior karma; and because the succession of different karmas is beginningless. Therefore, it is established that the concordance of the Vedas (*śruti-samanvaya*) is appropriately with Nārāyaṇa.
And the same applies even in the case of intentional meanings and so forth.

Now, one might object: "What is the use of postulating an unseen force (adṛṣṭa)? For the diversity [of the world] can be accounted for solely by the diversity of defects such as passion, hatred, and delusion. Anticipating this doubt, he sets forth the aphorism to dispel it.

"And likewise in the case of intentions and so forth. This is the meaning: since even in the case of intentions and other such things, namely defects like desire and anger, the diversity [of experience] must be explained as arising solely from the diversity of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) and so on; therefore, because it is necessary, the diversity of the unseen alone is the cause of the diversity among individual souls (jīvas), and not the diversity of defects and the like—this is the sense.

Thus, since the diversity of defects must ultimately be attributed to the unseen (adṛṣṭa) even for the sake of accounting for that diversity, and because a diversity is observed at every moment even in the absence of a diversity of defects; and since it is not only in the case of passion and other qualities denoted by the term "intention" (*abhisaṃdhi*) that this diversity arises from the non-restriction of the unseen, but rather—because the moment-to-moment diversity residing in a single person can only occur through the very restriction of the unseen—it cannot arise from any other cause. Therefore, it is established that the harmony with the Śruti is logical.
If it is argued that [the whole exists] because of its presence in a particular part, we say no, because [the whole] is included within [the parts].

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the diversity among gods and humans is already accounted for by the very diversity of their locations—such as 'the gods reside in heaven' and 'humans reside on earth'—what is the need for a diversity of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)? Anticipating this, he presents the aphorism that refutes it.

"From place and so forth—if this is argued, it is not so, because [the variety] is included within [adṛṣṭa]. This is its meaning: Now, one might object: "Let the diversity among gods, humans, and other beings arise simply from the diversity of places—such as heaven, earth, and so on—and not from the diversity of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit). If this is said, we reply: No. Why? Because of inclusion (*antarbhāva*). When one searches for the cause of the diversity of places, that cause is found to be included within the very diversity of *adṛṣṭa*, since it is of that nature.
Therefore, the meaning is that because it is necessary, the diversity of *adṛṣṭa* alone is the regulator of the diversity among gods, humans, and others.

And thus, since even the attainment of heaven and other such states is accomplished through the unseen (adṛṣṭa), and because diversity is observed among those situated in a single location; and since that very [reflection] does not entail any contradiction with reason regarding its technical definition as "reflective image" (pratibimba); and because of the scriptural statement, "It is neither a part nor a relation"; and because there is no contradiction even when [the scripture] refers to the absence of being a face-to-face reflection or a physical reflection—since the technical definition of "reflective image" is established by the scripture stating "form after form"—it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Nārāyaṇa is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter.
Śrīḥ!
Om. May there be auspiciousness. May Hari protect you.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the second chapter.
In this section (pāda), contradictions with scripture that are accompanied by logical reasoning are refuted.
The contradiction with scripture regarding the production of the sense organs is thus resolved;
the same applies to the vital breaths.

But is it not the case that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are not subject to origination, on account of the scriptural text, "The vital breaths themselves"? Nor should it be argued that there is also a scriptural text regarding their origination, namely, "From this [Self]... For the scriptural text concerning non-origination is stronger, as its meaning is explicit and thus leaves no room for alternative interpretation. The scriptural text, "From this it is born," can also be interpreted as referring to manifestation; therefore, being of indistinct meaning, it is weaker. Furthermore, this is supported by reasoning: the vital breaths are not subject to origination because they lack a material cause (*upādāna*). Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*).

Because it is established by the Smṛti that there is no material cause (upādāna), and because this contradicts powerful Śruti texts, the Śruti concerning origination is indeed non-authoritative; thus, the status of the Lord as the cause of the world is not established through the concordance of Śruti. To this objection, the following was aphorized:

"Likewise, the vital breaths (prāṇas)"—the meaning of this is as follows: just as ether and the other elements are produced from Viṣṇu, so too the vital breaths, which are the sense organs, are indeed produced; the meaning is that they are not unproduced.

Thus, the vital breaths (prāṇas) indeed possess origination, because the reasons that establish the origination of space are present here as well. Consequently, they possess the attainment of specific qualities dependent on another; therefore, since their origination from the Supreme Self is established, it is proven that Brahman is the cause of the world through the consistent interpretation of the scriptures (śruti-samanvaya). This is established.
Because a figurative sense is impossible.

"Because of the impossibility of a secondary sense" (gauṇyasaṃbhavāt). This is its meaning: the scriptural statement regarding beginninglessness—namely, "The vital breaths alone are indeed beginningless"—is secondary (gauṇī), that is, non-literal. It refers to the absence of origination in a subtle form. Why? Because of impossibility; for it is impossible for the senses to possess primary beginninglessness. Furthermore, it means because of the incompatibility with the scriptural statement, "From this [Self]... (etasmāt).

And thus, even though there is such a scriptural statement, because it lacks a primary sense and possesses only a figurative sense—since a primary sense is impossible due to the contingency of [the prāṇas] being equal to the Supreme Self—and because it contradicts reason, as in "the prāṇas have an origin, because they possess limited power," it is therefore established that the prāṇas are produced from the Supreme Self.
And because it would contradict the initial proposition.

He introduces the sūtra which establishes the origin of the sense organs by means of the argument against the abandonment of the initial proposition (pratijñāhāni) stated in the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa).

"And because of the non-contradiction of the proposition. The meaning of this is as follows: because there would otherwise be a contradiction with the proposition that "He created all this," and in order to conform to that proposition, it must be accepted that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are produced. This is the sense.

And thus, by accepting the origination of the vital breaths (prāṇas), there is no contradiction with the scripture stating "He [breathed forth] this"; therefore, it is established that the vital breaths originate from the Supreme Self (paramātman) without contradicting the Śruti.
Thus ends the section concerning the origin of the vital breaths.
Here, the contradiction with the Vedic texts regarding the origin of the mind is resolved:
"And because of the scriptural statement prior to that."

Is it not the case that there is no origination of the mind? For scripture states, "The mind is eternal because it is beginningless. Nor is it appropriate to interpret this scriptural statement regarding its beginninglessness as being figurative—following the pattern of the scriptural statements regarding the origination of the senses—simply because the origination of the mind is mentioned specifically after declaring the impermanence of the senses. Furthermore, if the mind were to have a beginning, the Person (Puruṣa), who is beginningless, would at times have to exist without it; yet that is impossible, for if that were so, it would follow that there could be no transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) at those times.

Because the mind is the cause of saṃsāra, and because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "the mind alone [is the cause] for human beings," the mind is therefore eternal. Thus, since the scriptural statements regarding specific logical arguments are more powerful, the scriptural statements concerning origination lack authority when they contradict them; consequently, the status of the Lord as the cause of the world cannot be established through the reconciliation of the scriptures (śrutisamanvaya). This being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"And because of its being heard prior to those. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to conjoin [the reason] "because of its non-origination" [with the previous one]. "Of that" means of the mind (manas). "Prior to those" means before the other sense organs (indriyas), by virtue of having originated earlier. "Because of its being heard" refers to the scriptural statement, "The mind and all the sense organs. The meaning is that the mind is indeed something that originates; it is not unoriginated.

And thus, it is not logical that the mind is non-originated, because there is a scriptural statement regarding its origination. Nor is there any other alternative for this [scripture], since it is a specific scriptural statement (viśeṣa-śruti) designating the birth of the mind as distinct [from the self]. Nor is the separate mention of the mind’s object [as distinct from the objects of] the other senses redundant if the mind, like the other senses, possesses origination; for that [separate mention] is justified by the intention to show that the mind originates prior even to the other senses. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning non-origination, because those refer to the mind in its subtle form.

Nor is there any contradiction with the statement regarding its specific eternality, for that statement intends to convey that it undergoes less accumulation than the other sense organs. Therefore, since the mind's origination from the Blessed Lord is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman, the cause of the universe, is logical. Thus it is established.
Thus concludes that preceding section.
Here, the contradiction between the scriptural statement regarding the origination of speech and the scriptural statement regarding its non-origination is resolved by the principle:
"Because speech is preceded by that [mind]."

Now, it might be argued that speech is not something produced, because of the scriptural text, "Speech indeed [is eternal]. Nor should it be said that this scripture refers only to the Vedas; for it is impossible for this [scripture] to be the locus of the very scripture [itself], as expressed in the phrase "in this scripture it abides. Furthermore, if speech were to have a beginning, the contradiction with the inference—"speech is unproduced because it is the locus of the eternal scripture"—would be difficult to avoid, since a produced thing is never seen to be the locus of an eternal thing. Nor can the scripture regarding its beginninglessness refer to a subtle form [of speech], because it is impossible for a subtle form to be the locus of the scripture consisting of the capacity to utter the eternal heard-scripture. To this objection, the following is set forth in a Sūtra:

"Because speech is preceded by that. This is the meaning: "Of speech," that is, of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*). "Because it is preceded by that" means that since scripture declares the mind (*manas*) to be its prior form—that is, its cause—the organ of speech is indeed something produced, and not something unproduced.

And thus, speech possesses the quality of being produced (*utpattimat*), because it is heard in scripture as having a subsequent form, which implies it is an effect. Nor is its status as an effect untenable due to a lack of a cause; for its causality by means of the mind is established through the scriptural statement in another recension, "The mind is the prior form," and thus its nature as an effect is logically consistent. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with scripture, for that scripture declares its eternality only in a figurative sense. Nor is its eternality established by the argument that it must have an eternal substratum.

Since it is accepted that speech possesses the fitness for eternal presence in the Śruti, it is not accepted as the substratum of a Śruti endowed with an eternal fruit; rather, through a consideration of the meaning of the Śruti, only a figurative eternity is obtained. For only when this is the case does the meaning of the sentence "I praise [Him] who is eternal by being the substratum of the Vedas and non-eternal by being the substratum of the Purāṇas" become logically consistent, and not otherwise. Therefore, since its origin is established without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that the concordance of the Śruti with respect to Hari, the cause of the world, is appropriate for speech.
Thus concludes the section concerning [the fact that] it is preceded by that.
Here, the contradiction regarding the number of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) found in the scriptures is resolved.

Now, one might object that because the scriptural statements "seven vital breaths arise" and "or twelve" are mutually contradictory, they lack determinative authority. Nor is it logical for one scriptural statement to sublate another, as they are of equal strength. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that because there are seven presiding deities (*abhimānin*), there must likewise be only seven vital breaths, based on the rule that the number of presiding deities and the objects they preside over must be equal. Finally, it cannot be claimed that the scripture stating the number seven is more authoritative due to its being supported by reasoning.

In the Śruti passage stating "twelve," since the twelve months are mentioned with the intention that the vital breaths (prāṇas), the months, and so forth, share a single deity, it must be asserted that because there are twelve presiding deities of the vital breaths, the vital breaths themselves are also twelve; for the reasoning stated here applies equally in this case as well. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction between the two Śruti texts on the grounds that even seven [vital breaths] are possible among the twelve, because it would be illogical to speak of "seven" when there is no specific reason for limiting the number to twelve. Consequently, since the two Śruti texts would lack authority, it is not tenable that the Lord's status as the cause of the world is established through the concordance of the Śrutis. To this objection, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "But [the number] is based on the similarity of the functions. (ŚBh 2.4.17) This means that the number twelve is based on the similarity of the functions of the various organs. Just as the eyes, though two, function as a single unit in seeing, and the ears function as one in hearing, so too the ten vital breaths, together with the mind and intellect, perform their respective functions as a single collective entity. Thus, the number twelve is used figuratively to denote the unity of these functions, and there is no contradiction between the two Śruti passages. Therefore, the concordance of the Śrutis remains valid, and the Lord's causality of the world is established.

"And because of the specification of the seven in relation to movement. This is the meaning [of the sūtra]. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the authority [of the scripture] that states, "the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), however, are for the sake of cognition. Regarding "movement" (*gateḥ*), it means cognition (*jñāna*). The conclusion is simply that the sense organs which produce [cognition] are seven in number; it is not a matter of uncertainty. Why? Because of being specified (*viśeṣitatvāt*). The meaning is that in the Vedic text stating "seven vital breaths," they are designated with specific attributes as being placed within the cave [of the heart] for the purpose of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Thus, there are exactly twelve vital breaths (*prāṇas*), according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating "twelve. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural mention of seven; for even among the twelve *prāṇas*, the number seven is also present. Nor is it improper to speak of the number seven when the reason for the twelvefold nature of the *prāṇas* exists; for since hearing, sight, touch, taste, smell, mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*) are the organs that serve as instruments for knowledge, the mention of seven is possible by intending to refer to them. Nor is their status as being for the purpose of knowledge unknown.

This is because it is established by the completion of the sentence [in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]: "They are placed within the cave. Therefore, since the authority of both scriptural passages is maintained without contradiction, it is proven that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the universe is logically established through the harmonization of the scriptures (śrutisamanvaya).
But since [the body] persists, hands and so forth do not [cease]; therefore, it is not thus.

Now, if there were the existence of vital breaths other than the seven, then in this Atharvaṇa scripture, where they are stated to be born from the Supreme Self, the reading would have been "seven plus five vital breaths" along with those seven. Here, the absence of such a joint enumeration could be due to either the beginninglessness of the Supreme Self or because He is not their cause; however, both of these are contradicted by the statement "so too the vital breaths. Furthermore, there is no other reason for the absence of joint enumeration, whether it be regarding the Supreme Self or His not being their cause.

Furthermore, the arising of an effect without a cause is illogical. Consequently, since there is no mention of them alongside the others in the scriptural enumeration, it follows that there are no vital breaths (*prāṇas*) other than the seven; such being the prima facie view, the author of the Sūtras recites the following aphorism to resolve it: **"But the hands and so forth [are distinct], for their function is established; therefore it is not so."** The meaning of this is as follows: The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. "Hands and so forth" refers to the organs of action, such as the hands. "Established" (*sthite*) means their specific activity is fixed; the locative case here denotes purpose, meaning they exist for the sake of action. Therefore, because of this distinction from the others, they are not enumerated together with the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). Thus, the fact that they number seven is indeed established.

And thus, since the recitation together [of the elements] is justified by relying on the distinct characteristics of the five, beginning with the hands, as being the causes of stability, it is established that the determination of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is logical, due to the harmony of the scriptures and their authoritative validity through the absence of contradiction between the two scriptural passages.
Thus concludes the section on the seven destinies.
Here, the contradiction regarding the size of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) found in the scriptures is resolved:
"And [the prāṇas] are atomic."

[Objection: Surely the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are all-pervading, because of the scriptural statement regarding their pervasion, "Like the eye in the sky," and because of their connection with the observation and hearing of distant objects. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural statements concerning their atomicity (*aṇutva*); for this [latter] scripture is more authoritative since it describes the pervasion of the eye by means of an illustration of Viṣṇu's pervasion. Therefore, since it contradicts the stronger scriptural testimony of pervasion, the scripture concerning atomicity is simply not a valid authority. To this, the Sūtra replies: *Śeṣatvāt puruṣārthavādo yathānyeṣv iti jaiminiḥ.* (3.4.2) "Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose, as in the case of other [subsidiary acts]; so says Jaimini. (3.4.2) [Commentary: Because the *prāṇas* are subordinate to the Self, the mention of their "human purpose" (i.e., their benefit to the person) is merely a figurative expression of praise, just as in the case of other subsidiary rites. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding pervasion refers to the *prāṇas* insofar as they are dependent on the omnipresent Self; it does not mean that the *prāṇas* themselves are inherently all-pervading. Moreover, the statement regarding pervasion is intended to show that the *prāṇas* are capable of perceiving distant objects through their connection with the omnipresent Self, not that they are themselves all-pervasive. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statements concerning their atomicity. Consequently, the *prāṇas* are indeed atomic. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding pervasion is not more authoritative than the statement regarding atomicity. This is because the pervasion of the *prāṇas* is established through their dependence on the omnipresent Self, whereas the pervasion of Viṣṇu is established through His own essential nature. Since the two cases are not analogous, the strength of the scriptural testimony is equal. Thus, there is no contradiction between the two types of scriptural statements. "And they are atomic" (aṇavaśca). The meaning of this is: the vital breaths, that is, the sense organs, are atomic, meaning they are minute by their very nature. The word "and" (ca) signifies that they are not only atomic, but are also pervaded by light (tejas).

Thus, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed atomic (*aṇu*), because of such scriptural testimony. Nor can their lack of atomicity be established on the grounds of contradiction with the powerful scripture stating, "As the eye in the sky," for atomicity itself is established by the even more powerful scripture, "For it is as if atomic" (*tadyathā hyaṇu*). And this does not result in a state of indecision; for the scripture "as if atomic" is more authoritative than the scripture concerning pervasiveness, owing to its explicit nature. Nor is that [scripture] invalid.

For instance, by following the scriptural statement "the atom is not," and by determining that the scriptural passage concerning pervasion refers to the pervasiveness of light, the contradiction with reasoning has been set aside. Therefore, it is established that the prāṇas are atomic in accordance with scripture and without contradicting it.
Thus concludes the section concerning the atom (aṇvadhikaraṇa).
Here, the contradiction among scriptural passages concerning the origin of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is resolved.
And [the Sūtra says]: "And he is the best."

[Objection: But surely the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is not subject to origination, because of the scriptural text, "This is not breath. Nor can this scriptural text be interpreted otherwise—just as the text regarding the non-origination of the principal air (*mukhya-vāyu*) is interpreted—on the grounds that it is illogical for it to have origination and so forth since it is the cause of birth and death. For the scriptural texts concerning its beginninglessness, which are supported by reasoning, possess greater authority. Therefore, since the scriptural text on origination lacks authority due to its contradiction with the more powerful scriptural texts on beginninglessness, the concordance of the scriptures with the Supreme Lord as the cause of the world is untenable. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: *na vāyukriye pṛthagupadeśāt* (Sūtra 2.4.9). [The principal breath] is neither air nor mere function, because of the separate teaching [of them]. [Note: This is the full Sūtra. [Explanation: It is not the case that the principal breath is not subject to origination. Although there is the text, "This is not breath," that text does not deny its origination; rather, it denies that the term "breath" applies to the individual soul (*jīva*), based on the common usage of the word "breath" for the vital functions of the body. Furthermore, the denial of origination found in the text concerning the principal air cannot be used here as a precedent for interpreting this text differently. This is because the scriptural texts asserting its beginninglessness—which are consistent with reason—are more authoritative than the text concerning its being the cause of birth and death, which would imply its own origination. Thus, since the scriptural text on origination is sublated by the more powerful scriptural texts on beginninglessness, it lacks authority. Consequently, the objection that the concordance of the scriptures with the Supreme Lord as the cause of the world is impossible is raised. To this, the Sūtra says: *na vāyukriye pṛthagupadeśāt*. [The principal breath is] neither air nor mere function, because of the separate teaching [of them]. [Note: This is the full Sūtra. [Explanation: The principal breath is not merely air, nor is it merely the function of air. Why? Because of the separate teaching [of them]. In the passage, "From him are born breath, mind, and all the sense organs" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1), the principal breath is taught separately from the sense organs, which include the function of air. If it were merely air or its function, it would not be taught separately. Therefore, the principal breath is a distinct entity produced from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the concordance of the scriptures with the Supreme Lord as the cause of the world is established.

"And the best" (śreṣṭhaḥ). The meaning of this is as follows: just as the other vital breaths (prāṇas) arise, so too the "best," the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), arises from Viṣṇu; it does not mean that it is unoriginated.

And thus, just as the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*) arise, so too the preeminent *mukhya-prāṇa* possesses origination; for the scripture states, "Indeed, it exists by way of subtlety. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its beginninglessness, because it is taught that while it always exists in a subtle form, it arises at times in a gross form; for this gross state and the like do not constitute its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Although it shares no distinction from other living beings in this regard, nevertheless, this [grossness] belongs only to the body and such, and not to the consciousness (*caitanya*) as it does for other living beings.

Because there exists a specific distinction—namely, that [the former] possesses particular modifications produced by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of those [elements]—therefore, since the birth of the primary air is established without contradicting the Śruti, it is proven that the status of being the cause of the world belongs to Vāsudeva through the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Śruti.
The vital breath and its functions are not distinct [from the Self], because they are taught separately.

Now, since the scriptural statement regarding beginninglessness is more powerful due to its being supported by reasoning, the scriptural statement concerning origination should be interpreted accordingly as referring to external air; for even in the sentence "and of those two, in [their] movement," it is stated that they are denoted by the word *prāṇa*, and thus there is no contradiction in accepting their origination, as there is no statement to the contrary. To this prima facie view, the author presents the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the breaths are] not [produced], because of the non-origination of the chief [breath]. (BrSū 2.4.1) This means: But the breaths are not produced, because the chief breath—the one called *prāṇa*—is not subject to origination. For it is said: "From this very self, these sixteen parts arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.7.1), and "He sent forth the breaths from his own self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). Since the chief breath is mentioned here, and since the word *prāṇa* is used for all the breaths in the passage "And of those two, in [their] movement" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2), the non-origination of the chief breath implies the non-origination of the others as well. Furthermore, the scripture declares its eternity: "The breath indeed is the eternal among the breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). Therefore, the scriptural statement regarding origination must be explained as referring to the manifestation of the breaths at the time of creation, just like the manifestation of the individual soul. Thus, the breaths are not produced. This is the established conclusion.

"Nor are they air and its function, because of their separate teaching. This is the meaning: "Air and its function"—that is, the action known as the movement of external air—are not what are taught by this [scriptural passage] regarding the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Rather, it is the primary air itself that is taught therein. Why? Because of their separate teaching. The meaning is that in passages such as "He created the *prāṇa*," the origin of the primary air is heard separately from the origins of air and its function.

Thus, having stated in the Śruti that "He created the Prāṇa along with life" (*saprāṇam asṛjata*) that the Prāṇa possesses the quality of being produced, and because the Śruti further declares the distinct origination of movement and the vital air (*vāyu*) from the Prāṇa; and likewise because the Smṛti also states, "The elements, the mantras, and movements [were born]"; nor can it be argued that there is no origination for it on account of its being the cause of the origin of all beings or its status as the most excellent, since even that great Prāṇa has birth from Viṣṇu, who is even greater than it. Therefore, it is established that the primary Prāṇa originates, in accordance with the Śruti and without contradiction.
Thus ends the section on the most excellent [offering].
Here, the contradiction between scriptural passages regarding the independence and lack of independence of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is resolved:
"But it [the chief vital breath] is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them, and for other reasons."

Is it not the case that the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is indeed independent? For scripture states that it "depends on something. Nor does this contradict the scriptural statement of its dependence, namely, "of the breath" (*prāṇasya*), because the scripture asserting independence is stronger, being supported by the reasoning that it sets all the world in motion, which establishes its independence. Furthermore, the scripture asserting dependence is not stronger on account of the reasoning that it possesses an origin; for those who maintain its independence do not admit its birth, and even the scriptural texts concerning its birth lack authority due to their contradiction with this [present] scripture.

Even if [the scripture] were authoritative, since it is possible for Him to assume a physical form through divine play (*līlā*), that [scripture] lacks the power to prove His dependence; thus, the scriptural texts concerning dependence lack logical consistency. Therefore, because the contradiction with more powerful scriptural passages remains unresolved, the scripture regarding dependence is not authoritative. Consequently, since Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause of the universe is not established through the systematic interpretation of the scriptures (*śrutisamanvaya*), this being the position reached, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"But like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them, etc. This is the meaning: the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of emphasis (*eva*). The principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), too, is dependent upon the Supreme Self just like the eye and other organs; it is not independent. Why? Because of its being taught together with them, etc.; for in the scripture, "All this indeed is He," the dependence of the principal breath along with those [organs] such as the eye is stated. And because of the logical arguments stated in such passages as "the maker of all," etc.

And thus, the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), like the eyes and other senses, is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Self; for by the statement "all this indeed," its subordination to Him is declared along with the eyes and the rest. It is logical that the principal air is not independent, because it is devoid of the capacity for seeing and so forth without the impulsion of the Blessed Lord. Nor is this unproven, as it is established by the scripture stating, "There is none other than this. Even though the *prāṇa* is the agent of all, it must nevertheless be admitted to be dependent on the Lord; otherwise, it would not even be a *prāṇa*.

It is established that what has been stated is correct, because if the sovereignty of the Supreme Self were denied, there would be no arising of the world and so forth; and since two independent entities are impossible, the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) is subject to the Lord is proven without contradicting the Śruti. Thus it is settled.
"And because it is not something to be performed, there is no fault; for thus [the scripture] shows."

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is indeed dependent on the Lord just like the eyes and other organs, then—since its status as a subordinate lord (avāntareśvaratva) and so forth would be impossible—the scriptural statement regarding its independence, 'The breath is nothing whatsoever,' would be rendered meaningless. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the following sūtra:

"And because it is not an instrument, there is no fault; for [the scripture] shows this. This is its meaning: Since the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is not an instrument—because it is distinct from instruments in the sense that they are employed by an agent—and since the eyes and other senses possess that nature [of being instruments], the superiority of the principal breath over the others is established precisely due to this difference. "There is no fault" means that there is no fault consisting in the scriptural texts declaring the independence of the principal breath having another referent, such as a subordinate Lord (*avāntareśvara*). If it is asked, "Why should it be interpreted thus?", [the text says] "Because" (*hi*), which means: for this reason.
The Śruti indeed declares "tāni ha vai" in the manner thus described; it reveals or makes known [this]. Therefore is the meaning.

And thus, although all [beings] are equal in their dependence on the Lord (Īśvara), there is a distinction because the others are directed by an agent (kartṛ), whereas the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) lacks that; furthermore, this distinction is established through reasoning based on the presence or absence of activity during states such as deep sleep, and by the scriptural text beginning with "tāni ha vai. Therefore, its status as a subordinate lord is justified, and consequently, the subordination of the vital breath to the Lord is established without contradicting scripture.
Thus ends the section concerning the eye and the other [senses].
Here, the contradiction with scripture regarding whether the prāṇa, apāna, and so forth are of the nature of the chief prāṇa or are its servants is resolved.
"The fivefold function is designated as being like the mind."

Is it not the case that both scriptural passages—the one stating "All these are indeed the chief's servants" and the other stating "They are the very forms of the chief"—are invalid as authorities? This is because they do not determine the true meaning. If one person, relying on the scripture "they are the very forms of the chief" and the reasoning of their possessing manifest good qualities, were to say that the [other] vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the forms of the chief vital breath; then the other might also, by his command, rely on the scripture "All these are indeed [servants]" and the reasoning of their performing actions, and say that the vital breaths are merely servants.

Therefore, if one were to say on the basis of logic and scripture that these [beings] are indeed slaves from the beginning, then the opponent might likewise say on the basis of ancient scripture and logic that they are indeed of their own nature (svarūpa). Since both positions possess equal strength, it is impossible to sublate either one through scripture. Thus, because there is no determination of the meaning and both scriptures would consequently lack authority, the status of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world cannot be established by the force of scripture. To this objection, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Having five functions, it is designated like the mind. This is its meaning: "Like the mind" means just as the mind possesses five modes—namely, those called manas, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, citta, and cetanā—so too the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) has five functions, consisting of the forms of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. Why? Because in the scripture [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19.2], it is thus designated—that is, it is set forth as having five functions. Therefore, this is the sense.

Thus, we do not say that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are exclusively the essential forms (*svarūpa*), which would lead to an irresolvable contradiction due to mutual inconsistency. Rather, on the basis of the scriptural statement "this [is] fivefold in its function," they are like the mind: the vital breaths and so forth are twofold—both essential forms and servants (*dāsa*). Consequently, there is no sublation because the two scriptural passages have different objects of reference. Nor is there a contradiction with the manifest possession of good qualities (*sadguṇatva*) if the vital breaths are servants, for even servants are admitted to possess those qualities. Furthermore, there is no impossibility of the relationship between master and servant.

Since the existence of those [qualities] is established in the case of the masters as well, by virtue of their possessing manifest good qualities, it follows that the nature of the vital breaths and so forth is established without contradicting scripture. Therefore, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman, the cause of the world, is established.
Thus concludes the section on the fivefold function.
Here, the contradiction regarding the size of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) found in the scriptures is resolved:
"And it is atomic."

[Objection: But surely this prāṇa is all-pervading, because of the scriptural statement regarding its pervasion: "Prāṇa alone is below. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural statement of its atomicity [on the grounds that it is] minute; for the scriptural statement of pervasion is more powerful, as it is supported by the logical reasoning of being the sustainer of the entire world. Therefore, since it contradicts a more powerful scripture, the scriptural statement of atomicity is not authoritative. To this, the Sūtra says:

"And it is subtle" (aṇuśca). The meaning of this is: the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is subtle by way of its nature as *prāṇa*, and it is all-pervasive by way of its nature as air (*vāyu*). This is the sense.

Thus, the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) is indeed atomic (aṇu), according to the scriptural text: "This, verily, is that prāṇa. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its all-pervasiveness; for those refer to the air existing outside the body. This is because of the specific scriptural distinction: "Within it is atomic, without it is great," and because of the reasoning regarding its movement through the channels (nāḍīs). Therefore, since the atomic nature of the principal prāṇa is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman—the cause of the universe—is logically consistent.
Thus ends the section concerning the atom (aṇvadhikaraṇa).
Here, the contradiction with the senses, their objects, and the Vedic scriptures is resolved:
"But the presiding [deities] are fire and the rest, because of the scriptural teaching thereof."

[Objection: "Surely the senses are the instruments of the individual soul (jīva). For there is a scriptural statement regarding their connection with the soul, namely: 'They call them the instruments of the soul. Nor does this contradict another scriptural text stating that [the senses] belong to Brahman; for the scriptural statement that they are the instruments of the soul is stronger, as it is supported by the reasoning that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are observed to be under the control of the soul. Consequently, because the scriptural statement regarding Brahman as the instrument would lack authority due to its contradiction with this [other] scripture, the fact that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world is not established through the harmonization of the scriptures. To this, the author recites the Sūtra: *na tadvacanādāmnānāt* (Sūtra 2.4.5). [Response: No, because of that [scriptural] declaration and because of the traditional record. The scriptural statement that the senses belong to the soul is not more powerful than the statement that they belong to Brahman. Why? Because of the declaration: "The senses are indeed Brahman" (*brahmaiva prāṇāḥ*). Furthermore, the traditional record (*āmnāna*) of the *Śatarudriya* mantra—beginning with "Obeisance to Rudra" (*namo rudrāya*) and ending with "Obeisance to the One who has entered the senses" (*namo hṛdayāya*)—establishes that these [senses] belong to Śiva. Moreover, the scriptural statement that the senses are the instruments of the soul is not more powerful than the statement that they are the instruments of Brahman. Why? Because the scriptural statement that they are the instruments of Brahman is supported by the reasoning that the soul itself is dependent on Brahman. Therefore, since the scriptural statement regarding Brahman as the instrument possesses greater force, the harmony of the scriptures establishes that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

"But the presiding over light and so forth belongs to That, because of the teaching concerning That. This is the meaning: the phrase "the presiding over light and so forth" is repeated; it is connected with the word "That" (tat). Thus, the presiding over light and so forth—that which impels the elements such as fire—is that very Brahman. The presiding over light and so forth—that which impels the eyes and other organs—is not the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the teaching concerning That; the meaning is that this is established by such passages as, "He who dwells in the eye," and so forth.

And thus, the instruments belonging to Brahman alone are the means for the individual soul’s knowledge and other faculties; they are not, however, the instruments of the soul. This is because, being superior to the soul, it is impossible for them to be employed by the soul; for that alone is truly one's own which is fit to be deployed according to one's will. Nor should it be argued that [the organs] do not belong to Brahman simply because they are so; for since all elements, beginning with fire—the source of these organs—are governed by Brahman, these organs are all the more subject to His control.

And because of such scriptural passages as, "He who dwells in the eye," and so forth; therefore, since the fact that the vital breaths have Brahman as their cause is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Hari as the cause of the world is logical.
[The soul exists] because of sound in one who possesses breath.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the organs do not belong to the individual soul (jīva), then would it not follow that the scriptural texts declaring them to be its organs would lose their authority? Anticipating this doubt, he presents the following sūtra:

"By means of the senses belonging to the one endowed with breath, on account of the scriptural statement. This is its meaning: the Supreme Self causes the seeing and other activities to be performed by the individual soul (jīva) acting as the agent, who is endowed with breath, through the instruments such as the eyes which are themselves employed by Him; not by means of instruments employed by the individual soul. Why? "On account of the scriptural statement," that is to say, because of the Śruti text: "For he [the Self] indeed causes him [the soul] to act by this [instrument]. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.28).

And thus, since the scriptural text expressing instrumentality is possible as authoritative by virtue of its intent being that Brahman causes seeing and so forth through its own instruments—possessing a slight connection like a borrowed axe—and since the authority of that text is also possible when intended to refer to the beginningless and eternal connection with the instruments of the individual soul (jīva); for indeed, in the world, it is observed that there is a figurative usage of ownership (*tadīyatva*) regarding things belonging to another with which one has been connected for a long time.

If it is argued that since the sense organs are instruments of Brahman, the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) must likewise be an instrument for the same reason—as was stated previously—and therefore the chief vital breath alone is not a non-instrument, making its status as an instrument untenable; we say no. There is a distinction: the Lord impels the eyes and other senses by the will of a particular individual soul, whereas the chief vital breath acts by its own will. Since this distinction exists, such an interpretation is justified. Furthermore, because there exist scriptural statements such as "the cause by means of the instruments," it is established that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman as the cause of the universe is logical, without contradicting the sacred texts.
And because that [Brahman] is eternal.

Thus, although the sense organs are dependent on the Lord, they are called "instruments" (*karaṇa*) because they serve as the means for action performed by the independent individual soul (*jīva*). Just as one who cuts with another person’s axe is said to have that axe as his instrument, so too [the organs belong to the soul]. Having thus explained the primary meaning of the scriptural statement regarding the soul's possession of instruments, he now introduces the aphorism which establishes another primary meaning.

"And because of its eternity. This is the meaning: although the eyes and other organs are instruments of Brahman, since that [Brahman], the individual soul (jīva), the instrument, and the relationship between the two are eternal, the scriptural statement regarding the soul's status as an instrument is also justified by intending to refer to that [eternal reality]. This is the sense.

And thus, since we observe the figurative usage of "belonging to someone" even with respect to an object belonging to another when it has been associated with that person for a long time, so too here—in the case of the sense organs belonging to the Lord—the scriptural statement regarding their being His instruments proceeds because of the existence of a long-term association with the individual soul; for the scripture possesses a figurative meaning. Furthermore, this is supported by the scripture stating they are "inseparable. Therefore, it is established that the systematic harmony of the scriptures with the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the world, is logical without contradicting the sacred texts.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
Here, the contradiction regarding whether the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is a sense-organ (*indriya*) or not a sense-organ, as found in the scriptural texts, is resolved:
"Those [others] are the sense-organs, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one."

Is it not the case that all vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed sense organs (*indriyas*), according to the scriptural text, "The vital breaths are the sense organs"? Since this general scriptural statement applies universally, it cannot be sublated by the specific scriptural statement that "there are only twelve sense organs. This is because the general scriptural statement is stronger due to its logical consistency with the nature of flowing [toward objects]. Furthermore, it would be difficult to restrict the status of being a sense organ to only twelve, as it is impossible to exclude any one of them. Without a restrictive principle, if one were to be discarded, the same would apply to another, resulting in the loss of the fixed number twelve.

Therefore, since the second [interpretation] contradicts reason and scripture, it lacks authority; thus, the conclusion being reached that scripture is not applicable to Brahman, the following was set forth as a sūtra:

"Those [other breaths] are the sense organs (indriyas), because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one. This is the meaning: "With the exception of the best one," that is, the principal breath (mukhya-prāṇa); those other breaths are indeed the sense organs, but the principal breath is not. Why? "Because of their designation as such," meaning that in the Śruti it is stated, "The sense organs are exactly twelve."

Thus, not all vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are sense organs (*indriyas*); rather, excluding the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), there are only twelve. This is because of the specific scriptural statement that "there are only twelve sense organs. Nor should it be asked how this [chief breath], which possesses the quality of flowing (*dravaṇavat*), can be non-sensory; for while it possesses the state of being a master (*svāmitva*) over their flowing, it lacks this [specific] flowing itself. Since there exists the statement, "Because of the flowing toward their respective objects, they [are called sense organs]," the non-sensory nature of the chief vital breath is established without contradicting scripture. Therefore, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman, the cause of the world, is logically consistent.
Because of the scriptural teaching of difference.

Now, if the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is not an organ (*indriya*), then the eye also would not be one; for there is no difference whatsoever between the eye and the principal vital breath. This objection—based on the fact that the author of the Sūtras has not stated that [the eye] exists by way of the state of being stationary (as opposed to the state of moving), and because such a reason is irrelevant—is raised; in response, the Sūtra says:

"Because of the scriptural statement of distinction. This is its meaning: since the scripture declares that the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) possesses distinguishing attributes consisting of being the agent and the instigator of all actions, while others lack these, and since this is established in the Vedic text, it follows that the chief vital breath is not identical to the eyes and other senses. This is the sense.

And this being so, since the Śruti explicitly states that the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) possesses qualities such as being the agent and instigator of all actions, strength and the giver of strength, the supporter and the sustainer—thereby declaring its equality with the Lord—it follows that it lacks the status of being an instrument directed by an agent. Consequently, the non-sensory nature of the chief vital breath is established without contradicting the Śruti.
And because of the difference in nature.

Now, is this principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) under the control of the Lord or not? In the first case, its status as a non-sense organ (anindriya) is unestablished, because it is identical [to the senses] in being subject to the Lord. Furthermore, this subordinate distinction—such as its state of remaining stationary rather than moving—is possible even in the case of the sense organs. In the second case, there is a contradiction with what was stated regarding the eyes and so forth. This being the position reached, the author states the aphorism as a resolution: [The sūtra: "But that [is] the principal one, on account of its difference from those [senses]. (VS 2.4.9) This means: But that [breath] is the principal one, because of its difference from those [other senses]. It is indeed a sense organ, yet it is distinguished from the others by its specific nature, such as its immobility and its function of sustaining the body. Therefore, it is not a sense organ like the eyes and so forth, which are characterized by movement and the perception of external objects. Thus, the objection is refuted. The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the doubt raised. The word "that" (saḥ) refers back to the principal breath mentioned previously. The word "principal" (mukhya) indicates its preeminence due to its superior power. The phrase "on account of its difference from those" (tadvailakṣaṇyāt) expresses the reason for its distinction from the other senses. The term "those" (tat) refers to the group of senses beginning with the eyes. The word "difference" (vailakṣaṇya) denotes the possession of contrary characteristics. The meaning is that it is a sense organ, yet it is distinct from the others due to its unique attributes. The word "but" (tu) is used to exclude the possibility of it being a sense organ like the eyes and so forth. The word "on account of" (iti) signifies the cause. The word "therefore" (ataḥ) implies the conclusion. The meaning is: therefore, it is not a sense organ like the eyes and so forth. Thus, the objection is refuted.
