"And because of their difference in nature" (vailakṣaṇyāt). This is the meaning: since there exists a difference in nature between the principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) and the other vital breaths—consisting in the former's being dependent solely on the Lord and the latter's being dependent on both the Lord and the individual soul (jīva)—the status of being a sense organ (indriyatva) does not belong to the former, but only to the eyes and the rest. This is the meaning.

And thus, although the senses are dependent on the primary Lord, they function under the control of both the Lord and the individual soul (jīva), whereas the primary [prāṇa] possesses a distinct nature consisting of activity that is dependent on the Lord alone. Since this aforementioned distinction among the senses is established by direct perception, and since the primary [prāṇa] is established by the scripture stating "the fires are the prāṇas," it is therefore proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Hari as the cause of the universe is logical and not in contradiction with the sacred texts.
Thus ends the section concerning the sense organs.
Here, the contradiction with scripture regarding name and form is resolved:
"But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, because of the scriptural teaching."

[Objection: Is it not Viriñca alone who is the creator of names and forms? For there is a scriptural text stating, "Viriñca [is he]," and so forth. Nor does this contradict the other scriptural text beginning with "Then why? because this latter scripture is more authoritative due to its being supported by reasoning. Furthermore, this scripture does not intend to establish him as the instrumental agent; rather, since a primary meaning is impossible, a secondary meaning must be accepted. Therefore, since the other scripture contradicts this [latter] scripture which is supported by reasoning, that other scripture is not authoritative. To this, the author reads the Sūtra: *na sāmānyādapyupalabdhermṛtyuvanna hi lokāpattiḥ //* (Sūtra 2.4.13) [Response: Not so, even on account of commonality, because [the creatorship] is perceived [in another], just as in the case of Death; for there is no attainment of the world [of Viriñca]. (Sūtra 2.4.13) This means: It is not the case that Viriñca is the creator of names and forms merely on the basis of commonality. Why? Because [creatorship] is perceived in another [entity, namely Brahman], according to the scriptural text, "He who is the maker of these names and forms" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.12.7). Nor is there a contradiction with the other scriptural text beginning with "Then why? because that [text] refers to the Supreme Lord, whereas the text concerning Viriñca refers to a subordinate agent. Moreover, the text concerning Viriñca is not intended to establish him as the instrumental agent; rather, it intends to show that he is the material cause. Since a primary meaning is possible here, one should not resort to a secondary meaning. Thus, the other scripture is not non-authoritative, as it is not contradicted by a scripture supported by reasoning. This is the sense. As for the example "just as in the case of Death," it is like the scriptural text, "Death, verily, is a seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.20), where "Death" is a name of the Supreme Lord. Or, it is like the scriptural text, "From death, indeed, O Gārgī, from death one goes to immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3), where "death" refers to the body. In the same way, here too, the term "Viriñca" refers to the Supreme Lord. Nor is there an attainment of the world [of Viriñca] here, because the context concerns the Supreme Self. Therefore, Viriñca is not the creator of names and forms. This is the conclusion.

"But the fashioning of names and forms [proceeds] from Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching. This is the meaning: the word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. The "fashioning of names and forms" is the production of the manifold world consisting of bodies and senses, which are of the nature of name and form. This occurs solely from the Supreme Self who performs the tripartition—that is, who effects the mixture of earth, water, and fire—and not from Viriñca (Brahmā). Why? Because of the scriptural teaching; the meaning is that it is so stated in the Śruti: "The Wise One, having willed all forms... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7).

Thus, the Supreme Self alone is the creator of names and forms, according to the Śruti: "All forms... Nor is there any Śruti regarding Viriñca (Brahmā) as the creator; for since the creation of names and forms depends upon the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), the agency of the creator of that tripartition must primarily be declared as the agency of the creator of names and forms. Consequently, any Śruti mentioning Viriñca refers merely to him as an instrumental cause. Therefore, the objection based on the logical inconsistency of Viriñca’s status is also refuted. Thus, since it is established through non-contradiction with the Śruti that the body has Hari as its creator, it is proven that His causality of the universe is established by the harmonization (*samanvaya*) of the Śruti texts.
Thus concludes the section on designations.
Here, the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the cause of the body is resolved:
"The [body] consisting of flesh and so forth is composed of the earth element; the other two [elements] are likewise according to the scriptural statements."

Is it not the case that the body consists of water alone? For there is the Vedic scripture stating, "For this [body] arises from the waters," and because we observe that among the limbs of the body, such as the flesh and so forth, there is the presence of that which nourishes through unrighteousness (or: the presence of the watery element). Yet, it does not consist of the three elements [earth, water, and fire], because if that were so, specific designations such as "the waters are the body" or "the body of Hiraṇyagarbha" would be untenable. Alternatively, it is earthen; for it is stated that "the body goes back to earth," indicating its dissolution into the earth, and because it possesses qualities such as solidity. Or else, it is fiery; for there is the Vedic scripture, "He [arose] from the fire-god," and because heat is observed [in the body].

Therefore, since these three deities [are mutually exclusive], the Vedic scripture lacks authority; thus, it is argued that the status of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world cannot be established through the reconciliation of the scriptures. To this, the author states the Sūtra:

"Earthly [parts] such as flesh and so forth, according to their respective sounds, and likewise for the other two. This is its meaning: "earthly" (*bhauma*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). That which in the body is solid, such as flesh and so forth, is thus earthly or made of earth (*pārthiva*), but not the entire body. Rather, it is "according to their respective sounds," following the Vedic scripture that "that which is solid is earth. Furthermore, the effects of the other two—water and fire—must be admitted in the form of blood, marrow, and so forth. Just as flesh and so forth are earthly, being the effects of earth.
The meaning is that it is not only the effect of earth, but indeed the effects of the other two—water and fire—as well, which must be accepted according to scripture.

And thus, that which in the body is solid, such as flesh and so forth, is indeed the earthly (pārthiva) element; that which is blood and so forth is the watery (āpya); and that which is marrow and so forth is the fiery (taijasa). The body, however, is composed of all three [earth, water, and fire], because of the Vedic scripture stating, "That which is solid is earth. Nor does this contradict the scripture, "Water, verily, is flesh," for we do not maintain that flesh is exclusively earthly; rather, in accordance with scripture, it is intended that flesh is also an effect of water and the other elements. Therefore, since the five-elemental nature (pāñcabhautikatva) of the body is established without contradicting scripture, it is proven that the concordance of the scriptures with Brahman, the cause of the world, is logical.
But on account of its preponderance, there is a designation of that; indeed, there is a designation of that.

Now, it may be argued that if the body were not composed of multiple elements as its material cause (*prakṛti*), then the specific designation [of it as "earthy," etc. would be untenable; or, even if there were a specific conjunction of elements within the body or in flesh and so forth, since all elements are present in every body, it would be impossible to speak of specific designations like "earthy" based on the intended predominance of one particular element. Furthermore, since the meaning can be understood through the distinction of the subject matter, the repetition of the words of the Sūtra at the end of the chapter would be unnecessary for the purpose of signaling the conclusion of the chapter; otherwise, such a repetition would have occurred at the end of each section (*pāda*) as well. To this objection, he states the Sūtra: *na viśeṣāt* (Not so, because of the specific distinction). This means: It is not the case that the specific designations are improper. Why? Because of the specific distinction. For although all elements are present in every body, there is a specific distinction in the degree of their manifestation. Just as in the case of a mixture of water and milk, where the predominance of one is perceived despite the presence of both, so too in bodies, the predominance of earth and the other elements is observed respectively in flesh, blood, heat, and movement. Thus, the specific designations are justified by this distinction. Moreover, the repetition of the words of the Sūtra is appropriate for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the chapter, as it serves to distinguish the subject matter from what precedes; otherwise, if it were not for this purpose, the repetition at the end of the *pādas* would indeed be redundant. Therefore, the Sūtra is correctly stated.

"But on account of preponderance, there is that designation; that designation. This is its meaning: the specific designations "earthy," "watery," and "fiery" are appropriate because of preponderance (*vaiśeṣya*), depending upon the particular conjunction of each respective body with the elements such as earth and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural statement]. The repetition at the end of the chapter is for the purpose of confirming the entire subject matter taught in this chapter.

And thus, since bodies composed of the elements possess specific designations based on the presence of particular conjunctions with those respective elements, their distinct appellations are logically justified. Nor is there any contradiction regarding the absence of the aforementioned specific conjunctions, because of the statement "of earthly bodies. Nor is there a contradiction of redundancy, because the repetition of a word at the final sūtra of every chapter is performed for the purpose of ascertaining the meaning of that chapter.

Therefore, it is established that since the five-elemental nature of the body is proven without contradicting the Śruti, the concordance of the Śruti with Viṣṇu as the creator of the world is logical.
Thus concludes the section on meat.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter.
Thus the second chapter is completed.
Śrīḥ.
Hari Oṃ.
Now begins the third chapter.
This chapter is an investigation into the means of accomplishment.
Now begins the first quarter.
In this section, the determination of the states of existence and so forth is undertaken for the purpose of cultivating detachment.
In this context, the non-separation of the living being from the elements is established for the sake of dispassion toward the means of attaining the Blessed One.
*Oṃ*. Upon entering the intermediate state, it departs enveloped [by the elements], as is shown by both the question and the answer. *Oṃ*.

Now, it might be argued that the means (sādhana) need not indeed be practiced; for a means is to be practiced only for the sake of a result, and the result here is the cessation of bondage. This [cessation] does not differ from death, since bondage is the connection with the elements (bhūta), according to the statement: "The world-process (saṃsāra) is the bondage of the elements. Nor should the means be practiced merely for the sake of death, because death is observed even without the practice of detachment (vairāgya) and other such qualities. Consequently, this scripture would be rendered useless. To this, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Oṃ. Upon reaching the next state, it departs enveloped, according to the question and the explanation. This is the meaning: "Upon reaching the next state"—that is, for the purpose of attaining another body—the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped, joined with the elements such as earth and the rest; it is known that having abandoned this body, it goes to another world. Why? Because of the question and the explanation: from King Pravāhaṇa’s question to the seer Śvetaketu, "Do you know how...?
and from the answer given by Pravāhaṇa, "Yes, indeed..."—this is the sense.

And thus, because there exists a fruit in the form of the cessation of bondage, death itself is not the cessation of bondage; for it is accepted that at the time of death, the individual soul (jīva) departs while still enveloped by the elements (bhūta). This is because in the question "Or does he go? and in its corresponding answer, the envelopment by the elements of the deceased is explicitly stated. As for the statement regarding the "withdrawal of the elements," it is intended to mean the withdrawal of the *portion* of the elements [belonging to the subtle body], and thus there is no contradiction. Therefore, since liberation cannot occur through mere death, it is established that the means must indeed be practiced, and the scripture is purposeful.
Thus ends the section concerning the intermediate state.

In this context, the movement of the individual soul (jīva), enveloped by all the elements, is established for the purpose of attaining dispassion toward the means of reaching the Blessed One. Oṃ. But because it consists of the three [guṇas] and because of their predominance. Oṃ.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that only water accompanies the individual soul (jīva) and not all the elements? For the scripture states, 'Water is man' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.4). Otherwise, the scripture would have said 'the elements' (bhūtāni). Therefore, since the deceased lacks any connection with the totality of the elements, death itself is liberation; thus, detachment and the like are useless. To this, the Sūtra replies: sūkṣmaṃ pramāṇataśca tathopalabdheḥ || 3.1.7 || [The soul is] subtle, on account of the authority [of scripture], and because it is perceived as such. || 3.1.7 || The word "subtle" (sūkṣmam) here refers to the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which is composed of the five elements in their subtle state. This is established by the authority of scripture, such as "He consists of earth, he consists of water" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and by the fact that it is perceived as such through inference based on the experience of dreams and the like. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul's departure accompanied by the subtle elements: "When he departs, he departs together with the breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2), and "He takes these elements with him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1). Thus, the objection is refuted. The mention of "water" in the specific passage is merely illustrative, intended to show that the soul is accompanied by material elements. Therefore, since the soul remains bound to the subtle body until final liberation, detachment and other spiritual disciplines are indeed necessary.

"Oṃ. But because [water] consists of the three [elements] and because it is predominant. This is its meaning: The individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by all the elements, not by water alone. The specific mention of "water" is because water consists of the three elements—earth, water, and fire—and because among those, water is the most abundant and predominant. Thus, there is no contradiction; this is the sense.

And thus, because of the scriptural statement regarding "re-origination" (*punarutpatti*) in the phrase "and even so, water," re-origination is not possible in the absence of an embrace by all the elements (*sarvabhūta*). For bondage by the elements alone constitutes *saṃsāra*; in their absence, there would follow the consequence of liberation. Furthermore, a single element cannot constitute bondage. Nor is there any contradiction with specific scriptural texts; for since water is the cause of earth, fire, and air when they have been triplicated (*trivṛtkṛta*), the mention of water alone necessarily includes all of them.

Nor is there any reason to abandon the term "waters" (*āpaḥ*) and instead employ another word for earth and fire as well, on the grounds that they too are causes of the threefold-composed triad of elements—just as the waters are; for in all bodies, it is the plurality of the waters alone that serves as the determining factor. Therefore, it is established that all elements proceed by embracing the individual soul (*jīva*); and since liberation does not occur through natural death, it follows that dispassion (*vairāgya*) and other such means must be practiced.
Thus concludes the section concerning the threefold nature.
In this context, the departure of the individual soul together with the elements is established for the sake of proving dispassion.
Om. And because of the departure from the body. Om.

[Objection: Surely the elements do not go along [with the soul], because there is no proof for it. Nor are the question and the explanation [in the scripture] proof, since even in those two cases, the departure together with the elements is not perceived. Furthermore, an implied assumption (ārthika-kalpanā) is impossible without a specific means of knowledge (viśeṣa-pramāṇa). Therefore, liberation is simply natural death; so, enough with dispassion and the like. To this, the Sūtra says:

"Oṃ. And because of the departure of the vital breaths. This is its meaning: because it is heard in scripture that the senses—which are designated by the term "vital breaths" (prāṇa) and are pervaded by the elements—depart along with the individual soul (jīva), the meaning is that the soul departs enveloped by the elements.

And thus, since there exists the following inference—"The elements possess motion along with the individual soul (jīva), because they pervade the vital breaths that move together with it"—there is no lack of pervasion (vyāpti). For the scripture, in the passage beginning "Where indeed the elements [are]," declares the mutual relationship of pervader and pervaded between the elements and the vital breaths. Therefore, since the embrace of the individual soul by all the elements is established, liberation occurs through mere death; hence, it is proven that detachment and the like are not required.
Thus ends the section concerning the movement of the vital breath.

Here, the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) together with the individual soul (*jīva*) is established. Om. [The opponent objects: "Because of the absence of fire, and because there is no proof for the movement of the vital breaths, there can likewise be no movement of the elements; thus, death itself is liberation, and detachment and the like are useless. Having raised this objection, the author recites the aphorism (*sūtra*) to provide the resolution: "On account of the mention of fire. Thus, since there is movement of the vital breaths, the elements also move along with them. Therefore, death is not liberation, and detachment and the like are not in vain.

"Oṃ. 'Because of the scriptural statement regarding the departure toward fire and so forth'—if this is argued, it is not so, because that is figurative. This is its meaning: If it is argued that there is no departure together with the individual soul (jīva) because of the scriptural statement regarding the departure toward fire and so forth—stated in the passage "where [the breaths go] toward fire and so forth"—we say no. Why? Because it is figurative. The meaning is that the scriptural statement "where" refers to a portion of the vital breaths (prāṇa)."

And thus, because of the existence of the scriptural statement, "Verily, by these [they depart] not," there is no contradiction with the specific scriptural mention of fire (*agni*)—namely, that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) go to fire and so forth by way of their respective parts. This is because of the statement, "In the opinion of some. Furthermore, since it is accepted that at the time of regaining a body, those parts that had entered fire and so forth re-enter the parts accompanying the individual soul (*jīva*), there is no total departure [of the elements]. Likewise, even for the gross elements (*bhūtas*), there is a departure along with the soul by way of their parts; they proceed to fire and so forth by way of their parts.

Furthermore, when the body is acquired again, the portions of the elements that had gone toward fire and the other elements accompany the individual soul (jīva); this is understood through discernment. Therefore, since the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart along with the soul, the elements likewise depart; thus, liberation does not occur merely by death, and it is established that the means [to liberation] must be practiced.
Here, the departure of the elements together with the individual soul (jīva) is raised as an objection and then resolved.
Oṃ. [Sūtra 1.4.5: "If it be said that [the elements do not depart] because they are not mentioned in the first [case], we say no; for it is precisely those [elements] that are logical. Oṃ.

[Objection: "Surely there must be a departure of the elements (bhūta) along with the individual soul (jīva), because in that very passage [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2], 'In this very fire...,' the oblation is described as being accompanied by faith (śraddhā). Since the elements also depart together, it would follow from the introductory statement that they do so likewise. Therefore, for one who asserts that liberation is merely the cessation of the elements due to their lack of co-departure, it would absurdly follow that death itself is liberation; thus, the teaching on dispassion (vairāgya) would be rendered useless. Having raised this objection, the author recites the aphorism to provide a resolution.

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul does not go] because it is not heard of in the first [case], we say no; for it is those very [waters] that are referred to on account of the logical consistency. This is the meaning: "In the first"—that is, at the beginning of that [section]; "in the first," namely, in that which is called the sky; "because of the hearing of the oblation" in the first fire, and because there is no hearing of the elements accompanied by the living soul. If it be argued that the soul does not go accompanied by the elements, we say no. Why? Because "those very" waters under discussion are what are expressed by the word *śraddhā* (faith) occurring in the opening passage. Therefore, why is this so? "On account of the logical consistency" (*upapatteḥ*).
That is to say, because the concluding statement, "The waters become human speech," is logically consistent [only if the soul goes with water].

And thus, because it is heard in the case of the first fire that there is an oblation (*homa*) accompanied by the elements (*bhūta*), it must be stated that the elements go along with [the soul]. Furthermore, the word *śraddhā* (faith) denotes the living being (*jīva*) qualified by faith through a *jahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (a metaphorical indication where the primary meaning is abandoned). This is because, in the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), the movement of the waters together with the living being is heard. And since the beginning (*upakrama*) must be interpreted in accordance with the conclusion, it cannot be argued that the conclusion refers merely to the act of coming back; for no mention is made of the abandonment of those [elements] at the time of death.

Since no conjunction with the elements is mentioned in the interim, and because the phrase "the waters" must be understood as a restatement (anuvāda) in connection with the very act of departing, it is established that because the elements do indeed depart along with the individual soul (jīva), death is not liberation; therefore, the necessary means such as dispassion (vairāgya) and so forth are required.
Thus ends the first section.
Here, the departure of the individual soul (jīva) together with the elements is established.
Oṃ. If it be argued that this is not so because [the elements] are not mentioned in scripture, we say no; for those who perform sacrifices and other rites are known [to depart thus]. Oṃ.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no departure of the elements along with the individual soul (jīva), because there is no such scriptural statement. Nor is the simultaneous departure of the waters and the vital breaths (prāṇas) heard in scripture; therefore, by implication, the departure of the elements is also established as being scripturally taught. This objection is refuted by the fact that since there is no direct scriptural hearing regarding "the waters and the vital breaths," any implied scriptural teaching must be rejected. Furthermore, since reasoning operates only where there is the existence of direct scriptural hearing regarding a Vedic matter, even through reasoning that [departure] cannot be established. Consequently, since death itself would result in liberation, dispassion and the like would become non-performable. Having raised this objection, the author reads the Sūtra which refutes it: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] not so, on account of the going of the other [elements], according to scripture. (3.1.4) This means: It is not the case that the elements do not depart. Why? Because of the going of the others—namely, the waters and the vital breaths—as directly heard in scripture. Since the departure of the elements follows from the departure of those others, the objection does not hold. Moreover, because the departure of the soul is established by scripture, and because the soul's departure implies the departure of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which consists of the elements, the departure of the elements is necessarily established. Thus, since the soul departs at death for the purpose of attaining another body, liberation is not attained merely by death; therefore, dispassion and the other means are indeed to be practiced. This is the sense.

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the elements] do not accompany [the soul] because it is not so heard, we say no, because it is perceived in the case of those who perform sacrifices and the like. This is the meaning: if it be argued that the elements do not accompany [the soul] because there is no direct scriptural hearing (pratyakṣa-śravaṇa) of their departure along with the living self—as there is in the case of speech merging into fire (*agniṃ vāgapyeti*) and so forth—we say no. Why? Because of the perception (*pratīti*) of those who perform sacrifices and oblations (*iṣṭādikārin*) through the scripture beginning with "Then him... (*athainam*); the meaning is that the separation from and the conjunction with the elements are understood through direct perception itself.

Thus, since there is no direct scriptural statement [to the contrary], one must accept the non-hearing [of the soul by the elements]; for it is impossible to consider that the elements do not accompany [the soul] because they do not hear [it]. Furthermore, even an implied hearing contradicts non-hearing; and since the accompaniment of the elements with the soul at the death of the sacrificer is clearly stated, the movement of the elements is established everywhere by that very example. Therefore, because there is indeed an accompaniment of the elements with the living soul, liberation does not occur at death; hence, it is established that detachment and other such qualities must indeed be practiced.
Thus ends the section concerning the fact that [the soul] is not mentioned [in the context of the creation of the elements].

In this context, by stating that actions have unstable fruits for the sake of attaining the Blessed One, it is established that detachment and other such qualities are necessary means. Oṃ. "Or [the status of being a knower of Brahman] is figurative, because they do not know the Self; for thus the scripture shows. Oṃ.

Now, it might be argued that detachment (*vairāgya*) and the like need not be practiced by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because liberation is accomplished through ritual action alone, as the scripture states: "We have drunk the Soma. Nor should it be said that detachment and so forth must also be practiced because both are means [to the same end], for when a lighter means exists, a heavier means is not to be respected. Therefore, since liberation is accomplished by the easily performed ritual action, there is no further purpose for detachment and the like. To this, the following is stated in the aphorism:

"Or [the immortality] is figurative because they do not know the Self; for thus [the scripture] shows. This is the meaning: the immortality mentioned for those who perform rites for the sake of desires (*kāmyakarmin*) is figurative, that is, secondary. Why? Because they do not know the Self, since they lack knowledge of Brahman. By the word "or" (*vā*), the Sūtra indicates two alternative views: first, that even the immortality produced by the non-desirous rites performed by the seeker of knowledge (*jijñāsu*) and the knower (*jñānin*) does not consist of the primary immortality characterized by the cessation of *saṃsāra*; rather, it consists of the unsurpassed, supreme, and primary [immortality] in the form of the excellence of bliss resulting from the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, it points toward these two positions.

Why is this so? Because the Śruti—through the passages "or he who knows the immortal," "he [the teacher] leads him," "by means of action," and "the Self"—shows and establishes these very points as they have been stated; that is the meaning.

And thus, since liberation is not established if dispassion and the other [means] are not practiced, there is no contradiction with the Śruti. For action is of two kinds: that performed for desire (kāmya) and that not performed for desire (akāmya). Even the action not performed for desire is of two kinds: that which precedes knowledge and that which follows it. All of this is indeed the meaning of the Śruti, due to the difference in the qualifications of the practitioners (adhikāribheda). When the Śruti refers to action performed for desire, it does not speak of primary immortality, but rather of a figurative sense consisting in living for a long time.

However, when [the text] refers to optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) that precede knowledge (*jñāna*), it speaks primarily of their being a means to immortality; indeed, it does not say this directly, but rather states that for one whose nature is purified by action, these rites serve as a means to liberation through the mediation of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth. On the other hand, when it refers to rites subsequent to knowledge, it says that they provide an excellence (*atiśaya*) to liberation once it has been accomplished by knowledge. Since such a distinction exists, in no way does [the text] directly state that action is the primary means to liberation.
Therefore, since liberation is not established without the practice of dispassion and so forth, it is proven that the scripture teaching those [practices] is not useless.
Thus concludes the section concerning figurative application.
Here, the necessity of practicing the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) is established.
Oṃ. "At the end of [the fruit of] what has been performed, one possesses residual karma (*anuśaya*), according to both perception and scripture. Oṃ.

Now, it may be argued that there is no need for dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, since liberation from *saṃsāra* is possible simply through the exhaustion of karma already endowed with such qualities by means of its experience alone; for when the seed [of karma] is absent, the absence of *saṃsāra* necessarily follows. Nor should it be said that liberation from *saṃsāra* does not occur because other karmas might be performed during the time of experiencing [the fruits], for although there is a rule regarding the performance of karma during the time of experience in this world, such performance is absent in places like heaven; thus, when all karma is exhausted through experience right there [in heaven], liberation from *saṃsāra* becomes possible.

"Oṃ. 'Upon the exhaustion of what has been performed, one returns with a remainder, according to perception and scripture. This is its meaning: when there is an exhaustion—that is, a depletion—of the performed karma through enjoyment in heaven and so forth, it is known that one returns to this world possessing a remainder, that is, possessing only that which was not fully enjoyed. Why? Because of perception and scripture; the meaning is: because of the scripture indicated by the word 'perception' in the phrase 'then by the remainder,' and because of the Smṛti which speaks of 'the remainder of what was enjoyed.'"

And thus, since it has been established by both Śruti and Smṛti that there is no total exhaustion of those very actions that bring about heaven and other results, the impossibility of the destruction of all karma is even more certain. For when one action is being experienced, because of the performance of endless other actions, that experience remains incomplete; and even after two or three cycles, there is no destruction of all karma, according to the Smṛti which states, "until the fourteenth year. Therefore, it is established that the means such as detachment (vairāgya) are indispensable.
Thus concludes the section concerning those whose transgressions have been expiated.

Om. "In the same way as they came, and also not so. Om.

"Oṃ. 'In the same way and not otherwise. The meaning of this is: by which path (*yathā*) the individual soul (*jīva*) has gone—that is, reached heaven and so forth—in that very way (*tathā*), and also "not otherwise" (*anevam*), by another path, the soul returns to this world; such is the meaning.

And thus, because there is the specific scriptural statement, "From smoke to the cloud," and because there is no contradiction with the previous scripture since it is accepted that the return follows the same path as the ascent up to the ether; and because there is no conflict with that [scripture] since reasoning is not applicable due to the soul's lack of independence in the return; therefore, it is established that one must become dispassionate even toward the fruit of heaven, as the return and so forth involve excessive hardship.
Thus ends this section.
In this context, it is established that coming and going constitute the fruit of karma.
Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul's departure] is due to its "going forth" (caraṇāt), we say no; Kārṣṇājini holds that this is for the purpose of indicating [all actions]. Oṃ.

But is it not the case that coming and going is the fruit of conduct (*caraṇa*) alone, and not of rituals such as sacrifice, because of the scriptural text, "Those who here..."; and because conduct is distinct from ritual action, given the scriptural text, "As he acts," and the traditional law (*smṛti*), "Conduct" (*ācāra*); and because of the scriptural text, "And those who here...," it follows that coming and going is the fruit of sacrifice alone, and not the fruit of conduct? No. For [the word] "conduct" (*caraṇa*) is used in the sense of "action" (*karman*). This is understood from the scriptural text, "As he acts," and from the traditional law, "Conduct. Furthermore, the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is employed to denote all ritual actions; for it is seen that the word "sacrifice" is applied to other actions as well, as in the passage, "The sacrifice, gift, austerity, etc., performed by one who does not believe. Therefore, the meaning is that coming and going is the fruit of all ritual actions, including both good and evil. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural text, "Those who here... Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural text, "And those who here... because the latter refers to those who perform sacrifices and the like, while the former refers to those who do not. Hence, there is no inconsistency. Moreover, the scriptural text, "He reaches the world of Brahmā," shows that the fruit of sacrifice is indeed the attainment of the world of Brahmā. Therefore, the conclusion is that coming and going is the fruit of all ritual actions. Furthermore, the scriptural text, "Having reached the end of his deeds in that world," indicates that the fruit of ritual action is subject to exhaustion. And the scriptural text, "From there he returns again according to his deeds and according to his knowledge," shows that the fruit of ritual action is characterized by returning. Thus, it is established that coming and going is the fruit of ritual action. Therefore, the statement, "For him there is no return to this world," is made in reference to the person who possesses knowledge, because for him there is no return at all. But for the person who lacks knowledge, there is a return to this world. Consequently, the scriptural text, "From there he returns again according to his deeds and according to his knowledge," is appropriate. Thus, the meaning of the entire section has been explained. Now, the following doubt arises: since the fruit of knowledge is liberation, which is eternal, why is it said that "he returns no more"? To resolve this, the text says: "Because he has reached the end of his deeds. The meaning is: because he has reached the end of all works that produce fruits to be experienced in this transmigratory existence. Alternatively, the meaning is: because he has reached the end of the works that cause rebirth. Since he has reached the end of those works, he returns no more. However, the works whose fruits have already begun to manifest must necessarily be exhausted through experience. This is what is meant by the phrase, "Having reached the end of his deeds in that world. Therefore, the meaning of the entire section is as follows: the fruit of knowledge is liberation, which is eternal and characterized by the absence of return; whereas the fruit of ritual action is transitory and characterized by coming and going. Thus, having distinguished between the two, the text concludes with the words, "For him there is no return to this world. This is the meaning. Now, the doubt arises: if the fruit of knowledge is liberation, which is eternal, then how can the scriptural text, "He becomes one with Brahman" (*brahma-saṃsthaḥ*), be interpreted? To resolve this, it is said: "One who is established in Brahman is one who has renounced all actions and is intent on meditation. This is the meaning.
