The word "iṣṭāpūrte" (sacrifices and charitable works) is explained by the prefix "upa," which denotes proximity, thereby referring to the conduct [of the Vedic way], while the term "iṣṭāpūrte" itself denotes sacrifice. Since both types of results are indicated by the passage beginning with "they attain the smoke," and since the two kinds of heaven are mentioned, and because the word "atha" (then) in the scripture indicates that this is the fruit of conduct, one might argue that since the coming and going has other fruits, and since a heaven free from rebirth is established through ritual action alone, there is no need for dispassion and the like. To this, the Sūtra states:

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the attainment of results] is due to conduct (*caraṇa*), we say no; for Kārṣṇājini holds that this is intended as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of both sacrifice and conduct]. This is the meaning: the coming and going [to higher or lower worlds] does not result from sacrifice and the like alone, but rather from conduct—that is, from the very practice which constitutes a limb of sacrifice. If it be argued that this is not so because the scripture mentions only "conduct," why? Because the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains that the scriptural statement is intended to indicate both sacrifice and conduct by means of a definition that does not abandon its own primary sense (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*). Such is the meaning.

And thus, by the scriptural text "nor by another path," the fact that the fruit which is empty—consisting of going and returning—is to be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*) is prohibited; for both the scriptural text "sacrifices and works of public utility" (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and the Smṛti text "of those who know the three Vedas" (*traividyānām*) declare that going and returning is the fruit of ritual action. Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural text "those who here... (*tad ya iha*), since, in accordance with the previously cited scriptural passages and others, that text can be explained as having the purpose of [encouraging] sacrifice and so forth, through *jahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication where the primary meaning is abandoned). This is also evident from the clear scriptural text beginning with "by sacrifice" (*atha yajñena*).
Moreover, the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains this very view; therefore, it is established that there is an absence of the status of being a fruit of karma for what has gone and returned.
Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Veda] is purposeless, we say no, because it depends upon that. Oṃ.
Having raised an objection to what was stated, he provides a resolution and explains the sūtra.

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the word *caraṇa*] is purposeless, we say no, because it is dependent upon that. This is the meaning: if the word *caraṇa* were intended merely as an indirect indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would be purposeless. Why? Because the performance of good and evil deeds could already be indicated by the words "pleasant" (*ramaṇīyaka*) and "foul" (*pūya*) respectively. If this is argued, we say no. Why? "Because it is dependent upon that. That is to say, it is dependent upon that—namely, the possession of good or bad sacrifices and so forth—which in turn depends upon conduct (*ācāra*) and the like. Thus, the meaning is that the word is purposeful insofar as it serves to convey that [specific quality].

And thus, since it has been stated that there would be a contradiction with the Śruti and other authorities if one were to deny that "conduct" (caraṇa) serves as an indicator for sacrifice and so forth—given the resulting consequence of conduct being purposeless—it is accepted that the word "conduct" is used to indicate sacrifice and the like, while its specific function is merely to make known that for those who perform sacrifices and such acts, their pleasantness arises solely from their good or bad conduct. Therefore, it is established that because going and returning is the fruit of karma, one must become detached from both that process and its results, which are means of suffering.
Oṃ. But Bādari [maintains] that it is only good and evil deeds [that follow]. Oṃ.
He recites the sūtra which explains the scriptural passage concerning conduct (caraṇa) by means of another method.

"Oṃ. But Bādari [holds that] only good and evil deeds [are meant]. This is its meaning: "Good and evil deeds" refers to virtuous and non-virtuous actions; however, the teacher Bādari maintains that the word *caraṇa* found in the Śruti denotes only the performance of those constituent parts [of the rites]. By the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates that this is his own established position.

Thus, the word *caraṇa* denotes precisely sacrifices and the like. Even if one accepts the meaning "perform dharma," there is no contradiction because of the usage *carati*. Since *karoti* and *carati* are synonyms, it is established for all that the word *kṛta*—which denotes that which has been accomplished—applies to every ritual action such as sacrifice that serves as a means to merit (*puṇya*) and is denoted by the term *dharma*; therefore, since they are synonyms, it is unavoidable that the word *caraṇa*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, also applies to such actions. Moreover, the teacher Bādari maintains this very view.

Therefore, since coming and going are the fruits of karma, it is established that one must become dispassionate toward that which accomplishes the afflictions and toward that which is accomplished by them.
Thus concludes the section concerning the feet.
Here it is established that even for those who perform undesirable deeds and so forth, there exists the suffering of going and returning and the like.
Oṃ. It is also heard [in scripture] regarding those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. Oṃ.

Is it not the case that the affliction of coming and going belongs only to those who perform meritorious acts such as *iṣṭi* sacrifices? For they are possessed of fear regarding injunctions and prohibitions, according to the maxim: "Fearing, one falls from the tree. Furthermore, desire is indeed the cause of the fruit of action only when it is conjoined with the performance of the ritual act, but not as something manifested by it. And those performers of *iṣṭi* and other rites, being full of desire, bind themselves by their own accord through injunctions and prohibitions; for only one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) is subject to injunctions and prohibitions, whereas those who have not been initiated are like children.

For it cannot be said that the scripture beginning with "the twilight devotions every day" applies to those who have not been initiated; otherwise, it would follow that Śūdras and others are also subject to it. Therefore, the suffering of coming and going belongs only to those who perform meritorious and sinful deeds, and not to those who are intoxicated by sin alone; rather, for them there is only liberation. Thus, one must cultivate detachment toward merit and its fruits, and not engage solely in the performance of sin. To this, the Sūtra says:

"Oṃ. And also for those who perform undesirable acts, according to scripture. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to include other types of suffering. It is not only those who perform desirable acts such as sacrifices who undergo the process of going and returning; rather, this applies even to those who perform sinful acts contrary to rites such as sacrifice—acts denoted by the term "undesirable. Why? Because it is so stated in scripture; that is, because it has been declared in the Śruti passage beginning with "Those here... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7). This is the sense.

And thus, for those who have performed [actions] with a specific intention (*saṃkalpa*), there is no reckoning of merit and demerit; rather, there is the affliction of coming and going and so forth even for those who are intoxicated by, or devoted to, demerit alone. This is because the cited scripture describes the affliction of coming and going for each [type of being] individually. Therefore, it is established that what was stated is correct.
Oṃ. But for others, after experiencing [the results] in Saṃyamaṇa, there is ascent and descent, because their destiny is seen [in scripture]. Oṃ.

It is not merely the coming and going of those who perform undesirable deeds; rather, there is another thing of extreme suffering indicated by the word "and" (ca) in the preceding sūtra. With this meaning in mind, he introduces the following sūtra to establish it.

|| Oṃ || "But for others, after experiencing [the results] in Saṃyamana, there is ascent and descent, because their destination is seen. This is the meaning: the word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. The locative case is used in the sense of the accusative. In *saṃyamane*, that is, in the hell [of Yama]. For those others—meaning those other than the performers of sacrifices and the like—who remain after having fully experienced the governance of Yama, there is "ascent and descent": for some there is ascent, which is rising up from hell; for others there is descent, which is falling even further down into a place of woe, into an eternal hell. Why? Because their destination is seen [in scripture].
The meaning is: "because of their going there"—that is, because of the scriptural statement that "all" go by such a path for those who perform undesirable deeds and so forth.
Thus it is established that what has been stated is logical.
Oṃ. And they remember. Oṃ.
Supporting the stated meaning with a scriptural citation, he recites the Sūtra:
"|| Oṃ || And they remember. The meaning of this is: the authors of the Smṛtis establish the stated point by means of such Smṛti passages as "they go," and so forth.

Thus, there is no contradiction with the absence of fear, desire for rewards, and so forth; for even one who is not afraid and is devoid of desire for results may perceive that a particular object of enjoyment is a cause of death. Therefore, since even those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin) are far removed from liberation due to the great harm [involved], it is established that one must be dispassionate toward that [world] as well.
Thus ends the section concerning that which is undesirable.
Here, the eternality of hell as the fruit of hating the Blessed One and so forth is established.
Om. Even seven times. Om.

[Objection: Is it not the case that hell is not a means to suffering [only] after one has emerged from it? For in passages such as "as long as there are fourteen Indras," a limit is heard. Nor is it logical for both [the eternity of hell and its being a means to suffering] to be true, because of their contradiction. Nor can there be a systematic arrangement based on different persons, since emptiness is declared in the statement, "He made hell empty. Consequently, what was stated previously—that some descend after having experienced [the fruit] in Saṃyamana—is incorrect; therefore, one should cultivate an even greater detachment toward hatred of the Lord than toward other sins. This being the position reached, the Sūtra is stated: [The answer: No, because of the scriptural declaration of a limit. It is not that the word "limit" refers to the cessation of the experience of suffering, for that would contradict the fact that the experience itself is eternal. Rather, the limit refers to the end of the state of being a denizen of hell. For it is said: "Having experienced [the fruit] in Saṃyamana, they descend," which implies that after the experience is finished, they emerge from that state. Therefore, the objection that the previous statement is incorrect is refuted. Thus, one should indeed cultivate a superior detachment toward hatred of the Lord compared to other sins. This is the established conclusion.
"Oṃ. 'Even seven'—the meaning of this is as follows: the authors of the Smṛtis establish, through their traditional texts (smṛtis), that there are seven kinds of hells, beginning with Raurava."

And this would indeed be so if there were only a single hell; but it is not so. For, based on the statement "What indeed is Raurava?", there are seven groups of hells. The phrase "the wheel of hell" refers to the five hells beginning with Raurava. The passages beginning with "they do not rise up at all" refer to Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra. Furthermore, there are many other minor hells, and these also yield impermanent results. Therefore, since the fruit of hatred toward the Blessed One and similar acts consists of eternal hell, it is established that one must inevitably go to that very place [Vaivasvata] as a consequence far exceeding other sins.
Thus ends the section on the "even seven."
Here, the fact that hell is characterized by suffering is established. Oṃ. And even in that case, there is no contradiction because of its operation. Oṃ.

Is it not the case that hell is not characterized by suffering? For if it were, it would follow that even God (Īśvara) would experience suffering. Just as in the case of the power-distinction (*śaktivaiśeṣya*)—wherein, because the earth lacks the inherent nature of producing suffering for all those dwelling upon it, only the individual soul (*jīva*) experiences suffering and not God when both reside together on earth—it might be argued that such a distinction is possible here. However, since hell possesses the inherent nature of producing suffering for all who dwell within it, such a partiality (*vaiṣamya*) is impossible. Nor can it be argued that there is no consequence of suffering for God because He is absent from there.

Since the scripture states that "He emits everything," the Lord is the cause of all effects; therefore, in the absence of a Lord there, suffering would be even more impossible. Consequently, since the absence of suffering is possible in both cases [whether one accepts or rejects the Lord], it follows that one need not cultivate detachment toward that [state]. To this objection, the Sūtra provides the following response:

"Even there, there would be a contradiction regarding His activity and so forth. This is the meaning: the word "ca" (and) indicates the sense of "even without the experience of suffering. Thus, even in that case, if the Lord were to remain in hell and exercise control over the living beings residing there, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti which states "all [this is pervaded by Him]. If He exercises such control, there would be the experience of suffering; therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction in either of these two positions.

And thus, even regarding hell, since the agency of Īśvara is accepted, the defect of being without a cause does not arise. For hell also is under His control; by experiencing [the state] as such, he acts as its impeller, and thus there is no acquisition of suffering for Him. This is because of the Vedic revelation, "He is heaven," and the Smṛti statement, "even in hell. And so it is established that, since hell is characterized by suffering, one must cultivate detachment toward it precisely therein.
Thus ends the section on that as well.
Here, the independence of living beings regarding their destiny is refuted. Oṃ. But [the soul's movement depends] on knowledge and action, because these are the subjects under discussion. Oṃ.

[Objection: Surely living beings (jīvas) are indeed independent with respect to the fruits such as going [to heaven] and so forth, because of the statement, "Now, of these two... For if there were no independence, the designations "they go" and "they do not go" would not be appropriate. Nor should it be said that the independence of the living beings has not been established; for we accept that they possess an independence granted by the Lord, similar to their possession of instruments and fruits. Therefore, according to the maxim that "one who has already obtained the fruit at the root does not desire to go to the tip of the branch," since independence exists only with respect to the fruit, what is the need for the means of dispassion (vairāgya)? [Response: To this, the Sūtra states:

"‘But because ignorance and action are the subjects under discussion’—this is the meaning [of the Sūtra]. The word ‘but’ (tu) is used for emphasis. In the Śruti passage, ‘Of these two paths,’ the phrase ‘of these two’ refers specifically to knowledge and action, and not to the paths of smoke and light, by which the soul’s independence regarding the fruit [of its actions] might be established. Why? Because they are the subjects under discussion; that is to say, because those two [knowledge and action] are also the subjects under discussion in the preceding text, ‘Those who live thus...’"

And thus, there is no evidence for the independence of living beings regarding their movement and so forth. Now, as for the word "of these two" (*etayoḥ*) occurring in the scripture, since both the path of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the path of ritual action (*karman*)—introduced by the phrase "those who [know] thus"—are under discussion, this sentence establishes [the reference] by referring back to them; for its nature consists in pointing out [their] independence. Nor can it be argued that there is no definitive conclusion due to doubt—as to which [path] this refers—on the grounds that both the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths are equally under discussion, just like the paths of knowledge and ritual action.

Because the reference [to the means] is established by the statement "the path of knowledge" (vidyāpatha), it follows that since there is no independence regarding the fruit, the required proximate causes such as dispassion (vairāgya) and so forth are established.
Thus concludes the section on knowledge (vidyādhikaraṇa).
In this context, it is established that blind darkness consists of nothing but suffering.
Oṃ. [Sūtra: "Not so in the third case, because it is perceived as such. Oṃ.

"Is it not the case that even the deepest darkness (andha-tamas) is indeed endowed with happiness? Because it is joined with suffering; for suffering is inseparable from happiness, according to the saying: 'Where there is suffering, there is happiness. Therefore, since happiness exists even in the deepest darkness, there is no need for extreme detachment toward it. Anticipating this objection, the author states the sūtra:

"Oṃ. Not in the third, because it is perceived as such. This is its meaning: "In the third"—that is, in the third darkness among the downward destinies (adhogati) described as the animal realm and the hells—there is no happiness; this is the ellipsis. Why? Because it is perceived as such; that is to say, because it is experienced as such.

Thus, since there is the existence of the scriptural statement, "And so, the ignorant one [performs] action," and the Smṛti passage, "Not for those submerged in blind darkness," it is established that because there is an absence of even a trace of happiness in that blind darkness, there must be detachment toward it and its means.
Oṃ. And it is also recorded in common worldly usage: Oṃ.
Establishing this very point through both memory and inference, he introduces the Sūtra.

"Oṃ. And it is also recorded in the world. This is the meaning: "In blinding darkness" refers to the absence of happiness; this is both recorded by the author of the *Smṛti* and established by the *Smṛti* itself. Furthermore, the meaning is that this is also established in the world by means of inference based on universal observation (*lokadṛṣṭavyāpti*).

And thus, according to the Smṛti statement "likewise among animals," it is established that those under dispute do not possess happiness, because they are not so intended by the Lord. For there exists the following inference: whatever is not intended by the Lord in a certain way is not so [endowed]; just as a crested one (a peacock), being undesired [by the Lord] as having horns, is not horned. And this state of being undesired by the Lord is established by the reason of being disliked by Him. Therefore, it is proven that there is an absence of even a trace of happiness in the blinding darkness.
Oṃ. And because it is seen [in scripture].
Establishing this point even through direct perception, the Sūtra says:

|| Oṃ || "And from [the] vision" (darśanāt). The meaning of this is: the absence of happiness in the third [state] is established by the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of Hiraṇyagarbha; such is the sense.

And thus, by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, with the eye of knowledge fully developed, he himself—without depending on the mouth of another—spoke of the absence of happiness upon seeing the Four-faced One (Brahmā). Therefore, it is established that there is not even a trace of happiness in the blinding darkness.
Oṃ. In the third [case], there is the apprehension of sound for one born of grief. Oṃ.
He introduces a sūtra that supports this point through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

"Oṃ. In the third, there is the obstruction of sound for that which is born of grief. This is its meaning: the word "in the third" is repeated. It refers to the third darkness; even there, in the third, blinding darkness, with respect to that object, there is the "obstruction"—that is, the attainment—of sound for that which is born of grief, meaning for delusion (*moha*) produced by intense sorrow. This is the sense.

Thus, since it is otherwise inexplicable that those who hear of the lower darkness (adhara-tamas) should fall into delusion merely by hearing of it, and because it is established that the suffering therein is limitless and lacks even a trace of happiness due to its intensity, it is proven that there is an absence of even a fraction of happiness in the blinding darkness (andha-tamas).
Oṃ. And because of recollection. Oṃ.

Now, how is it known that hearers fall into confusion upon hearing the nature of the third state? Anticipating the objection that the absence of pleasure there is understood through the principle of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*)—since it cannot otherwise be accounted for—the author recites the Sūtra as a refutation.

"Oṃ. And because of the Smṛti. The meaning of this is as follows: the fact that hearing about the third type of darkness (the third *tamas*) results in delusion for the listener is established by both [scriptural authority] and the Smṛti statement, "And great darkness (*mahātamas*). Thus, both [points] are proven.

Thus, it is not the case that the attainment of delusion by those who merely hear [this teaching] is unestablished, for there is the traditional authority (smaraṇa) stating, "The great darkness is threefold. Therefore, since there is an absence of even a fragment of happiness in the blinding darkness, it is established that there must be detachment toward that [darkness] and toward its causes.
Thus ends the third section.
In this case, the state of being smoke and so forth is excluded for one who performs ritual action.
Oṃ. That [Self] attains the state of being of that [Brahman], because it is logical. Oṃ.

[Objection: Surely it must be accepted that for the performer of rituals there is either the attainment of smoke and so forth, or identity with them, because of the statement, "having become smoke" (*dhūmo bhūtvā*). By virtue of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in this sentence, both the state of being smoke and so forth and the attainment thereof are perceived; this is just as a king's son attains the title of "king" through the power of affection, or as Arjuna attained identity with Indra—both cases being equally plausible. Therefore, since even in these two ways there is no possibility of attaining supreme bliss until the end of the kalpa for those who perform sacrifices but once, dispassion toward ritual action and its fruit is useless. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: *na sāmānyādapyupalabdhermṛtyuvat* (Sūtra 3.1.24). [The answer is: No, because even on the basis of similarity, [the meaning] is perceived, as in the case of death. (Sūtra 3.1.24) [Commentary: It is not the case that the performers of rituals attain identity with smoke and so forth. Why? Because even on the basis of similarity, such a meaning is perceived. Just as in the world, when one says, "He has become like his father," it is understood that he has attained a similarity to his father, not identity. Likewise, here too, the statement "having become smoke" (*dhūmo bhūtvā*) means that they attain a state similar to smoke, not identity with it. Furthermore, the word *bhūtvā* ("having become") denotes the attainment of a state of similarity. This is because the root *bhū* is used in the sense of attaining a state of similarity, as seen in expressions like "he became like his father" (*pitṛvad abhavat*). Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is perceived from the context, whereas identity is not. For example, when it is said, "Having entered the enemy's city, he dwelt there," it is understood that he merely entered the vicinity of the city, not that he became the city itself. Similarly, in the passage beginning with "Having become smoke, he becomes mist" (*dhūmo bhūtvā megho bhavati*), the attainment of smoke and so forth is understood from the context, while identity is not. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a transformation of the body, whereas identity is not, because it would entail the impossibility of returning [to earth]. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the subtle body. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the gross body, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the gross body. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the senses, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the senses. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the vital breaths. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the elements, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the elements. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the mind, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the mind. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the intellect. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the ego. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the latent impressions. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the field (*kṣetra*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the field. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the knower of the field. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the Lord (*īśvara*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the Lord. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the individual soul. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the Supreme Self. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the unmanifest. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the manifest (*vyakta*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the manifest. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the cause (*kāraṇa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the cause. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the effect (*kārya*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the effect. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the means (*upāya*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the means. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the goal (*upeya*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the goal. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the path (*mārga*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the path. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the destination (*gati*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the destination. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of time (*kāla*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of time. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of space (*deśa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of space. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of action (*karma*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of action. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of knowledge (*jñāna*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of knowledge. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of ignorance (*ajñāna*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of ignorance. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of merit (*puṇya*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of merit. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of demerit (*pāpa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of demerit. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of dharma, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of dharma. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of adharma, whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of adharma. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the world (*loka*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the world. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the non-world (*aloka*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the non-world. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the seen. Moreover, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the unseen. Furthermore, the attainment of smoke and so forth is logical because it is a modification of the heard (*śruta*), whereas identity is not, because it would result in the destruction of the

|| Oṃ || "The attainment of that very nature [occurs] because it is logical. This is its meaning: in the case of the ritual action, there is the "attainment of that very nature" (*tatsvābhāvyāpatti*). That is, the attainment of the very nature—or of a nature similar to the nature—of those deities such as Dhūma. It is not identity with them, nor is it the attainment of their station. Why? Because it is logical (*upapatteḥ*). The meaning is that this alone is the correct sense, since the identity of one thing with another has never been observed.

Thus, because the existence of one thing as another is impossible, and because that state (tatpada) is attainable only through knowledge by those with fixed eligibility, and because it is impossible for many performers of ritual action (*karmi*) gathered together simultaneously to attain the same state; therefore, the meaning of the scripture is that the attainment of its own essential nature consists precisely in becoming like that—such that when it moves, there is movement, and when it stands still, there is standing still. Consequently, since there is no identity between the smoke and so forth [of the path], it is established that detachment from those actions and their fruits is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section on "having that as its inherent nature."
In this context, it is established that for the ritualist who has descended from heaven, the attainment of dwelling in a womb and so forth occurs before long.
Oṃ. "Not very long, because of a specific statement. Oṃ.

But surely, Karma, having departed from heaven, obtains a body in another kalpa; for in passages such as "returning by the same path through space," there is scriptural mention of reaching many places at the time of his return. Furthermore, that journey cannot occur without delay, because it would be possible for him to experience immense pleasure in each respective place according to its own nature, and thus there would be no purpose in leaving them to return. Nor can it be argued that a long duration of stay is untenable due to the smallness of his merit.

This is because, through the actual presence of the deity there, it is possible to acquire the favor of the deity, which is the cause for remaining [in that state]. For it is not possible that a discerning person, while in the presence of a generous and great lord, would fail to obtain their desired object without having propitiated him. Nor should it be argued that, such being the case, there is no attainment of a body even at the end of the kalpa; for at the end of the kalpa, since one's own familiar deity has attained liberation, there is no possibility of propitiating another deity due to the absence of familiarity with them.

And since, by the mere practice of desires, there exists happiness for an aeon (akalpa), what is the use of detachment from action and its fruit?—this being the position reached, the author recites the aphorism:

"Oṃ. 'Not after a very long time, because of a distinction'—this is its meaning: Having departed from heaven, the person performing ritual action (karmī) returns to earth and attains a birth as a Brāhmaṇa or other [caste] not after a very long time, but indeed without delay. Why? Because of a distinction; that is to say, because of the specific statement, 'Those here... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).

Thus, since there is the scriptural teaching [of transmigration] and the existence of the Smṛti stating "from heaven," and because it is impossible for the fruit of action to persist for an excessive duration given that its time is fixed, and because the Lord has established that the acquisition of merit occurs in this very world, it is impossible to perform further worship of deities there; therefore, it is established that one must become detached from action at its very outset, since the sufferings of dwelling in a womb and so forth will inevitably follow shortly thereafter.
Thus ends the section [concerning] "not long after."
In this context, the absence of suffering caused by becoming rice and so forth for those who perform ritual actions is established.
Om. "In that which is presided over by another, as before, because of the scriptural statement. Om.

But surely, for those performers of ritual acts, there exists a powerful suffering—distinct from the incidental suffering that arises immediately—that is not absent for them; for it is heard in scripture that "they [become] rice and so forth" (*te iha vrīhyādi-bhāva-śravaṇāt*). And since suffering necessarily follows from the cutting and so forth involved in that state, such a claim is untenable. It should not be argued that this scriptural passage, regarding sacrifices and the like, refers merely to the entry into the form of rice and does not intend their actual transformation into that state; for when there is no subverting evidence, one cannot abandon the primary meaning. Furthermore, if one accepts merely the entry into rice and so forth, suffering remains unavoidable.

Even when one dwells among those who suffer, the cause for not experiencing that suffering is precisely the fruit of actions such as sacrifices. Therefore, since the karma taught in the Veda is a means to suffering, it produces pain; consequently, because there would be no confidence even in detachment (vairāgya) and other means taught as causes of liberation, it follows that such karma is not to be practiced. To this objection, the Sūtra replies:

"Oṃ. 'In another presided over [by another], as before, because of the statement. This is its meaning: for the one who performs ritual actions (*karmī*), there is only entry into a body such as rice or barley that is "presided over by another"—that is, a body in which another living being has the sense of self-identification (*abhimāna*)—but not the state of identifying with it oneself, whereby suffering would arise. If this is so, how is the statement of non-difference, "He becomes rice and barley," to be explained? To this it is said: "as before. Just as in passages such as "having become smoke," there is a statement of becoming smoke and so forth, so it is here. Why is this so? "Because of the statement" (*abhilāpāt*). The meaning is that it is so stated in the scripture: "He went downwards" (*so 'vāggataḥ*).

And thus, in the absence of any authoritative proof (*māna*), one should not consider that there is suffering for those performing ritual actions (*karmin*) by virtue of their becoming rice and other such grains. For this scriptural passage merely states the entry of the performer of rituals into the bodies of rice and so forth. Nor does the attainment of suffering follow from coexistence with suffering, because coexistence is not the causal factor (*prayojaka*); rather, it is the absence of that causal factor [of suffering]. It is not the case, however, that the meaning of the scripture is merely the entry into the bodies of rice and so forth, nor that they become those very things. If you ask, "On what basis is this certain?"—that has already been explained below.

Because of the scriptural designation "entering into stationary beings" and because of the mention [of such states], it is established that the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*) is appropriate, since sacrifices and other rites are taught as means for attaining happiness.
Om. If it be argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śruti). Om.

Now, having raised the objection that because sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma involve injury, they are the basis for sin, and therefore suffering is unavoidable even in the form of rice and other grains, the author states the sūtra which provides the resolution:

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the sacrifice] is impure, we say no, because of the scriptural word. This is its meaning: if it is argued that because the sacrifice takes the form of violence, the action is impure and a means to suffering, we say no. Why? Because of the scriptural word; that is to say, because it is enjoined by Vedic statements.

And thus, although external violence is a cause of sin, the violence prescribed by such injunctions as "one should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" is a cause of merit; therefore, sacrifices and the like are not mixed with sin. This is because of the Smṛti text: "Violence [that is] Vedic is not [sinful]. Consequently, since that which is taught as a means to happiness—such as sacrifice—is not a cause of suffering, it is established that the practice of dispassion (vairāgya) is appropriate.
Thus ends the section concerning other [deities].
Here, the entry of the father [into the child] of one who has descended from heaven is established.
Om. Now, the connection with the progenitor. Om.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no entry of the father into the *jīva*, because of the statement "only [into] the mother"? Nor does this contradict the Śruti text, "He who becomes a householder," because that Śruti—being supported by the reasoning of the absence of purpose—is weaker than the other Śruti and thus intends to prohibit the father’s entry even by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku-svara*). Consequently, since there is an absence of excessive hardship, an extreme degree of dispassion toward ritual action and the like is not required. This being the position reached, the Sūtra states: *na ca paryāyādapyavirodhaḥ pariśeṣāt* (Sūtra 3.1.18). [Response: And there is no contradiction even on account of succession, because of the remainder. (Sūtra 3.1.18) The meaning is as follows: The Śruti, "He who becomes a householder," is indeed not contradicted. For the phrase "he who becomes" (*yo bhavati*) is intended to indicate the sequence of stages of life (*āśrama*), meaning "he who, having been a student, becomes a householder. Since the father’s entry is established by the Śruti, "From the father he is born again," and since the mother’s entry is established by the statement, "Only into the mother," there is no conflict. Furthermore, the Śruti regarding the father’s entry is not set aside by the reasoning of the absence of purpose; rather, it is more powerful. Therefore, because there is excessive hardship, an extreme degree of dispassion toward ritual action and the like is indeed required. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

"Oṃ. 'First, the union with the seed-sower'—the meaning of this is as follows: for the performer of ritual action (karmī), first occurs the union with the seed-sower, that is, the connection or relationship with the father who pours the seed; in other words, entry into him. Then, immediately after that, entry into the mother occurs, but not at the very beginning."

Thus, the entry of the father into the soul [of the child] certainly exists, because of the Vedic scripture stating, "From that [father], the seed [comes] for the soul. Nor does this mean that there is no entry of the father; for the entry of the father is possible for the soul that is about to be born, as it serves to purify that soul through the creative power (*kalpā*) of the Lord. Furthermore, the scriptural statement "only from the mother's womb" is not invalid, because the entry of the mother is also accepted as occurring after the entry of the father. Nor is the restrictive emphasis "only from the mother" untenable.

This is because, when the term "smṛti" refers to the common state of the individual soul (jīva), we accept that the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) has the sense of excluding what is impossible (*ayogavyavaccheda*); however, when it refers to the state of the soul entering the perfected body of one dwelling in the womb, there is also the sense of excluding what is other (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Therefore, since the attainment of the ancestors is still present [at that stage], it is established that there must be intense detachment toward ritual action and the like.
Thus ends the section concerning the seed.
In this context, the attainment of a body by the individual soul (jīva) after entering the womb through the father is established. Om. From the womb, the body [is produced]. Om.

Is it not the case that for one who has come from heaven, there is no acquisition of a body by entering the mother through the vaginal door—just as in the case of a father—and then proceeding through the stages of the *kalala*, *budbuda*, and so forth? Rather, for some who have come from heaven and entered the father, there is the attainment of a body by entering the mother without sexual contact, solely by virtue of merit; while for another, even without entering the father, there is such attainment by entering the mother through food and other means, due to possessing even greater merit than the former.

In both cases, there is the attainment of a perfected body—either while still within the mother’s womb in the *jarāyu* (membrane), or upon emerging from it for another; however, there is no fixed rule that for anyone coming from heaven, the attainment of a body through the mother’s womb via the gateway of the birth canal must necessarily follow the sequence of the embryo (*kalala*), the bubble (*budbuda*), and so forth, as is the case with sinners. Consequently, since there is an absence of great hardship, it follows that there is no need for intense dispassion (*vairāgya*). To this, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the attainment of a body] occurs through the conjunction of the soul with a body brought about by past karma, and through the agency of the *guṇas*. (YS 3.22) [Commentary: However, even for one who has come from heaven, the attainment of a body occurs through the conjunction of the soul with a body produced by past karma, and through the agency of the *guṇas*. Just as in the case of a sinner, the attainment of a body through the mother’s womb follows the sequence of the embryo, the bubble, and so on, so too for one returning from heaven, the attainment of a body occurs through the conjunction of the soul with a body brought about by past karma, and through the agency of the *guṇas*. Therefore, because of the presence of great hardship, there is indeed a need for intense dispassion. Thus, the Sūtra is stated.

"Oṃ. 'From the womb, the body'—this is its meaning. The ablative case here is used in the sense of an elided verbal suffix (*lyap*). The meaning is that the agent, having entered the mother's womb by way of the father, then obtains a body therein; it is not obtained without that [entry]."

And thus, because there exists a fixed rule—namely, that even for one who has come from heaven, there is first entry into the father, then entry into the mother through the birth canal, and thereafter the acquisition of a body through the sequence of the *kalala* and so forth—and because of the scriptural statement, "those who dwell in heaven," there is no contradiction with the passage stating, "the body situated in the womb. For since such a condition applies only to some, those statements refer exclusively to them and do not apply to all inhabitants of heaven.

Therefore, since entry as a father or other relative at the time of ordinary birth is invariably accompanied by great suffering—such as the loss of heaven and so forth—it is established that the Lord should be worshipped by one who is dispassionate.
Thus ends the section concerning the womb.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter.
Śrīḥ.
Om. May there be auspiciousness. May Hari be victorious.
Now begins the second quarter.
Devotion is taught in this section.

Here, for the sake of devotion which is the means to attaining the Blessed Lord, the greatness of the dream-world—which consists of the knowledge of objects—as being dependent upon the Blessed Lord is described. "The creation in the intermediate state [is real], for so the scripture says."

[Objection: But surely the object of a dream is not dependent on the Lord, because it is non-existent. Nor is the reason unproven, because [the object] is not perceived before or after [the dream]. Nor should it be argued that the absence of perception before and after is not a defect, since we accept that its creation occurs at that specific time; for there is a lack of evidence [for such a claim]. To this, the Sūtra says: *na bhāvo 'nupalabdheḥ.* (2.2.29) [The dream object is] not [non-existent], because it is not [absolutely] unperceived. (2.2.29) [Commentary: It is not the case that the dream object does not exist. Why? Because it is not [absolutely] unperceived. For it is perceived during the time of the dream. And it is not the case that its existence is contradicted by the fact that it is not perceived before or after the dream, because we accept that its manifestation occurs precisely at that time. Furthermore, the reason—that it is not perceived before or after—is not unproven, because it is indeed perceived at the time of the dream. Moreover, the argument that there is no proof for the claim that the Lord creates the dream object at that specific time is invalid, because there is scriptural authority for it. As the scripture says: "He makes bodies with one, two, or many limbs; he makes them similar or dissimilar; he, the wise one, being himself without limbs, creates all. Therefore, the dream object is indeed dependent on the Lord. Thus, the conclusion stands. || 2.2.29 ||*

"Regarding the intermediate state, there is creation, for so the scripture says. This is its meaning: "For" (*hi*) means because; the scripture, in the passage beginning with "Then [he creates] chariots," states that the Lord's creation occurs in the intermediate state—that is, in the dream state which exists between waking and deep sleep. Therefore, there is creation; the meaning is that the creation of the objects of the dream state arises from the Lord alone.

Thus, the objects of a dream are indeed dependent upon Īśvara, because they exist [only during that time]. Nor does it follow that they should be perceived before or after that time, for it is accepted that their creation occurs only at that specific time. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for this, as the Śruti states, "He creates chariots... Therefore, since it is established that the objects of a dream are under the control of the Blessed Lord, His supreme majesty is proven; thus, it is logical that devotion toward Him is appropriate. This is established.
And some [hold that the Lord is] the creator, as well as sons and so forth.

One might object: "Since there is no agent, a creation occurring during the time of sleep is not logical. For the individual soul (*jīva*) is not its agent, because it is asleep; nor is the Lord (*īśvara*), because there is no evidence for him [in that context]. Furthermore, in neither of these two cases is creation tenable, since no agent of production and destruction is perceived at that very time. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the following sūtra to resolve it:

"And some [mention] the creator, as well as sons and so forth. This is its meaning: "And" (*ca*) means "because. Some followers of particular recensions (*śākhins*) remember this Blessed One—as the one who creates the objects of dreams, according to the text "He who [creates] while these [others] sleep"—while others mention "sons and so forth," saying that they are born from Viṣṇu alone. Therefore, the meaning is that the creation of the dream state belongs to Viṣṇu alone.

And thus, there is no impossibility of creation due to the absence of a creator, because the agency of the Lord alone is accepted based on the scriptural passages: "He who [is] in these" and "From Him alone. Therefore, it is established that the dream-creation belongs to Viṣṇu alone, and devotion toward Him therein is appropriate.
But [the Lord is] indeed Māyā, because His essential nature is not manifested in its entirety.

If it is argued that dreams are indeed perceived as external objects, and that these are perceived by everyone both before and after [the dream], we reply: if one accepts that [the self] perceives external objects while remaining within the body, there would be the undesirable consequence of not seeing Meru, Mandara, and other such distant mountains. If, on the other hand, one maintains that [the self] goes outside [the body], then for one who has fallen asleep in the Kuru region and sees the Pañcāla region [in a dream], it would follow that his entry back into the body occurs only after he has awakened. Furthermore, there is the perception of spring by one who has slept during the winter.

And at that time, there is no existence of the soul (sattā) by which it might see, whether remaining within the body or having gone outside; nor is there a cause for the cognition of external objects, because the sense organs have ceased to function and because the mind lacks independence with respect to external objects—this being the position reached, the Sūtra states:

"But it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its true nature is not fully manifested. This is the meaning [of the sūtra]: the word "tu" (but) has the sense of emphasis; the intermediate state (saṃdhyam) is mere illusion, constructed solely by the two things designated by the word "māyā"—namely, desire (icchā) and latent impressions (vāsanā)—which serve as its efficient and material causes, and not by external causes. Why? Because its true nature is not fully manifested; that is to say, because its true nature is not perfectly manifested, unlike external objects.

And thus, because the material cause (*upādāna*) exists by way of its objective basis (*nimitta*): for it is accepted that mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in the mind serve as the material cause through the power of memory, while the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Since objects such as Mount Meru, which consist of latent impressions, can be perceived by the mind alone, there is an absence of external causes. Furthermore, there is no contingency of perceiving the prior stages such as the lump of clay or the subsequent stages such as the potsherds [in the case of dream objects]. Therefore, since it is established that the objects of a dream depend upon the Blessed Lord, it is proven that devotion toward Him is appropriate therein.
For the scripture indicates it, and those who know that [reality] declare it so.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the objects of a dream were produced by external things, then they would not possess reality, just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the following sūtra:

"And because it is indicative, for those who know it declare so according to scripture. This is the meaning: "And" (*ca*) is used because [it is so]; the object of a dream is "indicative" (*sūcaka*), meaning it makes known good and evil fortune. For this reason also, it is not unreal. Why? Because of the scripture that says "when... (*yadā*); and because of the observation of results through direct perception—this is the sense of the word "for" (*hi*). Furthermore, "those who know it," namely the experts on dreams such as Vyāsa and others, "declare so. The meaning is that even the scriptures, when stating "when...", speak of the dream objects possessing causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

And thus, because reality alone is determined to be the cause of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; and because, through the two scriptural statements "when [there is] action" and "the person," as well as by perception accompanied by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the causality [of the Lord] is established; moreover, Vyāsa and others consider it so, or [they hold it] on the strength of the statement, "Whatever a Brāhmaṇa may say, that is the deity. Therefore, since the object of the dream is established as being dependent upon the Blessed One, His majesty is proven, and it is thus established that devotion toward Him is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section on the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
Herein is described the majesty of the Blessed One as the concealer of the dream-like state:
"But through meditation on the Supreme [Lord], [the self] is concealed; for from that [concealment] arise its bondage and its opposite (liberation)."

Now, an objection is raised: "The disappearance of the dream state is not dependent upon the Lord. Since that [disappearance] is produced by external cognition, it follows from the destruction of ignorance that the continuity [of the dream] persists; thus, because the disappearance of the dream is possible through the destruction of ignorance by means of cognition, it is not dependent on the Lord, and therefore He does not possess supreme majesty. To this, the Sūtra says:

"But by meditation on the Supreme, [the soul's nature] is concealed; for from that [Supreme] come its bondage and its opposite. This is the meaning: "For" (*hi*) means because; "from that" (*tataḥ*) means from the Supreme Self; "of this" (*asya*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*); "bondage and its opposite" (*bandhaviparyayau*) means bondage and liberation. Therefore, "by meditation on the Supreme" (*parābhidhyānāt*)—that is, solely through the will of the Supreme Self—the intermediate state (*saṃdhyam*) becomes concealed or dissolved. The meaning is that it does not arise from any other cause.

And thus, since both knowledge and ignorance lack independence due to their insentience, just as bondage and liberation are dependent upon the Lord, the cessation of dreams is likewise dependent on Him. Therefore, it is established that devotion toward Him is appropriate because of His supreme majesty.
Thus ends the section concerning the meditation on Parā.
Here, the greatness of Viṣṇu as the initiator of the world is described;
even his dwelling [arises] from his connection with a body.

[Objection: Is it not the case that waking is not dependent upon the Lord? For it is dependent upon time. Nor can it be argued that its dependence on Him is untenable because time is insentient; for since the dependence on time is established by direct experience (*anubhava*), the inference of its insentiency has its object sublated. Furthermore, this experience is not an error, as there is no sublater (*bādhaka*). Therefore, since the waking state is not dependent on the Lord, the Lord does not possess such great majesty [in relation to it]. To this, the Sūtra states: [The answer: It is not so, because of the scriptural statement regarding the Lord's sovereignty over all states. (BrSū 2.3.39) The meaning is as follows: waking is indeed dependent upon the Lord. This is because of the scriptural declaration of His sovereignty over all states: "He who controls the waking state from within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11). Nor is it contradictory that an insentient entity like time should be subject to the will of a sentient being. Just as the body, though insentient, is controlled by the soul, so too is time controlled by the Lord. Nor is the experience of time's independence a delusion, for there is no sublater. On the contrary, the very fact that time is perceived as a distinct category proves its dependence, just as the perception of a body as distinct from the soul proves its subservience to the soul. Thus, the waking state is indeed dependent on the Lord, and His majesty is therefore unsurpassed.

"Even the state of being clothed [in a body] arises from the conjunction with a body. This is its meaning: even the waking state, which consists of abiding through the identification with a body, arises solely from the supreme contemplation (parābhidhyāna) and not from anything else; such is the sense.

And thus, because of the scriptural statement, "He alone is awake in the waking state," even the inference of insentience serves to negate [the idea that He is] dependent on time. Since perception is invalid when it contradicts scripture, whereas perception regarding time as a mere instrumental cause remains valid due to the absence of sublation; therefore, it is established that devotion to Hari is appropriate, given His supreme majesty as the instigator of the waking state.
Thus ends the section on the conjunction with a body.
Here, the greatness of being attained during sleep is described:
"The absence [of that state] occurs in the channels; [its presence] in the Self, because of the scriptural statement to that effect."

Now, an objection may be raised: sleep does not occur in the Supreme Self alone, nor in that which is qualified by its location in the channels (nāḍīs), nor in the connection with the channels; for this would entail the occurrence of suffering. For even when the individual soul (jīva) resides in the Lord who is situated in the eyes and other organs during the waking and other states, suffering is observed due to its connection with the body. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion, because it is established by subsequent recollection that at the time of deep sleep there is the experience of nothing but bliss. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: [The Sūtra: "But [the soul] is connected with the channels, because of the scriptural statement. (BrSū 3.2.7) This means: the soul is indeed connected with the channels during sleep, because scripture declares so. As it is said: "When a man sleeps here, he becomes united with the prāṇas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). Furthermore, the soul's connection with the channels is not the cause of suffering, because the channels are merely the pathways for the movement of the soul; they do not themselves constitute the locus of experience. Moreover, the soul's connection with the channels is not possible in the absence of the Supreme Self, for the soul cannot exist independently of Him. Therefore, the soul remains in the Supreme Self while being connected with the channels during sleep. This is confirmed by the fact that upon waking, the soul remembers the state of blissful sleep, which would be impossible if it had experienced suffering. Thus, the objection is refuted.

"His absence [of waking and dreaming] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of the scriptural statement regarding them; thus it is said. This is the meaning: for this individual soul (*jīva*), his "absence"—that is, the absence of the waking and dreaming states—occurs in the channels and in the Self, which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing within the channels; deep sleep (*suṣupti*) arises. At that time, his entry into that [Self] takes place. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "Then he is in these channels," meaning that such is heard in the scripture. He states the logical justification for this point by using the word "thus" (*ha*).

Thus, deep sleep occurs in the Supreme Self (paramātman) residing within the channels (nāḍī). Otherwise, one of the two scriptural statements—"In these [channels]" (Chāndogya 8.6.3) and "With the Existent, O gentle one" (Chāndogya 6.8.1)—would result in being invalid. Furthermore, there is no attainment of suffering; for while the connection with the channels is accepted for the Supreme Self alone, it is not accepted for the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, since the Lord resides in the channels and possesses the great majesty of being the goal attained in deep sleep, it is established that devotion toward Him is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section on the non-existence of that [world].
Herein, the majesty of Hari’s power to awaken those who are asleep is described.
Therefore, awakening arises from this.

Now, it might be argued that not every instance of awakening from sleep is dependent upon the Lord, since in some cases we observe that things such as the beating of a drum serve as the cause. Therefore, since there is no awakening of all beings [simultaneously], he does not possess supreme sovereignty. To this objection, the Sūtra states:

"Therefore, awakening is from Him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2). This is its meaning: the awakening of this individual soul (jīva)—its rising from sleep—occurs only from this Supreme Self (paramātman) and not from anything else. Why? Because it is heard in scripture that "He alone [awakens him]" (eṣa eva...); such is the meaning.

And thus, since living beings are indeed asleep within the Blessed One, awakening is impossible without His command; furthermore, because the perception that the beating of a drum and so forth are independent causes is contradicted by the Śruti and is therefore invalid, it is established that since He alone is the cause of all awakening, unsurpassed devotion is appropriate toward Him who possesses such great majesty.
Thus ends the section on the locus of awakening.
Herein is described the majesty of the Lord's sovereignty over all persons, at all times, and in all states.
And He alone [is the cause], on account of the scriptural texts concerning action, remembrance, and injunctions.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the Lord is not the impeller of all things in all times and in all states? Because He is the sovereign, like a king; for since it is possible to interpret [the scripture] as referring to some other controller, there is no contradiction with the Śruti text, "For this one alone... Nor can the status of being the controller of all—which contradicts reason—be accepted as the meaning of the Śruti in the absence of a clear scriptural designation. Therefore, since He does not impel all states, Hari does not possess universal sovereignty. To this, the author of the Sūtras reads the following:

"And that very [Lord] alone [is the impeller], on account of the action, the recollection, the word, and the injunction. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "also. "That very one" means the Lord alone; he is the impeller of all beings at all times and in all states, and there is no other in another place or time. Why? On account of action, recollection, the word, and the injunction. For there is the scriptural revelation that actions are dependent upon the Lord: "For he alone... There is also the corroborating traditional recollection stating that he is the "director. Furthermore, there is the word "this one" (eṣa), and the injunction "himself" (ātmānam). Such is the meaning.

And thus, because He is the regulator of all actions, and because states such as deep sleep are included therein; because the cited Śruti and Smṛti exist as authoritative evidence; and because of the injunction, "He [creates] these dreams"; and because if anything other than Him were the instigator of dreams and so forth, it would be impossible for the Supreme Self alone to be the object of worship—it is established that devotion is appropriate toward the Lord of great majesty, who impels all states of existence.
Thus ends the section concerning the recollection of karma.
Herein is described the greatness of the Lord as being attainable by the individual soul (jīva) residing in His intermediate state:
"In the state of swoon, there is partial attainment [of Brahman], because of the remainder."

Now, it might be argued that delusion does not belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) with respect to anything other than the Blessed Lord, but rather [it belongs] to the Supreme Self alone, because [the state of delusion] is distinct from the states of waking and dreaming; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of their confusion. Nor does the acceptance of delusion in the Supreme Self entail the consequence of it being merely a part of deep sleep, for that part is accepted precisely because its objects are external things. Thus, when it is established that delusion belongs to the individual soul only insofar as it pertains to the Supreme Self, the Sūtra says:

"In the state of fainting (mugdha), there is half-attainment [of the Self], because of the method of elimination (pariśeṣāt). This is its meaning: "In the state of fainting" means in a swoon; "half-attainment of the individual soul" (jīva) means its partial entry into the Supreme Self. Why? "Because of the method of elimination"—that is to say, by means of an inference preceded by the negation of all other possible alternatives.

And thus, in the case of the Lord, there is only a half-entry of the individual soul (jīva) into delusion (moha), not a complete entry; this follows by the method of elimination (pariśeṣāt). To explain: regarding delusion, there is indeed a half-entry consisting of distance from, proximity to, or entry into the Supreme Self. However, these three alternatives are not possible, because they are attributes belonging to the states of waking and so forth. And since the other [alternatives] have been negated and no other possibility remains, the remaining half-entry of the soul into delusion must be accepted. This would be the case if delusion were distinct from the three states. If it is asked, "How is that so? [the answer follows].

On this point, it must be asked: is it said that delusion (*moha*) is included within the state of deep sleep (*supta*), or within the states of waking (*jāgrat*) and dreaming (*svapna*)? It cannot be the first, because of the differences [between them]. To explain: one who is deluded sometimes breathes heavily; his body trembles; his face becomes terrifying; and his eyes are wide open. One who is asleep, however, has a serene face, breathes regularly and repeatedly, and his eyes are closed; nor does his body tremble.

By merely pressing with the hand, they can awaken one who is asleep, but not one who is in a state of swoon (*mugdha*). Even with the blow of a mallet, there is a difference between the cause of swooning and that of sleep; for swooning has its cause in the blow of a pestle and the like, whereas sleep has its cause in deep tranquility (*succhāyā*). Therefore, they do not say that one who is swooning is "asleep. Nor is it included within the states of dreaming or deep sleep, because its objects are not seen to be distinct from those of suffering and time. Thus, swooning is indeed a separate state.
Consequently, it is established that devotion toward the Blessed Lord is appropriate, owing to His great majesty as the one attained through the state of swoon.
Thus ends the section on attainment.
Here, the fact that the Lord, in all His forms, is free from defects and possesses every perfection is established:
"Even on account of His abode, the Supreme does not possess both characteristics [of being with and without qualities], for everywhere [He is described as such]."
