"Even from the standpoint of location, the Supreme possesses neither dual characteristics, for everywhere [it is so]. This is the meaning: "Of the Supreme," that is, of the Paramātman; "even from the standpoint of location," that is, even due to the difference in locations such as the eye and so forth; "dual characteristics," that is, a divided form, does not exist. Rather, the form situated in all places—every location—is one and the same. Why? Because there is a scriptural statement (śruti) here beginning with "for" (*hi*), which means "because" (*yasmāt*) [it is so] in all cases. Therefore is the sense.

Thus, it should be understood that Hari, though appearing in diverse forms such as Viṣṇu and others and occupying distinct locations, is indeed non-different. This is because the inference of His difference based on His occupation of distinct locations is sublated by the Śruti text "in all [He is one]. Therefore, it is established that devotion toward Him is appropriate, for He is devoid of internal difference and is endowed with the fullness of all attributes everywhere.
If it is argued that [the whole] does not [exist] because of the difference [of its parts], we say no, because each [part] is not stated to be that [the whole].

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that non-difference between the universe and so forth is untenable? For it has been stated [in the commentary] that because the scripture speaks of 'cause and effect,' there is the designation of distinguishing attributes," and so on. Having raised this objection, he sets forth the aphorism as a resolution.

"If it be argued that there is no non-difference because of difference, we say no, because each is individually declared to be not that. This is the meaning: If it be argued that there is no non-difference among the forms such as Viśva and the rest, on account of their being bound by cause and effect—that is, because one hears of the distinguishing property of being the generator of the experiences of dream and waking—[we reply] "no. Why? Because each [of them] is individually declared to be not that; the meaning is that there is scriptural evidence for their non-difference in the passage, "Those which are these selves... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20).

Thus, because such scriptural passages as "This indeed is His Self," "He is this very one," and "This is indeed Hari" convey non-difference; and furthermore, because the scripture stating "He is without measure, yet of infinite measures" declares the non-difference of the root-form from the infinite forms such as the Universal (Viśva) and others; therefore, it is established that devotion should be directed toward Hari, who is devoid of internal difference.
Moreover, some [hold] thus.

Now, it may be argued that it is not proper for the scriptures teaching non-difference to sublate the scriptures teaching difference, because the former have scope as they refer only to certain specific aspects [of the Lord]. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural text "This one is indeed the three Haris," since in that passage there is no mention of mutual non-difference even in their fundamental forms, and non-difference is not clearly perceived there as it is in the text "This is your Self. Therefore, the author recites the sūtra which dispels the doubt that, on the strength of the scriptures teaching difference, Viṣṇu and the others must indeed be distinct.

"Moreover, 'thus some [read] as one'": because some followers of certain recensions (śākhins) read in the scripture, "Thus, as one," both non-difference and the state of having manifold forms; the meaning is that even in the case of non-difference, the designation of difference is justified by the difference of locations and so forth.

And thus, certain followers of other recensions (śākhins) read of non-difference [of the Lord] with the forms beginning with Viśva; therefore, it is established that devotion toward Hari is appropriate because He is devoid of internal difference and is full of all auspicious qualities.
Thus ends the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Not even from the standpoint of place" (na sthānato 'pi).
Here, Viṣṇu’s non-material form is established:
"For that [form] is indeed like the formless, because it is the primary [subject]."

Objection: Should not supreme devotion (*bhakti*) toward the Lord be rejected? For if one accepts that the Lord possesses a form (*rūpitva*), there follows the contingency of His being non-eternal; and if He is formless (*arūpa*), there follows the contingency of the scriptural testimony (*śruti*) being invalid. Consequently, devotion would be lost, for unsurpassed devotion is not possible toward a non-eternal body, nor is it tenable if the scripture declaring formlessness is invalid. Since the same logic applies if the scripture on formlessness were invalid, and since the qualities that motivate devotion are established by the very fact that scripture as a whole is authoritative, devotion would be untenable; thus, this [fourth] quarter [of the book] would be useless. To this, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Indeed, it is like that which is formless, because it is the primary [subject]. This is its meaning: Brahman is indeed "like that which is formless," meaning it is devoid of natural (prākṛta) form. Why? Because it is the primary subject—that is, because it is superior to primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth. Furthermore, the word "hi" (indeed) indicates the scriptural authority of the Śruti passage, "Not coarse" (asthūlam). Such is the meaning.

And thus, devotion to the Blessed One is indeed required; for His formlessness is free from defects such as the invalidation of scriptural authority regarding the nature of His impermanence. Nor is His formlessness unestablished, since His lack of material form is established by the excellence of His primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, since devotion is thus logically justified, it is established that this chapter (pāda) is meaningful.
And like light, it is not purposeless.

One might object: "If Brahman lacks form, then scriptural passages describing it as having a golden hue and so forth would be rendered meaningless; moreover, it would follow that beauty, auspicious marks, and other such qualities are absent. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the following sūtra to refute it:

"And like light, [the scriptures] are not purposeless. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) indicates a reason. "Like light" means just as in the case of extraordinary light such as that of the eyes, there is no such conventional usage as "there is no light. "Not purposeless" means that the scriptural texts describing the form of Brahman do not lack authority. Why? Because even though it is formless, it is accepted that it possesses an extraordinary form; this is the sense.

Thus, there is no futility of scriptural passages such as "of golden color" (rukmavarṇam), nor is there an absence of beauty and the like, because an aprākṛta (non-material) body is accepted. Therefore, it is established that devotion to the Lord is indeed required.
And it says: "That alone."

Now, an objection is raised: How can Brahman possess a nature distinct from the world, by virtue of which there is an absence of defects such as impermanence? For it is a rule that all forms are essentially composed of primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth; moreover, no distinction has been stated regarding His form in comparison to other forms. To this, the author of the Sūtras reads the following aphorism:

And it says, "consisting of that alone" (tanmātra). The meaning of this is as follows: because the Śruti states that Brahman is "of a single essence," it declares—that is, speaks of—Brahman as consisting of that alone, having the unique nature of consciousness and bliss. Therefore, the sense of the word "and" (ca) is that there is no statement of any difference [between them].

And thus, because the existence of scriptural authority as indicated is present, it is established that Brahman possesses a nature distinct [from the world] and is free from defects such as impermanence.
Moreover, it is shown [in scripture] and also recorded in traditional texts (smṛti).

[Objection: "But has it not been stated that in the two cited scriptural passages, only Brahman’s nature as consisting of knowledge, bliss, and so forth is expressed, and not that bliss and the rest are the body of Brahman? Therefore, since the scriptural statement regarding 'having a body' (dehitva) mentioned by the word *rūpin* lacks a subject matter in the form of a shape unlike that of the world, its purposelessness and the absence of beauty remain unresolved. Nor can it be argued that because the form (*rūpa*) and the possessor of form (*rūpin*) are non-different, that [beauty] is also intended by the scripture—as was said in the *Tattvapradīpa*. For, due to the lack of explicit statement, there is no definitive conclusion. Anticipating this doubt, he recites the following sūtra to dispel it:

"And it shows, moreover, it is also recorded in Smṛti. This is the meaning: the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). It is not only that [the scripture] shows that Brahman has the nature of bliss and so forth; rather, by the phrase "through the knowledge of That," the Śruti also shows—that is, establishes—that knowledge itself has the nature of Brahman. The word "atho" (moreover) indicates another point. Furthermore, the fact that knowledge also has the form of Brahman is recorded in the Smṛti by Vyāsa and others in such passages as "like pure crystal," and so on.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is not without scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*) that knowledge and bliss have the nature of Brahman.

And thus, since it is established that Brahman possesses a nature distinct [from the world] and that its various forms are mutually non-different—and because of the Smṛti statement, "It resembles pure crystal"—that very [Brahman] is logically accessible through devotion; therefore, it is proven that this quarter [of the verse] is meaningful.
Thus ends the section concerning the formless realm.
Here, the difference-in-identity (bhedābheda) between the Lord and the individual soul is refuted.
For this very reason, there is the analogy [of the Lord] being like the sun and its reflections, and so forth.

Now, it is established by scripture and other means that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and this is accepted by you as well. This being the case, the following argument is employed: "The individual soul is non-different from the Supreme Self, because it is conscious, and because it is a part of Him, like the fish [and other analogies]. Thus, even though the Lord is distinct from the individual soul, since non-difference also exists, and since if there were identity with the soul's defects He would necessarily be subject to corruption, devotion toward the Supreme Self would not be appropriate. To this, the author states the aphorism: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly before the actual *sūtra* is quoted.]

"And for this very reason, the comparison is like that of the sun and so forth. This is its meaning: "For this very reason" means precisely because of the statement of non-difference between the Lord and His forms; and "for this very reason" means precisely because of the reasons such as sentience. "The comparison" refers to the soul's similarity to the fish and so forth. If it is argued that there is non-difference from the Lord as in the case of the fish and so forth, the word "no" is to be supplied. By the word "and" (*ca*), he combines the similarity of difference. Why?

The meaning is that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection, it is distinct [from Brahman], just as the reflection of the sun and so forth in water is distinct from the sun and so forth. Alternatively: for this very reason, because it is stated that there is no difference between the fish and others [who are emanations] and Brahman in terms of qualities such as knowledge; for this very reason, "like the reflection of the sun and so forth"—the comparison is with the reflection of the sun and so forth. Since the soul possesses a portion equal to the fish and others, and since there would otherwise be no distinction [between them], the comparison is that it is a reflection of Brahman.

Therefore, the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not non-different from Brahman, precisely because it is a reflection of Brahman, like the sun's reflection in water and so forth. Alternatively: "ataeva" means precisely because of the two qualities under discussion—dependence on Him and similarity to Him. The comparison "like the sun's reflection and so forth" is an illustration; it is due to being a reflection of the Lord, and not due to dependence on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the like. The meaning is that the status of being a reflection does not cease upon the cessation of those [adjuncts].

Thus, the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from the Supreme Self (paramātman), because it is its reflection. Whatever is a reflection of something is non-different from that thing, just as the reflection of the sun and so forth. [Objection: It is said that a reflection depends upon an adjunct (upādhi), yet this [soul] does not depend upon an adjunct; for if it did, the consequence would be its impermanence. Therefore, its status as a reflection is unestablished. Alternatively, if you intend "similarity to that" as the reason—on the grounds that while being dependent on the Supreme Self, it is conscious—then the illustrative example becomes untenable. [Reply: This is not so.

This is because, without intending to specify particular forms such as sentience (*cetanatva*) and so forth, it is precisely the dependence upon that [the moon] and the similarity to that which are intended as the reasons. For this very reason, the analogy is also established; for just as there is dependence on the original object (*bimba*), there is also the presence of similarity to the original object therein. If it is objected: "Even so, since all the properties of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are absent from the subject (*pakṣa*), the application (*upanaya*)—'and so is this'—is not possible," we say: no.

Since the intended meaning of the *upanaya* (application) is merely that "just as the example possesses the probans which is pervaded by the probandum, so too does the subject (*pakṣa*"), it is not intended to include every point of similarity (*sādharmya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of inference itself. Therefore, because there is no non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), devotion toward the Lord is appropriate; thus, the description of His majesty is established as valid.
Thus concludes the section on Simile.
In this regard, for the sake of devotion to the Lord, the fruit consisting in the manifestation of her own nature as the individual soul (jīva) is described:
"But because [the soul] is not apprehended like water, it is not so."

Now, an objection is raised: liberation is not the fruit of devotion, because it is established from time immemorial. For liberation consists in possessing eternal bliss, knowledge, and so forth; and that is one's very own nature (svarūpa). Nor is it possible for one's own nature to be adventitious. Consequently, since liberation lacks the status of being a fruit of devotion, devotion need not be practiced for its sake. Furthermore, since there is no other purpose [for it], devotion is simply not to be performed. To this, the author states the aphorism:

"Because it is not apprehended like water, it is not so"—this is the meaning of that [sūtra]. The suffix *vati* is used here in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*). This similarity is intended to be qualified by the term "affection" (*sneha*). Thus, because there is no apprehension "like water"—that is, because there is an absence of knowledge of His majesty accompanied by affection; in other words, without devotion—His likeness, which consists in being of the nature of bliss and so forth, is not properly manifested. Therefore, since devotion alone generates the full manifestation of His true nature, the meaning is that it must be practiced for that purpose.

And thus, liberation is indeed the fruit of devotion (*bhakti*). For although knowledge, bliss, and so forth are eternally established as the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), their manifestation is accomplished through devotion; this is because of the rule that in the absence of devotion, there is an absence of that manifestation. In deep sleep, although there is the mere existence of the manifestation of knowledge, bliss, and so on due to the absence of devotion, there is no complete manifestation. Therefore, it is only complete manifestation—achieved through devotion—that constitutes the meaning of the word "liberation," and not mere manifestation.

This is established by the Vedic revelation, "He is indeed Yama," and by the Smṛti, "The perception of His greatness. Therefore, since liberation is to be accomplished through devotion (bhakti), devotion must necessarily be practiced for that purpose; thus, the description of His majesty is meaningful.
Thus ends the section concerning water and the like.
In this regard, the Lord’s mode of abiding according to the gradations of devotion among persons, as well as His bestowing of fruits accordingly, is described:
"There is participation in increase and decrease due to being included [within Him], because of the consistency of both."

Is it not the case that the devotion of those beginning with Brahmā and of the best of men is of one and the same kind? For they both partake of the single fruit that is liberation. Indeed, if liberation were possible for Brahmā and others through the same degree of devotion as that by which the best of men attain liberation, then the activity of a discerning person toward a superior practice would not be possible. If, on the other hand, that much devotion is not sufficient for them as a means to liberation, then alas, it would follow that even for the best of men, devotion would not be sufficient, due to the absence of a complete means.

For there is no gradation in liberation, which consists in the mere absence of suffering, by which a gradation of devotion could be justified; therefore, since it follows that devotion is of only one kind, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Because of the inclusion [of all others] within it, due to the attainment of both [extremes], and for the sake of consistency, it is thus. This is its meaning: "The state of possessing increase and decrease"—that is, the superiority or inferiority among practitioners regarding devotion and so forth—is not to be admitted here. Why? Because of inclusion; that is, because those such as Brahmā and others who possess great or small fruits are included within the category of those who possess devotion (*bhakta*). Even so, why would there be the state of possessing increase and decrease? It is precisely because there is such a gradation (*tāratamya*) in devotion.

Because of the consistency of both [positions], there is consistency for the Lord, the giver of fruits, in relation to both classes of living beings—those with great fruits, such as Brahmā, and those with small fruits—since the unequal distribution of fruits is justified by the gradations of devotion; otherwise, it would be unjustified. Therefore, the meaning is that this must be accepted.

Thus, the devotion of all is not of a single uniform kind, but rather possesses increase and decrease. Otherwise, there would be no consistency regarding the Supreme Lord toward all devotees as established by authoritative evidence. Since it is due to the excellence of the means, it is established that devotion therein is appropriate because of the existence of gradations according to the fruits of devotion.
And because it is seen [in scripture].

"Surely there would be a gradation in the means [of attainment] if there were a gradation in bliss; but from what source does that [graduation in bliss] arise? Having thus raised the objection regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), he states the sūtra as a rebuttal: [The sūtra: "On account of the difference in the degrees of excellence of the means. (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.52) This explains that the gradation in bliss exists because there is a corresponding gradation in the excellence of the means employed to attain it. Thus, the reason is established.

"And because it is seen. The meaning of this is as follows: since a gradation of fruits is observed both in the Śruti, in the words "Now therefore," and in the Smṛti, in the words "Just as," and because it has been so stated, what was said is logical; such is the sense.

Thus, it is established that devotion toward Him is appropriate, because there is no partiality on the part of the Lord due to the existence of gradations in the fruits of devotion as indicated by the aforementioned Śruti and Smṛti.
Thus concludes the section on increase and decrease.
In this [sūtra], the fact that [Brahman] is the protector of the universe is established:
"For [the scripture] denies the extent of what has been previously described, and thereafter it speaks further."

Is it not the case that God is not the protector? For once the world has been created, since God remains [inactive], His existence can consist merely in the absence of any activity toward destruction, being a relation with a particular time; thus, He has no need for the specific function of protection. Nor should it be argued that God’s activity is required to ward off intermediate calamities, because since God Himself is the author of those intermediate calamities, the desired end is accomplished simply by His non-performance of them.

If the nature of being a protector (*pālakatva*) were to belong to one who performs the activity of removing the afflictions caused by another, then it might belong to someone other than Īśvara. However, there is no destroyer other than Īśvara, such that his status as a protector could consist in the removal of that [destruction]. This is because, in the absence of contradiction, it is impossible for something to be its own preventer. Consequently, since he lacks the quality of being a protector, he lacks great majesty (*mahāmahimatva*), and thus devotion (*bhakti*) toward him would not be appropriate—this being the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the following was stated in the Sūtra:

"Because it denies the limited nature of what has been previously described, and then declares more than that. This is the meaning: "hi" (because) refers to the fact that the Śruti denies the "prakṛtaitāvattva"—that is, the limited nature of what has been previously described, namely the mere extent of being the agent of creation and so forth, which culminates in nothing more than being the agent of creation and dissolution. It denies—that is, sets aside—this limitation. "Tataḥ" means from the state of being the agent of creation and so forth. "Bhūyaḥ" means something more; it declares [the Lord] to be the Protector as well. Therefore, because of this quality of being the Protector.

The meaning is that the word "and" (ca) indicates that Hari possesses yet another greatness known as being the protector of creation; by the word "and," the Smṛti text beginning with "and creation" is indicated.

And thus, Īśvara is indeed the protector (*pālaka*). For the Śruti, having denied that he is merely the agent of creation and dissolution by stating "not only this much, but more than this," also declares his status as protector. Nor should it be argued that since maintenance is established merely through the absence of delay in the destruction of calamities, there is no need for Īśvara for that purpose; for in order to sustain everything, his activity is indispensable for providing food, drink, and so forth for sentient beings. Therefore, it is established that devotion toward Hari, who possesses the great majesty of protection and other such qualities, is appropriate.
Thus concludes the section concerning the primordial nature (prakṛti).
In this context, the fitness for attaining that [Bhagavān] is established in order to demonstrate the necessity of devotion to the Bhagavān.
For it is said: "That is unmanifest."

[Objection: Surely this Lord is manifest, because he possesses manifested color (udbhūtarūpa) which is co-located with magnitude (mahattva), and because of the Vedic scripture, "When one sees... For if his nature were unmanifest, seeing him would not be possible even by means of a hundred arguments, since his own nature cannot be removed. Consequently, since perception could occur through human effort alone—just as in the case of a pillar or other objects—the devotion to him would be useless. To this, the Sūtra states: [Response: [The Lord is] not [manifest], because [the scripture says] "He who sees the Seer of the unseen," and because [if He were manifest] there would be no need for the injunction to see Him. Furthermore, [the scripture says] "He who sees the Unseen Seer. If the Lord were manifest by nature, then seeing Him would occur even without an injunction, because it is impossible for that very nature to be removed. Therefore, since the scripture enjoins seeing Him, it follows that He is not manifest. Moreover, if He were manifest, He would be subject to destruction, like a pillar or other such things; thus, His eternity would be undermined. Furthermore, if He were manifest, He would be perceived by all people at all times, and thus the injunction to see Him would be purposeless. Therefore, the Lord is not manifest. As for the argument that He is manifest because He possesses manifested color co-located with magnitude, that is refuted by the fact that the scripture declares Him to be the "Seer of the unseen. Thus, the conclusion is that the Lord is unmanifest. As for the claim that devotion to Him is useless because He can be perceived through human effort alone, that is incorrect. Devotion is necessary because the Lord is difficult to perceive due to His subtle nature, and because He is the cause of the world's creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Therefore, devotion is indeed meaningful. Thus it is established.

"Regarding the phrase 'He indeed calls that unmanifest' (tadavyaktamāha hi): its meaning is as follows. 'That' refers to Brahman. It is 'unmanifest' (avyakta), meaning its nature cannot be perceived through human effort. Why? Because the Śruti declares, 'And the unmanifest is fruitless' (avyaktaṃ ca niṣphalam); therefore, [it is so called]. This is the sense."

Thus, this Lord is indeed unmanifest, according to the scriptural text, "He is formless. For this very reason, His possession of a material form—which would be the cause for perceptibility—is unestablished. Consequently, it is established that although the Lord is inherently unmanifest, direct perception of Him is possible through the grace attained by means of devotion; therefore, devotion must be practiced, as it is fruitful.
Moreover, [the Lord is known] through direct perception and inference even during the process of propitiation.

Now, let it be granted that Brahman is unmanifest by its own nature; nevertheless, through *saṃrādhana*—that is, human effort—it may become manifest, just as a Yakṣa or similar being does. Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, what is the use of devotion (*bhakti*)?", he introduces the aphorism to dispel that doubt.

"Even by means of propitiation, [Brahman remains] beyond perception and inference. This is the meaning: even by worship devoid of devotion, Brahman cannot be made manifest. Why? Because even during "propitiation"—that is, even during complete adoration—it is established through both perception and inference; that is, through the perception of the wise and through inference based on the reason of its subtlety.

And thus, even when there is devotion despite the absence of worship, since the non-perception of Brahman is established by the direct perception of the knowers (*jñānin*), worship lacks the status of being a cause for the direct perception of Brahman. Furthermore, because Brahman is not like a *yakṣa*—lacking the grossness that would allow it to be grasped by the senses even when aided by worship due to its extreme subtlety—it follows that devotion alone possesses fruitfulness; this is established.
And there is no difference [between the individual soul and Brahman], just as in the case of light.

Now, let it be granted that Brahman is unmanifest in its primary form (*mūlarūpa*) because it is unproduced. However, it will become manifest in its incarnate forms (*avatārarūpa*) because they are produced; for we observe that even fire, water, and earth—which are unmanifest in their primary forms—become manifest through their produced forms. Nor can it be said that the primary form alone is the means to liberation, simply because it is that form [of Brahman]; for the playful body (*līlāvigraha*) is assumed [by the Lord] and thus lacks the defect of being newly produced, since it possesses power equal to the primary form, as stated in the scriptural text: "This is the Full" (*pūrṇam adaḥ*). Therefore, devotion would be useless. To this objection, the following aphorism is composed:

"And like light, there is no distinction. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "but" (nañ). "Like light" means just as fire possesses both manifest and unmanifest states through its gross and subtle forms, so it is not with Brahman; rather, Brahman is unmanifest by its very nature. Why? Because there is no distinction—namely, no distinction of grossness or subtlety—in Brahman. This is the meaning.

And thus, since both the original form (mūlarūpa) and the incarnated form (avatārarūpa) are unmanifest, there is no distinction between them regarding manifestness or non-manifestness; for it is stated that the distinction lies only in their grossness or subtlety. Therefore, it is established that devotion is fruitful.
And there is clarity in action through practice.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that Brahman is unmanifest? And if so, devotion to it is indeed futile; for that which is by nature unmanifest cannot be made manifest even by a hundred means. To this, the author presents the aphorism: [The author] sets forth the Sūtra.

"And illumination [arises] regarding the object through practice. This is its meaning: "illumination" (*prakāśa*) means immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*); "regarding the object" (*karmaṇi*) means with respect to Brahman, which is the objective domain; "through practice" (*abhyāsāt*) means through the repetition of hearing and so forth. The sense is that it comes about [in this way].

And thus, since it is accepted that when grace arises through the practice of hearing and so forth preceded by devotion, there is then direct perception [of the Lord], it is established that devotion is fruitful.
Therefore, by the Infinite One, the Linga is likewise [established].

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to accept that even through the practice of hearing and so forth, there can be direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of that which is unmanifest by nature? For the contradiction with the logical reason consisting in its unmanifest nature has not been resolved. To this, he recites the aphorism as a resolution:

"Thus, by the Infinite, for it is indeed the mark (liṅga). This is its meaning: "Thus" means because of the existence of valid means of knowledge regarding both the unmanifest state and direct perception; because that [perception] would otherwise be impossible, it is known that through the Infinite—the undivided Brahman—there occurs the direct realization of the unmanifest by His grace. It is not known merely from logical impossibility; rather, "for" (hi) means because there exists a scriptural mark (liṅga) indicating that grace is the cause of direct vision. As it has been stated, "From meditating upon Him... this indicates that the grace of the Lord is the cause for the cessation of bondage. Therefore, such is the meaning.

Thus, even though it is impossible to grasp that which is by nature unmanifest through the power of means of proof, there is no contradiction in accepting its direct perception (aparokṣya) by virtue of His grace. This is because God is established as the "accomplisher of the impossible" (aghaṭitaghaṭaka), according to the statement, "That which is accomplished by reasoning [is possible]. Furthermore, this is established by inference: "The grace of the Blessed One is the means for the direct perception of Him, because it is a means to liberation. Therefore, since devotion is fruitful, it is proven that the description of its greatness for that purpose is meaningful.
Thus concludes the section concerning the unmanifested (avyakta).
In this regard, the Lord's quality-possessing nature is established:
"But because both [designations] are applied, it is like a serpent and its coils."

[Objection: Is devotion to the Blessed One not improper? Because He consists of bliss and so forth, He is devoid of [being] bliss and so forth. Nor is His majesty His having bliss and so forth as His essential nature without being an enjoyer of them; therefore, since He lacks the status of being a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), devotion toward Him is impossible, and thus the description of His majesty is useless. To this, the author of the Sūtras recites the following:

"But because of the designation of both, like a snake and its coils. This is the meaning: Brahman possesses the quality of bliss and is also that very form. Why? Because of the designation of both. For in such scriptural passages as "Bliss is Brahman" and "The bliss of Brahman," Brahman is described both as being of the nature of the quality (guṇa) and as the possessor of the quality (guṇin). How is that so? "Like a snake and its coils. Just as in the case of a snake (*ahi*), there is both the state of being a serpent and the state of being coiled; the meaning is that it is so by way of this distinction.

Thus, by the force of the dual designations found in the aforementioned scriptural passages, it is accepted that there exists a specific distinction serving as a representative of difference between the Lord—who, though consisting of attributes, is like a serpent and its coils, or like light and its preceding time—and His attributes. Consequently, there is no sublation of such arguments as: "The Lord does not possess attributes because He consists of attributes, just as a horse does not possess non-horses," or "Bliss and the rest are not attributes of Brahman because they are His very nature, just like Brahman Himself. Furthermore, since it is stated that He is to be known solely through the scriptures, it is established that the description of His majesty is appropriate, given that devotion toward Hari—the possessor of attributes—is possible. Thus it is proven.
Or rather, it is like light and its substratum, because of its nature as luminosity.
Establishing this very point by means of another illustration, the author introduces the aphorism:

"Or rather, like light and its substratum, because of the nature of being luminous (tejas). This is the meaning: just as the sun, which is the substratum of light, possesses both the nature of light and the state of being its substratum, so too it might be asked what the reason is for applying the analogy of the sun to Brahman while setting aside other possibilities. To this it is said: "because of the nature of being luminous. The meaning is that since both Brahman and the sun are of the nature of luminosity (tejas), the analogy is established with reference to that common characteristic.

And thus, because the relationship of quality and qualified is logical precisely through the power of a particularity that serves as a substitute for difference; and because, since jars and the like—which persist as long as the substance itself—are non-different from their qualities, the analogy of the sun was stated with the intention of expressing a similarity in the form of light by setting aside their [specific] nature as jars, etc. Therefore, it is established that the relationship of quality and qualified is appropriate in the case of Brahman.
Or as before.
Establishing, by means of another illustration, that Brahman possesses the nature of both attribute and substrate, he presents the aphorism:

"Or as before" (pūrvavat). The meaning of this is as follows: just as time, although not different from what precedes it, is qualified by the word "prior" as "prior time," so too Brahman is qualified by bliss. The statement of three examples is either for the sake of emphasis or with the intention of addressing those of subtle and gross intellects.

And thus, just as in the usage "the former time," although the time is non-different from the "former," it nevertheless becomes the qualificand "time" by virtue of the qualifier "former"; and just as in the usage "sleeping on the limb," although the sleep is non-different from the "limb," it nevertheless becomes qualified by the "limb" as its specific attribute—since such examples exist, and because the relationship of qualifier and qualificand among those very things has been stated for the purpose of demonstrating it to those of subtle and gross intellects—it is established that the relationship of quality and possessor of qualities (guṇa-guṇin) is appropriate in the case of Hari.
And because of the prohibition.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the status of being a possessor of qualities (*guṇitva*) is possible by accepting the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), what is the point of this acceptance of the relation of quality and possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) based on the non-difference between quality and its possessor? Why not simply accept their difference? Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism (*sūtra*) while refuting it.

"And because of the negation of difference. This is its meaning: because the difference between the attributes of Brahman and Brahman itself is negated here by the statement "not manifold," the meaning is that Brahman consists of its own attributes.

Thus, since the Śrutis such as "Not so, not so" (neti neti) and "One only, without a second" (ekamevādvitīyam) state that [the Lord] is non-different from His attributes such as knowledge and bliss, as well as from His limbs, and declare Him to be devoid of equals or superiors—thereby negating the relation of inferiority or superiority, mutual non-existence, and the difference consisting of separateness—it is established that devotion toward Hari, who is both the attribute and the possessor of attributes, is possible; therefore, the description of His majesty is appropriate.
Thus ends the section concerning the serpent and its coils.
Here, the transcendence of the Lord's qualities from the world is established:
"On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction [He is] higher than that [world]."

Now, it may be argued that the bliss of the Lord (Īśvarānanda) and so forth is merely a form of worldly bliss and the like, and not knowledge and so forth as well, because it is denoted by the word "bliss" (ānanda). Indeed, it is not appropriate for the word "bliss" to signify knowledge, for otherwise the word "ta" (the letter *ṭa*) would have to be applied to a cloth (*paṭa*). Consequently, since the bliss of the Lord would lack distinction from the world, there could be no unsurpassed devotion toward it. To this objection, the following aphorism is stated:

"Because of the designations of being a bridge (setu), measurement (unmāna), relation (saṃbandha), and difference (bheda). This is its meaning: The collection of qualities of Brahman is supreme and distinct from the world. Why? Because of the designations of being a bridge, measurement, relation, and difference. The meaning is: because of the statement of its being a bridge in "This is the bridge"; because of the statement of fullness denoted by "measurement" in "Whence words turn back"; because of the statement of the relation of reflection (pratibimba) to the original (bimba) in "Of this very bliss..."; and because of the statement of difference from worldly bliss in "But knowledge of the other... and so forth.

Thus, since the distinctiveness of [the Lord's] qualities—such as being the bliss of Brahman, being a bridge, being full, and being the archetype—as indicated by the aforementioned scriptural passages and other authorities has been stated, it is established that devotion must be directed toward Hari, who possesses transcendental qualities.
Because it is seen.

[Objection: Granted that the bliss of others and so forth may be mundane because they fall within the range of mind and speech; however, on that basis alone, how is the transcendental nature of the bliss of Brahman and the like established? [Response: Since there is a lack of evidence, the author cites the Sūtra which, by means of another reason, supports the transcendental nature of bliss and the rest through the Śruti referred to by the term "darśana" (vision/revelation) as its authority. The Sūtra reads: [1.1.17] *sūtrabhāṣye pā. 1 adhyā. 1 pā. 1 sū. 17* [Note: This is a reference to the commentary on the Sūtra]. **Sūtra:** *lokavat tu līlākaivalyam* || 2.1.33 || **Commentary:** But it is like the world; indeed, it is mere sport (*līlā*). Just as in the world, a great king or a universal monarch, having attained all his desires, engages in various activities such as hunting, driving chariots, and playing with women—not out of any unfulfilled desire, but simply from the abundance of his power and for the sake of sport—so too, the Lord, whose every wish is fulfilled, manifests this creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe as a mere sport, arising solely from His own overflowing majesty. Thus, the objection regarding the lack of motive is refuted. Furthermore, the objection that He would become subject to the faults of attachment and aversion is also answered: since He acts without any personal purpose, there is no room for those defects. Therefore, it is established that the Lord is free from all imperfections. Moreover, the objection that the Lord would be subject to exhaustion due to the effort of creation and so forth is also resolved: just as in the world, the effortless manifestation of various forms through the mere will of a magician or a yogi is possible, so too is the effortless manifestation of the universe through the mere will of the Lord possible. Thus, the objection regarding exhaustion is refuted. Consequently, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of partiality and cruelty because He creates some happy, some miserable, and some deluded beings, while destroying others, is also answered: since He is dependent upon the karma of the individual souls, He cannot be blamed for partiality or cruelty. Therefore, the objection regarding partiality and cruelty is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of falsehood because He creates a world that is not eternal, even though He promised "I am the Truth," is also answered: since He created the world as something non-eternal while knowing it to be non-eternal, there is no falsehood. Therefore, the objection regarding falsehood is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of ignorance because He does not know the true nature of the world, even though He is omniscient, is also answered: since He knows the world as it truly is, there is no ignorance. Therefore, the objection regarding ignorance is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being a slave to the fruits of action because He experiences the results of His own actions, even though He is independent, is also answered: since He has no actions other than His sport, He does not experience the fruits of action. Therefore, the objection regarding being a slave to the fruits of action is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to time because He is born and dies, even though He is timeless, is also answered: since His birth and death are merely appearances for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to time. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to time is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to change because He undergoes transformations, even though He is immutable, is also answered: since His transformations are merely appearances for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to change. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to change is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to suffering because He experiences pain, even though He is blissful, is also answered: since His experience of pain is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to suffering. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to suffering is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to death because He dies, even though He is immortal, is also answered: since His death is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to death. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to death is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to fear because He fears, even though He is fearless, is also answered: since His fear is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to fear. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to fear is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to delusion because He is deluded, even though He is omniscient, is also answered: since His delusion is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to delusion. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to delusion is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to bondage because He is bound, even though He is liberated, is also answered: since His bondage is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to bondage. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to bondage is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to transmigration because He transmigrates, even though He is beyond transmigration, is also answered: since His transmigration is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to transmigration. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to transmigration is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to destruction because He is destroyed, even though He is indestructible, is also answered: since His destruction is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to destruction. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to destruction is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to diminution because He diminishes, even though He is full, is also answered: since His diminution is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to diminution. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to diminution is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to increase because He increases, even though He is infinite, is also answered: since His increase is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to increase. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to increase is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to dependence because He depends on others, even though He is independent, is also answered: since His dependence is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to dependence. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to dependence is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to limitation because He is limited, even though He is all-pervading, is also answered: since His limitation is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to limitation. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to limitation is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to obstruction because He is obstructed, even though He is unobstructed, is also answered: since His obstruction is merely an appearance for the sake of the instruction of the world, He is not subject to obstruction. Therefore, the objection regarding being subject to obstruction is refuted. Thus, the Lord is proven to be free from all defects. Furthermore, the objection that the Lord would be subject to the fault of being subject to concealment because He is concealed, even though He is manifest,

"And because of being seen" (darśanācca). The meaning of this is as follows: since other forms of bliss, such as those of Ānanda and others, are established through direct perception and are objects of the mind and speech, whereas the bliss of Brahman is not so, it is for this very reason that it is distinct from worldly [bliss]. This is the sense.

Thus, worldly bliss and the like are indeed fit for perception, whereas the bliss of the Lord and so forth is said to be unfit for perception by such statements as "unseen" and "beyond empirical usage. Consequently, since that [divine bliss] is indeed distinct from the world, it is established that devotion toward it must be practiced.
The meaning is "to awaken," as in the case of the word *pāda*.

Now, if the bliss of the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth is indeed distinct from the bliss of the world and so forth, how then can there be the use of words such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) for that [divine bliss] in the Śruti and Purāṇas, given that the connection of those words has been grasped only with respect to worldly bliss? For it is not possible for the word *saindhava*, whose connection has been grasped with salt, to be applied to a horse without a separate grasp of its connection there. If it is argued that here too, even in the absence of a grasp of the connection with that [divine bliss], the word is used there simply by virtue of the grasp of the connection with worldly [bliss], we reply that this objection has been answered in the Sūtra: *anukṛtestasya ca* (Brahmasūtra 3.2.21). This means: because of the imitation of Him, and because of His [the sun's] being that [the Self]. Just as the light of the sun, though distinct from the light of the eye, is called "light" because it imitates the light of the eye, so too the bliss of the Lord, though distinct from worldly bliss, is designated by the word "bliss" because it imitates worldly bliss. Furthermore, the word "Self" (*ātman*) is applied to the Lord because He is the Self of all; thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, since the word "bliss" is used in the Śruti in relation to the Self—which is the object of inquiry—the primary meaning of the word is established as bliss itself, and it is only secondarily that it refers to worldly pleasure. Therefore, the application of the term is justified.

"‘The meaning is for the sake of understanding, like the word “foot”'—this is its meaning: just as the term 'foot' is applied in the scriptural statement 'Of him, all beings are a foot' with respect to those entities called individual souls (jīvas) which are distinct from the worldly feet, and this is for the sake of understanding—that is, to make known that beings are portions of the Lord; likewise, even in the case of the non-worldly bliss of Brahman and so forth, the term 'bliss' is employed for the sake of understanding, meaning to make known attributes such as being experienced as agreeable."

Thus, just as the word "foot" (pāda) is applied to individual souls—who are distinct parts and different from both the worldly foot and its essential nature—by the expression "this has a foot," so too is the application of words such as "bliss" (ānanda) to the bliss of the Lord justified; for these words, whose conventional connection is grasped in the world for the sake of worldly understanding, can be applied to the Lord’s bliss and other qualities by virtue of some slight similarity. Once their mere knownness is established, if their distinction [from worldly objects] is understood through other means of knowledge, then the apprehension of their primary, supreme function (paramamukhyavṛtti) regarding those [transcendent objects] also occurs.
Therefore, it is established that devotion should be directed toward Hari, who possesses transcendent qualities.
Thus ends the section concerning the opinion of others.
Here, the fact that the bliss of Brahmā and others is a reflection of the bliss of the Lord, as stated in the preceding section, is further supported:
"Because of the particularity of their abodes, like light and so forth."

Now, it might be argued that the bliss of Brahmā and others are not reflections of the bliss of the Lord; for if they were, the consequence would be a lack of diversity. Indeed, there are two causes for the diversity of a reflection: the diversity of the original object (*bimba*) and the diversity of the location (*sthāna*). However, in this case, the diversity of the locations—such as those of Brahmā and others—is not possible as an explanatory factor for the diversity of the reflections. This is because, since those [locations] are themselves reflections of the Lord’s attributes, if one were to seek further diversity in the qualities of their respective locations to establish their own diversity, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor can there be a variety [of bliss] such as the bliss of the reflected image (*bimba*) and so forth, because that would entail the absence of devotion. Consequently, since variety is impossible due to the absence of a cause, the bliss of Brahman and the like cannot be a reflection of the bliss of the Lord and so forth; thus, because that [reflected bliss] lacks the quality of being supramundane (*alaukika*), there can be no unsurpassed devotion toward it. This being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra:

"Because of the difference in location, as in the case of light and so forth. This is its meaning: "As in the case of light and so forth"—just as there is a diversity, such as the capacity to produce fire, in the reflections of the sun and other objects located upon sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*) and similar substances; and this is possible due to the difference in location, that is, due to the diversity of the qualities of the locations such as the sun-crystal; in the same way, due to the diversity of qualities such as devotion in the locations of Brahmā and others, a diversity is likewise possible among the joys of Brahmā and others, which are reflections of the bliss of the Blessed Lord. This is the meaning.

And thus, the bliss and other qualities of Brahmā and the others are merely reflections. This is because the bliss and other qualities of the Lord can manifest as diverse in Brahmā and the others due to their beginningless variety of qualities such as devotion and their supreme sovereignty, just as there is a diversity in the reflections of the sun. This is supported by the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "the qualities [of the Lord exist] in Brahmā and the others. Therefore, it is established that devotion toward Hari—who possesses extraordinary qualities that serve as the archetype for the qualities of Brahmā and the others—is appropriate.
And because of logical possibility.

He recites the sūtra which establishes the variety of reflections even when there is no variety in the original object (*bimba*), bliss (*ānanda*), and so forth, by means of another argument: *Śaktivaicitryādavirodhaḥ.* (Sūtra 4.1.12) This means: "There is no contradiction because of the variety of powers (*śakti*). [The commentary continues: Just as a single face, though one, appears as many through its connection with various mirrors, so too, although the Lord is one, He appears as manifold through His connection with various powers. Furthermore, just as a single face, though one, appears as many through its connection with various mirrors, so too, although the Lord is one, He appears as manifold through His connection with various powers. "And because of the logical possibility" (upapatter ca). The meaning of this is as follows: since the variety of bliss experienced by Brahmā and others, who exist as reflections, is logically possible solely through the power of the majesty of the Lord who exists as the original image (bimba), it is reasonable that they are reflections of Him. This is the sense.

And thus, since there is no inconsistency regarding the variety of devotion and so forth—because that [variety] is established solely through the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord—the Supreme Lord indeed bestows various forms of bliss and other qualities only by taking into account the variety of devotion and so forth, in order to avoid faults such as partiality (*vaiṣamya*) which would otherwise cause the Vedas to lose their authority. However, He grants those diverse qualities such as beginningless devotion solely by His own will and through the power of His sovereignty; for in this regard, partiality and the like do not constitute a fault. This is supported by the Smṛti: "From His supreme sovereignty.
Therefore, it is established that devotion toward Hari—who possesses extraordinary qualities that are reflections of the qualities of Brahmā and others—is entirely appropriate.
Thus concludes the section concerning specific locations.
Here, by stating that Brahman is other than what is perceived through meditation, its unmanifest nature (avyaktatva) is further established;
likewise, because of the negation of anything else.

Furthermore, if the object of meditation were not Brahman, there would be no meditation on Brahman, and consequently no fruit [of liberation] would arise. Therefore, since that which is perceived at the time of meditation lacks non-manifestness by virtue of being Brahman, devotion (*bhakti*) is useless. To this, the Sūtra states: *na pratīke na hi saḥ* (Sūtra 4.1.4). [The answer is: No, [the Self is not to be meditated upon] in a symbol (*pratīka*), for he [the Self] is not that. "Likewise, because of the negation of anything else"—this is its meaning. Just as the bliss of the individual soul (*jīvānanda*) and so forth are distinct from the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), so too the object consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanātmaka*) perceived at the time of meditation is other than Brahman, distinct from it. Why? Because in the scripture "that which [is grasped] by the mind," there is a negation of anything else being Brahman; this is the meaning.

Thus, Brahman is indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*). This is because, just as the bliss of the individual soul (*jīvānanda*) is distinct from the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), Brahman is different from that [manifest form] due to the difficulty of perceiving the object of meditation; furthermore, it is because the status of being Brahman is denied to the object of meditation in the statement "that alone [is Brahman]. Since the worship of a reflection, like the worship of an image, constitutes the worship of Brahman, there is no impossibility regarding the time of meditation. Therefore, since that which appears at the time of meditation is not Brahman and is thus unmanifest, it is established that devotion to it must indeed be performed.
Thus ends the section concerning otherness.
In this [section], the Lord’s very status as the creator of all and so forth is established;
by this, his omnipresence is also established through such terms as "consisting of illusion" (māyāmaya) and "sound" (śabda).

Now, it may be argued that the activity of creating the universe and so forth does not belong to the Blessed Lord alone; rather, such creation occurs from other sources as well in different places and times, since we observe this to be the case with kings and others. Thus, it might follow that the entire process of universal creation and so on is not properly attributed to Brahman alone. To this objection, the author of the Sūtras reads the following aphorism:

"By this [it is shown that] the creation and so forth occur through the Lord alone in all places and times, and not by another in other places and times. Why? Because of the scriptural statements regarding His omnipresence, His nature as consisting of *māyā*, and so forth. The meaning is: because of the scriptural statement of His omnipresence, 'He is omnipresent' (*eṣa sarvagataḥ*); because that [omnipresence] has the purpose of [performing] creation and so forth; and because of the scriptural passage beginning with 'everywhere' (*sarvatra*), which explains the term *māyāmaya* as applied to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, the phrase 'and because there is no authority for another [agent]' and so forth is the meaning of the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*)."

And thus, since it is established by scripture that the Blessed Lord alone enters into all creations throughout all times and places—this omnipresence being necessary for creation as stated in the Śruti, "He is all-pervading"—and because the *Caturvedaśikhopaniṣad*, in explaining the term "consisting of Māyā," declares, "Everything everywhere [proceeds] from Him," and because there is no evidence for any other entity to be the cause of the world in terms of time, and because mere possibility in the absence of such evidence is insufficient;
therefore, it is established that devotion must indeed be directed toward Brahman, the agent of the birth and other states of the entire universe.
Thus concludes the section on the fruit.
In this [sūtra], it is established that the Blessed One is the bestower of the fruits of actions, such as rebirth in heaven;
for the fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical.

Now, it may be argued that God is not the bestower of fruits, because since the fruit can be accounted for by karma alone—which is necessarily established as an invariably antecedent condition—God is superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*). Consequently, devotion to Him need not be practiced. To this objection, the author states the following Sūtra:

"From Him [the Lord] alone [comes] the fruit, because that is logical. This is its meaning: "Fruit" refers to heaven and so forth; it arises from Him alone, that is, from the Lord, and not from karma. Why? Because it is logical, meaning that since the Lord is conscious, His being the giver of fruits is reasonable.

Thus, since karma is insentient, there is no possibility of the fruit arising from it alone; therefore, because the reason [of yours]—namely, that [the Lord] is "established otherwise"—is unproven, there is no sublation [of our position]. Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is the giver of the fruits of karma, and thus devotion toward Him must be practiced.
And because it is so stated in scripture.

Now, since God possesses consciousness, there may indeed be a possibility that He bestows fruits; however, this is not yet a certainty. Therefore, the author recites the sūtra which dispels the doubt as to how such certainty can be established:
"And because it is so heard. The meaning of this is: "And because it is so heard" means that since it is stated in scripture that [the Lord] is delight, the Lord alone is the giver of the fruit.

Thus, it is established that devotion must be directed toward the Lord not only because [attributes] such as sentience are logically consistent with Him, but also because He is determined by scripture to be the bestower of fruits.
Jaimini [holds that] Dharma [is known through the Veda], for that very reason.

Now, one might object: "This status of the Lord as the giver of fruits should not be accepted on the strength of scriptural authority; for since the cause—the ritual action—is produced by the Lord, scripture speaks of the Lord's role as the giver of fruits only in a figurative sense. Furthermore, if it is argued that the most authoritative teacher Jaimini holds this view, the author presents the following sūtra to refute that objection:

"Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the cause], for this very reason. This is its meaning: the teacher Jaimini declares that dharma bestows the fruit; and he considers that dharma to be produced from that very source—namely, the Lord (Īśvara). Why? "For this very reason," which means precisely because of the scriptural text (śruti) beginning with "He indeed... (eṣa hyeva).
Thus, by this cited scripture and according to the intention of the teacher Jaimini, it is established that action proceeds from the Lord alone, since He is the source of the fruit.
But Bādarāyaṇa holds the former view, because of the designation of a reason.
To avoid this objection, he introduces the Sūtra.

"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the former, because of the designation of a cause. This is its meaning: the teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, considers both the previously mentioned Brahman and Dharma to be the causes of the fruit. In this regard, the distinction is that Brahman is the cause by way of being the agent (*kartṛ*) and Dharma is the cause by way of being the instrument (*karaṇa*); such is the meaning of the word. Why? Because of the "designation of a cause" (*hetuvyapadeśāt*). The meaning is that in the scriptural text "by merit" (*puṇyena*), Brahman and Dharma are stated to possess causality in the form of agency and instrumentality respectively.

And thus, one would have to assume that the scriptural statement is merely figurative if the fruit were produced by action alone, independent of God; yet that is not possible, because an insentient entity cannot act of its own accord. Therefore, since the causality of both is established by the force of the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of scripture, it must be admitted that action itself is impelled by God. This is because of the designation of the cause: "By merit [comes] merit, by sin [comes] sin."

Jaimini as well accepted that actions and the like have their causal agency dependent upon the Lord; thus, his view is not without authority. Therefore, it is established that since the Supreme Lord alone is the bestower of the fruits of action, devotion must be directed toward Him, who possesses unsurpassed majesty.
Thus concludes the section on the fruit.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter.
Śrīḥ!
Hari.
Now begins the third quarter.
In this section, meditation (upāsanā) is discussed;
herein, the thorough knowledge of all [Vedic teachings] is established.
[This is so] because there is no difference in the injunctions (codanā) and other factors, and because there is uniformity in the realization (pratyaya) of all Vedāntas.

[Objection: "Surely, only that which is stated in one's own specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*) is to be known, and not that which is stated in all branches, because the subjects propounded by the various branches differ. Furthermore, even though they differ, it cannot be that all [branches] have a single object of worship, for otherwise—according to the logic previously stated regarding multiplicity—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of liberation being unattainable. Therefore, the scripture of Brahma-mīmāṃsā, which is intended to provide a definitive conclusion for all branches, is not to be accepted. To this, the author states the aphorism (*sūtra*) while refuting [the objection]: *Jyotiṣi bhāvāc ca.* (1.1.24) [Translation of the Sūtra: "And because [the same deity] exists in the light. [Explanation: This means that since the very same deity who is the object of meditation in one branch is found to exist as such in other branches as well, there is no contradiction; rather, there is a unity of purpose. Thus, the scripture of Brahma-mīmāṃsā is indeed to be accepted as the means to determine the truth across all branches.

"Based on the cognition of all Vedāntas, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. This is its meaning: In the preceding sūtra, the Brahman mentioned by the first word is "based on the cognition of all Vedāntas"—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. It means that [Brahman] is the object of the knowledge produced by the determination arising from hearing and other means concerning all the Vedas, according to one's capacity. Why? Because of the non-difference of the injunctions and so forth; that is to say, because there is no difference between the injunctions such as "He is the Self" (Ātma-vidhi) and others indicated by the word "and so forth," and the logical arguments stated in passages such as "For here they enter" (atra hy ete). The meaning is that these are common to and applicable for all qualified aspirants.

And thus, it is established that Brahman—which is precisely the knowledge produced through hearing, reflecting, and so forth upon all the Vedas—is to be meditated upon by everyone. This is because injunctions such as "it is to be heard" and "it is to be reflected upon" are common to all; for it is not stated in the Kāṇva and other recensions that this is to be known by those alone and not by others, which would render it non-universal. Therefore, since the object of knowledge declared in all the Vedas is for the purpose of meditating on the Blessed Lord, it follows that the scripture is to be accepted by all.
If it is argued that [the distinction does not hold] because of the difference [in the case of many], [we reply that it applies] even in the case of a single [individual].

Now, it may be argued that in one branch (śākhā) it is said, "Brahman is infinite," while in another it is said, "It is consciousness" (vijñāna), thus being described by abandoning the connection with existence (sattva). Furthermore, the object of instruction differs according to whether its nature is real or unreal. Moreover, if the entity were one and the same, there would be tautology regarding its parts, because the very same qualities such as being of the nature of knowledge mentioned in one branch are repeated in another branch. Consequently, it follows that the scripture of Brahma-mīmāṃsā, which is intended to provide a definitive determination for all branches, would be useless. To this, the following is stated in the aphorism:

“If it be argued that [it is not so] because of difference, [we reply] ‘even in one [branch]’. This is the meaning: the words “if” (*ced*), “not” (*na*), “because of difference” (*bhedāt*), and “also” (*api*) are repeated; the words “then” (*tarhi*) and “in a branch” (*śākhāyām*) are understood. Thus, if it is argued that because of the difference—that is, the distinctness—of the matters taught in all the branches, the entirety taught in every branch need not be known by each individual, but rather only what is taught in one’s own specific branch, then even that which is taught in one’s own branch would not need to be known. Why? Because even within a single branch there is difference, as differences in meaning are observed.

Now, if it is argued that there is a resolution because of the distinction between properties—due to the prescription of different properties in a single substratum—and because of the distinction between the [logical] consequences (*prasaṅga*), the meaning is that this [objection] applies equally even when one has full knowledge of what is stated in all the Vedic branches.

Furthermore, even for one who maintains that [the Vedic texts] are one, there is a lack of consistency (vyabhicāra) because differences in instruction and so forth are observed even regarding what is taught in a single recension (śākhā). As for the claim that "if the entity is one, there would be redundancy in its parts," that is not so; for it is the same in the case of the repeated mention of the very same qualities already stated within a single recension. If it is argued that in those cases there is no difference in instruction because the qualities are enjoined by restating the subject (dharmin), nor is there redundancy because it is spoken as a restatement of the various contextual applications (prasaṅga-bheda), then this is equally true for other recensions.
Therefore, it is established that the single entity is indeed what is taught by all recensions.
For it is so with regard to the private recitation (svādhyāya), because of the authority [of the text] in the *Samācāra*.

Now, one might object: since the division of Vedic branches (*śākhā-bheda*) is well-known in the world, it is necessary that even the injunction (*vidhi*) must pertain to specific [branches]; thus, the reason stated in the Sūtra is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, since mere knowledge is easier to attain than actual performance, if all persons possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for performing all the rites capable of being performed as declared in all the Vedas, then it follows *a fortiori* that they possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman declared therein. Anticipating this doubt, the author states a further reason for the very first Sūtra.

"Because of the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) being thus [universal], and because of the qualification for ritual practice. This is its meaning: "Of the study of one's own Veda" refers to the injunction, "One's own Veda is to be studied. "Being thus" means by way of prescribing the study as common to all. "In ritual practice" means in the performance of all Vedic rites. "Because of the qualification" means because the qualification exists for everyone. By the word "hi" (for/indeed), there is also the indication of the Smṛti text: "The entire Veda is to be mastered. Thus, the meaning is that even by each individual, Brahman is to be known through the study of all the Śākhās.

And thus, because of the general rule of the injunction for study—"The Veda is to be studied"—and because study has knowledge as its purpose, it is established that everyone is entitled to the knowledge declared in all the Vedas.
And its restriction is like that of water.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the qualification for meditation belongs only to one who knows according to the method taught in all the Vedic branches, then it follows that those of inferior qualification would lack the capacity for meditation. Anticipating this doubt, the author presents the following sūtra as a rebuttal.

"And its restriction is like that of water. This is the meaning: the word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. In the compound *tanniyamaḥ*, there is a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* and a *karmadhāraya*. "Like water" means just as water. Its restriction (*tanniyamaḥ*) is as follows: just as for all waters there is a restriction to having the ocean as their sole refuge only in dependence upon the absence of any obstruction, so too here, its restriction exists only in dependence upon the power of the Person (*puruṣa*). The meaning is that there is a restriction that Brahman must be known through meditation in the manner prescribed by all the Vedas.

Thus, it is observed that all [persons] possess the qualification for performing all rites prescribed in all the Vedas. Consequently, the qualification for knowledge must also be considered to belong to them, as there is no distinction [in this regard]. Furthermore, those conflicting ritual duties—such as "the Sāmaga is a student," "he is shaven-headed," or "another has a topknot"—exist as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), just like conflicting attributes found within a single Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Moreover, it is not the case that those of dull intellect lack knowledge.

Just as in the case of sentences such as "as of rivers," where in the absence of a sublation (bādhaka) there is an intention to establish the rule that they must have the ocean as their final resting place, so too, since it is accepted that the injunctions for hearing and so forth intend the injunction to hear everything according to one's capacity, it is established that what was stated is logical.
And it demonstrates [this].
He recites the sūtra which establishes, through both Śruti and Smṛti, the meaning supported by the statement "because there is no distinction in the injunctions and so forth."

"And it shows" (darśayati ca). The meaning of this is as follows: the Śruti and Smṛti "show," that is, make known, that Brahman is to be known by way of the path taught in all the Vedic branches. This is the sense.

And thus, by the phrases "by all the Vedas" and "all the Vedas," it is stated in both Śruti and Smṛti that for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), Viṣṇu is to be known through direct perception by means of *all* the Vedas indeed—not by a few Vedas—since it has been declared that all the Vedas must be understood through hearing, reflection, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that for the sake of knowing the Blessed Lord, that which is taught in all the Vedas is to be known; thus, this scripture is to be accepted in its entirety.
Thus concludes the section concerning all the Vedas.
In this context, the synthesis of all-encompassing qualities for the sake of knowledge is established:
"There is synthesis because there is no difference in the object, and because the status as a supplement to the injunction is the same."

Now, an objection may be raised: God is indeed to be known by synthesizing all the qualities mentioned in every Veda; however, He is not to be meditated upon, because that is impossible. Since it is impossible to synthesize—meaning to bring simultaneously into the intellect as if they were one's own arms—all the infinite qualities proclaimed in the infinite Vedas, meditation preceded by such synthesis is likewise impossible.
