Consequently, the effort to attain omniscience for that purpose would be futile. To this, the Sūtra replies: [The Sūtra states: "But [He is to be meditated upon] on account of the combination [of qualities], because of the teaching. (BS 3.3.1) This means that although it is impossible to know all the qualities of the Lord simultaneously, He is nevertheless to be meditated upon by combining those qualities that are taught in the various scriptures. For meditation does not require the simultaneous mental apprehension of every single attribute, but rather the focused contemplation of the Lord as possessing a synthesized totality of His divine attributes as revealed in the sacred texts. Thus, the attainment of omniscience for the sake of meditation is not futile.

"Upasaṃhāra (synthesis) occurs because the purpose is not different, even when the status of being a supplement to an injunction is the same. This is its meaning: "Like that which is enjoined by an injunction"—that is, just as the Sandhyā-vandana and other such rites must necessarily be performed because they are enjoined by an injunction, so too [is the synthesis]. "Because the purpose is not different": *bheda* means division. Because there is no difference—that is, no division—among the qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and the absence of defects such as sinlessness (*apahatapāpmatva*), which constitute the meaning of all the Vedas; that is to say, one should not divide them.

The "combination" (*upasaṃhāra*) is the bringing together of all qualities in the form of their being presented to a single cognition. Because it is enjoined in scripture that "one [quality] is to be meditated upon," it must be performed. Furthermore, this applies only when the objects are similar and have the same scope; it concerns only those qualities in Brahman that are suitable and do not contradict its perfection. It does not concern unsuitable qualities such as weeping and the like, for if it were so, it would lead to misfortune. This is the meaning.

Thus, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self by way of a synthesis of all the qualities of bliss and so forth, as well as certain absences of defects such as freedom from sin mentioned in all the Vedas, without making a distinction between those that are to be combined and those that are not. For it is enjoined that "all qualities indeed are to be meditated upon. Otherwise, there would be the fault of transgression (pratyavāya) for failing to perform what is enjoined, such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vandana). Furthermore, only those attributes that constitute the intended meaning (tātparya) are to be meditated upon, and not those that do not constitute the intended meaning.

Since weeping and other such effects of suffering—understood from passages such as "He wept"—are impossible in the case of the Supreme Lord, and since meditation on what is unfitting is a cause of misfortune, it is established that the synthesis of all attributes must be performed, and thus the complete knowledge of everything is indeed meaningful.
If it is argued that there is a change [in the Veda] because of the word [of the author], we say no, because there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Now, since it has been enjoined that one should meditate merely on the Self—on the grounds that the injunction "one should meditate [on him] as the Self" prohibits the combination of other qualities—it follows that if all qualities were combined, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the enjoined practice. To this, the Sūtra replies:

"And if it be argued that there is a change [in the rule] on account of the scriptural statement, we say no, because there is no distinction. This is the meaning: "Change" refers to the alteration of what was previously stated—that the combination of all qualities must be performed. One must necessarily admit that such a change is not to be made. Why? If it be argued that it is "on account of the scriptural statement"—namely, the scriptural text regarding non-combination, "One should meditate [on Brahman] as the Self alone"—we say no. Why? "Because there is no distinction," meaning there is an absence of any specific authority to the effect that these qualities are not to be combined. For, on the contrary, there exists specific authority for combining them without distinction, namely, by means of all qualities. This is the sense.
The sense is that the particle "eva" in the phrase "ātmaiveti" serves to exclude non-connection (ayoga-vyavaccheda).

Furthermore, there is no evidence to suggest that these qualities should not be combined. Moreover, there is a specific scriptural statement to the effect that "the Lord alone is to be worshipped with all His qualities, and never with defects. As for the restriction in the passage "one should meditate on Him as the Self alone," it serves only to exclude the defect of non-selfhood due to its conflict with this [other] scripture which leaves no room for alternative interpretations; it does not, however, exclude other qualities. Therefore, that [restriction] is also not a proof against the combination of qualities. Thus, it is established that the combination of all qualities must be performed.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of "the higher than the high" (parovarīyas) and other such instances.

Anticipating the objection that "this compendium of all qualities is not tenable because it is impossible," he refutes it by way of an *abhyupagama-vāda* (a concessionary argument) and explains the sūtra "na vā" through the application of the words "upasaṃhāraḥ" and "kāryaḥ" from the preceding and following contexts respectively.

"Or rather, [the qualities] are not to be combined because of the difference in context, as in the case of 'being higher than the high' (parovarīyastva) and so forth. This is the meaning: just as in the case of "being higher than the high" and other such qualities—which were described by the words "He is this"—only those qualities are to be combined for the purpose of meditation that consist of being the unsurpassed highest of all, and not all qualities; likewise, the combination of all qualities need not be performed. Why? Because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*), that is, because of the difference in context such as that of "being higher than the high" and "Vaiśvānara. The meaning is that otherwise, that [distinction] would not exist.

Thus, let there indeed be no synthesis of all qualities, because of the difference in context; otherwise, the contexts would not be distinct. One should not think that a synthesis of all [qualities] must be performed on the grounds that all contexts are intended to signify all qualities by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇatayā*). For the context concerning the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and so forth is concerned only with the qualities actually heard therein. Furthermore, since it is possible to indicate all qualities by a single word in another instance, the words "udgītha" and so forth would become redundant.
Therefore, it is established that what has been stated is correct.
If it is argued that it exists as a designation, it has already been stated that even that [designation] exists.

"Is it not the case that the synthesis of all qualities must indeed be performed? For all the Vedas have the Blessed One as their name and thus denote His qualities, and the denotation of qualities serves precisely the purpose of meditation. Having raised this objection, the author states the aphorism by way of refutation:

"If it is argued that [the attributes] are based on name, it has been stated that even that exists. This is the meaning: "Based on name" means that because all the qualities of all the sciences are expressed in the form of the names of the Lord, the collection of the qualities mentioned in all the sciences must be performed. If this is argued, the response is that this very point was addressed in that objection; the resolution—that this is indeed desired—was stated by that Sūtra on Collection (*Upasaṃhāra-sūtra*). This is not established merely by reasoning; rather, there is also scriptural authority for this point, namely the statement, "Or these are indeed names," which means that such authority certainly exists.

And let it be so; for we also accept this, since the inclusion of all qualities has been stated by us. Furthermore, the word "or" (*nāma*) is authoritative because it is prescribed in the *Kauṇḍinya-śruti*. Therefore, since the inclusion of all qualities must be performed, it is established that the complete knowledge of all [qualities] is indeed purposeful.
Thus ends the section concerning the withdrawal [of the prāṇas].
Here, it is established that the previously mentioned performance and non-performance [of certain rites] are to be carried out according to the distinction between types of persons;
and this is because [the practice] is well-established by tradition.

Now, it may be argued that the previously mentioned conclusions—namely, that [the meditations] are either to be combined or not combined—are not tenable due to contradiction. For the simultaneous performance of two contradictory things by a single person is impossible. Nor can both be established on the basis of a difference in qualified persons (adhikārin), because there is no restrictive rule (niyāmaka) [to that effect]. To this, the author states the aphorism: [The opponent says: "But surely, the previously stated conclusions regarding combination and non-combination are not logical, because they are contradictory. It is impossible for one person to perform two contradictory things simultaneously. Nor is the establishment of both possible through a difference in qualified persons, as there is no restrictive rule. This being the position reached, the Sūtra says:

"And because [the rule] of attainment is consistent. This is its meaning: it is "consistent" (samañjasa), that is, appropriate, that both the performance and non-performance of the inclusion [of qualities] should be carried out. Why? Because of "attainment" (prāpteḥ); the meaning is that since those two are established according to the distinction between various persons suited for them, there is no contradiction attained.

Thus, the application and non-application [of the attributes] are established in this very way. The distinction is that for those such as Rudra, however many qualities appear clearly manifest, they do so simultaneously, like one's own two arms; whereas for others, it is according to their respective capacities. Therefore, because these two cases are consistent, what was stated previously is proven.
Thus concludes the section on acquisition.
Here, the necessity of performing the synthesis of many qualities is established by stating the excellence of the resulting fruit.
These others [are included] because of the non-difference from all.

Now, it might be argued that one need not combine all the various qualities [of the object of meditation], because there is no authoritative basis for the view that the gradation of results follows the gradation of the meditations. To this, the author of the Sūtras states the following:

"Because of the non-difference of all [attributes] from another [form]," so it is said. This is its meaning: these [meditators], such as Brahmā and others, who perform the compendium of all attributes, "from another"—that is, from those who do not perform that compendium—become possessors of a great fruit that is distinct from the fruit of the latter; they become partakers of that [great fruit]. Why? Because of the non-difference of all [attributes]. The meaning is: because of meditating upon [the Lord] by way of compendiously gathering the attributes declared in all the Vedas without division.

Thus, the synthesis of many qualities must indeed be performed. This is because there is a rule that the gradation of results follows the gradation of means; for those who possess the great meditations (mahopāsana) taught in the Vedas, it is impossible for there to be an absence of superior results. Therefore, it is established that the synthesis of many qualities must be performed.
Thus ends the section concerning the non-difference of all.
Here, the qualities to be meditated upon, which are common to all seekers of liberation, are determined:
"Bliss and the rest [belong] to the Principal."

Now, it may be argued that there are indeed no established qualities (guṇas) intended for common meditation, because there is no restrictive rule [to determine them]. Consequently, since there is an absence of such an establishment, primary meditation would be impossible; thus, meditation in general would be unattainable. To this objection, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Bliss and the rest belong to the primary [goal]. This is its meaning: bliss, knowledge, that which is denoted by the word "Being," and faultlessness—these four qualities, along with sovereignty denoted by the word "Self," are the attributes. The meaning is that they are to be meditated upon for the sake of the primary goal, namely liberation, by all those seeking liberation.

Thus, the qualities that are the objects of worship for all seekers of liberation are already established, because bliss, knowledge, and the absence of suffering are required by everyone in liberation. For the sake of attaining those, they must first be worshipped by the knower of reality (*tattvavit*). Furthermore, since "lordship" (*svāmitva*)—which is synonymous with "selfhood" (*ātmatva*)—is itself a means of pleasing the Lord through the recollection of His bonds, that too is to be worshipped. And so, it is established that every form of worship is appropriate, given the determination of the primary object of worship.
Thus ends the section concerning Bliss (Ānandādhikaraṇa).

In this context, regarding the meditation on Brahman, the rule that [the four attributes] apply to all is established by refuting the view that qualities such as "having pleasure as the head" are common to all qualified aspirants.
[The sūtra states: "Qualities such as having pleasure as the head are not attained [by all], for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference."

[Objection: But surely qualities such as "having bliss as the head" (priyaśirastva) and so forth must also be meditated upon by all, because they are comprised within [the category of] bliss and the rest; otherwise, since bliss and the other qualities would not have been properly meditated upon, liberation (mokṣa) could not be achieved. Consequently, it is incorrect to say that only four qualities are to be meditated upon by all. To this, he presents the Sūtra: *na vā viśeṣāt* (Or rather not, because of the distinction). This means: It is not the case that all these qualities are to be meditated upon by everyone, because there is a specific distinction [regarding which qualities are to be included]. The word "or rather" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view. The sense is that the inclusion of qualities such as "having bliss as the head" is not universal, because there is a distinction based on the specific scriptural context. For instance, in the passage beginning "The Self, dear one, is to be seen," the qualities "having bliss as the head" and so forth are mentioned in connection with the meditation on the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), whereas in the passage beginning "The True, the Knowledge, the Infinite is Brahman," the qualities "bliss, knowledge, and infinity" are mentioned in connection with the meditation on the small ether (daharavidyā). Thus, since the inclusion of these qualities is restricted by the specific context, the rule that only the four qualities—truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss—are to be meditated upon by all remains valid. Therefore, the objection is refuted.

"Because there is no attainment of [attributes] such as 'having pleasure as the head,' for distinction consists in the increase and decrease [of qualities]. This is its meaning: For all qualified aspirants, there is no attainment of [attributes] such as "having pleasure as the head"—that is, they lack the fitness for the meditation on attributes such as "pleasure is indeed its head," as stated in the Śruti; rather, this applies only to some. Why? Because (hi) it is well known that there is a distinction among them—that is, a distinction in results and a gradation of results. There is no traditional teaching (smṛti) stating that this applies to everyone.

And because, for the sake of establishing a difference in the fruits [of action], increase and decrease—meaning growth and decline, or rather, gradation—are required in the practice [of meditation], therefore [the self must be manifold]; such is the meaning.

And thus, qualities such as "having joy as the head" (priyaśirastva) and so forth are not to be meditated upon by all. For if one were to meditate on them by taking their specific distinctions—such as bliss (ānanda)—as the basis, it would follow that everyone must meditate on all qualities, since it is possible to state that even all other qualities are specific instances of the four beginning with bliss. Furthermore, there is no absence of liberation if one does not meditate on "having joy as the head" and the rest; for according to the scripture, "according to the multitude of qualities [one is fit for]," the attainment of the fruit is possible through the meditation on only those qualities for which one is qualified, even when specific [other] qualities are not meditated upon. Therefore, it is established that because qualities such as "having joy as the head" are unique [to specific texts], only the four [qualities beginning with bliss] are to be meditated upon by all.
Thus ends the section concerning the head being the beloved.

In this [section], the meditation upon the many qualities, such as having the beloved as the head and so forth, belonging to those other than the gods of the Vedic word—starting from the gods and ending with the Gandharvas—is established.
"But the others, on account of the similarity of their purpose."

Now, an objection may be raised: surely only four qualities are to be meditated upon by deities other than Viriñca, and no more, because it has been determined that all seekers of liberation (mumukṣus) possess the fitness for the meditation on these four qualities, whereas no determination regarding any further [qualities] exists; therefore, since the intermediate qualities are not to be meditated upon, their inclusion [in the meditation] is untenable. To this, the following aphorism is stated:

"But the others, however, on account of the similarity of purpose" (Itare tv arthasāmānyāt). This is its meaning: the word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed). "On account of the similarity of purpose" (arthasāmānyāt): this is a fifth case ending caused by the elision of the suffix *lyap*. Having regard for the equality of the respective fruits to be attained through meditation, the meaning is that the "others"—that is, all those qualities other than the four [already mentioned], namely the intermediate qualities—must indeed be combined by the gods and others.

And thus, qualities four times greater [than those previously mentioned] are indeed to be worshipped by the gods and others. Having first determined the fruits to be attained as required by them, and subsequently determining the means, it is established that the determination of fitness is possible through the instruction of either Brahman or another omniscient teacher; therefore, since even those of middling qualities are fit to be worshipped by the gods and others, the statement regarding their inclusion is justified. This is proven.
Here begins the section concerning the other [case].
In this regard, the authority for whether or not there should be a compendium of all qualities is stated:
"For the purpose of meditative reflection, because of the absence of any other purpose."

Now, it may be objected that the combination of all qualities need not be performed, because there is no authoritative evidence for it; and because liberation arises even for those who do not combine them, such as those who worship only four qualities, there is no contradiction with the Śruti statement, "One [attains] the Supreme. Furthermore, since that which is inconsistent cannot be a means, it is not a means; for a statement that presents something as a means when it is not would lack authority. Nor should it be said that because all meditations (vidyās) denote the qualities of the Lord, the combination of those qualities must be performed.

Since the qualities have been mentioned in various places, there is no purpose for a final summary (upasaṃhāra) of them; thus, such a summary would be fruitless. Consequently, because the description of the Lord’s qualities would not have that [summary] as its purpose, it would lack authority in that regard. And so, meditation (upāsana) would not be appropriate—this being the prima facie view, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Regarding the statement 'for the sake of meditation, because there is no other purpose': the meaning of this is as follows. In the Vedas, the description of all attributes and their synthesis are intended for *ādhyāna*—that is, for the sake of perfect knowledge and meditation. Why? Because there is no other purpose; that is to say, apart from meditation, there is no purpose for the description of attributes or their synthesis."

Thus, the synthesis (upasaṃhāra) must indeed be performed, because all the qualities of the Lord are designated by His names and thereby express His attributes. Furthermore, since there is no other purpose for them, they serve the purpose of meditation preceded by such synthesis. Nor is this synthesis fruitless, as there exists the fruit characterized by the excellence of bliss. Accordingly, with the exception of Viriñca (Brahmā), others should perform the synthesis of only certain qualities, not all, because there exists scriptural authority for non-synthesis, such as "One should meditate [on Him] as the Self alone" (Ātmaivopāsīta).
Therefore, it is established that meditation is appropriate.
And because of the word "Self."
Thus, he introduces the sūtra which establishes both the inclusion of all qualities and the non-inclusion based on the capacity [of the subject], by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

"And because of the word 'Self' (ātman). This is its meaning: In the passage "One should meditate [on him] as the Self alone," the word "Self" emphasizes the state of being and is restrictive. The "word 'Self'" refers to the term that enjoins meditation on the mere state of being the Self—the phrase "one should meditate [on him] as the Self alone. Therefore, the meaning is that non-inclusion [of other qualities] is established by this word which, having first excluded other attributes, enjoins meditation on the state of being the Self.

And thus, since the scripture cited is authoritative for the inclusion of minor qualities implied by the mode of worship (*upāsanā*), otherwise there would be an inconsistency because the instruction here would be solely for the worship of the Self preceded by the exclusion of other qualities. Nor should it be argued that the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) has a different meaning, since it was stated in the Sūtra that its function is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedaka*); how then can it be said to have the function of excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavacchedaka*)?

Because there is no contradiction due to the difference in the qualifications of the practitioners—just as in the cases of "inclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*) and "non-inclusion"—where for those of superior qualification, such as Brahmā and others, there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), while for those of inferior qualification, there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*); therefore, since both inclusion and non-inclusion must be performed, it is established that meditation (*upāsana*) is appropriate.
Thus ends the section concerning meditation.

In this context, the restriction of the four qualities beginning with bliss (*ānanda*) in the meditation (*upāsanā*) is established. [Sūtra: "The Self is grasped [as the object of meditation], as in other cases, because of what follows."

Now, one might raise the following doubt: "Is it not the case that the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) alone is to be meditated upon by all, and not the four qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth? This is because of the restrictive statement, 'The Self alone' (*ātmaiveti*). Furthermore, meditation on the mere nature of the Self is easy to perform when other qualities are set aside, and it brings about the swift attainment of direct intuition (*aparokṣya*) of the Lord along with its attendant benefits. Therefore, since the nature of the Self alone is the object of universal meditation, the statement that 'bliss and the rest belong to the Principal [Brahman]' is incorrect. To resolve this suspicion, the author recites the following Sūtra:

"Because of the inclusion of the Self, as in other cases, on account of what follows. This is its meaning: since, "as in other cases," just as in the passage concerning Truth, Knowledge, and so forth, the inclusion of other qualities occurs through words such as "Truth," so too in the sentence "the Self alone," the inclusion of the four qualities is possible by means of the word "Self. Why? Because of what follows; that is, because of the subsequent statement, "For here one would obtain these. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with that [teaching], as it refers to the meditation upon the four qualities.

Thus, Ānanda and the other three are also indeed objects of meditation. For, just as the word "Self" (ātman) [is used here], these words such as "Truth" (satya) and so forth denote multiple meanings due to the force of the subsequent statement, "For all these," which indicates that they signify Ānanda and the rest. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, what has been stated is established as correct.
Thus ends the section concerning the grasping of the self.
Here, the objection that the word "Self" (ātman) lacks the quality of being a restatement of what was previously mentioned is raised and then resolved:
"If it be argued [that it is not a restatement] because of the positive concomitance (anvaya), [we reply] it would be so because of the restrictive determination."

[Objection: Surely all qualities are to be meditated upon; they are not designated by the word "Self" (ātman) in their specific, exclusive sense, because that term denotes all qualities. Consequently, this [word "Self"] cannot serve as a basis for non-inclusion [of qualities]. To this, the Sūtra replies:

"If it be argued that [the attributes apply] because of their connection (anvaya), [we reply] that it would be so because of the restriction (avadhāraṇa). This is the meaning: Now, it might be argued that it is improper for the sentence "or as the Self" (*ātmeti vā*) to lack a concluding summary. Why? Because of the connection; that is, because all attributes are connected with the word "Self. If this is said, then what has been stated by the opponent would indeed be so. Nevertheless, there is no inconsistency. Why? Because of the restriction: because of the restriction "as the Self alone" (*ātmeti eva*). Nor is there a lack of determination.
For the meaning is that the word "Self" denotes all attributes only with respect to Brahmā and others, and not with respect to anyone else; thus, a definitive conclusion is possible.

This being the case, although the word *ātman* denotes all qualities, it does not do so for everyone. Rather, it denotes those specific qualities for each individual according to their respective capacity. Consequently, since the qualities denoted by the word *ātman* are to be meditated upon by whoever perceives as many qualities as appear to them, it is established that the statement regarding the universal meditativeness of the qualities expressed by the word *ātman* is logical.
Thus concludes the section on positive concomitance (anvayādhikaraṇa).
Here, it is established that only supermundane qualities are to be combined [in meditation]. [Sūtra: "Because of the mention of the effect, there is something new."

[Objection: "Surely the qualities of the Blessed One should be meditated upon only as worldly things; otherwise, since they are not experienced as non-worldly, there would be the undesirable consequence that meditation—which consists of recollection—could not exist due to the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā). And meditation must indeed be performed. Therefore, the qualities of the Blessed One are only worldly. To this, the Sūtra says:

"Because of the description of an effect, [the meditation] is something not previously known. This is its meaning: because liberation, which is the effect of meditation, is stated to be non-worldly (*alaukika*), therefore a collection of qualities that is "not previously known"—that is, non-worldly—must be meditated upon. This is the sense.

Thus, the qualities of the Blessed One are to be meditated upon precisely as they are supramundane, because their effect—liberation—is itself supramundane. Nor does it follow that meditation on them is impossible due to the non-perception of supramundane qualities; for such perception is possible through instruction by way of defining characteristics, just as in the case of Indra and others. Therefore, it is logical that only the supramundane qualities are to be meditated upon, and thus the previously stated supramundane nature of the Blessed One’s qualities is established.
Thus concludes the section on the effect.
In this context, the equality or inequality of the worship of Brahmāṇī and Brahmā is established in order to prove that such worship yields a fruit corresponding to itself.
"And likewise, it is equal because of non-difference."

Is it not the case that the worship of the Blessed One does not have the inherent nature of bestowing a fruit corresponding to itself? For in the case of the worship of Brahmāṇī and Brahman, there is an absence of the production of a fruit corresponding to themselves. Indeed, it cannot be said that whatever is of a certain kind must possess the inherent nature of producing something of that same kind if it does not produce it; otherwise, it would follow that a bamboo seed has the inherent nature of producing the trunk of a plantain tree. Nor should one suspect the absence of a suitable location for the cause; for the worship of those two may be either equal or unequal, but never both equal and unequal simultaneously.

Because they are contradictory; however, the fruit is both equal and unequal, since even when the stations are the same, there exists a gradation of qualities. Thus, since there is no fixed rule regarding the fruits corresponding to the meditations, it was stated [in the previous Sūtra] that "because of the similarity of the meaning in each case. This being the position reached, the following is set forth as a Sūtra:

"Samāna evaṃ cābhedāt" (And likewise, because of non-difference). This is its meaning: "And likewise" means even so; although the qualities of Brahman are transcendental (*alaukika*), the inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of Vāṇī's qualities applies only to those that are suitable, and not to unsuitable actions. In that regard, because of non-difference—that is, with reference to non-difference—the occasional actions such as the three-striding (*trivikrama*) are included within the eternally similar acts of striding, and thus their inclusion occurs. This is the sense.

Thus, worship indeed bestows a fruit corresponding to itself; for since the worship of Brahmāṇī and Brahmā is equal or unequal, there exists a fruit for each that corresponds precisely to their respective worship. And so, it is established that the stated principle—that the fruit exists in liberation according to the nature of the worship—is correct.
In this same way, it is so elsewhere as well, simply by virtue of the connection.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even for Viriñca, the withdrawal of specific activities such as the three strides (*trivikrama*) and so forth is not possible? For, since those activities are non-eternal, they would be absent at the time of meditation. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the following sūtra:

"Thus, it is also [the case] elsewhere because of the connection. This is its meaning: "But for Hiraṇyagarbha, even in other specific actions such as the 'three-striding' (trivikrama) and so forth, such a universal withdrawal [of all powers] is appropriate. Why? Because of the connection; that is to say, because of the eternality [of these actions] through their connection with Brahman in the form of identity (tādātmya)."

And thus, Brahmāṇī indeed meditates upon all qualities by fully incorporating them, as does Brahmā; however, she incorporates Trivikrama and others within his eternal acts of striding and so forth, and not as separate entities, because of the lack of such suitability. But Brahmā always meditates upon Trivikrama and others by fully incorporating them [within himself]. Since even the state of being Trivikrama and so forth is eternal due to its being the very nature of Brahman, it is established that what was said regarding the existence of the fruit in liberation according to the mode of meditation is correct.
Thus ends the section on coreferentiality.
Here, it is established that the meditation on the qualities denoted by the word "Self" must be performed by all;
[this is so] because there is no distinction.

Now, it might be argued that the injunction "one should meditate [on Brahman] as 'Not this, not this'" (neti neti) is common to all qualified aspirants, because it contains the word "ātman," which denotes infinite attributes. Nor should it be said that, although the word "ātman" denotes all attributes for the highest [aspirants], it denotes only those attributes appropriate to each [lower aspirant] for others—thereby being established as common to all—because such a thing is impossible. For a word is not an intelligent being.

Since it might follow that [the scripture], having taught all qualities with respect to a specific qualified person for whom [the Lord] is supreme, teaches only a few with respect to another because [the Lord] is not supreme for him; and since, consequently, the statement that there is no authority for non-inclusion (anupasaṃhāra) would be incorrect—this being the prima facie view, the following was aphorized:

"Or rather, not so, because of the distinction. This is its meaning: it is not accepted that by the word "Self" (*ātman*) occurring in the sentence, all qualities are grasped. Why? Because of the distinction; the meaning is that, depending on the specific qualification of the seeker (*adhikārin*), that word denotes only those qualities for which he is fit.

And thus, this injunction is common to all qualified aspirants, because it designates those various qualities that are appropriate for each respective individual. Nor is there any impossibility [of its application], for just as the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) produces either valid knowledge or non-valid knowledge depending on the qualification [of the hearer], so too the word *ātman*, which denotes all qualities, can convey those qualities only by depending upon the specific fitness of the individual. Therefore, it is established that all the qualities expressed by the word *ātman* are to be meditated upon by everyone.
And it is also shown.

[Objection: But since even for one who meditates on [the Self] as possessing four qualities, there is the possibility of understanding it as possessing five qualities due to the word "Self" (ātman), a specific restriction would be impossible; thus, meditation [on the specific number of qualities] would be untenable. To this, the Sūtra is recited, supporting with scripture the point established by reasoning, namely: "Because of the distinction. [The Sūtra: "But because of the distinction. (Brahmasūtra 3.3.58) [Commentary: Although the word "Self" is common to both, the distinction between the two meditations—consisting of the difference in the number of qualities—is established by reasoning. This same point is supported by scripture as well. Thus, the Sūtra is stated.
"And it shows" means: the meaning of this is that the Śruti demonstrates its own stated meaning with respect to "all."

And thus, since it is possible to establish the rule that as many qualities as are perceived by the word "Self" (ātman) simultaneously—as in the case of one's own two arms—so many alone are to be meditated upon; and because of the scriptural statement, "all qualities"; therefore, it is established that what was said is correct, on account of all the qualities expressed by the word "Self" being objects of meditation.
Thus ends the section [beginning with] "Or rather not."
In this regard, it is stated that the qualities such as "supporting" (saṃbhṛti) and so forth do not belong to every object of meditation:
"And because of supporting, pervading heaven, and so on."

[Objection: Is it not the case that for all beings, beginning with humans, the qualities of *saṃbhṛti* (sustenance) and *dyubhyāpti* (pervasion of heaven) are objects of meditation, because they possess the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*), just like the gods? This is because their respective fruits—the sustaining of one's own lower state and the pervasion of light—are things to be realized (*bhāvya*). Nor does this entail the meditation on all qualities [of the Lord], because there is no desire for those other fruits. Consequently, the restriction to the meditation on only four qualities would be violated. Alternatively: The gods and others are not fit for the meditation on *saṃbhṛti* and *dyubhyāpti*, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Nor should it be said that their qualification for that meditation is established merely by their desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). For if the gods were qualified for meditations such as the *saṃbhṛti* on account of their desire for liberation, then humans would likewise be so qualified, since there is no distinction between them; thus, the position is contradicted by reasoning (*tarkabādha*). For this very reason, the qualification of the gods is not established by their desire for the fruit [of those meditations]. Consequently, the superiority of the gods over humans remains unproven. Thus, having reached this second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author states the aphorism (*sūtra*) which provides the resolution.

Regarding the phrase "and also because of the collection and pervasion": its meaning is as follows. By the word "api" (also), the negative particle "na" is drawn back [from the previous context]. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only). "Collection and pervasion" refers to perfect gathering and the pervasion of light. These do not apply to every object of worship; rather, they apply only to those worshipped by the gods and others. Why? Because, precisely for that reason, there exists a specific distinction in the fitness of the qualified aspirant (adhikārī). This is the meaning.

And thus, the two meditations on *saṃbhṛti* (the supporting) and *dyu-vyāpti* (pervasion of heaven) are not for all worshippers, because humans lack the fitness for such meditation. Nor is there a failure to achieve the light and other qualities required for liberation, since that is accomplished precisely by the light and so forth as they are perceived within the manifestation of the Lord's form. Consequently, there is no violation of the rule regarding the meditation on the four qualities mentioned above. Alternatively: Devas and others possess the meditations on *saṃbhṛti* and so forth, because in the context of the deities' eligibility, there exists a distinction from the eligibility of others. Since the meditations on *saṃbhṛti* and *dyu-vyāpti* exist for the deities as their objects of worship, there is no loss of excellence [in the meditation]. Thus, two possible conclusions have been stated.
Thus ends the section concerning the collection of materials.
Here it is established that the collection of qualities from all the vidyās must be performed;
for even in the Puruṣavidyā, the others are not mentioned.

Now, an objection might be raised: "There should be no collection of qualities scattered [across different texts], because there is no purpose for it. Nor can it be said that such a collection is for the sake of meditating on the qualities appropriate to oneself; for those of superior intellect would achieve their goal merely through the collection of qualities mentioned in a single meditation that declares many qualities, while those of duller intellect would achieve it merely through the collection of qualities mentioned in a single meditation that declares few qualities. Therefore, since the collection is useless, all knowledge [of all qualities] is not required. To this, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Also in the Puruṣavidyā, because others are not mentioned. This is its meaning: even in the Puruṣavidyā—which is proposed as the highest of all vidyās—namely the vidyā called the Puruṣasūkta—the qualities of "others," that is, those qualities other than those mentioned therein, are not mentioned; therefore, the combination of the qualities of all vidyās must indeed be performed. This is the sense.

Thus, the collection of qualities scattered [in various places] must indeed be performed, because there exist superior practitioners who worship all qualities. Furthermore, even in the *Puruṣasūkta*, which is the most excellent among meditations (*vidyā*), not all qualities are enumerated; nor is there a rule that those qualities required by those of duller intellect must be mentioned in a single place. Therefore, since the collection of qualities from everywhere is something that must be done, it is established that what was stated is correct.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Person (Puruṣādhikaraṇa).
In this [section], the fact that qualities such as "piercing" (vedha) and so forth are to be meditated upon in all [meditations] is refuted,
because there is a difference in their meaning, such as piercing and the like.

"Now, [it may be argued that] qualities such as 'piercing,' mentioned in the passage beginning with 'O Agni, pierce the skin of the sorcerer' (RV 7.104.16), are to be meditated upon by all, because the result of those qualities—the subjugation of the wicked—is required by everyone. Therefore, since piercing and the other qualities are to be meditated upon by all, there is no restrictive rule that meditation should consist of only four qualities. This being the prima facie position, the Sūtra states:

"Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing, and so forth. This is its meaning: because of the difference in purpose—that is, because the fruit of meditations on piercing and so forth is distinct from the fruit appropriate for ascetics and others, such as non-violence—piercing and the like (as expressed in "Pierce!", "Split!", "Cut!"), are not to be practiced by everyone who meditates. This is the sense.

And thus, piercing (*vedha*) and the other methods are not to be practiced by everyone; for ascetics (*yati*) and others lack the qualification for their results, such as the piercing of the *brahmarandhra*. Therefore, since piercing and the rest are not to be practiced by all, it is established that the previously stated rule is not violated.
Thus ends the section concerning piercing.
In this context, the persistence of the meditation even in liberation is established:

"But in the case of abandonment, because of the supplementary nature of the word 'approaching' (upāyana), it is like the kuśa grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the chanting; so it has been said."

Now, it may be argued that meditation is not performed by one who is liberated. For if one accepts that meditation is prescribed for the liberated, it would follow that there is still something to be attained as a fruit, and it would follow that liberation itself has not been achieved. Conversely, if one does not accept this [that meditation is for the liberated], it would follow that there is still a fruit to be attained; and since activity toward something is untenable when there is no expectation of something yet to be attained, it follows that meditation is necessarily qualified (sopādhika). Thus, meditation should be performed solely because it is a means to liberation, and there should be no excessive attachment to meditation itself. To this, the Sūtra says:

"But in the case of abandonment, because it is supplementary to the word 'approaching' (upāyana), it is like the kuśa-grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; that has been stated. The meaning of this is as follows: The particle "tu" (but) serves for emphasis. Since, in the case of "abandonment"—that is, in liberation characterized by the abandonment of bondage—it has been stated in scripture that "this Sāman belongs to the liberated ones," therefore their worship (upāsana) certainly exists even in liberation. Furthermore, that [worship] is just like the use of *kuśa* grass, the chanting of meters, the praise, and the singing; it is not [enjoined] by a formal injunction (*vidhi*).

Just as for those whose Brahmayajña is obligatory and whose twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) is obligatory, there is the study of both names by their own will—just as one might perform praise or chanting at will even after the obligatory rites—so too [the study of these names] is by will alone, not from scriptural injunction. Why? Because of the subordinate nature of the word "attainment" (upāyana). "Attainment" means liberation (mokṣa). The meaning is that since the injunctions for meditation are supplementary to the statements concerning liberation, how could those injunctions enjoin them even in that context? This is the sense.

Thus, meditation must indeed be practiced even in the state of liberation, because of the scriptural statement, "This is the Sāman. Nor does liberation possess the same characteristics as transmigratory existence merely by virtue of being bound by injunctions; for it is accepted that meditation occurs by one's own will even without an injunction. Furthermore, it is observed that even after the obligatory daily study of the Veda (svādhyāya) known as the Brahma-yajña, the study and other activities of the twice-born occur by their own will alone, such as covering [the texts] with kuśa grass. Therefore, it is established that what was stated is logical.
Because in the hereafter there is nothing left to be crossed over; for thus it is with others as well.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that for one who is liberated, meditation is not undertaken by his own will, but rather only for the purpose of avoiding undesirable results that may occasionally arise even in liberation? For no one is ever seen to engage in fruitless activity. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the following Sūtra:

"Because in the state beyond [death], there is nothing to be crossed over; for thus say others. This is its meaning: "In the *saṃparāya*—that is, in liberation (*mokṣa*)—meditation must be accepted as being undertaken by one's own will alone, and not for the sake of averting what is undesirable. Why? Because there is nothing to be crossed over; that is, because for those who are liberated, there is simply no undesirable thing to be avoided. And why is that? Because, for this reason (*hi*), other Śākhins recite the scriptural text: 'For he has already crossed over' (*tīrṇo hi*). Therefore is the meaning.

And thus, in the state beyond death (*saṃparāya*), there is nothing further to be crossed. Moreover, even yoga and the like are practiced by the liberated; how much more so meditation (*upāsana*)? For the *Bhārata* states: "The two [sons] were liberated by the liberated. Therefore, it is established that since meditation continues even in liberation, it must be performed without qualification while in saṃsāra.
Thus ends the section concerning the loss [of merit].
In this regard, the absence of restriction regarding the activity of the liberated ones is established by the principle that they act according to their own will,
since this does not conflict with either [state].

[Objection: Surely the liberated ones must necessarily perform ritual action, because their practice consists of the worship of Viṣṇu and because they possess the capacity for such action; otherwise, they would not even perform meditation necessarily, as there would be no distinction [between them and others]. Therefore, since for the liberated there is equality regarding both ritual action and meditation, it follows that prior [to liberation] one should not perform meditation as something superior to ritual action. To this, the Sūtra states:

"According to their own will, because there is no contradiction with either [of the two]. This is its meaning: liberated beings perform actions solely by following their own will (*svecchā*), not according to injunction (*vidhi*). Why? Because there is no contradiction with either; that is to say, because there is an absence of both the binding force of injunction and the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance.

And thus, for those who are liberated, there is no fixed rule regarding action; rather, they act sometimes by their own will and sometimes do not act, because there is an absence of both injunction and the fear of sin—which are the causes that necessitate the performance of an action as a rule. Therefore, since there is no necessity for action for the liberated one, it is established that even while in saṃsāra, meditation (upāsana) must be performed with excellence.
The purposefulness of the movement [of the soul] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.

Now, one might ask: why is it that for the liberated there is simply an absence of injunctions, bonds, and transgressions, such that there is no restriction regarding action? To this, he provides the answer in the following sūtra:

"Because liberation has purposefulness in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. This is the meaning: "hi" indicates the reason. "In both ways" means precisely because of the absence of both bondage and transgression. "Gati" means liberation. Its status as a human goal [is established]. "Otherwise," that is, if bondage and transgression were present in liberation, there would be a "contradiction"—the meaning being that there would be a contradiction in the form of liberation not being a human goal, as it would be equal to saṃsāra.

And thus, it is established that one must accept the absence of any restrictive rule regarding karma even for liberation; otherwise, liberation would not constitute a human goal (puruṣārtha). Therefore, it is proven that even while in saṃsāra, meditative worship (upāsana) should be practiced with particular intensity.
It is established because of the perception of objects characterized by those [marks], as in the case of the world.

[Objection: But surely the absence of injunctions and so forth regarding liberated beings exists only for the sake of conceiving a restriction on their karma, not for the sake of establishing it; for there is deviation in the case of the Lord’s actions. Therefore, since there is no establishing factor, this restriction is simply untenable. To this, the Sūtra says:

"Because [the performance of action] is possible for them due to the perception of an object characterized by that [action], just as in the world. This is its meaning: just as in the world there is no rule requiring the performance of the ritual act of Viṣṇukramaṇa—which is an auxiliary part of a sacrifice—after the completion of the sacrifice; rather, it is performed only occasionally, so too it is possible and reasonable that liberated beings sometimes perform actions and sometimes do not. Why is this so? "Because of the perception of an object characterized by that": because of the perception, that is, the attainment, of liberation, which is an object characterized by that [action] and is ultimately achievable through action.

Thus, it is established that once [liberation] has arisen, they perform actions at times according to their own will and not at others; such is the state of affairs. This is because liberation, which is the fruit thereof, has been attained, and because once that fruit has been attained, there is no further impulsion to act. Just as in the world, after the completion of a sacrifice—which is the characteristic fruit—there is no further impulsion toward acts such as the Viṣṇukramaṇa, but rather the impulsion arises solely from one's own will. Here is the formal argument: liberated beings do not possess a fixed necessity for the performance of ritual action.

Because there is no specific cause [for cessation] and because he has already attained that fruit—just like the sacrificer—it is established that for one who is liberated, since there is no restriction regarding karma, meditation must be performed with even greater intensity, even while in the state of saṃsāra.
Thus concludes the section on the meters.
Here, it is established that for all those who have attained knowledge of Brahman through the practice of Upāsana, liberation is certain.
[Sūtra: "There is no restriction for all, because there is no contradiction with scripture and inference."

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that liberation does not accrue to all knowers? For in some knowers, unfitness is produced by the curses resulting from treachery toward their own superiors; and indeed, the attainment of that [liberation] is not possible for those who are unfit. If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even the unfit would have to perform the synthesis of all qualities [of the Lord]. Therefore, since liberation is absent for all knowers, one should not practice meditation free from doubt. To this, the following is stated as a sūtra:

"Non-restriction [applies] to all, because there is no contradiction, on account of scripture and inference. This is its meaning: "non-restriction" means that among those possessing immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), there is no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) such that for some there is liberation and for others there is not; this is understood. Why? Because there is no contradiction—that is, an absence of any prohibitor—regarding the liberation of all. Furthermore, it is known from both scripture and inference: from the scriptural statement "not anyone at all," and from the inference based upon that.

And thus, liberation must belong to all who possess knowledge. One who asserts that "liberation belongs only to some, not to all" must be questioned: Is it because of the presence of an obstacle (*bādhaka*) that not all attain liberation, or because of the absence of a means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*)? The first case is not tenable, because such an obstacle does not exist. Nor can an obstacle be something that produces incapacity (*ayogyatā*), for according to the statement "those which are objects of knowledge," the production of incapacity is not admitted. The second case is also untenable, as it would result in a contradiction with the Śruti text: "There is no one [who does not know]."

Furthermore, there is the inference: "Those who possess knowledge are destined for liberation because they possess knowledge, just like the person universally acknowledged [as liberated]. Since this is not contradicted by any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) and is rooted in the Śruti, it cannot be invalidated by an inference based on mere summary (*upasaṃhāra*). Therefore, it is established that because liberation is certain for those possessing knowledge, one should practice meditation without hesitation.
Thus concludes the section on the lack of fixed rule.
In this regard, the restriction of qualification for worship is established:
"The persistence of those holding office lasts as long as their office."

[Objection: Is it not the case that those who possess meditative worship (*upāsanā*) do not have a restriction regarding their qualification [for liberation], because there is a lack of evidence? Nor is the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the gradations of bliss in liberation a valid means of proof; for even if such gradation were established by evidence, it could be otherwise accounted for simply by the gradations in the effort of meditative worship. Thus, since there is no restriction on the qualification for the object of worship, [the opponent] arrives at this conclusion. To this, the Sūtra states: *na, niyamātad-darśanāt* (Not so, because of the rule [of qualification] and because of the observation of that). This means: It is not so, because there is a rule regarding qualification, and because we observe that very rule in scripture. For it is observed in the scriptures that there is a restriction on the qualification for the object of worship, as seen in passages such as, "The Brahmin should desire to know Him through the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22), and "One who knows these two paths becomes fit for immortality" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.6.6). Furthermore, the gradations of bliss in liberation are indeed established by evidence, and they cannot be explained away merely by the gradations in the effort of worship; rather, they must be understood as resulting from the gradations in the excellence of the knowledge of Brahman itself. Therefore, there is a restriction on the qualification for the object of worship. Thus, the Sūtra has been formulated.

"Until their office is fulfilled, there is persistence for those who hold office. This is the meaning: for those who hold office—namely Brahmā and others who are habituated to meditation according to their respective capacities—their liberation occurs precisely in accordance with their own offices. The meaning is that for those who persist [in their roles], the fruit of their liberation is determined solely by the gradations in their meditative practice.

And thus, there is indeed a restrictive rule (niyama): "This person is fit for the meditation on these qualities, but this one is not. For without that, it would be impossible even to explain the gradations of bliss mentioned in the Śruti; since even the gradation of effort is dependent upon the gradation of fitness, as expressed by the saying, "Effort is greater according to the qualification. Therefore, it is established that what was stated regarding the restriction in the context of meditative worship (upāsanā) is correct.

But there is no contradiction regarding the cognitions of the syllables, because of their commonality and the presence of that [nature], as in the case of the *aupasada* offerings; so it has been stated.

Objection: Surely, gradation in bliss within liberation is not tenable; for if there were inequality among the liberated, it would result in mutual conflict, as such is observed in the world. Furthermore, scriptural texts concerning gradation refer only to the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). If gradation were admitted in liberation, it would entail the occurrence of hatred, envy, and so forth. Therefore, since there is no restriction on eligibility for the means [to liberation], and since [liberation] is attained [equally by all], the claim that "it is consistent" and so on is incorrect. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated:

"But there is no contradiction regarding the cognitions of the Imperishable, on account of the commonality and the existence thereof, as in the case of the Aupasadās; that has been stated. This is the meaning: the word "but" (tu) has the sense of "also" (api). Regarding "the cognitions of the Imperishable" (akṣaradhiyām), this refers to those who possess knowledge of Brahman. Even though there is inequality [among them], there is no contradiction; that is, no conflict exists. Why? Because they possess the cognition of Brahman. Furthermore, it is because of the commonality and the existence thereof—due to the absence of defects in all of them and because the lower ones do not provide assistance to the higher ones. How so? It is like the Aupasadās, that is, like good disciples. Moreover, "that has been stated."
The meaning is that even though there is inequality, there is no contradiction; this is stated in the *Tura-śruti* by the word "not manifold" (*nānā*), and therefore there is no contradiction.

And thus, there is no possibility of contradiction. For in the case of a contradiction, the causes are a greed for objects, envy, and so forth, as well as the state of being non-beneficial; these do not occur in liberated beings because they possess the knowledge of Brahman and are free from defects. Furthermore, there is no lack of beneficence, since the existence of the counter-positive [the benefactor] is established by valid means of knowledge. Therefore, it is established that what was stated regarding the restriction in the context of meditative worship is logical.
Thus ends the section on legal cases.

In this context, it is established that those qualified for the meditative worship (upāsanā) have their existence terminated with the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇa), on account of the scriptural declaration to that effect.
|| [Sūtra 14] || "On account of the declaration of this much. || [Sūtra 15] || 1.3.14–15 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that those who hold office do not have their lives terminated by the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)? For the vital breath is governed by its own superior office-holder, because it is an office, just like the name and so forth. Since this contradicts the aforementioned inference, the claim that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is fit for the meditation on all qualities—on the grounds that office-holders do not have their lives terminated by the departure of the vital breaths—is incorrect. To this, the Sūtra states: [The answer follows: "But [the office] is subordinate to the one who has attained the highest state. (BS 4.3.16) [This means: But the office is subordinate to the one who has attained the highest state, because it is an office, just like the name and so forth. Therefore, since the office is subordinate to the one who has attained the highest state, the objection based on the inference regarding the non-termination of the lives of office-holders is refuted. Thus, Hiraṇyagarbha alone is indeed fit for the meditation on all qualities. This is the established conclusion.

"Because of the scriptural statement to this effect. This is its meaning: the gradation of eligibility extends only this far—that is, it culminates precisely at the vital breath (prāṇa). Why? Because of the scriptural statement; the meaning is that it is so because of the Śruti text, "The vital breath, verily... and so forth.

And thus, it is established that for the qualified practitioner, the state of ending with the breath alone is indicated by scripture; furthermore, there is no sublation of this because inference has its object already contradicted [by scripture]. Consequently, since the qualified practitioners end with the breath, it is proven that he alone is fit for the meditation on all qualities.
If it is argued that [the soul] exists in the interval like a collection of living beings, that has already been answered.
Having raised an objection to what was stated, he reads the sūtra as a resolution.

“If it be argued that [the case] is like that of the group of beings, we say: ‘That has already been answered. This is the meaning: Just as in the group of beings—that is, in the collection of vital breaths (prāṇa) beginning with name—one is seen to be the one and supreme, so too might there be someone superior to the vital breath among those between [the individual soul and Brahman], excluding the Supreme Self and Śrī; if this is argued, the answer is ‘no,’ which is the sense of the ellipsis. For that has already been stated regarding the absence of anyone superior to the vital breath; the authority for this was stated as ‘not indeed’ (na hi). Therefore is the meaning.”

And thus, because the aforementioned inference is not contradicted by the scriptural text "Prāṇa indeed [is Brahman]," there is no conflict; therefore, it is established that what was stated is correct.
If it is argued that otherwise the distinction [between the two] would be untenable, we say no; for it is like the case of instruction.

Now, it might be argued that on the strength of the scriptural text "Prāṇa indeed [is Brahman]," it is not possible to assert the supreme excellence of Prāṇa; for if that were so, since two Lords are untenable, it would follow that Prāṇa and the Supreme Self are one and the same. To this objection, the Sūtra states:

"If it be argued that otherwise the distinction [between them] would be untenable, we say: 'No, as in the case of the instruction. This is its meaning: "Otherwise," that is, if there were no superiority over the vital breath (prāṇa), the distinction between the vital breath and the Supreme Self (paramātman) would be untenable—if this is argued, we say "no. Why? Because "as in the case of the instruction": just as it is stated in the Śruti, so it is accepted. Therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply; such is the meaning.

And thus, by accepting a restriction of the word "all" according to the method stated in the Chāndogya Śruti, it is established that Prāṇa is the most excellent among all eligible aspirants (adhikārin), because Mahālakṣmī is superior to him, and the Supreme Self is superior to her; therefore, since the eligibility of aspirants culminates in Prāṇa, he alone is fit for the meditation on all qualities.
Thus ends the section concerning the mention of "so much."
Here, the superiority of the Supreme Lord over the vital breath (prāṇa) of those qualified for worship is established:
"There is a mutual exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [Him] as being like the others."

Now, an objection may be raised: it is not logical that Viṣṇu possesses the status of being the supreme of all, because after declaring the pre-eminence of Prāṇa, no such pre-eminence is stated for Him. Indeed, even though there exists something superior to Prāṇa, there is no reason for its non-mention by which we might disregard that omission and perceive Viṣṇu’s superiority over Prāṇa. Nor should it be argued that it is illogical for Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the word "Satya," to possess superiority over Prāṇa; for, in the absence of any factor distinguishing the context, "truthfulness" (satyatva) is merely an attribute of Prāṇa. Thus, since Viṣṇu does not possess the status of being the object of worship for all, this prima facie view is addressed by the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [He is] the one [denoted by 'Truth'], on account of the subsequent [statement]. (Brahmasūtra 1.1.22) This means: But He—Viṣṇu—is indeed the one [intended as the Supreme], because of what follows later. For the subsequent passage—"From whom truth, knowledge, and infinity proceed"—is a statement concerning the nature of the Supreme Self, and it serves to exclude others. Since the attributes of truth, knowledge, and infinity are impossible in anything other than the Supreme Self, they establish Viṣṇu alone as the subject of the context. Furthermore, the fact that the term "Prāṇa" is used here is due to the proximity of the two words "Prāṇa" and "Satya" in the preceding sentence, and not because the word "Prāṇa" denotes the individual vital breath. Therefore, Viṣṇu is the one to be worshipped by all. Thus, the conclusion is established.

"Exchanging [the questions and answers] because they distinguish [him], as in the other case. This is its meaning: An exchange of the questions and answers must be made immediately after the section on Prāṇa and before the section on Viṣṇu. Why? Because (hi), for the reason that, just as in the case of Name and so forth, the Chāndogyas—those who teach Viṣṇu under the name Satya—distinguish [him] from the teacher of Prāṇa by means of the word "but" (tu) in the phrase "But he indeed [knows]" (eṣa tu vai). Therefore, this is the sense.

And thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the supreme of all is indeed logical. Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of [the names] Nāman and so forth, there is no intention to establish anyone superior to Prāṇa because of the absence of a question and answer; for by the force of the general context (*prāyapāṭha*), a question and answer can be inferred. Nor should it be argued that there is no supplying of a question and answer because there is no break in the context; for the word "but" (*tu*) exists as a marker of a break in the context.

And thus, since the seer of the mantra has stated, following a sequence of questions and answers, that Viṣṇu’s superiority is greater than that of Prāṇa, it is established that his status as the object of all worship is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning the exchange (vyatihāra).
Here, the superiority of Viṣṇu alone over Prāṇa is established;
for that [Brahman] is indeed [described as] "consisting of truth" and so forth.

Now, an objection may be raised: Is Viṣṇu alone, denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*), superior to *prāṇa*? Or rather, are there many? For it is stated that after "Truth," there follow "Knowledge," "Faith," "Devotion," "Action," "Bliss," "Abundance," "Ego," and "Self. Since there is no evidence for the identity of Truth and the others, and since many are superior even to *prāṇa*, it follows that Viṣṇu’s status as the supreme of all—without qualification—is untenable, as he would not be the sole supreme being. To this, the Sūtra provides the following answer: [The Sūtra: "But [He is] the one, on account of the designation of difference. (BrSū 1.1.22) [Commentary: "But" (*tu*) serves to refute the objection. Viṣṇu alone is the supreme of all, even among those mentioned after *prāṇa*. Why? Because of the designation of difference. For although the words "Truth" and so forth denote Viṣṇu, they are used with distinct attributes such as "the Truth of truths" (*satyānāṃ satyam*), "the Knowledge of knowledges" (*vijñānānāṃ vijñānam*), and so on. This distinction is established by the fact that these terms are applied to Him who is the cause of the manifestation of the respective qualities, just as the term "king" is applied to one who causes the manifestation of royal power. Furthermore, the various designations are appropriate because He possesses diverse powers; otherwise, the use of different words would be purposeless. Moreover, the statement "He who knows the Truth becomes immortal" (*satyaṃ jñātvā'mṛtībhavati*) indicates that the knowledge of Truth leads to immortality, which is a result of knowing Viṣṇu. Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is the supreme of all. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

"Indeed, she alone is [the one denoted by] 'Truth' and so forth. This is the meaning: "hi" (indeed) because; the categories beginning with "Truth" and ending with "I am the Self" are that very same supreme deity called Īśvara. Therefore, there are not many things superior to Prāṇa; rather, the meaning is that Śrī and that Lord are indeed one and the same.

And this being so, since Truth (Satya) and all the others are the Supreme Deity, there is no absence of statements regarding non-difference. For when "Truth" is questioned, the instruction of another object pervaded by that [Truth]—beginning with "Just as indeed"—cannot in any way be intended to convey anything other than the fact that Consciousness possesses the attribute of Truth; and because an attribute is non-different from the substrate of that attribute. Furthermore, liberation is declared to result from the knowledge of the Self as the "I" in the passage beginning with "He, verily, this one," and fullness is declared in the passage beginning with "He alone is below."

Furthermore, since in another Vedic text (*śruti*) such as "Truth is full" (*satyaṃ pūrṇam*), fullness (*pūrṇatva*) is stated to be a defining characteristic of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), it follows from that as well that all [qualities] beginning with Truth are one with Him. Therefore, it is established that because everything from Truth up to the Self (*ātman*) constitutes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Blessed Lord, the statement that He alone is superior to Prāṇa is logically sound.
Thus concludes the section on Truth (Satyādhikaraṇa).
Here, it is established that Śrī lacks the qualification for worship [of Brahman].
[The Sūtra states: "Because of desire elsewhere, and because of the abode and so forth there."

[Objection: Is it not the case that *prakṛti* (primordial matter) alone is the qualified agent? Nor should it be said that this is so because [the qualification] is not mentioned in the context of names and so forth; for that reason is unproven (*asiddha*). Nor does it follow that [liberation] must be heard [only by humans]; for we accept that even an unuttered statement may be intended by the seer (*ṛṣi*). Nor is transmigratoriness unproven; for it is established by the observation of birth, death, and so forth in the cases of Sītā, Rukmiṇī, and others. Consequently, since there is no restriction to the end of life for those who are qualified, [the following] was set forth as a sūtra: [The answer: This is not so. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding the departure [of the soul]. For the scripture declares that the soul departs from the body at the time of death. And it is not the case that this applies only to human beings; rather, it is understood that this is common to all embodied beings. Furthermore, the transmigratory nature of *prakṛti* is not established, because it is devoid of the experience of pleasure and pain. Nor is it reasonable to assume that the scripture intends an unuttered statement, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and contradict the fact that the qualification is indeed mentioned in connection with names and so forth. Moreover, the transmigratory nature of Sītā, Rukmiṇī, and others is established through their subordination to another; for they were born as the wives of others and died upon the death of those others. Therefore, since they are not independent agents, the aforementioned objection does not apply. Thus, the conclusion is that liberation occurs only at the end of life for those who are qualified. This is what was set forth in the sūtra.

"Elsewhere than that, and there as well, she manifests incarnations out of desire, on account of her abodes and so forth. This is its meaning: Lakṣmī, while remaining there in the presence of the Blessed One, also manifests incarnations elsewhere, such as on the earth and other places, solely by the will of the Lord (kāmāt). Why? "On account of her abodes and so forth" means because of scriptural passages such as "she who has all abodes," which establish her omnipresence.

And thus, primordial nature (prakṛti) is not an eligible agent, because it is unbound. Nor is its status established by birth and so forth, since there is no origination for Sītā, Rukmiṇī, and others, as they are manifested [forms]; for the Vatsa-śruti states that she is "the abode of all" and "existing at all times. Therefore, since primordial nature lacks eligibility, it is established that the soul's state ends with the vital breaths (prāṇa).
There is no omission [of the rite] due to reverence.

Now, one might object: "If Ramā were not subject to transmigratory existence (asaṃsāritva), then, being one who has already accomplished all that was to be done (kṛtakṛtyatva), she would lack the practice of worshiping the Lord and so forth. Yet this is not tenable, because it contradicts scriptural authorities such as *'That which is worshiped is Brahman'* and others, since these state that she is 'worshiped,' 'meditated upon,' and 'honored. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism (sūtra) that dispels it.

"Due to reverence, there is no omission. This is its meaning: "Due to reverence"—that is, due to an excess of unconditioned devotion toward the Blessed One—"there is no omission," meaning that there is no absence of service to the Blessed One by Śrī.

And thus, although Śrī is eternally liberated and unbound, because she is under the influence of a devotion that is unsurpassed by anything else and free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), her worship of the Lord is established as a matter of necessity; this is evident from the statement, "just as Śrī. Therefore, it is proven that what has been said is logical.
Because of the mention of that [attainment] in the context of presence.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for Ramā to possess eternal liberation (*nityamuktatva*), because there is no cause for it; nor can it be said to exist by her own nature, because she lacks independence. Having raised this objection, the author presents the aphorism (*sūtra*) to resolve it:

"Because of her presence and because of that statement. This is the meaning: It is appropriate that Śrī is eternally liberated. Why? Because of her presence—that is, because she always remains in the proximity of Hari. And Śrī’s state of being eternally in his proximity is known from that statement, namely from the statement regarding their eternal connection: "These two [are inseparable]. This is the sense.

And thus, since it is established that Ramā stands in close proximity [to the Lord] based on the scriptural statement "two," and because the cause known as the preeminent grace of the Lord exists, it is proven that—given her state of eternal liberation and the absence of any office of authority—it is logical that her departure occurs at the end of her vital breaths (prāṇa). This is established.
Thus concludes the section on desire.
Here, the necessity of performing the entire process of worship—consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*)—is established.
"The restrictive rule for the sake of determining that [meditation] exists, because it is seen [in scripture]; for the fruit is distinct and unobstructed."

Is it not the case that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) alone are what must be performed? For once ignorance, doubt, and error have been removed by those two, vision (*darśana*) arises from its own cause alone. If it be argued that because the obstacles to ignorance are firm, the removal of those obstacles occurs only through meditation (*dhyāna*), then let knowledge arise from meditation alone; hearing and reflection would not be for the sake of knowledge. Furthermore, there is no evidence for their being causes of knowledge when combined, nor is there any utility for hearing and reflection in the actual production of knowledge.
Therefore, since the meditation on the whole must necessarily be performed, the injunction for it would be rendered useless; this being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra:

"Because there is a restriction for the purpose of determining that; for its perception is indeed separate, as it has an unobstructed fruit.
