Since the immediate succession of the year is possible for both paths through these different routes, and since there is

"Varuṇa is after lightning because of their connection"—this is the meaning of that [statement]. Its sense is as follows: "After lightning" means after reaching lightning, Varuṇa is to be reached. Why? Because of the connection; that is to say, because of Varuṇa's connection with what is above lightning.

And thus, the immediate succession of the year for both [the lightning and Varuṇa] should not be accepted; rather, there is only one path. On that path, immediately after the year, one goes to the lightning itself. Nor is there any contradiction with other scriptural passages, because it is logical that Varuṇa is to be reached immediately after the lightning, as that is the purpose [of the sequence]. This is because of the scriptural mention of the connection "after the lightning" (*taṭitaḥ*) in the sense of "above" (*upari*). Therefore, it is established that the recollection [of the path] is consistent due to the unity of the path.
Thus ends the section concerning lightning.
Here, the nature of Vāyu as an *ativāhika* (conductor) for one who has reached the *arcis* (flame) immediately thereafter is established:
"He is a conductor because of its characteristic mark."

[Objection: Is it not the case that Vāyu is primary, since it was mentioned first as being reached [by the soul] in the statement, "He goes to Vāyu"? For the word "Vāyu" has its primary sense in that very context, and one should not abandon the primary meaning unless there is a subverting reason. Furthermore, even if it is primary, it is still something to be reached. Therefore, because Vāyu is reached immediately after Arcis, it cannot be considered superior. To this, the author of the Sūtras recites the following:

"Ātivāhika, because of its characteristic mark. This is the meaning: the wind previously mentioned as the second stage to be reached is indeed *ātivāhika* (conveying), not primary. Why? Because of its characteristic mark—that is, from the word "wind" which indicates it is a stage to be reached prior [to the next], and from the statement "he [reaches] light," which implies its form, attributes, and so forth.

And thus, on account of the mark of "going forward" (*pūrvagamanaliṅga*). Although the mere fact of "going forward" does not prove that [the soul] is led by the deities of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*)—since it could apply to other cases—it is indeed appropriate that it proves this when conjoined with the ascertainment of its being air (*vāyu*). For example, although the mere fact of having three castes or more does not prove that one belongs to the lowest caste (*antyaja*), it is appropriate that it proves *śūdra*-hood when conjoined with the ascertainment of caste. Thus, it is established that this air is indeed the primary leader (*ativāhika*) first reached, and so the primacy of the primary is proven.
Because that [cognition] is established through the delusion of both.

But even so, this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) does not hold, because there exists a subverting factor (bādhaka) in the form of the undesirable consequence that the primary [attainment] would not be reached, since it is not accepted as being attained first. Now, if it is thought: "Having gone from heaven to lightning, he reaches its lord, Vāyu"—thus the attainment of Vāyu is heard again; that will be the primary one, and therefore the attainment of the primary is not a defect—then, in response to this, the author recites the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "On account of the word 'therein' (tatra), [the primary attainment is] not [implied]. (Brahmasūtra 4.3.1) This means: although Vāyu is mentioned again, the primary attainment is not established here, because of the word "therein" (tatra). This indicates that the context refers back to the previously mentioned Brahman, which is the primary object of attainment. Thus, the attainment of the primary is indeed free from defect. Therefore, the conclusion stands.

"Because its establishment [occurs] from the confusion regarding both. This is the meaning: the ablative case is used in the sense of the locative. "From the confusion regarding both" means that there is doubt as to whether the previously mentioned wind is the primary *ativāhika* (conveying) one, or whether the subsequently mentioned wind is the primary one. "Because of its establishment" means that because the primacy of that subsequently mentioned wind is established by the qualification "lord of the day," there is no lack of determination.

If it is argued that, because there is no reason to dispel the doubt—namely, "Is this the previously mentioned *ativāhika* (conductor), or another? Likewise, is it the *ativāhika* mentioned later, or yet another?"—the certainty that "this is the *ativāhika*" is not possible, we say: No. For, by the qualification "Lord of the Day" (*divaspati*) in the subsequent [text], the primary nature of Vāyu is ascertained; and in the latter [text], the status of being the *ativāhika* is established through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Furthermore, this is supported by the Smṛti text, "But having departed... (*utkrāntastu*). Therefore, since the first [Vāyu] reached is the *ativāhika*, it is established that the primary [Vāyu] possesses primacy.
Thus concludes the section concerning the subtle body (the *ātivāhika*).
In this regard, the finality of the primary wind is established by the very fact that it is mentioned last in the scriptural passage concerning the lightning.

But is it not the case that there exists a destination beyond the wind and prior to Brahman? Since there is no subverting argument against such an admission, it follows that the wind does not possess the specific greatness of being the means for attaining Brahman. To this prima facie view, the Sūtra states:

"Then, by that [passage], 'by the lightning alone' (vaidyutenaiva)"; this is its meaning: the knower goes to Brahman by the lightning alone—that is, by the wind produced from lightning—and not through anything else in between. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding that [wind]: "He leads them to Brahman" (sa enān brahmagamayati), which declares that the wind itself is the one who causes them to go to Brahman.

And thus, there is indeed no destination for the wind other than the immediate one; for the attainment of Brahman occurs through the wind alone at the moment of the lightning-flash, not by any other means, because that [other] lacks the capacity to lead one to Brahman. The existence of the scriptural text, "He leads them," serves as the authority for the wind's capacity, and there is also the traditional teaching (smṛti) stating, "The lightning-flash. Therefore, since the wind is the final point of arrival, it is established that its preeminence is justified.
Thus concludes the section concerning the lightning.
In this regard, the destination of those of limited qualification who have traveled by the path beginning with light (arcis), as previously investigated, and of the gods, is now determined:
"Bādari [holds that it is] the effected [Brahman], because the going of this [soul] is possible."

Now, it might be argued that for all those who have traveled by the path beginning with light (arcirādi), there is only the attainment of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman) and not the Supreme (para), because the attainment of that [effected Brahman] alone is logically consistent; furthermore, since the statement "except for the gods" establishes that those other than the gods are unfit for the attainment of the Supreme—this being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [the soul] having reached [Brahman], [there is non-return], on account of the scriptural declaration. (4.3.7) This means: But having reached the Supreme Brahman, there is no return, because of the scriptural declaration: "Those who go by this path do not return to human existence" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6). The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the aforementioned doubt. It is not possible that those who have reached the Supreme Brahman would return from that state, because the scripture declares their non-return. Nor is it logical that they should reach the effected Brahman, because the scripture speaks of them as having attained immortality. For it is said: "Immortal indeed becomes he when he sees that subtle Self through the grace of the Creator" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). Furthermore, the term "immortality" is used in a primary sense regarding the Supreme Brahman, whereas it is used in a secondary sense regarding the effected Brahman. Therefore, it is established that those who have reached the Supreme Brahman do not return. As for the gods, however, their non-return is understood from the specific exclusion: "Except for the gods. This is because the gods, being already in the proximity of the Supreme Brahman, are not subject to rebirth in the manner of transmigrating beings. Thus, the conclusion is that the souls of those who travel by the path of light attain the Supreme Brahman and do not return.

"Badari [holds that] it is the effected [Brahman], because of the possibility of its being reached. This is the meaning: the teacher Badari considers that the scriptural statement, "Vāyu leads him," refers to the effected Brahman—namely, that which has an origin and is called Caturmukha (the Four-faced One). Why? Because for this very Caturmukha, there is the possibility of being reached; that is to say, the possibility of his being attained.

Thus, since it is established by the force of reasoning that for those who have departed [from the body], the attainment of the Supreme is impossible—given that they are distinct from the gods and are still bound—it is accepted that the scriptural mention of Brahman does not have its primary sense. This is because it is admitted that the gods attain Brahman directly either at the stage of liberation after the dissolution of the body, or, in the case of those gods born as humans prior to that [dissolution], immediately after departure while still in a state of bondage. It is thus proven that Bādari maintains that the "effected" (kārya) Brahman leads those who have traveled by the path beginning with light to Brahman before the liberation of the four-faced Brahmā.
And because it has been specified.

The author of the Sūtras states that regarding the attainment of the effect itself, neither mere reasoning nor Smṛti is the authority, but rather a specific scriptural statement (viśeṣa-śruti) as well.

"And because of being specified. This is its meaning: the sense is that it is appropriate to state [the above], because in the scriptural passage beginning with "If," the Brahman to be attained is specified by the term "Caturmukha" (the Four-faced One).

And thus, even though one perceives the Supreme Self through the scriptural text "evam vai ya iha ātmānam," it is established that for a knower distinct from the gods at the time of bondage, the attainment of Brahman is specifically that known as Caturmukha (the Four-faced One), because it is stated by the authority of the scriptures that the attainment of one thing follows from the knowledge of another, and because the aforementioned specific qualifications are present. Therefore, what has been said is logical; this is proven.
But that designation [of the Self] is due to its proximity.

"An objection may be raised: would this not contradict the direct statement that 'the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)? For that [statement] means that the attainment of the Supreme occurs immediately after the attainment of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma). To refute this, the author states the Sūtra: [The Sūtra: "But [it is] from that very [effected Brahman], because of the scriptural teaching. (Sūtra 4.3.7) This means: But the attainment of the Supreme is indeed from that very effected Brahman, because the scripture teaches it thus. The meaning is that the scripture teaches that the Supreme is attained by proceeding through that very effected Brahman. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word "but" (tu) in the Sūtra is intended to set aside the previously stated objection. The phrase "from that very" indicates that the attainment of the Supreme is from that same effected Brahman which was mentioned as being near to the Supreme. The word "because of the scriptural teaching" (śabdāt) refers to the scriptural teaching such as: "From Him, departing, he reaches the worlds of Brahman; in them he dwells for uncountable years" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1). The word "unaccountable" (asaṃkhyeya) here signifies eternity, because it is used in proximity to the mention of liberation. Therefore, since the scripture teaches that one attains the Supreme by proceeding from the effected Brahman, there is no contradiction with the statement that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Thus, the conclusion is established.

"But that designation [of him] is due to proximity. This is its meaning: because there is the designation "knower of Brahman" (brahmavit), there is the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. [The objection is: "Is this not a contradiction? [The answer is: It is due to proximity; having reached the Four-faced One (Caturmukha), one attains the Supreme after a short time. It is precisely due to this temporal proximity that [the designation] proceeds accordingly. Therefore, there is no contradiction with that—this is the meaning.

And thus, since the scripture cited refers to the commencement [of the path] solely due to the proximity of time between the task (*kārya*) and the attainment of the Supreme (*paraprāpti*), its meaning is that for the knower (*jñānin*), the task is accomplished in a proximate period and the Supreme is attained even more swiftly; because, being devoid of restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), there is no negation of the attainment of the task. Furthermore, the sublation of a general scripture by a specific scripture is logically consistent. Therefore, it is established that for the knowers, there is the attainment of that task during the dissolution (*pralaya*), owing to the existence of prior attainment.
Upon the completion of the task, he departs together with its supervisor, because of the scriptural statement that he goes beyond from there.

Now, what is the meaning of "he attains the Supreme Brahman from near at hand"? Does it mean before the dissolution (*pralaya*), or at the very moment of dissolution? It cannot be the first, because the state of being bound—which was stated as an obstacle to the attainment of the Supreme at the outset—is equally an obstacle here as well; otherwise, the attainment of the Supreme would have been possible right from the beginning. Nor can it be the second, because there is no specific evidence [to that effect]. Having reached this position, the author presents the aphorism (*sūtra*) as a rebuttal.

"Upon the dissolution of the effect, he goes with its presiding deity, because of the statement that [he attains] what is beyond this. This is the meaning: "Upon the dissolution of the effect" means at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). "With its presiding deity" means together with the four-faced one (*caturmukha*), the lord of the effect. "Beyond this" means higher than the four-faced one; the knower of Brahman goes to the Supreme Brahman. Why? "Because of the statement," meaning because of such scriptural testimony (*śruti*).

And thus, since it is accepted that after the dissolution of all effects, the seeker of liberation attains the Supreme through the grace of the four-faced Lord (Caturmukha), who is the presiding lord over those effects; and since during the dissolution (pralaya) there is no contradiction regarding the state of being bound—given the absence of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) for the knowers due to their liberation from it; and because there exists the scriptural authority for this in the form of the text "te ha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5); therefore, it is established that because Caturmukha is the one authorized over the phenomenal world of effects, it is logical that those desiring to go to Brahman should travel together with him alone.
And on account of Smṛti.
To establish this point even by means of tradition (smṛti), he cites a sūtra and presents that tradition.

"And because of Smṛti. The meaning of this is: since there exists a Smṛti stating "by Brahmā," it is established that the knower attains the Supreme together with Caturmukha (the four-faced one). This is the sense.

And thus, it is established that the aforementioned scriptural statement shows that the liberated knowers of the Supreme Self, after a hundred years of Brahmās have elapsed, enter into Brahman along with the four-faced one when the dissolution arrives; therefore, their departure together with the effected (kārya) Brahman is logical.
Jaimini [holds that the word "self"] refers to the Supreme [Self], because it is the primary meaning.
He introduces the sūtra that indicates another prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

"Jaimini [holds that the knower attains] the Supreme, because of the primary sense of the word. This is its meaning: the knower attains the Supreme Brahman alone, and not the effected (kārya) Brahman. Why? Because of the primary sense; for the teacher Jaimini maintains that the word "Brahman" has its primary sense only with respect to the Supreme Brahman.

Thus, since the word "Brahman" in the Vedic sentence "And so he leads them" has its primary meaning in the Supreme Brahman alone, the teacher Jaimini maintains that it is Vāyu who leads them to the Supreme Brahman, and not to the effected (kārya) Brahman; this is the established conclusion.
And because it is seen [in scripture].

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if the word *brahman* has its primary meaning in the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), since that [primary sense] cannot be accepted due to the contradiction with the previously cited logical arguments, scriptures, and traditional texts (*smṛti*), it is proper to assume a non-primary (secondary) meaning. Anticipating this doubt, he presents the aphorism (*sūtra*) which dispels it.

"And because of seeing" (darśanāt). This is its meaning: the knower goes to the Supreme Brahman itself. Why? Because by means of hearing and so forth, he has seen the Supreme Brahman alone; this is the sense.

And thus, since the knowers have realized the Supreme Brahman itself through direct perception by means of the practices such as hearing (śravaṇa), and since nothing else has been seen by them, it is established that it is logical for Vāyu to lead them to the Supreme.
And there is no intention to engage with the effect.
He introduces the sūtra which establishes the point that the attainment of the other [state] is indeed logically established through a different reason:

"And there is no intention for attainment regarding the effected [Brahman]. This is the meaning of this [sūtra]: For this reason also, the attainment of the effected Brahman by the knower is untenable. Why? Because (the word) "ca" means "since. Regarding the object that is the effected Brahman, there is no intention for attainment on the part of the knower. "Attainment" (pratipatti) means worship (upāsti); "intention" (abhisaṃdhi) means the desire, "May I attain [it]. [Such an intention] does not exist. This is the meaning.

And thus, for the knowers (jñānins), there is no [attainment of] the effected [Brahman], because of the absence of both comprehension (pratipatti) and intention (abhisaṃdhi); however, with respect to the Supreme [Brahman], there is no such absence of those two, according to the Smṛti text: "Whatever a person meditates upon... Therefore, it is established that Vāyu leads them only to the Supreme, not to the effected [Brahman].
"Badarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads [the soul] because it does not depend on any support; for there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of its resolve."
He introduces the sūtra which establishes that both [results] are attained according to the difference in the qualified aspirants (adhikārin).

"Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] Vāyu leads those who do not rely on symbols, because there are defects in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve" (Brahmasūtra 4.3.15). The meaning of this is as follows: Vāyu leads those who do not rely on symbols—that is, qualified aspirants who meditate upon the all-pervading [Brahman]—to the Supreme Brahman; he leads others who rely on symbols—that is, those who meditate within the body, which is designated by the word "symbol"—to the effected Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha). The teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers that such is the meaning of the scriptural passage, "He leads them. Why? Because there are defects in both cases.

If one does not accept this established rule and instead accepts that everyone attains each [of the goals], then—whether one accepts the attainment of the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahman*) or the supreme Brahman (*para-brahman*)—the defects mentioned for both positions regarding the attainment of the effected and the supreme Brahman would necessarily follow. Now, one might object: since there is the statement, "One attains that which one desires to attain," it is possible to attain each respective goal through the mere desire for it; therefore, the aforementioned rule need not be accepted. To this, he says: "And [it is] according to his resolve" (*tat-kratuśca*). By this, the scriptural passage beginning with "As is his desire, so is his resolve" (*sa yathākāmo bhavati tatkraturbhavati*) is understood.

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because. Because the Śruti states, "As he [wishes]," it negates the attainment of various things through the mere desire for their attainment and declares that their attainment occurs only through the direct realization resulting from the knowledge and meditation upon them. Therefore, the meaning is that attainment does not logically follow from the mere desire for those things.

And thus, Vāyu leads those humans who have the "pratīka" as their support to the effected state (kārya). This is because the meaning of the Śruti is that for those who do not have the "pratīka" as their support, "a hundred of the Ṛṣis and a hundred of the Kings go further. For there would be a logical flaw if the meaning were "he leads all to the effected state," or if the meaning were "he leads all to the supreme state [immediately]. Nor should it be argued that the acceptance of specific qualifications such as "not having the pratīka as support" is useless, since the attainment of either the effected state or the supreme state cannot occur by the mere power of one's will alone.

In the Śruti text, "He [obtains] according to his desire," there is a prohibition against attaining that [Brahman] for those who merely desire its attainment; furthermore, the Smṛti text "the symbol" (pratīka) exists as an authoritative basis for the distinction between those who rely on symbols and others. Therefore, it is established that the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that both attainments occur according to the difference in the qualifications of the knowers.
And he demonstrates the distinction.

Regarding the statement that attainment does not occur according to one's desire, but rather through a sequence beginning with the support of symbols (*pratīka*) and so forth—that is not tenable. There might be the following doubt: since there is no authoritative evidence for a fixed rule that some are "without the support of symbols" while others are "with the support of symbols," it is possible to assume, at will, that [all] are without the support of symbols. To dispel this doubt, the author recites the following sūtra:

"And it shows a distinction"—this is the meaning of that statement. The word "ca" (and) means "because. The scripture, by stating "they are inwardly luminous," shows—that is, establishes—a distinction, namely a difference between some who have non-symbols as their support and some who have symbols as their support. Therefore, what has been said is logical; this is the sense.

And thus, since the distinction between the support of a symbol (*pratīka*) and the non-symbolic support is established by the scripture stating "those who have light within" (*antaḥprakāśāḥ*), it is proven that the statement beginning with "those who do not rely on symbols" (*apratīkālaṃbanān*) is logical.
Thus ends the section concerning the effect.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter.
Śrīḥ.
Om. May there be auspiciousness. May Hari protect you.
Now begins the fourth quarter.
In this quarter, there is the experience of enjoyment.
In this context, it is established that the experience of objects of enjoyment by the liberated one occurs precisely without overstepping Brahman.
Having attained [the state of Brahman], he does not depart from his own [nature], because of the scriptural statement.

Objection: Is it not the case that the liberated one, having transcended Brahman, enjoys pleasures in liberation? For, since it is stated that "having crossed this bridge" (*etaṃ setuṃ tīrtvā*), the manifestation of his true form occurs immediately after the transcendence of Brahman, it is impossible for one who remains without having transcended it to experience his own essential nature. Therefore, because there is a rule that the liberated one must transcend Brahman, [Brahman] is not something to be reached by him. To this, the Sūtra says: [The Sūtra: *saṃpadyāvirbhāvaḥ svenaśabdāt* (Sūtra 4.4.1). "Upon attaining [Brahman], there is the manifestation [of his true nature] by means of his own [nature], because of the word 'own'. This means: Having attained Brahman, the liberated one's true nature manifests; he does not enjoy external objects. Why? Because of the word "own" (*svena*) in the scriptural passage: "Having attained [Brahman], he emerges in his own true nature" (*saṃpanno virājate svena rūpeṇa*). Since the word "own" is used, it follows that his true nature is manifested by means of that very nature, and not by means of anything else. Furthermore, the word "own" excludes the possibility of enjoying external objects. Thus, the liberated one does not transcend Brahman, but rather abides within it while experiencing his own essential nature. Therefore, Brahman is indeed reachable by the liberated one. This is the conclusion.

"Having attained [Brahman], not having abandoned [it], by his own [nature], on account of the scriptural statement. This is its meaning: Having attained Brahman—that is, having reached Brahman—the knower, not having abandoned it—that is, not deviating from Brahman—remains established in his own manifested nature and experiences enjoyments. Why? Because of the scriptural statement; the meaning is that this is so because of the Śruti text: "He who knows thus... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).

And thus, having attained Brahman, he enjoys the objects of enjoyment without even leaving [the body], according to the Śruti: "He, being thus," and the Śruti: "The supreme light. Since there is no contradiction in the fact that the crossing [of the river] is for the purpose of attaining Brahman, as per the Śruti: "To him [Brahman]," it is established that because there is no sequential order of worlds such as Brahmā for the liberated one, Brahman alone is the destination.
Thus concludes the section concerning the attainment [of Brahman].
In this context, it is established that the enjoyer of experiences attains liberation by reaching Brahman and not departing from it:
"The liberated [remains there], because of the scriptural promise."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the one described in the scripture as "he wanders there" is not liberated? For the verb "wanders" implies action, and action is impossible for the liberated one, since his purpose has been accomplished. Nor is such enjoyment impossible for one who is not yet liberated; for even if it was impossible previously, it becomes possible after attaining [Brahman]. Furthermore, if the one mentioned in the scripture were not liberated, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "in his own nature. [Reply: No, because in that passage, the manifestation of the true nature is being described specifically for the meditator on the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.

Because in that context, enjoyment is described for one who is still unliberated while practicing the meditation on the small (dahara-vidyā); therefore, since the scripture states he is unliberated, it follows that there is no enjoyment for one who is liberated—this being the prima facie view, the Sūtra states:

"Because of the declaration [that he is] liberated. This is its meaning: In the scripture stating "he moves about there," it is the liberated one alone who is spoken of. Why? Because of the declaration; for, having prohibited divine enjoyment for anyone other than the liberated, the scripture states that it is the liberated one alone who attains Brahman and thereby experiences divine enjoyment. This is the sense.

And thus, since it is stated in the aforementioned scripture that this belongs only to one who is liberated—because such enjoyment is impossible without liberation, because of the statement regarding the manifestation of one's true nature (svarūpa), and because when a single context is possible, it is improper to assume a different context—otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)—it is therefore established that the experience of the liberated one is indeed logical.
Thus concludes the section on those who have attained liberation.
Here, it is established that the light to be attained by the liberated is Brahman:
"The Self [is meant], because of the context."

Objection: Is it not the case that the one denoted by the term "supreme light" (paraṃjyotis) is not Viṣṇu, but rather the sun? For there is a scriptural designation [of the sun] as "light" (tejas). And if this is so, there would be no enjoyment for the liberated soul in the proximity of Brahman. To this, the Sūtra replies:

"Because of the context, it is the Self. This is its meaning: by the term "supreme light," it is the Self, the Supreme Self alone that is denoted, not the sun. Why? Because of the context; that is to say, because this passage occurs within the context of the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, since this passage begins with "He who is the Self" (*evaṃ ca ya ātmā*) as taught by the Blessed One himself, it belongs to that specific context (*tat-prakaraṇatva*). Context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than mere name (*samākhyā*). Moreover, the statement "he becomes united with that light" (*sa tejasīti*) is not without scope, as it refers to the attainment of the sun prior to reaching the world of *Tudhna*, given the acceptance that evil karma is destroyed immediately after reaching the solar orb. Additionally, the term "supreme light" (*paraṃjyotiḥ*) does not occur elsewhere [referring to anything other than Brahman].
Therefore, it is established that the supreme light is indeed Brahman, and that the liberated one enjoys pleasures without departing from the attainment of that very [Brahman].
Thus concludes the section on the Self.
In this regard, it is established that those who possess union (sāyujya) enjoy the same objects of enjoyment as those enjoyed by the Lord;
for they are seen to be non-different [from Him].

[Objection: Surely the liberated souls enjoy those objects of enjoyment that have not been enjoyed by the Supreme Self, because they have attained the supreme human goal (*mahāpuruṣārtha*). Otherwise, even if the liberated souls should at some time desire enjoyment, since their desires would already be fulfilled (*avāptakāmatva*), there would be no enjoyment for them if the Supreme Self did not desire it, because their enjoyment is impossible without the enjoyment of the Supreme Self. Consequently, since they enjoy what has not been enjoyed by the Lord, He would not be the enjoyer of everything. To this, the Sūtra replies: *na vā, anubhūtatvād asya* (Sūtra 4.4.16). "Because they are seen to be without distinction. This is its meaning: the enjoyments enjoyed by those liberated in succession are enjoyed without distinction from those enjoyed by the Supreme Self. Why? Because it is so seen; the meaning is that this is established by the Śruti text, "Whatever I [enjoy]."

And thus, liberated souls enjoy only those enjoyments that have already been enjoyed by the Lord, according to the Śruti: "Those very [enjoyments] which I hear them enjoying," and the Smṛti: "Having attained [the state], the liberated [souls enjoy]. Therefore, since liberated souls enjoy the enjoyments already enjoyed by the Blessed Lord, it is established that His status as the enjoyer of all is logical.
Thus concludes the section on non-differentiation.
In this regard, the enjoyment of one who has attained Brahman and is liberated through union (*sāyujya*) is established:
"Jaimini [holds that it is] by means of the state of Brahman, on account of the introductory statements and so forth."

Now, an objection is raised: enjoyment is not appropriate for those who are liberated, because they lack a body; for if one were to admit the existence of a body for them, their state of liberation would be contradicted. Thus, since enjoyment is impossible in liberation, it follows that liberation is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha). To this, the following aphorism has been composed:

"Jaimini [holds that the liberated soul enjoys] by means of a body belonging to Brahmā, on account of the introductory statements and so forth. This is its meaning: the liberated one enjoys enjoyments by means of a body connected with Brahmā (*brāhma*) alone. Why? On account of the introductory statements and so forth; that is to say, because of the Śruti statement "by means of Brahmā," and because of the Smṛti passage indicated by the word "and so forth" (beginning with) "He gives [the body]," and because of logical reasoning—this is what the teacher Jaimini maintains.

And thus, since enjoyment by means of a *brāhma* body is appropriate even for the liberated despite the absence of a physical body—and because of the cited Śruti and Smṛti texts, as well as the authoritative status of what was stated by Jaimini which does not contradict the words of Bādarāyaṇa—it is established that the possibility of enjoyment in liberation makes liberation a valid human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
"Auḍulomi [says] that [the soul is of the nature of pure consciousness], because it consists of that very consciousness."
Having thus established the experience of the liberated one by accepting the absence of a body, [the author] now introduces the sūtra that establishes it by accepting the existence of a body.

"Because [the liberated soul] consists of that [consciousness] alone, by means of pure consciousness; thus says Auḍulomi. This is its meaning: By means of "pure consciousness"—that is, by means of a body whose sole nature is knowledge—the liberated one enjoys objects of experience because he consists of that [consciousness]. Since the very nature of the liberated one is a body consisting of pure consciousness, and since that [body] is not a cause for transmigratory existence, this is what the teacher Auḍulomi maintains.

And thus, because the liberated ones exist separately as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and because their bodies exist separately by virtue of having the nature of consciousness, and because they consist of consciousness while the body made of consciousness is the very nature of the liberated one, and because that nature—being uncreated—does not bring about transmigratory existence; the liberated ones enjoy themselves through pure consciousness alone, distinct from the body of Brahman, after having abandoned all [other] bodies. This is based on the Śruti text: "Or he becomes everything" (*sarvaṃ vā*). Thus the teacher Auḍulomi thinks.
Therefore, it is established that enjoyment is possible in liberation.
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] there is no contradiction because of such an introductory statement and because [the soul] exists previously.

One might object: "Are not the two solutions stated in the two Sūtras untenable? For there is a contradiction between the absence and presence of a body. Anticipating this doubt, the author recites the following Sūtra to dispel it.

"Because of such a presentation and because of its prior existence, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] there is no contradiction. This is the meaning: Because of the presentation of this very method stated by Auḍulomi—since it is declared in the Śruti, "He who is this"—and because of its prior existence, that is, because of the presence of authoritative evidence even in the former position stated by Jaimini; the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers there to be no contradiction between these two positions.

And thus, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers there to be no contradiction between these two views. For although the scripture stating "everything" (*sarvaṃ vā*) speaks only of the liberated soul having a body consisting of consciousness (*cit-śarīra*), the scripture stating "he indeed is this" (*sa vā eṣa*) also presents the experience of that conscious body as taught by Auḍulomi; and because there is no contradiction when both Jaimini’s view—that there is experience for pure consciousness through the Brahmanic state—and the scriptural evidence are taken into account. This is because the first [view] refers to a body consisting of pure consciousness, while the second refers to the absence of a material (insentient) body.
Therefore, since enjoyment is possible even in liberation, it is established that liberation is a goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha).
Thus concludes the section concerning Brahmā.
Here, it is established that the liberated one possesses enjoyments accomplished by mere volition.
And because of the scriptural statement that [the creation] proceeds from mere volition (saṃkalpa) alone.

[Objection: But surely liberation is something to be accomplished by means of various specific practices, because it is an enjoyment residing in a locus, like the enjoyment of a transmigrating being residing in a locus such as the earth; otherwise, it would contradict common worldly experience. Consequently, since liberation would lack the quality of being achievable through volition (saṃkalpa), it would not be a human goal (puruṣārtha). To this, the following aphorism is stated:

"And because of the scriptural statement that it is from mere volition alone. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to exclude the opposing view. Liberated souls enjoy objects of experience solely through volition—that is, in accordance with their own will. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding that matter; the meaning is that this is established by the scripture beginning with the words "sa yadi" (if he...).

And thus, because those who are liberated are independent of effort regarding enjoyments and the like—according to the scriptural text, "If he should desire the worlds"—there is no contradiction with the world. For it is only logical that such a state [of effortless enjoyment] should exist in the faultless abode of the Blessed Lord. Therefore, since the enjoyment of the liberated is accomplished by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), it is established that liberation is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus concludes the section on the resolve (saṃkalpa).
In this context, the enjoyment of those liberated ones who have attained Brahman is established by their freedom from being subject to any lower controller;
for this very reason, it is said: "And he has no other lord."

But surely, the liberated ones are subject to their own lower [beings], because they reside in the abode of universal sovereignty, like ministers residing in the royal palace. For even ministers are seen to be governed by gatekeepers, though they are of lower rank, when they have entered the king’s command. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with worldly experience. Thus, since the liberated one is subject to those below him, liberation possesses the same characteristics as transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). To this objection, the Sūtra states: [The Sūtra: "Not so, on account of the scriptural statement of the absence of such subjection. (BrSū 4.4.21) This means: It is not so that the liberated one is subject to others. Why? Because of the scriptural declaration of the absence of such subjection. For scripture declares that the liberated one is no longer subject to anything: "He has transcended all sorrows" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.2); "For him there is no delay; having become Brahman, he is merged in Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7). Furthermore, the state of being subject to others arises from the presence of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), which are the causes of the body and organs. But for the liberated one, these do not exist, as scripture declares: "His actions perish entirely upon the vision of Him who is the high and the low" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8). Therefore, the liberated one is not subject to others. As for the analogy of the minister, it is not a valid proof here, because the case is dissimilar. Ministers are indeed subject to others due to their dependence on the king's favor, but the liberated one has no such dependence. Moreover, the example of the minister is itself subject to qualification: a minister may be subject to a gatekeeper while remaining outside the royal palace, but once he has entered the palace, he is no longer subject to the gatekeeper. Similarly, the liberated one is subject to none while still within the sphere of the body and organs; but when he has entered the abode of universal sovereignty—that is, when he has attained identity with the Self consisting of bliss—he is subject to none. Consequently, there is no equality between liberation and transmigratory existence. This is the established conclusion.

"And for this very reason, he has no other superior. This is the meaning: the word "and" (*ca*) serves to exclude the possibility of a contradiction. "Having no other superior" means that the liberated one is not joined with any other superior, whether higher than himself or belonging to his own class. Why? "For this very reason," which means: because of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*).

And thus, because the Supreme Self is the sovereign lord of all—from the gods beginning with Prāṇa down to the deities ending with Nāman—and because He is the sovereign lord even of those teachers in whom knowledge is well-established, since there is no one else lower than Him who could be a sovereign lord; and because His will is true, for in the world only that which is not dependent [on another] exists, and that is appropriate only for the liberated one due to His very nature of having a true will; and because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "He is the supreme sovereign lord"—therefore, it is established that the difference between liberation and transmigratory existence is logical, owing to the liberated one's being devoid of any inferior sovereign lord.
Thus ends the section on the lack of sovereignty over anything else.
Here, the impossibility of enjoyment for those who have attained the Supreme Lord is refuted.
Bādari says it is non-existence, for thus [the scripture] declares.

Now, it may be objected that experience is not possible for the liberated, because there is a contradiction between the presence and absence of a body. If one accepts an external body for the liberated, there follows the consequence of suffering; if one does not accept it, experience is impossible, since experience is not possible without a body. Nor can experience be established by means of a "consciousness-body" (*ciccharīra*), for even though such a body exists during states like deep sleep, it is not observed to serve as a locus for experience. Nor can it be established by means of a "Brahma-body," for a body belonging to another cannot serve as a locus of experience for someone else.

Therefore, since it is impossible for those who are liberated to experience anything devoid of suffering, liberation would lack the status of a human goal (apuruṣārthatva); this being the position reached, the author states the Sūtra:

"Badari says there is non-existence, for thus [the scripture] declares. This is its meaning: Having accepted the absence of the natural (prākṛta) body, the teacher Badari maintains that there is enjoyment for the liberated one who possesses a body consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra). Why? Because—the word "hi" meaning "since"—the scripture states, "Indeed, he is bodiless," referring to the absence of the natural body. Therefore is the sense.

And thus, because of the existence of the body consisting of pure consciousness alone, although there is an absence of a locus for experience at the time of deep sleep and so forth—since [pure consciousness] is then veiled by ignorance and the like—it is possible [for such a locus] to exist immediately after the cessation of that ignorance. For it is not correct to say that simply because a cause does not produce its effect when obstructed, it will likewise not produce the effect once that obstruction has ceased. Nor does this entail the consequence of suffering, because of the absence of an external body; for the scripture states, "Verily, he is bodiless" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 2.1.2). This is the view of the teacher Bādari.
And thus it is established that the enjoyment of the liberated is indeed logical.
Jaimini [maintains that] there is existence [of the intermediate state], because it is mentioned without distinction.
Those who accept the continued existence of the body for liberated beings propose a subtle [body].

"Bhāvaṃ Jaiminirvikalpāmnānāt" (Jaimini [holds] that there is existence [of a body], because of the scriptural mention of an option). The meaning of this is as follows: Jaimini maintains that for the liberated there is "bhāva"—the existence of a body distinct from pure consciousness (cinmātra). Why? Because of the scriptural mention of an option; that is to say, because scripture establishes an option between two kinds of bodies, stating, "either with consciousness or without consciousness."

And thus, the teacher Jaimini sometimes maintains that even for a certain liberated and supreme being, there may be the existence of a material body by virtue of his own will for the sake of enjoyment; this is because there exists scriptural authority for it. Consequently, it is established that liberated beings possess enjoyment.
Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that both [the rites] are like those of the twelve-day sacrifice.

Now, since these two views are mutually contradictory and because it is impossible for both the existence and non-existence of a body to occur simultaneously, one might ask: "What then is his own view? In response to this expectation, he recites the Sūtra.

"Like the twelve-day sacrifice, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] both; therefore. This is its meaning: Bādarāyaṇa considers his own view to be twofold—namely, that which consists of the presence and absence of the natural body. Why? Because there is evidence for this. How is this appropriate? "Like the twelve-day sacrifice"; the meaning is that just as the twelve-day sacrifice is of a dual nature, being both an *ahīna* and a *sattra*, so it is here.

And thus, since there is no impossibility regarding the existence or non-existence of a body, on the contrary, just as a sacrifice completed in twelve days is an *ahīna* when performed by a single agent through desire, and a *sattra* when there are multiple agents, so too the existence or non-existence of a body for liberated souls is logically consistent with their desire. Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the two views.
Because it is logical that [the self] exists even in the absence of a body, just as [a person exists] in the absence of an assembly.

Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no contradiction between the existence and non-existence of the body, even so, how can experience (bhoga) be possible? If there were a body, there would be suffering and the like; thus, experience would be impossible. Since this objection has already been stated as being untenable, the author of the Sūtras provides the following resolution: [The Sūtra: "Not so, because of the absence of contact with the organs. (Yogasūtra 4.32) This means: It is not the case that experience is impossible. Why? Because of the absence of contact with the organs (indriya-saṃyoga-abhāvāt). Even though the body exists, experience does not occur unless there is contact between the self, the mind, the sense organs, and their objects. Therefore, since such contact is absent in that state, there is no experience of pleasure, pain, or the like. Thus, the objection is refuted.

"Because [the experience] is possible even in the absence of a body, just as in the case of the intermediate state (saṃdhi). This is its meaning: "Just as in the case of the intermediate state"—that is, just as in the state of dream there is a connection with experience despite the absence of an external body—"so too in liberation. "Even in the absence of a body"—that is, even in the absence of a material body—"because of the possibility," meaning because experience is logically consistent, the position that there is no body is tenable.

And thus, since experience is possible even in the absence of a body—just as in a dream—in accordance with the scriptural statement, "The intermediate state is the third," what has been said is established as logical.
In the state of existence, it is like the waking state.

But surely, since a counter-example can also be stated—asking why there might not be an absence of experience, just as in deep sleep and so on, just as there is experience in the twilight state and in the waking state—how is it that experience occurs in the presence of a body like in the waking state, while there is no experience in the absence of a body like in a dream? To this, the Sūtra says:

"In the case of existence, as in the waking state. This is its meaning: "As in the waking state," that is, just as in the waking condition there is the occurrence of experience even while the body exists, so too in liberation. The meaning is that experience is appropriate even when there is "existence," i.e., the existence of a material body.

And thus, just as for those who have entered the state of dream, experience is possible even without the ordinary identification with a body, so too for the liberated one—having voluntarily assumed certain bodies of the nature of light and experienced [objects] as in the waking state—there may at some time be a relinquishing, according to the Smṛti. Therefore, it is established that there is experience for the liberated.
The entry [of the self into multiple bodies] is like that of a lamp; for thus scripture shows.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that, while in the state of having a body, the enjoyment of liberated beings through an external body is intended to be like that of the waking state? If that were so, suffering would also follow. To this, the author reads the aphorism as a resolution: The objection is as follows: Since the liberated ones possess a body during their embodied state, their enjoyment through an external body must be understood to be similar to that of the waking state. This being the case, it follows that they would also experience suffering. To this, the author recites the sūtra as a response.

"Like a lamp, there is an entry; for thus it shows. This is its meaning: "Like a lamp" means just as a lamp enters a lantern and so forth, experiencing the oil and such contained therein, yet not experiencing the blackness and so forth [of the vessel]; in the same way, the entry of the liberated ones is their entry into an insentient body. In that state, there is the experience of auspicious enjoyments and the non-experience of suffering and the like. Why? Because of the word "hi" (for), which refers to the Śruti text: "He has indeed crossed over. "Thus it shows" means it establishes or demonstrates this; therefore is the sense.

Thus, as in the aforementioned illustration, even though the liberated one has entered into an external body, since there is the actual existence of enjoyment consisting solely of bliss, it is established that the experience of the liberated ones is an enjoyment devoid of suffering.
"Because it is revealed as referring to either deep sleep or union [with Brahman]."

[Objection: Might this sentence, "He has indeed crossed over," not rather have heaven and the like as its subject? For there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. Thus, this is not a proof for the absence of suffering among the liberated; for by the words "in the heavenly world" and so forth, the absence of suffering in heaven is established. To this, the following is stated in the Sūtra:

"Because it has been made manifest that [the statement] 'in the world of heaven' depends on either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union (sampatti). This is its meaning: the sentence "in the world of heaven" depends on either deep sleep or union; that is, it refers to one or the other. Why? Because, for this reason—since the scripture, by stating "here his father is no longer his father," has made manifest, i.e., revealed, that this [state] pertains to the subject of deep sleep or liberation. Therefore is the sense.

Thus it has been stated that this is logical; therefore, it is established that the experience of the enjoyment of freedom from suffering by the liberated is indeed logical, and thus the status of liberation as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) is proven.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence.
Here, the limit of the enjoyments of one who has attained Brahman and is liberated is established:
[it is] "excluding the activity of the world."

[Objection: But surely even the liberated ones attain the world-activity of the Supreme Lord, according to the Śruti text, "All desires. Nor can the word "all" be restricted [in its meaning], as there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka) to do so; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with their "possession of true desires" (satyakāmatva), and if those desires were not attained, the consequence of suffering would follow. Therefore, it is improper for the definition-sūtra to attribute the agency of the creation and so forth of the world to the liberated. "Except for the activity of world-management": the meaning of this is that the liberated one attains all desires in such a way as to be exempt from the activity of creating the world and so forth.

And thus, since there is no evidence for the liberated souls' attainment of all desires—given that the scriptural statement "all desires" signifies only the attainment of those desires for which they are qualified—it is established that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (the definition-sūtra) is correct, because the liberated souls lack involvement in the governance of the world.
Because of the context and because of the lack of proximity.

[Objection: But surely, because the scriptural statement "all desires" refers to the Lord and not to the individual soul (jīva), it is more appropriate as an answer to say that the governance of the world by the liberated soul is established by this scripture. To this, the following sūtra was composed:

"Because of the context and because of the lack of proximity. This is its meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the probandum. In the scriptural text "all desires," the individual soul (jīva) is spoken of. Why? Because of the context; that is, because this passage belongs to the section concerning the individual soul. And thus, in that case, the enjoyment of all desires by the soul is not applicable without restriction, but only with restriction. Why? Because of the lack of proximity; the meaning is that the souls are far removed from the capacity for the activity of governing the world.

And thus, because the subsequent [interpretation] is more reasonable—given that the scriptural statement "and all desires" must be understood as having a restricted scope for the sake of establishing the individual soul (jīva) as the subject; because the scripture refers to the individual soul; because the context concerns the individual soul, as indicated by the phrase "having departed from the body"; and because the restriction of the scripture is necessary since the individual soul lacks such capacity—furthermore, because of the Smṛti text stating "in the attainment of its own superior bliss," it is established that the Sūtra defining [the Lord] is correct, since liberated souls do not possess the activity of creating the world.
If it be argued that [the soul's ascent] is due to direct scriptural instruction, we say no; for that instruction refers to one who resides within the [divine] circles of authority.

Now, one might object: "Is not the sovereignty over the world indeed possessed by the liberated ones? For there is a direct scriptural teaching stating, 'All the gods [belong] to him,' and so forth. Having thus raised this objection, he explains the Sūtra which provides the resolution.

"If it be argued that [the liberated soul possesses sovereignty over the world] because of direct scriptural instruction, we say no, because of the statement regarding those situated in the spheres of office. This is its meaning: It must be admitted that liberated souls possess sovereignty over the world. Why? Because of direct scriptural instruction; for the scripture, "He who knows Him," clearly establishes that the liberated one is worshipful to all deities. If this is argued, we say no. Why? Because of the statement regarding those situated in the spheres of office (*adhikārika-maṇḍala-stha*); the meaning here is that in this passage, only the liberated Hiraṇyagarbha is designated as worshipful to the multitude of deities appointed to their respective offices.

And thus, if by this scriptural passage one were to accept the attainment of sovereignty over the entire universe for all liberated souls, it would be contradicted by the fact that the passage refers specifically to the Four-faced One (Brahmā). For, while accepting that [sovereignty] for the Four-faced One, the text describes him as having lordship only over the circle of those qualified for liberation, and does not describe him as having sovereignty over everything; furthermore, there is the statement, "The Self alone is the highest. Thus, it is established that what has been stated is logical.
And it does not abide in the modifications, for thus the scripture shows.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why is it accepted that Brahmā and the other gods possess only the power to govern those who are liberated? Why could they not also be the governors of those in saṃsāra? Anticipating this doubt, he presents the following sūtra.

"Furthermore, it does not abide in the modifications, for the Scripture shows this. This is the meaning: the word "and" (ca) serves to draw in the preceding [term]. For those who are liberated, there is no abiding in the modifications—that is, no engagement with the modifications, which is to say, the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Why? Because the Scripture shows, that is, establishes, this very point; such is the meaning.

And thus, by the scriptural passage cited and by the statement "by their own authority," the activities of the liberated ones regarding the sphere of saṃsāra are negated; therefore, it is established that the definition-sūtra is correct because there is an absence of world-activity for the liberated.
Thus concludes the section concerning the world's activity.
Here, the increase or decrease of those who have attained Brahman and are liberated through enjoyment and so forth is refuted.
He states their continued existence, for both perception and inference demonstrate it thus.

"He states the state [of liberation] with the words: 'And thus perception and inference show'. This is its meaning: the state of the liberated one is in exactly that manner, and there is neither increase nor decrease. Why? Because the scripture beginning with "He is this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1) declares his state to be an abiding in only one single mode. Not only this much, but perception and inference—perception by the knower and inference based on the absence of causes [for change]—also show and make known the very same point stated in the scripture. Therefore is the meaning.

Thus, from the Jābāla Śruti, and from the inferential mark (liṅga) that one who is liberated through the direct perception of the Great Ones does not possess growth and so forth because he is devoid of its causes; and likewise from the Smṛti, which declares that there is no decrease because such a state of being established in this single manner has been made known—it is established that liberation does not share the same attributes as transmigratory existence due to the absence of growth and the like in the case of the liberated.
And because there is a scriptural indication of equality regarding enjoyment alone.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no cause for the increase or decrease of the bliss of the liberated? For it is observed that sometimes there is an increase in experience and sometimes its absence. Let there be no decrease; however, there will be an increase, because since he possesses true desires (*satyakāmatva*), an increase is possible through the attainment of everything desired. Nor is it reasonable to say that he does not desire, for since the increase of bliss is desirable, it is impossible not to admit the presence of desire. To this, the author of the Sūtras reads the following: *na karmāvibhāgāditi cennānāditvāt* (BS 4.4.8). [The objection continues: "If it be said that [there is no increase] because of the non-division of karma... etc. [The Sūtra refutes this by stating... "No, because [the cycle] is beginningless. [The commentary explains: Since the sequence of karma is beginningless, there is no contradiction, even though the Lord is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, the Lord’s power is such that He can bring about the manifestation of His own qualities at will, without depending on the ripening of karma. Therefore, the increase of bliss is indeed possible. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

"And because of the mark of equality in enjoyment alone. This is its meaning: Even though there is no lack of distinction elsewhere, despite the existence of distinctions in enjoyment, there is no specific variety of enjoyment [for the liberated soul] on account of the mark consisting of the statement of a single mode denoted by the word "equality" (sāmya). Therefore, since that [equality] is the cause for the absence of increase and so forth, the meaning is that the liberated soul does not possess increase and so forth.

And thus, because the scripture states "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), and because it is declared that upon the increase or decrease of enjoyments there is no difference from the bliss of liberation, the increase or decrease of the enjoyments of liberation does not cause an increase or decrease in that bliss. This is because [liberated bliss] has already been attained by one who is fit [for it], and because it is improper to accept desires—since desire for what is unfit is prohibited by the statement "even the liberated one has no [unfit desires]"—and because of the scriptural declaration that [liberated bliss] is of a nature devoid of increase or decrease. Nevertheless, occasional particularities must indeed be admitted.
Therefore, it is established that because liberation is devoid of growth and so forth, it does not share the same characteristics as saṃsāra.
Thus concludes the section on abiding.
Here, the non-return of the liberated one who has attained Brahman and is enjoying the objects of experience is established:
"Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement."

But is it not the case that the liberated one is subject to return, because he has left his own place and gone elsewhere, like one who has gone to heaven and so forth? Nor should it be argued that while return is appropriate for one who has gone to heaven—since he dwells there for only a period of a *yuga*, a *manvantara*, or the like—it is not so for the liberated one, who dwells in his true state for infinite time; for it is possible that even the entirety of time might at some point come to an end. Furthermore, it is not the case that because time is infinite, its termination is impossible.

Since even in an infinite period of time, the completion [of liberation] is possible—just as the thirteenth day of the lunar fortnight can consist of multiple moments up to the fifteenth—and since there is thus the possibility of returning again, liberation would not be the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). To this objection, the author of the Sūtras reads the following aphorism:

"Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement. This is its meaning: for the liberated one there is no return—that is, no returning again. Why? "On account of the scriptural statement," meaning because of the Vedic revelation (śruti) stating, "And he does not return. The repetition is for the purpose of emphasis, signifying that it is exactly so.

And thus, being liberated, he is not subject to return. This is because of the scriptural statement, "He does not return, he does not return," and because of the Śruti text, "All desires. Furthermore, for one who has become liberated and whose desires have become true (satyakāma), a reversal from liberation is not logical, due to the absence of desire. Moreover, there is no returning because of his abiding for infinite time. Nor should it be argued that there might be a reversal after the completion of even that infinite time.

Because it would be contradictory for the existence of time to be asserted again immediately after declaring the completion of infinite time; therefore, since there is no returning for those who are liberated, it is established that liberation is indeed the supreme human goal.
Thus concludes the section on non-returning.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
Thus the fourth chapter is completed.
